questions.loText: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.
questions.source: Workbook A18.3 • S1, S6 • Map #36
questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a large EUR-denominated pension fund allocates assets across more than 20 external equity managers using a funds-of-funds approach, so each manager’s nonsystematic risk is largely diversified away. She must choose between two candidate managers. Annual data for the evaluation period are:

|  | Fund X | Fund Y | Market index |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average return | 17% | 13% | 10% |
| Standard deviation | 18% | 24% | 15% |
| Beta | 1.4 | 0.8 | 1.0 |

The average risk-free rate was 4%. Which of the following correctly identifies the preferred fund and the supporting measure?

options.text: Fund X, because its Sharpe ratio is 0.72 versus 0.38 for Fund Y
Fund Y, because its Treynor measure is 11.25 versus 9.29 for Fund X
Fund Y, because its Treynor measure is 16.25 versus 12.14 for Fund X
Fund X, because its Jensen’s alpha is 4.6% versus 4.2% for Fund Y

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Choose the measure**

Each manager is one of many components of the overall risky portfolio and nonsystematic risk diversifies away, so only beta matters: the Treynor measure.

**Step 2 – Excess returns**

$$r\bar{_{X}} - r\bar{_{f}} = 17\% - 4\% = 13\%, r\bar{_{Y}} - r\bar{_{f}} = 13\% - 4\% = 9\%$$

**Step 3 – Treynor measures**

$$T_{X} = \frac{13\%}{1.4} = 9.29\%, T_{Y} = \frac{9\%}{0.8} = 11.25\%$$

⇒ Per unit of beta, Y delivers 11.25% of excess return and X 9.29%; the market’s Treynor is 6%, so both beat the SML, Y by more.

**Step 4 – Sharpe ranking (to see the flip)**

$$S_{X} = \frac{13\%}{18\%} = 0.72, S_{Y} = \frac{9\%}{24\%} = 0.375, S_{M} = \frac{6\%}{15\%} = 0.40$$

⇒ On total risk X is far better: Y carries a lot of nonsystematic risk, which washes out in a multi-manager structure.

**Interpretation**

The rankings flip because Y’s volatility is mostly nonsystematic (high $\sigma$, low $\beta$). Sharpe ranks a stand-alone overall portfolio; Treynor ranks one of many.

**LO:** IM-7 b: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant. IM-7 c: Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures. • **Reference:** Bodie, Kane and Marcus, Investments 12e, Ch.24 (GARP 2025 Ch.8), The Treynor Ratio (Table 8.1, Figure 8.3)

IM-7 • Portfolio Performance Evaluation • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

a.reason: Right numbers, wrong lens (sibling swap): the Sharpe ratio uses total risk, relevant only if the fund were the investor’s entire risky portfolio.

c.reason: Used raw returns instead of excess returns: 13%/0.8 = 16.25 and 17%/1.4 = 12.14. Right fund, wrong values.

d.reason: The alphas are right (17 − (4 + 1.4 × 6) = 4.6%; 13 − (4 + 0.8 × 6) = 4.2%), but highest alpha is not a selection rule: GARP’s Table 8.1 shows the lower-alpha portfolio winning on Treynor.

questions.question: A performance analyst at a Toronto pension consultant is preparing training slides on the graphical representation of risk-adjusted performance measures. One chart plots average return against standard deviation and shows the capital market line (CML) and the capital allocation line (CAL) of an active portfolio P. A second chart plots average return against beta and shows the security market line (SML) and the T-line of P. Which of the following statements about the two charts is correct?

options.text: M$^{2}$ is the difference in slope between P’s capital allocation line and the CML, so it is measured in Sharpe-ratio units.
M$^{2}$ is the vertical distance, at the market’s standard deviation, between the market portfolio and the point on P’s capital allocation line.
T$^{2}$ is the vertical distance, at P’s own beta, between portfolio P and the security market line.
On the beta chart, the portfolio with the steeper T-line is always the one with the higher Jensen’s alpha.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where M**$^{2}$ **sits**

P$^{*}$ is formed by moving along P’s CAL (mixing P with T-bills, or borrowing) until its standard deviation equals the market’s. GARP: “M$^{2}$ is the vertical distance between points M and P$^{*}$”.

⇒ B is correct: a vertical distance at $\sigma_{M}$ , in return units.

**Step 2 – Test the beta-chart claims**

At P’s own beta, the gap between P and the SML is Jensen’s alpha, not T$^{2}$. T$^{2}$ is the gap at $\beta= 1$ between P$^{*}$ and M. And in Table 8.1 the steeper T-line (U) belongs to the portfolio with the lower alpha.

**Interpretation**

Three distances, three measures: M$^{2}$ at $\sigma_{M}$ on the standard deviation chart; T$^{2}$ at $\beta= 1$ on the beta chart; alpha at the portfolio’s own beta on the beta chart. The slopes themselves are the Sharpe and Treynor ratios.

**LO:** IM-7 c: Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures. • **Reference:** Bodie, Kane and Marcus, Investments 12e, Ch.24 (GARP 2025 Ch.8), Example 8.1 and Figure 8.2; The Treynor Ratio, Table 8.1 and Figure 8.3

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-7 c.1), built from GARP Ch.8 (Figures 8.2 and 8.3).

a.reason: The slope difference is $S_{P} - S_{M}$ ; M$^{2}$ multiplies it by $\sigma_{M}$ to turn it into a return.

c.reason: Sibling swap: the vertical distance to the SML at P’s own beta is Jensen’s alpha; T$^{2} = \alpha/\beta$.

d.reason: Absolute claim: GARP’s U has the steeper T-line (13.75 against 12.80) but the lower alpha (3.0% against 3.5%).

questions.question: An investment consultant at a USD family oﬀice is presenting to newly hired analysts how to express the risk-adjusted performance of a concentrated portfolio P that the family holds as its entire risky portfolio. Over the period, P returned an average of 22% with a standard deviation of 28% and a beta of 1.3. The market index returned 12% with a standard deviation of 16%. The average T-bill rate was 4%. Which of the following correctly states the Sharpe ratio of P and its M$^{2}$?

options.text: Sharpe ratio 0.64; M$^{2}$ 0.14%
Sharpe ratio 0.64; M$^{2}$ 2.29%
Sharpe ratio 0.64; M$^{2}$ 4.00%
Sharpe ratio 0.79; M$^{2}$ 0.57%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Sharpe ratios**

$$S_{P} = \frac{22\% - 4\%}{28\%} = 0.643, S_{M} = \frac{12\% - 4\%}{16\%} = 0.500$$

⇒ P earns 0.64% of excess return per 1% of total volatility, against 0.50% for the index.

**Step 2 – Weight in P that matches the index’s volatility**

$$w_{P} = \frac{\sigma_{M}}{\sigma_{P}} = \frac{16\%}{28\%} = 0.5714$$

⇒ Hold 57.14% in P and 42.86% in T-bills so P$^{*}$ has a 16% standard deviation.

**Step 3 – M**$^{2}$

$r_{P^{*}} = 0.5714 \times22\% + 0.4286 \times4\% = 14.286\%, M^{2} = 14.286\% - 12\% = 2.29\%$

**Step 4 – Check**

$$(S_{P} - S_{M} ) \sigma_{M} = 0.143 \times16\% = 2.29\%$$

**Interpretation**

At the index’s volatility P would have beaten the index by 2.29 points a year. Because P is the family’s whole risky portfolio, total risk is the right measure; the beta of 1.3 is a red herring (it would feed T$^{2}$).

**LO:** IM-7 c: Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures. IM-7 b: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant. • **Reference:** Bodie, Kane and Marcus, Investments 12e, Ch.24 (GARP 2025 Ch.8), The M$^{2}$ Measure and the Sharpe Ratio (Eq. 8.1, Example 8.1)

**Source:** Tier workbook, Tier A, section A18, Performance Measures and Attribution (question A18.4). Printed in the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook as question IM-7 c.3.

a.reason: Reported $S_{P} - S_{M} = 0.143$ as a return of 0.14%; the Sharpe difference must be scaled by $\sigma_{M}$ .

c.reason: Scaled the Sharpe difference by $\sigma_{P}$ instead of $\sigma_{M}$ : 0.143 × 28% = 4.00%, which matches P’s volatility rather than the index’s.

d.reason: Used raw returns throughout: $S_{P} = 22/28 = 0.79$, $S_{M} = 12/16 = 0.75$, $M^{2} = (0.786 - 0.75) \times16\% = 0.57\%$, equivalent to dropping the T-bill leg $(1 - w)r\bar{_{f}}$ .

questions.question: A consultant at a Johannesburg asset manager is explaining the firm’s performance attribution system to new trustees of a client pension fund. The system uses a bogey that holds neutral weights across equity, bonds and cash, and an index within each market. Which of the following statements about the system is correct?

options.text: The asset allocation contribution multiplies each market’s active weight by the manager’s own return in that market.
The security selection contribution multiplies each market’s return in excess of its index by the bogey’s weight in that market.
The neutral weights are set with the client according to its risk tolerance, so the same manager decisions can show different allocation contributions for two clients.
A manager who holds exactly the bogey’s market weights can still show a nonzero asset allocation contribution when the market indexes move.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the bogey is**

Neutral weights across markets, “determined in consultation with the client” according to its risk tolerance, and an index within each market.

**Step 2 – Why it changes the allocation effect**

The allocation effect is $\sum(w_{P} - w_{B})r_{B}$. A different neutral $w_{B}$ changes every active weight, so identical holdings can show a different allocation contribution for each client.

⇒ C is correct. GARP’s Concept Check 8.5 shows it: moving the bogey from 60/30/10 to 70/25/5 turns the same portfolio’s allocation effect from +0.31% into −0.17%.

**Interpretation**

The attribution result is always relative to a benchmark chosen with the client. Before reading an allocation effect, ask what the neutral weights were.

**LO:** IM-7 i: Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution. • **Reference:** Bodie, Kane and Marcus, Investments 12e, Ch.24 (GARP 2025 Ch.8), 8.5 Performance Attribution Procedures, Concept Check 8.5

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-7 i.1), built from GARP Ch.8, Section 8.5.

a.reason: Wrong returns: allocation uses the index return of each market. Using the manager’s returns mixes selection into allocation.

b.reason: Wrong weights: GARP’s selection effect uses the manager’s weights (the bogey-weight version leaves out the interaction).

d.reason: If $w_{P} = w_{B}$ in every market, every active weight is zero and the allocation effect is zero, whatever the indexes do.

questions.question:
A performance analyst at a Swiss pension fund is attributing the monthly return of a balanced mandate. The bogey holds 50% in equity; the manager holds 60%. Inside the equity component, the manager’s sector weights and returns, and the equity index’s sector weights and returns, were:

| Sector | Manager weight | Index weight | Manager return | Index sector return |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Technology | 40% | 30% | 8.0% | 6.0% |
| Financials | 25% | 30% | 4.0% | 3.0% |
| Energy | 10% | 20% | −1.0% | −2.0% |
| Consumer | 25% | 20% | 5.0% | 4.0% |

Which of the following correctly states the sector allocation effect measured within the equity component, and the contribution of security selection within equity sectors to the total portfolio’s excess return?

options.text: Sector allocation 0.85%; security selection contribution 0.70%
Sector allocation 0.95%; security selection contribution 0.78%
Sector allocation 0.85%; security selection contribution 0.84%
Sector allocation 0.85%; security selection contribution 1.40%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Equity returns**

Manager: 0.40(8) + 0.25(4) + 0.10(−1) + 0.25(5) = 5.35%. Equity index: 0.30(6) + 0.30(3) + 0.20(−2) + 0.20(4) = 3.10%. Equity excess 2.25%.

**Step 2 – Sector allocation within equity**

$$\sum(w_{P ,s} - w_{B,s}) r_{s} = 0.10(6) - 0.05(3) - 0.10(-2) + 0.05(4)$$

$s$

= 0.60 − 0.15 + 0.20 + 0.20 = 0.85%

⇒ The tilt towards technology and away from energy added 85 basis points inside equity.

**Step 3 – Security selection within sectors**

2.25%−0.85% = 1.40%. Check: $\sum_{s} w_{P ,s}(r_{P ,s} -r_{s}) = 0.40(2)+0.25(1)+0.10(1)+0.25(1) =$ 1.40%.

**Step 4 – Contribution to the portfolio**

1.40% × 0.60 = 0.84%, using the manager’s equity weight.

**Interpretation**

At portfolio level, sector allocation contributes 0.85×0.60 = 0.51% and security selection 0.84%, together the equity component’s 2.25 × 0.60 = 1.35%. The bogey’s 50% equity weight is a red herring here: it matters only for the asset allocation effect.

**LO:** IM-7 i: Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution. • **Reference:** Bodie, Kane and Marcus, Investments 12e, Ch.24 (GARP 2025 Ch.8), 8.5 Sector and Security Selection Decisions, Tables 8.8 and 8.9

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-7 i.7), built from GARP Ch.8, Table 8.8.

a.reason: Multiplied by the bogey’s equity weight: 1.40 × 0.50 = 0.70%.

b.reason: Used the manager’s sector returns in the sector allocation effect: 0.10(8) − 0.05(4) − 0.10(−1) + 0.05(5) = 0.95%, leaving 2.25 − 0.95 = 1.30%, times 0.60 = 0.78%.

d.reason: Stopped at the equity-level figure, 1.40%, without multiplying by the equity weight.

questions.question:
A fund-of-funds analyst at a Canadian pension plan is preparing a monthly attribution report for a balanced manager. The neutral (bogey) weights, the manager’s weights, and the returns are:

| Market | Bogey weight | Manager weight | Index return | Manager’s return in market |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equity | 55% | 65% | 4.0% | 5.2% |
| Fixed income | 35% | 20% | 1.2% | 1.6% |
| Cash | 10% | 15% | 0.4% | 0.4% |

A separate sector analysis of the equity component shows that the manager’s sector weights within equity contributed 0.80% of the equity component’s excess return over the equity index. Which of the following correctly states the contribution of the asset allocation decision to the portfolio’s excess return, and the contribution of security selection within equity sectors to the portfolio’s excess return?

options.text: Asset allocation 0.24%; security selection within equity 0.40%
Asset allocation 0.24%; security selection within equity 0.78%
Asset allocation 0.30%; security selection within equity 0.26%
Asset allocation 0.24%; security selection within equity 0.26%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Bogey, portfolio and excess return**

$$r_{B} = 0.55(4.0\%) + 0.35(1.2\%) + 0.10(0.4\%) = 2.66\%$$

$$r_{P} = 0.65(5.2\%) + 0.20(1.6\%) + 0.15(0.4\%) = 3.76\%, r_{P} - r_{B} = 1.10\%$$

**Step 2 – Asset allocation contribution (active weight times index return)**

(0.10)(4.0%) + (−0.15)(1.2%) + (0.05)(0.4%) = 0.40% − 0.18% + 0.02% = 0.24%

⇒ Overweighting equity in a month when the equity index returned 4% added 24 bp.

**Step 3 – Equity component: total selection, then split**

Equity excess = 5.2% − 4.0% = 1.20%; security selection within sectors = 1.20% − 0.80% = 0.40%.

**Step 4 – Contribution to the portfolio (multiply by the equity weight)**

0.40% × 0.65 = 0.26%

⇒ Stock picking inside equity sectors added 26 bp to the whole portfolio.

**Step 5 – Check: the full decomposition**

Sector allocation in equity 0.80%×0.65 = 0.52%; bond selection 0.20×(1.6%−1.2%) = 0.08%; total 0.24 + 0.52 + 0.26 + 0.08 = 1.10%.

**Interpretation**

All decisions added value this month, with most of it coming from sector bets inside equity rather than from the asset mix or stock picking.

**LO:** IM-7 i: Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution. • **Reference:** Bodie, Kane and Marcus, Investments 12e, Ch.24 (GARP 2025 Ch.8), 8.5 Performance Attribution Procedures (Tables 8.6 to 8.9)

a.reason: Stopped at the equity-level figure 1.20% − 0.80% = 0.40% without multiplying by the 65% equity weight (GARP multiplies 147 bp by 0.70).

b.reason: Intermediate result: took the whole equity selection effect, 1.20%×0.65 = 0.78%, which still contains the sector allocation decision.

c.reason: Asset allocation computed with the manager’s own returns instead of index returns: 0.10(5.2%) − 0.15(1.6%) + 0.05(0.4%) = 0.30%, which mixes selection into allocation.

questions.question: A senior analyst in the alternatives team of a Dutch pension fund is presenting four hedge fund managers to the investment committee. Which of the following descriptions is correct?

options.text: Manager W runs fixed-income arbitrage: it buys a convertible bond and sells short the issuer’s stock, rebalancing the hedge as the bond’s delta changes in order to monetize volatility.
Manager X runs merger arbitrage on a share-for-share deal: it buys the target and sells short the acquirer, accepting that losses if the deal fails can far exceed gains if it closes.
Manager Y runs global macro: it makes large, leveraged directional bets across rates, currencies and commodities, and it tends to trade less liquid instruments than other strategies.
Manager Z runs passive distressed investing: it sits on creditor committees and litigates to steer the workout, accepting that the restructuring may take longer than expected.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Test each mechanic against the reading**

Merger (risk) arbitrage: in a share-for-share merger the arbitrageur “may short the acquirer’s stock while simultaneously purchasing the target’s stock”. If the deal fails, the target falls back to (or below) its pre-announcement price and the acquirer may rise, and “the losses from a failed deal can far exceed the gains earned when a deal is successfully completed”.

⇒ B is correct.

**Interpretation**

Each strategy is identified by its legs and its payoff shape. Merger arbitrage resembles a short put on deal completion: a small, likely gain against a large, less likely loss. That is why the hedge fund’s edge is legal and antitrust expertise in judging the probability that the deal closes (IM-8 c).

**LO:** IM-8 a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. IM-8 b: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies. IM-8 c: Describe the mechanics and risks of event-driven strategies such as merger arbitrage. IM-8 d: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations that may arise when implementing this strategy. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.12 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 90)

IM-8 • Hedge Fund Investment Strategies • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Tier workbook, Tier A, section A24, Hedge Funds: Strategies, Survivorship and Other Biases, and Madoff (question A24.1). It is one of the questions recalled from the August 2026 exam. Printed in the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook as question IM-8 a.7.

a.reason: Sibling swap: the mechanic described (long convertible, short stock, delta hedging, monetizing volatility) is convertible arbitrage. Fixed-income arbitrage trades yield divergences between similar bonds, such as on-the-run against off-the-run Treasuries (IM-8 b).

c.reason: Polarity flip: global macro funds “tend to trade in more liquid instruments”.

d.reason: Role misassignment: sitting on creditor committees, supervising the workout and litigating describe active distressed investors; passive investors stay uninvolved and prefer less complex situations (IM-8 d).

questions.question: A convertible arbitrage fund buys USD 50 million of a convertible bond and sells short the issuer’s stock against it. The fund’s controller is classifying the expected cash flows of the position for the next quarter. Which of the following is correctly classified as a cost of the strategy rather than a source of return?

options.text: The coupons received on the convertible bond.
The interest earned on the cash proceeds of the short sale.
The gains from rebalancing the delta hedge as the share price moves.
The dividends paid to the stock lender on the borrowed shares.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – List the sources of return**

The hedge itself (monetizing volatility through rebalancing), the bond’s coupons, the interest earned on the short sale proceeds, and any cheapness in the convertible.

**Step 2 – List the costs**

Borrowing fees paid to the stock lender, and the dividends that must be paid to the lender on the borrowed shares.

⇒ The dividends owed on the borrowed shares are a cost.

**Interpretation**

A short seller owes the lender every dividend the shares pay while they are on loan. A high-dividend issuer makes the short leg expensive to carry, which cuts into the coupon and rebate income.

**LO:** IM-8 b: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.12 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 90, LO 90.b, Convertible Arbitrage)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-8 b.5), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 90.

a.reason: Sibling swap: coupons are income earned by the long bond leg.

b.reason: Sibling swap: the interest on short proceeds (the rebate) is a source of return.

c.reason: Sibling swap: rebalancing gains are how the strategy monetizes volatility; they are the hedge’s return, not a cost.

questions.question: A convertible arbitrageur is long a convertible bond with a delta of 53% and short the corresponding number of the issuer’s shares. Over the next week the share price rises 8% and the bond’s delta rises to 61%. Which action keeps the position delta neutral, and what does the pattern of such adjustments achieve over time?

options.text: Buy back some shares, because the higher delta means the short is now too large; the adjustments lock in the bond’s coupon.
Sell more shares short; adjustments of this kind sell stock after rises and buy it back after falls, which monetizes volatility.
Leave the short unchanged, because the hedge ratio is fixed by the conversion ratio at inception; the profit comes from the coupon alone.
Sell more shares short; adjustments of this kind buy stock after rises and sell it after falls, which earns the interest rebate.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Which way must the hedge move?**

The number of shares to short is delta times the conversion ratio. Delta has risen from 53% to 61%, so the hedge needs more shares: sell more short.

⇒ After a rise, the arbitrageur sells stock.

**Step 2 – What the pattern does**

After a fall, delta drops and the arbitrageur buys shares back. Repeatedly selling after rises and buying after falls is buying low and selling high: the rebalancing harvests the stock’s movement. Because the convertible’s price is convex in the share price, the hedged position gains on moves in either direction.

⇒ This is how the hedge monetizes volatility.

**Interpretation**

The hedge ratio is a moving target precisely because the embedded call is nonlinear. A fixed hedge would leave the fund long equity after rises and short equity after falls.

**LO:** IM-8 b: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.12 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 90, LO 90.b, Convertible Arbitrage)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-8 b.6), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 90.

a.reason: Direction reversed: a higher delta needs a larger short, not a smaller one, and coupons are earned whether or not the hedge is adjusted.

c.reason: The hedge ratio depends on delta, which moves with the share price; continuous rebalancing is the defining mechanic.

d.reason: Right action, wrong mechanism: the adjustments sell after rises and buy after falls (not the reverse), and their payoff is the volatility gain, not the rebate.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager compares two ways of holding a convertible bond bought at USD 1,013.75 per USD 1,000 par when the issuer’s stock trades at USD 41.54. The bond’s delta is 53%, its conversion ratio is 21.2037 shares and its annual coupon is USD 2.50. The desk’s pricing model gives:

| Share price move | −5% | +5% |
|---|---|---|
| Convertible price (USD) | 991.78 | 1,038.07 |

Strategy 1 holds the bond unhedged. Strategy 2 also sells short the delta-equivalent number of shares (about 11.24 per bond). Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Strategy 2 shrinks both the gain on a rise and the loss on a fall, but it still loses money when the stock falls 5%.
Strategy 2 removes all risk from the position, including the bond’s interest rate and credit risk.
Strategy 2 gains whether the stock rises or falls 5%, because the convertible’s price is convex in the share price and lies above the hedge line.
Strategy 2 gains more than Strategy 1 when the stock rises 5%, because the short position adds to the bond’s gain.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Strategy 1, unhedged**

The bond’s price moves by −21.97 or +24.32; with the \$2.50 coupon the outcomes are −\$19.47 and +\$26.82. It is a leveraged bet on the stock.

**Step 2 – Strategy 2, hedged**

The short of 11.24 shares gains or loses 11.24 × 2.077 = \$23.34. On a fall the bond loses \$21.97 and the short gains \$23.34: +\$1.37. On a rise the bond gains \$24.32 and the short loses \$23.34: +\$0.98.

⇒ The hedged position gains in both cases (before carry).

**Step 3 – Why**

The convertible’s price curve is convex: it gains more than the hedge loses on a rise and loses less than the hedge gains on a fall (Figure 3).

**Interpretation**

The hedge does not merely shrink the downside; it changes its sign, and it gives up most of the upside to do so. This is Schweser’s example (Figure 4).

**LO:** IM-8 b: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.12 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 90, LO 90.b, Example: Convertible arbitrage)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-8 b.7), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 90.

a.reason: Sign error: the hedged position gains \$1.37 on a 5% fall; it does not merely lose less.

b.reason: Absolute claim: the short stock hedges share-price risk only; the bond’s interest rate and credit sensitivities remain.

d.reason: Polarity flip: on a rise the short position loses \$23.34, so Strategy 2 gains far less than Strategy 1 (\$0.98 against \$26.82).

questions.question: A risk analyst at a multi-strategy fund is documenting the firm’s relative value arbitrage book. Which of the following descriptions is correct?

options.text: Statistical arbitrage can earn a return by providing liquidity: when an institution sells a large block, the fund buys the temporarily depressed stock and shorts a related stock until prices normalise.
Index arbitrage requires trading every constituent of the index against the futures contract, so firms that already hold the constituents have no cost advantage.
Pairs trading buys the stock that has risen and shorts the stock that has fallen, betting that the divergence between the two peers will continue.
Fixed-income arbitrage earns large returns per trade by taking outright directional positions on the level of interest rates.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Statistical arbitrage**

Stat arb spreads the pairs idea over many long and short positions using factor models. Schweser names liquidity provision as one source of return: after a large block sale depresses a price, the fund buys it, shorts a related stock to hedge market risk, and holds until the price normalises.

⇒ A is correct.

**Step 2 – Check the other descriptions**

Index arbitrage trades an optimal subset of constituents chosen by algorithm, and firms that already hold the shares source them internally at lower cost. Pairs trading buys the undervalued peer and shorts the overvalued one, betting on reversion. Fixed-income arbitrage is a relative value trade with small, steady gains.

**Interpretation**

Every arbitrage strategy bets on convergence. An option that bets on a divergence continuing, or that takes an outright directional view, has left the arbitrage family.

questions.question: An event-driven portfolio manager files each new idea under one of the five categories of event-driven opportunity in Stowell’s framework. Which of the following pairings is correct?

options.text: A position taken after a merger agreement collapses, exploiting the dislocation in the target’s price (a broken risk arbitrage situation): technical opportunity.
A stub trade that isolates the discount between a holding company’s share price and the value of its underlying assets: technical opportunity.
A position taken ahead of an anticipated credit rating change: operational opportunity.
A position based on the synergies expected from a merger: legal/regulatory opportunity.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall the five categories**

Strategic (hard catalysts), financial, operational, legal/regulatory and technical (Section 1).

**Step 2 – Place each idea**

Broken risk arbitrage situations are listed under technical opportunities, next to secondary offerings. Stub trades are strategic; credit re-ratings are financial; merger synergies are operational.

The live deal and the collapsed deal sit in different rows: risk arbitrage on an announced deal is a strategic opportunity, while the dislocation left behind when a deal breaks is a technical one.

questions.question: An activist hedge fund has built a 6% stake in a conglomerate and is campaigning for the spin-off of a division and a share buyback. Which of the following best describes the strategy and how it succeeds or fails?

options.text: The fund profits from the spread between an announced offer price and the target’s current price, and loses if the deal breaks.
The fund must stay passive, because only creditors sitting on a creditor committee may seek to influence management.
The fund’s return comes mainly from the interest rebate on its short sale proceeds, so the campaign itself is a hedge.
The fund seeks to influence the board, for example by soliciting proxy votes; it succeeds if management adopts the initiatives and the share price responds, and fails if no meaningful change is made.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The mechanics of activism**

Take an equity or derivative position, then seek to influence management or the board, for example by soliciting proxy votes, toward governance changes, spin-offs, cost cuts, buybacks, higher dividends or more leverage.

**Step 2 – Success and failure**

Success needs management to adopt the initiatives and the share price to respond; failure is a campaign that produces no meaningful change.

⇒ D.

**Interpretation**

A spin-off and a buyback are both on Stowell’s list of activist demands. The event is created by the fund itself, which is what separates activism from merger arbitrage, where the event (the offer) is given.

b.reason: Polarity flip and sibling swap: activists engage on purpose; creditor committees belong to active distressed investing.

c.reason: True fact about the wrong strategy: the interest rebate is a return source of strategies with short books, such as equity long/short.

questions.question: After a share-for-share acquisition is announced, a long-only mutual fund and a hedge fund both review the target’s stock. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Long-only funds are usually drawn to the trade, because the gap between the offer value and the post-announcement price is large and the outcome is certain.
If the deal fails, the hedge fund’s short position in the acquirer offsets the loss on the target, so a failed deal is roughly neutral for the arbitrageur.
The hedge fund can apply legal and antitrust expertise to judge the probability that the deal closes, and its short position in the acquirer adds incremental return.
The hedge fund would short the acquirer at the exchange ratio even if the offer were in cash, because the short leg is what defines merger arbitrage.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why long-only funds stay away**

The potential gain, the acquisition price less the post-announcement price, is relatively small, and there is uncertainty about whether the deal closes. Mutual funds are therefore not attracted.

**Step 2 – What the hedge fund brings**

Specialised legal and antitrust expertise to assess the likelihood of completion, and the short position in the acquirer, which generates incremental return (interest on the short proceeds, and extra profit if a competing bid lifts the target and depresses the acquirer).

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

The edge is judgement about $C$, the probability of completion. In the return formula of Section 5, $L$ is usually several times $G$, so a small error in $C$ swings the expected return sharply.

**LO:** IM-8 c: Describe the mechanics and risks of event-driven strategies such as merger arbitrage. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.12 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 90, LO 90.c, Merger Arbitrage)

questions.question: Two hedge funds buy the bonds of a retailer that has just filed for bankruptcy. Fund 1 joins the creditor committee, supervises the workout and is prepared to go to court. Fund 2 avoids involvement and prefers distressed situations that are less complex and less time intensive to analyse and monitor. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Fund 1 is an active investor that seeks to influence the restructuring and protect its position; Fund 2 is a passive investor.
Fund 1 is an active investor, but its involvement must end if the restructuring moves out of court, because workouts are reserved for the debtor’s banks.
Fund 2 is an active investor, because choosing simpler situations is itself a way of influencing the restructuring.
Both funds are active investors, because every holder of a distressed bond automatically sits on the creditor committee.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What active investors do**

They try to influence the restructuring: they participate on a creditor committee, supervise the workout process (out of court or in court) to protect their interests, and engage in legal proceedings when that could improve their position. Fund 1 does all three.

**Step 2 – What passive investors do**

They choose not to get involved and prefer distressed investments that are less complex and less time intensive to analyse and monitor. That is Fund 2.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

This is the swap tested in option D of Workbook A24.1: a “passive” investor who sits on the committee and litigates is a contradiction.

**LO:** IM-8 d: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations that may arise when implementing this strategy. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.12 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 90, LO 90.d, Investor Approaches)

b.reason: Scope error: active investors supervise the workout whether it is an out-of-court restructuring or an in-court bankruptcy.

c.reason: Role misassignment: choosing simpler situations and staying uninvolved is the definition of passive.

d.reason: Absolute claim: committee membership is a choice of active investors, not automatic for every bondholder.

questions.question: A distressed debt analyst expects that, as a struggling issuer restructures, its senior secured loans will be repaid in full while its subordinated bonds will recover little. The market currently prices both at similar discounts to face value. Which trade best exploits this view?

options.text: Buy the subordinated bonds and short the senior loans, expecting junior claims to gain relative to senior claims.
Buy the senior loans and short the subordinated bonds, expecting senior claims to appreciate relative to junior claims.
Buy both the senior loans and the subordinated bonds, since the whole capital structure trades at a discount.
Short only the equity, because a restructuring always leaves the equity worthless.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the view**

Senior claims will be repaid in full; junior claims will recover little. The market prices them alike, so the senior claim is cheap relative to the junior claim.

**Step 2 – Set the legs**

Buy the senior loans and short the subordinated bonds. As the restructuring proceeds, the senior claim should appreciate relative to the junior claim, and the spread between them should widen toward the recovery difference.

⇒ B: the capital-structure trade.

**Interpretation**

This is the structure of the NOV example one level up the ladder: long the claim that ranks first, short the claim that ranks behind it. Priority decides recovery, so priority decides the trade.

**LO:** IM-8 d: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations that may arise when implementing this strategy. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.12 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 90, LO 90.d, ways to profit)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-8 d.5), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 90.

a.reason: Legs reversed: it bets that junior claims gain on senior claims, the opposite of the analyst’s view.

c.reason: A long position in both is a bet on the whole firm’s recovery, not on the mispricing between the two claims; the subordinated leg loses under the analyst’s view.

d.reason: Absolute claim: equity is not always worthless (firms can emerge from restructuring), and a short in the equity alone does not express the senior against junior view.

questions.question: A fund holds the 5% bonds of a real estate company expected to file for bankruptcy. It bought them at 30 per 100 of face value against an estimated liquidation recovery of 35, and it is short the company’s stock. Which of the following developments would most directly threaten the bond leg of the trade?

options.text: The company’s stock falls to zero in liquidation.
Restricted institutions were forced to sell the bonds before the fund bought them, depressing its entry price.
The equity holders receive nothing until the bondholders’ claims are met in full.
The court approves new debtor-in-possession financing that ranks ahead of the existing bonds.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the bond leg depends on**

Its profit comes from the liquidation recovery (estimated at 35 per 100) exceeding the price paid (30), plus any coupons received. Anything that cuts the recovery threatens the leg directly.

**Step 2 – Test each development**

New debtor-in-possession financing that ranks ahead of the existing bonds takes its share of the liquidation value first, so less is left for the bonds. Schweser lists DIP financing and new senior debt among the developments that can erode recovery values.

⇒ D.

**Interpretation**

A recovery estimate is only as good as the claims ranked above it. The distressed investor must watch the whole capital structure, not just its own claim, which is why the strategy needs legal and restructuring expertise.

**LO:** IM-8 d: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations that may arise when implementing this strategy. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.12 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 90, LO 90.d, Challenges, Risks, and Key Considerations)

IM-9 • Risk, Regulation and Organizational Structure • Vardeez: IMPORTANT

a.reason: This is the gain on the short leg: the stock going to zero is what the equity short is for.

b.reason: Forced selling by restricted institutions is the source of the discount the fund bought at, not a threat to the recovery.

c.reason: This is the priority that the trade relies on: bondholders are paid before shareholders.

options.text: Style drift
Key person risk
Unrelated business taxable income (UBTI)
Correlation spikes

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall the two lists**

Portfolio-level: benchmarking issues, survivorship bias, UBTI. Investment-level: counterparty risk, conflicts of interest, key person risk, strategy failure, style drift, regulatory changes, correlation spikes.

⇒ UBTI is the portfolio-level risk.

**Step 2 – Why UBTI matters to this investor**

An endowment is tax exempt, but debt-financed income earned through a levered fund can become taxable to it. Investing through an offshore fund (the offshore feeder of IM-9 d) can mitigate the problem.

**Interpretation**

The test for the level: does the risk come from holding hedge funds in a portfolio (a tax, a benchmark, a biased database), or from how one fund is run (its people, its counterparties, its strategy)?

questions.question: A risk analyst summarises hedge fund leverage for an investment committee, using Stowell’s discussion and the 2020 findings of the US Treasury’s Oﬀice of Financial Research. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Most hedge fund leverage is uncollateralised borrowing, which is why leverage makes funds sensitive to liquidity shocks.
Leverage can be on-balance-sheet (direct borrowing) or off-balance-sheet (for example, derivatives), and relative value funds carried the highest average leverage in the 2020 data.
Managed futures funds carried the highest average leverage in the 2020 data, because their individual trades earn the smallest returns.
Leverage amplifies gains but not losses, because lenders are repaid only out of the fund’s profits.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The forms of leverage**

Stowell: on-balance-sheet leverage (direct borrowing) or off-balance-sheet leverage (for example, derivatives).

**Step 2 – The 2020 data**

Relative value funds carried the highest average leverage, about 3.0 times NAV; managed futures the lowest, about 1.4 times (Figure 1).

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

Relative value trades earn small, steady returns per trade, so they need leverage; that same leverage makes them vulnerable to liquidity shocks. Most hedge fund leverage is collateralised with cash or assets held by the fund.

**LO:** IM-9 a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.a, Leverage and Figure 91.2)

a.reason: Polarity flip: most hedge fund leverage is collateralised; true uncollateralised borrowing is rare. The sensitivity to liquidity shocks comes from leverage itself.

c.reason: Sibling swap: managed futures carried the lowest average leverage in the data.

d.reason: Polarity flip: leverage amplifies losses just as it amplifies gains; the loan must be repaid whatever the fund earns.

questions.question: A pension fund trustee asks why short selling and limited transparency appear among the incremental risks of hedge fund investing. Which response is correct?

options.text: A short position’s loss is capped at the sale proceeds, while a long position’s loss is unlimited.
Once collateral is posted at the start of a short sale the lender cannot ask for more, so a squeeze cannot force a fund to close a short.
Hedge funds publish their positions to investors daily, so transparency risk arises only from exit gates.
Short sellers can be caught in squeezes in which forced covering pushes prices higher, and funds keep strategies secret to protect trades from crowding, which makes their risks harder to monitor.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Short selling**

A long position cannot lose more than its value; a short position’s loss is theoretically unlimited, because a price has no upper bound. In a squeeze, a heavily shorted stock rises quickly, short sellers are forced to buy to close, and the forced buying pushes the price up further.

**Step 2 – Transparency**

When a trade becomes crowded the profit disappears, so funds keep their strategies secret. Investors then find it harder to monitor risks and to check that the strategy has not shifted; gates and other liquidity limits can stop them leaving.

⇒ D.

**Interpretation**

Both risks come from the hedge fund edge itself: the freedom to short creates the squeeze risk, and the arbitrage nature of many strategies creates the need for secrecy.

**LO:** IM-9 a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.a, Short Selling and Transparency)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-9 a.6), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91.

a.reason: Short and long reversed: the long loss is limited; the short loss is unlimited.

b.reason: Polarity flip: short sellers must add collateral as required; that is part of how a squeeze forces covering.

c.reason: Polarity flip: hedge funds are often highly secretive; gates add to the transparency problem, they are not its only source.

questions.question: The CRO of a US university endowment is preparing a report for the board on the risks of investing in hedge funds and on how hedge funds are regulated and structured. Which of the following statements is correct to include in the report?

options.text: A fund holding USD 100 of stock on a USD 75 loan that sees a 10% price fall must sell USD 30 of stock to return to its target leverage, the forced-selling channel through which hedge funds can spread losses.

In a master-feeder structure, US tax-exempt investors such as pension funds invest through the onshore feeder, which keeps debt-financed income from creating unrelated business taxable income for them.
Because hedge funds can transmit losses to banks and markets, the reading recommends the strictest feasible regulation of hedge funds as the most effective way to reduce their systemic risk.
In the limited partnership, investors act as the general partners and the manager as a limited partner, and the performance fee can be taxed at capital gains rates if assets are held at least a year.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Verify the leverage spiral**

Before: stock 100, loan 75, equity 25, debt to equity 3.0x. After a 10% fall: stock 90, loan 75, equity 15, so 5.0x. To get back to 3.0x with equity of 15 the loan must fall to 45: sell 75 − 45 = 30 of stock, leaving stock 60, loan 45, equity 15.

⇒ A 10% price fall forces the sale of 30% of the original position, with no fundamental reason to sell: this is how forced selling becomes contagion.

**Interpretation**

Stowell’s two systemic channels are fire-sale contagion from a failing strategy and losses imposed on lenders and counterparties (revenue, credit and counterparty risk for banks, as in Archegos). The spiral in A is the first channel (IM-9 b, Figure 1).

**LO:** IM-9 a: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds. IM-9 b: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk. IM-9 c: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds. c.reason: Absolute claim: the mitigants are conservative bank lending, lower leverage with more diversification, and reasonable regulation; excessively strict regulation can reduce the liquidity hedge funds supply as investors of last resort and may raise systemic risk.

d.reason: Role misassignment: the manager is the general partner and the investors are the limited partners. The tax clause is true (carried interest).

questions.question: A financial stability analyst at a central bank is writing a briefing on how hedge funds can add to systemic risk. Which of the following best summarises the two channels identified by Stowell?

options.text: Hedge funds add to systemic risk mainly through their high fees and through the survivorship bias in their reported returns.

A failing strategy can be forced to unwind at fire-sale prices, spreading losses to other holders of similar assets, and a fund’s failure can impose large losses on the institutions that lend to it or trade with it.
Hedge funds add to systemic risk only when they are larger than the largest banks, because size is the only way losses can be transmitted.
Hedge funds add to systemic risk mainly by lending to banks, so that a fund’s failure cuts off the banks’ funding.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The activities channel**

The failure of a fund’s strategy can trigger contagion if it is forced to unwind positions at fire-sale prices: prices fall for every other holder of similar assets.

**Step 2 – The exposure channel**

Hedge funds can impose large losses on the financial institutions that lend to them or act as their counterparties (revenue, credit and counterparty risk for banks).

⇒ B states both channels.

**Interpretation**

The LO wording itself splits the two: “the activities of hedge funds” (fire sales) and “exposure to hedge funds” (banks).

c.reason: Absolute claim: a fund far smaller than a bank can transmit losses through fire sales and counterparty exposures, as LTCM and Archegos showed.

d.reason: Roles reversed: banks lend to hedge funds, through margin loans and derivatives, not the other way round.

questions.question: A prime broker’s risk manager is explaining to a new analyst why leveraged hedge funds can amplify price declines. A client fund finances its stock positions with margin loans and keeps a fixed target ratio of debt to equity. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: When prices fall the loan is unchanged while equity shrinks, so leverage rises; restoring the target requires selling stock worth a multiple of the loss, and the sales can push prices down further.
When prices fall leverage falls, because the collateral falls faster than the loan; the fund can then add to its positions.
When prices fall the fund needs to sell only an amount of stock equal to the loss on its position, so forced selling cannot exceed the market move.
Forced selling of this kind happens only when the assets’ fundamental value has fallen, so it does not spread to other markets.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What a price fall does to leverage**

The loan does not change when prices fall; the whole loss comes out of equity. Debt to equity therefore rises (3.0x to 5.0x in Figure 1).

**Step 2 – What restoring the target requires**

The permitted loan is $k$ times the reduced equity, so the fund must sell $L - kE^{'}$, which equals $k$ times the loss: at 3x, a \$10 loss forces \$30 of selling.

⇒ The forced sale is a multiple of the loss, and the selling itself can push prices lower and start the cycle again.

**Interpretation**

The selling is driven by the leverage constraint, not by any change in the assets’ fundamental value, which is exactly why it spreads to other holders and to otherwise unrelated assets.

**LO:** IM-9 b: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.b, Figure 91.3)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-9 b.2), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91.

b.reason: Polarity flip: leverage rises after a fall, because equity absorbs the whole loss while the loan stays put.

c.reason: Intermediate result: selling only the amount of the loss (\$10 in the example) leaves leverage at 65/15 = 4.3x, above the target.

d.reason: Polarity flip: forced selling happens for no fundamental reason; that is what makes it contagious.

questions.question: After the 2021 collapse of Archegos Capital, the CRO of a global bank reviews the bank’s exposure to hedge fund clients. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Archegos was a hedge fund that defaulted on exchange-traded futures, so its lesson concerns clearinghouses rather than bank exposure.

**Step 1 – What Archegos was**

A family oﬀice, not a hedge fund. Its total return swaps gave it exposures that closely resembled those of a highly leveraged hedge fund.

**Step 2 – What it cost**

The case is in the reading because the systemic exposure came from the structure of the trades, not from the legal form of the client. A bank that monitored only its “hedge fund” clients would have missed it.

questions.question: A risk consultant is preparing case studies on hedge fund failures and systemic risk for a bank’s board. Which of the following pairings of case and lesson is correct?

options.text: LTCM (1998): the Bank of England concluded that key intermediaries contribute far more to systemic risk than hedge funds do.
Amaranth Advisors (2006): assets that normally behave independently became highly correlated in extreme stress, showing the need to monitor liquidity and leverage.
Amaranth Advisors (2006): its failure settled the debate by showing that hedge funds are the main source of systemic risk.
LTCM (1998): the need to monitor liquidity and leverage, because assets that typically behave independently can become highly correlated in extreme stress.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – LTCM**

The 1998 failure underscored the importance of monitoring liquidity and leverage, and showed that assets that typically behave independently can become highly correlated in extreme stress.

**Step 2 – Amaranth**

The 2006 failure raised the question of how systemic hedge funds are. The Bank of England concluded that key intermediaries contribute far more to systemic risk than hedge funds; critics disagree, pointing to leverage and nonlinear strategies.

⇒ D is the correct pairing.

**Interpretation**

Two cases, two verdicts: LTCM is the warning about leverage and correlation; Amaranth produced the Bank of England’s view that the intermediaries, not the hedge funds, are the bigger systemic risk.

**LO:** IM-9 b: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.b)

a.reason: Case swap: the Bank of England’s conclusion followed Amaranth.

b.reason: Case swap: the correlation-in-stress lesson is LTCM’s.

c.reason: Polarity flip and absolute claim: the Bank of England reached the opposite view, and the debate is not settled.

questions.question: A securities regulator’s policy paper groups its hedge fund objectives under the three high-level concerns identified in the reading. Which of the following correctly matches each concern with the way it is addressed?

options.text: Investor protection: limiting leverage; market integrity: restricting participation to sophisticated investors; financial stability: monitoring insider trading.

Investor protection: restricting participation to investors presumed sophisticated enough to evaluate the risks; market integrity: the same insider-trading rules and enforcement as other markets; financial stability: limiting leverage and requiring timely, accurate posting of collateral.
Investor protection: mandatory central clearing; market integrity: Form PF filings; financial stability: a ban on short selling.
Investor protection: registration under the Investment Company Act of 1940; market integrity: caps on performance fees; financial stability: a cap on the number of investors.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Investor protection**

The worry is fraud; the tool is restricting participation to investors presumed sophisticated enough to evaluate hedge fund risks.

**Step 2 – Market integrity and financial stability**

Market integrity: insider trading, policed with the same rules and enforcement as the rest of the markets. Financial stability: limiting leverage and requiring timely and accurate posting of collateral.

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

Each concern has its natural tool: who may invest (protection), how trading is policed (integrity), how much leverage and collateral (stability). The distractors shuffle the tools.

c.reason: True facts about the wrong concerns: central clearing and Form PF are stability and monitoring tools, and short selling is restricted (in China, to 50 names), not banned, in the reading.

d.reason: Polarity flip: hedge funds avoid ’40 Act registration through exemptions; that registration is what they are structured to stay outside.

questions.question: The general counsel of a US hedge fund is reviewing how the fund stays outside the Investment Company Act of 1940 and the related US rules. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: A fund relying on Section 3(c)(1) may accept any number of investors, provided each is a qualified purchaser.
Under Regulation D, a fund sold by private placement may accept any number of nonaccredited investors, provided it does not advertise.

A fund relying on Section 3(c)(7) is limited to qualified purchasers (individuals with more than USD 5 million in investment assets) and must register under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 if it has 500 or more investors.
To stay outside ERISA, a fund must keep benefit-plan investors above 25% of total fund assets.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The two ’40 Act exemptions**

Section 3(c)(1): fewer than 100 investors. Section 3(c)(7): only qualified purchasers (individuals with more than USD 5 million in investment assets), but 500 or more investors trigger registration under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

⇒ C is correct.

**Step 2 – Regulation D and ERISA**

Reg D allows only accredited investors, with Rule 506 permitting up to 35 nonaccredited investors. Funds stay outside ERISA by keeping benefit-plan participation below 25% of fund assets.

**Interpretation**

Every number here is a ceiling the fund is organised to stay under, which is why IM-9 d reads the structure as a set of constraints.

**LO:** IM-9 c: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.c, U.S. Regulatory Framework)

a.reason: Sibling swap: 3(c)(1) is the fewer-than-100-investors exemption; the qualified purchaser test belongs to 3(c)(7).

b.reason: Absolute claim: Rule 506 permits up to 35 nonaccredited investors, not any number.

d.reason: Polarity flip: benefit-plan assets must stay below 25% of the fund.

questions.question: A US adviser manages USD 2 billion across several hedge funds. Before 2010 it advised fewer than 15 funds and relied on the private adviser exemption. Under the Dodd-Frank Act, which of the following best describes its obligations?

options.text: It remains exempt from SEC registration as long as it advises fewer than 15 funds.
It must register with the SEC and file Form PF annually; quarterly filing applies only to advisers below USD 150 million.
It reports to ESMA, which both interprets and enforces the rules for hedge funds marketed in the United States.
It must register with the SEC, appoint a chief compliance oﬀicer, keep records available to the SEC, face periodic examinations and file Form PF quarterly; its reports also reach the FSOC.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Registration**

Title IV eliminated the private adviser exemption, so the 15-fund threshold no longer helps. An adviser managing at least USD 150 million must register with the SEC, maintain extensive records and make them available, appoint a chief compliance oﬀicer and undergo periodic examinations.

**Step 2 – Reporting**

Reports go to the SEC and the FSOC. Form PF is filed annually from USD 150 million of AUM and quarterly above USD 1.5 billion; at USD 2 billion the adviser files quarterly.

⇒ D.

**Interpretation**

Dodd-Frank turned hedge fund oversight into a systemic-risk tool: the FSOC receives data on AUM, leverage, counterparty exposures and strategies.

**LO:** IM-9 c: Summarize different approaches taken by regulators to mitigate risks related to hedge funds. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.a, Regulation; LO 91.c, Title IV and Form PF)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-9 c.5), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91.

a.reason: Outdated: the exemption was eliminated by Title IV.

b.reason: Thresholds reversed: quarterly filing applies above USD 1.5 billion; USD 150 million is the threshold for annual filing.

c.reason: Jurisdiction swap: ESMA interprets the EU’s AIFMD, and enforcement there sits with member states; it has no role for US advisers.

questions.question: A global allocator compares hedge fund regulation in four jurisdictions. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Under the AIFMD, ESMA interprets the directive’s provisions, while enforcement remains the responsibility of the individual EU member states.
Singapore requires every hedge fund, whatever its size, to register with the Monetary Authority of Singapore and to publish audited quarterly reports.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The EU**

The AIFMD (2010) brought registration, leverage limits and reporting, disclosure and marketing rules. ESMA, created in 2011, interprets its provisions; enforcement remains the responsibility of the individual member states.

The EU row is a who-does-what distinction: one body interprets, many enforce. That split is why enforcement emphasis differs by country (Portugal, France, Germany).

questions.question: A prospective investor asks how a typical hedge fund is organised legally. Which of the following descriptions is correct?

options.text: It is a closed-end corporation: the manager owns the voting shares and investors hold notes that cannot be redeemed.
It is an open-ended limited partnership in which the investors are the general partners and the manager is a limited partner.

It is an open-ended limited partnership: the manager is the general partner and the investors are limited partners, who can enter and redeem subject to the lockups and gates in the partnership agreement.
It is a limited partnership that cannot admit new investors after launch, because the partnership agreement fixes the number of partners.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The legal form and the roles**

A limited partnership: the hedge fund manager is the general partner; the investors are the limited partners.

**Step 2 – Open-ended**

The partnership can issue new interests to incoming investors and redeem investors who want to leave, subject to the lockups and gates in the partnership agreement.

⇒ C.

**Interpretation**

The general partner runs the fund and earns the fees; the limited partners provide the capital and have limited liability. Lockups and gates are how an open-ended fund protects itself from redemptions it cannot meet.

**LO:** IM-9 d: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.d, Organizational and Structural Design)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-9 d.1), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 91.

a.reason: Wrong form: a hedge fund is typically an open-ended limited partnership, not a closed-end corporation.

b.reason: Roles swapped: the manager is the general partner and the investors are limited partners (option D of Workbook A24.2).

d.reason: Polarity flip: the fund is open-ended; it admits new investors and redeems existing ones, within the agreement’s terms.

questions.question: A manager is choosing the domicile for a new family of funds. Which of the following statements about domicile is most accurate?

options.text: An offshore domicile can reduce taxes at the fund level, but the manager is still taxed on its fees and investors on their gains in their home jurisdictions.
An offshore domicile removes all tax: neither the manager’s fees nor the investors’ gains are taxed anywhere.
Bermuda hosts the majority of offshore hedge funds, followed by the British Virgin Islands.
The main purpose of an offshore domicile is to qualify the fund for the EU Passport.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why funds choose a domicile**

To minimise taxes and reduce regulatory oversight: Delaware onshore; the Cayman Islands (55%), the British Virgin Islands (15%) and Bermuda (10%) offshore.

**Step 2 – What it cannot do**

Domicile can reduce taxes at the fund level, but managers still pay tax on the fees they earn and investors are still taxed on their gains at home.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

Domicile shifts where the fund itself is taxed; it does not make the people behind it tax free. Tax-exempt access is the feeders’ job (Section 3).

**LO:** IM-9 d: Describe a typical organizational structure for a hedge fund and explain motivations for adopting this structure. • **Reference:** Stowell and Stowell 4e, Ch.14 (SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 91, LO 91.d, Organizational and Structural Design)

d.reason: True fact about the wrong topic: the EU Passport is a benefit of EU-domiciled funds under EU regulation, not the purpose of an offshore domicile.

questions.question: A risk analyst at a Canadian public pension fund reviews the fund’s commitment to a closed-end private credit fund. About 40% of the commitment is still uncalled. The credit fund has granted revolving credit lines to many of its middle-market borrowers. The pension fund’s investment committee asks how the credit fund’s liquidity risk could reach the pension fund. Which answer is most consistent with the IMF’s analysis of private credit?

options.text: It cannot: because the closed-end fund permits no withdrawals, liquidity risk is eliminated for the fund and for its investors.
If many borrowers draw on their credit lines at the same time, the fund may need to call capital, shifting the liquidity strain to investors such as the pension fund.
Mainly through the floating-rate coupons on the loans, which reset lower when policy rates rise and cut the cash the fund distributes.
Mainly through other limited partners redeeming early, because closed-end private credit funds offer quarterly redemption windows.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the closed-end structure does**

Closed-end funds and CLOs do not permit withdrawals, which greatly mitigates the redemption side of liquidity risk.

**Step 2 – The channel it does not close**

Revolving credit lines to borrowers are a call on the fund’s cash. If many borrowers draw at the same time, the fund may need extra funding and can call it from investors’ uncalled commitments.

⇒ The liquidity risk is shifted to the investors, here a pension fund with 40% of its commitment still uncalled.

**Interpretation**

The IMF adds that investors’ uncalled commitments may exceed their current private credit holdings, and that pension funds already face margin and collateral calls on their derivatives. A capital call arriving in the same stress is how a fund’s liquidity problem becomes an investor’s.

**LO:** IM-10 c: Describe and assess the risks and vulnerabilities related to private credit, and explain how private credit can pose risks to financial stability. • **Reference:** IMF, Global Financial Stability Report, April 2024, Ch.2; Schweser-Notes 2026 Book 5, Reading 92, LO 92.c (Liquidity Risks; Interconnectedness Risks)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-10 c.6), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 92.

a.reason: Absolute qualifier: closed-end structures mitigate redemption risk, but they do not eliminate the capital-call channel.

c.reason: Floating-rate coupons reset higher when rates rise, and their effect runs through the borrowers’ credit risk, not through the fund’s liquidity.

d.reason: Closed-end funds do not offer redemption windows; scheduled redemptions are a feature of semiliquid evergreen funds.

questions.question: A senior risk consultant is advising a Brazilian securities regulator on a draft framework for private credit funds, which are increasingly sold to retail investors through semiliquid evergreen structures with quarterly redemption windows. The funds’ loans have no secondary market and are marked by the managers each quarter, and their reported NAVs have barely moved through a period in which listed leveraged-loan prices fell. Which of the following recommendations is consistent with the IMF’s analysis of private credit risks?

options.text: Permit more frequent redemption windows for retail investors, since more frequent redemptions reduce both the liquidity risk and the conduct risk of these funds.
Where valuations are significant or prone to error, require more frequent external valuations and audits of valuations, since stale marks can defer losses and overstate fees.
Rely on leverage reported at the fund level, since most closed-end private credit funds use little leverage and leverage across the private credit system is therefore low.
Leave monitoring of the loans’ credit quality to external rating agencies, so that funds holding large private credit exposures need not run bank-like monitoring of their own.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Diagnose the symptom**

Flat NAVs while public loan prices fall are stale valuations: few comparables, infrequent marks, no secondary market. Private credit values change less and respond more slowly than public debt, so price and NAV can diverge for several quarters.

⇒ Stale marks may overstate asset values and returns, inflate manager fees, and defer losses that are later recognised all at once.

**Step 2 – Match the IMF policy fix**

Valuation: greater regulatory oversight of valuation methods; more frequent external valuations where valuations are significant and/or prone to error; audits of valuations to fix deficiencies in methods and controls.

**Step 3 – Check the retail angle**

The liquidity fixes are closed-end structures, less frequent redemptions, longer notice and settlement, liquidity tools and stress tests, and clear disclosure. The conduct fix is to disclose conflicts and make sure retail investors understand the credit, liquidity and redemption restrictions.

**Interpretation**

B is correct. The regulator’s framework should pair the valuation fix with the liquidity and conduct fixes, because evergreen retail funds combine all three risks. Note that the fix is targeted (significant or error-prone valuations), not “mark everything more often”: more frequent marks full of estimation error can add volatility and short-termism.

**LO:** IM-10 c: Describe and assess the risks and vulnerabilities related to private credit, and explain how private credit can pose risks to financial stability. IM-10 d: Assess potential policy recommendations that could help mitigate the risks associated with private credit. • **Reference:** IMF, Global Financial Stability Report, April 2024, Ch.2; Schweser-Notes 2026 Book 5, Reading 92, LO 92.c and 92.d

c.reason: Scope error: low leverage in closed-end funds does not extend to the system; leverage is layered at investor, fund (SPVs, collateralized fund obligations) and borrower level, and fund-level reports can obscure it.

d.reason: Role misassignment: the IMF wants funds with substantial private credit to run more rigorous, bank-like monitoring themselves; reliance on internal valuations and rating agencies is the weakness, not the fix.

questions.question: The chief risk oﬀicer of a European life insurer tells the board that private credit is now a material share of the general account, held through direct lending funds and private credit CLO tranches. The insurer judges the loans’ credit quality from the managers’ internal valuations and from external credit ratings. Which action is most consistent with the IMF’s policy recommendations on private credit credit risk?

options.text: Cap the allocation at 3% of assets under management, the level the IMF reports for insurers and pension funds, since exposures at that level carry no credit risk.
Put in place more rigorous, bank-like processes to monitor the performance of the underlying loans, with close scrutiny of the managers’ underwriting policies.
Rely on the private equity sponsors that back most borrowers, since sponsor support has kept private credit losses below those of high-yield bonds.
Require every borrower to obtain a public credit rating before the insurer invests, so that the rating agencies take over the monitoring of the loans.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The gap**

Insurers and pension funds have no requirement to monitor the creditworthiness of the underlying loans, so they lean on internal valuations and rating agencies, which “may not provide much confidence”.

**Step 2 – The IMF’s fix**

Funds that hold a substantial amount of private credit should adopt more rigorous processes, similar to banks’, to monitor loan performance in structured products and direct lending, and underwriting policies and credit risks need careful scrutiny.

⇒ B is the credit-risk recommendation.

**Interpretation**

Monitoring sits with the institution that holds the risk. The insurer’s current approach (internal valuations plus ratings) is the weakness the IMF describes, not a substitute for the fix.

**LO:** IM-10 d: Assess potential policy recommendations that could help mitigate the risks associated with private credit. • **Reference:** IMF, Global Financial Stability Report, April 2024, Ch.2; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 92, LO 92.d (Credit Risks)

a.reason: Misuses a number: about 3% of AUM describes current exposure, not a policy cap, and no level of exposure is free of credit risk.

c.reason: A true fact used as a wrong policy: sponsor support has reduced defaults, but it is not monitoring, and the PE ties are themselves an interconnectedness risk.

d.reason: Wrong party: reliance on rating agencies is the problem; the IMF does not propose mandatory public ratings for private borrowers.

questions.question: A securities regulator in Singapore is consulting on rules for private credit funds that are now sold to retail investors through semiliquid structures. The funds hold illiquid corporate loans with no secondary market. Which package of measures is most consistent with the IMF’s recommendations on the liquidity risk of these funds?

options.text: Require daily dealing at a daily NAV, so that the funds’ liquidity terms match those of retail bond funds.
Permit only closed-end structures or less frequent redemptions, require longer notice and settlement periods, and mandate liquidity management tools and stress testing.
Allow frequent redemption windows as long as the loans are floating rate, since floating-rate loans hold their value when rates rise.
Address the risk mainly through leverage caps on the funds, since liquidity mismatches in private credit arise from fund-level borrowing.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The risk**

Illiquid loans inside a fund that lets retail investors out at regular dates: a liquidity mismatch, made worse if many unsophisticated investors try to leave together in stress.

**Step 2 – The IMF’s remedies**

Limit the outflows (only closed-end funds, or less frequent redemptions), slow them (more notice, more time to settle), prepare for them (mandatory liquidity management techniques and stress testing where mismatches are large), and explain them (thorough, understandable disclosure of risks and redemption limits).

⇒ B is the package.

**Interpretation**

These are the structural fixes in the list: they change the product, at the cost of the liquidity that made semiliquid funds attractive to retail investors. Disclosure completes the package and doubles as a conduct fix.

**LO:** IM-10 d: Assess potential policy recommendations that could help mitigate the risks associated with private credit. • **Reference:** IMF, Global Financial Stability Report, April 2024, Ch.2; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 92, LO 92.d (Liquidity Risks)

a.reason: Polarity flip: daily dealing on illiquid loans maximises the mismatch.

c.reason: Wrong mechanism: floating rates protect coupons, not the ability to sell a loan; they do nothing for a fund facing redemptions.

d.reason: Sibling swap: leverage caps are the contingency fix for leverage risk; the liquidity mismatch here comes from redemption terms.
