questions.loText: Describe potential explanations for the risk anomaly.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.3 (Ang), Agency Problems
questions.question: A trustee argues that Berkshire Hathaway’s long-run outperformance is mostly a low-risk anomaly trade. The CIO cites Frazzini, Kabiller and Pedersen (2012), who measure Buffett’s alpha from 1976 to 2011 against several benchmarks: 12.5% a year against the Fama-French and momentum benchmark, 11.1% when a betting-against-beta (BAB) factor is added, and 7.0% when a factor for company quality is also added. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Low-risk factors explain most of Buffett’s alpha, since adding BAB removes most of the 12.5%.
Some of Buffett’s outperformance comes from selecting low-risk stocks, but most of it comes from finding high-quality companies, which the reading treats as true skill.
Because 7.0% of alpha remains after both factors are added, the low-risk factor explains none of Buffett’s performance.
Because adding BAB lowers the alpha, the beta anomaly must be concentrated in large stocks such as Berkshire’s holdings rather than in small stocks.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What BAB removes**

12.5% − 11.1% = 1.4 points: a slice, not most, of Buffett’s alpha.

**Step 2 – What quality removes**

11.1% − 7.0% = 4.1 points more.

**Step 3 – GARP’s reading**

“Some of Buffett’s investing prowess is due to Buffett selecting stocks with low risk, but most of Buffett’s investment prowess comes from ferreting out gems with high underlying quality: true skill that is unrelated to just holding low-volatility stocks.”

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

The example sits in GARP’s agency-problems discussion: Berkshire is “well known for its ability to go against the crowd and avoid common agency issues”, so it can harvest low-risk stocks that benchmarked institutions avoid.

**LO:** IM-3 i: Describe potential explanations for the risk anomaly. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management, Ch.10 (GARP 2025 Ch.3), 3.5, Agency Problems

IM-4 • Portfolio Construction • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-3 i.6), built from GARP Ch.3 (Ang), Agency Problems.

a.reason: BAB removes only 1.4 of 12.5 points.

c.reason: Absolute claim: 1.4 points is not “none”.

d.reason: Wrong conclusion and wrong fact: the beta anomaly shows up more in small stocks (BAB loads positively on SMB).

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.4 • S2
questions.question: An analyst presents Grinold and Kahn’s two-stock example to an investment committee. Both stocks cost USD 100, and buying or selling either stock costs USD 0.75 per trade. Stock 1 rises to USD 102 over six months and then stays flat; the manager expects to find a similar stock every six months and to switch into it. Stock 2 rises to USD 108 over 24 months. Both positions earn an annual alpha of 4%, the risk-free rate is zero, and the manager starts and ends in cash. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Because both positions earn the same 4% annual alpha, they deliver the same annual return after transaction costs.
The six-month series pays a round-trip cost every six months, so its annualized transaction cost is four times that of the single 24-month holding.
The 24-month holding carries the higher annualized cost, because the round-trip cost is multiplied by the longer holding period.
Transaction costs should be amortized over one year for every position, so the two positions carry the same annualized cost.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Count the round trips**

The six-month series buys at 0 and sells at 24 months, and switches at 6, 12 and 18 months: four round trips in two years, costing USD 0.75, 1.50, 1.50, 1.50 and 0.75, a total of USD 6.00. The 24-month holding makes one round trip, USD 1.50.

⇒ Four times the cost for the same two-year period.

**Step 2 – Apply the amortisation rule**

Round trip 1.5%. Six-month holding: 1.5%/0.5 = 3% a year. 24-month holding: 1.5%/2 = 0.75% a year.

⇒ The ratio is 3/0.75 = 4; dividing by the holding period, not multiplying, is what produces it.

**Interpretation**

Same annual alpha, very different net returns: 1% a year for the six-month series against 3.25% for the single holding. Short-horizon alpha has to clear a much higher annual cost hurdle, which is the bridge to the revision trade-offs of IM-4 f.

**LO:** IM-4 d: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction. • **Reference:** Grinold and Kahn, Active Portfolio Management 2e, Ch.14 (GARP 2025 Ch.4), 4.4 Transactions Costs (the two-stock example)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-4 d.3), built from GARP Ch.4, 4.4.

a.reason: Ignores the costs: equal alphas give equal returns only before costs (1.00% against 3.25% after).

c.reason: Multiplies by the holding period instead of dividing: the longer holding has the lower annual cost.

d.reason: Amortises every cost over one year; the rate of amortisation must follow the anticipated holding period.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.4 (and note 5)
questions.question: A consultant tells a pension fund’s investment committee: “Accurate estimation of transaction costs is just as important as accurate forecasts of exceptional return.” Based on Grinold and Kahn, which of the following is the most appropriate assessment of the consultant’s statement?

options.text: Correct: transaction costs are as uncertain as alphas, so perfect information about either input is equally valuable.
An understatement: transaction costs are the least certain input to portfolio construction, so they matter more than the alphas.
Irrelevant: transaction costs are paid once, when a position is opened, so they can be left out of portfolio construction.
An overstatement: returns are much less certain than transaction costs, so perfect information about returns is much more valuable, although costs still play a crucial role.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall what GARP says about the claim**

“It has been said that accurate estimation of transactions costs is just as important as accurate forecasts of exceptional return. That is an overstatement, but it does point out the crucial role transactions costs play.”

**Step 2 – The reason (note 5)**

“Perfect information regarding returns is much more valuable than perfect information regarding transactions costs. The returns are much less certain than the transactions costs.”

⇒ Overstatement, yet costs still matter: they add a second trade-off and force precision on the alphas.

**Interpretation**

The asymmetry in certainty is why costs are treated as an input to the optimiser (“we will assume that we know the cost for each anticipated trade”), while the alphas need a whole procedure of refinement (IM-4 b, c).

**LO:** IM-4 d: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction. • **Reference:** Grinold and Kahn, Active Portfolio Management 2e, Ch.14 (GARP 2025 Ch.4), 4.4 Transactions Costs and note 5; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 86, LO 86.d

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-4 d.4), built from GARP Ch.4, 4.4 (and note 5).

a.reason: Wrong on certainty: alphas are much less certain than costs, so perfect alpha information is worth more.

b.reason: Polarity flip: costs are not the least certain input; alphas are the least reliable.

c.reason: Costs are paid on construction, rebalancing and liquidation and must be amortised into the objective; they cannot be dropped.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.4
questions.question: The CIO of a quantitative equity fund finds that the alphas sent to the optimizer have about twice their proper scale. Before transaction costs were added to the optimizer, the team offset the problem by raising the active risk aversion. The optimizer now includes transaction costs. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Raising the risk aversion can restore the trade-off between alpha and active risk, but not the trade-off between alpha and transaction costs, so the alphas themselves must be rescaled.
Raising the risk aversion still corrects the problem fully, because transaction costs act as one more component of active risk.
The fund should lower the risk aversion, because transaction costs already penalize the large positions that overscaled alphas create.
The scale of the alphas no longer matters, because trades are now driven by transaction costs rather than by alphas.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Without costs: one knob**

“Finding the correct trade-off between alpha and active risk is a one-dimensional problem. By turning a single knob, we can find the right balance.” Doubling the alpha scale and doubling $\lambda_{A}$ leave the optimal active positions unchanged.

**Step 2 – With costs: two trade-offs**

“Transactions costs make this a two-dimensional problem.” Alpha must now also be traded off against costs. Overscaled alphas make every trade look twice as valuable relative to its cost, and the risk aversion does not touch that comparison.

⇒ The manager overtrades unless the alphas themselves are rescaled. “We therefore must be precise in our choice of scale.”

**Interpretation**

This is one of the two implications Schweser lists for LO 86.d: costs “increase the importance of both precision in estimating alphas and of the choice of scale”. Rescaling is the IM-4 b procedure: alpha scale $= \text{volatility} \times$ IC.

**LO:** IM-4 d: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction. • **Reference:** Grinold and Kahn, Active Portfolio Management 2e, Ch.14 (GARP 2025 Ch.4), 4.4 Transactions Costs; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 86, LO 86.d

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-4 d.5), built from GARP Ch.4, 4.4.

b.reason: Costs are not a component of active risk; the alpha-against-cost comparison is a separate dimension.

c.reason: Polarity flip, and still the wrong tool: a lower risk aversion would enlarge positions further, and the costs do not correct the alpha scale.

d.reason: Costs make the scale more important, not irrelevant: “transactions costs force greater precision on our estimates of alpha”.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.6 • S3
questions.question: A risk analyst reviews the rebalancing rule of an equity optimizer. For each stock $n$, the optimizer compares the marginal contribution to value added, MCVA$_{n} = \alpha_{n} - 2\lambda_{A}\psi_{P} \text{MCAR}_{n}$, with the stock’s purchase cost PC$_{n}$ and sales cost SC$_{n}$. Which of the following statements about the resulting no-trade region is correct?

options.text: The region runs from $-\text{SC}_{n}$ to $+\text{PC}_{n}$, so its width is PC$_{n} + \text{SC}_{n}$; the risk aversion and MCAR$_{n}$ shift the matching band for $\alpha_{n}$ but do not change its width.
The region is symmetric around zero, from $-\text{PC}_{n}$ to $+\text{PC}_{n}$, because only the cost of the next purchase has to be recovered.
When new information moves MCVA$_{n}$ to a point inside the region, the manager should still trade toward the new optimum that ignores costs.
A higher active risk aversion widens the no-trade band for $\alpha_{n}$, because it raises the penalty on active risk.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where the band comes from**

A purchase pays if MCVA$_{n} > \text{PC}_{n}$; a sale pays if MCVA$_{n} < -\text{SC}_{n}$. Between the two, no trade pays: $-\text{SC}_{n} \le\text{MCVA}_{n} \le\text{PC}_{n}$.

$\Rightarrow\text{Width PC}_{n} + \text{SC}_{n}$ (1.25% in GARP’s example), centred on zero only if the two costs are equal.

**Step 2 – Rewrite it for alpha**

$2\lambda_{A}\psi_{P} \text{MCAR}_{n} - \text{SC}_{n} \le\alpha_{n} \le2\lambda_{A}\psi_{P} \text{MCAR}_{n} + \text{PC}_{n}$. The risk terms appear at both ends with the same sign.

⇒ They move the band; only the costs set its width.

**Interpretation**

The two halves of the correct statement are the two numbers you need in any band question: where the edges are (costs, plus the risk charge for alpha) and how wide the band is (costs only).

**LO:** IM-4 g: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs. • **Reference:** Grinold and Kahn, Active Portfolio Management 2e, Ch.14 (GARP 2025 Ch.4), 4.6, Eqs. 4.7 to 4.9

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-4 g.1), built from GARP Ch.4, 4.6.

b.reason: The sales cost sets the lower edge: the band is $[-\text{SC}_{n}, +\text{PC}_{n}]$ and is symmetric only if SC$_{n} = \text{PC}_{n}$.

c.reason: Polarity flip: inside the region “we should not react to new information”; trading toward the cost-free optimum loses more in costs than it gains.

d.reason: Width versus location: a higher $\lambda_{A}$ raises the risk charge and shifts the alpha band up; the width stays PC$_{n} + \text{SC}_{n}$ (see the correction box in Section 3).

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.6 • S3
questions.question:
A quantitative equity manager’s portfolio was optimal before this morning’s alpha update. For every stock, the purchase cost is 0.50% and the sales cost is 0.75%, both amortized and expressed in percent per year. After the update, the optimizer reports:

| Stock | Active weight | MCVA (% per year) |
|---|---|---|
| P | +1.2% | +0.65 |
| Q | −0.4% | −0.60 |
| R | +2.0% | −1.30 |
| S | 0.0% | +0.95 |

Which of the following correctly states the trades the manager should make and the net benefit of the most valuable trade?

options.text: Buy S only and sell R only; the most valuable trade is the sale of R, with a net benefit of 0.55%.
Buy P and S and sell R only; the most valuable trade is the sale of R, with a net benefit of 0.55%.
Buy S only and sell Q and R; the most valuable trade is the sale of R, with a net benefit of 0.80%.
Buy P and S and sell Q and R; the most valuable trade is the sale of R, with a net benefit of 1.30%.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Set up the band**

$-\text{SC} \le\text{MCVA} \le$ PC: from −0.75% to +0.50%. Buy above 0.50%, sell below −0.75%.

**Step 2 – Test each stock**

P: 0.65 > 0.50, buy, net 0.65 − 0.50 = 0.15%. Q: −0.75 ≤ −0.60 ≤ 0.50, hold. R: −1.30 \< −0.75, sell, net 1.30 − 0.75 = 0.55%. S: 0.95 > 0.50, buy, net 0.95 − 0.50 = 0.45%.

⇒ Buy P and S, sell R, hold Q.

**Step 3 – Most valuable trade**

Net benefits 0.15% (P), 0.55% (R), 0.45% (S): the sale of R, 0.55%.

**Interpretation**

P and Q are the asymmetry tests. P’s MCVA (0.65%) would sit inside a band built on the sales cost alone, and Q’s (−0.60%) would trigger a sale if the purchase cost were used on the downside. The active weights are a red herring: the decision depends only on MCVA and the two costs.

**LO:** IM-4 g: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs. • **Reference:** Grinold and Kahn, Active Portfolio Management 2e, Ch.14 (GARP 2025 Ch.4), 4.6, Eq. 4.8 and the worked costs of 0.50% and 0.75%

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-4 g.3), built from GARP Ch.4, 4.6.

a.reason: Used the sales cost on both sides (±0.75%): P is wrongly held.

c.reason: Swapped the ends of the band (−0.50% to +0.75%): P is held, Q is sold, and R’s net benefit becomes 1.30 − 0.50 = 0.80%.

d.reason: Traded on the sign of MCVA with no band and reported R’s gross 1.30% as its net benefit.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.6 • S3
questions.question: A portfolio manager has just bought stock K up to its optimal holding. For stock K the purchase cost is 0.40% and the sales cost is 0.60%, both amortized (percent per year). The stock’s marginal contribution to active risk is 0.30, the manager’s active risk aversion is 0.05 and the portfolio’s active risk is 4%. Assuming the marginal contribution to active risk and the other inputs stay unchanged, by how much must stock K’s alpha fall before the manager would consider selling it?
questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Where the stock sits now**

Just after a purchase up to the optimal holding, MCVA$_{K} = \text{PC}_{K} = +0.40\%$: the top edge of the band.

**Step 2 – Where selling starts**

A sale pays only once MCVA$_{K} < -\text{SC}_{K} = -0.60\%$.

**Step 3 – Distance**

With MCAR and the other inputs fixed, MCVA moves one-for-one with alpha, so alpha must fall by

PC$_{K} + \text{SC}_{K} = 0.40\% + 0.60\% = 1.00\%$

⇒ The full width of the band. GARP: “The alpha would have to decrease by 1.25 percent before we would consider selling the stock” with its costs of 0.50% and 0.75%.

**Interpretation**

The risk charge, 2(0.05)(4)(0.30) = 0.12%, is a red herring: it sits inside MCVA at both ends and cancels. The same logic after a sale: alpha must rise by PC + SC before the manager buys back.

**LO:** IM-4 g: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs. • **Reference:** Grinold and Kahn, Active Portfolio Management 2e, Ch.14 (GARP 2025 Ch.4), 4.6, Eq. 4.8

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-4 g.5), built from GARP Ch.4, 4.6.

a.reason: Treated MCVA turning negative as the sell signal: a fall of 0.40% only brings MCVA to zero, the middle of the band.

b.reason: Started the stock at zero instead of at the top of the band, so counted only the sales cost.

d.reason: Added the risk charge of 0.12% to the width; it does not change.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.6 (Leland) • S3
questions.question: A pension fund’s strategic allocation is 60% equities and 40% bonds. Following Leland’s analysis of rebalancing with linear transaction costs, the fund’s consultant has estimated a no-trade region of 55% to 65% equities around the target. After a strong equity rally, the portfolio has drifted to 68% equities. Which of the following actions is consistent with Leland’s result?

options.text: Sell equities to restore the 60/40 target, because the target allocation is the optimal portfolio.
Wait for the next scheduled quarterly rebalancing date, then trade back to the 60/40 target.
Leave the portfolio at 68/32, because outside the no-trade region the cost of trading exceeds the benefit.
Sell equities until the allocation reaches 65/35, the boundary of the region, which roughly halves turnover and costs with effectively no change in risk over time.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Is the portfolio outside the region?**

68% equities is above the 65% boundary, so the no-trade rule no longer protects it: a trade is required.

**Step 2 – Trade to where?**

Leland: outside the region, “the optimal strategy is to trade back to the boundary”. Sell 3 points of equities to 65/35, not 8 points to 60/40.

⇒ “Trading only to the boundary, not to the target allocation, cuts the turnover and transactions costs roughly in half, with effectively no change in risk over time.”

**Interpretation**

Two features separate Leland’s rule from ordinary rebalancing: the trigger is the boundary, not the calendar, and the destination is the boundary, not the target. The region’s size depends on costs, risk aversion and the assets’ expected returns and risks.

**LO:** IM-4 g: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs. • **Reference:** Grinold and Kahn, Active Portfolio Management 2e, Ch.14 (GARP 2025 Ch.4), 4.6 (Leland, 1996)

IM-4 • Portfolio Construction • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-4 g.7), built from GARP Ch.4, 4.6 (Leland).

a.reason: Trades to the target: about twice the turnover and cost for effectively no reduction in risk.

b.reason: Calendar rebalancing; Leland motivates rules driven by the boundaries, not by the passage of time.

c.reason: Polarity flip: it is inside the region that the costs exceed the benefit; outside it, a trade to the boundary pays.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the following portfolio construction techniques: screens, stratification, linear programming, and quadratic programming.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.7 • S4
questions.question: A consultant compares two proposals for a US equity mandate drawn from a followed list of 200 stocks. Proposal 1 sorts the stocks into 10 economic sectors and 3 size groups, screens by alpha within each of the 30 cells, and weights each cell at its benchmark weight. Proposal 2 characterizes every stock by industry, size, volatility and beta, and maximizes alpha less transaction costs while staying close to the benchmark on each of those characteristics. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Proposal 2 is a stratification approach, because it requires the risk dimensions to split the stocks into mutually exclusive categories.
Proposal 2 is a linear program, and its main strength is that it produces portfolios with exactly the number of stocks the manager specifies.

Proposal 1 is a stratification approach: it is robust to alpha biases across categories, but it cannot slightly overweight one category and underweight another, and its risk control fails if an important dimension is left out.
Proposal 1 uses all of the information in the alphas, including their magnitudes, and departs from benchmark category weights wherever the alphas justify it.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Name the proposals**

Proposal 1 uses exclusive cells (10 sectors × 3 sizes), screens within each and holds cells at benchmark weights: stratification, “glorified screening”. Proposal 2 uses overlapping risk characteristics and maximises alpha less costs near the benchmark: linear programming, “space-age stratification”.

**Step 2 – Check the properties claimed**

Stratification “ignores any biases in the alphas across categories” but “does not consider slightly over-weighting one category and underweighting another”, and “if some important risk dimensions are excluded, risk control will fail”.

⇒ C is correct.

**Interpretation**

The two proposals differ in exactly the way GARP separates them: exclusive categories against non-exclusive dimensions. Both match the benchmark on risk; LP uses all the alpha information, stratification only the rankings inside each cell.

**LO:** IM-4 h: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the following portfolio construction techniques: screens, stratification, linear programming, and quadratic programming. • **Reference:** Grinold and Kahn, Active Portfolio Management 2e, Ch.14 (GARP 2025 Ch.4), 4.7 Stratification and Linear Programming

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-4 h.3), built from GARP Ch.4, 4.7.

a.reason: Sibling swap: LP “does not require that these dimensions distinctly and exclusively partition the stocks”; that requirement belongs to stratification.

b.reason: Polarity flip: “the linear program has diﬀiculty producing portfolios with a prespecified number of stocks”.

d.reason: Stratification ignores some information (it screens on ranks within cells) and holds categories at benchmark weights.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the following portfolio construction techniques: screens, stratification, linear programming, and quadratic programming.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.4, 4.7 (Figure 4.2) • S4
questions.question: A quantitative manager tests a simple cash-versus-market quadratic program in which the true market volatility is 17%. Following Grinold and Kahn, the manager studies how much of the optimal value added is lost when the optimizer uses an estimated volatility instead of the true one. Which of the following conclusions is correct?

options.text: Overestimates of volatility are more damaging than underestimates of the same size, because the optimizer then takes positions that are too large.
Estimation errors in the covariance inputs cancel out in optimization, as they do in ordinary risk estimation, so their quality matters little.
Because covariance errors make implementation ineﬀicient, the manager should abandon quadratic programming in favour of screens.
An estimate within about 1 percentage point of 17% costs little value added, but errors beyond about 3 points are costly, especially underestimates, and an estimate of 12% makes value added negative.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the loss curve**

GARP: “market volatility estimates within 1 percent of the true market volatility will not hurt value added very much, but as estimation error begins to exceed 3 percent, the effect on value added becomes significant, especially if the error is an underestimate of volatility. In fact, an underestimate of 12 percent market volatility … leads to a negative value added.”

**Step 2 – Check with the rebuilt curve**

Loss $= (1 - 17^{2}/\hat{\sigma}^{2})^{2}$: 1.7% at 16%, 1.2% at 18%, 22.5% at 14%, 7.7% at 20%, 101% at 12%.

⇒ D is correct.

**Interpretation**

An underestimate makes the market look safer than it is, so the optimiser takes positions that are too large; the loss grows much faster than for an overestimate. The two lessons: covariance errors cause ineﬀicient implementation, and good covariance estimates are vital.

**LO:** IM-4 h: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the following portfolio construction techniques: screens, stratification, linear programming, and quadratic programming. • **Reference:** Grinold and Kahn, Active Portfolio Management 2e, Ch.14 (GARP 2025 Ch.4), 4.7 Quadratic Programming, Eq. 4.11 and Figure 4.2

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-4 h.5), built from GARP Ch.4, 4.7 (Figure 4.2).

a.reason: Polarity flip: underestimates do more damage, and it is underestimates that make positions too large.

b.reason: Errors largely cancel in ordinary risk estimation but are “an obstacle in optimization”, because the optimiser exploits them.

c.reason: “Rather than abandon the attempt, try to do a good job”: the lesson is better estimates, not a cruder technique.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and compare the following types of risk: absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk.
questions.reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
questions.topic: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
questions.source: Workbook C4.1 • S1, S2, S5 • Map #35
questions.question:
A risk analyst at an Australian superannuation fund with AUD 8,000 million of assets is asked by the investment committee for the fund’s one-year VaR at the 99% confidence level, calculated by the policy-mix method. Returns are assumed normal and the analyst uses $\alpha= 2.33$.

| Asset class | Policy weight | Current weight | Benchmark volatility | Managers’ TEV |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Domestic equities | 50% | 45% | 15% | 3.0% |
| Global equities | 20% | 20% | 17% | 4.0% |
| Fixed income | 30% | 35% | 6% | 1.5% |

Benchmark correlations: domestic/global equities 0.60; domestic equities/fixed income 0.10; global equities/fixed income 0.05. Which of the following is closest to the policy-mix VaR?

options.text: AUD 1,571 million
AUD 1,794 million
AUD 1,910 million
AUD 2,367 million

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Choose the inputs**

Policy-mix risk is “the risk of a dollar loss owing to the policy mix selected by the fund”: the first term of Eq. 6.2, $\sum_{i} w^{p}_{i}R^{b}_{i}$. So the weights are the policy weights and the volatilities are the benchmark volatilities. The current weights and the managers’ TEVs describe active-management risk and are not inputs here.

**Step 2 – Variance of the policy-mix return**

$$\sigma^{2}_{p} = (0.50 \times0.15)^{2} + (0.20 \times0.17)^{2} + (0.30 \times0.06)^{2}$$

\+ 2(0.50)(0.20)(0.60)(0.15)(0.17) + 2(0.50)(0.30)(0.10)(0.15)(0.06)

\+ 2(0.20)(0.30)(0.05)(0.17)(0.06)

= 0.005625 + 0.001156 + 0.000324 + 0.003060 + 0.000270 + 0.000061 = 0.010496

$$\sigma_{p} = \sqrt{0.010496} = 10.25\%$$

⇒ A passive implementation of the policy mix would have an annual volatility of about 10.25%.

**Step 3 – Policy-mix VaR**

VaR$_{\text{policy}} = \alpha\sigma_{p}W = 2.33 \times0.10245 \times8{,}000 = 1{,}909.7$

⇒ There is a 1% chance that the chosen policy mix alone loses more than about AUD 1,910 million over a year.

**Interpretation**

The individual risk budgets are 2.33 × 0.15 × 0.50 × 8,000 = 1,398, 2.33 × 0.17 × 0.20 × 8,000 = 634 and 2.33 × 0.06 × 0.30 × 8,000 = 336; their sum, 2,367, is the undiversified VaR, and diversification removes about 458. The managers’ TEVs would feed a separate active-management VaR; as at OTPPB, the fund’s asset VaR need not equal the sum of the two, so the committee should not add them.

**LO:** IM-6 e: Describe and compare the following types of risk: absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk. IM-6 h: Describe the risk budgeting process and calculate risk budgets across asset classes and active managers. • **Reference:** Jorion, Value at Risk 3e, Ch.17 (GARP 2025 Ch.6), 6.2 Eq. 6.1, 6.2 and 6.5

**Source:** Tier workbook, Tier C, section C4, Policy-Mix VaR and Risk Budgeting (question C4.1). Printed in the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook as question IM-6 e.3.

a.reason: Ignored the correlations (treated benchmark returns as uncorrelated): $\sqrt{0.005625 + 0.001156 + 0.000324} = 8.43\%$, 2.33 × 0.0843 × 8,000 = 1,571.

b.reason: Used the current weights (45/20/35) instead of the policy weights: volatility 9.62%, VaR 2.33 × 0.0962 × 8,000 = 1,794. The tilt away from policy is a deviation from the policy mix, which Jorion places in active-management risk.

d.reason: Summed the individual risk budgets, 1,398 + 634 + 336 = 2,367: the undiversified VaR, as if all correlations were 1.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and compare the following types of risk: absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk.
questions.reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
questions.topic: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
questions.source: Workbook C4.3 • S2 • Map #35
questions.question: The CRO of a Canadian defined-benefit teachers’ pension plan is preparing a report for the board’s risk committee, which has asked for a clear statement of how the plan’s risk types differ. Which of the following statements is correct to include in the report?

options.text: Funding risk is measured on the surplus; because nominal pension liabilities behave like a short position in a long-term bond, a fall in interest rates can reduce the surplus even in a year when the plan’s equities rise.
Sponsor risk has two parts: cash-flow risk, the variation in the total economic earnings of the plan sponsor, and economic risk, the year-to-year fluctuation in contributions to the fund.
Policy-mix risk and active-management risk are additive, so the plan’s total asset VaR always equals the policy-mix VaR plus the active-management VaR reported for its managers.
Funding risk is borne by the plan sponsor in a defined-contribution plan, which must make up any shortfall of the fund’s assets relative to the benefits promised to retirees.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why A is correct**

Funding risk is “the risk that the value of assets will not be suﬀicient to cover the liabilities of the fund”; the relevant variable is the surplus $S = A-L$, with $R_{S} = R_{\text{asset}} -R_{\text{liabilities}}(L/A)$. Jorion: when liabilities consist mainly of nominal payments, “their value in general will behave like a short position in a long-term bond. Thus decreases in interest rates, while beneficial for equities on the asset side, can increase even more the value of liabilities, thereby negatively affecting the surplus.”

⇒ The board should judge the plan on the surplus, not on asset returns alone.

**Interpretation**

The minimum-risk position is an immunized portfolio matching asset and liability durations, at an opportunity cost.

**LO:** IM-6 e: Describe and compare the following types of risk: absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk. • **Reference:** Jorion, Value at Risk 3e, Ch.17 (GARP 2025 Ch.6), 6.2 (Funding Risk, Sponsor Risk, Policy Mix and Active Management Risk)

IM-6 • VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Tier workbook, Tier C, section C4, Policy-Mix VaR and Risk Budgeting (question C4.3). Printed in the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook as question IM-6 e.8.

b.reason: Sibling swap: the labels are reversed. Cash-flow risk is “the risk of year-to-year fluctuations in contributions”; economic risk is “the risk of variation in total economic earnings of the plan sponsor”.

c.reason: Absolute claim: total VaR comes from the policy-mix VaR, the active-management VaR and a cross-product term. At OTPPB, 19.6% and 1.6% gave an asset VaR of 19.3% because of a slightly negative correlation.

d.reason: Role misassignment: a defined-benefit plan’s shortfall “will have to be made up by the fund’s owner”; “defined-contribution plans put the risk on the employees”.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe the risk budgeting process and calculate risk budgets across asset classes and active managers.
questions.reading: IM-6: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
questions.topic: VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
questions.source: Workbook C4.2 • S3, S4, S5 • Map #35
questions.question:
A senior analyst at a Dutch pension fund is setting risk budgets for the EUR 600 million domestic equity sleeve. The sleeve can be split between two active managers and a passive index fund (TEV 0%). The investment committee wants to maximize the sleeve’s information ratio subject to an overall tracking-error volatility of 3%. The managers’ active returns are assumed independent of each other.

- Manager X: expected excess return over the benchmark 2.5%; TEV 5%
- Manager Y: expected excess return over the benchmark 2.4%; TEV 8%

Using the optimal relative risk budgets, which of the following is closest to the weight allocated to Manager Y and the expected excess return of the sleeve?

options.text: Weight to Y 14.1%; expected excess return 1.28%
Weight to Y 19.3%; expected excess return 1.75%
Weight to Y 19.3%; expected excess return 1.20%
Weight to Y 37.5%; expected excess return 2.46%

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Managers’ information ratios**

IR$_{X} = \frac{\mu_{X}}{\omega_{X}} = \frac{2.5\%}{5\%} = 0.50, \text{IR}_{Y} = \frac{2.4\%}{8\%} = 0.30$

⇒ X earns 0.50 units of excess return per unit of active risk (“good”, top quartile); Y earns 0.30.

**Step 2 – Portfolio IR with independent managers**

IR$_{P} = \sqrt{0.50^{2} + 0.30^{2}} = \sqrt{0.34} = 0.5831$

**Step 3 – Relative risk budgets and weights (Eq. 6.7)**

$$x_{Y} \omega_{Y} = \frac{\text{IR}_{Y}}{\text{IR}_{P}}\omega_{P} = \frac{0.30}{0.5831}(3\%) = 1.5435\% \Rightarrow x_{Y} = \frac{1.5435\%}{8\%} = 19.29\%$$

$$x_{X}\omega_{X} = \frac{0.50}{0.5831}(3\%) = 2.5725\% \Rightarrow x_{X} = \frac{2.5725\%}{5\%} = 51.45\%$$

index = 100% − 51.45% − 19.29% = 29.26%

⇒ Check: $\sqrt{2.5725^{2} + 1.5435^{2}} = 3.00\%$, the TEV target. The 29.3% left in the index is the slack needed to hit exactly 3%.

**Step 4 – Expected excess return of the sleeve**

$\mu_{P} = x_{X}\mu_{X} + x_{Y} \mu_{Y} = 0.5145(2.5\%) + 0.1929(2.4\%) = 1.286\% + 0.463\% = 1.749\%$

$\Rightarrow\text{Equivalently IR}_{P} \times\omega_{P} = 0.5831 \times3\% = 1.749\%$: the sleeve’s IR of 0.58 exceeds both managers’, because independent active bets diversify.

**Interpretation**

In money terms the 99% relative risk budgets are $2.33 \times2.5725\% \times600 = \text{EUR} 36.0$ million for X and $2.33 \times1.5435\% \times600 = \text{EUR} 21.6$ million for Y; the sleeve’s budget is 2.33 × 3% × 600 = EUR 41.9 million, smaller than their sum because of diversification. Within those budgets the managers trade without seeking approval.

**LO:** IM-6 h: Describe the risk budgeting process and calculate risk budgets across asset classes and active managers.

- **Reference:** Jorion, Value at Risk 3e, Ch.17 (GARP 2025 Ch.6), 6.5 Eq. 6.4 to 6.7, Table 6.4

**Source:** Tier workbook, Tier C, section C4, Policy-Mix VaR and Risk Budgeting (question C4.2). Printed in the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook as question IM-6 h.6.

c.reason: Correct weights, but computed the sleeve’s excess return as the average manager IR times the TEV: 0.40 × 3% = 1.20%, ignoring the diversification of independent active bets.

d.reason: Split the whole sleeve in proportion to the IRs with nothing in the index: $x_{Y} = 0.30/0.80 = 37.5\%$, $\mu_{P} = 0.625(2.5\%) + 0.375(2.4\%) = 2.46\%$. This ignores the TEV constraint: the sleeve’s TEV would be $\sqrt{3.125^{2} + 3.0^{2}} = 4.33\%$.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between the time-weighted and dollar-weighted returns of a portfolio and describe their appropriate uses.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.8 and SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 89
questions.question: The investment committee of a Canadian university endowment reviews the external equity manager who runs a CAD 400 million account. Contributions and withdrawals are decided by the endowment’s treasurer, not by the manager. Over the year the account returned +5%, +4%, −8% and +5.5% in the four quarters, and the treasurer added CAD 200 million at the end of the second quarter. The account’s time-weighted return for the year is 6.0% and its dollar-weighted return is 3.6%. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The manager should be judged on the 3.6% dollar-weighted return, because it reflects the money that was actually invested in the weak third quarter.
The manager should be judged on the 6.0% time-weighted return; the gap arises because the treasurer’s contribution put more money to work in the weak quarter.
The time-weighted return is the IRR of the account’s cash flows, so the 6.0% already reflects the timing of the treasurer’s contribution.
The gap shows that the manager timed the market poorly in the third quarter, a weakness that the time-weighted return understates.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Check the two numbers**

Time-weighted: 1.05 × 1.04 × 0.92 × 1.055 − 1 = 5.99%. The account is worth CAD 436.8 million at mid-year, CAD 636.8 million after the contribution and CAD 618.1 million at year-end. Dollar-weighted: solve $400(1 + r) + 200(1 + r)^{0.5} = 618.08$, giving $r_{D} = 3.62\%$.

**Step 2 – Explain the gap**

The CAD 200 million arrived just before the −8% quarter, so more money was at work in the worst quarter. The IRR weights that quarter more heavily; the time-weighted return does not.

**Step 3 – Choose the measure for the manager**

The treasurer, not the manager, chose the size and timing of the contribution.

⇒ The manager is judged on the time-weighted 6.0%.

**Interpretation**

The 3.6% is still a true and useful number: it is what the endowment earned on the money it committed, and it reflects the treasurer’s timing decision. It is the wrong number for judging the manager.

**LO:** IM-7 a: Differentiate between the time-weighted and dollar-weighted returns of a portfolio and describe their appropriate uses. • **Reference:** Bodie, Kane and Marcus, Investments 12e, Ch.24 (GARP 2025 Ch.8), 8.1 and Adjusting Returns for Risk (comparison universes); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 89, LO 89.a

IM-7 • Portfolio Performance Evaluation • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-7 a.8), built from GARP Ch.8 and SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 89.

a.reason: Sibling swap: the dollar-weighted return mixes in the treasurer’s timing, which the manager did not control.

c.reason: Definition swap: the IRR is the dollar-weighted return; the time-weighted return is built to ignore the flows.

d.reason: Wrong person: the timing that hurt the result was the treasurer’s contribution. The manager’s own decisions are what the 6.0% captures.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe style analysis.
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.8, Section 8.2
questions.question: A consultant at a Hong Kong wealth manager runs Sharpe’s style analysis on an actively managed equity fund using 60 months of returns and seven style indexes. The constrained regression gives nonzero slopes of 0.58 on a large-cap index, 0.37 on a mid-cap index and 0.05 on a growth index, an R$^{2}$ of 97%, and an intercept of 0.28% per month. Which of the following conclusions is correct?

options.text: Because the R$^{2}$ is 97%, security selection contributed almost nothing to the fund’s average return over the period.
The intercept measures the fund’s average monthly return from security selection, and it can be positive even when the R$^{2}$ is close to 100%.
The 3% of variability that the styles leave unexplained is the fund’s average return from security selection, about 3% a year.
The slopes show that the fund held 58% of its assets in large-cap stocks at every month-end of the sample period.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the R**$^{2}$ **says**

97% of the month-to-month variability of returns moves with the style benchmark. It says nothing about the average level of the unexplained part.

**Step 2 – What the intercept says**

The intercept is the average return from security selection relative to the style benchmark: 0.28% a month here, about 3.4% a year before compounding.

⇒ A fund can have a very high R$^{2}$ and a positive intercept at the same time, as Magellan did (97.5% and 32 basis points a month).

**Interpretation**

GARP warns that a high R$^{2}$ is often read as evidence against the importance of security selection, and that this reading “misses the important role of the intercept”. A manager who beats the style benchmark by a steady amount every month adds return without adding unexplained variance.

**LO:** IM-7 e: Describe style analysis. • **Reference:** Bodie, Kane and Marcus, Investments 12e, Ch.24 (GARP 2025 Ch.8), 8.2 Style Analysis, Table 8.4 and Figure 8.4

IM-14 • Madoff: A Riot of Red Flags • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-7 e.6), built from GARP Ch.8, Section 8.2.

a.reason: The misreading GARP names: a high R$^{2}$ does not rule out a positive average selection return.

c.reason: Confuses a share of variance with a return: $1 - R^{2} = 3\%$ is the variability left unexplained, not 3% of return.

d.reason: Absolute claim: the slopes are effective average exposures implied by returns, not the fund’s holdings at each month-end.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund and describe the fund’s reported strategy and its reported performance.
questions.reading: IM-14: Madoff: A Riot of Red Flags
questions.topic: Madoff: A Riot of Red Flags
questions.source: New • built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 96
questions.question: A compliance trainer at a broker-dealer uses Madoff’s career to show how a strong reputation can discourage questions. Which statement about the history of BMIS’s brokerage business is correct?

options.text: Madoff used NYSE Rule 390 to become a specialist on the NYSE floor, which gave BMIS its competitive edge in listed stocks.
The brokerage was a front from the start: it never executed client orders and existed only to hold the advisory clients’ money.
BMIS paid brokers about one cent a share to route orders to it, which helped it handle more than 5% of trading volume by 1989.
BMIS earned most of its brokerage profits from management and performance fees charged to the brokers that sent it orders.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – How the brokerage grew**

BMIS made markets in NYSE-listed stocks off the exchange, earning the bid-ask spread, and paid brokers USD 0.01 a share to route orders to it. This payment for order flow, controversial in the industry, gave it more than 5% of trading volume by 1989 and about 10% by 2008.

⇒ C is correct.

**Step 2 – Rule 390**

Rule 390 allowed NYSE-listed stocks to trade away from the floor and its specialists. NYSE members could not make markets in those stocks off the exchange, so the edge went to a non-member: Madoff joined the Cincinnati Stock Exchange instead.

**Interpretation**

The brokerage was genuine and successful, and Madoff chaired NASDAQ’s board. That reputation is what made investors and regulators reluctant to question the advisory business.

**LO:** IM-14 a: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund and describe the fund’s reported strategy and its reported performance. • **Reference:** Gregoriou and Lhabitant (2009); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 96, LO 96.a (BMIS Background and Growth)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-14 a.2), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 96.

a.reason: Reversed: the opening was to trade listed stocks away from the floor and its specialists, not to become one.

b.reason: The brokerage was a real business; the fraud was in the advisory arm.

d.reason: Sibling swap: management and performance fees belong to asset management; the brokerage earned spreads.

questions.question: In 2007 a due diligence analyst at a European fund of hedge funds tries to evaluate BMIS’s advisory business directly and finds that she cannot. Which description of how the business was organised best explains why?

options.text: BMIS ran a single offshore hedge fund in limited partnership form, and its offering memorandum was available only to existing limited partners.
The advisory business was run from a separate city by independent staff, so the brokerage could not release any of its records.
BMIS managed thousands of small retail accounts directly, so no single investor was large enough to demand an on-site visit.
Most of its 23 discretionary accounts were feeder funds, so end investors were clients of the feeders, and Madoff allowed no visits or questions.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – How the advisory business was organised**

Its 2008 Form ADV listed 23 discretionary accounts with about USD 17 billion. Most were feeder funds that opened brokerage accounts at BMIS and gave it full trading authority; the feeders were marketed to investors worldwide.

**Step 2 – What that meant for due diligence**

End investors were clients of the feeder funds, not of BMIS, so they could examine only the feeders. Madoff did not let investors visit, ask questions or deal with him directly.

⇒ D explains why the analyst cannot reach BMIS.

**Interpretation**

The reading calls this distinction “central to understanding the Madoff story”: investors had to rely on the feeder funds to do the due diligence they could not do themselves.

**LO:** IM-14 a: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund and describe the fund’s reported strategy and its reported performance. • **Reference:** Gregoriou and Lhabitant (2009); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 96, LO 96.a (BMIS Background and Growth)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-14 a.3), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 96.

a.reason: BMIS was not a hedge fund in limited partnership form; it managed discretionary accounts.

b.reason: Reversed: the advisory firm was in the same building as the brokerage, which blurred the two.

c.reason: A small number of large accounts, mostly feeder funds, not thousands of retail accounts.

questions.question: A risk analyst tests the split-strike conversion strategy as Madoff described it, with out-of-the-money options struck either side of the index level at the start of each holding period. In one period the S&P 100 falls 15%; in another it rises 12%. Ignoring option premiums, which statement is correct?

options.text: The position loses about 15% in the falling period, because the puts were sold, and gains the full 12% in the rising period.
The loss in the falling period is limited to about the distance to the put strike, and the gain in the rising period is capped at about the distance to the call strike.
The position gains in both periods, because the two option legs make the strategy market-neutral whatever the index does.
The loss in the falling period is limited by the short calls, and the gain in the rising period is increased by the long puts.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The falling period**

The index ends below the put strike. The long put pays the difference, so losses on the stocks below the strike are offset: the position loses only about the distance from the start to the put strike (the floor in Figure 2).

**Step 2 – The rising period**

The index ends above the call strike. The short call costs the difference, so gains above the strike are given up: the position gains only about the distance to the call strike (the ceiling).

⇒ B describes both outcomes.

**Interpretation**

This is the payoff the investors were promised. Note what it does not do: in a period when the index falls by less than the distance to the put strike, the collar loses the whole fall. That is why almost no losing months was impossible (IM-14 b).

**LO:** IM-14 a: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund and describe the fund’s reported strategy and its reported performance. • **Reference:** Gregoriou and Lhabitant (2009); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 96, LO 96.a (Reported Investment Strategy and Performance)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-14 a.5), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 96.

a.reason: Polarity flip: the puts were bought, not sold, and the short calls cap the 12% gain.

c.reason: Absolute claim: a collar is long the market between the strikes, so it loses when the index falls.

d.reason: Legs swapped: the long puts limit losses and the short calls cap gains.

questions.question: A risk analyst at a multi-asset manager screens two proposed market-driven scenarios with the Mahalanobis distance, using the same covariance matrix. Scenario 1 shocks two policy variables. Scenario 2 shocks nine policy variables that are close to uncorrelated, each by one standard deviation, so its Mahalanobis distance is about 3.0, the same as Scenario 1’s. The analyst concludes that the two scenarios are equally severe and equally plausible. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.text: The conclusion is correct, because the inverse covariance matrix in the Mahalanobis distance already adjusts for the number of policy variables.

The conclusion is flawed: the distance tends to grow with the square root of the number of policy variables, so the scenarios should be compared on scenario z-scores, which would rank Scenario 2 as less severe.
The conclusion is flawed: Scenario 2 should be ranked as more severe, because a scenario that shocks more variables at once is always less plausible.
The conclusion is correct, because a Mahalanobis distance of 3.0 describes a three-standard-deviation scenario whatever the number of variables shocked.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Why the two distances match**

With nine uncorrelated shocks of one standard deviation each, MD$^{2} = 1^{2} + \cdots+ 1^{2} = 9$ and MD = 3.

⇒ Scenario 2 reaches 3.0 by adding up nine ordinary moves, not through any single unusual one.

**Step 2 – The scaling problem**

The MD tends to grow with the square root of the number of policy variables: under normality its expected square equals $n$. Raw distances therefore penalize the scenario with more variables.

**Step 3 – Use the scenario z-score**

The scenario z-score rescales the MD so that it does not increase with $\sqrt{n}$, and expresses severity in standard deviations. On that scale Scenario 2 is the less severe, more plausible scenario.

**Interpretation**

Rescaling is what lets scenarios built on different numbers of policy variables, and the historical events on a risk ruler, sit on one scale. Lower scenario z-score means more plausible.

**LO:** IM-15 b: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 97, LO 97.b, Scenario Z-Score; Golub (ed.), BlackRock’s Guide to Fixed-Income Risk Management, Ch.5

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-15 b.2), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 97.

a.reason: The inverse covariance matrix adjusts for each variable’s volatility and for the correlations, not for how many variables there are. That is why a separate rescaling exists.

c.reason: Polarity flip and absolute claim. More variables do not by themselves make a scenario less plausible; here every move is ordinary, so Scenario 2 is the milder one.

d.reason: Absolute claim. A distance of 3.0 means very different things for two variables and for nine; ignoring the $\sqrt{n}$ effect is the error the scenario z-score was introduced to fix.

questions.question: A risk manager at a US credit fund tests two candidate scenarios on the same two policy variables, a US equity index and a US high-yield credit index, whose returns have a correlation of +0.8 in the chosen covariance matrix. Each scenario moves each index by 2.4 standard deviations. In Scenario A both indices fall. In Scenario B the equity index falls and the high-yield credit index rallies. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The two scenarios have the same scenario z-score, because each shock is the same number of standard deviations in both scenarios.
The two scenarios have the same volatility z-score, but Scenario B has the higher scenario z-score and the higher correlation z-score.
Scenario A has the higher scenario z-score, because two indices falling together produce a larger combined loss than offsetting moves.
The two scenarios have the same correlation z-score, because the correlation z-score does not depend on the absolute size of the shocks.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Volatility z-score (correlations set to zero)**

Both scenarios have two shocks of 2.4 standard deviations, so the zero-correlation distance is $\sqrt{2.4^{2} + 2.4^{2}} = 3.39$ in both.

⇒ Same magnitude, same volatility z-score.

**Step 2 – Scenario z-score (correlation** +0.8 **included)**

MD$_{A} = \sqrt{\frac{2.4^{2} + 2.4^{2} - 2(0.8)(2.4)(2.4)}{1 - 0.8^{2}}} = \sqrt{\frac{2.304}{0.36}} = 2.53$

MD$_{B} = \sqrt{\frac{2.4^{2} + 2.4^{2} + 2(0.8)(2.4)(2.4)}{1 - 0.8^{2}}} = \sqrt{\frac{20.736}{0.36}} = 7.59$

⇒ A moves with the correlation; B cuts across it. B’s scenario z-score is far higher.

**Step 3 – Correlation z-score**

It normalizes for magnitude and depends on the signs and relative sizes of the factor z-scores. The sizes are identical and only B’s sign pattern contradicts the +0.8 correlation, so B’s correlation z-score is high and A’s is low.

**Interpretation**

These are points A and B of Figure 1. A univariate screen, or the volatility z-score alone, would treat the two scenarios as equally extreme. The figures in Step 2 are there only to show the direction: the question is answered by the definitions.

**LO:** IM-15 b: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 97, LO 97.b, Volatility Z-Score and Correlation Z-Score (Kinlaw and Turkington, 2014)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-15 b.4), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 97.

a.reason: Univariate thinking: equal factor z-scores do not give equal scenario z-scores once the correlation enters (2.53 against 7.59).

c.reason: Confuses portfolio loss with statistical plausibility. The z-scores measure distance from history, not P&L, and A is the scenario that sits with the grain.

d.reason: A true fact applied wrongly: the correlation z-score is independent of the absolute size, but it does depend on the signs, and B flips one.

questions.question: A risk team is building a risk ruler of historical stress events for its market-driven scenario program. The same event receives a scenario z-score of 6.8 when the covariance matrix uses five years of weekly data before the event, 4.1 when it uses one year of weekly data before the event, and 3.2 when it uses the current covariance matrix. A committee member asks what the differences mean. Which of the following responses is most appropriate?

options.text: Only the five-year figure is valid, because a longer equally weighted window always gives the most reliable scenario z-score.
The event’s shocks must have been mismeasured, because an event has a single scenario z-score whatever covariance matrix is used.
Each matrix makes the same event look more or less surprising and gives a different risk ruler, so the matrix should match the conditions of the scenario being modeled.
The current matrix should always be used, because the most recent data always describe the conditions under which the next stress will occur.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What a z-score is measured against**

Every scenario z-score standardizes the shock vector by a covariance matrix. Change the matrix and the yardstick changes. Slow data (five years weekly before the event), fast data (one year weekly before the event) and recent data (the current matrix, which may reflect post-event dynamics) are the three common choices.

**Step 2 – Read the numbers**

The z-score falls from 6.8 to 4.1 to 3.2. The shorter window and the current matrix carry more volatility (or correlations closer to the event’s own pattern) than the five-year window, so the same moves are fewer standard deviations.

⇒ Each matrix produces a different risk ruler for the same events.

**Step 3 – Which one to use**

The appropriate matrix depends on the scenario being modeled: data from similar crashes for a crash scenario; recent data for Brexit, which had no comparable precedent (IM-15 c).

**Interpretation**

None of the three numbers is “the” z-score of the event. The committee should ask which window describes the conditions of the scenario under review, and keep the choice consistent across the ruler.

**LO:** IM-15 b: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 97, LO 97.b, Covariance Matrix Selection and Figures 97.2 to 97.4

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-15 b.6), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 97.

a.reason: Absolute claim: a long equally weighted window is not always best. For a crash it dilutes the crisis correlations and understates the stress.

b.reason: A scenario z-score is not a property of the event alone; it depends on the covariance matrix used to standardize the shocks.

d.reason: Absolute claim: recent data suit some scenarios (Brexit) and not others, and the current matrix may reflect post-event dynamics.

questions.question: A portfolio risk manager at a London asset manager is drafting internal guidance on building plausible stress scenarios, drawing on the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach and on lessons from the supervisory bank stress tests. Which of the following statements should the manager keep in the guidance?

options.text: The scenario z-score measures how consistent a set of policy shocks is with the chosen covariance matrix, so a value close to zero signals a coherent scenario.
The set of policy variables should be kept large, so that the regression that implies the nonpolicy factor shocks leaves less room for arbitrariness.
The 2009 SCAP achieved coherence with a rich scenario of more than 70 trading-book risk factors and eight macro factors for each participating country.
For a market crash scenario, the covariance matrix should be estimated from periods with similar crashes, since correlations among risky assets spike in crises.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Covariance choice (IM-15 b, c)**

Z-scores and implied nonpolicy shocks both depend on the covariance matrix. “If you are modeling a market crash, you should use data or a covariance matrix from periods that experienced similar crashes, because correlations among risky assets typically spike during market crises. Relying only on ‘normal’ data would likely understate the severity of the stress.”

**Step 2 – Map the other statements to their true owners**

Consistency with the covariance structure belongs to the correlation z-score; a small policy set is the MDS rule; the 70-plus factor scenario belongs to EBA 2011, while SCAP used GDP, unemployment and house prices plus a historical market shock.

**Interpretation**

D is correct. Its supervisory counterpart in ORR-17 is the same lesson from the other side: a historical shock gives loose coherence but “does not test for anything new”, so the data window must match the stress being modelled.

**LO:** IM-15 b: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios. IM-15 c: Explain steps in the process of defining and developing market-driven scenarios, and describe the application of the MDS approach in the example provided. ORR-17 b: Explain challenges in designing stress test scenarios, including the problem of coherence in modeling risk factors. • **Reference:** Golub (ed.), BlackRock’s Guide to Fixed-Income Risk Management, Ch.5 (via SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 97, LO 97.b and 97.c); Schuermann, Stress Testing Banks, Section 17.3

IM-15 • Market-Driven Scenarios: An Approach for Plausible Scenario Construction • Vardeez: VERY IMPORTANT

**Source:** Tier workbook, Tier C, section C9, Stress-Testing Practices and Scenario Design (question C9.2). Printed in the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook as question IM-15 b.8.

a.reason: Sibling swap: the scenario z-score measures severity (lower means more plausible). The correlation z-score normalizes for magnitude and shows consistency with the covariance matrix: near zero consistent, above 1.0 a warning.

b.reason: Polarity flip: “keeping the number of policy variables small helps minimize arbitrariness in the resulting perturbation vector”; a large set invites multicollinearity (do not add a variable with adjusted $R^{2}$ of 90% or more).

c.reason: Sibling swap (case cross-mapping): over 70 trading-book factors and eight macro factors for each of 21 countries describe the 2011 EBA test. The 2009 SCAP state space had only three dimensions with a historical market shock from June to December 2008.

questions.question: A newly hired risk analyst at a London asset manager is documenting the firm’s market-driven scenario (MDS) process. Which of the following lists the five steps in the correct order?

options.text: Select policy variables; define a market event; generate nonpolicy factor shocks; calibrate shock sizes; estimate the portfolio stress test P&L.
Define a market event; select policy variables; calibrate shock sizes to the policy variables; generate nonpolicy factor shocks; estimate the portfolio stress test P&L.
Define a market event; calibrate shock sizes to all risk factors; select policy variables from the largest shocks; estimate the portfolio stress test P&L; generate nonpolicy factor shocks.
Define a market event; select policy variables; generate nonpolicy factor shocks; calibrate shock sizes to the implied shocks; estimate the portfolio stress test P&L.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Start from what each step needs**

Policy variables can be chosen only for a defined event; shocks can be sized only once the policy variables exist; nonpolicy shocks are implied from the sized policy shocks; the P&L needs the full perturbation vector.

**Step 2 – Read off the order**

(1) Define a market event; (2) select policy variables; (3) calibrate shock sizes to the policy variables; (4) generate nonpolicy factor shocks from the policy shocks; (5) estimate the portfolio stress test P&L.

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

Each step consumes the output of the one before, so the order follows from the logic. Vardeez’s four-step version (see the correction box) is a common source of a wrong “count” or a wrong order.

**LO:** IM-15 c: Explain steps in the process of defining and developing market-driven scenarios, and describe the application of the MDS approach in the example provided. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 97, LO 97.c, Steps for Defining and Developing MDSs

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-15 c.1), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 97.

a.reason: Selects policy variables before the event they are meant to represent is defined, and implies nonpolicy shocks before the policy shocks are sized.

c.reason: Calibrates shocks to all risk factors directly, which defeats the conditional design (the experts shock only the few policy variables), and computes the P&L before the perturbation vector is complete.

d.reason: Implies nonpolicy shocks before the policy shocks are sized, then calibrates to the implied shocks: the dependency runs the other way.

questions.question: The risk team of a US fund that holds only US Treasury securities is asked to propose the market event for its next market-driven scenario. Which of the following proposals best meets the criteria for defining a market event?

options.text: A 25 basis point cut in the federal funds rate at the next policy meeting, which futures markets price with a 95% probability.
A sharp rotation from growth stocks into value stocks, triggered by a surprise in technology sector earnings.
A 120 basis point rise in 10-year Treasury yields within one week, triggered by a failed Treasury auction amid rising fiscal concerns.
A significant deterioration in global financial markets at some point over the next two years, from causes still to be identified.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The four Step 1 criteria**

Low probability but plausible, and not already priced in; defined precisely (size and direction); relevant to the portfolio; a specific catalyst.

**Step 2 – Test each proposal**

A: priced at 95%, so it is a known risk, not a low-probability one. B: equity style shocks are irrelevant to a Treasury-only portfolio (the reading’s own example). C: precise size and direction, directly relevant, unlikely but possible, with a named catalyst. D: no size, no direction, no catalyst.

⇒ C meets all four criteria.

**Interpretation**

The criteria reduce the two uncertainties of a scenario: whether the event happens, and how markets react if it does. A precise, relevant event with a catalyst also gives the team something it can monitor.

**LO:** IM-15 c: Explain steps in the process of defining and developing market-driven scenarios, and describe the application of the MDS approach in the example provided. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 97, LO 97.c, Step 1: Define a market event

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-15 c.2), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 97.

a.reason: Fails “low probability”: a risk the market already prices teaches nothing new.

b.reason: Fails “relevant”: shocks to value versus growth would have little relevance for a portfolio invested solely in US Treasuries.

d.reason: Fails “precise” and “catalyst”: the expected impact is open to interpretation and nothing triggers it.

questions.question: In February 2016 a risk team is sizing the policy shocks for a Soft Brexit scenario. The closest historical episode, sterling’s 1992 exit from the Exchange Rate Mechanism, was driven mainly by currency policy and did not capture the broader economic effects of leaving the European Union. Which of the following approaches to calibrating the shock sizes is most consistent with the MDS process?

options.text: Copy the 1992 shocks exactly, since a historical episode is the only objective basis on which shock sizes can be set.
Set the shocks to a target frequency based on the team’s view of the scenario’s likelihood, measured by the scenario z-score against the risk ruler.
Size every policy shock at the same number of standard deviations, so that the correlation z-score of the scenario is zero by construction.
Choose the largest shocks the covariance matrix will accept, since the purpose of the scenario is to quantify the worst-case tail loss.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The two calibration routes**

(1) Identify a historical period that resembles the scenario; (2) set a target frequency from a subjective view of the scenario’s likelihood, the likelihood of a scenario at least as extreme, measured by the scenario z-score.

**Step 2 – Which route fits here**

The stem rules out route (1): the 1992 episode was about currency policy and the reading notes that direct historical comparisons offered limited guidance for Brexit.

⇒ Route (2), using the risk ruler to place the scenario against historical events.

**Interpretation**

The risk ruler turns “how likely do we think this is?” into a number of standard deviations. Soft Brexit sat between Remain (more likely) and Adverse Brexit (far less likely).

**LO:** IM-15 c: Explain steps in the process of defining and developing market-driven scenarios, and describe the application of the MDS approach in the example provided. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 97, LO 97.c, Step 3 and the Brexit example (Figure 97.6)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-15 c.5), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 97.

a.reason: Absolute claim: an analogue is one of two routes, and the stem says this one does not resemble the scenario.

c.reason: Equal sizing does not make a scenario coherent: the correlation z-score depends on the signs and relative sizes against the correlations, so nothing is “zero by construction”.

d.reason: Purpose error: MDS aims at plausible scenarios, not at the largest acceptable shock, and it is not designed to quantify tail losses.

questions.question: A risk manager is reviewing how the market-driven scenario approach was applied to the 2016 UK referendum on leaving the European Union. Which of the following statements about the Soft Brexit scenario is correct?

options.text: Policy shocks were spread across asset classes, because mixing equity, rate and currency shocks in one block gives the most realistic correlations.
Gilts were assumed to sell off, because investors were expected to exit UK fixed income in both of the leave scenarios.
The covariance matrix was estimated over the 1992 ERM crisis, because it was the closest historical analogue to a vote to leave.
The policy variables focused on UK markets, and shocks to Italian sovereign debt and the Mexican peso were kept small to dampen contagion.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall the policy variables**

The Soft Brexit policy variables focused on UK markets: the FTSE All Share index, the 10-year gilt yield and sterling.

**Step 2 – Recall the design choices**

A few shocks, such as those to Italian sovereign debt and the Mexican peso, were kept small on purpose, to dampen contagion outside the UK and stop those factors overwhelming the covariance matrix. Shocks were generally restricted to the same asset class.

⇒ D is correct.

**Interpretation**

Each design choice protects the covariance step: small peripheral shocks and single-asset-class blocks keep the implied shocks from being driven by spurious relationships.

**LO:** IM-15 c: Explain steps in the process of defining and developing market-driven scenarios, and describe the application of the MDS approach in the example provided. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 97, LO 97.c, Applying the MDS Approach: Brexit Example (Figures 97.5 and 97.7)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-15 c.6), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 97.

a.reason: Reverses the rule: shocks were restricted to the same asset class to avoid spurious correlations.

b.reason: Scenario swap: gilts were a safe haven in Soft Brexit; rising yields were the Adverse Brexit assumption.

c.reason: No comparable event existed; the 1992 ERM exit was only loosely related, and a matrix based on recent data was used.

questions.question: A risk committee reviews a table of Soft Brexit policy shocks with a column headed “scenario z-score delta”: the change in the scenario z-score if a policy shock were moved from its stressed value to its expected value conditional on the other shocks. The delta is close to zero for every policy variable except the 10-year gilt yield. Which of the following conclusions is most appropriate?

options.text: The rate shock is the least consistent with the other shocks under the chosen covariance matrix, so the safe-haven assumption for gilts deserves the closest challenge.
The rate shock is the most consistent with the other shocks, since a delta away from zero shows that the covariance matrix explains it well.
All shocks except the rate shock should be removed from the scenario, since a delta near zero shows that they add no information to it.
The scenario z-score of the full scenario is close to zero, so the scenario is too mild to be of use as a stress test of the portfolio.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the delta measures**

How much the scenario z-score changes when one policy shock is moved to the value the covariance matrix would expect given the other shocks. Near zero: that shock already sits where the other shocks imply.

**Step 2 – Read the table**

Every delta is near zero except rates, so the shocks are largely consistent with one another, with the exception of rates.

⇒ The gilt rally is the assumption that departs most from what the matrix implies.

**Step 3 – Link to the example**

Rates were also the most debated variable: safe haven or exit from UK fixed income. The team kept the safe-haven assumption for Soft Brexit, but this is where the judgment is concentrated and must be defended.

**Interpretation**

A large delta does not prove the assumption wrong; it marks where the scenario leans hardest on expert judgment rather than on history.

questions.question: The board of a multi-strategy hedge fund asks its new chief risk oﬀicer to explain fund liquidity risk after a reputational problem involving one of the fund’s star managers. Which of the following statements is most consistent with best practice?

options.text: It is the risk of being unable to obtain enough liquidity to meet redemptions; it can arise as a byproduct of poor performance or reputational problems, and is best met with top-down governance.
It is the risk that the fund’s holdings fall in value as bid-ask spreads widen; it does not depend on investor behavior, so a reputational problem leaves it unchanged.
It arises only on the asset side of the fund, so a fund whose holdings are all liquid has no need for a liquidity risk management framework.
It is best managed bottom-up, with each portfolio manager setting liquidity limits for his or her own book and no separate fund-wide framework.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Define the risk**

Fund liquidity risk is the risk that a fund may be unable to obtain enough liquidity to meet investor redemptions.

**Step 2 – Where it comes from**

It can arise as a byproduct of other issues, such as poor fund performance or reputational problems involving managers: exactly the board’s situation.

**Step 3 – The best-practice response**

A robust, top-down governance structure supported by a clearly defined liquidity risk framework that operates independently within the fund.

⇒ A.

**Interpretation**

The star manager’s problem is a redemption trigger. The board should expect the risk to show up on the liability side first, and the framework should already have measured how fast the assets can be turned into cash.

**LO:** IM-16 a: Explain best practices for managing liquidity risk in an investment fund. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 98, LO 98.a; Golub (ed.), BlackRock’s Guide to Fixed-Income Risk Management, Ch.7

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-16 a.1), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 98.

b.reason: Wrong risk: a fall in asset values is market risk. Fund liquidity risk is about meeting redemptions, and reputational problems drive redemptions.

c.reason: Absolute claim: redemptions can still exceed what can be sold without stranding the remaining investors, and the framework also covers redemption patterns.

d.reason: Polarity flip: best practice is top-down governance with an independent framework, not bottom-up limits.

questions.question: The chief risk oﬀicer of a credit fund is writing job descriptions for two teams within the fund’s liquidity risk framework. Which of the following correctly distinguishes the liquidity risk measurement element from the liquidity risk management element?

options.text: Measurement monitors the liquidity profile against limits; management identifies and quantifies the sources of liquidity risk.
Measurement escalates concerns to the CIO; management maintains the fund’s backup credit lines and other extraordinary tools.
Measurement identifies, assesses and quantifies the key sources of liquidity risk; management monitors the liquidity profile and evaluates redemption risks against limits.
Measurement and management are the same element, because quantifying liquidity risk automatically keeps it within the fund’s limits.
