questions.question: A credit analyst at a regional bank reviews a borrower’s latest annual report while preparing its annual credit review. Which observation is most consistent with an early warning signal of financial distress?

options.text: Revenue dipped in the first quarter, in line with the firm’s usual seasonal pattern.
The tax charge appears low relative to the earnings the firm reports.
Almost all of the year’s earnings were generated by the firm’s core operations.
The firm kept the same auditor and the same fiscal year-end as in prior years.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall the early-warning questions**

The reading’s accounting questions include: are earnings generated from core operations, and does the tax charge appear low relative to reported earnings?

⇒ A tax charge that looks low against reported earnings suggests the earnings may be overstated: an early warning signal.

**Step 2 – Check the other observations**

A dip that follows the usual seasonal pattern is the kind of temporary fluctuation the analyst must separate from a permanent deterioration. Earnings from core operations, and an unchanged auditor and fiscal year-end, are the healthy answers to the reading’s questions.

**Interpretation**

The tax line is hard to inflate along with profits: when reported earnings rise but the tax charge does not, ask what kind of earnings they are.

**LO:** IM-13 a: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.a

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-13 a.2), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95.

a.reason: A seasonal dip is a temporary fluctuation, not by itself a distress signal.

c.reason: Earnings from core operations are the reassuring answer to the first question.

d.reason: Changes of auditor or fiscal year-end are warning signs; keeping them is not.

questions.question: A distressed-debt analyst is preparing a training note on why firms default. Which statement about performing well below expectations as a cause of financial distress is correct?

options.text: It is the most common cause of distress, and in a recession the key challenge is to judge whether the downturn itself or management’s decisions drive the deterioration.
It is a rare cause of distress, because recessions can be forecast and their effect on revenue hedged in advance.
It covers products that lose demand as preferences shift, which the reading classifies as a crisis of confidence.
In a recession, the deterioration should always be attributed to the business cycle rather than to management’s strategy.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall the reading’s statement**

“Performing well below expectations. This is the most common cause of financial distress.” Its two triggers are economic downturns and uncompetitive products or services.

**Step 2 – The diagnostic challenge**

For downturns, “the key challenge is determining whether the downturn itself is driving the deterioration, or whether management decisions and strategies are the underlying cause”.

⇒ A states both points.

**Interpretation**

The diagnosis matters for the remedy: a cyclical problem may need time and liquidity; a management problem needs a new plan, and extra capital can simply give weak management more time to destroy value (IM-13 b).

**LO:** IM-13 a: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.a

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-13 a.3), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95.

b.reason: Polarity flip: it is the most common cause, and the business cycle “is unavoidable”.

c.reason: Sibling swap: obsolete products are the second trigger of performing below expectations; a crisis of confidence is usually fraud.

d.reason: Absolute claim: the reading asks the analyst to separate the cycle from management’s decisions, not to assume the answer.

questions.question: A distressed-debt analyst groups four troubled borrowers by the main cause of their distress. Which grouping is correct?

options.text: A roll-up of 40 regional dental practices whose expected economies of scale never materialised: performing well below expectations.
A chemicals maker facing a class action over groundwater contamination that its insurance may not cover: unexpected liabilities.
A retailer whose sales collapsed after its customers moved online: crisis of confidence.
A logistics firm whose former CFO is found to have inflated revenue for five years: unrealistic business plan.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Recall the five families**

Leverage and business performance; unexpected liabilities (tort, contract); performing well below expectations (downturns, uncompetitive products); crisis of confidence (often fraud); unrealistic business plans (LBOs, roll-ups, too many entrants).

**Step 2 – Place each borrower**

Class action for environmental harm: a tort liability, under unexpected liabilities, often underestimated by management and possibly uninsured. Roll-up whose economies of scale never came: unrealistic business plan. Retailer losing customers to online rivals: uncompetitive products, under performing below expectations. CFO fraud: crisis of confidence.

⇒ Only B is grouped correctly.

**Interpretation**

Markets typically “assume the worst” about a tort claim and discount the firm’s securities before the award is known.

**LO:** IM-13 a: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.a

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-13 a.5), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95.

a.reason: Roll-ups are one of the reading’s three unrealistic business plans.

c.reason: Obsolete products are performing below expectations, not a crisis of confidence.

d.reason: Accounting fraud is the classic crisis of confidence (Enron), not an unrealistic plan.

questions.question: Shortly after a manufacturer discloses that its former CFO falsified three years of revenue, a credit analyst at an insurer that holds the firm’s bonds is asked what to assess first. Which approach is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Treat only the three restated years as unreliable, since information from outside the fraud period is unaffected.
Assess how far the fraud contaminates all previously reported information, and whether it could trigger a liquidity crisis through cash balances, credit lines and loan acceleration.
Focus on whether the firm’s products remain competitive, since a crisis of confidence is mainly a problem of customer demand.
Wait for the next audited statements before acting, since market prices overreact to fraud news and then recover.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Reliability of historical information**

“Once financial fraud is uncovered, all previously reported financial information becomes suspect.” The analyst assesses the informational contagion and whether there is a practical cutoff point for reliable data.

**Step 2 – Liquidity and the likelihood of bankruptcy**

The analyst asks whether the fraud could trigger liquidity problems: cash balances, the availability of credit lines and the risk of loan acceleration.

⇒ B covers the two areas of focus the reading names.

**Interpretation**

A crisis of confidence turns a reporting problem into a funding problem: lenders who no longer trust the numbers can pull lines or accelerate loans.

**LO:** IM-13 a: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.a

a.reason: Too narrow: the contagion can reach information outside the restated years; that is why a cutoff point must be found.

c.reason: Sibling swap: competitiveness belongs to performing below expectations.

d.reason: Waiting ignores the immediate liquidity question, which is the more urgent of the two.

questions.question: A distressed-debt analyst notes that a retailer’s senior bonds now trade at 45 per 100 of face value, down from 92 six months ago. Which interpretation of the debt trading level is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: The lower trading level signals that the market expects more severe distress, and it informs the analyst about which restructuring solutions are realistic.
The lower trading level signals that the market expects milder distress, because cheaper bonds make open market repurchases more attractive.
The trading level is informative only for bank loans, because bond prices mainly reflect changes in interest rates.
The trading level measures the bonds’ coupon relative to market yields and says nothing about the restructuring options.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the trading level is**

The debt trading level is the current market price of the debt relative to its full repayment value.

**Step 2 – What it tells the analyst**

It “serves as an indicator of the market’s expectations about distress severity and potential restructuring options”. A fall from 92 to 45 means the market expects far less to be repaid.

⇒ A: deeper expected distress, and a guide to the realistic solutions.

**Interpretation**

The price is the market’s verdict on the stage of distress. Near full value, the problem looks like liquidity; far below it, the market is pricing in a restructuring of the claim itself.

**LO:** IM-13 b: Describe methods firms can use to remedy a financial distress situation at different stages of distress and explain the potential implications and challenges to using each method. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20 (after Moyer, 2005); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.b

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-13 b.1), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95.

b.reason: Polarity flip: a lower price signals more severe expected distress. Cheaper bonds can make a discounted buyback attractive, but only for a firm with cash to spare.

c.reason: The reading applies the trading level to a firm’s actively traded debt; a fall from 92 to 45 is a credit signal, not a rate move.

d.reason: The trading level is a price relative to repayment value, and the reading links it directly to the restructuring options.

questions.question: A distressed industrial firm with almost no cash wants to cut its bond debt. It offers bondholders new secured notes in exchange for their existing unsecured bonds, and warns that bondholders who do not take part may end up worse off than those who do. Which method is the firm using?

options.text: A noncoercive exchange offer.
A cash tender offer.
A coercive exchange offer.
A direct purchase from bondholders.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Identify the family**

The firm lacks cash and offers new securities for its distressed debt: an exchange offer, not a cash tender or a direct purchase.

**Step 2 – Coercive or noncoercive**

Exchange offers “may be coercive, meaning participants are warned that nonparticipants may be disadvantaged”; noncoercive offers encourage participation by highlighting the opportunity’s attractiveness.

⇒ The warning makes it a coercive exchange offer.

**Interpretation**

Coercion is the firm’s answer to the holdout problem: if staying out looks worse than taking part, fewer creditors hold out (IM-13 c).

**LO:** IM-13 b: Describe methods firms can use to remedy a financial distress situation at different stages of distress and explain the potential implications and challenges to using each method. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.b

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-13 b.4), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95.

a.reason: A noncoercive offer persuades with attractive terms, not with a warning.

b.reason: A tender offer pays cash; this firm has almost none.

d.reason: A direct purchase is a negotiated deal with individual holders, usually for cash.

questions.question: A restructuring adviser briefs the board of a distressed company on the implications of different ways to raise capital and reduce leverage. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: A private equity sponsor holding more than 50% of the equity is generally positive for creditors, because the sponsor realises value only after the debt claims are satisfied.
Assets generally fetch better prices after a bankruptcy filing, so a distressed firm should delay asset sales until it has filed.
Secured financing is usually the easiest source of cash for a distressed firm, because its most valuable assets are rarely pledged.
An equity injection from new outside investors can usually be arranged faster than one from the firm’s incumbent investors.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The equity sponsor**

“A private owner with more than a 50% stake is generally positive for distressed investors. A majority equity holder realizes value only after debt claims are satisfied, which aligns incentives.”

⇒ A is correct.

**Step 2 – Test B, C and D**

Asset sales: a favourable price is “generally easier to obtain before a bankruptcy filing”. Secured financing: “often limited”, since the most valuable assets were pledged in earlier restructurings. Equity: incumbent capital “can typically be arranged quickly”, while new investors take longer because of due diligence.

⇒ B, C and D each reverse the reading.

**Interpretation**

Each method’s implication follows from timing and incentives: sell early, expect the collateral to be gone, and look to existing owners first for fast equity.

**LO:** IM-13 b: Describe methods firms can use to remedy a financial distress situation at different stages of distress and explain the potential implications and challenges to using each method. • **Reference:** Ippolito, Private Capital Investing (2020), Ch.20; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 95, LO 95.b

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-13 b.5), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 95.

b.reason: Polarity flip on timing: sell before filing.

c.reason: Polarity flip: the best assets are usually already pledged.

d.reason: Reversed: incumbents are faster; newcomers need time for due diligence.

questions.question: The head of risk at a global asset manager tells the board that the firm’s market-driven scenario (MDS) process is designed to meet James Surowiecki’s three criteria for good collective decisions. Which of the following correctly matches a feature of the MDS process with the criterion it satisfies?

options.text: Requiring every expert to adopt the firm’s house economic view before proposing shocks satisfies the criterion that opinions be independent.
A centralized process run by the risk management department to aggregate the ideas into a collective view satisfies the criterion of an objective aggregation mechanism.
Passing the policy shocks through a covariance matrix satisfies the criterion that each individual possess specialized knowledge not available to others.
Letting the experts settle the scenario among themselves, without the risk function, satisfies the criterion of an objective aggregation mechanism.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – The three criteria**

(1) Each individual has specialized knowledge not available to others; (2) opinions are independent and not influenced by groupthink; (3) there is an objective mechanism for aggregating private views into a collective assessment.

**Step 2 – Match the MDS features**

The diverse group of professionals supplies (1). The firm’s risk management department “develops a centralized process to aggregate these ideas into a collective view”: that is (3).

⇒ B.

**Interpretation**

The mapping explains why the aggregation sits with risk management rather than with any one investment team: an aggregator that has no stake in a particular view is what makes the mechanism objective.

**LO:** IM-15 a: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 97, LO 97.a (Surowiecki, The Wisdom of Crowds)

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-15 a.2), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 97.

a.reason: Polarity flip: imposing a house view is the groupthink that the independence criterion rules out.

c.reason: Sibling swap: the covariance matrix is a statistical tool that implies the nonpolicy shocks; specialized knowledge comes from the diverse experts.

d.reason: Removing the central risk function removes the objective aggregator; a consensus reached among the experts themselves invites groupthink.

questions.question: At an investment committee meeting, the CIO of a balanced fund proposes replacing the fund’s 99% VaR limit with the loss from the firm’s Soft Brexit market-driven scenario, which he describes as “our new measure of tail loss”. Which of the following responses is most consistent with the purpose of the MDS approach?

options.text: The proposal is appropriate, because the MDS approach is designed to quantify the tail loss of a portfolio at a stated confidence level.
The proposal is appropriate, because a scenario’s P&L can be converted into an exact probability of loss without any further assumptions.
The proposal misreads the approach: MDS does not quantify tail losses or set targets; it integrates views in a structured way and prompts managers to reassess their convictions.
The proposal misreads the approach: MDS scenarios are built only from historical episodes, so they cannot inform any forward-looking decision.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What the approach is for**

“The goal of the MDS approach is not to quantify tail losses or force risk managers to target specific outcomes. Instead, it is a tool for integrating insights from different perspectives in a structured way.”

**Step 2 – What it gives instead**

By quantifying returns under scenarios of varying plausibility, it encourages managers to reassess their strategic convictions and increases awareness of alternative outcomes.

⇒ The CIO’s proposal misreads the approach: C.

**Interpretation**

A scenario loss is the outcome of one coherent story, with no confidence level attached. It complements a VaR limit; it does not replace it.

**LO:** IM-15 a: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios. • **Reference:** SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 97, LO 97.a and LO 97.c (closing paragraph of the Brexit example)

a.reason: Purpose error: quantifying tail losses at a confidence level is what the reading says MDS is not for.

b.reason: Absolute claim: scenario z-scores give only relative probabilities; an absolute probability needs further assumptions (IM-15 b).

d.reason: Right verdict, wrong reason: MDS scenarios are forward-looking, not built only from historical episodes.

questions.question: The head of real estate at a Canadian pension plan unsmooths the quarterly returns of the plan’s appraisal-based property index before the annual asset allocation review. The reported series has a first-order autocorrelation of 0.70, and the properties are reappraised once a year. Which of the following statements about the unsmoothed series is correct?

options.text: Its average quarterly return will be well below the reported average, because unsmoothing restores the losses that the appraisers failed to record.
Its average quarterly return will be close to the reported average, because smoothing spreads each shock over several quarters without removing it.
A first-order AR(1) filter is suﬀicient for this index, because the annual reappraisal cycle affects the level of the index but not the lag structure of its returns.
Its volatility will be lower than the reported volatility, because the filter removes the noise that appraisal errors add to the reported returns.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – What smoothing does to the level**

Each true shock is spread over several quarters but still counted in full, so the index ends where the true index ends. Summing the filter gives $\sum r_{t} = \sum r^{*}_{t} + \frac{\phi}{1-\phi}(r^{*}_{T} - r^{*}_{0})$, a single end term.

⇒ The average return is essentially unchanged: Ang’s first property.

**Step 2 – What it does to dispersion**

The filter adds noise back, so volatility rises: with $\phi= 0.70$ a pure AR(1) filter would scale it by $\sqrt{1.7/0.3} = 2.38$.

**Step 3 – What the reappraisal cycle does**

Annual reappraisals put a fourth-order lag into quarterly returns. A first-order filter misses it; Ang’s third property is that unsmoothing is an art, best done with an ARMA model and knowledge of how the market is valued.

**Interpretation**

Unsmoothing changes the path, not the destination. Individual bad quarters become much worse, which is easy to mistake for a lower mean.

**LO:** IM-17 d: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management (2014), Ch.13, Unsmoothing (three properties), as reported in Vardeez IM-17 d and Workbook D9; SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 99, LO 99.d

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-17 d.4), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 99.

a.reason: Confuses deeper individual quarters with a lower mean: unsmoothing affects risk estimates, not expected returns.

c.reason: Annual reappraisal creates a fourth-order lag in quarterly data; one lag is not enough.

d.reason: Polarity flip: unsmoothing adds noise back and raises volatility.

questions.question:
A risk manager at a Dutch insurer presents the following statistics for a private real estate index to the investment committee. Over the same period the quarterly volatility of US equities was about 7.5%.

|  | Reported | Unsmoothed |
|---|---|---|
| First-order autocorrelation | 0.78 | close to 0 |
| Quarterly volatility | 2.25% | 6.26% |
| Correlation with the S&P 500 | 9.2% | 15.8% |
| Worst quarter (December 2008) | −8.3% | −36.3% |

Which of the following conclusions should the risk manager draw?

options.text: Real estate’s expected return was overstated by about 28 percentage points, so the index mean must be lowered before it enters the optimiser.
Real estate’s Sharpe ratio is lower on unsmoothed data, and an optimiser fed the unsmoothed statistics will allocate less to real estate.
Because the unsmoothed correlation is still below 20%, smoothing biased the volatility estimate but not the correlation estimate.
Because reported volatility is less than a third of equity volatility, real estate is a low-risk diversifier whose allocation can be raised.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the table**

Unsmoothing multiplies quarterly volatility by 6.26/2.25 = 2.8, to a level close to equities (7.5%), raises the correlation with the S&P 500 from 9.2% to 15.8%, and turns a −8.3% quarter into −36.3%.

**Step 2 – Effect on the Sharpe ratio**

The mean is unchanged by unsmoothing, so the excess return stays the same while volatility is 2.8 times larger.

⇒ The Sharpe ratio falls to about a third of its reported value.

**Step 3 – Effect on the allocation**

Higher volatility and higher correlation with equities both reduce the optimal mean-variance weight.

⇒ The optimiser allocates less to real estate on unsmoothed data.

**Interpretation**

Reported appraisal data make real estate look like a near-riskless diversifier. The committee should put unsmoothed statistics into the optimiser.

**LO:** IM-17 d: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management (2014), Ch.13, Unsmoothing (NCREIF example); SchweserNotes 2026 Book 5, Reading 99, LO 99.c and 99.d

**Source:** Written new for the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook (question IM-17 d.5), built from SchweserNotes 2026 Reading 99.

a.reason: The −36.3% is one quarter’s unsmoothed return, not a bias in the mean; the expected return is unchanged by unsmoothing. The 28 points is 36.3−8.3, a gap in one quarter’s return.

c.reason: The correlation rose from 9.2% to 15.8%: smoothing biases correlations downward too.

d.reason: The 2.25% is the smoothed figure. Unsmoothed, real estate volatility (6.26%) is close to that of equities.

questions.question: A member of the investment committee of a Canadian university endowment is reviewing a consultant’s report that relies on two data sets: an appraisal-based institutional real estate index whose quarterly returns show a first-order autocorrelation of 0.75, and a commercial database of venture capital returns to which reporting is voluntary. Which of the following statements is correct to include in the committee’s response to the consultant?

options.text: Unsmoothing the real estate index with an AR(1) filter will raise its estimated volatility, correlation and beta with equities, but will leave its estimated expected return essentially unchanged.
Survivorship bias in the venture capital database makes reported returns understate true returns, because funds that drop out of the database tend to be those with above-average returns.
Selection bias in the venture capital database, which arises because values are recorded mainly when they are high, is corrected by applying the same Geltner-Ross-Zisler unsmoothing filter.
The downward bias in the real estate index’s volatility is a small-sample problem that will disappear once the consultant uses a suﬀiciently long history of reported quarterly returns.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Read the autocorrelation**

A first-order autocorrelation of 0.75 signals appraisal smoothing. Infrequent trading makes “estimates of risk, volatilities, correlations, and betas” too low; unsmoothing adds noise back to recover the true returns.

**Step 2 – Apply Ang’s first property**

“Unsmoothing affects only risk estimates and not expected returns”, because smoothing spreads shocks over several periods but still counts all of them, so the first and last prices are unchanged.

⇒ A is correct. For NCREIF, volatility rose from 2.25% to 6.26% a quarter and the correlation with the S&P 500 from 9.2% to 15.8%.

**Interpretation**

The committee should ask for unsmoothed risk estimates before the real estate allocation enters a mean-variance optimiser; raw appraisal data make the asset look like a near-riskless diversifier. With $\phi= 0.75$ a pure AR(1) filter would scale the reported volatility by $\sqrt{1.75/0.25} = 2.65$.

**LO:** IM-17 c: Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets. IM-17 d: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing. • **Reference:** Ang, Asset Management, Ch.13 (LTR source text Ch.19), 19.4

**Source:** Tier workbook, Tier D, section D9, Illiquid Assets (question D9.1). Printed in the Risk Management and Investment Management P1–P3 workbook as question IM-17 d.6.

b.reason: Polarity flip: survivorship bias “results from the tendency of poorly performing funds to stop reporting”, so reported returns overstate true returns.

c.reason: Sibling swap: unsmoothing corrects infrequent trading. Selection bias is addressed with Heckman (1979) selection models, which let the threshold above which returns are observed vary over time.

d.reason: Scope error: Ang states that the infrequent-observation bias “is not a ‘small sample’ problem, which goes away when our sample becomes very large; it is a ‘population’ problem”.

questions.loText: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-1 b Q1
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a SGD 60 billion Singapore pension fund is presenting the history of asset pricing theory to newly hired analysts. She wants one slide to capture what made the CAPM revolutionary when it was formulated in the 1960s. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Before the CAPM, risk was usually measured by an asset’s covariance with the market; the CAPM replaced this with the asset’s own volatility, which is simpler to estimate.
The CAPM showed that an asset’s own volatility is irrelevant to investors in every model of risk, a conclusion that later factor research has fully confirmed.

The CAPM held that the risk of an asset is not how it behaves in isolation but how it moves in relation to other assets and the market, measured by its covariance with the market portfolio (its beta).
The CAPM held that the risk of an asset is how it covaries with whatever portfolio the individual investor already owns, so the relevant beta differs from one investor to the next.

questions.solution:
Q1: A pension-fund analyst picks the statement that captures what made the CAPM revolutionary.

**Concept and theory**

Any pricing model must answer one question first: what is “risk”? Before the CAPM, the common answer was an asset’s own volatility, the spread of its returns looked at on their own. The CAPM (Treynor, Sharpe, Lintner and Mossin, building on Markowitz’s mean-variance diversification) was the first cogent theory to say that this is the wrong lens. An investor never holds an asset in isolation; she holds it inside a diversified portfolio, and in CAPM equilibrium that portfolio is the market. What matters is therefore how much the asset adds to the risk of the market portfolio, which is its co-movement with the market:

$\beta_{\text{i}} = \frac{\text{cov}(\text{r}_{\text{i}}\text{, r}_{\text{m}})}{\text{var}(\text{r}_{\text{m}})}$ ,

where $\text{r}_{\text{i}}$ is the asset’s return and $\text{r}_{\text{m}}$ the market return. The part of an asset’s volatility that does not move with the market is diversified away and earns nothing.

|  | Pre-CAPM view | CAPM view |
|---|---|---|
| Risk is | the asset’s own volatility | co-movement with the market |
| Measure | $\sigma_{\text{i}}$ | $\beta_{\text{i}} = \text{cov}(\text{r}_{\text{i}}$, $\text{r}_{\text{m}})$/ var$(\text{r}_{\text{m}})$ |
| Reference portfolio | none (asset in isolation) | the market portfolio |

GARP adds a caveat: own volatility does turn out to matter (Chapter 2 on factors), but for describing the CAPM it is ignored.

**Applying it to this question**

The slide must state (1) the direction of the shift, from isolation to co-movement, and (2) the reference portfolio, the market. Only one option gets both right and makes no claim beyond the source.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: the CAPM moved risk from own volatility to covariance with the market; the reference is the market portfolio, not the investor’s portfolio.

**Reference**

LO 83.b: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM. GARP Chapter 1, Factor Theory, Section 1.4 CAPM (opening discussion). Schweser Reading 83, LO 83.b. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 b, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Reverses the direction of the historical shift: before the CAPM risk was own volatility, and the CAPM moved it to covariance with the market. A would be correct only if the stem asked what the CAPM replaced, with the two measures swapped back.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** Turns “irrelevant for the CAPM” into “irrelevant in every model” and claims full confirmation. GARP explicitly says asset volatility itself matters (Chapter 2); it is set aside only for describing the CAPM. B would be correct if it read “within the CAPM, own volatility is not priced”.

c.reason: GARP 1.4: the CAPM “was the first cogent theory to recognize that the risk of an asset was not how that asset behaved in isolation but how that asset moved in relation to other assets and to the market as a whole”; the relevant measure “was how the asset covaried with the market portfolio, the beta of the asset”. Schweser 83.b says the same. C restates this exactly.

d.reason: **Scope error.** Replaces the market portfolio with each investor’s own portfolio. In the CAPM everybody holds the same MVE portfolio, which is the market, so there is one beta per asset, measured against the market. D would describe a partial-equilibrium marginal-risk calculation for a non-CAPM investor, not the CAPM.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-1 b Q2
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Canadian property and casualty insurer is ranking three TSX-listed stocks by their CAPM risk premiums for an investment committee note. The CAPM is assumed to hold, the market risk premium is 5.0%, and the volatility of the market portfolio is 18%. The analyst has collected the following data.

| Stock | Volatility (%) | Correlation with market | Market cap (CAD bn) |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | 45 | 0.40 | 60 |
| Q | 20 | 0.85 | 85 |
| R | 30 | 0.70 | 25 |

Which of the following correctly ranks the three stocks from the highest to the lowest CAPM risk premium?

options.text: R, then P, then Q
P, then R, then Q
Q, then R, then P
Q, then P, then R

questions.solution:
Q2: An insurer’s treasury analyst ranks three stocks by CAPM risk premium from volatility, correlation and (irrelevant) market cap.

**Concept and theory**

In the CAPM the risk premium of an asset is proportional to its beta, E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} = \beta_{\text{i}} (\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )$, so with a positive market premium the ranking of premiums is the ranking of betas. Beta can be written in two equivalent ways (GARP, Lesson 5):

$\beta_{\text{i}} = \frac{\text{cov}(\text{r}_{\text{i}}\text{, r}_{\text{m}})}{\text{var}(\text{r}_{\text{m}})} = \frac{\rho_{\text{i,m}} \sigma_{\text{i}} \sigma_{\text{m}}}{\sigma^{2}_{\text{m}}} = \frac{\rho_{\text{i,m}} \sigma_{\text{i}}}{\sigma_{\text{m}}}$ ,

where $\rho_{\text{i,m}}$ is the correlation of the asset with the market, $\sigma_{\text{i}}$ the asset’s volatility and $\sigma_{\text{m}}$ the market’s volatility. Beta therefore needs both ingredients: a very volatile asset with low correlation can have a modest beta, and a highly correlated but calm asset can too. Market capitalisation tells you the asset’s weight in the market portfolio, not its exposure to the market factor.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i,m}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}}$ with $\sigma_{\text{m}} =$ 18%, then premium $= \beta_{\text{i}} \times$ 5.0%.

$\beta_{\text{P}} =$ 0.40 × 45/18 = 1.000, $\text{premium}_{\text{P}} =$ 1.000 × 5.0% = 5.00%

$\beta_{\text{Q}} =$ 0.85 × 20/18 = 0.944, $\text{premium}_{\text{Q}} =$ 0.944 × 5.0% = 4.72%

$\beta_{\text{R}} =$ 0.70 × 30/18 = 1.167, $\text{premium}_{\text{R}} =$ 1.167 × 5.0% = 5.83%

Ranking: R (5.83%) > P (5.00%) > Q (4.72%). Meaning: R is the stock whose returns contribute most to the market’s swings, so it is the one investors must be paid most to hold.

**Fragile fact.** $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i,m}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}}$: correlation times the asset’s volatility divided by the market’s volatility (not the reverse ratio, not squared).

**Reference**

LO 83.b: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM. GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.4 CAPM, “CAPM Lesson 5: Risk Is Factor Exposure” (beta formula, Equation 1.2). Schweser Reading 83, LO 83.b and Lesson 5 under LO 83.c. GARP gives $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i,m}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}}$; Schweser gives only cov / var. Same quantity.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 b, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: GARP: “the higher the co-movement (the higher cov$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}$, $\text{r}_{\text{m}})$), the higher the asset’s beta” and the risk premium “is a function of that stock’s beta”. Using $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i,m}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}}$ gives R, P, Q.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: total volatility for beta.** Ranks by $\sigma_{\text{i}}$: P (45%) > R (30%) > Q (20%). This is the pre-CAPM measure of risk that the CAPM rejected. B would be correct if all three stocks had the same correlation with the market, since then beta would be proportional to $\sigma_{\text{i}}$.

c.reason: **Dropped term: correlation alone.** Ranks by $\rho_{\text{i,m}}$: Q (0.85) > R (0.70) > P (0.40), dropping the $\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}}$ factor. C would be correct if all three stocks had the same volatility.

d.reason: **Wrong input twin: market cap for exposure.** Ranks by market capitalisation: Q (85) > P (60) > R (25). Cap weight sets how much of the stock the market portfolio holds (CAPM Lesson 1), not how sensitive the stock is to the market factor. D would answer “rank the stocks by weight in a cap-weighted index”.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-1 b Q3
questions.question: The chief risk officer of a BRL 25 billion Brazilian asset manager is reviewing a draft board memo that explains how the CAPM treats factor risk. The memo will be used to justify moving the equity book toward market-factor exposure. Which of the following statements should the CRO approve as the most accurate description of the CAPM?

options.text: The CAPM allows several systematic factors, with the market the most important, and an asset’s risk premium is the sum of its exposures to each factor times that factor’s premium.
Under the CAPM both an asset’s exposure to the market and its idiosyncratic risk earn risk premiums, but the premium on idiosyncratic risk is smaller because it can be partly diversified.
The single CAPM factor is the market return in excess of T-bills, and any asset whose total volatility equals the market’s volatility earns exactly the market risk premium.
The single CAPM factor is the market return in excess of T-bills; every asset’s risk premium is set solely by its exposure (beta) to that factor, and the greater the exposure, the higher the premium.

questions.solution:
Q3: A Brazilian asset manager’s CRO picks the accurate description of how the CAPM treats factor risk.

**Concept and theory**

Factor theory says assets earn premiums because they are bundles of factor risks; it is the factor exposures, not the asset labels, that are rewarded. The CAPM is the most basic factor theory: it specifies exactly one factor, the market portfolio, whose return in excess of T-bills is the factor return. Three consequences follow.

1. One factor drives all expected returns: the market excess return E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ .
2. Each asset’s premium depends only on its exposure (beta) to that factor: E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} = \beta_{\text{i}}(\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) -$ $\text{r}_{\text{f}} )$. Greater exposure means a higher premium when the market premium is positive.
3. Idiosyncratic (non-factor) risk is diversified away in the market portfolio and earns no premium (in Ang’s analogy, it is the part of food with no nutritional value).

|  | CAPM | Multifactor models (LO 83.d) |
|---|---|---|
| Factors | one: the market excess return | several (macro or tradeable) |
| Premium | $\beta_{\text{i}}\times$ market premium | $\sum_{\text{k}} \beta_{\text{i,k}}\times$ factor k premium |
| Bad times | low market returns | each factor defines its own |

**Applying it to this question**

The memo must say: one factor, defined as the market return over T-bills; the premium set solely by beta; higher beta, higher premium. Check each option for a second factor, a rewarded idiosyncratic component, or a substitute for beta.

**Fragile fact.** The CAPM factor is the market return in excess of T-bills, and the premium depends solely on beta; idiosyncratic risk earns zero, not a small premium.

**Reference**

LO 83.b: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM. GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.3 Factor Theory and Section 1.4 CAPM (“CAPM Lesson 1: Don’t Hold an Individual Asset, Hold the Factor” for the unrewarded idiosyncratic risk). Schweser Reading 83, LO 83.b and Key Concepts LO 83.b. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 b, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: multifactor property.** The sum of factor betas times factor premiums is the multi-beta relation of multifactor models (APT, Equation 1.9), not the CAPM. A would be correct if the stem asked about multifactor models.

b.reason: **Scope error: reward extended to idiosyncratic risk.** GARP: individual stocks “also have idiosyncratic risk, which is not rewarded by a risk premium”. There is no small idiosyncratic premium. B would be correct with “idiosyncratic risk earns no premium because it is diversified away”.

c.reason: **Sibling swap: total volatility for beta.** The first half is right, but premium depends on beta, not volatility. An asset with $\sigma_{\text{i}} = \sigma_{\text{m}}$ has $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i,m}}$, which equals 1 only if it is perfectly correlated with the market. C would be correct with “any asset whose beta equals one”.

d.reason: GARP 1.3: “The CAPM states that there is only one factor driving all asset returns, which is the market return in excess of T-bills. All assets have different exposures to the market factor and the greater the exposure, the higher the risk premium.” Schweser 83.b: “the only relevant factor is the market portfolio, and risk premiums are determined solely by beta.” D matches both.

questions.loText: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-1 b Q4
questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Japanese life insurer is setting the CAPM expected return for a JPY-denominated equity holding to use as a hurdle rate. Her estimates are shown below.

| Input | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Covariance of the stock’s return with the market return | 0.0180 |
| Volatility of the market portfolio | 0.15 |
| Volatility of the stock | 0.35 |
| Expected return on the market portfolio | 0.065 |
| Risk-free rate | 0.005 |

According to the CAPM, the expected return on the stock is closest to:
questions.solution:
Q4: A Japanese life insurer’s PM sets a CAPM hurdle rate from covariance, market volatility and an irrelevant stock volatility.

**Concept and theory**

The CAPM’s second pricing relationship is the security market line (SML), GARP Equation 1.2:

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} = \frac{\text{cov}(\text{r}_{\text{i}}\text{, r}_{\text{m}})}{\text{var}(\text{r}_{\text{m}})} \left(\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} \right) = \beta_{\text{i}}\left(\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} \right)$.

Here E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}})$ is the asset’s expected return, $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ the risk-free rate, E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ the market risk premium and $\beta_{\text{i}}$ the asset’s exposure to the market factor. This is exactly how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM: one factor, one price of risk (the market premium), and each asset’s quantity of risk is its beta. The asset’s own volatility does not appear; it enters only through the covariance, and only to the extent that it co-moves with the market.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first: E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) = \text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{i}} (\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )$, $\beta_{\text{i}} = \text{cov}(\text{r}_{\text{i}}$, $\text{r}_{\text{m}})$/$\sigma^{2}_{\text{m}}$.

var$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) =$ $\text{0.15}^{2} =$ 0.0225

$\beta_{\text{i}} =$ 0.0180/0.0225 = 0.80

E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} =$ 0.065 − 0.005 = 0.060

risk premium = 0.80 × 0.060 = 0.048

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) =$ 0.005 + 0.048 = 0.053 = 5.30%

Meaning: the insurer should require 5.30% a year on the holding; 4.80 percentage points of that is compensation for market-factor exposure. The stock’s 35% volatility is not used (it implies a correlation of 0.018/(0.35 × 0.15) = 0.34, which is already inside the covariance).

**Fragile fact.** Divide the covariance by the market variance (0.0225), not the market volatility (0.15); and beta multiplies the market premium, not the market return.

**Reference**

LO 83.b: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM. GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.4 CAPM, “CAPM Lesson 5: Risk Is Factor Exposure” (Equation 1.2, the SML). Schweser Reading 83, LO 83.b (premiums determined solely by beta) and Lesson 5 under LO 83.c (SML formula). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 b, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **Intermediate result.** 0.80 × 6.0% = 4.80% is the risk premium E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ , not the expected return; the risk-free rate was not added back. A would be correct if the question asked for the risk premium.

b.reason: It applies GARP Equation 1.2 with $\beta_{\text{i}} =$ cov / var and adds back $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ , as the SML requires.

c.reason: **Dropped term.** 0.5% + 0.80 × 6.5% = 5.70% multiplies beta by the market’s total expected return instead of the market premium, so $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ is not subtracted inside the bracket. This method agrees with the SML only when the risk-free rate is zero (with $\text{r}_{\text{f}} =$ 0 both give 0.80 × 6.5% = 5.20%), so C would be right only in a stem with $\text{r}_{\text{f}} =$ 0 and the same market return.

d.reason: **Sibling swap: own volatility for beta.** Uses the irrelevant input: $\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}} =$ 0.35/0.15 = 2.333, then 0.5% + 2.333 × 6.0% = 14.50%. This treats total volatility as the measure of risk and drops the correlation. D would be correct only if the stock were perfectly correlated with the market ($\rho=$ 1), which the given covariance rules out.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-1 b Q5
questions.question:
A risk consultant is advising the investment committee of a GBP 4 billion UK university endowment on how the CAPM links risk premiums to bad times. She drafts the following statements.

I. In the CAPM, bad times are defined as periods of low (or negative) returns on the market portfolio.

II. An asset that tends to pay off when the market has losses has a low beta, and investors accept a low expected return to hold it.

III. High-beta assets must offer high expected returns because, with investors risk averse on average, the gains these assets deliver in good times do not cancel out their losses in bad times.

IV. In the CAPM, bad times are periods of high inflation or low economic growth, whichever the individual investor fears more.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I, II and III only
I and II only
I, III and IV only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Q5: An endowment’s consultant decides which statements correctly link CAPM risk premiums to bad times.

**Concept and theory**

Factor theory says every factor defines a set of bad times, and investors exposed to losses in those bad times are paid premiums in normal times. The CAPM has one factor, the market, so it has one definition of bad times: low (or negative) market returns. The logic, from GARP Lesson 6:

- An asset that loses when the market loses has a high beta. Investors are risk averse on average, so the gains it delivers in good times do not cancel out the pain of its losses in bad times. It is risky and must offer a high expected return to be held in equilibrium.
- An asset that pays off when the market loses has a low beta. It is valuable as insurance, so investors need little compensation: its premium is low.

Multifactor models keep this intuition but define bad times more broadly, for example high inflation or low economic growth.

**Applying it to this question**

I: CAPM definition of bad times, true. II: pays off when the market falls, low beta, low expected return, true. III: risk aversion means good-time gains do not offset bad-time losses, true (GARP’s own reasoning). IV: macro definition of bad times, which belongs to multifactor models, false. Correct set: I, II and III.

**Fragile fact.** In the CAPM, “bad times” means low market returns and nothing else; inflation and growth bad times belong to multifactor models.

**Reference**

LO 83.b: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM. GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.4 CAPM, “CAPM Lesson 6: Assets Paying Off in Bad Times Have Low Risk Premiums”; Section 1.3 Factor Theory (bad times). Schweser Reading 83, LO 83.b. Boundary: the six lessons as lessons belong to LO 83.c; here only the CAPM’s definition of bad times and the compensation logic named in LO 83.b are tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 b, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: GARP Lesson 6: “Bad times are defined in terms of the factor, which is the market portfolio, so bad times correspond to low (or negative) market returns”; “Investors are, on average, risk averse so that the gains during good times do not cancel out the losses during bad times. Thus, high beta assets are risky”; “if the asset pays off when the market has losses, the asset has a low beta ... the expected return on the asset can be low”. Schweser 83.b: premiums “compensate investors for losses during bad times”.

b.reason: **I and II only: drops a true statement.** Rejects III, perhaps reading “gains do not cancel losses” as a contradiction of symmetric mean-variance preferences. It is GARP’s own explanation of why high-beta assets need high returns. B would be correct if III had said investors were risk neutral.

c.reason: **I, III and IV: sibling swap in IV, drops II.** Accepts IV, which attributes a multifactor definition of bad times (inflation, growth) to the CAPM, and rejects II, which is GARP’s statement of Lesson 6. C would be correct for a multifactor model if II were false.

d.reason: **II, III and IV: sibling swap in IV, drops I.** Rejects the CAPM’s own definition of bad times and accepts the macro definition. D reverses the roles of I and IV.

questions.question:
The treasurer of an AUD 90 billion Australian superannuation fund is evaluating a gold-linked asset as a crisis hedge. Assume the CAPM holds and the asset is priced on the security market line. The fund’s data are shown below.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Correlation of the asset with the market | −0.20 |
| Volatility of the asset (%) | 20.00 |
| Volatility of the market portfolio (%) | 16.00 |
| Asset’s historical average return, last 10 years (%) | 6.00 |
| Expected return on the market portfolio (%) | 8.00 |
| Risk-free rate (%) | 3.00 |

Which of the following best describes the asset’s CAPM expected return and its interpretation?

options.text: 4.25%: the asset carries a positive risk premium of 1.25% because its diversification benefit is a source of risk that investors must be paid to bear.
−1.25%: the asset’s expected return is negative, so investors give up 1.25% a year in absolute terms to hold it.
1.75%: the asset’s expected return is below the risk-free rate because it tends to pay off when the market falls, so investors accept a negative risk premium to hold it.
1.75%: the asset’s expected return is below the risk-free rate, which signals under the CAPM that the asset is overvalued and should be avoided by all investors.

questions.solution:
Q6: A superannuation treasurer computes and interprets the CAPM expected return of a negative-beta, gold-linked hedge.

**Concept and theory**

Beta can be negative: if $\rho_{\text{i,m}} <$ 0, then $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i,m}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}} <$ 0 and the SML gives a negative risk premium, so E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) < \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ . GARP’s interpretation: low-beta assets “have tremendous diversification benefits and are very attractive to hold”; if their payoffs are high enough when the market return is low, “investors are willing to pay to hold these assets rather than be paid”. Gold, and sometimes government bonds, are GARP’s examples of low or negative beta assets that pay off when the stock market crashes. A low expected return here is not a sign of mispricing; it is the equilibrium price of insurance against the CAPM’s bad times.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first: $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i,m}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}}$, then E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) = \text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{i}}(\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )$.

$\beta_{\text{i}} = -$0.20 × 20/16 = −0.25

E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} =$ 8.00% − 3.00% = 5.00%

risk premium = −0.25 × 5.00% = −1.25%

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) =$ 3.00% + (−1.25%) = 1.75%

Meaning: investors accept 1.25% a year less than the risk-free rate because the asset tends to rise when the market falls. The 6.00% historical average return is irrelevant to the CAPM expected return.

**Fragile fact.** Negative beta gives a negative risk premium, so the expected return is below $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ ; it is negative in absolute terms only if $|\beta_{\text{i}}|(\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) > \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ .

**Reference**

LO 83.b: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM. GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.4 CAPM, “CAPM Lesson 5: Risk Is Factor Exposure” (low and negative beta assets, gold and government bonds) and “CAPM Lesson 6”. Schweser Reading 83, LO 83.b; Lesson 5 under LO 83.c (safe havens with negative expected returns in 2007 to 2009). Note: GARP and Schweser write “negative expected returns” loosely for what the SML gives as a negative risk premium; this paper keeps the two separate.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 b, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: **Sign error.** Uses $|\beta| =$ 0.25: 3.00% + 0.25 × 5.00% = 4.25%, and then rationalises diversification as a risk to be paid for. This reverses GARP: diversification benefits lower the premium. A would be correct if the correlation were +0.20 (and the explanation were about market exposure).

b.reason: **Intermediate result.** −1.25% is the risk premium E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ , not the expected return; $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ was not added back. B would be correct if the question asked for the risk premium.

c.reason: It gives the right number and GARP’s interpretation: the asset pays off in bad times, so it is valuable and its premium is low, here negative.

d.reason: **Polarity flip on attractiveness.** The number is right, but it reads a $\text{below-r}_{\text{f}}$ expected return as overvaluation. The stem says the asset plots on the SML, so it is fairly priced; its low expected return reflects how valuable it is. D would be correct only if a forecast return lay below the SML-required return (a mispricing question, LO 83.c).

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a CNY 3 trillion Chinese commercial bank is validating the model documentation for the bank’s equity hurdle-rate engine, which is built on the CAPM. The documentation lists the following items under “Assumptions of the CAPM”.

I. Investors have only financial wealth.

II. Investors have mean-variance utility.

III. Large institutional investors set prices, while individual investors are price takers.

IV. Information is costless and available to all investors.

Which of the listed items are genuine assumptions of the CAPM?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Q7: A bank auditor checks which listed items in a model document are genuine CAPM assumptions.

**Concept and theory**

The CAPM is derived from very strong assumptions. GARP Section 1.6 lists seven:

| # | CAPM assumption (GARP 1.6) | What it rules out |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Investors have only financial wealth | labour income, liabilities |
| 2 | Investors have mean-variance utility | asymmetric (downside) preferences |
| 3 | Single-period investment horizon | dynamic rebalancing |
| 4 | Investors have homogeneous expectations | differing beliefs |
| 5 | No taxes or transactions costs | any frictions |
| 6 | Individual investors are price takers | trades that move prices |
| 7 | Information is costless and available to all investors | costly or private information |

The assumptions are not empirical claims; they are the conditions that make every investor hold the same MVE portfolio and make the market the single priced factor.

**Applying it to this question**

I matches assumption 1. II matches assumption 2. IV matches assumption 7. III splits investors into price setters and price takers; the CAPM assumes that individual investors are price takers, with no investor large enough to move prices, so III is not a CAPM assumption. Answer: I, II and IV only.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the CAPM makes every investor a price taker; “large investors set prices” is the real-world departure, not the assumption.

**Reference**

LO 83.b: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM. GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.6 Failures of the CAPM (list of assumptions). Schweser Reading 83, “Shortcomings of the CAPM” under LO 83.c. Conflict: Schweser’s text lists seven assumptions but its Key Concepts list for LO 83.c shows six, omitting “information is free and available to everyone”; GARP lists seven, and GARP is followed. Schweser writes “All investors are price takers” where GARP writes “Individual investors are price takers” (same meaning). Boundary: the list is placed by Schweser under LO 83.c shortcomings; LO 83.b names the assumptions, so identifying them is tested here and their real-world failures are left to LO 83.c.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 b, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: **I and II only: drops a true assumption.** Omits IV, perhaps because Schweser’s Key Concepts list for LO 83.c shows only six shortcomings and leaves out the information assumption. GARP and Schweser’s own text both list it. A would be correct if the stem asked for the first two assumptions on the list.

b.reason: GARP 1.6 items 1, 2 and 7 correspond to I, II and IV word for word; III contradicts item 6.

c.reason: **II, III and IV: role misassignment in III, drops I.** Accepts III, which assigns price-setting power to large institutions. In the real world large investors do move prices (this is a shortcoming, LO 83.c), but the CAPM assumes no one does. C also drops I.

d.reason: **All four: role misassignment in III.** Accepts III along with the three true items. D would be correct if III read “all individual investors are price takers”.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-1 b Q8
questions.question: A supervisor at a Japanese financial regulator is reviewing how a life insurer’s model manual restates the assumptions behind the CAPM used to set JPY equity return assumptions. The manual contains the four restatements below. Which restatement is least accurate?

options.text: Investors care only about the mean and variance of portfolio returns, so they treat a loss and a gain of the same size symmetrically.
Investors hold only financial wealth, so labour income and liabilities play no role in their portfolio choice.
Individual investors are price takers, so no investor’s trades are large enough to move prices.
Taxes and transaction costs are permitted provided they are identical across all securities, because uniform frictions leave relative prices unchanged.

questions.solution:
Q8: A regulator finds the least accurate restatement of the CAPM assumptions in an insurer’s model manual.

**Concept and theory**

Each CAPM assumption has a precise content, and exam traps usually corrupt one word of it.

- Mean-variance utility: investors care only about mean and variance, so risk is treated symmetrically; more realistic utility is asymmetric because investors are more distressed by losses than pleased by gains.
- Only financial wealth: investors’ unique income streams and liabilities are left out (in reality inflation, growth and labour income risk become factors).
- Price takers: individual investors cannot move prices.
- No taxes or transactions costs: markets are frictionless. The assumption is that frictions are absent, not that they are equal. GARP notes that taxes affect expected returns and can be regarded as a systematic factor, and that transaction costs vary across securities.

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and C each restate an assumption with its correct implication. D replaces “no taxes or transactions costs” with “uniform taxes and costs are allowed”, which is a different (weaker) condition that the CAPM does not make.

**Fragile fact.** Condition: the CAPM assumes no taxes or transaction costs, not equal ones.

**Reference**

LO 83.b: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM. GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.6 Failures of the CAPM, items 1, 2, 5 and 6. Schweser Reading 83, “Shortcomings of the CAPM” (LO 83.c) and Module Quiz 83.1 answer 5 (“it assumes there are no taxes or transaction costs”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 b, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: **Accurate; trap: mistaking symmetry for a flaw in the restatement.** Mean-variance utility does imply symmetric treatment of risk; asymmetry is the real-world departure. A would be the inaccurate one if it said mean-variance investors dislike losses more than they like gains (a polarity flip).

b.reason: **Accurate; trap: thinking the CAPM accounts for liabilities.** GARP item 1: investors have only financial wealth, so income streams and liabilities are outside the model. B would be inaccurate if it said the market portfolio hedges investors’ labour income.

c.reason: **Accurate; trap: actor confusion.** GARP item 6: individual investors are price takers. C would be inaccurate if it said only small investors are price takers while large ones set prices (a role misassignment).

d.reason: GARP 1.6, item 5: “No taxes or transactions costs.” Schweser: “Markets are frictionless (no taxes or transaction costs).” D changes the condition from absence to uniformity, which is a scope or condition error.

questions.question: A risk manager at a EUR 150 billion French asset manager is training new analysts. She asks which CAPM assumption bridges the gap between “every investor solves a mean-variance problem” and “in equilibrium the market portfolio is the only factor”. Which of the following statements best describes the role of that assumption?

options.text: Because all investors share the same means, volatilities and correlations, they all hold the same MVE portfolio in different quantities, so in equilibrium the MVE portfolio becomes the market portfolio.
Because all investors share the same risk aversion, they all hold the same mix of the riskfree asset and the MVE portfolio, so in equilibrium the MVE portfolio becomes the market portfolio.
Because all investors share the same means, volatilities and correlations, they all hold the market portfolio in the same quantity, so in equilibrium no investor holds the risk-free asset.

Because all investors share the same means, volatilities and correlations, they hold the same MVE portfolio, and it is arbitrage by hedge funds, not equilibrium, that turns it into the market portfolio.

questions.solution:
Q9: A French asset manager’s risk manager explains how homogeneous expectations turn the MVE portfolio into the market.

**Concept and theory**

Mean-variance investing on its own gives each investor a capital allocation line (CAL): a mix of the risk-free asset and the mean-variance efficient (MVE), maximum Sharpe ratio, tangency portfolio. The amount in each depends on the investor’s risk aversion. Nothing yet says the MVE portfolio is the market. The bridge has two steps.

1. **Homogeneous expectations.** Assume the set of means, volatilities and correlations is the same for all investors. Then all investors compute the same frontier and hold the same MVE portfolio, “just in different quantities depending on their own risk aversion”.
2. **Equilibrium.** Demand must equal supply. If everyone’s risky portfolio gave zero weight to some stock, its price would fall (its expected payoff stays constant, so its expected return rises) until investors want to hold exactly the shares outstanding. Since everyone holds the same MVE portfolio, it must be the market portfolio, with cap weights.

GARP: this assumption “ensures that all investors hold the same MVE portfolio in the CAPM world and that, in equilibrium, the MVE portfolio becomes the market portfolio”.

**Applying it to this question**

The correct statement must name (1) common means, volatilities and correlations, (2) the same MVE portfolio but different quantities, and (3) equilibrium as the mechanism. Each distractor breaks one of these.

**Fragile fact.** Homogeneous expectations equalise the risky portfolio across investors, not their quantities; equilibrium, not arbitrage, makes it the market.

**Reference**

LO 83.b: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM. GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.4 CAPM, “Equilibrium” (the strong assumptions) and Section 1.6 Failures of the CAPM, item 4. Schweser Reading 83, “Shortcomings of the CAPM” item 4 and “Equilibrium” under LO 83.c. Note: Schweser does not spell out the role of homogeneous expectations in making the MVE portfolio the market; GARP does, and GARP is used. Boundary: the equilibrium price-adjustment mechanism itself belongs to LO 83.c and is used here only as the link that the assumption feeds.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 b, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: It reproduces GARP’s chain in the Equilibrium section and Section 1.6 item 4 exactly.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: risk aversion for expectations.** Common risk aversion is not the CAPM assumption; investors differ in risk aversion, which is why they sit at different points on the CAL (Lesson 2). B would be correct only in a model that assumed identical investors, which is not how GARP states the CAPM.

c.reason: **Absolute or scope error: same quantity.** Keeps the right assumption but overextends it: homogeneous expectations make the risky portfolio the same, not the quantity. Investors still hold different amounts of the risk-free asset; only the average investor is 100% in the market. C would be correct if all investors also had the market’s average risk aversion.

d.reason: **Role misassignment: arbitrage instead of equilibrium.** The step from the MVE portfolio to the market portfolio is the supply-equals-demand equilibrium argument, not arbitrage; GARP stresses that equilibrium premiums “will not disappear because clever hedge funds go and trade them”. D would describe an APT-style argument (LO 83.d), not the CAPM.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-1 b Q10
questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a USD 12 billion US charitable foundation is reviewing a consultant’s report that summarises the empirical standing of the CAPM. The member wants to check which summary is consistent with Ang’s assessment. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Empirical studies broadly support the CAPM’s prediction that beta alone determines risk premiums, although its prediction that only one factor matters has been rejected.
Since both of its central predictions have been rejected, the CAPM has been abandoned by practitioners and its intuition about how risk is rewarded has been discarded.
The CAPM’s implication that every investor holds the market portfolio is strongly supported by data on investors’ actual holdings, even though beta pricing has failed.
Both central predictions have been rejected, yet the intuition that risk premiums compensate for losses in bad times still holds and the CAPM remains the workhorse model of finance.

questions.solution:
Q10: A foundation board member checks a consultant’s summary of the CAPM’s empirical standing.

**Concept and theory**

Discussing the CAPM means knowing both what it predicts and how it has fared. Ang is blunt: the CAPM “is well known to be a spectacular failure”. It makes two central predictions:

1. asset risk premiums depend only on the asset’s beta, and
2. only one factor matters, the market portfolio.

“Both of these predictions have been demolished in thousands of empirical studies.” The implication that every investor holds the market portfolio is “outright rejected in data”. Yet the failure is “glorious”: the basic intuition survives, that the factors underlying assets determine risk premiums, that premiums compensate investors for losses in bad times, and that risk is a property of how assets move together, not of an asset in isolation. The CAPM “remains the workhorse model of finance” (about 75% of finance professors advocate it and 75% of CFOs use it in capital budgeting); it works approximately for most applications but fails badly in some.

**Applying it to this question**

The summary must say: both predictions rejected; intuition intact; still widely used. Any option that keeps one prediction alive, says the model was abandoned, or says the holdings implication is supported is wrong.

**Fragile fact.** Both predictions failed (beta-only premiums and one factor); what survives is the intuition, and the model is still the workhorse.

**Reference**

LO 83.b: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM. GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.4 CAPM (opening discussion and “What does the CAPM get right?”); Section 1.4, “CAPM Lesson 1” for the rejected holdings implication. Schweser Reading 83, Exam Focus (“recognizing the model’s limitations in a real-world setting”). Note: the empirical verdict is in GARP only; Schweser’s LO 83.b summary does not report it.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 b, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error: partial rejection.** Keeps beta pricing alive. GARP says both predictions, beta-only premiums and the single factor, have been demolished. A would be correct if it said both were rejected.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** Turns empirical rejection into abandonment. GARP: the CAPM remains the workhorse model, and its intuition about how risk is rewarded is what keeps it in use. B would be correct only for the predictions, not for the intuition or for practice.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says the implication that every investor holds the market portfolio is “outright rejected in data”. C reverses that verdict.

d.reason: It matches GARP 1.4: both predictions demolished, the basic intuition “still holds true”, and “it remains the workhorse model of finance”.

questions.loText: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-1 b Q11
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Singapore private bank compares two equities for a client who wants “more risk for more return”. The analyst assumes the CAPM holds, with a market risk premium of 6% and a market volatility of 15%.

| Equity | Volatility (%) | Correlation with market |
|---|---|---|
| X | 12 | 0.90 |
| Y | 36 | 0.30 |

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Y should earn the higher risk premium because its total volatility is three times that of X, so it carries three times the risk.
X and Y have the same beta of 0.72 and therefore the same CAPM risk premium of 4.32%; Y’s extra volatility is diversifiable and is not rewarded.
X should earn the higher risk premium because its higher correlation with the market means it offers less diversification than Y.
Y has a beta of 2.40 and X a beta of 0.80, so Y’s CAPM risk premium is three times X’s, consistent with the client’s preference.

questions.solution:
Q11: A private-bank analyst compares two equities with different volatilities and correlations but the same beta.

**Concept and theory**

GARP calls beta “the CAPM’s measure of risk” and “a measure of the lack of diversification potential”. Writing $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i,m}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}}$ shows it is the product of two forces: how much the asset moves ($\sigma_{\text{i}}$ relative to $\sigma_{\text{m}}$) and how much of that movement is in step with the market ($\rho_{\text{i,m}}$). The lower the correlation, the greater the diversification benefit, because the asset is more likely to do well when the portfolio does badly. Volatility that is not in step with the market is idiosyncratic and is diversified away, so the CAPM does not reward it. Two assets with very different volatilities can therefore have exactly the same beta and the same premium.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i,m}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}}$, premium $= \beta_{\text{i}} \times$ 6%.

$\beta_{\text{X}} =$ 0.90 × 12/15 = 0.72

$\beta_{\text{Y}} =$ 0.30 × 36/15 = 0.72

$\text{premium}_{\text{X}} = \text{premium}_{\text{Y}} =$ 0.72 × 6% = 4.32%

Meaning: Y’s extra volatility buys the client no extra expected return under the CAPM; it is idiosyncratic risk that carries no premium. “More risk” in the CAPM sense means more beta, not more volatility.

**Fragile fact.** Beta needs both correlation and relative volatility; high beta means low diversification benefit, and only beta is rewarded.

**Reference**

LO 83.b: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM. GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.4 CAPM, “CAPM Lesson 5: Risk Is Factor Exposure” (beta as lack of diversification potential, $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i,m}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}}$) and “CAPM Lesson 1” (idiosyncratic risk unrewarded). Schweser Reading 83, LO 83.b. Conflict: Schweser’s Lesson 5 text says beta “looks at idiosyncratic risk and the lack of diversification”; GARP says beta measures the lack of diversification potential and that idiosyncratic risk is unrewarded. GARP is followed; the Schweser phrasing looks like a condensation slip rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 b, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: total volatility for beta.** Treats $\sigma_{\text{Y}} =$ 3$\sigma_{\text{X}}$ as three times the risk, the pre-CAPM view. A would be correct if both equities had the same correlation with the market (then beta would scale with volatility).

b.reason: Equal betas imply equal premiums because risk premiums are “determined solely by beta” (Schweser 83.b) and idiosyncratic risk “is not rewarded by a risk premium” (GARP Lesson 1).

c.reason: **Dropped term: correlation alone.** Uses $\rho$ only and ignores the volatility ratio. X does offer less diversification per unit of volatility, but Y’s larger volatility exactly offsets its lower correlation. C would be correct if both had the same volatility.

d.reason: **Dropped term: volatility ratio without correlation.** Computes $\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}}$: 36/15 = 2.40 and 12/15 = 0.80, dropping $\rho_{\text{i,m}}$. These would be the betas only if both equities were perfectly correlated with the market.
