questions.question:
A risk analyst at an Italian insurer is building a CAPM hurdle rate for a new EUR equity mandate. The risk-free rate and market premium are not published internally, but two existing holdings are known to plot exactly on the security market line.

| Holding | Beta | Expected return (%) | Volatility (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Holding 1 | 0.6 | 6.2 | 14 |
| Holding 2 | 1.4 | 10.2 | 26 |
| New mandate | 1.1 | ? | 30 |

According to the CAPM, the expected return on the new mandate is closest to:
questions.solution:
Q12: An Italian insurer’s analyst backs out $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ and the market premium from two SML holdings, then prices a beta 1.1 mandate.

**Concept and theory**

The SML, E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) = \text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{i}}(\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )$, is a straight line in (beta, expected return) space. Its intercept is the risk-free rate (the return on a zero-beta asset) and its slope is the market risk premium, the single price of factor risk in the CAPM. Any two correctly priced assets pin the line down completely, and every other asset’s expected return then depends only on its beta. Volatility is not an input.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first: slope $= \frac{\text{E}(\text{r}_{2}) - \text{E}(\text{r}_{1})}{\beta_{2} - \beta_{1}}$ , intercept $\text{r}_{\text{f}} = \text{E}(\text{r}_{1}) - \beta_{1}\times$ slope.

E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} = \frac{\text{10.2\%} - \text{6.2\%}}{1.4 - 0.6} = \frac{\text{4.0\%}}{0.8} =$ 5.0%

$\text{r}_{\text{f}} =$ 6.2% − 0.6 × 5.0% = 3.2%

check: 3.2% + 1.4 × 5.0% = 10.2%

$\text{premium}_{\text{new}} =$ 1.1 × 5.0% = 5.5%

E$(\text{r}_{\text{new}}) =$ 3.2% + 5.5% = 8.70%

Meaning: the mandate should be held to an 8.70% hurdle, of which 5.5 percentage points pay for its market-factor exposure. Its 30% volatility is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** The SML intercept is $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ , not zero; slope equals the market premium, so expected returns are not proportional to beta.

**Reference**

LO 83.b: Discuss the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) including its assumptions and explain how factor risk is addressed in the CAPM. GARP Chapter 1, Section 1.4 CAPM, “CAPM Lesson 5: Risk Is Factor Exposure” (Equation 1.2, the SML). Schweser Reading 83, LO 83.b and Lesson 5 under LO 83.c. No conflict. Boundary: comparing a forecast return with the SML to call an asset over- or undervalued is LO 83.c and is not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 b, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: **Intermediate result.** 1.1 × 5.0% = 5.50% is the mandate’s risk premium; $\text{r}_{\text{f}} =$ 3.2% was not added. A would be correct if the question asked for the risk premium.

b.reason: **Dropped term: beta applied to the market return.** Computes E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) =$ 3.2% + 5.0% = 8.2%, then 1.1 × 8.2% = 9.02%, applying beta to the total market return and omitting the (1 $- \beta)\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ term. B would be correct only if $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ were zero.

c.reason: It uses the SML (GARP Equation 1.2) with the intercept and slope implied by the two correctly priced holdings.

d.reason: **Dropped term: zero intercept.** Scales holding 2 by the beta ratio: 10.2% × 1.1/1.4 = 8.01%, which assumes the SML passes through the origin. D would be correct only if the risk-free rate were zero.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a public pension fund is presenting the CAPM’s case for diversification to newly hired analysts. Her draft slide contains four statements about why investors should hold the market factor rather than individual assets.

Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Investors keep diversifying until they hold the global minimum-variance portfolio, because under the CAPM that portfolio offers the best risk-return trade-off available.
Diversifying across assets that are not perfectly correlated raises the Sharpe ratio, and market risk affects every investor except one who is infinitely risk averse and holds only risk-free assets.
Because diversification guarantees that losses on one asset are fully offset by gains on others, an investor who holds the market portfolio bears no risk that needs to be rewarded.
Individual stocks earn a risk premium for their idiosyncratic risk as well as for their market exposure, so holding the market factor gives up part of the premium available.

questions.solution:
Pension fund analyst’s slide on why investors hold the market factor rather than individual assets.

**Concept and theory**

CAPM Lesson 1 is “don’t hold an individual asset, hold the factor.” The CAPM says there is exactly one factor, the market portfolio, in which every stock is held in proportion to its market capitalization (an index fund). Each individual stock has two pieces of risk:

| Piece of risk | CAPM treatment |
|---|---|
| Market (systematic) exposure | Pervasive, affects all assets; carries the risk premium (GARP’s “nutrient”) |
| Idiosyncratic (firm-specific) risk | Can be diversified away; earns no risk premium (“no nutritional value”) |

Why diversify? The CAPM rests on mean-variance utility, and the key idea of mean-variance investing is diversification: absent perfect correlation, when one asset does badly some other assets do well, so gains partly offset losses. Holding many imperfectly correlated assets improves the reward-to-risk trade-off, that is, raises the Sharpe ratio. Investors keep diversifying until they hold the most diversified portfolio possible, the market portfolio, which in Figure 1.1 is the mean-variance efficient (MVE) portfolio, the maximum Sharpe ratio tangency portfolio. Market risk then affects all investors, with one exception: an investor who is infinitely risk averse and holds only risk-free assets.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are (i) diversification across imperfectly correlated assets raises Sharpe ratios and (ii) the single exception to bearing market risk is the infinitely risk-averse investor in risk-free assets. Option B states both precisely. Each other option distorts one element: the destination portfolio (A), the strength of the offset (C), or which risk is rewarded (D).

**Fragile fact.** The market is the maximum Sharpe ratio portfolio, not the minimum-variance portfolio; and the only investor not exposed to market risk is the infinitely risk-averse one.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.4 CAPM, “CAPM Lesson 1: Don’t Hold an Individual Asset, Hold the Factor” and Figure 1.1. Schweser R83, “Implications of Using the CAPM,” Lesson 1 and “Mean-variance efficient portfolio.” No conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q1 of 15.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps the MVE (tangency, maximum Sharpe ratio) portfolio for its sibling on the frontier, the global minimum-variance portfolio. Investors diversify until they hold the market portfolio, which has the highest Sharpe ratio; it is the lowest-volatility portfolio only among portfolios that share the market’s mean. A would be correct if the stem asked which frontier portfolio an investor who cared only about variance, with no risk-free asset available, would choose.

b.reason: GARP, Lesson 1: “This balance across many assets that are not perfectly correlated improves Sharpe ratios” and “Market risk also affects all investors, except those who are infinitely risk averse and hold only risk-free assets.” B restates both. Schweser’s module quiz 83.1 Q2 confirms the infinitely risk-averse investor as the only exception to holding the MVE portfolio.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** GARP says gains can partly offset losses. Diversification removes idiosyncratic risk only; the market (systematic) risk that remains cannot be diversified away and is exactly the risk that earns the premium. C would be right only for a hypothetical portfolio of perfectly negatively correlated assets, which is not the market.

d.reason: **Polarity flip on what is rewarded.** Idiosyncratic risk “is not rewarded by a risk premium.” Holding the factor removes unrewarded risk and keeps the whole premium, which is why it dominates. D would be true only in a world where firm-specific risk could not be diversified, which contradicts the CAPM.

questions.question:
A risk consultant at a sovereign wealth fund is validating an equilibrium model built on the CAPM assumptions. In the first run of the model, every investor’s optimal risky portfolio assigns a zero weight to Stock AA, even though AA has shares outstanding.

Which of the following best describes how the CAPM says this situation is resolved?

options.text: AA’s expected payoff rises until investors want to hold it, so its price stays where it is while its expected return increases.
AA’s price rises, because zero demand at the current price signals that AA is underpriced relative to its expected payoff.
AA drops out of the market portfolio, so the equilibrium market factor is the capitalization-weighted portfolio of the remaining stocks.
AA’s price falls while its expected payoff stays constant, raising its expected return until investors want to hold exactly the shares outstanding.

questions.solution:
Consultant validating a CAPM equilibrium model in which no investor wants to hold Stock AA.

**Concept and theory**

Equilibrium means investor demand for every asset exactly equals its supply. Under the CAPM’s strong assumptions (everyone shares the same means, volatilities and correlations) every investor holds the same MVE portfolio, in different amounts. Because everyone holds it and every share outstanding must be held by someone, the MVE portfolio must contain every asset in proportion to its market capitalization: the MVE portfolio becomes the market portfolio, and the market is the factor.

The adjustment mechanism is a price mechanism. Under CAPM assumptions an asset’s expected payoff is fixed. Expected return links payoff and price:

E$(\text{r}_{\text{AA}}) = \frac{\text{E}(\text{payoff}_{\text{AA}})}{\text{P}_{\text{AA}}} -$ 1.

If nobody wants AA, AA must be overpriced: its expected return is too low. Its price falls; with the payoff fixed, its expected return rises. The price keeps falling until investors want to hold exactly the shares outstanding. At that point supply equals demand and the expected return is the equilibrium one.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem describes the exact GARP thought experiment: zero weight in everyone’s optimal risky portfolio, shares outstanding. Three facts decide it: the payoff is fixed, the price falls, and the process ends when demand equals the shares outstanding.

**Fragile fact.** The payoff is the constant and the price is the variable: price down, expected return up. Zero demand means overpriced, not underpriced.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.4 CAPM, “Equilibrium.” Schweser R83, “Equilibrium” paragraph under Lesson 1. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q2 of 15.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: payoff for price.** It moves the wrong variable. Under the CAPM the expected payoff is held constant and the price adjusts. A would be correct only in a model where firms change cash flows in response to investor demand, which is outside the CAPM.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Zero demand means AA is overpriced, so its price falls. B reverses the direction. It would be correct if every investor wanted more AA than the shares outstanding (excess demand), when the price would rise and the expected return fall.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Equilibrium requires that someone holds AA so that supply equals demand; an asset with shares outstanding cannot be dropped. The market consists of each asset at its capitalization weight. C would be correct only if AA had zero shares outstanding.

d.reason: GARP, Equilibrium: “If no one wants to hold AA, then AA must be overpriced and the expected return of AA is too low. The price of AA falls. The expected payoff of AA stays constant under CAPM assumptions, so that as the price of AA falls, the expected return of AA increases. AA’s price falls until investors want to hold exactly the number of AA shares outstanding.” D reproduces this chain.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Japanese life insurer is checking whether Stock AA is priced consistently with CAPM equilibrium over a one-year horizon. Under the CAPM assumptions the expected payoff of AA is fixed, so any adjustment must come through its price. The analyst has gathered the following data.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Current price of AA | JPY 1,100 |
| Expected payoff of AA in one year (price plus dividend) | JPY 1,166 |
| Beta of AA | 1.5 |
| Total volatility of AA | 35% |
| Risk-free rate | 1.0% |
| Expected return on the market portfolio | 7.0% |

Which of the following best describes AA and the price at which it would be held in equilibrium?

options.text: AA is overpriced; its equilibrium price is about JPY 1,060.
AA is overpriced; its equilibrium price is about JPY 1,046.
AA is overpriced; its equilibrium price is about JPY 1,070.
AA is underpriced; its equilibrium price is about JPY 1,210.

questions.solution:
Japanese insurer: is Stock AA consistent with CAPM equilibrium, and at what price would it be held?

**Concept and theory**

In CAPM equilibrium two relations hold at once. First, the security market line (SML) gives the expected return that investors require for the asset’s factor exposure:

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) = \text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{i}} [\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ]$,

where $\beta_{\text{i}}$ is the asset’s exposure to the market factor and E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ is the market risk premium. Second, with the expected payoff fixed, the price is whatever makes the asset’s expected return equal that required return:

$\text{P}^{*}_{\text{i}} = \frac{\text{E}(\text{payoff}_{\text{i}})}{1 + \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{i}})}$ .

This is the traditional discount rate form of the CAPM (GARP Equation 1.5). If the current price implies an expected return below the SML return, the asset is overpriced and, as in the GARP AA example, its price falls until it is willingly held.

**Applying it to this question**

Step by step:

Market risk premium = 7.0% − 1.0% = 6.0%

Required return E$(\text{r}_{\text{AA}}) =$ 1.0% + 1.5 × 6.0% = 10.0%

Expected return at current price = 1,166/1,100 − 1 = 6.0%

Equilibrium price $\text{P}^{*} =$ 1,166/1.10 = JPY 1,060

The current price offers 6.0%, below the 10.0% the SML requires, so AA is overpriced. Its price must fall by JPY 40 (with the payoff fixed) to JPY 1,060, at which point its expected return is 10.0% and investors hold exactly the shares outstanding. The total volatility of 35% is irrelevant: the CAPM prices only beta.

**Fragile fact.** An expected return below the SML means overpriced; with a fixed payoff, the price must fall to raise the expected return.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.4 CAPM, “Equilibrium” and “CAPM Lesson 5: Risk Is Factor Exposure” (Equation 1.2); Equation 1.5 (Section 1.5, “Pricing Kernels versus Discount Rate Models”) for the price form. Schweser R83, “Equilibrium” and Lesson 5. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q3 of 15.

a.reason: A combines the correct direction (overpriced, so the price falls) with the correct equilibrium price from the SML return. This is GARP’s Equilibrium logic (“the expected return is too low. The price of AA falls”) with the Lesson 5 SML providing the equilibrium expected return.

b.reason: **Wrong input twin: market return used as the premium.** E$(\text{r}) =$ 1.0% + 1.5 × 7.0% = 11.5% and 1,166/1.115 = JPY 1,046. The SML multiplies beta by the excess market return. B would be correct if 7.0% were the market risk premium rather than the market return.

c.reason: **Dropped term: risk-free rate omitted.** E$(\text{r}) =$ 1.5 × 6.0% = 9.0% and 1,166/1.09 = JPY 1,070. The SML gives the risk premium; the required return adds $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ back. C would be correct if the question asked for the price at a 9.0% discount rate, for example with $\text{r}_{\text{f}} =$ 0.

d.reason: **Direction error: compounding instead of discounting.** 1,100 × 1.10 = JPY 1,210 grows today’s price at the required return and then reads the higher number as “underpriced.” The equilibrium price discounts the fixed payoff. D’s direction would be right only if the expected return at the current price exceeded 10.0%, for example a payoff above JPY 1,210.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Canadian wealth manager advises three clients who all accept the CAPM assumptions, including identical expectations of means, volatilities and correlations. Their current allocations are shown below (Client R borrows CAD at the risk-free rate).

| Client | Market portfolio (%) | Risk-free asset (%) |
|---|---|---|
| P | 40 | 60 |
| Q | 100 | 0 |
| R | 130 | −30 |

Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Client P should replace the market portfolio with a low-beta risky portfolio, because a more risk-averse investor needs a different risky portfolio.
Client Q’s risk aversion equals the simple, equal-weighted average of the risk aversions of all investors in the economy.
All three hold the same risky portfolio in different quantities; Client Q sits at the tangency point and has the risk aversion of the market.
Client R’s risk aversion sets the market risk premium, because leveraged investors are the marginal buyers of the market portfolio.

questions.solution:
Canadian wealth manager: three CAPM clients at 40%, 100% and 130% in the market portfolio.

**Concept and theory**

With identical expectations, every investor solves the same mean-variance problem and finds the same MVE portfolio. Risk aversion then decides only how much of it to hold against the risk-free asset. In Figure 1.1 each investor sits at a different point on the capital allocation line (CAL), which in equilibrium is the capital market line (CML).

| CAPM lesson | What it says about holdings |
|---|---|
| Lesson 2 | Each investor has his own optimal exposure to factor risk: same MVE portfolio, different proportions, different points on the CAL |
| Lesson 3 | The average investor holds the market: 100% in the MVE portfolio, the tangency point; this investor’s risk aversion is the market’s risk aversion |
| Footnote 2 | The market is the wealth-weighted average across all investors |

More risk-averse investors hold less of the market and more of the risk-free asset; less risk-averse investors borrow to hold more than 100%.

**Applying it to this question**

Client P (40%) is more risk averse than average, Client R (130%) less. All three hold the identical risky portfolio. Client Q, with exactly 100% in the MVE portfolio, is at the tangency point and so has the market’s risk aversion. The deciding facts: same risky portfolio, and the 100% investor’s risk aversion is that of the market.

**Fragile fact.** The actor with “the risk aversion of the market” is the investor holding exactly 100% in the market portfolio, and the averaging is by wealth.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.4 CAPM, “CAPM Lesson 2: Each Investor Has His Own Optimal Exposure of Factor Risk,” “CAPM Lesson 3: The Average Investor Holds the Market” and footnote 2. Schweser R83, Lessons 2 and 3. Schweser does not mention wealth weighting; GARP does (detail only, not a conflict).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q4 of 15.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: different risky portfolio instead of different quantity.** Under homogeneous expectations risk aversion changes the mix of risk-free asset and MVE portfolio, not the composition of the risky portfolio. A would be correct for an investor with heterogeneous beliefs or a nonfinancial hedging need (relaxed CAPM assumptions), not inside the CAPM.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: equal weighting for wealth weighting.** GARP footnote 2: “the market is the wealth-weighted average across all investors,” and $\bar{\gamma}$ weights each investor’s risk aversion in proportion to wealth. B would be correct only if every investor had the same wealth.

c.reason: GARP, Lesson 2: “all investors will hold the market portfolio, just in different proportions”; Lesson 3: “This tangency point represents the average investor. The risk aversion corresponding to this 100% portfolio position is the risk aversion of the market.” C states both.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** The investor whose risk aversion sets the market premium is the average (100%) investor, Client Q, not the leveraged one. Client R simply bears more market risk than average. D would be correct only if R’s position happened to be the wealth-weighted average, which a 130% position is not.

questions.question:
An economist at a central bank is estimating the equilibrium market risk premium for a stylized CAPM economy that contains three groups of investors. Market volatility is 16% and the risk-free rate is 3.5%.

| Investor group | Wealth (GBP bn) | Risk aversion $\gamma$ |
|---|---|---|
| Pension funds | 600 | 4.0 |
| Households | 300 | 2.0 |
| Hedge funds | 100 | 1.0 |

Under the CAPM, the market risk premium is closest to:
questions.solution:
Central bank economist: equilibrium market risk premium for an economy of three investor groups.

**Concept and theory**

CAPM Lesson 4 gives the market risk premium an economic story. The CML pins down the premium in terms of investor preferences and market risk (GARP Equation 1.1):

E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} = \bar{\gamma}$ $\sigma^{2}_{\text{m}}$,

where $\bar{\gamma}$ is the risk aversion of the average investor and $\sigma^{2}_{\text{m}}$ is the variance of the market portfolio. The average is taken weighting each investor’s risk aversion in proportion to that investor’s wealth:

$\bar{\gamma}$ $= \sum_{\text{k}} \text{w}_{\text{k}} \gamma_{\text{k}}$, $\text{w}_{\text{k}} = \frac{\text{Wealth}_{\text{k}}}{\sum_{\text{j}} \text{Wealth}_{\text{j}}}$ .

Note on the source: the equation image is lost in the GARP text extraction. The surrounding GARP text says the premium “is proportional to market variance” and the definition of $\bar{\gamma}$ is given; Schweser writes E$(\text{R}_{\text{M}}) - \text{R}_{\text{F}} = \bar{\gamma}$ $\sigma^{2}_{\text{M}}$. The formula is reconstructed on that basis. There is no factor of one-half.

**Applying it to this question**

Step by step:

Total wealth = 600 + 300 + 100 = GBP 1,000 bn

Wealth weights = 0.60, 0.30, 0.10

$\bar{\gamma}$ = 0.60(4.0) + 0.30(2.0) + 0.10(1.0) = 2.4 + 0.6 + 0.1 = 3.10

$\sigma^{2}_{\text{m}} =$ $\text{0.16}^{2} =$ 0.0256

E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} =$ 3.10 × 0.0256 = 0.07936 ≈ 7.94%

The risk-free rate of 3.5% is not needed for the premium; it would only be added to obtain the expected market return. A 7.94% premium means the wealth-weighted average investor needs about 7.9 percentage points above $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ to hold the market portfolio willingly.

**Fragile fact.** Variance, not volatility; wealth-weighted, not equal-weighted; and no one-half.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.4 CAPM, “CAPM Lesson 4: The Factor Risk Premium Has an Economic Story” (Equation 1.1) and “CAPM Lesson 3” footnote 2. Schweser R83, Lesson 4. GARP’s extracted text defines $\sigma_{\text{m}}$ as the market volatility next to an equation image that is missing; the text states proportionality to variance, matching Schweser’s $\sigma^{2}_{\text{M}}$.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q5 of 15.

a.reason: **Wrong averaging: equal weights.** Simple average $\gamma= ($4 + 2 + 1)/3 = 2.333, and 2.333 × 0.0256 = 5.97%. It ignores that the large, more risk-averse pension funds dominate wealth. A would be correct if all three groups had equal wealth.

b.reason: **Intermediate twin: expected market return, not the premium.** 3.5% + 7.94% = 11.44% is E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}})$, which adds the irrelevant input. B would be correct if the question asked for the expected return on the market portfolio.

c.reason: **Wrong formula twin: mean-variance utility one-half.** 0.5 × 3.10 × 0.0256 = 3.97% imports the $\frac{1}{2}$ from a mean-variance utility function. The CAPM premium relation has no one-half. C would be correct only if the stem defined the premium as $\frac{1}{2} \bar{\gamma}$ $\sigma^{2}_{\text{m}}$.

d.reason: D uses the wealth-weighted $\bar{\gamma}$ and market variance, as GARP Lesson 4 specifies (“$\bar{\gamma}$ is the average risk aversion across all investors, where the average is taken weighting each individual’s degree of risk aversion in proportion to the wealth of that agent”).

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at an Australian superannuation fund is stress testing the CAPM market risk premium for a volatility shock. Expected payoffs on equities are assumed unchanged by the shock.

| Input | Before shock | After shock |
|---|---|---|
| Average investor’s risk aversion $\bar{\gamma}$ | 2.5 | 2.5 |
| Market volatility (%) | 14.0 | 22.0 |
| Risk-free rate, AUD (%) | 4.0 | 4.0 |

Which of the following best describes the CAPM’s prediction after the shock?

options.text: The market risk premium rises to 7.70% and equity prices fall contemporaneously.
The market risk premium rises to 12.10% and equity prices fall contemporaneously.
The market risk premium rises to 12.10% and equity prices rise contemporaneously.
The market risk premium stays at 4.90% and equity prices are unchanged.

questions.solution:
Australian super fund stress test: market volatility rises from 14% to 22% with risk aversion fixed at 2.5.

**Concept and theory**

Lesson 4: E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} = \bar{\gamma}$ $\sigma^{2}_{\text{m}}$. Under the CAPM investors have mean-variance preferences: they dislike variance and like expected return. So the premium is proportional to market variance, and it rises with either higher variance or higher average risk aversion. Because expected payoffs are fixed, a higher required return can only be delivered by a lower price today. GARP: “as the market becomes more volatile, the expected return of the market increases and equity prices contemporaneously fall, all else equal,” as in 2008 and 2009, when volatility soared, prices nosedived, and realized returns in 2009 and 2010 were high.

**Applying it to this question**

Step by step:

Before: E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} =$ 2.5 × $\text{0.14}^{2} =$ 2.5 × 0.0196 = 4.90%

After: E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} =$ 2.5 × $\text{0.22}^{2} =$ 2.5 × 0.0484 = 12.10%

Change = +7.20 percentage points

Volatility rises by a factor of 22/14 = 1.571, so variance rises by $\text{1.571}^{2} =$ 2.469 and so does the premium. The risk-free rate (4.0%) is irrelevant to the premium. With payoffs unchanged, the higher required return is achieved by an immediate fall in equity prices.

**Fragile fact.** Volatility up means expected returns up and prices down at the same time; the premium scales with the square of volatility.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.4 CAPM, “CAPM Lesson 4: The Factor Risk Premium Has an Economic Story” (Equation 1.1). Schweser R83, Lesson 4 (“During volatile market times . . . equity prices typically fall and expected returns increase”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q6 of 15.

a.reason: **Unit slip: premium scaled with volatility, not variance.** 4.90% × (22/14) = 7.70% treats the premium as proportional to $\sigma_{\text{m}}$. A would be correct only if the premium were $\bar{\gamma}$ $\sigma_{\text{m}}\times$constant, which is not the CAPM relation.

b.reason: B pairs the variance-based premium of 12.10% with the GARP direction “equity prices contemporaneously fall.”

c.reason: **Polarity flip on prices.** The premium is right but prices move the wrong way. Higher expected returns with fixed payoffs require lower prices. C would describe a fall in volatility (prices rise as required returns fall), not a rise.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Singapore bank is reviewing a training module that explains how the CAPM determines the size of the market risk premium.

Which of the following statements in the module is NOT correct?

options.text: The market portfolio has the lowest volatility of all portfolios sharing its mean and removes all idiosyncratic risk, so the risk that remains must be rewarded.
The risk aversion in the premium is a wealth-weighted average across investors, so the premium reflects the preferences of everyone in the economy.
Because the market premium is a pricing anomaly, it will be competed away once enough hedge funds trade the market factor aggressively.
If the average investor becomes more averse to variance, the market risk premium rises even if market volatility is unchanged.

questions.solution:
Singapore bank auditor: which statement in a training module on the CAPM market risk premium is false?

**Concept and theory**

Lesson 4 explains why the market earns a premium and why it persists:

- The market portfolio has the lowest volatility of all portfolios with the market’s mean (equivalently, the highest Sharpe ratio). It removes all idiosyncratic risk, so the risk that remains is systematic and has to be rewarded.
- The premium depends on the preferences of everyone: $\bar{\gamma}$ is a wealth-weighted average, so the market premium “reflects the full setup of all people in the economy.”
- As the average investor becomes more averse to variance ($\bar{\gamma}$ rises), the premium rises.
- The premium is an equilibrium reward for bearing systematic risk. It will not disappear because clever hedge funds trade it; it disappears only if the economy totally changes. Investors cannot arbitrage away the market factor.

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and D each restate a GARP sentence. C calls the premium an anomaly that trading eliminates, the opposite of GARP’s equilibrium argument. The question asks for the statement that is NOT correct, so C is the answer.

**Fragile fact.** A factor premium is an equilibrium reward for systematic risk, not an arbitrage opportunity; trading does not remove it.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.4 CAPM, “Equilibrium” and “CAPM Lesson 4: The Factor Risk Premium Has an Economic Story.” Schweser R83, “Equilibrium” (“risk premiums will not disappear since investors cannot use arbitrage to remove systematic risk”) and Lesson 4. Schweser writes that “market variance removes all idiosyncratic risk”; GARP’s wording is that the market removes it. GARP wording used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q7 of 15.

a.reason: **True.** GARP Lesson 4: “The market portfolio is the portfolio that has the lowest volatility among all portfolios that share the same mean as the market . . . The market removes all idiosyncratic risk. This remaining risk has to be rewarded.” A would become false under a sibling swap to “lowest volatility of all portfolios” (global minimum variance).

b.reason: **True.** Lesson 4 defines $\bar{\gamma}$ with wealth weights, and the Equilibrium section says the premium “reflects the full setup of all people in the economy.” B would be false if it said “equal-weighted.”

c.reason: GARP, Equilibrium: “Equilibrium factor risk premiums will not disappear because clever hedge funds go and trade them; these types of investment strategies are not factors. Investors cannot arbitrage away the market factor and all other systematic factors.” C contradicts this.

d.reason:
**True.** “As the average investor becomes more risk averse to variance (so $\bar{\gamma}$ increases), the risk premium of the market also increases.” D would be false under a polarity flip (“falls”).

The corruption in C is a polarity flip: “will not disappear” became “will be competed away.”

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a EUR-denominated asset manager is computing CAPM required returns for two stocks. Market volatility is 18%, the risk-free rate is 2.0% and the expected return on the market portfolio is 8.0%.

| Stock | Correlation with the market | Total volatility (%) |
|---|---|---|
| X | 0.30 | 45 |
| Y | 0.90 | 20 |

The CAPM required returns on X and Y are closest to:
questions.solution:
EUR asset manager: CAPM required returns for a high-volatility, low-correlation stock X and a low-volatility, high-correlation stock Y.

**Concept and theory**

Lesson 5: risk is factor exposure. The risk of an asset is its exposure to the market factor, measured by beta, and the SML prices it:

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} = \beta_{\text{i}} [\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ]$, $\beta_{\text{i}} = \frac{\text{cov}(\text{r}_{\text{i}}\text{, r}_{\text{m}})}{\text{var}(\text{r}_{\text{m}})} = \frac{\rho_{\text{i,m}} \sigma_{\text{i}}}{\sigma_{\text{m}}}$ ,

where $\rho_{\text{i,m}}$ is the correlation of asset i with the market, $\sigma_{\text{i}}$ its volatility and $\sigma_{\text{m}}$ the market’s volatility. GARP stresses that beta is “a measure of the lack of diversification potential”: the lower the correlation with the portfolio, the greater the diversification benefit. Total volatility matters only through the product $\rho_{\text{i,m}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$; the uncorrelated part of $\sigma_{\text{i}}$ is idiosyncratic and unpriced.

**Applying it to this question**

Step by step:

$\beta_{\text{X}} =$ 0.30 × 0.45/0.18 = 0.135/0.18 = 0.75

$\beta_{\text{Y}} =$ 0.90 × 0.20/0.18 = 0.180/0.18 = 1.00

E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} =$ 8.0% − 2.0% = 6.0%

E$(\text{r}_{\text{X}} ) =$ 2.0% + 0.75 × 6.0% = 6.5%

E$(\text{r}_{\text{Y}} ) =$ 2.0% + 1.00 × 6.0% = 8.0%

X is more than twice as volatile as Y but requires the lower return, because most of its volatility is uncorrelated with the market and diversifies away; Y moves almost one-for-one with the market and offers little diversification.

**Fragile fact.** $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i,m}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}}$: a high-volatility asset can have a low beta if its correlation with the market is low.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.4 CAPM, “CAPM Lesson 5: Risk Is Factor Exposure” (Equation 1.2 and $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i,m}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}}$). Schweser R83, Lesson 5 gives $\beta_{\text{i}} = \text{cov}(\text{R}_{\text{i}}$, $\text{R}_{\text{M}})$/ var$(\text{R}_{\text{M}})$; the correlation form is GARP’s.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q8 of 15.

a.reason: A applies $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i,m}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}}$ and the SML exactly as GARP Lesson 5 writes them.

b.reason: **Dropped term: correlation omitted.** Using $\beta= \sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{m}}$ gives $\beta_{\text{X}} =$ 2.5 and $\beta_{\text{Y}} =$ 1.111, so E$(\text{r}_{\text{X}} ) =$ 2% + 2.5 × 6% = 17.0% and E$(\text{r}_{\text{Y}} ) =$ 2% + 1.111 × 6% = 8.7%. This prices total volatility, the pre-CAPM view of risk. B would be correct only if both stocks were perfectly correlated with the market.

c.reason: **Wrong input twin: correlation used as beta.** E$(\text{r}_{\text{X}} ) =$ 2% + 0.30 × 6% = 3.8%, E$(\text{r}_{\text{Y}} ) =$ 2% + 0.90 × 6% = 7.4%. Correlation equals beta only when $\sigma_{\text{i}} = \sigma_{\text{m}}$. C would be correct if both stocks had 18% volatility.

d.reason: **Wrong input twin: market return used as the premium.** E$(\text{r}_{\text{X}} ) =$ 2% + 0.75 × 8% = 8.0%, E$(\text{r}_{\text{Y}} ) =$ 2% + 1.00 × 8% = 10.0%. Betas are right but are multiplied by E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}})$ instead of E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ . D would be correct if 8.0% were the market risk premium.

questions.question:
A member of the risk committee at a Chinese insurer, whose CNY equity portfolio is already well diversified, asks why the CAPM requires a higher expected return on high-beta stocks than on low-beta stocks.

Which explanation is most accurate?

options.text: High-beta stocks carry more idiosyncratic risk, and investors must be compensated for bearing that firm-specific risk.
High-beta stocks tend to pay off when the market falls, and investors require high returns on assets whose payoffs arrive in bad times.
High-beta stocks move with the diversified portfolio already held, so they add little diversification benefit and must offer high expected returns to be held.
High-beta stocks require a higher expected return only when their total volatility is also higher than the volatility of the market portfolio.

questions.solution:
Chinese insurer risk committee: why does the CAPM require higher returns on high-beta stocks for an already diversified investor?

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s intuition for Lesson 5 is that “mean-variance investing is all about diversification benefits” and beta is “a measure of the lack of diversification potential.” Start from a diversified portfolio:

| Asset | Behavior | CAPM consequence |
|---|---|---|
| High beta | Goes up when the market goes up and down when it goes down; acts like the portfolio already held | Low diversification benefit, unattractive, requires a high expected return |
| Low beta | Pays off when the market tanks | Large diversification benefit, attractive, needs little compensation |

**Applying it to this question**

The committee member’s portfolio is already diversified, exactly GARP’s starting point. The deciding fact is that high-beta stocks replicate what the investor already holds, so they add little diversification and must be paid for with expected return.

**Fragile fact.** High beta means low diversification benefit; low beta means high diversification benefit.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.4 CAPM, “CAPM Lesson 5: Risk Is Factor Exposure.” Schweser R83, Lesson 5 (“Higher betas imply lower diversification benefits”). Conflict noted: Schweser’s phrase linking beta to “idiosyncratic risk” differs from GARP; GARP used, and it looks like a condensation slip rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q9 of 15.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: idiosyncratic for systematic risk.** Beta measures co-movement with the market, systematic risk; idiosyncratic risk is unrewarded under the CAPM. Caution: Schweser’s sentence “beta looks at idiosyncratic risk and the lack of diversification” is loosely worded; GARP’s version, used here, is that beta measures the lack of diversification potential. A would be correct only in a world without diversification, which is not the CAPM.

b.reason: **Polarity flip on when the payoff arrives.** Assets that pay off when the market falls are low-beta assets, and they are valuable, so they need low returns. B attaches a high-beta label to low-beta behavior. B’s reasoning would apply to assets that lose in bad times.

c.reason: GARP: “investors find assets with high betas, those assets that tend to go up when the market goes up, and vice versa, to be unattractive. These high beta assets act like the diversified portfolio the investor already holds, and so they require high expected returns to be held by investors.” C states this.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error: added condition.** The required return rises with beta regardless of total volatility; total volatility is not an SML input. D would be correct only if beta and total volatility moved one-for-one, which requires a correlation of one with the market.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Brazilian bank is preparing a note on how the CAPM prices assets that behave differently in market crashes. The BRL risk-free rate is 4.0% and the market risk premium is 6.0%.

| Asset | Beta | Total volatility (%) | Behavior when the market crashes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gold fund | −0.20 | 24 | Rises |
| Utility equity | 0.60 | 12 | Falls modestly |
| Bank equity | 1.40 | 30 | Falls sharply |

Which statement should the analyst include in the note?

options.text: The gold fund’s CAPM risk premium is −1.2%: its payoffs are high when market returns are low, which makes it valuable to hold.
The gold fund’s CAPM risk premium is +1.2%: holders must be rewarded for an asset that pays off when market returns are low.
The utility equity is the most valuable of the three assets to hold, because its total volatility is the lowest of the three.
The gold fund’s CAPM expected return is −1.2%: investors pay to hold it because it pays off when market returns are low.

questions.solution:
Brazilian bank note: CAPM pricing of a gold fund, a utility and a bank stock that behave differently in crashes.

**Concept and theory**

Lesson 6: assets paying off in bad times have low risk premiums. In the CAPM, bad times are defined by the factor: low (or negative) market returns. The risk premium is a reward for how an asset pays off in bad times:

- Losses when the market loses: high beta, risky, high premium. Because investors are risk averse, good-time gains do not cancel bad-time losses.
- Payoffs when the market loses: low beta, valuable, low premium. If the bad-time payoffs are large enough, investors pay to hold the asset rather than being paid: low enough betas give negative expected returns. Gold and government bonds are GARP’s examples.

The SML quantifies this: risk premium $= \beta_{\text{i}}[\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ]$, expected return $= \text{r}_{\text{f}} +$ risk premium.

**Applying it to this question**

Step by step:

Gold fund premium = −0.20 × 6.0% = −1.2%, E$(\text{r}) =$ 4.0% − 1.2% = 2.8%

Utility premium = 0.60 × 6.0% = 3.6%, E$(\text{r}) =$ 7.6%

Bank premium = 1.40 × 6.0% = 8.4%, E$(\text{r}) =$ 12.4%

The gold fund has the lowest (negative) premium because it pays off in crashes; it is the most valuable asset to hold. Total volatilities are deliberately irrelevant inputs.

**Fragile fact.** A negative premium is not a negative expected return; add back $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ before judging whether investors “pay to hold” the asset.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.4 CAPM, “CAPM Lesson 5: Risk Is Factor Exposure” (low beta assets and negative expected returns, gold and government bonds) and “CAPM Lesson 6: Assets Paying Off in Bad Times Have Low Risk Premiums.” Schweser R83, Lessons 5 and 6. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q10 of 15.

a.reason: A gives the right premium (−1.2%) and GARP’s reason: “if the payoff of an asset tends to be high in bad times, this is a valuable asset to hold and its risk premium is low.”

b.reason: **Sign error and polarity flip on the reward.** +1.2% drops the negative sign of beta and claims that paying off in bad times must be rewarded. It is the reverse: such assets are hedges, so investors accept a low or negative premium. B’s reasoning would hold for an asset that pays off in good times and loses in crashes.

c.reason: **Sibling swap: total volatility for beta.** Value in the CAPM depends on payoffs in bad times (beta), not on own volatility. The utility’s lowest total volatility (12%) is irrelevant; with $\beta=$ 0.60 it loses when the market loses. C would be correct only if the CAPM measured risk by stand-alone volatility, the pre-CAPM view.

d.reason: **Dropped term: risk-free rate omitted.** −1.2% is the risk premium, not the expected return; E$(\text{r}) =$ 4.0% + (−1.2%) = 2.8%, which is positive. GARP’s “negative expected returns” needs a beta low enough that $\beta_{\text{i}}[\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ] < -\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ , here $\beta< -$0.67. D would be correct if $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ were 0%.

questions.question:
A risk consultant advising a UK defined benefit pension fund is explaining what happens to asset pricing when two CAPM assumptions, that investors have only financial wealth and that they have mean-variance utility, are relaxed. She lists four statements.

I. Because liabilities are often set in real terms and incomes fall when growth is low, inflation and economic growth become important factors.

II. Taking labor income risk into account has been found to improve the performance of the CAPM substantially.

III. Because investors dislike losses more than they like gains, stocks with greater downside risk should earn lower returns than the CAPM implies.

IV. Higher-moment risks, such as skewness and kurtosis, have been found to carry risk premiums. Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I, III and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
UK DB pension consultant: consequences of relaxing the CAPM’s financial-wealth-only and mean-variance utility assumptions.

**Concept and theory**

GARP 1.6 examines each CAPM assumption and what happens when it is relaxed. The general rule (1.6 summary): when an assumption is violated, additional risk premiums appear.

| Assumption | Reality | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Only financial wealth | Investors have income streams and liabilities; liabilities often in real terms; income falls when growth is low | Inflation and growth become important factors; human capital (labor income risk) drives returns; Jagannathan and Wang (1996) find large CAPM improvements when labor income risk is included |
| Mean-variance utility | Investors are more distressed by losses than pleased by gains (asymmetric) | Deviations among stocks with different downside risk: greater downside risk, higher returns (Ang, Chen and Xing, 2006); skewness and kurtosis (higher moments) also carry premiums |

**Applying it to this question**

I: true (real liabilities and growth-sensitive income make inflation and growth factors). II: true (labor income risk improves the CAPM). III: false, the direction is reversed. IV: true (higher-moment risks carry premiums). Correct set: I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** More downside risk means higher required returns than the CAPM implies, because investors dislike losses more than they like gains.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.6 Failures of the CAPM, items 1 (Investors have only financial wealth) and 2 (Investors have mean-variance utility). Schweser R83, “Shortcomings of the CAPM,” items 1 and 2. Schweser omits the Jagannathan and Wang evidence and the higher-moment premiums; content from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q11 of 15.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Omits IV, a true GARP statement; the error is a scope error (treating the higher-moment evidence as outside the assumption). A would be the key if IV were false, for example if it claimed higher moments carry no premium.

b.reason: **I, III and IV only.** Includes III, whose polarity is flipped (“lower” should be “higher”), and omits II. B would be the key if III said “higher” and II were false.

c.reason:
**II, III and IV only.** Includes the polarity-flipped III and drops I, which is the core of the financial-wealth shortcoming. C would be the key if I and III were swapped in truth value.

The corruption in statement III is a polarity flip: loss aversion means investors demand more for downside risk.

d.reason: GARP 1.6 item 1 supports I and II; item 2 states “stocks with greater downside risk have higher returns” and “higher moment risk, like skewness and kurtosis, also carry risk premiums,” supporting IV and refuting III.

questions.question:
A junior quantitative analyst at a US university endowment is drafting a memo on the CAPM’s assumption that investors have a single-period investment horizon.

Which statement should the memo include?

options.text: It is the most damaging CAPM assumption, because the model’s pricing relation no longer holds in any period once it is extended to many periods.
By itself it is minor, since a dynamic extension keeps the CAPM holding each period, but long-term investors should rebalance while the average investor does not.
Because the average investor holds the market portfolio, the average investor is the one who must rebalance most often to restore market weights.
Its key implication is that long-term investors should buy and hold the market portfolio without rebalancing, exactly as the average investor does.

questions.solution:
US endowment memo on the CAPM’s single-period horizon assumption.

**Concept and theory**

GARP 1.6 item 3 makes two separate points that must not be merged:

|  |  |
|---|---|
| For CAPM pricing theory | Minor. Merton (1971, 1973) extends the CAPM to a dynamic setting in which the CAPM holds in each single period. |
| For portfolio choice | Huge implication. The optimal strategy for long-term investors is to rebalance. The average investor, who holds the market portfolio by definition, does not rebalance. |

The average investor holds the market, whose weights drift with prices automatically, so no trading is needed to stay at market weights. Long-horizon investors who differ from the average should rebalance, a multi-period strategy that a single-period model cannot represent.

**Applying it to this question**

The memo must state both halves: unimportant for the pricing relation, important for long-horizon portfolio choice, with the correct actor for each (long-term investors rebalance; the average investor does not).

**Fragile fact.** Long-term investors rebalance; the average investor holding the market does not. Minor for pricing, major for portfolio choice.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.6 Failures of the CAPM, item 3 (Single-period investment horizon). Schweser R83, “Shortcomings of the CAPM,” item 3. Schweser omits the Merton extension; content from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q12 of 15.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP calls the assumption minor for the theory, and in Merton’s extension the CAPM holds in each period. A would be correct only if the dynamic extension broke the period-by-period relation.

b.reason: GARP: “By itself an investment horizon of one period is a minor assumption. Merton (1971, 1973) provides a famous extension of the CAPM to the dynamic case. In this setting, the CAPM holds in each single period . . . The optimal strategy for long-term investors is to rebalance. The average investor, who holds the market portfolio by definition, does not rebalance.”

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** Rebalancing belongs to long-term investors who are not average. The average investor holds the market by definition and does not rebalance. C would be correct for a long-term investor with a fixed target mix that differs from market weights.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It extends the average investor’s no-rebalancing result to all long-term investors. GARP says the optimal strategy for long-term investors is to rebalance. D would be correct only for a long-term investor who happens to be the average investor.

questions.question:
A regulator at a securities commission is reviewing a local equity market in which short selling is prohibited and investors disagree sharply about the prospects of listed companies.

Which of the following best describes the effect on CAPM pricing?

options.text: Disagreement alone would leave a version of the CAPM intact, but with the short-sale ban prices reflect only optimists’ beliefs and beliefs become a systematic factor.
With the short-sale ban, prices reflect only pessimists’ beliefs, because optimists are already fully invested and cannot buy more of the stocks.
Disagreement alone causes large deviations from the CAPM, so lifting the short-sale ban would leave the size of the deviations unchanged.
The pricing effect arises only in behavioral models; in a rational setting, a short-sale ban has no effect on prices relative to the CAPM.

questions.solution:
Securities regulator: CAPM pricing in a market with a short-selling ban and sharply differing investor beliefs.

**Concept and theory**

Homogeneous expectations ensure that all investors hold the same MVE portfolio, which becomes the market portfolio. GARP is precise about how much relaxing this matters:

- Alone, heterogeneous expectations are not important: a version of the CAPM holds in which expected returns are simply averages across all investors’ beliefs (Williams, 1977).
- Combined with trading frictions such as an inability to short, they produce significant deviations. Pessimists would like to short but cannot, so their beliefs are not impounded into prices. Prices reflect only optimists’ beliefs, and investor beliefs become a systematic factor.
- The original setting of this idea, Miller (1977), was rational, although behavioral versions also exist.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem contains both ingredients: disagreement and a short-sale ban. The deciding facts are that disagreement alone is benign, that the ban lets optimists set prices, and that beliefs then become a systematic factor.

**Fragile fact.** Under a short-sale ban optimists set prices; heterogeneous beliefs matter only in combination with the ban.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.6 Failures of the CAPM, items 4 (Investors have homogeneous expectations) and 5 (No taxes or transactions costs). Schweser R83, “Shortcomings of the CAPM,” items 4 and 5. Conflict: Schweser presents heterogeneous expectations as a source of significant departures on their own; GARP says only in combination with trading frictions. Resolved from GARP; this looks like Schweser condensation, not a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q13 of 15.

a.reason: GARP 1.6 item 4: “By itself, the homogeneous expectations assumption is not important . . . But, in combination with the next assumption, heterogeneous expectations can produce significant deviations from the CAPM”; item 5: “Optimists may prevail in pricing because the pessimists’ beliefs are not impounded into stock prices . . . Thus, investor beliefs become a systematic factor.”

b.reason: **Polarity flip: optimists swapped for pessimists.** The ban silences pessimists, who cannot express negative views by shorting; optimists set prices. B would be correct under a ban on buying (or leverage limits binding on optimists).

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It credits the deviation to disagreement alone. GARP says disagreement alone is not important; the combination with the short-sale constraint creates the deviation, so lifting the ban should shrink it. Caution: Schweser’s condensed item 4 says heterogeneous expectations “can produce significant departures” without the “in combination” condition; GARP is the authority and is more precise.

d.reason: **Sibling swap: behavioral for rational.** GARP: “While there are behavioral versions of this story, the original setting of Miller (1977) . . . was a rational setting.” D would be correct only if the effect required irrational investors.

questions.question:
The CRO of an asset manager about to launch a fund of illiquid small-cap emerging market stocks asks a risk analyst to summarize where the CAPM’s assumptions of no taxes or transaction costs, price-taking investors and costless information break down.

Which statement in the summary is NOT correct?

options.text: Taxes affect expected returns and can themselves be regarded as a systematic factor.
In very illiquid markets with high transaction costs, larger deviations from the CAPM should be expected.
Informed investors trade on knowledge others lack, but their large trades leave prices unchanged, so the price-taker assumption survives.
Several deviations from the CAPM are strongest in small-cap stocks traded in illiquid markets where information is not spread efficiently.

questions.solution:
CRO of an illiquid small-cap fund: which summary statement on frictions, price taking and costly information is false?

**Concept and theory**

GARP 1.6 items 5 to 7:

| Assumption | What GARP says when it is relaxed |
|---|---|
| No taxes or transactions costs | Taxes matter, affect expected returns and can be regarded as a systematic factor. Transaction costs vary across securities; very illiquid markets with high costs show more deviations from the CAPM (liquidity premiums, Chapter 4) |
| Investors are price takers | The informed investor trades and moves prices because he has knowledge others do not; large trades move prices |
| Information is costless and available to all | Collecting and processing information is costly and not available to all; information can itself be a factor; additional premiums are expected in more inefficient markets; several deviations are strongest in small-cap stocks in illiquid markets where information is not promulgated efficiently |

Summary: failures of the CAPM should be most apparent in illiquid, inefficient markets.

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and D restate items 5 and 7. C says informed trades leave prices unchanged, the opposite of item 6. Because the question asks for the statement that is NOT correct, C is the answer.

**Fragile fact.** Informed investors are price setters: their large trades move prices.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.6 Failures of the CAPM, items 5 (No taxes or transactions costs), 6 (Individual investors are price takers) and 7 (Information is costless and available to all investors). Schweser R83, “Shortcomings of the CAPM,” items 5 to 7. Schweser’s Key Concepts list six shortcomings and omits costless information, while its main text and GARP list seven; GARP’s seven used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q14 of 15.

a.reason: **True.** Item 5: “Taxes matter. Taxes affect expected returns and can be regarded as a systematic factor.” It would be false if it said taxes are diversifiable. Schweser does not state the systematic-factor point; it is GARP content.

b.reason: **True.** Item 5: “for very illiquid markets with high transactions costs, there may be more deviations from the CAPM.” It would be false under a polarity flip (“fewer deviations”).

c.reason: GARP item 6: “The informed investor is trading and moving prices because he has some knowledge that others do not have. But when these trades are large, they move prices.” Price taking fails precisely for informed, large traders, and especially in the illiquid market this fund will trade.

d.reason:
**True.** Item 7: “Several deviations from the CAPM are strongest in stocks that have small market capitalizations and trade in illiquid markets where information is not promulgated efficiently.” It would be false if it named large-cap liquid stocks.

The corruption in C is a polarity flip on the price impact of informed trading.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-1 c Q15
questions.question:
A board member at an Australian general insurer asks the CRO for a short verdict on the CAPM before the investment committee reviews its use in setting hurdle rates.

Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Empirical work supports its prediction that premiums depend only on beta, while rejecting its prediction that the market is the only factor that matters.
Its predictions that premiums depend only on beta and that only the market factor matters are rejected, yet its intuition that premiums reward losses in bad times survives.
Its failures should be most apparent in the most liquid, efficient markets, where many arbitrageurs trade heavily against its mispricings.
It works approximately for most applications and never fails badly, which explains why most CFOs still use it in capital budgeting decisions.

questions.solution:
Australian insurer board member: short verdict on the CAPM’s empirical standing.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s overall assessment of the CAPM has three layers:

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Predictions | Risk premiums depend only on beta, and only one factor (the market) matters. Both “demolished in thousands of empirical studies.” The implication that every investor holds the market portfolio is “outright rejected in data.” |
| Surviving intuition | Factors underlying assets determine risk premiums; premiums compensate for losses during bad times; risk is about how assets move together, not assets in isolation |
| Practical standing | Still the workhorse: 75% of finance professors advocate it, 75% of CFOs use it in capital budgeting. It works approximately, but fails miserably in certain situations |

Section 1.6 adds that failures should be most apparent in illiquid, inefficient markets, and that violated assumptions produce additional premiums.

**Applying it to this question**

The verdict must reject both predictions and keep the bad-times intuition. Only B does both; A keeps one prediction, C reverses where failures appear, and D overstates reliability.

**Fragile fact.** Both predictions (beta only; market only) are rejected; the intuition survives, and failures concentrate in illiquid, inefficient markets.

**Reference**

LO 83.c: Explain the implications of using the CAPM to value assets, including equilibrium and optimal holdings, exposure to factor risk, its treatment of diversification benefits, and shortcomings of the CAPM. GARP FRM Part II RMIM (2025), Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.4 CAPM (introductory assessment and “What does the CAPM get right?”) and Section 1.6 Failures of the CAPM (summary paragraph). Schweser R83, “Shortcomings of the CAPM” introduction (assumptions break down especially in illiquid, inefficient markets). Schweser does not carry the empirical-rejection and practitioner-usage points; content from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 c, where it is Q15 of 15.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error: half the verdict.** It keeps the beta-only prediction alive, but GARP says both predictions were demolished. A would be correct if the evidence rejected only the single-factor claim.

b.reason: GARP 1.4: “It predicts that asset risk premiums depend only on the asset’s beta and there is only one factor that matters, the market portfolio. Both of these predictions have been demolished . . . The basic intuition of the CAPM still holds true: that the factors underlying the assets determine asset risk premiums and that these risk premiums are compensation for investors’ losses during bad times.”

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP: “We should expect failures of the CAPM to be most apparent in illiquid, inefficient markets.” C would be correct only if liquidity and efficiency worsened the fit.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** GARP: it “works approximately, and well enough for most applications, but it fails miserably in certain situations.” The CFO statistic is right; “never fails badly” is the corruption. D would be correct if “never” were replaced by “fails badly in certain situations.”

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-1 d Q1
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Brazilian pension fund is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts that explains, in one sentence, how multifactor models change the CAPM’s notion of “bad times”. Which of the following statements best describes that change?

options.text: Multifactor models replace the CAPM’s separate bad times with one composite bad time, which arises only when every factor in the model performs poorly in the same period.
Multifactor models keep low market returns as the only bad times and use the extra factors to explain the idiosyncratic part of each asset’s return, which then earns its own premium.
Each factor in a multifactor model provides its own definition of bad times, so periods of high inflation or low economic growth can count as bad times, not only periods of low market returns.
Multifactor models define bad times through each asset’s own poor returns, because once several factors are used, risk becomes a property of how an asset behaves in isolation.

questions.solution:
Onboarding slide: how multifactor models change the CAPM’s definition of bad times.

**Concept and theory**

Factor theory says that assets earn risk premiums because they lose money in bad times, and investors who bear those losses must be paid for doing so in good times. The question every model must answer is: what counts as a bad time?

The CAPM gives the narrowest answer. It has one factor, the market portfolio, so bad times are simply periods of low (or negative) market returns. GARP calls this “very restrictive: there are many more factors than just the market.”

Multifactor models keep every CAPM intuition but broaden the definition: “Multifactor models recognize that bad times can be defined more broadly than just bad returns on the market portfolio” and “each factor in a multifactor model provides its own definition of bad times.” With macro factors, bad times are periods of high inflation, low economic growth, or both. With investment factors, they are periods of low market returns, value underperforming growth, or both. The chapter summary puts it in one line: the CAPM defines bad times as times of low market returns, whereas multifactor models capture multiple definitions of bad times across many factors and states of nature.

| Feature | CAPM | Multifactor models |
|---|---|---|
| Number of factors | One (the market) | Several (market, macro, styles) |
| Bad times | Low market returns | Each factor’s own bad times |
| Example | Market falls | High inflation, low growth, or both |

**Applying it to this question**

The slide must state the change in the definition of bad times. The deciding fact is that each factor brings its own set of bad times, and the sets combine with “or” rather than “and”. Check each option for (i) whether more than the market counts, and (ii) whether the sets combine correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Factors combine with “or”: a bad time for any one factor is a bad time. The CAPM is the special one-factor case whose only bad time is a low market return.

**Reference**

LO 83.d: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM. Schweser Reading 83, Module 83.2, “Multifactor Models” (LO 83.d and its Key Concepts). GARP Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.1 “Chapter Summary”; end of Section 1.4 (after “CAPM Lesson 6: Assets Paying Off in Bad Times Have Low Risk Premiums”); Section 1.5 “Multifactor Models” (opening paragraph and the two-factor examples). Schweser and GARP agree.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 d, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** GARP’s examples say bad times are high inflation, low growth, “or both”. Requiring every factor to be poor at once turns “or” into “and” and throws away most bad times. A would be correct only for a model defined to recognise joint stress alone, which is not how GARP describes multifactor models.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** B keeps the CAPM’s definition of bad times and then gives the extra factors the job of pricing idiosyncratic risk. In both frameworks idiosyncratic risk is diversified away and earns no premium (Lesson 1). B would describe the CAPM’s bad times correctly if the stem asked about the CAPM, but the pricing of idiosyncratic risk is wrong in either model.

c.reason: C restates GARP Section 1.5 directly: each factor provides its own definition of bad times, so high inflation or low growth are bad times in their own right, not only low market returns. It also matches Schweser: the CAPM “defines bad times as low returns to the market portfolio. By contrast, multifactor models incorporate other risk factors, including low economic growth, low GDP growth, or low consumption.”

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Treating risk as an asset’s own behaviour in isolation is the pre-CAPM view that the CAPM overturned. GARP stresses that risk “is a property not of an asset in isolation but how the assets move in relation to each other”, and that intuition carries over to multifactor models. D would be correct only for a description of the pre-CAPM own-volatility view.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-1 d Q2
questions.question: A risk consultant hired by an Australian superannuation fund is reviewing four sentences in the fund’s AUD-denominated training manual describing the arbitrage pricing theory (APT). Which sentence is most accurate?

options.text: The APT, developed by Stephen Ross, is an early multifactor model; it uses the word “arbitrage” because its factors, like the CAPM’s market factor, cannot be arbitraged or diversified away, so investors must be compensated in equilibrium for bearing them.

The APT, developed by Stephen Ross, is an early multifactor model; it uses the word “arbitrage” because arbitrageurs who trade its factors steadily remove the factor premiums, so the premiums shrink toward zero as more capital follows them.

The APT, developed by Stephen Ross, is an early multifactor model; like the CAPM, it captures bad times solely through low returns on the market portfolio, but it estimates each asset’s market beta from several macroeconomic variables.

The APT, developed by Stephen Ross, is an early multifactor model; it describes expected returns as a linear function of exposures to firm-specific risk factors, which are rewarded because a single asset’s own risks cannot be diversified.

questions.solution:
Consultant reviews four training-manual sentences on the arbitrage pricing theory.

**Concept and theory**

The arbitrage pricing theory (APT) of Stephen Ross (1976) is where multifactor models begin. GARP calls it “the first multifactor model”; Schweser calls it “one of the earliest”. Its core claims:

- **Several systematic factors.** Expected returns depend on exposures to common (macroeconomic) risk factors; Schweser describes expected returns as a linear function of these exposures.
- **Why “arbitrage”.** GARP: “It uses the word ‘arbitrage’ because the factors cannot be arbitraged or diversified away, just like the single market factor in the CAPM.”
- **Compensation.** “In equilibrium, investors must be compensated for bearing these multiple sources of factor risk.”
- **Bad times.** “While the CAPM captures the notion of bad times solely by means of low returns of the market portfolio, each factor in a multifactor model provides its own definition of bad times.”

The name is easy to misread: the word does not say arbitrageurs remove the premiums; it says the factors are the part of risk that arbitrage and diversification cannot remove.

**Applying it to this question**

All four sentences share the same correct opening, so the discrimination lives in the second clause: what “arbitrage” refers to, how bad times are defined, and what kind of factor is priced. Only one second clause matches the source.

**Fragile fact.** “Arbitrage” in APT means the factors cannot be arbitraged or diversified away, so they must be rewarded. It does not mean arbitrageurs eliminate them.

**Reference**

LO 83.d: Describe multifactor models and compare and contrast multifactor models to the CAPM. Schweser Reading 83, Module 83.2, “Multifactor Models” (LO 83.d and its Key Concepts). GARP Chapter 1 Factor Theory, Section 1.5 “Multifactor Models” (opening paragraphs); Section 1.4 “Equilibrium” for the persistence of factor premiums. Wording difference: GARP calls the APT “the first multifactor model”, Schweser “one of the earliest”; Schweser adds “linear function of exposures to common (i.e., macroeconomic) risk factors”. Not a content conflict; the question uses “an early multifactor model”. The APT’s role in efficient market theory (arbitrageurs driving returns toward equilibrium) belongs to LO 83.f and is not tested here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-1 d, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: A reproduces GARP Section 1.5: the factors cannot be arbitraged or diversified away, exactly like the CAPM’s market factor, and investors must be compensated for bearing them in equilibrium.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** B reverses the meaning of the name: it says arbitrage removes the premiums, whereas the source says the factors cannot be arbitraged away. GARP adds in Section 1.4 that equilibrium factor premiums “will not disappear because clever hedge funds go and trade them”. B would be correct only for a mispricing (a pure anomaly) rather than a systematic factor.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Defining bad times solely by low market returns is the CAPM’s property, attributed here to the APT. In the APT each factor provides its own definition of bad times. C would be correct if “APT” were replaced by “CAPM” and the beta clause dropped.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** The APT’s factors are common (macroeconomic, systematic) factors, not firm-specific ones; firm-specific risk is diversifiable and unrewarded in both frameworks. D would be correct if “firm-specific” read “common (macroeconomic)” and the reason were that these factors cannot be diversified away.
