questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a Chinese insurer’s asset management arm is reviewing four CNY client mandates that propose selling volatility protection through index put options. Which client is most suitable to be a seller of volatility protection?

options.text: A long-horizon, unleveraged endowment with no large payouts due in market stress, which can sit through very large losses when volatility spikes and risky assets fall together.
A leveraged fund that must meet margin calls and investor redemptions during market stress, but which values the high and steady premiums earned in calm periods.
A pension plan that reasons that, because the price of volatility risk is negative, selling put protection is a way to reduce the risk of its existing equity holdings.

The test therefore has two parts: can the investor absorb very large losses, and can it do so at the very time its other risky assets are also falling?

Schweser Reading 84, Module 84.2, Volatility Premiums, Professor’s Note. No conflict.

questions.question: At a US foundation, a board member argues that the foundation’s policy of rebalancing quarterly to fixed 60/40 equity/bond weights (USD 900 million in total) has nothing to do with volatility risk. The foundation’s risk analyst is asked to respond. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Rebalancing is a long volatility strategy: by buying assets after they fall, it pays off in left-tail episodes much like owning a put.
Rebalancing is a short volatility strategy, and its crash losses are potentially steeper than those of selling volatility in derivatives markets.
The investor who never rebalances, holding 100% of the market, collects the long-run volatility premium that the rebalancer gives up.
Rebalancing is a short volatility strategy that reaps a long-run volatility premium, but it trades physical assets rather than option volatility.

US foundation’s analyst responds to the claim that fixed-weight rebalancing has nothing to do with volatility risk.

GARP: “Rebalancing as a portfolio strategy is actually a short volatility strategy.” A rebalancer sells assets that have risen and buys those that have fallen. This earns a long-run volatility risk premium, and “the person who does not rebalance, the average investor who owns 100% of the market, is long volatility risk and loses the long-run volatility risk premium.” Like a volatility seller, the rebalancer “is exposed to the possibilities of fat, left-hand tail losses.”

GARP then lists two differences from selling volatility in derivatives:

|  | Rebalancing | Derivatives volatility selling |
|---|---|---|
| What is traded | Physical assets; does not directly trade volatility | Risk-neutral (option) volatility, which carries an additional volatility risk premium |
| Severity of losses | Less steep | Potentially much steeper |
| Stance on returns | Done to earn the underlying factor premiums; boosted by mean reversion | Can be delta-hedged, taking no stance on expected returns |

The board member claims there is no link. The deciding facts are the direction (short volatility), who earns the premium (the rebalancer, not the buy-and-hold investor) and the comparison of loss severity (derivatives steeper). The USD amount and the 60/40 weights are irrelevant.

LO 84.c: Assess methods of mitigating volatility risk in a portfolio and describe challenges that arise when managing volatility risk. B would be right if “rebalancing” and “derivatives” were swapped in the comparison.

questions.question: A model validator at a Swiss asset manager is reviewing the documentation for a valuation model that links the market risk premium to market variance through E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} = \gamma\sigma^{2}_{\text{m}}$. The documentation contains four statements. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.text: In the relation, the market risk premium is proportional to market variance, and $\gamma$ is the wealth-weighted average risk aversion of investors.
Because $\gamma$ is positive in theory, empirical studies have consistently estimated a stable positive value, so the relation is easy to build into models.
A single seminal study reports positive, negative and zero estimates of $\gamma$, and theory shows that the relation can be negative and change over time.
Whatever the sign of $\gamma$, when volatility rises dramatically assets tend to produce losses, so only loss-tolerant investors should sell volatility protection.

Swiss model validator finds the incorrect statement about $\gamma$ in the risk-premium/variance relation.

GARP’s last challenge is modeling: “Constructing valuation models with volatility risk can be tricky because the relation between volatility and expected returns is time varying and switches signs and is thus very hard to pin down.” The relation studied is Equation (2.1), which repeats Equation (1.1):

E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} = \gamma\sigma^{2}_{\text{m}}$,

where E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ is the market risk premium (expected market return in excess of the risk-free rate), $\sigma^{2}_{\text{m}}$ is the variance of the market return, and $\gamma$ is the risk aversion of the average investor, the average weighting each investor’s risk aversion by wealth (Chapter 1). Under the CAPM, mean-variance investors dislike variance, so the premium is proportional to variance and $\gamma$ should be positive.

In the data: estimates “are positive, negative, or zero”; one seminal study, Glosten, Jagannathan and Runkle (1993), “contains all three estimates in the same paper”; and theory shows the relation “can indeed be negative and change over time.” What is undisputed is that “when volatility increases dramatically, assets tend to produce losses,” so only investors able to tolerate large losses should sell volatility protection.

LO 84.c: Assess methods of mitigating volatility risk in a portfolio and describe challenges that arise when managing volatility risk. | Period | Market return (%) | Risk-free rate (%) | Market vol (%) | Months |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 8.1 | 1.8 | 15 | 60 |
| P2 | −1.5 | 1.5 | 30 | 24 |
| P3 | 2.2 | 2.2 | 18 | 36 |

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Singapore sovereign wealth fund is presenting to newly hired analysts. She explains why the fund’s investment committee implements its factor exposures through dynamic factors such as size and value rather than by targeting macro factors such as inflation and economic growth directly. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Dynamic factors are attractive mainly because they are unrelated to macro risk, so they give the fund return streams that are independent of the fundamental risks of the economy.
Economic growth is the one macro factor that is traded in scale, so growth exposure can be implemented directly, while inflation exposure has to be obtained through dynamic factors.
Macro factors such as inflation and growth are usually not directly traded in scale, volatility being the exception, whereas dynamic factors can be easily implemented and still reflect macro risk.
Because they are tradeable, dynamic factors fully replace macro factors, so a fund holding size and value factor portfolios no longer carries any exposure to inflation or growth shocks.

questions.solution:
A sovereign wealth fund analyst explains why factor exposures are implemented through dynamic factors rather than macro factors.

**Concept and theory**

Factor theory says that assets earn risk premiums because they are exposed to factors that do badly in bad times. GARP Chapter 2 sorts factors into two families. Macro, fundamental-based factors are economy-wide variables: economic growth, inflation, volatility, productivity and demographic risk. Investment, or style, factors are tradeable investment strategies: the market portfolio, value-growth, momentum and so on.

The two families are linked. GARP says the tradeable factors “reflect macro risk and at some level should reflect the underlying fundamental risks of the economy”. The practical difference is implementation. The CAPM market factor is tradeable through low-cost index funds, exchange-traded funds and stock futures. Other dynamic factors are tradeable too. Macro factors such as inflation and growth, however, are not usually directly traded, at least not in scale, with the exception of volatility. So dynamic factors have a big advantage: they can be easily implemented in investors’ portfolios. That is the motivation for building multifactor models such as Fama-French (1993) out of dynamic factors.

|  | Macro factors | Dynamic factors |
|---|---|---|
| Examples | Growth, inflation, volatility, productivity, demography | Market, SMB (size), HML (value), WML (momentum) |
| Directly traded in scale? | Usually not (volatility is the exception) | Yes: long-short portfolios, index products |
| Link to macro risk | They are the macro risks | They reflect macro risk |

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks why the fund implements exposures through dynamic factors. Two facts decide it: (1) macro factors are generally not tradeable in scale, volatility being the stated exception, and (2) dynamic factors are easy to implement while still reflecting macro risk. Any option that breaks the link to macro risk, names the wrong exception, or claims complete replacement fails.

**Fragile fact.** Exception to “macro factors are not traded in scale” is volatility, and dynamic factors reflect (do not escape) macro risk.

**Reference**

LO 84.d: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example. GARP Chapter 2 Factors, Section 2.4 Dynamic Factors (opening paragraph); Section 2.2 Value Investing (two types of factors). Schweser Reading 84, Dynamic Risk Factors, says the same in condensed form (“volatility risk is the exception”); no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 d, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says dynamic factors reflect macro risk; A reverses this into “unrelated to macro risk”. A would be correct only if the stem asked about a strategy deliberately built to be orthogonal to the economy, which no factor in this reading is.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** The one macro factor GARP names as traded in scale is volatility, not economic growth. B swaps in a sibling macro factor. B would be correct if the word “growth” were replaced by “volatility” (for example, through derivatives).

c.reason: C restates GARP Section 2.4 directly: macro factors “are not usually directly traded (at least not in scale, with the exception of volatility), and so dynamic factors have a big advantage that they can be easily implemented”, and these factors “reflect macro risk”.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** D promises that dynamic factors “fully replace” macro factors and remove “any” macro exposure. Because dynamic factors reflect macro risk, holding them does not eliminate exposure to inflation or growth shocks. D would be closer to correct if it said only that dynamic factors are a practical way to obtain factor exposure.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Canadian public pension plan is reviewing a glossary drafted by the plan’s factor investing team. The glossary contains the following four entries.

I. In the assigned reading, “style factors”, “investment factors” and “dynamic factors” are used interchangeably, and practitioners often call the same factors “smart beta” or “alternative beta”.

II. The author prefers the term “dynamic factors” to “smart beta” because, strictly, a beta measures exposure to a factor rather than the factor itself: investors invest in factor portfolios, not betas.

III. The CAPM market factor is a dynamic factor, because its risk premium can be collected only by constantly trading different types of securities.

IV. Many hedge funds and private equity investments are essentially bundles of static factors, which is why they can be replicated by simply going long the market.

Which of the entries are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
II and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
An internal auditor reviews four glossary entries on factor terminology and static versus dynamic factors.

**Concept and theory**

The reading uses several labels for the same family of tradeable factors. In Section 2.4, Ang uses “style factors”, “investment factors” and “dynamic factors” interchangeably, and notes that practitioners often call them “smart beta” or “alternative beta”. In footnote 18 he explains why he prefers “dynamic factors”: technically, beta has the strict meaning of measuring exposure to a factor, rather than the factor itself. “We invest in factor portfolios, not betas.”

Section 2.2 adds a second distinction inside investment factors:

|  | Static factor | Dynamic factor |
|---|---|---|
| How harvested | Simply go long to collect the risk premium | Only by constantly trading different types of securities |
| Example | The CAPM market factor | SMB, HML (and momentum) |
| Packaged as | Index funds, ETFs, futures | Long-short factor portfolios; many hedge funds and private equity investments are bundles of dynamic factors |

Note a small inconsistency inside GARP: Section 2.2 says investment factors include both static and dynamic factors, while Section 2.4 uses “investment factors” interchangeably with “dynamic factors”. Entry I is phrased as the Section 2.4 usage, which is how the reading states it.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each entry against the source. I: matches Section 2.4 word for word (and Schweser’s Professor’s Note). True. II: matches footnote 18. True. III: GARP calls the market a static factor that “we simply go long”. False. IV: GARP says hedge funds and private equity are bundles of dynamic factors, not static ones. False. So only I and II are correct.

**Fragile fact.** Market factor = static (just go long); SMB, HML, WML = dynamic (constant trading); hedge funds and private equity = bundles of dynamic factors.

**Reference**

LO 84.d: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example. GARP Chapter 2 Factors, Section 2.4 Dynamic Factors and footnote 18; Section 2.2 Value Investing (static versus dynamic investment factors). Schweser Reading 84, Professor’s Note under Dynamic Risk Factors, gives the interchangeable terms but omits the static versus dynamic distinction and footnote 18; GARP used for those (Schweser compression, not a version difference).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 d, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: A (I and II only) is the only combination that contains both true entries and neither false entry.

b.reason: **Includes IV: sibling swap.** Entry IV swaps “dynamic” for its sibling “static”. Hedge fund returns come from active trading strategies, which is why GARP calls them bundles of dynamic factors. B would be correct if IV read “bundles of dynamic factors”.

c.reason: **Includes III: sibling swap, omits I.** Entry III attributes the defining property of a dynamic factor (constant trading) to the market factor, which is static. C would be correct only if III described SMB or HML instead of the market, and I were false.

d.reason: **Includes III and IV.** D accepts both sibling swaps and rejects the true footnote 18 point. It would be correct only if static and dynamic were reversed throughout the source.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Japanese asset manager is preparing a short report on the Fama-French (1993) model for the firm’s equity desk. She drafts four statements and must decide which to include.

I. SMB is the return on a portfolio of small stocks minus the return on a portfolio of big stocks, where small and big refer simply to market capitalization.

II. The book-to-market ratio is market capitalization divided by book value, so HML goes long the stocks whose prices are high relative to book value.

III. A value strategy buys stocks with low prices normalized by book value, sales, earnings or dividends; academics often normalize by book value, while practitioners also build value factors on other measures.

IV. Fama and French discovered the size and value effects: before their 1993 paper, neither effect had been documented.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I, III and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
A junior analyst chooses which of four statements on SMB, HML, the book-to-market ratio and the origin of the effects to include in a report.

**Concept and theory**

The Fama-French (1993) model explains expected returns with three factors: the CAPM market factor plus two long-short factors.

- **SMB** (small minus big): the return on small stocks minus the return on big stocks, where small and big refer simply to market capitalization. It captures the outperformance of small firms relative to large firms.
- **HML** (high minus low): the return on a portfolio of high book-to-market stocks minus a portfolio of low book-to-market stocks.

The book-to-market ratio is

$\frac{\text{B}}{\text{M}} = \frac{\text{book value of equity}}{\text{market capitalization}}$ ,

the inverse of equity value normalized by book value. A value strategy buys stocks with low prices normalized by book value, sales, earnings, dividends and so on, and sells stocks with high normalized prices. Academics often normalize by book value; practitioners use other measures when they build their (often proprietary) value factors. So value stocks have low prices relative to book (high B/M) and growth stocks have high prices relative to book (low B/M).

On history, GARP is explicit: Merton (1973) and Ross (1976) developed the multifactor framework, size was documented by Banz (1981) and Reinganum (1981), and modern research into value began with Basu (1977). “Fama and French did not discover these effects; they just provided a parsimonious model to capture their effects.”

**Applying it to this question**

I: correct definition of SMB. True. II: inverts the ratio (market over book) and so reverses which stocks HML buys. False. III: matches GARP’s description of normalization. True. IV: contradicts GARP’s statement that Fama and French did not discover the effects. False.

questions.question: A risk consultant at a Brazilian pension fund is validating a factor data vendor’s methodology note before the fund licenses its Fama-French factor series. The note contains four statements about how the SMB and HML factors are constructed. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.text: SMB and HML are factor mimicking portfolios, constructed to capture the size premium and the value premium respectively.
Because SMB and HML are long-only portfolios of small stocks and of value stocks, holding them adds to an investor’s exposure to the market portfolio.
The factors use the concept of diversification, averaging across many stocks, to ensure that they capture size and value effects.
The construction of HML exploits the common covariation of value stocks, a large part of which cannot be diversified away.

questions.solution:
A consultant validates a vendor’s four statements on how SMB and HML are constructed; find the one that is NOT correct.

**Concept and theory**

A factor in a multifactor model must be something whose return we can observe and, ideally, trade. Fama and French therefore construct SMB and HML as factor mimicking portfolios: portfolios whose returns track the size and value premiums. Three design features matter.

- **Long-short.** Each factor is long one group (small stocks; high book-to-market stocks) and short another (big stocks; low book-to-market stocks). The factors therefore “take positions away from the market portfolio”: they are spreads, not additional market exposure.
- **Diversified.** They use the CAPM and multifactor concept of diversification, averaging across many stocks, so that the factor captures the size or value effect rather than the idiosyncratic moves of a few names.
- **Common covariation.** Value stocks tend to move together; some value risk can be diversified away, but a large amount cannot. Fama and French exploit this common covariation when constructing HML (Section 2.5).

Because each factor is a spread, the average stock has only market exposure: every stock cannot be small and every stock cannot be large.

**Applying it to this question**

This is a NOT question, so look for the single statement that contradicts the source. A, C and D restate GARP. B calls the factors long-only and claims they add market exposure; GARP says they are long-short and take positions away from the market.

**Fragile fact.** SMB and HML are long-short and sit away from the market; long-only small-cap or value funds carry market exposure, the factors themselves do not.

**Reference**

LO 84.d: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example. GARP Chapter 2 Factors, Section 2.4, subsection Fama-French (1993) Model; Section 2.5, Rational Theories of the Value Premium (common covariation). Schweser Reading 84 mentions factor-mimicking portfolios but not the long-short and diversification points; GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 d, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **True.** GARP: SMB and HML “are constructed to be factor mimicking portfolios” that capture size and value premiums. A would be the answer only if it swapped the factors, for example “SMB captures the value premium”.

b.reason: B is the only false statement. Since SMB and HML are long-short spreads, their net market exposure is approximately zero; they add size and value tilts, not market exposure.

c.reason: **True.** GARP: the factors “use the (CAPM and multifactor) concept of diversification to ensure that the factors capture size and value effects by averaging across many stocks”. C would be false if it said the factors were built from a handful of representative stocks.

d.reason: **True.** GARP Section 2.5: “a large amount of value movements cannot be diversified away. (In fact, Fama and French exploit this common covariation in constructing the HML factor.)” D would be false with an absolute claim such as “all value risk can be diversified away”.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at an Australian superannuation fund is comparing two domestic stocks with the Fama-French model. Stock V trades at a high book-to-market ratio, and its management likes to buy companies trading below book value. Stock G trades at a low book-to-market ratio and has grown rapidly through a series of acquisitions. Both stocks have the same market beta, both have SMB betas of approximately zero, and the expected HML return is positive. Relative to the CAPM expected return of each stock, which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Both stocks have positive HML betas because HML carries a positive premium, so the Fama-French model raises both expected returns, with Stock V raised by more.
Stock G has a positive HML beta because fast-growing firms earn high returns, so its expected return is adjusted upward, while Stock V’s is adjusted downward.

Stock V has a positive HML beta and its expected return is adjusted upward by $\beta_{\text{V,HML}} \times$ E$(\text{HML})$; Stock G has a negative HML beta and its expected return is adjusted downward.

Stock V has a positive HML beta and Stock G a negative one, but since E$(\text{HML})$ is positive, both products $\beta\times\text{E}(\text{HML})$ are positive and both expected returns are adjusted upward.

questions.solution:
A portfolio manager compares a high book-to-market stock and a low book-to-market acquisitive stock, both size neutral, against their CAPM expected returns.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Equation (2.2):

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) = \text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{i,MKT}} \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) + \beta_{\text{i,SMB}} \text{E}(\text{SMB}) + \beta_{\text{i,HML}} \text{E}(\text{HML})$,

where $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ is the risk-free rate, E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )$ the market risk premium, E$(\text{SMB})$ and E$(\text{HML})$ the expected returns (premiums) of the size and value factor portfolios, and the $\beta$s are stock i’s loadings on each factor.

With the same market beta in both models, the difference from the CAPM is the extra terms:

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}})^{\text{FF}} - \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{i}})^{\text{CAPM}} = \beta_{\text{i,SMB}} \text{E}(\text{SMB}) + \beta_{\text{i,HML}} \text{E}(\text{HML})$.

HML is constructed to have a positive premium: it goes long high book-to-market (value) stocks, which have high returns, and short low book-to-market (growth) stocks, which have low returns. GARP’s two examples:

| Stock | Type | Sign of $\beta_{\text{i,HML}}$ | Adjustment relative to CAPM |
|---|---|---|---|
| “Huffet” | Value | Positive | Up by $\beta_{\text{i,HML}} \times\text{E}(\text{HML})$ (“valueness”) |
| “Inron” | Growth | Negative | Down, since $\beta_{\text{i,HML}} \times\text{E}(\text{HML}) <$ 0 |

**Applying it to this question**

SMB betas are approximately zero, so only the HML term separates each stock from its CAPM expected return. Stock V: high B/M, a value stock, so $\beta_{\text{V,HML}} >$ 0 and $\beta_{\text{V,HML}}\text{E}(\text{HML}) >$ 0: adjusted up. Stock G: low B/M and acquisitive growth (GARP’s Inron), so $\beta_{\text{G,HML}} <$ 0 and $\beta_{\text{G,HML}}\text{E}(\text{HML}) <$ 0: adjusted down.

**Fragile fact.** Value: $\beta_{\text{i,HML}} >$ 0, adjusted up; growth: $\beta_{\text{i,HML}} <$ 0, adjusted down. The premium E$(\text{HML})$ is positive for both; only the beta sign changes.

**Reference**

LO 84.d: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example. GARP Chapter 2 Factors, Section 2.4, subsection Fama-French (1993) Model (Huffet and Inron examples). Schweser Reading 84, Dynamic Risk Factors, matches; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 d, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error.** A extends the sign of the factor premium to every stock’s beta. The premium is positive, but a stock’s beta sign depends on whether it behaves like value or growth. A would be correct only if both stocks were value stocks with different degrees of valueness.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** B reverses the betas: it gives the growth stock a positive HML beta on the intuition that growth firms earn high returns. In the source, growth stocks have low returns and sit in the short leg of HML. B would be correct only if HML were defined as low minus high book-to-market.

c.reason: C states exactly GARP’s result: the value stock’s expected return is adjusted upward by $\beta_{\text{i,HML}} \times$ E$(\text{HML})$ and the growth stock, with a negative HML beta, is adjusted downward.

d.reason: **Sign error.** D gets the beta signs right but then multiplies a negative beta by a positive premium and reports a positive product. (−) × (+) = (−). D would be correct only if E$(\text{HML})$ were negative, which contradicts the construction of HML.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Chinese life insurer is estimating the expected annual CNY return on a listed stock with the Fama-French three-factor model. She has gathered the following inputs.

| Expected return input | % p.a. | Stock factor loading | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Risk-free rate | 2.0 | Market beta | 0.90 |
| Market portfolio | 8.0 | SMB beta | 0.40 |
| Small-cap portfolio | 10.5 | HML beta | −0.60 |
| Big-cap portfolio | 7.3 | Stock return volatility | 28% |
| High book-to-market portfolio | 11.2 |  |  |
| Low book-to-market portfolio | 6.4 |  |  |
| Past winners / past losers portfolios | 14.0 / 5.0 |  |  |

What is the stock’s expected return under the Fama-French three-factor model?
questions.solution:
An insurer’s analyst computes a stock’s Fama-French expected return from portfolio leg returns, with momentum legs and volatility as irrelevant data.

**Concept and theory**

In Equation (2.2), each dynamic factor enters as an expected return on a long-short portfolio, not as the return on one leg. The market factor enters as an excess return over the risk-free rate.

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) = \text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{i,MKT}} \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) + \beta_{\text{i,SMB}} \text{E}(\text{SMB}) + \beta_{\text{i,HML}} \text{E}(\text{HML})$

with

E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) = \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ , E$(\text{SMB}) = \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{small}}) - \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{big}})$,

E$(\text{HML}) = \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{high B/M}}) - \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{low B/M}})$.

Each beta is the stock’s sensitivity to that factor; a negative beta on a positive premium lowers the expected return.

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1, market risk premium:

E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) =$ 8.0% − 2.0% = 6.0%

Step 2, size premium:

E$(\text{SMB}) =$ 10.5% − 7.3% = 3.2%

Step 3, value premium:

E$(\text{HML}) =$ 11.2% − 6.4% = 4.8%

Step 4, factor contributions:

$\beta_{\text{i,MKT}} \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) =$ 0.90 × 6.0% = 5.40%

$\beta_{\text{i,SMB}} \text{E}(\text{SMB}) =$ 0.40 × 3.2% = 1.28%

$\beta_{\text{i,HML}} \text{E}(\text{HML}) = -$0.60 × 4.8% = −2.88%

Step 5, expected return:

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) =$ 2.0% + 5.40% + 1.28% − 2.88% = 5.80%

The winner and loser returns are irrelevant (the three-factor model has no WML term), and the stock’s volatility is irrelevant (only factor loadings price risk in the model). The result means that the stock’s growth tilt (negative HML beta) costs it 2.88 points of expected return, more than offsetting its small-cap tilt.

**Fragile fact.** Market enters as E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ ; SMB and HML enter as leg differences; keep the sign of a negative HML beta.

**Reference**

LO 84.d: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example. GARP Chapter 2 Factors, Section 2.4, subsection Fama-French (1993) Model, Equation (2.2). Schweser Reading 84 prints the same three-factor equation (image not extracted in the text file; the notation here follows GARP).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 d, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: 5.80% is the Equation (2.2) value with every factor premium formed as long leg minus short leg and every beta applied with its sign.

b.reason: 2.0% + 5.40% = 7.40% is the CAPM part of the computation: the analyst stopped before adding the SMB and HML terms. It would be correct if both SMB and HML betas were zero.

c.reason: The market return was used in place of the market risk premium: 2.0% + 0.90 × 8.0% + 1.28% − 2.88% = 7.60%. It would be correct if the table listed 8.0% as the market risk premium.

d.reason: The negative HML beta was treated as positive: 2.0% + 5.40% + 1.28% + 2.88% = 11.56%. It would be correct if the stock were a value stock with an HML beta of +0.60.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a UK general insurer is asked by a board member why the insurer’s investment team uses the Fama-French model rather than the CAPM to set expected returns for its equity portfolio. Which of the following statements best describes what the Fama-French model does and does not do?

options.text: Like the CAPM for the market factor, the Fama-French model supplies an economic theory that explains and determines the size of the value premium.
The Fama-French model replaces the CAPM market factor with SMB and HML, so a stock’s market beta no longer enters its expected return.
Under the CAPM logic retained in the model, stocks with high market betas are expected to earn lower average returns than the market, because they fall in parallel when the market falls.
The Fama-French model adds SMB and HML alongside the market factor, giving a parsimonious model of size and value effects that is silent on why value carries a premium.

questions.solution:
A CRO explains to a board member what the Fama-French model adds to the CAPM and what it leaves unexplained.

**Concept and theory**

The CAPM is a single-factor model. Its insight: when the market does poorly, high-beta stocks also do badly (they “tank in parallel when the market tanks”), so over the long run they must offer higher average returns than the market to compensate investors for losses in bad times, which the CAPM defines as low market returns.

Merton (1973) and Ross (1976) built the theoretical multifactor framework, but it took two decades of empirical work to show that factors other than the market mattered. The Fama-French model keeps the market factor and adds SMB and HML alongside it. Fama and French did not discover the size and value effects; they provided a parsimonious model to capture them.

What the model does not do is explain the value premium. GARP: “The Fama-French model itself is silent on why value carries a premium. In contrast, the CAPM provides a theory of how the market factor is priced and even determines the risk premium of the market.” Explaining the premium requires the rational and behavioral stories of LO 84.a and 84.e.

|  | CAPM | Fama-French (1993) |
|---|---|---|
| Factors | Market only | Market + SMB + HML |
| Theory of factor pricing | Yes (market risk premium determined) | No: silent on why value is priced |
| Role of market beta | Sole driver | Still enters, alongside size and value betas |

**Applying it to this question**

The board member asks what the model does and does not do. The deciding facts: it adds (does not replace) factors, it is a parsimonious empirical description, and it offers no theory for the value premium.

**Fragile fact.** CAPM: theory that prices the market factor. Fama-French: adds size and value, explains none of them.

**Reference**

LO 84.d: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example. GARP Chapter 2 Factors, Section 2.4, subsection Fama-French (1993) Model (CAPM recap, Merton and Ross); Section 2.5, Rational Theories of the Value Premium (model silent on why value is priced). Schweser Reading 84 covers the CAPM recap but not the “silent” point; GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 d, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** A attributes to the Fama-French model the CAPM’s property of providing a pricing theory for its factor. A would be correct if it said “the CAPM supplies a theory that determines the market risk premium”.

b.reason: **Scope error.** SMB and HML are added to, not substituted for, the market factor; the market beta still enters Equation (2.2). B would be correct only for a pure size-and-value model that drops the market term, which is not the Fama-French model.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** The CAPM predicts that high-beta stocks earn higher average returns than the market, as compensation for falling with the market in bad times. C reverses “higher” to “lower”.

d.reason: D captures all three points: SMB and HML are added alongside the market factor, the model is parsimonious, and it is silent on why value carries a premium.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a German manufacturer is reviewing the EUR equity allocation of the company’s pension scheme. One holding is a fund that fully replicates a broad capitalization-weighted index of the whole equity market. The analyst wants the fund’s expected return under the Fama-French model, using the following inputs.

| Input | % p.a. |
|---|---|
| Risk-free rate | 3.0 |
| Expected market return | 8.5 |
| Expected SMB return | 2.0 |
| Expected HML return | 3.5 |
| Expected WML (momentum) return | 6.0 |
| Fund return volatility | 15.2 |

What is the best estimate of the fund’s expected return?
questions.solution:
A treasury analyst estimates the Fama-French expected return of a fund that replicates the whole capitalization-weighted market.

**Concept and theory**

In the CAPM, the average stock has a beta of one, which is also the beta of the market. In the Fama-French model, the SMB and HML betas are centered around zero. GARP: “The market is actually size neutral and value neutral. Just as the average investor holds the market, the average stock does not have any size or value tilt. It just has market exposure.” This follows from construction: SMB and HML are long-short spreads, and every stock cannot be small and every stock cannot be large. An investor must deliberately choose a size or value tilt to earn those premiums.

| Portfolio | $\beta_{\text{i,MKT}}$ | $\beta_{\text{i,SMB}}$ | $\beta_{\text{i,HML}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Whole market (average stock) | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| Value tilt | around 1 | any | > 0 |
| Growth tilt | around 1 | any | \< 0 |

**Applying it to this question**

The fund replicates the whole market, so $\beta_{\text{i,MKT}} =$ 1, $\beta_{\text{i,SMB}} =$ 0, $\beta_{\text{i,HML}} =$ 0.

E$(\text{r}) = \text{r}_{\text{f}} +$ 1 $\times\left[\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} \right] +$ 0 $\times\text{E}(\text{SMB}) +$ 0 $\times\text{E}(\text{HML})$

E$(\text{r}) =$ 3.0% + 1 × (8.5% − 3.0%) = 3.0% + 5.5% = 8.50%

The SMB, HML and WML premiums and the fund volatility are excess data: the market has no tilt, and the three-factor model has no WML term. The answer means that, under Fama-French, the market earns exactly its CAPM expected return; size and value premiums are earned only by tilting away from it.

**Fragile fact.** Average stock: market beta 1, SMB and HML betas 0 (not 1).

**Reference**

LO 84.d: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example. GARP Chapter 2 Factors, Section 2.4, subsection Fama-French (1993) Model (betas centered around zero; market size and value neutral). Schweser Reading 84 states the same; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 d, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: 1 × (8.5% − 3.0%) = 5.50% is the market risk premium without adding back $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ . It would be correct if the question asked for the expected excess return.

b.reason: 8.50% applies GARP’s statement that the market is size and value neutral, so only the market term survives.

c.reason: 3.0% + 1 × 8.5% = 11.50% treats the expected market return as the market premium. It would be correct if 8.5% were labelled as E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )$.

d.reason: 3.0% + 5.5% + 1 × 2.0% + 1 × 3.5% = 14.00% carries the CAPM result “average beta equals one” over to SMB and HML. In the Fama-French model those betas are centered on zero. D would be correct for a fund deliberately built with unit loadings on both size and value.

The chief compliance officer of a US wealth manager is checking whether an external equity fund matches its stated “small-cap growth” mandate. The fund’s monthly excess returns over ten years are regressed on the Fama-French factors, with the following results.

| Coefficient | Estimate | t-statistic |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha (% per month) | 0.05 | 0.6 |
| Market | 1.08 | 31.4 |
| SMB | −0.35 | −6.2 |
| HML | 0.62 | 9.8 |

The regression $\text{R}^{2}$ is 0.91. Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: The fund tilts toward small-cap stocks and toward value stocks, so only the growth part of the mandate is contradicted.
The fund tilts toward large-cap stocks and toward growth stocks, so only the small-cap part of the mandate is contradicted.
The market loading of 1.08 shows that the fund essentially holds the market, so its size and value loadings can be disregarded as noise.
The fund tilts toward large-cap stocks and toward value stocks, so both parts of the mandate are contradicted.

questions.solution:
A compliance officer checks a “small-cap growth” fund’s Fama-French regression loadings against its mandate.

**Concept and theory**

Using dynamic factors in a multifactor model is not only about forecasting expected returns: the estimated loadings describe a portfolio’s style. Regress the portfolio’s excess return on the factor returns:

$\text{r}_{\text{p}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} = \alpha+ \beta_{\text{p,MKT}}(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) + \beta_{\text{p,SMB}}$ SMB $+ \beta_{\text{p,HML}}$ HML $+ \epsilon$.

Because SMB and HML betas are centered on zero for the market and the average stock, a loading far from zero is a deliberate tilt:

| Loading | Positive | Negative |
|---|---|---|
| SMB (small minus big) | Small-cap tilt | Large-cap tilt |
| HML (high minus low B/M) | Value tilt | Growth tilt |

**Applying it to this question**

SMB = −0.35 (t = −6.2): significantly negative, so the fund moves with big stocks against small stocks: a large-cap tilt. HML = +0.62 (t = 9.8): significantly positive, so the fund moves with value stocks against growth stocks: a value tilt. Mandate: small-cap (needs SMB > 0) and growth (needs HML \< 0). Both signs are the opposite of the mandate. Alpha, its t-statistic and $\text{R}^{2}$ are not needed for the style conclusion.

**Fragile fact.** Sign of the loading tells the side: positive SMB = small, negative SMB = big; positive HML = value, negative HML = growth.

**Reference**

LO 84.d: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example. GARP Chapter 2 Factors, Section 2.4, subsection Fama-French (1993) Model (definitions of SMB and HML; value has positive and growth negative HML beta; betas centered around zero). Schweser Reading 84 matches; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 d, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip on SMB.** A reads the negative SMB loading as a small-cap tilt. SMB is small minus big, so a negative loading means the fund behaves like big stocks. A would be correct if the SMB loading were +0.35.

b.reason: **Polarity flip on HML.** B reads the positive HML loading as a growth tilt. HML is long high book-to-market (value), so a positive loading is a value tilt. B would be correct if the HML loading were −0.62.

c.reason: **Scope error.** C uses the market loading near one to dismiss the other loadings. A market beta near one is consistent with any size or value tilt; the market itself has SMB and HML betas of zero, so loadings of −0.35 and +0.62 with large t-statistics are genuine tilts. C would be correct only if both loadings were close to zero and insignificant.

d.reason: D reads both signs correctly (large-cap, value) and therefore concludes that both parts of the mandate are contradicted.

| Risk-free rate | 1.5 | Market beta | 1.15 |
| Market risk premium, E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )$ | 5.5 | SMB beta | 0.30 |
| E$(\text{SMB})$ | 2.5 | HML beta | −0.85 |
| E$(\text{HML})$ | 4.0 |  |  |

Compared with the analyst’s CAPM expected return, the Fama-French expected return is:

options.text: 4.15 percentage points lower.
3.40 percentage points lower.
2.65 percentage points lower.
2.65 percentage points higher.

questions.solution:
A risk committee member compares a stock’s Fama-French and CAPM expected returns, holding the market beta fixed.

**Concept and theory**

With Equation (2.2) and the CAPM sharing the same market beta, the risk-free rate and the market term cancel when the two expected returns are compared:

$\Delta\equiv\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{i}})^{\text{FF}} - \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{i}})^{\text{CAPM}}$

$= \left[\text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{i,MKT}}\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) + \beta_{\text{i,SMB}}\text{E}(\text{SMB}) + \beta_{\text{i,HML}}\text{E}(\text{HML})\right]$

$- \left[\text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{i,MKT}}\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )\right]$

$= \beta_{\text{i,SMB}} \text{E}(\text{SMB}) + \beta_{\text{i,HML}} \text{E}(\text{HML})$.

GARP’s description: relative to the CAPM, a value stock’s expected return is adjusted up by $\beta_{\text{i,HML}} \times\text{E}(\text{HML})$, and a growth stock’s (negative $\beta_{\text{i,HML}}$) is adjusted down. When the stock also has a size loading, the SMB term adds its own adjustment.

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1, size adjustment:

$\beta_{\text{i,SMB}} \text{E}(\text{SMB}) =$ 0.30 × 2.5% = +0.75%

Step 2, value adjustment:

$\beta_{\text{i,HML}} \text{E}(\text{HML}) = -$0.85 × 4.0% = −3.40%

Step 3, total difference:

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}})^{\text{FF}} - \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{i}})^{\text{CAPM}} =$ 0.75% − 3.40% = −2.65%

Check by full computation: CAPM = 1.5% + 1.15 × 5.5% = 7.825%; Fama-French = 7.825% + 0.75% − 3.40% = 5.175%; difference −2.65 points. The risk-free rate, the market premium and the market beta are irrelevant to the difference. The meaning: the stock’s growth tilt cuts its required return by more than its small-cap tilt adds, so the CAPM forecast is too high.

**Fragile fact.** FF minus CAPM is only the extra factor terms; a negative HML beta pulls the expected return below the CAPM.

**Reference**

LO 84.d: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example. GARP Chapter 2 Factors, Section 2.4, subsection Fama-French (1993) Model, Equation (2.2) and the Inron (growth stock) example. Schweser Reading 84 matches; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 d, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: −0.75% − 3.40% = −4.15% treats the positive SMB term as negative. It would be correct if the SMB beta were −0.30 (a large-cap growth stock).

b.reason: −3.40% is only the HML adjustment, the textbook “growth stock adjusted down by $\beta_{\text{i,HML}}\text{E}(\text{HML})$” with the size term omitted. It would be correct if the SMB beta were zero.

c.reason: −2.65 points is the sum of both extra Fama-French terms with their signs: the Fama-French expected return is 2.65 percentage points lower.

d.reason: The magnitude is right but the direction is reversed, as if a negative HML beta raised the expected return. It would be correct if both loadings had the opposite signs, a large-cap value stock with $\beta_{\text{i,SMB}} = -$0.30 and $\beta_{\text{i,HML}} = +$0.85: −0.75% + 3.40% = +2.65%.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-2 d Q11
questions.question: A model validation analyst at a Japanese trust bank is reviewing an equity risk model that applies the Fama-French model with betas estimated on 2000 to 2006 data and then held fixed. In the 2008 financial crisis, realized losses on the bank’s risky equity holdings were materially larger than the model implied, even though the factor returns themselves were measured correctly. Which of the following statements best explains the shortfall?

options.text: The CAPM and Fama-French models both assume constant betas, but exposures of some assets to systematic factors rise during bad times, making losses larger than constant betas imply.
Unlike the CAPM, the Fama-French model allows betas to vary over time, so the shortfall must come from a missing factor rather than from variation in the betas themselves.
Betas tend to fall during bad times as investors reduce risk, so a constant-beta model should have overstated the losses; the shortfall must therefore reflect estimation error.
Only the market beta can vary over time: SMB and HML betas are centered around zero, so time variation in them cannot contribute to the shortfall.

questions.solution:
A model validator explains why a fixed-beta Fama-French risk model understated 2008 losses.

**Concept and theory**

Equation (2.2) treats each $\beta$ as a fixed number. GARP flags this as an important assumption of both the CAPM and the Fama-French model: “the betas are constant”. Empirically, the exposures of some assets to systematic factors vary over time and, in particular, increase during bad times (Ang and Chen, 2002). Two consequences follow:

- The variation of betas is itself a source of risk.
- Because betas rose in the financial crisis, the negative returns of risky assets were larger than they would have been had betas stayed constant.

A constant-beta model fitted in calm years therefore uses betas that are too low for a crisis and understates losses.

**Applying it to this question**

The factor returns were measured correctly, so the error lies in the exposures. Betas estimated on 2000 to 2006 and frozen are too low for 2008, when betas rose. The model understated the losses: exactly GARP’s mechanism.

**Fragile fact.** Betas rise (not fall) in bad times; the constant-beta assumption belongs to both the CAPM and Fama-French.

**Reference**

LO 84.d: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example. GARP Chapter 2 Factors, Section 2.4, subsection Fama-French (1993) Model, final paragraph and footnote 19 (Ang and Chen, 2002). Schweser Reading 84: “the CAPM and Fama-French models assume betas are constant, but empirical research indicates they vary and increase during bad times”; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 d, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: A states the assumption (constant betas in both models), the empirical fact (exposures vary and rise in bad times) and the consequence (larger losses than constant betas imply), all from GARP Section 2.4.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** B gives the Fama-French model a property it does not have. GARP says the assumption of constant betas is shared by both the CAPM and the Fama-French model. B would be correct only for a conditional (time-varying beta) model.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C reverses the direction of beta variation. Betas increase in bad times, so constant betas understate, not overstate, crisis losses. C would be correct if betas fell during crises.

d.reason: **Scope error.** D confuses the cross-sectional statement “SMB and HML betas are centered around zero” (true for the average stock at a point in time) with a claim that individual SMB and HML betas cannot change over time. GARP’s evidence on time-varying exposures is about factor exposures in general (and, in Section 2.5, value stocks’ betas rise in bad times). D would be correct only if the stem were about the average stock’s loadings.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a US asset manager is training new analysts on how a further dynamic factor, momentum (WML, past winners minus past losers), can be added to the Fama-French model:

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) = \text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{i,MKT}} \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) + \beta_{\text{i,SMB}} \text{E}(\text{SMB}) + \beta_{\text{i,HML}} \text{E}(\text{HML}) + \beta_{\text{i,WML}} \text{E}(\text{WML})$.

Which of the following statements about the extended model is most accurate?

options.text: Because the momentum premium is positive, adding WML raises the expected return of every stock relative to the three-factor model.
As with SMB and HML, momentum betas are centered around zero and winner stocks have positive momentum betas; the market, neither a relative winner nor loser, is simply the market.
Loser stocks have positive momentum betas because they are expected to rebound, so their risk premiums are adjusted upward under the extended model.
Momentum compares a single stock’s current return with its own past returns over time, so the market as a whole can have a large positive momentum beta.

questions.solution:
A trainer explains how adding momentum (WML) to the Fama-French model works.

**Concept and theory**

The Fama-French framework is open-ended: any tradeable dynamic factor can be added as a further long-short portfolio. Momentum is the standard example. WML (past winners minus past losers, also called UMD) is long stocks that have gone up over the past six or so months and short those with the lowest returns. Adding it gives GARP Equation (2.4):

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) = \text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{i,MKT}} \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) + \beta_{\text{i,SMB}} \text{E}(\text{SMB}) + \beta_{\text{i,HML}} \text{E}(\text{HML}) + \beta_{\text{i,WML}} \text{E}(\text{WML})$.

GARP: “The same intuition applies as with the Fama-French model. The momentum beta, $\beta_{\text{i,WML}}$, is centered around zero. Winner stocks have positive momentum betas; their risk premiums are adjusted upward. Loser stocks have negative momentum betas; their risk premiums are adjusted downward. The market, neither a relative winner nor a relative loser, is simply the market.” Like size and value, momentum is a cross-sectional strategy: it compares one group of stocks with another at the same time, and winners and losers are always relative. (Carhart (1997) first added momentum this way.)

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are the centering at zero, the sign pattern (winners positive, losers negative) and the market’s neutrality, all of which mirror SMB and HML.

**Fragile fact.** WML betas are centered on zero (not one); losers negative; the market has no momentum tilt.

**Reference**

LO 84.d: Explain how dynamic risk factors can be used in a multifactor model of asset returns, using the Fama-French model as an example. GARP Chapter 2 Factors, Section 2.5 Value Factor, subsection Momentum Investing, Equation (2.4) and footnote 33. Boundary note: Schweser prints the momentum extension in the LO 84.e text; it is included here once, only as an example of adding a dynamic factor to a multifactor model, and momentum’s risk and return profile is left to LO 84.e. No content conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 d, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** A says adding WML raises “every” stock’s expected return. Because momentum betas are centered on zero, losers (negative $\beta_{\text{i,WML}}$) are adjusted downward and the market is unchanged. A would be correct only for a portfolio known to have a positive momentum beta.

b.reason: B reproduces GARP’s description of Equation (2.4): same intuition as Fama-French, momentum betas centered around zero, winners positive, and the market is simply the market.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C gives losers positive momentum betas on a reversal intuition. In Equation (2.4) losers have negative momentum betas and their risk premiums are adjusted downward. C would be correct if WML were defined as losers minus winners.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** D describes a time-series comparison of a stock with its own past. GARP says momentum, like size and value, is cross-sectional: winners and losers are relative, so the market as a whole is neither. D would be correct only for a time-series trend rule applied to a single asset, which is not the WML factor.

questions.loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-2 e Q1
questions.question:
A junior quantitative analyst at a Singapore asset manager is preparing a training example for newly hired analysts. She ranks a six-stock universe and builds two long-short books. Each book is long the top two and short the bottom two stocks on its own ranking variable, and the middle two stocks are not held. One is a value-growth (HML-style) book and the other a momentum (WML-style) book. Market capitalization is shown for information only.

| Stock | Book-to-market | Past six-month return (%) | Market cap (SGD bn) |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | 1.92 | −18 | 0.9 |
| Q | 0.28 | +41 | 22.0 |
| R | 1.35 | +26 | 1.4 |
| S | 0.36 | −12 | 15.3 |
| T | 0.85 | +4 | 3.1 |
| U | 1.10 | −27 | 6.8 |

Which of the following statements about the two books is correct?

options.text: Stock U, with the worst past return and a book-to-market ratio above 1.0, is held long by the value book and short by the momentum book.
Stocks P and Q are held in opposite directions by the two books, while Stock R is held long by both books.
Stock Q is held long by the value book, because its high price relative to book value marks it as the market’s preferred stock.
Stock P is held long by both books, because momentum investors buy stocks that have fallen far enough to become cheap.

questions.solution:
Six-stock universe ranked on book-to-market (value) and on past six-month return (momentum); which stock positions are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Both strategies are dynamic, long-short factor portfolios, but they rank stocks on different variables. A value-growth strategy (the Fama-French HML factor) goes long stocks with high book-to-market ratios (value stocks: low prices relative to book value) and short stocks with low book-to-market ratios (growth stocks: high prices relative to book value). A momentum strategy (WML, “winners minus losers”, also called UMD, “up minus down”) buys stocks that have gone up over the past six (or so) months and shorts the stocks with the lowest returns over the same period. GARP stresses that momentum, like size and value, is a cross-sectional strategy: it compares one group of stocks against another group at the same time, so winners and losers are always relative to each other, and the market as a whole can go up or down. The same relativity holds for value: a stock is “value” only relative to the rest of the universe.

|  | Value (HML) | Momentum (WML / UMD) |
|---|---|---|
| Ranking variable | Book-to-market (price normalized by book) | Past return, about six months |
| Long leg | High book-to-market (value) | Past winners |
| Short leg | Low book-to-market (growth) | Past losers |
| Nature | Cross-sectional, relative | Cross-sectional, relative |

**Applying it to this question**

Value ranking (book-to-market, high to low): P 1.92, R 1.35, U 1.10, T 0.85, S 0.36, Q 0.28. Long P and R; short S and Q; U and T not held.

Momentum ranking (past return, high to low): Q +41, R +26, T +4, S −12, P −18, U −27. Long Q and R; short P and U; T and S not held.

Resulting positions: P is long value and short momentum; Q is short value and long momentum; R is long in both; S is short value only; U is short momentum only; T is in neither. Market capitalization is irrelevant: it is the ranking variable of the size factor, not of either book.

**Fragile fact.** Momentum sorts on past returns (about six months) and value sorts on price relative to book; both are relative, cross-sectional sorts, and a stock that has fallen hard is typically long in value and short in momentum.

**Reference**

LO 84.e: “Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Value Factor, subsection “Momentum Investing” (definition of WML/UMD, cross-sectional nature); Section 2.4 Dynamic Factors, “Fama-French (1993) Model” (construction of HML). Schweser Module 84.3, “Momentum Investing”. No GARP and Schweser difference on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 e, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The momentum half is right (U has the worst return, so it is shorted), but value is a relative ranking, not an absolute threshold of 1.0. U ranks third of six on book-to-market and is not held by the value book. A would be correct if the value book went long the top three stocks.

b.reason: P (cheap after a fall) and Q (expensive after a rise) are held in opposite directions, and R ranks second on both variables, so both books are long it. This matches the source definitions: value is long high and short low book-to-market; momentum is long past winners and short past losers.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** Value goes long low prices relative to book value (high book-to-market) and short high prices relative to book. Q has the lowest book-to-market, so value shorts it. C would be correct for a growth tilt (long low book-to-market).

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** “Buying what has fallen far enough to become cheap” is the value (negative feedback) behavior. Momentum shorts past losers, so it is short P. D would be correct only if the second book were a second value book.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Canadian public pension plan is preparing a report for the investment committee on the historical record of US style factors from January 1965 to December 2011, ahead of a proposed CAD 2 billion factor mandate. Which of the following statements is most appropriate to include in the report?

options.text: The cumulated value (HML) return peaked in the early 1980s, shortly after the effect was first published, and value has shown no reliable premium since then.
Momentum’s cumulated profits exceeded those of value and size by an order of magnitude, and its return distribution was positively skewed because winners kept winning.
Value produced gains in every multi-year window of the sample, which is why the value premium is described as earned consistently rather than only on average.
Momentum’s cumulated profits were an order of magnitude larger than those of value and size, but the strategy was negatively skewed and prone to periodic crashes.

questions.solution:
Report statement on the 1965 to 2011 record of value, size and momentum: which is most appropriate?

**Concept and theory**

A factor’s “return profile” has two sides: how much it has earned on average and how it earns it. GARP’s Figure 2.6 plots cumulated returns from January 1965 to December 2011 for SMB, HML and WML. Momentum returns “blow size and value out of the water”: cumulated momentum profits have been an order of magnitude larger than cumulated profits on size and value. The risk side is the opposite: momentum is prone to periodic crashes, some lasting for extended periods, and momentum strategies are negatively skewed (skewness of −1.43 for the strategy in Figure 2.6). Value, by contrast, is described as robust: unlike size, it has produced gains over the last fifty years, but with notable losing periods (the early-1990s recession, the late-1990s Internet bull market and the 2007 to 2008 financial crisis). Value is risky precisely because it can underperform growth for extended periods; its premium is earned on average, not consistently. Size is the factor whose cumulated returns peaked in the early 1980s, after Banz (1981) and Reinganum (1981) were published.

|  | Value (HML) | Momentum (WML) |
|---|---|---|
| Cumulated return 1965 to 2011 | Robust, positive | Order of magnitude larger |
| Main risk | Long losing spells (early 1990s, late 1990s, 2007 to 2008) | Periodic crashes, negative skew (−1.43) |

**Applying it to this question**

The report statement must get both the size of the momentum premium and the shape of its risk right. Only D says “order of magnitude larger” and “negatively skewed and prone to periodic crashes”.

**Fragile fact.** Momentum: much higher average return but negative skew (−1.43); value: robust but with long losing spells; size: peaked in the early 1980s.

**Reference**

LO 84.e: “Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Value Factor (opening discussion of HML in Figure 2.5), subsections “Momentum Investing” and “Implications for Asset Owners” (skewness −1.43); Section 2.4, “Size Factor”. Schweser Module 84.3 reports the WML dollar reaching more than \$60 and falling below \$30 in 2007 to 2009, read from Figure 2.6; the GARP text in the project does not state these figure values, so they are not used to decide the answer. Schweser omits the −1.43 skewness (GARP only).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 e, where it is Q2 of 14.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Peaking in the early 1980s right after publication, with no premium since, is the record of size (SMB), not value. Value is the robust factor. A would be correct if it described SMB.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** The magnitude claim is right, but momentum is negatively, not positively, skewed. “Winners keep winning” describes the average return, not the tail: the crashes give the left tail. B would be correct with “negatively skewed because of periodic crashes”.

c.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** Value lost money over several multi-year spells (early 1990s, late 1990s, 2007 to 2008). GARP says rational stories must define bad times “so that value earns a premium on average”. C would be correct only if “every multi-year window” were replaced by “on average over the sample”.

d.reason: GARP: “The cumulated profits on momentum strategies have been an order of magnitude larger than cumulated profits on size and value” and “Momentum strategies are negatively skewed; the skewness of the momentum strategy in Figure 2.6 is −1.43”; momentum “is prone to periodic crashes”.

questions.question: At a risk committee meeting of a Japanese life insurer that is considering a JPY 50 billion allocation split between a value (HML) sleeve and a momentum (WML) sleeve, a board member argues: “Value buys what has fallen and momentum buys what has risen, so the two premiums are mirror images. Holding both will net out, and a model containing both factors must be close to perfectly collinear.” Which response by the CRO, based on the US evidence for 1965 to 2011, is most accurate?

options.text: The HML-WML correlation was only about −0.16, so the returns are not mirror images; the strategies are opposite only in that value is negative feedback (stabilizing) and momentum is positive feedback (destabilizing).

The HML-WML correlation was only about −0.16, so the returns are not mirror images; the strategies are opposite only in that value is positive feedback (destabilizing) and momentum is negative feedback (stabilizing).

The HML-WML correlation was only about −0.16, so the returns are not mirror images; the strategies differ in that momentum compares each stock with its own past returns over time, while value is cross-sectional.
The HML-WML correlation was close to −1, so the member is right that the premiums largely offset, even though value is stabilizing and momentum is destabilizing in their feedback effects on prices.

questions.solution:
Board member claims value and momentum premiums are mirror images and collinear; which CRO response is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

It is tempting to see value and momentum as opposites: value buys stocks whose prices have fallen (they become cheap), while momentum buys stocks whose prices have risen. GARP separates two senses of “opposite”. In returns, they are not opposite: in Figure 2.6 (1965 to 2011) the correlation of HML with WML is only −16%, that is about −0.16. A correlation near −1 would mean one premium is the mirror image of the other; −0.16 means the two are close to independent with a mild negative tilt, so a portfolio holding both diversifies rather than nets out, and a four-factor model is not close to perfectly collinear. The one sense in which they are opposite is feedback. Value is a negative feedback strategy: stocks with declining prices eventually fall far enough to become value stocks, value investors then buy them, and value is inherently stabilizing. Momentum is a positive feedback strategy: stocks with high past returns are attractive, momentum investors keep buying them, they keep rising, and positive feedback strategies are ultimately destabilizing and subject to periodic crashes.

**Applying it to this question**

The member makes two claims: (i) returns are mirror images; (ii) the model must be near perfectly collinear. Both rest on a correlation near −1. The evidence of −0.16 rejects both, and the correct response must also locate the real sense of opposition, feedback, with the correct polarity: value negative and stabilizing, momentum positive and destabilizing.

**Fragile fact.** Correlation of HML with WML: only about −0.16 (not −1). “Opposite” refers only to feedback: value negative (stabilizing), momentum positive (destabilizing).

**Reference**

LO 84.e: “Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Value Factor, subsection “Momentum Investing”. Schweser Module 84.3 agrees; no difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 e, where it is Q3 of 14.

a.reason: GARP: “Momentum returns are not the opposite of value returns: in Figure 2.6, the correlation of HML with WML is only −16%” and “There is one sense in which momentum is the opposite of value. Value is a negative feedback strategy . . . Momentum is a positive feedback strategy.”

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Reverses both feedback labels. Value is the negative feedback, stabilizing strategy; momentum is the positive feedback, destabilizing one. B would be correct only with the two strategy names swapped.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Attributes a time-series nature to momentum. GARP is explicit that momentum, like size and value, is a cross-sectional strategy that compares winners with losers “rather than looking at a single stock over time”. C would be correct for a time-series trend rule, which is not the WML factor.

d.reason: **Wrong input, number.** Replaces the observed correlation of about −0.16 with about −1, which is exactly the member’s error. D would be correct only if HML and WML were near perfect negative correlates, which the 1965 to 2011 data reject.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-2 e Q4
questions.question:
A risk consultant is reviewing a client memo on how value and momentum strategies interact with market prices and with portfolio rebalancing. The memo contains the following statements:

I. Value is a negative feedback strategy: stocks whose prices decline eventually fall far enough to become value stocks, value investors then buy them, and this is inherently stabilizing.

II. Momentum is a positive feedback strategy: stocks with high past returns attract momentum buyers and keep rising, so the strategy is ultimately destabilizing and subject to periodic crashes.

III. Because momentum is a cross-sectional strategy, rebalancing should also be carried out primarily at the level of individual stocks, which can be relied on to exist over the long run.

IV. Momentum is primarily a cross-sectional strategy within an asset class, whereas rebalancing should be done primarily at the asset class or strategy level.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I, II and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Client memo with four statements on feedback and rebalancing: which are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Feedback describes how a strategy’s own trading pushes prices. Under negative feedback (value), a falling price eventually makes a stock cheap enough to be a value stock; value investors buy it, pushing the price back up, so the strategy leans against price moves and is inherently stabilizing. Under positive feedback (momentum), a rising price attracts momentum buyers whose buying makes it rise further, so the strategy amplifies price moves and is ultimately destabilizing and subject to periodic crashes.

GARP then links this to rebalancing. Momentum is “primarily a cross-sectional strategy within an asset class”, whereas “rebalancing, in contrast, should be done primarily at the asset class or strategy level because rebalancing requires the assets or strategies to exist over the long run while individual equities can disappear”. So holding momentum does not conflict with rebalancing: the two operate at different levels. Schweser condenses this to “An investor following a momentum strategy should still rebalance their portfolio.”

**Applying it to this question**

I: matches the value negative feedback description. True.

II: matches the momentum positive feedback description, including crashes. True.

III: claims rebalancing should be at the individual stock level because stocks exist over the long run; GARP says the opposite: individual equities can disappear, so rebalancing belongs at asset class or strategy level. False.

IV: matches GARP’s statement on levels. True.

Correct set: I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Momentum: cross-sectional within an asset class. Rebalancing: primarily at asset class or strategy level, because individual stocks can disappear. A momentum investor still rebalances.

**Reference**

LO 84.e: “Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Value Factor, subsection “Momentum Investing”. Schweser Module 84.3 (“should still rebalance”) omits the asset class versus stock level reasoning (GARP only).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 e, where it is Q4 of 14.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Brazilian multi-manager fund reviews two stocks in her BRL 800 million equity universe. Over the past six months, Stock X has fallen 35% and now has one of the highest book-to-market ratios in the universe, while Stock Y has risen 40% and now has one of the lowest. She wants to explain to her team how value and momentum investors acting on these stocks affect prices. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.text: Value buying of X is a positive feedback that destabilizes prices, while momentum buying of Y is a negative feedback that stabilizes prices.
Momentum investors are the natural buyers of X because it has fallen far enough to become cheap, and value investors are the natural buyers of Y because its rise confirms strong growth.
Value buying of X stabilizes prices, and momentum buying of Y is also stabilizing in effect, because behavioral models show that prices eventually revert to fundamentals.
Value buying of X tends to push its price back up, a stabilizing negative feedback; momentum buying of Y pushes it further up, a destabilizing positive feedback.

questions.solution:
A stock that fell 35% (high book-to-market) and one that rose 40% (low book-to-market): how do value and momentum trading affect prices?

**Concept and theory**

The two strategies react to the same price history in different ways. For value, a price fall is a buying signal once the stock is cheap relative to book: “stocks with declining prices eventually fall far enough that they become value stocks. Then value investors buy them”, which makes value “inherently stabilizing”. For momentum, a price rise is a buying signal: “Stocks with high past returns are attractive, momentum investors continue buying them, and they continue to go up! Positive feedback strategies are ultimately destabilizing and are thus subject to periodic crashes.”

The behavioral momentum literature adds that in both the overreaction and underreaction models prices eventually reverse when they revert to fundamentals in the long run. This reversion happens in spite of momentum trading, not because of it; it does not turn momentum into a stabilizing force.

**Applying it to this question**

Stock X: a large fall, now high book-to-market. It is a value stock, so value investors buy it, which pushes its price back up (negative feedback, stabilizing). Stock Y: a large rise, now low book-to-market. It is a past winner, so momentum investors buy it, which pushes it further up (positive feedback, destabilizing and crash-prone).

**Fragile fact.** Value buys falls (negative feedback, stabilizing); momentum buys rises (positive feedback, destabilizing). Long-run reversion to fundamentals does not make momentum stabilizing.

**Reference**

LO 84.e: “Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Value Factor, subsections “Momentum Investing” and “Characterizing Momentum Risk” (reversion in both behavioral camps). Schweser Module 84.3, “Momentum Investing”. No difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 e, where it is Q5 of 14.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Correct buyers, but the feedback labels are reversed: value is negative feedback and stabilizing; momentum is positive feedback and destabilizing. A would be correct only with “negative” and “positive” swapped.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Gives value’s buying motive (cheapness) to momentum and a growth or momentum motive (strong recent rise) to value. Momentum shorts X as a past loser; value would short Y as a growth stock. B would be correct only with the two strategy names exchanged.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Takes the long-run reversion to fundamentals in behavioral momentum models and extends it to claim momentum trading is stabilizing. GARP is explicit that positive feedback strategies are destabilizing. C would be correct only for value’s buying of X.

d.reason: D assigns the right buyer to each stock and the right feedback label and stability effect to each strategy, exactly as in GARP’s “Momentum Investing” paragraph.
