questions.question: An internal auditor at a UK asset manager is reviewing why the firm’s GBP 1.2 billion US equity momentum fund suffered its largest loss in early 2009. At the end of 2008, the fund was long past winners and short past losers, and the loser leg was dominated by large banks and an automaker whose share prices had collapsed during 2008. Over the following months, government support for these firms put a floor under their share prices, and the stocks rebounded sharply. Which lesson best explains the loss?

options.text: Like the size effect after its publication, rational investors learned of the momentum anomaly and bid up the loser stocks until the premium was arbitraged away.
Government bailouts put a floor under the loser stocks the fund was short, so they rebounded; momentum crashes cluster when policymakers interrupt the natural progression of prices.
Like a seller of out-of-the-money puts, the fund had collected small steady premiums and then lost when equity volatility spiked, since momentum is in essence a short-volatility position.
As with value in the late 1990s, a booming economy lifted the stocks the fund was short, so the loss reflects the strategy’s own definition of bad times rather than any policy event.

questions.solution:
UK auditor reviews a momentum fund’s early-2009 loss after government support lifted the bank and auto stocks it was short.

**Concept and theory**

Momentum’s risk profile is dominated by crashes. Daniel and Moskowitz (2012), as reported in GARP, study the eleven largest momentum crashes: seven occurred during the Great Depression in the 1930s, one in 2001 and three during the financial crisis in 2008. The 2008 to 2009 episode shows the mechanism. The loser stocks were tanking financials (Citi, Bank of America, Goldman, Morgan Stanley) and others hard hit, such as General Motors. Losers tend to keep losing, and these would have, “were it not for Uncle Sam riding to their rescue”. Government bailouts put a floor under their prices, they skyrocketed, and since momentum strategies were short them, momentum investors suffered large losses when they rebounded. The other big momentum drawdowns were concentrated in the Great Depression, when policymakers also had great influence on asset prices. GARP’s conclusion: momentum “seems to reflect monetary policy and government risk during extraordinary times”, which have also been times of high volatility.

**Applying it to this question**

The case gives every element of the 2009 mechanism: a short leg concentrated in collapsed banks and an automaker, government support putting a floor under their prices, and a sharp rebound. The lesson is policy and government risk interrupting the natural progression of momentum, not arbitrage, volatility selling or a value-type definition of bad times.

Each wrong option is the true lesson of another case in the reading.

**Fragile fact.** In 2009 the momentum loss came from the short leg (past losers) rebounding after government bailouts, not from the winners falling.

**Reference**

LO 84.e: “Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Value Factor, subsections “Characterizing Momentum Risk” and “Implications for Asset Owners”. Schweser Module 84.3 dates the three recent crashes to “the financial crisis starting in 2007”; GARP says “during the financial crisis in 2008”. This looks like a condensation difference; GARP is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 e, where it is Q6 of 14.

a.reason: **Sibling case: size.** Rational investors bidding up a published anomaly until it vanishes is GARP’s second explanation for the disappearance of the size effect (Grossman-Stiglitz near-efficient market). It does not describe a sudden rebound triggered by bailouts, and momentum has not disappeared. A would be correct for SMB after the mid-1980s.

b.reason: B reproduces GARP’s account: bailouts “put a floor underneath the prices of these stocks . . . Since momentum strategies were short these stocks, momentum investors experienced large losses when these stocks rebounded”, and declines are concentrated “in periods when policymakers have interrupted natural progressions of momentum”.

c.reason: **Sibling case: volatility selling.** Steady premiums followed by a crash when volatility spikes is the lesson of selling volatility protection (LO 84.c: the Merrill Lynch volatility index losing nearly 70% from September to November 2008, with skewness of −8.26). GARP does not characterize momentum as a short-volatility position; it notes only that crash periods were also times of high volatility. C would be correct for a put-writing fund.

d.reason: A booming economy hurting a strategy, so that the strategy needs its own definition of bad times, is the value lesson from the late-1990s Internet bull market. Early 2009 was not a boom, and the cause was explicitly a policy event. D would be correct for an HML fund in 1998 to 1999.

Which of the following statements in the draft is NOT correct?

Momentum strategies are negatively skewed: over January 1965 to December 2011 the skewness of the WML strategy was about −1.43.
Momentum profits appear to vary over the business cycle, to depend on the state of the stock market and to be linked to liquidity.
The largest momentum drawdowns have been concentrated in periods of high volatility in which policymakers interrupted the natural progression of asset prices.

questions.solution:
Briefing on momentum risk: which statement about crashes, skew, macro links and policy periods is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP characterizes momentum risk on four dimensions.

| Dimension | GARP evidence |
|---|---|
| Crash record | Eleven largest crashes: seven in the Great Depression (1930s), one in 2001, three in the 2008 financial crisis |
| Distribution | Negatively skewed; skewness of WML in Figure 2.6 is −1.43 |
| Macro links | Profits vary over the business cycle, depend on the state of the stock market, and are linked to liquidity |
| Policy and volatility | Drawdowns concentrated when policymakers interrupted natural progressions of momentum; these were also times of high volatility |

The rational story of momentum is still far from being fully fleshed out; the macro links are “tantalizing suggestions”. The most widely cited theories are behavioral.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each count and claim against the table. A allocates seven crashes to 2008 and three to the 1930s; the source says seven in the 1930s and three in 2008. B, C and D match the source.

**Fragile fact.** Crash count: 7 (1930s), 1 (2001), 3 (2008). Momentum skew −1.43; do not confuse with −8.26 for volatility selling.

**Reference**

LO 84.e: “Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Value Factor, subsections “Characterizing Momentum Risk” and “Implications for Asset Owners”. Schweser Module 84.3 lists the same crash counts and risks but omits the −1.43 skewness (GARP only).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 e, where it is Q7 of 14.

a.reason: GARP: “Of the eleven largest momentum crashes, seven occurred during the Great Depression in the 1930s, one occurred in 2001, and the other three occurred during the financial crisis in 2008.” A swaps the counts for the two episodes, so it is NOT correct.

b.reason: A true statement from “Implications for Asset Owners”: negative skew of −1.43. It would be the answer if it said positive skew or quoted −8.26, which is the skewness of volatility selling in LO 84.c (sibling number swap).

c.reason: A true statement from “Characterizing Momentum Risk” (business cycle, state of the market, liquidity). It would be the answer if it claimed momentum is unrelated to macro factors.

d.reason: A true statement combining the policy concentration of drawdowns with GARP’s remark that these “have also been times of high volatility”. It would be the answer if it said crashes occur in calm markets.

questions.question: The CRO of a US university endowment is comparing the rational (risk-based) explanations of the value and momentum premiums before approving USD 300 million of factor tilts. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Both rational stories are equally developed: just as value firms carry high and asymmetric adjustment costs, momentum firms are risky because their capital cannot be redeployed in bad times.
In the rational story, value risk can largely be diversified away across many value stocks, so the value premium compensates mainly for firm-specific losses that happen to coincide with recessions.

Value stocks move together, much of their risk cannot be diversified away and their betas rise in bad times such as low investment growth, whereas the rational story of momentum is still far from fully fleshed out.
Rational stories hold that value’s bad times always coincide with bad times for the economy, so the late-1990s boom, when value lost heavily, is inconsistent with any risk-based value premium.

questions.solution:
Endowment CRO compares the rational explanations of the value and momentum premiums.

**Concept and theory**

In the rational (pricing kernel) view, a risk premium exists because it compensates for losing money during bad times; the key is defining those bad times.

Value. Value stocks move together with other value stocks after controlling for market exposure (and covary negatively with growth stocks). Some value risk can be diversified in portfolios, but a large amount cannot; under the APT the undiversifiable remainder must be priced, giving a value premium. Value’s bad times do not always line up with the economy’s: value did badly in the late 1970s and early 1980s, the early-1990s recession and 2008, but also in the late-1990s boom. So rational stories “have to specify their own definitions of bad times” so that value earns a premium on average. Candidate factors: investment growth, labor income risk, nondurable or “luxury” consumption, housing risk and long-run consumption risk; in some of these bad times the betas of value stocks increase. Firm investment risk stories (Berk, Green and Naik; Cochrane and Zhang) add that value firms are burdened with unproductive capital and have high and asymmetric adjustment costs.

Momentum. GARP: “In the rational story of momentum (which is still far from being fully fleshed out in the literature), asset owners should examine how they behave facing the various sources of macro risk”. Some momentum profits correlate with macro factors, but the most widely cited theories are behavioral.

|  | Value | Momentum |
|---|---|---|
| Rational story | Well developed; undiversifiable co-movement, betas rise in bad times | Far from fully fleshed out |
| Leading explanation | Rational and behavioral both developed | Behavioral most widely cited |

**Applying it to this question**

The CRO needs a comparison. Only one option gets both sides right: value’s rational story (co-movement, undiversifiable risk, rising betas) and momentum’s (not yet fleshed out).

**Fragile fact.** Value: undiversifiable co-movement and betas that rise in bad times; its bad times need not be the economy’s. Momentum: rational story still incomplete; behavioral theories dominate.

**Reference**

LO 84.e: “Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Value Factor, subsections “Rational Theories of the Value Premium”, “Firm Investment Risk” and “Characterizing Momentum Risk”. Note: GARP says value stocks “covary negatively with growth stocks”; Schweser Module 84.3 says they “co-vary with growth stocks”, dropping “negatively”. This looks like a condensation error in Schweser; GARP is used. Boundary: the value premium explanations are also the subject of LO 84.a; here they are tested only in comparison with momentum, as LO 84.e requires.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 e, where it is Q8 of 14.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** High and asymmetric adjustment costs and capital that cannot be redeployed are the firm investment risk story for value firms (Cochrane-Zhang). GARP gives no such story for momentum, and it says the two rational stories are not equally developed. A would be correct for value versus growth firms only.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says a large amount of value risk cannot be diversified away, and it is that undiversifiable risk that is priced. B would be correct only for diversifiable, idiosyncratic risk, which earns no premium in the APT.

c.reason: C restates GARP’s “Rational Theories of the Value Premium” (value stocks move together, a large amount cannot be diversified away; betas increase in bad times defined by factors such as investment growth) and “Characterizing Momentum Risk” (rational story of momentum still far from fully fleshed out).

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** Rational stories do not need value’s bad times to coincide always with the economy’s; they must specify their own definitions of bad times. The late-1990s episode is exactly why. D would be correct only if rational theory required bad times to be recessions.

questions.question:
A senior analyst at a sovereign wealth fund is building a slide that links four behavioral mechanisms to the factor premium each is used to explain in the reading:

(1) Investors overextrapolate past growth rates into the future and bid glamour stocks up too high.

(2) Investors are loss averse and use mental accounting, so a stock burned by dismal prior performance is viewed as riskier.

(3) Informed investors are overconfident and attribute their successes to their own skill, pushing prices above fundamental values.

(4) News watchers receive signals of firm value with delay, and these are only partially incorporated into prices, while other investors trade only on past prices.

Which mapping is correct?

options.text: Value: (1) and (2); momentum overreaction: (4); momentum underreaction: (3)
Value: (1) and (2); momentum overreaction: (3); momentum underreaction: (4)
Value: (2) only; momentum overreaction: (1) and (3); momentum underreaction: (4)
Value: (1), (2) and (4); momentum overreaction: (3); momentum underreaction: none

questions.solution:
Map four behavioral mechanisms to value, momentum overreaction and momentum underreaction.

**Concept and theory**

Behavioral explanations say a factor premium arises from investor behavior that is not arbitraged away.

Value. (i) Overextrapolation (Lakonishok, Shleifer and Vishny, 1994): investors overextrapolate past growth rates into the future, so growth (“glamour”) stocks are bid up too high; when the growth does not materialize, their returns are low relative to value stocks. Value stocks are not fundamentally riskier, just cheap. (ii) Loss aversion and mental accounting (Barberis and Huang, 2001): a high book-to-market stock reached its low price through dismal prior performance; this burned investors, who view each stock separately and now see it as riskier, so they require higher average returns.

Momentum. Good news can generate momentum in two ways. Overreaction camp: delayed overreaction pushes prices persistently up; in Daniel, Hirshleifer and Subrahmanyam (1998), informed investors are overconfident and have biased self-attribution (success is skill, failure is bad luck), and they push prices above fundamental values. Underreaction camp: in Hong and Stein (2000), “news watchers” receive signals of firm value with delay and ignore price history, while other investors trade only on past prices; information is only partially incorporated, causing underreaction.

| Mechanism | Explains | Source model |
|---|---|---|
| (1) Overextrapolation of growth | Value premium | Lakonishok, Shleifer, Vishny (1994) |
| (2) Loss aversion and mental accounting | Value premium | Barberis and Huang (2001) |
| (3) Overconfidence and self-attribution | Momentum, overreaction | Daniel, Hirshleifer, Subrahmanyam (1998) |
| (4) Delayed news watchers | Momentum, underreaction | Hong and Stein (2000) |

**Applying it to this question**

(1) and (2) are value stories; (3) pushes prices above fundamental value, so it is overreaction; (4) partial incorporation of delayed news is underreaction.

**Fragile fact.** Overextrapolation and loss aversion with mental accounting explain value; overconfidence with self-attribution is momentum overreaction; delayed news watchers are momentum underreaction.

**Reference**

LO 84.e: “Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Value Factor, subsections “Behavioral Theories of the Value Premium” and “Characterizing Momentum Risk”. Schweser Module 84.3 matches; it does not name the momentum model authors, which come from GARP. GARP also mentions conservatism bias in Barberis, Shleifer and Vishny (1998); it is not tested here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 e, where it is Q9 of 14.

a.reason: **Sibling swap between the two momentum camps.** Puts the news watchers under overreaction and overconfidence under underreaction. Overconfident investors push prices above fundamentals (overreaction); delayed, partial incorporation is underreaction. A would be correct only with the two camp labels exchanged.

b.reason: B is the only mapping that puts both value stories under value and assigns (3) to overreaction and (4) to underreaction, matching GARP’s “Behavioral Theories of the Value Premium” and “Characterizing Momentum Risk”.

c.reason: **Sibling swap from value to momentum.** Moves overextrapolation of growth rates to momentum overreaction. The word “overreaction” appears in value’s behavioral story too (Schweser: “overextrapolation and overreaction”), but GARP attributes this mechanism to the value premium (LSV 1994). C would be correct only if the item described overreaction to firm-specific news about recent winners.

d.reason: **Sibling swap and incomplete set.** Places the news watchers mechanism under value (perhaps because value stocks are “underestimated”) and leaves the underreaction camp empty, although GARP names Hong and Stein as the standard underreaction reference. D would be correct only if GARP had no underreaction theory of momentum.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at an Australian superannuation fund is reviewing a training slide on behavioral explanations of the value and momentum premiums before it is shown to the fund’s AUD 40 billion growth-option team. Which statement on the slide is most accurate?

options.text: In the overextrapolation story, value stocks earn higher returns because they are fundamentally riskier than growth stocks, carrying more unproductive capital in bad times.
In the Barberis and Huang story, a high book-to-market stock has reached its low price through dismal prior performance, so loss-averse investors view it as safer and accept lower returns.
In both the overreaction and the underreaction models of momentum, prices drift away from fundamental values permanently, which is why momentum profits are so large.
Behavioral momentum stories split into an overreaction camp and an underreaction camp that are difficult to distinguish, and in both, prices eventually reverse as they revert to fundamentals.

questions.solution:
Superannuation training slide on behavioral explanations of value and momentum: which statement is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Behavioral stories and rational stories answer the question “why does the premium exist?” differently. In the behavioral value story, value stocks are not fundamentally riskier; they are cheap because investors underestimate their growth prospects (and growth stocks are expensive because investors overestimate theirs). In the Barberis-Huang story, a stock that has fallen hard is seen as riskier by loss-averse, mentally accounting investors, who therefore require higher returns. For momentum, the two behavioral camps (delayed overreaction; underreaction to news) are difficult to distinguish, and this “still bedevils the literature”. GARP adds a common feature: “In both the underreaction and overreaction models, prices eventually reverse when they revert to fundamentals in the long run.”

|  | Overreaction (momentum) | Underreaction (momentum) |
|---|---|---|
| Initial response to good news | Price pushed above fundamentals | Price rises too little |
| Next periods | Persistent upward drift | Investors learn; price rises again |
| Long run | Reverts to fundamentals | Reverts to fundamentals |

**Applying it to this question**

Test each slide line for the exact source claim: whether risk drives the extrapolation story (no), whether loss-averse investors see a fallen stock as riskier (yes), whether momentum mispricing is permanent (no), and whether the two momentum camps are hard to distinguish and both revert (yes).

**Fragile fact.** Behavioral value: not riskier, just cheap. Barberis-Huang: burned investors see the stock as riskier and demand more. Momentum camps: hard to tell apart, both revert to fundamentals in the long run.

**Reference**

LO 84.e: “Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Value Factor, subsections “Behavioral Theories of the Value Premium” and “Characterizing Momentum Risk”. Schweser Module 84.3 matches (“prices eventually revert to their fundamental values over the long run”).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 e, where it is Q10 of 14.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: rational into behavioral.** “Fundamentally riskier . . . unproductive capital in bad times” is the Cochrane-Zhang rational story. GARP stresses that in the extrapolation story “value stocks are not fundamentally riskier than growth firms”. A would be correct if labeled the firm investment risk story.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** In Barberis and Huang the burned investor views the stock as riskier and requires higher average returns, not safer with lower returns. B would be correct with “riskier” and “higher returns”.

c.reason: **Polarity flip on the long-run outcome.** GARP says prices eventually revert to fundamentals in both models; the deviation is not permanent. C would be correct only if no long-run reversal occurred, which contradicts the source.

d.reason: D combines two explicit GARP statements: distinguishing between the camps “is difficult”, and in both models “prices eventually reverse when they revert to fundamentals in the long run”.

questions.question:
A risk consultant in Frankfurt advises four EUR-based asset owners on factor tilts, using the reading’s implications for asset owners.

| Owner | Profile |
|---|---|
| 1 | University endowment: periods of low investment growth do not force it to cut spending, and it is able to act against the crowd. |
| 2 | Family office: knows that it overextrapolates past growth more than the average investor does. |
| 3 | Corporate pension plan: behaves like the average investor, with no distinctive bias or comparative advantage. |
| 4 | Insurer’s surplus portfolio: cannot tolerate large drawdowns; considering a large momentum sleeve. |

Which mapping of owners to the positions implied by the reading is most accurate?

options.text: 1: value tilt; 2: growth tilt; 3: market portfolio; 4: no large momentum sleeve
1: value tilt; 2: value tilt to offset its bias; 3: market portfolio; 4: no large momentum sleeve
1: growth tilt; 2: growth tilt; 3: market portfolio; 4: no large momentum sleeve
1: value tilt; 2: growth tilt; 3: market portfolio; 4: large momentum sleeve, as its positive skew offsets crash risk

questions.solution:
Four EUR asset owners with different exposures and biases: which tilts does the reading imply?

**Concept and theory**

Because the average investor holds the market, any factor tilt must be justified by how the owner differs from the average investor.

Rational implications (value). Each factor defines bad times; the owner asks whether those are bad times for her. If she does not need to cut consumption when investment growth is low, she has a comparative advantage in holding value stocks and can harvest the value premium. Owners who cannot shoulder value’s losses in bad times should hold growth stocks.

Behavioral implications (value). Do you act like the market, or can you avoid overextrapolating or overreacting? If you act like everyone else, hold the market portfolio. If you overreact more, perhaps unconsciously, you tilt toward growth stocks. If you can go against the crowd, value investing is for you.

Momentum. The owner should consider her own biases relative to the market’s, and “at a minimum, the investor should be able to tolerate large drawdowns induced by momentum strategies”, since momentum is negatively skewed (−1.43).

**Applying it to this question**

Owner 1: low investment growth is not a bad time for it and it can act against the crowd, so it holds a value tilt.

Owner 2: overextrapolates more than average, so the reading predicts a tilt toward growth.

Owner 3: acts like the average investor, so it holds the market portfolio.

Owner 4: cannot tolerate large drawdowns, which fails GARP’s minimum condition for momentum, so no large momentum sleeve.

**Fragile fact.** Overextrapolator leans growth; contrarian or comparative advantage in value’s bad times leans value; average investor holds the market; momentum requires tolerance of large drawdowns.

**Reference**

LO 84.e: “Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Value Factor, subsections “Rational Implications for Asset Owners”, “Behavioral Implications for Asset Owners” and “Implications for Asset Owners”. Wording difference: Schweser says those who “underreact will lean toward value stocks”; GARP says “If you can go against the crowd, then value investing is for you”. The stem uses GARP’s wording.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 e, where it is Q11 of 14.

a.reason: A matches all four GARP implications listed in (a).

b.reason: The reading says an investor who overreacts or overextrapolates more than the market tilts toward growth (Schweser: “Investors who overextrapolate will lean toward growth stocks”); it is the investor who can go against the crowd who suits value. B would be correct if Owner 2 knew it could resist extrapolation, that is, if it could go against the crowd.

c.reason: Owner 1 has the comparative advantage in bearing value’s bad times, so it is the natural value investor. C would be correct if low investment growth forced Owner 1 to cut spending (bad times for it), in which case it should hold growth.

d.reason: Momentum is negatively skewed; its crashes are not offset by positive skew, and GARP requires tolerance of large drawdowns. D would be correct only for an owner able to tolerate large drawdowns.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Chinese commercial bank is drafting a CNY 5 billion multi-asset factor proposal and must state how value and momentum carry over from equities to other asset classes. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Value is an equity-specific phenomenon; outside equities only momentum is observed, for example in commodities through commodity trading advisers.
In foreign exchange, the value strategy is carry: long low-interest-rate currencies such as the JPY and short high-interest-rate currencies such as the AUD.
In fixed income, value is riding the yield curve (a duration premium); momentum is observed in government and corporate bonds and, in commodities, is synonymous with commodity trading advisers.
In commodities, the value strategy is the roll return, whose sign is determined by the commodity’s past six-month price trend rather than by the slope of the futures curve.

questions.solution:
Chinese bank multi-asset proposal: how do value and momentum carry over from equities to other asset classes?

**Concept and theory**

Value in essence buys assets with high yields (low prices) and sells assets with low yields (high prices). The same strategy works in all asset classes under different names, and GARP notes value strategies have common components across asset classes (Koijen et al.; Asness, Moskowitz and Pedersen).

| Asset class | Value strategy is called | Momentum |
|---|---|---|
| Equities | Value-growth (HML) | WML / UMD |
| Fixed income | Riding the yield curve (a form of the duration premium) | Observed in government and corporate bonds |
| Commodities | Roll return; sign set by an upward- or downward-sloping futures curve | Synonymous with commodity trading advisory funds |
| Foreign exchange | Carry: long high-rate, short low-rate currencies | Observed in currencies |
| Other markets | Pervasive across asset classes | Industries, sectors, real estate, international equities |
| Implementation | Cheap and in size for a large investor; low-cost index products for small investors | Can be part of a long-run investor’s opportunistic strategy |

In FX carry, high yields play the role of low prices. Traditionally the high-rate currencies have been those of Australia and New Zealand, and the low-rate ones Japan and more recently the United States. Momentum “is also observed in every asset class” and “manifests across asset classes, as does value”.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option makes one claim about a non-equity market. Check the name of the value strategy, the direction of the carry trade, the determinant of the roll return’s sign, and the asset classes where momentum is observed.

**Fragile fact.** FX carry: long high-rate, short low-rate (high yield equals low price). Roll return sign: slope of the futures curve, not past trend.

**Reference**

LO 84.e: “Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Value Factor, subsections “Value in Other Asset Classes” and “Momentum Investing”. Schweser Module 84.3 matches. Boundary: the FX carry factor regression (GARP Equation 2.3) is treated as part of LO 84.d’s multifactor mechanics and is not tested here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 e, where it is Q12 of 14.

a.reason: **Scope error.** Value is not equity-specific; GARP calls it “a pervasive factor” present across fixed income, commodities and currencies. A would be correct only for the equity book-to-market label, not for value as a strategy.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Carry goes long high-interest-rate currencies (traditionally the AUD and NZD) and short low-interest-rate currencies (traditionally the JPY, more recently the USD). B would be correct with the long and short legs reversed.

c.reason: GARP: “In fixed income, the value strategy is called riding the yield curve and is a form of the duration premium”; momentum is observed in “government bonds, corporate bonds”; “In commodities, momentum is synonymous with commodities trading advisory funds.”

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Ranking on a past six-month price trend is momentum’s rule. The sign of the roll return is related to whether the futures curve is upward- or downward-sloping. D would be correct if it described commodity momentum rather than the roll return.

questions.loText: Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-2 e Q13
questions.question:
A risk consultant in Toronto is validating a CAD-denominated mutual fund that markets itself as a “growth” fund. She regresses the fund’s monthly excess returns on the four-factor model (market, SMB, HML and WML) and obtains the following loadings. The fund’s trailing three-year return of 41% is also reported.

| Factor | Loading |
|---|---|
| MKT | 1.04 |
| SMB | 0.03 |
| HML | −0.08 |
| WML | 0.46 |

Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: The fund’s distinctive exposure is to momentum, not growth: its positive WML loading raises its expected return by $\beta_{\text{WML}}\text{E}(\text{WML})$, as with many self-described growth funds.
The fund is effectively a value fund, because a negative HML loading means it is long high book-to-market stocks, and its WML loading confirms that it buys stocks that have fallen.
The WML loading is below one, so, just as market betas average one, the fund is underweight past winners relative to the average stock, which has a WML beta of one.
The fund’s large WML loading means it is well protected against momentum crashes, because its exposure to past winners is diversified across many stocks in the cross section.

questions.solution:
Toronto consultant validates a self-described “growth” fund with loadings MKT 1.04, SMB 0.03, HML −0.08, WML 0.46.

**Concept and theory**

Momentum is often added to the Fama-French model as a fourth factor (Carhart, 1997):

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) = \text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{i,MKT}}\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) + \beta_{\text{i,SMB}}\text{E}(\text{SMB}) + \beta_{\text{i,HML}}\text{E}(\text{HML}) + \beta_{\text{i,WML}}\text{E}(\text{WML})$,

where $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ is the risk-free rate, E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )$ the market risk premium, E$(\text{SMB})$, E$(\text{HML})$ and E$(\text{WML})$ the expected returns of the size, value and momentum factor portfolios, and each $\beta$ the stock’s or fund’s loading on the factor named in its subscript. “The same intuition applies as with the Fama-French model. The momentum beta, $\beta_{\text{i,WML}}$, is centered around zero.” Winners have positive momentum betas and their risk premiums are adjusted upward; losers have negative momentum betas and are adjusted downward; the market, neither a relative winner nor loser, is simply the market. GARP adds: “many investors who claim that they are growth investors are actually momentum investors, especially mutual funds, as pure growth underperforms value in the long run.”

**Applying it to this question**

MKT 1.04: roughly market exposure. SMB 0.03 and HML −0.08: close to zero, so almost no size tilt and only a slight growth tilt. WML 0.46: large and positive, so the fund holds past winners. Relative to a three-factor benchmark, its expected return is raised by 0.46 $\times\text{E}(\text{WML})$. The fund’s distinctive exposure is momentum, not growth, which is GARP’s point about self-described growth mutual funds. The trailing 41% return is irrelevant to interpreting loadings.

**Fragile fact.** WML betas are centered on zero (not one); winners positive, losers negative. Self-described growth funds often load on momentum.

**Reference**

LO 84.e: “Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Value Factor, subsection “Momentum Investing” (Equation 2.4 and the growth-fund remark); Section 2.4, “Fama-French (1993) Model” (betas centered on zero). Schweser Module 84.3 omits the growth-fund remark and the WML centering (GARP only).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 e, where it is Q13 of 14.

a.reason: A reads the positive WML loading correctly. It signals exposure to past winners, so the expected return is adjusted upward by the term $\beta_{\text{WML}}\text{E}(\text{WML})$, and it links this to GARP’s growth-fund remark.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** A negative HML loading indicates a (slight) growth tilt, not a value tilt; a positive WML loading indicates buying past winners, not stocks that have fallen. B would be correct with HML and WML loadings both of the opposite sign.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Applies the CAPM fact that the average market beta is one to WML. WML betas, like SMB and HML betas, are centered around zero; 0.46 is a substantial overweight to winners. C would be correct for a market beta of 0.46.

d.reason: **Scope error.** Diversifying across many winner stocks removes idiosyncratic risk, but not factor risk. A large WML loading increases exposure to momentum crashes, which occur when past losers rebound (for example after the 2009 bailouts). D would be correct only for a fund with a WML loading near zero.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a US asset manager is showing newly hired analysts how the momentum factor changes expected returns. Using the four-factor model (the Fama-French model plus WML) and the annual inputs below, she compares a past-winner stock W with a past-loser stock L.

| Input | Annual value (%) |
|---|---|
| Risk-free rate, $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ | 2.0 |
| Market risk premium, E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )$ | 5.5 |
| E$(\text{SMB})$ | 0.5 |
| E$(\text{HML})$ | 3.0 |
| E$(\text{WML})$ | 7.0 |

| Stock | $\beta_{\text{MKT}}$ | $\beta_{\text{SMB}}$ | $\beta_{\text{HML}}$ | $\beta_{\text{WML}}$ | 6m ret. (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| W | 1.10 | 0.20 | −0.30 | 0.60 | +38 |
| L | 1.10 | 0.20 | 0.40 | −0.50 | −24 |

Which of the following correctly states E$(\text{r}_{\text{W}} )$ and the gap E$(\text{r}_{\text{W}} ) - \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{L}})$?

options.text: E$(\text{r}_{\text{W}} ) =$ 12.35%; gap = 7.70 percentage points
E$(\text{r}_{\text{W}} ) =$ 7.25%; gap = −2.10 percentage points
E$(\text{r}_{\text{W}} ) =$ 11.45%; gap = −1.40 percentage points
E$(\text{r}_{\text{W}} ) =$ 11.45%; gap = 5.60 percentage points

questions.solution:
Four-factor expected returns for a past winner W and a past loser L, and the gap between them.

**Concept and theory**

The four-factor model (GARP Equation 2.4) prices each stock relative to the market by adding factor adjustments to the CAPM:

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) = \text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{i,MKT}}\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) + \beta_{\text{i,SMB}}\text{E}(\text{SMB}) + \beta_{\text{i,HML}}\text{E}(\text{HML}) + \beta_{\text{i,WML}}\text{E}(\text{WML})$.

A past winner has $\beta_{\text{i,WML}} >$ 0, so momentum raises its expected return; a past loser has $\beta_{\text{i,WML}} <$ 0, so momentum lowers it. Because a stock that has fallen often becomes cheap, a loser can carry a positive HML loading, which partly offsets its negative momentum adjustment. When two stocks share the same market and size loadings, those terms cancel in the gap:

E$(\text{r}_{\text{W}} ) - \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{L}}) = (\beta_{\text{W,HML}} - \beta_{\text{L,HML}})\text{E}(\text{HML}) + (\beta_{\text{W,WML}} - \beta_{\text{L,WML}})\text{E}(\text{WML})$.

**Applying it to this question**

Stock W:

CAPM part = 2.0 + 1.10 × 5.5 = 2.0 + 6.05 = 8.05%

size term = 0.20 × 0.5 = 0.10% ⇒ 8.15%

value term = −0.30 × 3.0 = −0.90% ⇒ 7.25% (three-factor result)

momentum term = 0.60 × 7.0 = +4.20% $\Rightarrow\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{W}} ) =$ 11.45%

Stock L:

CAPM part $+ \text{size term} =$ 8.05 + 0.10 = 8.15%

value term = 0.40 × 3.0 = +1.20% ⇒ 9.35% (three-factor result)

momentum term = −0.50 × 7.0 = −3.50% $\Rightarrow\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{L}}) =$ 5.85%

Gap check using the difference formula:

E$(\text{r}_{\text{W}} ) - \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{L}}) = (-$0.30 − 0.40) × 3.0 + (0.60 − (−0.50)) × 7.0

= −2.10 + 7.70 = 5.60 percentage points.

Meaning: the momentum factor adds 7.70 points in favor of the winner, but the loser’s value tilt claws back 2.10 points, so the winner’s expected return exceeds the loser’s by 5.60 points. The past six-month returns (+38%, −24%) are irrelevant: they explain the sign of the WML loadings but do not enter the model.

**Fragile fact.** Losers have negative WML betas, so momentum lowers their expected return; equal market and size betas cancel in the gap.

**Reference**

LO 84.e: “Compare value and momentum investment strategies, including their return and risk profiles.” GARP Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Value Factor, subsection “Momentum Investing” (Equation 2.4: winners adjusted upward, losers downward). Schweser Module 84.3 presents the same four-factor model (the equation image is lost in the text extraction; GARP’s Equation 2.4 is legible). No difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-2 e, where it is Q14 of 14.

a.reason: **Dropped term.** Omits the HML term for both stocks: E$(\text{r}_{\text{W}} ) =$ 8.15 + 4.20 = 12.35%, E$(\text{r}_{\text{L}}) =$ 8.15 − 3.50 = 4.65%, gap = 7.70. This is only the momentum part of the gap. A would be correct if both stocks had zero HML loadings.

b.reason: **Intermediate result.** Stops at the three-factor (Fama-French) values: E$(\text{r}_{\text{W}} ) =$ 7.25%, E$(\text{r}_{\text{L}}) =$ 9.35%, gap = −2.10. This ignores momentum entirely. B would be correct if the model had no WML factor.

c.reason: **Sign error.** Correct E$(\text{r}_{\text{W}} )$, but treats the loser’s $\beta_{\text{WML}} = -$0.50 as adding +3.50%: E$(\text{r}_{\text{L}}) =$ 9.35 + 3.50 = 12.85%, gap = 11.45 − 12.85 = −1.40. C would be correct only if L were a winner with $\beta_{\text{WML}} = +$0.50.

d.reason: E$(\text{r}_{\text{W}} ) =$ 11.45% and E$(\text{r}_{\text{L}}) =$ 5.85%, giving a gap of 5.60 percentage points, consistent with GARP: winners’ premiums are adjusted upward and losers’ downward by $\beta_{\text{i,WML}}\text{E}(\text{WML})$.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 a Q1
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Singapore life insurer is preparing an onboarding slide for newly hired analysts. The insurer holds SGD 1.8 billion of global equities and is considering a mandate that targets the low-risk anomaly. Which of the following statements best describes the low-risk anomaly that the slide should present?

options.text: Stocks with high market betas earn even higher returns than the CAPM predicts, while volatility shows no relation to subsequent returns.
Small-capitalisation stocks and stocks with high book-to-market ratios earn returns above those the CAPM predicts for their level of beta.
Risk, whether measured by market beta or by volatility, is negatively related to returns, contrary to the positive relation the CAPM implies.
Low-beta and low-volatility stocks outperform high-risk stocks in every period, so harvesting the anomaly is a riskless source of excess return.

questions.solution:
Q1: Junior analyst at a Singapore life insurer choosing the statement that best describes the low-risk anomaly.

**Concept and theory**

Standard theory says that investors demand compensation for bearing risk. In the capital asset pricing model (CAPM) the relevant risk is market beta, and expected return rises linearly with it:

E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) = \text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{i}} \left[\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} \right]$,

where E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}})$ is the expected return on asset i, $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ the risk-free rate, $\beta_{\text{i}}$ the asset’s beta with the market and E$(\text{r}_{\text{m}})$ the expected market return. A higher $\beta_{\text{i}}$ therefore means a higher expected return.

The low-risk anomaly is the empirical finding that runs the other way. GARP (3.5) defines it in one line: risk, measured by market beta or volatility, is negatively related to returns. The chapter summary (3.1) puts it as stocks with low betas and low volatilities having high returns. In the GM case (3.2) Martingale’s CIO pitched exactly this: stocks with low risk, measured by past volatility or past beta, had higher returns than stocks with high risk, which was contrary to generally accepted theory. Schweser’s Key Concepts for 85.a say the same: the anomaly appears to suggest the exact opposite of the CAPM’s positive risk-return relation.

|  | CAPM prediction | Low-risk anomaly (evidence) |
|---|---|---|
| Risk measure | Beta | Beta or volatility |
| Relation to returns | Positive | Negative |
| Status | Theory | Empirical regularity, an anomaly |

**Applying it to this question**

The slide must describe the anomaly itself. Two features decide: (i) both risk measures, beta and volatility, are involved; (ii) the relation is negative, which is what makes it an anomaly relative to the CAPM. Only option C contains both features without adding an extra claim.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: risk and return are negatively related under the anomaly; positively related under the CAPM. Both beta and volatility count as the risk measure.

**Reference**

LO 85.a (Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Low-Risk Anomaly”): “Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.” GARP Chapter 3, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly): 3.1 Chapter Summary; 3.2 GM Asset Management and Martingale; 3.5 Low Risk Anomaly (opening paragraphs). GARP and Schweser agree. Schweser also illustrates the anomaly with the iShares Edge MSCI Minimum Volatility USA ETF (68.75% cumulative return over 2011 to 2016 against 65.27% for the S&P 500 ETF); this example is Schweser only and is not in GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 a, where it is Q1 of 10.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the direction for beta (high-beta stocks earning even more than the CAPM predicts) and drops volatility. GARP says the reverse: low-beta and low-volatility stocks have high returns. A would be correct only for a stem asking what a steeper-than-CAPM security market line would look like, which is not the anomaly.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It describes the size and value effects, neighbouring anomalies. GARP 3.5 quotes Greenwood contrasting the risk anomaly with “yet one more variation of the size, value, or momentum anomaly.” B would be correct if the stem asked for the Fama-French size and value effects (Reading 85, LO 85.e).

c.reason: C restates GARP 3.5 almost exactly (risk measured by market beta or volatility negatively related to returns) and adds the contrast with the CAPM’s positive relation from GARP 3.2 and Schweser 85.a.

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** The anomaly is a tendency on average over long samples, not a guarantee in every period, and nothing in the source calls it riskless. GARP 3.6 notes that the strategy carries high tracking error, which is a real risk to the asset owner. D would be correct only for a stem describing a pure arbitrage, which no anomaly is.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 a Q2
questions.question:
A portfolio manager at an Australian superannuation fund with AUD 6.5 billion in equities is drafting a report for the fund’s investment committee that sets out the components of the low-risk anomaly. She lists four candidate statements:

I. Volatility is negatively related to future returns.

II. Realised beta is positively related to future returns, so the anomaly is confined to volatility as the measure of risk.

III. The outperformance of minimum variance portfolios relative to the market is a consequence of the volatility and beta effects rather than a separate, independent effect.

IV. The volatility and beta effects are themselves consequences of minimum variance portfolios doing better than the market.

Which of the statements should she include as accurate descriptions of the anomaly?

options.text: I and III only
I only
I, III and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Q2: Superannuation portfolio manager choosing which statements accurately describe the components of the low-risk anomaly.

**Concept and theory**

GARP 3.5 opens by decomposing the low-risk anomaly into three effects, “with the third a consequence of the first two”:

1. Volatility is negatively related to future returns.
2. Realised beta is negatively related to future returns.
3. Minimum variance portfolios do better than the market.

The logic of the ordering is simple. A minimum variance portfolio is built to hold the lowest-risk combination of stocks, so it is tilted towards low-volatility and low-beta names. If low volatility and low beta are each associated with higher future returns (effects 1 and 2), a portfolio tilted towards them should beat the market (effect 3). Effect 3 therefore follows from effects 1 and 2; it is not a separate source of the anomaly, and the causation does not run backwards from effect 3 to effects 1 and 2. Note too that both effects 1 and 2 concern future returns, so the anomaly is something an investor can act on ex ante.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I is effect 1, verbatim in substance: accurate. Statement II flips the sign for beta and then concludes the anomaly is confined to volatility: inaccurate. Statement III is GARP’s “third a consequence of the first two”: accurate. Statement IV reverses the direction of consequence: inaccurate. The accurate set is I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Order and direction of consequence: effect 3 (minimum variance beats the market) is the consequence; effects 1 and 2 (volatility and realised beta negatively related to future returns) are the causes.

**Reference**

LO 85.a (Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Low-Risk Anomaly”): “Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.” GARP Chapter 3, 3.5 Low Risk Anomaly (opening list of three effects). Schweser 85.a describes the anomaly without listing the three effects; this structure comes from GARP. The finer detail on lagged versus contemporaneous beta and volatility belongs to LO 85.h and is not tested here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 a, where it is Q2 of 10.

a.reason: A (I and III only) is the only option that includes both accurate statements and excludes both inaccurate ones, matching GARP 3.5’s list and its remark that the third effect is a consequence of the first two.

b.reason: **Scope error, I only.** It drops statement III, treating the minimum variance effect as if it were not part of the anomaly or not linked to the other two. GARP lists it as the third effect. B would be correct if the stem asked only which statement describes the volatility effect.

c.reason: **Role misassignment of cause and consequence, I, III and IV.** It adds IV, which assigns the role of cause to the minimum variance effect and the role of consequence to the volatility and beta effects. GARP assigns them the other way round. C would be correct only if GARP had said the first two effects were consequences of the third.

d.reason: **Polarity flip, adds II.** Statement II reverses the sign of the beta effect (GARP: realised beta is negatively related to future returns) and so wrongly confines the anomaly to volatility. D would be correct only if realised beta were positively related to future returns, as the CAPM would suggest, which is not the source’s account.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 a Q3
questions.question: A risk consultant reviewing a research note for a Brazilian asset manager with BRL 12 billion under management reads the claim that “the negative relation between volatility and returns is puzzling only once one asks what theory predicts.” He wants to add one sentence stating what the competing theories predict. Which of the following sentences is most accurate?

options.text: Under the CAPM, idiosyncratic volatility should carry a positive premium, because investors must be paid to bear risk that they cannot diversify away.
In models with noise traders who trade for reasons unrelated to fundamental value, higher volatilities are associated with lower risk premiums.
Multifactor extensions of the CAPM predict a negative relation between idiosyncratic volatility and expected returns, consistent with the evidence.
In markets segmented by clientele effects, where some agents cannot diversify, idiosyncratic volatility should be positively related to returns.

questions.solution:
Q3: Risk consultant adding a sentence on what the competing theories predict about volatility and returns.

**Concept and theory**

To evaluate the low-risk anomaly one must ask why it is an anomaly at all. GARP’s opening question in the volatility discussion is whether there should even be a relation between volatility and returns, and the answer depends on the model:

| Model | Prediction for volatility and expected returns |
|---|---|
| CAPM and multifactor extensions | Volatility itself should not matter; expected returns depend on how assets covary with factor risks. Idiosyncratic volatility (tracking error) should have no relation to expected returns under the CAPM. |
| Clientele (segmented markets) models | Where some agents cannot diversify, or prefer some assets for exogenous reasons, idiosyncratic volatility should be positively related to returns: agents must be paid for bearing it. |
| Noise-trader models | Where noise traders trade for reasons unrelated to fundamental value, higher volatilities are associated with higher risk premiums. |
| Evidence (Ang et al., 2006) | “Exactly the opposite”: a negative relation. |

So the evidence is anomalous twice over: against the CAPM family it should be zero, and against the clientele and noise-trader families it should be positive. It is negative.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option attributes a prediction to a model. The test is whether actor (model) and direction match GARP. Only the clientele statement pairs the right model with the right sign (positive) and the right condition (segmented markets where some agents cannot diversify).

**Fragile fact.** Actor-sensitive: CAPM and multifactor models predict zero relation; clientele and noise-trader models predict a positive relation; only the evidence shows a negative one.

**Reference**

LO 85.a (Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Low-Risk Anomaly”): “Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.” GARP Chapter 3, 3.5 Low Risk Anomaly, opening paragraph of “Volatility Anomaly” (should there even be a relation between volatility and returns; footnote 25 cites Merton (1981) for clientele models and Delong et al. (1990) for noise-trader models). Schweser 85.a frames the anomaly against the CAPM only; GARP gives the fuller set of theories. Boundary call: the theory paragraph is used because it is what makes the evidence anomalous (evaluate); the quintile evidence that follows it belongs to LO 85.h and is not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 a, where it is Q3 of 10.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** The positive premium for idiosyncratic risk belongs to clientele models, not to the CAPM. Under the CAPM idiosyncratic volatility should have no relation to expected returns, because it can be diversified away. A would be correct if “Under the CAPM” were replaced by “Under clientele models in segmented markets.”

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Noise-trader models associate higher volatilities with higher, not lower, risk premiums. B would be correct if “lower” were changed to “higher.”

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It assigns to multifactor models a negative prediction that belongs to the evidence. Multifactor extensions, like the CAPM, say volatility itself should not matter; expected returns depend on covariances with factors. C would describe the Ang et al. (2006) findings, not any model’s prediction, if the subject were “the evidence” rather than “multifactor extensions.”

d.reason: GARP: “in markets that are segmented due to clientele effects, where some agents cannot diversify . . . idiosyncratic volatility should be positively related to returns.” D states this with its condition intact.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 a Q4
questions.question: An internal auditor at a UK bank is checking the accuracy of a training module on the history of research into the low-risk anomaly before it is released to the bank’s asset management arm. Which of the following statements in the module is most accurate?

options.text: The negative relation between risk and returns was first documented by Ang, Hodrick, Xing and Zhang (2006); earlier tests such as Friend and Blume (1970) found risk-adjusted performance positively related to risk.
Studies showing a negative relation appeared in the late 1960s and early 1970s, but these results were largely forgotten before the literature revived strongly in the mid-2000s.
Friend and Blume (1970) found an inverse relation between risk-adjusted performance and volatility, but found no relation between risk-adjusted performance and CAPM beta.
Because the early findings of Haugen and Heins (1975) were widely adopted by practitioners, the anomaly has been exploited continuously since the 1970s and is now fully arbitraged away.

questions.solution:
Q4: Internal auditor checking a training module on the history of low-risk anomaly research.

**Concept and theory**

The low-risk anomaly is not a recent discovery. GARP’s “History” subsection traces it as follows:

| Study | What it found |
|---|---|
| Late 1960s and early | The first studies showing a negative relation between risk and |
| 1970s | returns appear. |
| Friend and Blume (1970) | Stock portfolio returns 1960 to 1968, with both CAPM beta and volatility as risk measures: in all cases risk-adjusted performance depends on risk, and the relation is inverse and highly significant. |
| Haugen and Heins (1975) | Data 1926 to 1971, beta and volatility: over the long run, portfolios with lesser variance in monthly returns had greater average returns than “riskier” ones; the data do not support the hypothesis that risk generates a special reward. |
| Afterwards | Most of these results were forgotten. |
| Ang, Hodrick, Xing and | Helped launch the new “risk anomaly” literature; the old |
| Zhang (2006) | results “have come roaring back.” |

Evaluating the anomaly requires knowing this: a pattern found in data from different eras and then rediscovered is harder to dismiss as a recent statistical accident.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are: (i) the early studies found an inverse relation, (ii) they did so for both beta and volatility, and (iii) the results were forgotten and later revived. Only B is consistent with all three.

**Fragile fact.** Sequence: early inverse findings (around 1970), then forgotten, then revival from 2006. Friend and Blume covered beta and volatility, not one of them.

**Reference**

LO 85.a (Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Low-Risk Anomaly”): “Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.” GARP Chapter 3, 3.5 Low Risk Anomaly, “History” subsection (and opening of “Volatility Anomaly” for the 2006 revival). Boundary note: Schweser quotes Haugen and Heins (1975) under LO 85.h as evidence for the volatility anomaly; GARP places it in the general history of the low-risk anomaly. This question tests only the historical arc, not the 85.h quintile evidence.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 a, where it is Q4 of 10.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Ang et al. (2006) revived the literature; they did not first document it, and Friend and Blume (1970) found the relation inverse, not positive. A would be correct only if the earliest studies had supported the CAPM’s positive relation, which GARP says they did not.

b.reason: B combines GARP’s statements that the first studies showing a negative relation appeared in the late 1960s and early 1970s, that most of these results were forgotten, and that they have recently come roaring back (Ang et al., 2006, launching the new literature).

c.reason: **Scope error.** Friend and Blume used both CAPM beta and volatility as risk measures and found the inverse relation “in all cases.” C narrows the finding to volatility alone. C would be correct only for a study that had tested volatility and found beta unrelated.

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** GARP says the early results were forgotten, not widely adopted, and in 3.6 that low-volatility strategies are still far from predominant. Claiming the anomaly is “fully arbitraged away” is an unsupported certainty. D would be correct only if the stem described a world in which institutions had heavily overweighted low-risk stocks.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 a Q5
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Canadian defined benefit pension plan with CAD 2.4 billion in assets is evaluating whether an external low-volatility equity strategy displays the low-risk anomaly relative to the cap-weighted index used as its benchmark. The manager reports the strategy’s statistics monthly; the index statistics are annual.

| Item | Value | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Strategy mean return | 0.90 | % per month |
| One-month T-bill return | 0.20 | % per month |
| Strategy standard deviation of returns | 3.40 | % per month |
| Strategy tracking error versus index | 6.30 | % per year |
| Strategy beta versus index | 0.74 |  |
| Index mean excess return over T-bills | 7.20 | % per year |
| Index standard deviation of returns | 16.00 | % per year |

Using one-month T-bills as the risk-free benchmark, which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The strategy’s annual Sharpe ratio is about 0.21, below the index’s 0.45, so the record does not display the anomaly.
The strategy’s annual Sharpe ratio is about 0.92, above the index’s 0.45, so the record displays the anomaly.
The strategy’s annual Sharpe ratio is about 0.71, above the index’s 0.45, so the record displays the anomaly.
The strategy’s annual Sharpe ratio is about 2.47, above the index’s 0.45, so the record displays the anomaly.

questions.solution:
Q5: Treasury analyst at a Canadian pension plan comparing a low-volatility strategy’s Sharpe ratio with its index.

**Concept and theory**

To evaluate whether a low-volatility strategy displays the low-risk anomaly, GARP’s GM case compares risk-adjusted performance: Martingale’s strategy had a mean excess return of 8.59% and a standard deviation of 12.22%, giving a Sharpe ratio of 8.59/12.22 = 0.70, against 0.45 for the Russell 1000. A lower-risk portfolio earning a higher reward per unit of risk is the anomaly in action.

The Sharpe ratio, with one-month T-bills as the risk-free benchmark, is

SR $= \frac{\bar{r} - \bar{r}_{\text{f}}}{\sigma}$ ,

where $\bar{\text{r}}$ is the average return, $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}}$ the average T-bill return and $\sigma$ the standard deviation of returns. It is not the information ratio, which divides alpha by tracking error. When data are monthly, annualise the mean by multiplying by 12 and the standard deviation by multiplying by $\sqrt{12}$ (returns assumed independent across months), so the annual Sharpe ratio equals the monthly one times $\sqrt{12}$.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, SR = ($\bar{\text{r}}$ − $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} )$/$\sigma$, on an annual basis for both series; then one step per line:

Monthly excess return = 0.90% − 0.20% = 0.70%

Annual excess return = 0.70% × 12 = 8.40%

Annual standard deviation = 3.40% $\times\sqrt{12} =$ 3.40% × 3.4641 = 11.78%

$\text{SR}_{\text{strategy}} =$ 8.40/11.78 = 0.713

$\text{SR}_{\text{index}} =$ 7.20/16.00 = 0.450

The strategy has lower volatility (11.78% against 16.00%), a higher excess return (8.40% against 7.20%) and a higher Sharpe ratio (0.71 against 0.45): lower risk paired with higher risk-adjusted return, which is the anomaly. Tracking error (6.30%), beta (0.74) and fund size are irrelevant to the Sharpe ratio.

**Fragile fact.** Annualise the mean by 12 and the standard deviation by $\sqrt{12}$; the Sharpe denominator is total volatility, not tracking error.

**Reference**

LO 85.a (Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Low-Risk Anomaly”): “Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.” GARP Chapter 3, 3.2 GM Asset Management and Martingale (Sharpe ratio 0.70 against 0.45). The Sharpe ratio itself is defined under LO 85.b (GARP 3.3, Definition of Alpha); it is used here only as evidence for evaluating the anomaly, as GARP does in 3.2. The annualisation convention is standard and not stated in the GARP chapter; it is needed only to put the two sets of figures on one basis.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 a, where it is Q5 of 10.

a.reason: **Unit slip, not annualised.** 0.70/3.40 = 0.206 is the monthly Sharpe ratio. Comparing it with an annual 0.45 mixes frequencies and reverses the conclusion. Annualising the mean by 12 and the standard deviation by 12 gives the same wrong 0.206. A would be correct only if the index’s 0.45 were also a monthly figure.

b.reason: **Dropped term, the risk-free rate.** (0.90 × 12)/11.78 = 10.80/11.78 = 0.917 uses the total return instead of the excess return over T-bills. B would be correct only if the T-bill rate were zero.

c.reason: C gives the correctly annualised Sharpe ratio (0.71) and the correct conclusion, mirroring GARP’s 0.70 versus 0.45 comparison for Martingale against the Russell 1000.

d.reason:
**Unit slip, only the mean annualised.** 8.40/3.40 = 2.47 annualises the excess return but leaves the standard deviation monthly. D would be correct only if 3.40% were already an annual standard deviation.

(Dividing by tracking error, 8.40/6.30 = 1.33, is the wrong-input-twin error of confusing the Sharpe ratio with the information ratio; it does not appear among the options but is the trap behind including tracking error in the table.)

questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a US corporate defined benefit pension plan is reviewing the case of GM Asset Management, which evaluated Martingale Asset Management’s low volatility strategy for the GM Pension Fund. The strategy had a historic tracking error of 6.16% against the Russell 1000. Which of the following statements best describes the considerations GM Asset Management weighed in judging whether the strategy was a good fit?

options.text: The tracking error was high relative to the below-6% levels of strategies usually considered, so it had to be offset or a benchmark change justified to the investment committee, yet lower risk and a higher correlation to pension liabilities fitted GM’s aim of reducing surplus volatility.

The tracking error was high relative to the below-6% levels of strategies usually considered, so it had to be offset or a benchmark change justified to the investment committee, yet lower risk and a lower correlation to pension liabilities fitted GM’s aim of reducing surplus volatility.

The tracking error was within the levels of strategies usually considered, so no offset or benchmark change had to be justified to the investment committee, and lower risk and a higher correlation to pension liabilities fitted GM’s aim of reducing surplus volatility.

The tracking error was high relative to the below-6% levels of strategies usually considered, but Scott, GM’s managing director, judged it irrelevant because only the pension liability mattered, so no case had to be made to the investment committee.

questions.solution:
Q6: Pension risk committee member summarising what GM Asset Management weighed in evaluating Martingale’s low volatility strategy.

**Concept and theory**

Evaluating the low-risk anomaly is not only about whether it earns alpha; it is also about whether exploiting it suits a particular asset owner. GARP’s GM case (3.2) sets out the trade-off:

| Consideration | What the case says |
|---|---|
| Tracking error | 6.16% against the Russell 1000: relatively high, since other US equity strategies the group considered had tracking errors below 6%. |
| Response required (Scott, managing director) | The equities group would need to offset that risk or convince the investment committee that a change of benchmark was warranted. |
| What ultimately mattered | Meeting the pension fund liability. |
| Fit (Herscovici, portfolio manager) | Low volatility had two factors consistent with GM’s direction to reduce surplus volatility: lower risk and a higher correlation to pension liabilities. |

Surplus volatility is the volatility of assets minus liabilities. Assets that are less volatile and move more closely with liabilities reduce it, which is why both features count in the strategy’s favour for a pension fund. Against this, tracking error relative to a market benchmark is a binding constraint for GM (GARP 3.5 and 3.6).

**Applying it to this question**

The correct description must contain: high tracking error relative to the usual below-6% level; the need to offset it or win a benchmark change from the investment committee; and the fit through lower risk and higher liability correlation. A has all three. The others alter exactly one element.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and direction: Scott (GM managing director) raised tracking error; Herscovici (GM portfolio manager) argued the fit; liability correlation is higher, not lower.

**Reference**

LO 85.a (Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Low-Risk Anomaly”): “Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.” GARP Chapter 3, 3.2 GM Asset Management and Martingale; 3.6 GM Asset Management and Martingale Redux (alpha is not the only consideration; high tracking error). Schweser does not present the GM case under 85.a; content is from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 a, where it is Q6 of 10.

a.reason: A matches GARP 3.2 on each element: the 6.16% figure as relatively high against strategies below 6%, Scott’s insistence on offsetting the risk or convincing the investment committee, and Herscovici’s view that lower risk and a higher correlation to pension liabilities are consistent with reducing surplus volatility.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the liability correlation. A lower correlation to liabilities would increase, not reduce, surplus volatility. B would be correct only for an asset owner seeking diversification from its liabilities rather than a hedge of them.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It says the tracking error was within usual levels, so nothing had to be justified. GARP says 6.16% was relatively high against strategies typically below 6%. C would be correct if the strategy’s tracking error had been below 6%.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It assigns to Scott a dismissal of tracking error. In the case Scott was the one who insisted that the risk be offset or a benchmark change be justified to the investment committee. GARP notes that what ultimately mattered was meeting the liability, but that did not remove the tracking error issue. D would be correct only if Scott had waived the tracking error constraint, which he did not.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a German insurer with EUR 9 billion in equities is preparing a report on whether low-risk strategies are a genuine source of alpha. She considers four statements:

I. Low-risk strategies appear to have significant alpha relative to standard market capitalisation-weighted benchmarks.

II. Once the benchmark controls for risk using dynamic value-growth and momentum factors along with the market portfolio, the alpha of low-risk strategies disappears.

III. If the benchmark were the low volatility strategy itself, the strategy would show no alpha, because alpha morphs into the benchmark.

IV. Because low-risk strategies deliver alpha against both market and factor benchmarks, alpha is the only consideration an asset owner needs when deciding whether to adopt one.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I, II and III only
III only
I, III and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
Q7: Senior risk analyst at a German insurer selecting accurate statements on low-risk strategies as a source of alpha.

**Concept and theory**

Alpha is the average return in excess of a benchmark, so whether the low-risk anomaly “is alpha” depends on the benchmark. GARP evaluates the anomaly on three benchmarks:

| Benchmark | Alpha of low-risk strategies |
|---|---|
| Standard market capitalisation-weighted benchmark | Significant (GARP 3.1, 3.6) |
| Sophisticated factor benchmark: market plus dynamic value-growth and | Still significant (GARP 3.1, 3.6) |
| momentum factors |  |
| The low volatility strategy itself | Zero by construction: alpha “morphs into the benchmark (or beta)” (GARP 3.6) |

The third row is not merely philosophical: GARP notes that GM might be able to run low volatility strategies internally, in which case the external manager’s “alpha” would be something the asset owner could obtain as a factor. GARP also stresses that alpha is not the only consideration: Martingale’s alpha comes with high tracking error relative to the Russell 1000.

**Applying it to this question**

I: accurate (significant alpha against cap-weighted benchmarks). II: inaccurate, since GARP says the alpha survives dynamic value-growth and momentum controls. III: accurate (alpha morphs into the benchmark). IV: inaccurate, since tracking error is also a consideration. The accurate set is I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Alpha against factor benchmarks is still significant (not zero); alpha against the strategy itself is zero.

**Reference**

LO 85.a (Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Low-Risk Anomaly”): “Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.” GARP Chapter 3, 3.1 Chapter Summary; 3.6 GM Asset Management and Martingale Redux. Schweser 85.a does not discuss benchmarks; the mechanics of benchmark choice (1.50% against 3.44%) belong to LO 85.c and are not tested here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 a, where it is Q7 of 10.

a.reason: **Polarity flip, adds II.** Statement II reverses GARP’s finding: the alpha remains significant relative to factor benchmarks with dynamic value-growth and momentum. A would be correct only if GARP had found the alpha to vanish under factor controls.

b.reason: **Scope error, III only.** It drops statement I, as if the anomaly’s alpha existed only in the trivial sense of III and not against standard market capitalisation-weighted benchmarks. GARP says the alpha against those benchmarks is significant. B would be correct only if the stem asked which statement holds by construction, whatever the evidence.

c.reason: **Absolute-claim trap, adds IV.** Statement IV says alpha is the only consideration. GARP 3.6: “alpha is not the only consideration for GM Asset Management”; the strategy’s alpha comes with high tracking error. C would be correct for an unconstrained investor with no tracking error limit, which the stem does not describe.

d.reason: D (I and III only) matches GARP 3.6: significant alpha against standard market capitalisation benchmarks and sophisticated factor benchmarks, no alpha against the strategy itself, and alpha not the only consideration.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a UK university endowment with GBP 3.1 billion in assets is presenting to trustees on whether a low-volatility equity allocation can rely on the low-risk anomaly continuing. Which of the following statements most accurately reflects Ang’s evaluation of whether the anomaly will persist?

options.text: He expects it to be arbitraged away soon, because most institutional investors are already overweight low-risk stocks and so low-volatility strategies have become predominant.

He doubts that it will disappear, because low-volatility strategies are far from predominant, most institutional investors appear to be underweight low-risk stocks, and the effect is pervasive across many markets.
He doubts that it will disappear, but only because the effect has been documented in US large-capitalisation equities, where institutional trading is concentrated, and not in other asset classes.
He expects it to disappear, because the explanations proposed for it, taken together, now fully account for the anomaly, so investors can be expected to trade it away.

questions.solution:
Q8: Endowment CRO reporting Ang’s evaluation of whether the low-risk anomaly will persist.

**Concept and theory**

An anomaly that is easy to exploit should, in principle, be traded away: investors buy the cheap low-risk stocks until their returns are no longer abnormal. Whether the low-risk anomaly will persist is therefore a central part of evaluating it. GARP 3.6 gives Ang’s view:

- He hopes it goes away as soon as possible, and calls it an enigma despite the many explanations proposed.
- He doubts it will disappear, for two reasons. First, low-volatility strategies are far from predominant, as most institutional investors appear to be underweight low-risk stocks. Second, and more fundamentally, the anomaly appears in many markets (US and international, stocks, bonds, commodities, foreign exchange and derivatives), which suggests a pervasive effect that requires a deep explanation.
- He closes with Greenwood’s description of it as the mother of all inefficiencies.

**Applying it to this question**

The test is the combination of the forecast (doubts it will disappear) and the reasons (not predominant, institutions underweight, pervasive across markets). B is the only option with both right.

**Fragile fact.** Institutions are underweight (not overweight) low-risk stocks; Ang hopes it disappears but doubts that it will.

**Reference**

LO 85.a (Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Low-Risk Anomaly”): “Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.” GARP Chapter 3, 3.6 GM Asset Management and Martingale Redux (“Will the risk anomaly persist?”). Schweser 85.a does not cover persistence; content is from GARP. The individual explanations (leverage constraints, agency problems, preferences) belong to LO 85.i and are not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 a, where it is Q8 of 10.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It says institutions are overweight low-risk stocks and that the strategies are predominant, the reverse of GARP, and reaches the reverse forecast. A would be correct only if institutions had in fact crowded into low-risk stocks.

b.reason: B restates GARP 3.6: “I doubt this will happen. Low-volatility strategies are far from predominant, as most institutional investors appear to be underweight low-risk stocks,” together with the pervasiveness argument.

c.reason: **Scope error.** It narrows the evidence to US large-capitalisation equities. GARP’s argument for persistence rests on the anomaly appearing across US and international stocks, bonds, commodities, foreign exchange and derivatives. C would be correct only if the effect had been found in a single market.

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** GARP calls the anomaly an enigma: a comprehensive explanation is still being sought, so no set of explanations “fully accounts” for it. D would be correct only if the explanations were complete and Ang expected arbitrage to follow, neither of which GARP says.
