questions.loText: Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 a Q9
questions.question: The treasurer of a Japanese life insurer holds JPY 180 billion in a low-volatility, low-beta equity portfolio. A board member asks what would happen to the insurer’s existing position if the low-risk anomaly disappeared because capital flowed into low-risk stocks. Which of the following is the most likely outcome?

options.text: The insurer would enjoy large capital gains as the inflow drives up the prices of low-risk stocks, while the anomalous returns available to new buyers would be removed.
The insurer would suffer capital losses as the prices of low-risk stocks fall back to levels consistent with the CAPM, while new buyers would earn higher returns.
The insurer’s position would be unaffected, because the disappearance of the anomaly would change only the future returns of low-risk stocks and not their current prices.
The insurer would enjoy large capital gains, and new buyers after the repricing would continue to earn the same anomalous returns on low-risk stocks indefinitely.

questions.solution:
Q9: Japanese life insurer’s treasurer on what happens to an existing low-risk position if the anomaly disappears.

**Concept and theory**

An anomaly in expected returns is, equivalently, a mispricing: low-volatility and low-beta stocks have returns that are too high because their prices are too low. If the anomaly disappears through capital flowing in, the mechanism is a repricing. GARP 3.6: capital should be drawn to these stocks, driving up their prices and removing the anomalous returns; if that happened, current low-risk anomaly investors would enjoy large capital gains, and the low-risk trades already put on by the smart money would pay off handsomely.

| Effect of the anomaly disappearing | Direction |
|---|---|
| Prices of low-risk stocks | Up |
| Existing holders | Large capital gains |
| Prospective (anomalous) returns for new buyers | Removed |

**Applying it to this question**

The insurer already holds the low-risk portfolio, so it is one of the “current low-risk anomaly investors.” The deciding facts are the direction of price change (up) and its timing (the gain accrues during the repricing), with future anomalous returns removed.

**Fragile fact.** Disappearance helps existing holders (capital gains now) and hurts prospective returns (anomalous returns removed).

**Reference**

LO 85.a (Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Low-Risk Anomaly”): “Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.” GARP Chapter 3, 3.6 GM Asset Management and Martingale Redux (“If it does disappear . . . ”). Schweser does not cover this; content is from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 a, where it is Q9 of 10.

a.reason: A states both halves of GARP 3.6: prices are driven up, giving existing holders large capital gains, and the anomalous returns are removed.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the price direction. Low-risk stocks are underpriced under the anomaly, so closing it raises their prices. B would describe the effect on holders of overpriced stocks, not of the underpriced low-risk stocks.

c.reason: **Dropped term, the price mechanism.** It treats returns and prices as independent. Removing anomalous future returns requires a higher current price; that price rise is precisely the capital gain. C would be correct only if the anomaly disappeared through some change that left current prices untouched, which is not the mechanism GARP describes.

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** Gains for existing holders are right, but GARP says the repricing removes the anomalous returns; new buyers cannot keep earning them “indefinitely.” D would be correct only if the anomaly persisted after the repricing, which contradicts the premise.

questions.question: A compliance officer at a US investment consultancy is reviewing teaching notes on the GM Asset Management and Martingale case before they are circulated to clients. Martingale’s Low Volatility LargeCap+ strategy is shown from January 1979 to April 2012 against the Russell 1000. Which of the following statements in the notes is NOT correct?

options.text: Returns up to December 2007 are as simulated by Martingale’s analysts, and performance from January 2008 onward is live.
Using one-month T-bills as the risk-free benchmark, the strategy’s full-sample Sharpe ratio was about 0.70 against 0.45 for the Russell 1000.
Robin Greenwood, a Harvard Business School professor and fellow adviser to Martingale, suggested the risk anomaly may be the “mother of all inefficiencies.”
The strategy’s average outperformance of the Russell 1000 since going live was lower than its full-sample outperformance, so the live record weakened the simulated evidence.

questions.solution:
Q10: Compliance officer finding the incorrect statement in teaching notes on the GM and Martingale case.

**Concept and theory**

How much weight to put on a low-volatility track record depends on what kind of record it is. GARP 3.2 is precise about Martingale’s:

| Fact | GARP 3.2 |
|---|---|
| Sample | January 1979 to April 2012, against the Russell 1000 |
| Simulated period | Up to December 2007, as simulated by Martingale’s analysts |
| Live period | From January 2008 |
| Outperformance of Russell 1000 | 1.50% full sample; 1.83% on average since going live |
| Sharpe ratio (T-bill benchmark) | 8.59/12.22 = 0.70 against 0.45 for the Russell 1000 |
| CAPM regression | Alpha 3.44%, beta 0.73 |

GARP separates the simulated and live portions of the record and notes that the strategy “had done even better after going live.” The live outperformance (1.83%) exceeded the full-sample figure (1.50%), so the live record strengthened rather than weakened the case. GARP 3.5 also records Robin Greenwood (Harvard Business School professor and, like Ang, an adviser to Martingale) saying in 2010 that the risk anomaly may be the mother of all inefficiencies.

**Applying it to this question**

This is a NOT-correct question, so three options must match the case and one must contradict it. A, B and C match GARP; D reverses the comparison between live and full-sample outperformance.

**Fragile fact.** Live (since January 2008) outperformance 1.83% is higher than the full-sample 1.50%; Jacques is Martingale’s CIO, Greenwood an academic adviser.

**Reference**

LO 85.a (Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Low-Risk Anomaly”): “Describe and evaluate the low-risk anomaly of asset returns.” GARP Chapter 3, 3.2 GM Asset Management and Martingale; 3.5 Low Risk Anomaly (opening, Greenwood quotation). Schweser does not present the case under 85.a; content is from GARP. The 3.44% alpha and 0.73 beta, and how benchmark choice turns 1.50% into 3.44%, belong to LO 85.c and are not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 a, where it is Q10 of 10.

a.reason: **True.** GARP 3.2: up until December 2007 the returns are as simulated by Martingale’s analysts; from January 2008 performance is live. A trap version would place the whole record as live or as simulated.

b.reason: **True.** GARP 3.2: mean excess return 8.59%, standard deviation 12.22%, Sharpe ratio 0.70, against 0.45 for the Russell 1000, with one-month T-bills as the risk-free benchmark. A trap version would quote the information ratio or swap the two Sharpe ratios.

c.reason: **True.** GARP 3.5: Greenwood, a professor at Harvard Business School and Ang’s fellow adviser to Martingale, said in 2010 that the mother of all inefficiencies may be the risk anomaly. A trap version would make him Martingale’s CIO, a role held by Bill Jacques (role misassignment).

d.reason: D is built by a polarity flip of GARP’s “it had done even better after going live, generating an average outperformance of 1.83% since 2008” against 1.50% over the full sample. The live record therefore supported, not weakened, the simulated evidence.

questions.loText: Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Shanghai life insurer is preparing an induction slide on performance measurement for newly hired analysts. The slide defines the excess return of an asset or strategy as $\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}} = \text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$, and she wants to add one accompanying statement. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Excess returns are called active returns because producing the benchmark return itself requires investment knowledge and continuous human intervention.
The benchmark return $\text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$ must come from a single published market index, since a combination of assets or asset classes cannot serve as a benchmark.
The benchmark return $\text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$ is by definition the risk-free rate, so every excess return in this equation is measured against the T-bill return.
Calling excess returns active returns presumes that the benchmark is passive and can be produced without investment knowledge, for example through a low-cost index fund.

questions.solution:
Induction slide on $\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}} = \text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$: which accompanying statement about excess (active) return is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Alpha cannot be defined until a benchmark is defined, so the starting object is the excess return. GARP (Equation 3.1) defines it period by period:

$\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}} = \text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$,

where $\text{r}_{\text{t}}$ is the return of the asset or strategy in period t and $\text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$ is the benchmark return for the same period. GARP adds that excess returns are sometimes called active returns, and explains the logic of that label: the terminology assumes that the benchmark is passive, that is, it can be produced without any particular investment knowledge or even human intervention. Common passive benchmarks are market-weighted portfolios such as the S&P 500 or the Russell 1000, which investors can track by buying low-cost index funds. If the benchmark is passive, any return beyond it must come from doing something different from it, which is by definition active.

Two further facts matter. First, the benchmark is general: GARP states that a combination of assets or asset classes can also serve as a benchmark (Martingale’s risk-adjusted benchmark of 27% T-bills and 73% Russell 1000 is exactly such a combination). Second, the risk-free rate is only one possible benchmark: GARP treats “the benchmark is the risk-free rate” as a special case, which produces the Sharpe ratio.

| Feature | What GARP says |
|---|---|
| Definition | $\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}} = \text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$ (Equation 3.1) |
| “Active” label | Presumes a passive benchmark, achievable without skill or intervention |
| What can be a benchmark | A market index, or a combination of assets or asset classes |
| Risk-free benchmark | A special case, not the general definition |

**Applying it to this question**

The slide already shows Equation 3.1. The task is to pick the accompanying statement that is true as stated. Three of the options corrupt one feature in the table above: the meaning of “active”, the range of admissible benchmarks, or the role of the risk-free rate. Only D reproduces GARP’s explanation of the label without distortion.

**Fragile fact.** “Active” return presumes a passive benchmark; the skill sits in the deviation, not in the benchmark.

**Reference**

LO 85.b: “Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.” GARP Chapter 3, Section 3.3 Active Management, “Definition of Alpha” (Equation 3.1 and the following paragraph) and “Benchmarks Matter” (combination of assets as a benchmark). Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Alpha, Tracking Error, Information Ratio, and Sharpe Ratio” says the same. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 b, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the presumption: the label “active” assumes the benchmark needs no investment knowledge or intervention. If the benchmark required skill, outperforming it would not identify the manager’s own active decisions. A would be correct only if the stem asked what the label does not presume, phrased as its negation.

b.reason: **Absolute claim / scope error.** GARP explicitly states that “a combination of assets or asset classes can also serve as a benchmark.” B forbids this. It would be correct only for a mandate that contractually names a single index as the sole admissible benchmark, which is a contract term, not a property of the definition.

c.reason: **Scope error.** It turns GARP’s special case into the general rule. The risk-free rate is the benchmark only in the special case that yields the Sharpe ratio; in general $\text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$ is whatever benchmark is defined (an index, a blend, a factor portfolio). C would be correct if the stem said the manager’s mandate benchmark is cash.

d.reason: GARP: “This terminology assumes that the benchmark is passive and can be produced without any particular investment knowledge or even human intervention. Common passive benchmarks are market-weighted portfolios, like the S&P 500 or the Russell 1000, which investors can track by buying low-cost index funds.” D states exactly this.

questions.loText: Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 b Q2
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Canadian university endowment is calculating the alpha of an external Canadian equity manager against its benchmark, the S&P/TSX Composite Index, over the last six months. Monthly returns are shown below.

| Month | Fund return (%) | Benchmark return (%) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1.40 | 1.10 |
| 2 | −0.60 | −0.90 |
| 3 | 2.10 | 1.50 |
| 4 | 0.80 | 0.95 |
| 5 | −1.20 | −1.65 |
| 6 | 1.90 | 1.30 |

Assets under management are CAD 850 million and the average one-month T-bill rate over the period was 0.30% per month. The endowment annualises a monthly average return by multiplying it by 12. What is the manager’s annualised alpha?
questions.solution:
Six months of fund and S&P/TSX returns, with AUM and a T-bill rate given: annualised alpha using the ×12 convention.

**Concept and theory**

GARP defines alpha as “the average return in excess of a benchmark.” With T observations of the excess return (Equation 3.1), Equation 3.2 is the sample mean:

$\alpha= \frac{1}{\text{T}} \sum_{\text{t}=1}^{\text{T}} \text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}} = \frac{1}{\text{T}} \sum_{\text{t}=1}^{\text{T}} \left(\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}\right)$ .

Two points follow. First, alpha is a mean, so it is computed from the benchmark the mandate defines; any other rate in the data (here the T-bill rate) is irrelevant unless it is the benchmark. Second, alpha is an average return, so it scales with time linearly: GARP annualises Berkshire Hathaway’s monthly alpha as 0.0072 × 12 = 8.6% per year. The square-root-of-time rule applies to standard deviations (tracking error, volatility), not to means.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: $\alpha_{\text{monthly}} = \frac{1}{6} \sum(\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}})$, then $\alpha_{\text{annual}} =$ 12 $\alpha_{\text{monthly}}$.

Step 1, monthly excess returns (%): 1.40 − 1.10 = 0.30; −0.60 − (−0.90) = 0.30; 2.10 − 1.50 = 0.60; 0.80 − 0.95 = −0.15; −1.20 − (−1.65) = 0.45; 1.90 − 1.30 = 0.60.

Sum of excess returns = 0.30 + 0.30 + 0.60 − 0.15 + 0.45 + 0.60 = 2.10%

$\alpha_{\text{monthly}} =$ 2.10/6 = 0.35%

$\alpha_{\text{annual}} =$ 0.35% × 12 = 4.20%

Meaning: on average the manager beat the S&P/TSX Composite by 35 basis points a month, or 4.20% a year on the endowment’s convention. The AUM (CAD 850 million) and the T-bill rate play no part.

**Fragile fact.** Alpha is a mean: annualise by ×12, never by $\sqrt{12}$; and measure it against the mandate benchmark, not against T-bills.

**Reference**

LO 85.b: “Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.” GARP Chapter 3, Section 3.3 Active Management, “Definition of Alpha” (Equations 3.1 and 3.2); Section 3.4 Factor Benchmarks, “CAPM Benchmark” (0.0072 × 12 = 8.6%). Schweser Reading 85 (Module 85.1) computes alpha as the average excess return for T observations and also annualises by ×12 (Berkshire, LO 85.e). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 b, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: **Intermediate result / unit slip.** 0.35% is the monthly alpha, the correct intermediate before annualising. It would be correct if the question asked for the monthly alpha.

b.reason: B applies Equation 3.2 to the stated benchmark and annualises a mean by multiplying by 12, as GARP does in Section 3.4.

c.reason: **Square-root-of-time misuse.** 0.35% $\times\sqrt{12} =$ 0.35 × 3.464 = 1.21%. Scaling by $\sqrt{12}$ is the rule for a standard deviation under independent returns; alpha is a mean. C would be correct if the question asked to annualise a monthly tracking error of 0.35%.

d.reason: **Wrong input twin: risk-free rate used as the benchmark.** Mean fund return = 4.40/6 = 0.7333%; minus the T-bill rate 0.30% gives 0.4333%; ×12 = 5.20%. This measures the average return over T-bills, the Sharpe-ratio numerator, not alpha against the S&P/TSX. D would be correct if the mandate benchmark were the one-month T-bill.

questions.loText: Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 b Q3
questions.question:
A risk committee member at a Hong Kong family office is reviewing a manager’s pitch book, which states: “Our alpha of 3.1% per year proves our skill.” She drafts four comments for the committee:

I. Alpha is first and foremost a statement about the benchmark against which it is measured, so the pitch must state that benchmark.

II. Alpha by itself could be produced by taking large amounts of risk, which is why it should be divided by the tracking error.

III. Because alpha is the average excess return over the sample, a positive alpha is sufficient evidence of manager skill.

IV. Alpha is the standard deviation of the manager’s excess returns, so the 3.1% figure also measures the manager’s active risk.

Which of the comments are consistent with the definition and interpretation of alpha?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
II and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Pitch claims a 3.1% alpha “proves skill”: which of four committee comments are consistent with the definition and interpretation of alpha?

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens Section 3.3 with a warning: “Alpha is often interpreted as a measure of skill. That is debatable. It is first and foremost a statement about a benchmark.” Alpha is computed as the average excess return over a benchmark (Equation 3.2); change the benchmark and the alpha changes. That is why the benchmark must always be stated with the alpha.

GARP then explains why alpha is not enough on its own: “Alpha by itself could be produced by a manager taking large amounts of risk. The information ratio divides the alpha by the risk taken, so it is the average excess return per unit of risk.” The risk in question is tracking error, the standard deviation of excess returns (Equation 3.3), a different statistic from alpha, which is their mean.

|  | Alpha $\alpha$ | Tracking error $\bar{\sigma}$ |
|---|---|---|
| Statistic of $\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}}$ | Mean (Equation 3.2) | Standard deviation (Equation 3.3) |
| Measures | Average outperformance | Dispersion around the benchmark |
| Role in IR | Numerator | Denominator |

**Applying it to this question**

Comment I restates “first and foremost a statement about a benchmark”: consistent. Comment II restates “alpha by itself could be produced by taking large amounts of risk” and the reason for dividing by tracking error: consistent. Comment III asserts that a positive average excess return is sufficient evidence of skill, which GARP calls “debatable”: inconsistent. Comment IV calls alpha a standard deviation: inconsistent. So I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Alpha is the mean of excess returns and is a statement about the benchmark; tracking error is their standard deviation.

**Reference**

LO 85.b: “Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.” GARP Chapter 3, Section 3.1 Chapter Summary; Section 3.3 Active Management (opening paragraph) and “Definition of Alpha” (Equations 3.2 to 3.4 and the paragraph “Alpha by itself could be produced. . . ”). Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1: “Alpha is often interpreted as a measure of investor skill, but it is really just a statement of average performance in excess of a benchmark.” No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 b, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: Only I and II reproduce GARP’s statements. GARP’s chapter summary reinforces I: alpha “tells us more about the set of factors used to construct that benchmark than about the skill involved in beating it.”

b.reason: **Absolute claim, via III.** B includes III, which promises that a positive alpha proves skill. GARP says the skill interpretation is debatable, alpha depends on the benchmark, and alpha can be generated by risk taking. III would be acceptable only if the claim were softened to “a positive alpha is consistent with skill, relative to this benchmark.”

c.reason: **Sibling swap, via IV; and omits I.** IV gives alpha the definition of its sibling, tracking error. The mean of excess returns says nothing about their dispersion. IV would be true if the word “alpha” were replaced by “tracking error”.

d.reason: **Absolute claim, via III.** D correctly includes I and II but adds III. It would be correct only if III were softened as described under B.

questions.loText: Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 b Q4
questions.question:
The CIO of a Dutch pension fund is reviewing three external European equity managers benchmarked to the MSCI Europe Index, whose volatility over the review period was 16.0% per year. Each mandate caps tracking error at 5.0% per year. Annualised statistics are below, where r is the portfolio return and $\text{r}^{\text{bmk}}$ the benchmark return (all in EUR).

| Manager | Portfolio volatility (%) | Mean of r $- \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}$ (%) | St. dev. of r $- \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}$ (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | 18.0 | 1.2 | 3.0 |
| Y | 15.0 | 2.4 | 6.0 |
| Z | 22.0 | 0.9 | 4.5 |

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Manager Z breaches the cap, because its volatility exceeds the benchmark volatility by 6.0 percentage points.
All three managers breach the cap, because each portfolio’s volatility, which is its tracking error, exceeds 5.0%.
Only Manager Y breaches the cap, even though its own volatility is below the volatility of the benchmark.
No manager breaches the cap, because the largest tracking error, Manager Y’s 2.4%, is below 5.0%.

questions.solution:
Three EUR managers under a 5.0% tracking error cap; data give total volatility, mean and standard deviation of r $- \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}$: which statement about breaches is accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Tracking error is defined in GARP Equation 3.3 as the standard deviation of the excess return:

Tracking Error $= \bar{\sigma}$ $= \text{stdev} (\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}}) = \text{stdev} \left(\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}\right)$ .

It “measures how disperse the manager’s returns are relative to the benchmark.” It is not the manager’s own volatility $\sigma$, and it is not the gap between the manager’s volatility and the benchmark’s volatility. Two portfolios with identical volatility can have very different tracking errors, depending on how closely their returns co-move with the benchmark’s. GARP also notes that tracking error constraints are imposed “to ensure a manager does not stray too far from the benchmark.” Why total volatility is the wrong measure: var$(\text{r} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}) = \sigma^{2}_{\text{r}} + \sigma^{2}_{\text{bmk}} -$ 2$\rho\sigma_{\text{r}}\sigma_{\text{bmk}}$. Even if $\sigma_{\text{r}} =$ $\sigma_{\text{bmk}}$, tracking error is large when the correlation $\rho$ is low. (This identity is standard variance algebra used only to illustrate the definition; it is not a GARP equation.)

**Applying it to this question**

The relevant column is “St. dev. of r $- \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}$”. Compare each value with the 5.0% cap:

X: $\bar{\sigma}$ = 3.0% \< 5.0% (complies)

Y: $\bar{\sigma}$ = 6.0% > 5.0% (breach)

Z: $\bar{\sigma}$ = 4.5% \< 5.0% (complies)

Meaning: only Y strays too far from MSCI Europe, even though Y’s own volatility (15.0%) is below the benchmark’s (16.0%). The portfolio volatility column and the benchmark volatility are distractors.

**Fragile fact.** Tracking error is the standard deviation of r $- \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}$, never $\sigma_{\text{r}}$ and never $\sigma_{\text{r}} - \sigma_{\text{bmk}}$.

**Reference**

LO 85.b: “Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.” GARP Chapter 3, Section 3.3 Active Management, “Definition of Alpha” (Equation 3.3 and the tracking error constraint sentence). Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1: “Tracking error is the standard deviation of excess returns.” No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 b, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **Wrong input: difference in volatilities.** 22.0 − 16.0 = 6.0 points is a gap between two standard deviations, not the standard deviation of the return gap. Z’s actual tracking error is 4.5%. A would be correct only if Z’s returns were perfectly correlated with the benchmark ($\rho=$ 1), in which case $\bar{\sigma}$ $= |\sigma_{\text{r}} - \sigma_{\text{bmk}}|$.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: total volatility for tracking error.** Portfolio volatility measures dispersion of returns around their own mean, not relative to the benchmark. B would be correct if the cap applied to total portfolio volatility rather than to tracking error.

c.reason: C applies Equation 3.3: the only tracking error above 5.0% is Y’s 6.0%. Low total volatility does not imply low tracking error.

d.reason: **Sibling swap: alpha for tracking error.** 2.4% is Y’s mean excess return, its alpha, not the standard deviation of its excess return. D would be correct if the cap were on alpha (a nonsensical mandate) or if the mean and standard deviation columns were swapped.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 b Q5
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Paris-based asset manager is reviewing the firm’s training material on tracking error before it is presented to new portfolio analysts. Which of the following statements in the material is NOT correct?

options.text: Tracking error constraints are imposed on active mandates to ensure that the manager does not stray too far from the benchmark.
The larger the tracking error that a mandate permits, the more freedom the manager has to deviate from the benchmark.
When the benchmark is risk adjusted, the tracking error of the strategy is what academics call idiosyncratic volatility.
A strategy with a beta well below one against an index will tend to show a low tracking error measured against that same index.

questions.solution:
Audit of four training statements on tracking error: which is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP attaches four facts to tracking error (Equation 3.3, $\bar{\sigma}$ $= \text{stdev}(\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}})$):

1. “Tracking error constraints are imposed to ensure a manager does not stray too far from the benchmark.”
2. “The larger the tracking error, the more freedom the manager has.”
3. “If the benchmark is risk adjusted, then academics like to call tracking error ‘idiosyncratic volatility’.” With a regression benchmark $\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} = \alpha+ \beta(\text{r}^{\text{m}}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) + \epsilon_{\text{t}}$, the excess return over the risk-adjusted benchmark is $\alpha+ \epsilon_{\text{t}}$, so its standard deviation is the residual standard deviation.
4. In the Martingale case, the tracking error of 6.16% versus the Russell 1000 “is high because Martingale’s product has a low beta of 0.73 relative to the same index.”

The intuition for the fourth fact: a beta-one benchmark moves one for one with the market, while a beta-0.73 strategy moves only 0.73 for one. In every market move, the strategy and the index drift apart by roughly 0.27 of the move, so the difference r $- \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}$ is volatile. Low beta means low market risk, but high risk relative to the index.

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and C restate facts 1, 2 and 3. D asserts that a beta well below one implies a low tracking error against the same index, which reverses fact 4. D is the incorrect statement.

**Fragile fact.** Low beta versus the index means high tracking error versus that index (Martingale: beta 0.73, tracking error 6.16%).

**Reference**

LO 85.b: “Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.” GARP Chapter 3, Section 3.3 Active Management, “Definition of Alpha” (Equation 3.3 and the following sentences) and “Benchmarks Matter” (tracking error of 6.16%, beta of 0.73). Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1 states the constraint and freedom points; it does not mention idiosyncratic volatility or the low-beta link, so those two facts rest on GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 b, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: **True statement.** This is GARP’s stated purpose of tracking error constraints. It would be the answer only if it claimed the constraints are imposed to raise alpha.

b.reason: **True statement.** GARP: the larger the tracking error, the more freedom the manager has. A polarity-flipped version (“the smaller the tracking error, the more freedom”) would be the answer.

c.reason: **True statement.** GARP: with a risk-adjusted benchmark, tracking error is idiosyncratic volatility. A sibling-swapped version (“tracking error is systematic volatility”) would be the answer.

d.reason: GARP attributes Martingale’s high tracking error directly to its low beta relative to the Russell 1000. D states the opposite direction.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 b Q6
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Tokyo trust bank is calculating the information ratio of a Japanese equity fund benchmarked to the TOPIX. Annual returns over five years are shown below.

| Year | Fund return (%) | TOPIX return (%) | Risk-free rate (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8.0 | 6.5 | 0.5 |
| 2 | −3.0 | −4.0 | 0.5 |
| 3 | 12.5 | 10.0 | 0.5 |
| 4 | 6.0 | 7.0 | 0.5 |
| 5 | 1.5 | 0.5 | 0.5 |

Using the sample standard deviation (divide by T − 1), which of the following is closest to the fund’s information ratio against the TOPIX?
questions.solution:
Five years of fund and TOPIX returns plus a constant risk-free rate: information ratio against the TOPIX with the sample standard deviation.

**Concept and theory**

The information ratio (GARP Equation 3.4) standardises alpha by tracking error:

IR $= \frac{\alpha}{\bar{\sigma}} = \frac{\frac{1}{\text{T}} \sum^{\text{T}}_{\text{t}=1} \text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}}}{\text{stdev} (\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}})}$ , $\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}} = \text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$.

Both numerator and denominator come from the same series of excess returns over the same benchmark. GARP describes the IR as “the average excess return per unit of risk”, the risk being the dispersion of the manager’s returns relative to the benchmark. The risk-free rate has no role when the benchmark is an index.

Sample standard deviation: $\bar{\sigma}$ $= \sqrt{\frac{1}{\text{T}-1} \sum_{\text{t}}(\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}} - \alpha)^{2}}$.

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1, excess returns $\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}}$ (%): 8.0 − 6.5 = 1.5; −3.0 − (−4.0) = 1.0; 12.5 − 10.0 = 2.5; 6.0 − 7.0 = −1.0; 1.5 − 0.5 = 1.0.

$\alpha= ($1.5 + 1.0 + 2.5 − 1.0 + 1.0)/5 = 5.0/5 = 1.00%

Deviations from $\alpha=$ 0.5, 0, 1.5, −2.0, 0

Sum of squared deviations = 0.25 + 0 + 2.25 + 4.00 + 0 = 6.50

$\bar{\sigma}$ $= \sqrt{\text{6.50/4}} = \sqrt{1.625} =$ 1.275%

IR = 1.00/1.275 = 0.784 ≈ 0.78

Meaning: the fund earned about 0.78% of average outperformance of the TOPIX for every 1% of tracking error it took.

**Fragile fact.** IR is alpha over tracking error, and both come from $\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$; the risk-free column is a decoy.

**Reference**

LO 85.b: “Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.” GARP Chapter 3, Section 3.3 Active Management, “Definition of Alpha” (Equations 3.1 to 3.4). Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1. GARP does not specify sample versus population standard deviation; the stem fixes the sample convention to remove ambiguity (the population version gives 1.00/1.140 = 0.88, not among the options).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 b, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: **Dropped term: benchmark not subtracted in the numerator.** Mean fund return = (8.0 − 3.0 + 12.5 + 6.0 + 1.5)/5 = 5.0%; 5.0/1.275 = 3.92. The numerator must be the excess return. A would be correct only if the benchmark return were zero in every year.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: total volatility in the denominator.** Standard deviation of fund returns: deviations from 5.0 are 3.0, −8.0, 7.5, 1.0, −3.5, squares sum to 142.5, $\sqrt{\text{142.5/4}} =$ 5.969%; 1.00/5.969 = 0.17. Total volatility is the Sharpe-ratio denominator. B would be correct only if the TOPIX return were constant over the sample, so that tracking error equalled the fund’s own volatility.

c.reason: C is alpha over tracking error, both computed from $\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$, exactly as in Equations 3.2 to 3.4.

d.reason: **Inverted ratio / intermediate result.** $\bar{\sigma}$ /$\alpha=$ 1.275/1.00 = 1.27; because $\alpha$ is exactly 1.00%, this is also numerically the tracking error itself, an intermediate result. D would be correct if the question asked for tracking error in percent, or for units of risk per unit of alpha.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 b Q7
questions.question:
A portfolio manager at an Australian superannuation fund is shortlisting four Australian equity managers, all benchmarked to the S&P/ASX 200 Index, and wants to rank them on risk-adjusted active performance. Annualised figures (in AUD terms) are:

| Manager | Alpha (%) | Tracking error (%) |
|---|---|---|
| P | 1.8 | 2.0 |
| Q | 4.2 | 7.0 |
| R | 3.0 | 2.5 |
| S | 0.9 | 1.2 |

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Ranked by information ratio from highest: R, P, S, Q; R’s ratio is above one, which is not common in practice.
Ranked by information ratio from highest: Q, R, P, S; Q adds the most alpha, so it adds the most per unit of risk.
Ranked by information ratio from highest: S, P, R, Q; the lowest tracking error marks the best active manager.
Ranked by information ratio from highest: Q, S, P, R; Q’s ratio of 1.67 is the highest of the four managers.

questions.solution:
Four AUD managers with alphas and tracking errors: which ranking statement is accurate?

**Concept and theory**

GARP: “Alpha by itself could be produced by a manager taking large amounts of risk. The information ratio divides the alpha by the risk taken, so it is the average excess return per unit of risk.” Because the IR puts every manager on the same per-unit-of-risk scale, Schweser adds that “active investment choices can be ranked based on their IR scores.” GARP also gives a sense of magnitude: “Information ratios above one are not common, although many hedge funds trying to raise money claim to have them,” and IRs on many funds have come down substantially since the financial crisis.

IR $= \frac{\alpha}{\bar{\sigma}}$ .

Ranking by alpha alone rewards risk taking; ranking by tracking error alone rewards closet indexing. Neither is a ranking by IR.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: IR $= \alpha$/$\bar{\sigma}$ for each manager.

$\text{IR}_{\text{P}} =$ 1.8/2.0 = 0.90

$\text{IR}_{\text{Q}} =$ 4.2/7.0 = 0.60

$\text{IR}_{\text{R}} =$ 3.0/2.5 = 1.20

$\text{IR}_{\text{S}} =$ 0.9/1.2 = 0.75

Ranking from highest: R (1.20), P (0.90), S (0.75), Q (0.60). R’s IR exceeds one, which GARP describes as not common. Q has the most alpha but the least alpha per unit of tracking error.

**Fragile fact.** Highest alpha is not highest IR; IR is alpha divided by tracking error, and IRs above one are uncommon.

**Reference**

LO 85.b: “Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.” GARP Chapter 3, Section 3.3 Active Management, “Definition of Alpha” (Equation 3.4 and the following two paragraphs). Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1 (ranking on IR scores). No conflict; the ranking remark is in Schweser and implied by GARP’s “per unit of risk”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 b, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: A gives the IR ranking computed from Equation 3.4 and correctly notes that an IR above one is uncommon.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: ranking by alpha.** Q, R, P, S is the order of alpha (4.2, 3.0, 1.8, 0.9). B’s reasoning is exactly what GARP warns against: alpha can be produced by taking large risk. B would be correct if all four managers had the same tracking error.

c.reason: **Polarity / sibling error: ranking by lowest tracking error.** S, P, R, Q is the order of tracking error from lowest (1.2, 2.0, 2.5, 7.0). Low tracking error means little deviation, not good performance per unit of deviation. C would be correct if all four managers had the same alpha.

d.reason: **Inverted ratio.** $\bar{\sigma}$ /$\alpha$: P = 1.11, Q = 1.67, R = 0.83, S = 1.33; ordering these from highest gives Q, S, P, R and the “1.67”. That ratio is risk per unit of alpha, so its highest value is the worst manager. D would be correct if the question asked to rank managers by tracking error per unit of alpha.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 b Q8
questions.question:
A risk consultant is validating a London asset manager’s performance report for a UK equity fund. The report measures alpha against a risk-adjusted benchmark of 20% T-bills and 80% FTSE All-Share, estimated by regressing the fund’s excess returns (over T-bills) on the index’s excess returns. Annual figures:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Regression intercept (%) | 2.60 |
| Regression slope (beta) | 0.80 |
| Standard deviation of regression residuals (%) | 3.25 |
| Average fund return minus FTSE All-Share return (%) | 1.40 |
| Standard deviation of fund return minus FTSE All-Share return (%) | 5.20 |
| Average FTSE All-Share return in excess of T-bills (%) | 6.00 |

Fund assets are GBP 1.2 billion. Which information ratio should the report show against the risk-adjusted benchmark?
questions.solution:
UK fund with regression alpha, residual volatility, naive alpha and naive tracking error: IR against the risk-adjusted benchmark.

**Concept and theory**

The IR (Equation 3.4) is alpha over tracking error, and both are statistics of the same excess return series $\text{r}^{\text{x}}_{\text{t}} = \text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$. If the benchmark changes, both the numerator and the denominator change. With a risk-adjusted benchmark estimated by regression, $\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} = \alpha+ \beta(\text{r}^{\text{m}}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) + \epsilon_{\text{t}}$, the benchmark is $\text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}} = ($1 $- \beta)\text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta\text{r}^{\text{m}}_{\text{t}}$ and the excess return over it is $\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}} = \alpha+ \epsilon_{\text{t}}$. Therefore:

- alpha against this benchmark is the regression intercept;
- tracking error against this benchmark is stdev$(\epsilon_{\text{t}})$, the residual standard deviation, which is why GARP says that with a risk-adjusted benchmark academics call tracking error “idiosyncratic volatility”;
- the IR against this benchmark is intercept divided by residual standard deviation.

GARP’s Martingale figures follow this logic: alpha 3.44% against 27% T-bills and 73% Russell 1000 gives an IR of 0.78, implying a tracking error against that benchmark of about 3.44/0.78 = 4.41%, lower than the 6.16% measured against the Russell 1000.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: $\text{IR}_{\text{risk-adj}} = \alpha_{\text{risk-adj}}$/$\bar{\sigma}_{\text{risk-adj}}$.

$\alpha_{\text{risk-adj}} = \text{regression intercept} =$ 2.60%

$\bar{\sigma}_{\text{risk-adj}} =$ residual standard deviation = 3.25%

$\text{IR}_{\text{risk-adj}} =$ 2.60/3.25 = 0.80

Consistency check: $\alpha_{\text{risk-adj}} - \alpha_{\text{index}} = ($1 $- \beta) \times\overline{(\text{r}^{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )} =$ 0.20 × 6.00% = 1.20%, and indeed 2.60% − 1.40% = 1.20%. The index excess return and the GBP 1.2 billion of assets are not needed for the IR.

Meaning: per unit of idiosyncratic risk, the fund adds 0.80 units of risk-adjusted alpha, an attractive but not implausible figure.

**Fragile fact.** With a risk-adjusted benchmark, the denominator is the residual (idiosyncratic) volatility, not the tracking error versus the raw index.

**Reference**

LO 85.b: “Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.” GARP Chapter 3, Section 3.3 Active Management, “Definition of Alpha” (Equations 3.3 and 3.4, idiosyncratic volatility sentence) and “Benchmarks Matter” (0.78 versus 0.24). Conflict: Schweser Reading 85 (LO 85.c section) computes the risk-adjusted IR as 0.0344/0.0616 = 0.5584, using the tracking error versus the naive Russell 1000. GARP’s 0.78 implies the tracking error against the risk-adjusted benchmark. GARP followed. This looks like a Schweser simplification (mismatched numerator and denominator), not a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 b, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling: naive benchmark IR.** 1.40/5.20 = 0.27 is the IR against the FTSE All-Share alone, which assumes a beta of one. It answers a different question. A would be correct if the report measured performance against the FTSE All-Share.

b.reason: **Mismatched benchmarks: naive alpha over idiosyncratic volatility.** 1.40/3.25 = 0.43 divides the naive alpha by the risk-adjusted tracking error. Numerator and denominator refer to different benchmarks. No consistent stem makes this correct.

c.reason: **Mismatched benchmarks: risk-adjusted alpha over naive tracking error.** 2.60/5.20 = 0.50 mixes the regression alpha with the tracking error versus the index. This is the same pairing that Schweser uses in its 85.c illustration (3.44/6.16 = 0.5584), which GARP does not use (GARP reports 0.78). C would be correct only if the residual standard deviation happened to equal 5.20%.

d.reason: D divides the alpha measured against the risk-adjusted benchmark by the tracking error measured against the same benchmark, as Equation 3.4 requires.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 b Q9
questions.question:
A junior analyst at a US charitable foundation is comparing two funds using the Sharpe ratio. Annualised data over the same sample:

| Item | Fund K (%) | Fund L (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Mean return | 9.4 | 7.6 |
| Volatility of returns | 14.0 | 8.0 |
| Tracking error versus the Russell 1000 | 5.0 | 4.0 |

Over the sample, the Russell 1000 returned 8.0% per year on average and one-month T-bills averaged 2.0% per year. Which of the following pairs gives the Sharpe ratios of Fund K and Fund L, respectively?
questions.solution:
Two US funds with mean returns, volatilities and tracking errors, plus the Russell 1000 return and the T-bill rate: Sharpe ratios of K and L.

**Concept and theory**

GARP presents the Sharpe ratio as a special case of the information ratio: when the benchmark is the risk-free rate $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ , alpha is the average return in excess of $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ and the information ratio coincides with the Sharpe ratio:

$$\text{SR} = \frac{\overline{\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}}}}{\sigma},$$

where the bar denotes the sample average of the excess return over the risk-free rate and $\sigma$ is the volatility of the asset. Schweser: “This measure has alpha in the numerator and the standard deviation of the asset in the denominator.”

|  | Information ratio | Sharpe ratio |
|---|---|---|
| Benchmark | Mandate benchmark (index, | Risk-free rate |
| Numerator | $\frac{\text{blend)}}{\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}}$ | $\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ |
| Denominator | Tracking error $\bar{\sigma}$ | Asset volatility $\sigma$ |

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: SR = ($\bar{\text{r}}$ $- \text{r}_{\text{f}} )$/$\sigma$.

$\text{SR}_{\text{K}} = ($9.4 − 2.0)/14.0 = 7.4/14.0 = 0.529 ≈ 0.53

$\text{SR}_{\text{L}} = ($7.6 − 2.0)/8.0 = 5.6/8.0 = 0.70

Meaning: Fund L earns more excess return over T-bills per unit of total risk, even though Fund K has the higher raw return. The Russell 1000 return and the tracking errors are irrelevant to the Sharpe ratio.

**Fragile fact.** Sharpe ratio: risk-free rate in the numerator, the asset’s own volatility in the denominator; neither the index return nor tracking error appears.

**Reference**

LO 85.b: “Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.” GARP Chapter 3, Section 3.3 Active Management, “Definition of Alpha” (special case of Equation 3.4, Sharpe ratio). Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 b, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: **Dropped term: risk-free rate omitted.** 9.4/14.0 = 0.67 and 7.6/8.0 = 0.95. A would be correct only if the risk-free rate were zero.

b.reason: B uses the risk-free rate as the benchmark and the asset’s own volatility as the denominator, exactly the special case GARP describes.

c.reason: **Wrong input twin: index return used as the benchmark.** (9.4 − 8.0)/14.0 = 0.10 and (7.6 − 8.0)/8.0 = −0.05. This uses the information-ratio benchmark with the Sharpe denominator. No consistent definition produces it; it would be correct only if the Russell 1000 return were the risk-free rate.

d.reason: **Sibling swap: tracking error in the denominator.** 7.4/5.0 = 1.48 and 5.6/4.0 = 1.40. Tracking error is the IR denominator. D would be correct only if each fund’s tracking error equalled its own volatility, as it does when the benchmark is a riskless rate.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 b Q10
questions.question: A risk consultant advising a Brazilian pension fund, which treats the short-term BRL deposit rate as its risk-free rate, is writing a methodology note on computing Sharpe ratios for its managers. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The risk-free rate is known at the beginning of each period, and the volatilities of excess and raw returns are generally almost the same unless risk-free rates are very volatile, as in some emerging markets.
The Sharpe ratio divides the fund’s average return in excess of the risk-free rate by the tracking error of the fund against a market-weighted index such as the Ibovespa.
The risk-free rate applied to the period from t − 1 to t is the rate observed at the end of the period, at t, since the asset’s return for that period is only known at t.
Since the risk-free rate is known at the beginning of each period, the volatilities of excess and raw returns are always exactly equal, in every market and in every sample period.

questions.solution:
Methodology note for a Brazilian pension fund on the Sharpe ratio: which statement on risk-free timing and excess versus raw volatility is accurate?

**Concept and theory**

In the Sharpe ratio, the benchmark is the risk-free rate. GARP adds two technical facts:

1. Timing: “the risk-free rate is known at the beginning of the period and applies from t − 1 to t.” A T-bill or deposit bought at t − 1 locks in its return for the period, unlike the risky asset whose return is learned only at t.
2. Volatility: footnote 2, “In practice, volatilities of excess returns or raw returns are generally almost the same, unless risk-free rates are very volatile, which happens in some emerging markets.”

The reasoning behind 2: var$(\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}_{\text{f ,t}}) = \text{var}(\text{r}_{\text{t}}) + \text{var}(\text{r}_{\text{f ,t}}) -$ 2 cov$(\text{r}_{\text{t}}$, $\text{r}_{\text{f ,t}})$. When $\text{r}_{\text{f ,t}}$ barely moves, the last two terms are tiny and excess-return volatility is close to raw volatility. When $\text{r}_{\text{f ,t}}$ moves a lot, as with some emerging market short rates, the two can differ. (The variance identity is standard algebra used to illustrate GARP’s footnote, not a GARP equation.)

**Applying it to this question**

The fund is in an emerging market with a short-term BRL rate as risk-free. The accurate note must get the timing (start of period) right and must state the volatility point with its condition (almost the same, unless risk-free rates are very volatile). Only A does both.

**Fragile fact.** Risk-free rate: known at the start of the period; excess and raw volatilities are almost equal, except where risk-free rates are very volatile (some emerging markets).

**Reference**

LO 85.b: “Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.” GARP Chapter 3, Section 3.3 Active Management, “Definition of Alpha” (special case of Equation 3.4, the timing parenthetical, footnote 2). Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1 does not mention the timing point or footnote 2, so this question rests on GARP alone.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 b, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: A reproduces GARP’s parenthetical on timing and footnote 2 with its emerging market condition intact.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: tracking error as the Sharpe denominator.** The Sharpe ratio divides by $\sigma$, the volatility of the asset, not by tracking error against an index. B would describe an information ratio computed with a mismatched numerator; it would be correct only if “tracking error versus the Ibovespa” were replaced by “the volatility of the fund”.

c.reason: **Polarity flip on timing.** GARP: the risk-free rate is known at the beginning of the period and applies from t − 1 to t. C moves it to the end. C would be correct for the risky asset’s return, which is only known at t, but not for the risk-free rate.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** D removes GARP’s “generally almost” and “unless risk-free rates are very volatile” and promises exact equality everywhere. Knowing the rate in advance does not make it constant across periods; if it varies, the volatility of $\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}_{\text{f ,t}}$ differs from that of $\text{r}_{\text{t}}$. D would be correct only if the risk-free rate were identical in every period of the sample.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 b Q11
questions.question:
The treasurer of a Singapore-listed company is reviewing an absolute return fund held in the company’s surplus cash portfolio. The fund’s mandate benchmark is the SGD three-month deposit rate, which is set at the start of each period and barely varied over the sample. Annualised data:

| Item | Value (%) |
|---|---|
| Mean fund return | 7.5 |
| Volatility of fund returns | 9.0 |
| Mean SGD three-month deposit rate | 3.0 |
| Mean return of the MSCI Singapore Index | 6.0 |
| Tracking error of the fund versus the MSCI Singapore Index | 6.5 |

Which of the following best describes the fund’s information ratio against its mandate benchmark?

options.text: 0.83, which is the fund’s Sharpe ratio, since cash earns no excess return.
0.23, since an information ratio must be measured against an equity index.
0.50, which coincides with the fund’s Sharpe ratio for this benchmark.
0.69, since an information ratio always uses tracking error versus an index.

questions.solution:
Absolute return fund with a cash (SGD deposit rate) mandate benchmark, plus irrelevant MSCI Singapore data: IR against the mandate benchmark and how to describe it.

**Concept and theory**

The information ratio is general (Equation 3.4): IR $= \alpha$/$\bar{\sigma}$ , where both are computed from $\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}}$ for the benchmark that applies. GARP: “A special case of Equation (3.4) is when the benchmark is the risk-free rate, $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ . Then, the alpha is the average return in excess of the risk-free rate, and the information ratio coincides with the Sharpe ratio.”

Why it collapses: with $\text{r}^{\text{bmk}}_{\text{t}} = \text{r}_{\text{f ,t}}$, the numerator becomes $\overline{\text{r}_{\text{t}} \text{r}_{\text{f}}}-$ , the Sharpe numerator. The denominator becomes stdev$(\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}_{\text{f ,t}})$, which by footnote 2 is almost the same as $\sigma$, the volatility of the asset, unless the risk-free rate is very volatile. So IR ≈ SR, and GARP writes them as coinciding.

Schweser makes the same point in mandate language: “Sometimes the benchmark for an asset manager is the risk-free rate. . . When the risk-free rate is the appropriate benchmark, the best way to measure risk-adjusted returns is to use the Sharpe ratio.”

**Applying it to this question**

The mandate benchmark is the SGD deposit rate, which “barely varied”, so excess-return volatility ≈ raw volatility of 9.0%.

$\alpha=$ $\bar{\text{r}}$ − $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} =$ 7.5% − 3.0% = 4.5%

$\bar{\sigma}$ $= \text{stdev}(\text{r}_{\text{t}} - \text{r}_{\text{f ,t}}) \approx\sigma=$ 9.0%

IR = 4.5/9.0 = 0.50 = SR

Meaning: against its own cash benchmark the fund’s IR is its Sharpe ratio, 0.50. The MSCI Singapore figures are irrelevant because the index is not the mandate benchmark.

**Fragile fact.** Cash benchmark: the information ratio is the Sharpe ratio; the denominator becomes the asset’s own volatility.

**Reference**

LO 85.b: “Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.” GARP Chapter 3, Section 3.3 Active Management, “Definition of Alpha” (special case of Equation 3.4 and footnote 2). Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1 and Key Concepts (risk-free benchmark, Sharpe ratio). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 b, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **Dropped term: benchmark not subtracted.** 7.5/9.0 = 0.83 omits the deposit rate. The claim that “cash earns no excess return” confuses cash’s zero excess return over itself with a zero return. A would be correct only if the deposit rate were zero.

b.reason: **Scope error: wrong benchmark.** (7.5 − 6.0)/6.5 = 0.23 is the IR against the MSCI Singapore Index. The IR is defined for whatever benchmark applies, and a cash benchmark is GARP’s explicit special case. B would be correct if the mandate benchmark were the MSCI Singapore Index.

c.reason: C applies Equation 3.4 to the benchmark the mandate actually uses and recognises that, for a risk-free benchmark, the IR coincides with the Sharpe ratio.

d.reason: **Mismatched benchmarks.** 4.5/6.5 = 0.69 divides the alpha over cash by the tracking error versus the equity index. Numerator and denominator refer to different benchmarks. No consistent stem makes this correct.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 b Q12
questions.question:
A member of the investment committee of a corporate pension plan is reviewing a summary of the GM Asset Management and Martingale case on Martingale’s low volatility strategy. The summary reports:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean return in excess of one-month T-bills (%) | 8.59 |
| Volatility of strategy returns (%) | 12.22 |
| Average outperformance of the Russell 1000 (%) | 1.50 |
| Tracking error versus the Russell 1000 (%) | 6.16 |
| Alpha versus 27% T-bills and 73% Russell 1000 (%) | 3.44 |
| Beta versus the Russell 1000 | 0.73 |
| Reported Sharpe ratio | 0.70 |
| Reported information ratio versus the Russell 1000 | 0.24 |
| Reported information ratio versus the risk-adjusted benchmark | 0.78 |

Which of the following statements correctly describes how one of the reported ratios is computed?

options.text: The 0.70 Sharpe ratio divides the 8.59% mean excess return over T-bills by the 6.16% tracking error versus the Russell 1000.
The 0.24 information ratio divides the 1.50% average outperformance of the Russell 1000 by the 6.16% tracking error versus that index.
The 0.78 information ratio divides the 3.44% risk-adjusted alpha by the 6.16% tracking error versus the Russell 1000.
The 0.24 information ratio divides the 1.50% average outperformance of the Russell 1000 by the strategy’s 12.22% volatility.

questions.solution:
GM Asset Management and Martingale case summary with reported Sharpe ratio and two information ratios: which statement on how a ratio is computed is correct?

**Concept and theory**

The case (GARP Section 3.2 and “Benchmarks Matter”) reports three ratios for Martingale’s Low Volatility LargeCap+ strategy, each pairing a numerator and a denominator measured against the same benchmark:

| Ratio | Benchmark | Numerator | Denominator |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sharpe 0.70 | One-month T-bills | 8.59% mean excess over T-bills | 12.22% volatility |
| IR 0.24 | Russell 1000 (beta assumed one) | 1.50% outperformance | 6.16% tracking error |
| IR 0.78 | 27% T-bills, 73% Russell 1000 | 3.44% alpha | About 4.41% (implied) |

The general rule is Equation 3.4, IR $= \alpha$/$\bar{\sigma}$ , with the Sharpe ratio as the special case of a risk-free benchmark, SR $= \overline{\text{r}_{\text{t}} \text{r}_{\text{f}}}-$ /$\sigma$. GARP adds that the Russell 1000 tracking error of 6.16% is high because the strategy’s beta is only 0.73, and that the Russell 1000 itself has a Sharpe ratio of 0.45.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each pairing arithmetically against the reported figure:

A: 8.59/6.16 = 1.39 ̸= 0.70

B: 1.50/6.16 = 0.2435 ≈ 0.24 ✓

C: 3.44/6.16 = 0.558 ̸= 0.78

D: 1.50/12.22 = 0.123 ̸= 0.24

The correct Sharpe calculation is 8.59/12.22 = 0.703 ≈ 0.70; the denominator of the 0.78 IR is implied as 3.44/0.78 = 4.41%, the tracking error against the risk-adjusted benchmark.

**Fragile fact.** Martingale: Sharpe 8.59/12.22 = 0.70; IR naive 1.50/6.16 = 0.24; IR risk-adjusted 0.78, which does not equal 3.44/6.16.

**Reference**

LO 85.b: “Define and calculate alpha, tracking error, the information ratio, and the Sharpe ratio.” GARP Chapter 3, Section 3.2 GM Asset Management and Martingale (8.59%, 12.22%, 0.70, 0.45, 1.50%, 6.16%, 3.44%, 0.73) and Section 3.3 Active Management, “Definition of Alpha” and “Benchmarks Matter” (0.78 and 0.24). Conflict: Schweser Reading 85 (LO 85.c section) reports the risk-adjusted IR as 0.0344/0.0616 = 0.5584 and the naive IR as 0.2435; GARP reports 0.78 and 0.24. GARP followed. The difference looks like a Schweser simplification (using the naive tracking error for both), not a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 b, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: tracking error for volatility in the Sharpe ratio.** 8.59/6.16 = 1.39. The Sharpe denominator is the asset’s volatility, 12.22%. A would be correct only if the benchmark for the tracking error were the T-bill rate (then tracking error ≈ volatility), which is not the 6.16% reported.

b.reason: GARP: over the full sample the strategy beat the Russell 1000 by 1.50%, its tracking error versus the Russell 1000 was 6.16%, and “the information ratio of the low volatility strategy relative to the naive Russell 1000 benchmark is just 0.24.” 1.50/6.16 = 0.24.

c.reason: **Mismatched benchmarks: risk-adjusted alpha over naive tracking error.** 3.44/6.16 = 0.56, not 0.78. The 0.78 needs the tracking error against the 27/73 benchmark (about 4.41%). This is the pairing Schweser uses in its LO 85.c text (0.5584); GARP’s 0.78 shows it is not how the reported IR is computed. C would be correct only if the tracking error against the risk-adjusted benchmark were also 6.16%.

d.reason: **Sibling swap: volatility for tracking error in the IR.** 1.50/12.22 = 0.12, not 0.24. The IR denominator is tracking error, not total volatility. D would be correct only if the Russell 1000 return were constant over the sample, so that tracking error equalled the strategy’s volatility.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 d Q1
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Singapore asset manager is presenting Grinold’s fundamental law of active management to newly hired analysts. She wants one slide that states what the law says and why its output carries a particular label. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The law gives the information ratio a manager will realize after transactions costs and trading restrictions, provided its IC and BR inputs are estimated without error.
The law formalizes the idea that a manager creates alpha by keeping holdings close to the benchmark, so that the most successful bets are the smallest deviations from it.
The law gives the maximum attainable information ratio, IR $= \text{IC} \times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$, because it ignores transactions costs, restrictions on trading and other real-world considerations.
The law holds as an exact identity, so a manager who achieves the stated IC and BR is assured of earning the resulting information ratio in every year.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at a Singapore asset manager: which statement best states what Grinold’s law says and why its output is labeled as it is?

**Concept and theory**

A portfolio manager creates alpha relative to a benchmark by making bets that deviate from that benchmark; the more successful the bets, the higher the alpha. Grinold (1989) made this intuition formal. The fundamental law links the information ratio (IR, alpha per unit of tracking error) to two properties of the manager’s process:

IR $= \text{IC} \times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$,

where IC (information coefficient) is the correlation of the manager’s forecasts with actual returns, a measure of how good the forecasts are, and BR (breadth) is how many independent bets are taken, which depends on the number of securities that can be traded and how frequently they can be traded.

GARP is careful with the label: the law gives the maximum information ratio attainable, because it ignores transactions costs, restrictions on trading and other real-world considerations. It is also an approximation within the mean-variance framework (GARP footnote 3), and Schweser accordingly writes that IR is “approximately equal” to IC $\times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$.

| What the law includes | What the law leaves out |
|---|---|
| Forecast quality (IC); number of independent bets (BR) | Transactions costs; trading restrictions; other real-world frictions; downside and higher-moment risk |

**Applying it to this question**

The slide must say two things: what the formula is, and why its output is called a maximum. The deciding fact is the reason GARP gives for “maximum”: the frictions the law ignores. Any statement that treats the output as a realized, after-cost or guaranteed IR contradicts that reason.

**Fragile fact.** The label is maximum attainable IR, and the reason is what the law ignores (costs, trading restrictions, real-world frictions), not what it includes.

**Reference**

LO 85.d (Schweser R85, verbatim): “Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.”

GARP Part II Book 5 (RMIM), Chapter 3 “Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)”, Section 3.3 “Active Management”, subsection “Creating Alpha”, Equation (3.5) and footnote 3. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Fundamental Law of Active Management”. Schweser says IR is “approximately equal” to IC $\times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$ and does not list the ignored frictions; GARP’s wording (maximum IR, because frictions are ignored) is used. No content conflict, only condensation.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 d, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It reverses the law’s stated condition: the law ignores transactions costs and trading restrictions, so it cannot give an after-cost realized IR, however accurately IC and BR are estimated. A would be correct only for an extended model that explicitly deducts costs and constraints, which is not Grinold’s law as GARP presents it.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says alpha is created by bets that deviate from the benchmark. B flips the direction to “keeping holdings close”. A portfolio that hugs the benchmark has small active bets and, all else equal, little alpha. B would be correct only if the question asked how to minimize tracking error, not how alpha is created.

c.reason: C reproduces GARP’s statement: the law gives the maximum attainable IR, IR $= \text{IC} \times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$, “since it ignores transactions costs, restrictions on trading, and other real-world considerations”. Real frictions can only pull the realized IR below this ceiling.

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** The law is an approximation in the mean-variance framework, gives a maximum rather than a promise, and IC is a correlation of forecasts with outcomes, so realized results vary from year to year. “Exact identity” and “assured in every year” promise certainty the source never gives. D would need a world with no frictions, an exact formula and no estimation noise.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 d Q2
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Canadian public pension plan is reviewing an external manager’s pitch book, which defines the two inputs of the fundamental law, IR $= \text{IC} \times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$. The pitch book contains the following statements:

I. The information coefficient is the correlation of the manager’s forecasts with the actual returns.

II. Breadth reflects both the number of securities that can be traded and how frequently they can be traded.

III. The information coefficient is the correlation of the manager’s realized returns with the benchmark’s returns.

IV. Breadth equals the number of securities in the benchmark index, irrespective of how often positions are revised.

Which of the statements are consistent with the definitions used in the law?

options.text: I and II only
I and IV only
II and III only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Canadian pension plan: which pitch-book definitions of IC and BR are consistent with the law?

**Concept and theory**

The law has exactly two inputs, and GARP defines each precisely.

| Input | GARP definition | What it is not |

questions.question:
A risk consultant at a Tokyo asset manager is validating the claimed information ratio of a quantitative equity strategy. The strategy covers a universe of stocks and revises its forecasts at the start of each month. The following data are available:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Stocks in the investable universe | 2,000 |
| Independent forecasts made each month | 30 |
| Information coefficient (IC) | 0.04 |
| Annual tracking error | 5.0% |
| Assets under management | JPY 85 billion |

Using the fundamental law of active management, the maximum attainable annual information ratio of the strategy is closest to:
questions.solution:
Risk consultant in Tokyo: maximum annual IR for a strategy with 30 independent monthly forecasts and IC of 0.04, with irrelevant data.

**Concept and theory**

The law gives the maximum attainable IR as IR $= \text{IC} \times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$. Breadth counts independent bets and depends on how many securities can be traded and how frequently. GARP’s market timer example makes the time unit explicit: a timer betting every quarter makes “only four bets a year” and needs IC = 0.25 for IR = 0.50 = 0.25 $\times\sqrt{4}$. So an annual IR requires annual breadth: independent bets per period times periods per year. Inputs such as universe size, tracking error and AUM do not enter the formula.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: IR $= \text{IC} \times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$.

$\text{BR}_{\text{annual}} =$ 30 forecasts per month × 12 = 360

$\sqrt{\text{BR}} = \sqrt{360} =$ 18.974

IR = 0.04 × 18.974 = 0.759 ≈ 0.76

The universe of 2,000 stocks, the 5.0% tracking error and the JPY 85 billion AUM are irrelevant: breadth is the count of independent forecasts, not names covered. An IR of about 0.76 is the ceiling before costs and trading restrictions.

**Fragile fact.** Breadth must be on the same time basis as the IR (annual bets for an annual IR), and only independent forecasts count, not names in the universe.

**Reference**

LO 85.d (Schweser R85, verbatim): “Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.”

GARP Part II Book 5 (RMIM), Chapter 3 “Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)”, Section 3.3 “Active Management”, subsection “Creating Alpha”, Equation (3.5) and the market timer and stock selector examples. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Fundamental Law of Active Management” (IR of 0.50 examples). No GARP vs Schweser difference affects this calculation.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 d, where it is Q3 of 14.

a.reason: Uses monthly breadth: 0.04 $\times\sqrt{30} =$ 0.219. This is a monthly IR, not an annual one. A would be correct if the question asked for the IR per month.

b.reason: Uses the universe size as breadth: 0.04 $\times\sqrt{2{,}000} =$ 1.789. Covering 2,000 names is not 2,000 independent bets. B would be correct only if the strategy made 2,000 independent forecasts a year.

c.reason: Multiplies IC by breadth instead of its square root: 0.04 × 360 = 14.40. C would be correct only if IR scaled linearly with breadth, which the law does not say.

d.reason: 0.76 uses annual breadth (360 independent bets) and the square root, exactly as GARP’s examples do (0.25 $\times\sqrt{4}$, 0.025 $\times\sqrt{400}$).

Manager X times the market by switching between a BRL equity index and a BRL government bond index, making one allocation decision at the start of each month. Manager Y is a stock selector who makes 25 independent stock bets each month. Assuming the fundamental law holds and all bets are independent, the minimum information coefficients required for Manager X and Manager Y, respectively, are closest to:

Brazilian pension CIO: required IC for a monthly equity/bond market timer and a stock selector making 25 independent bets a month, for an IR of 0.45.

**Concept and theory**

Rearranging the law gives the forecasting skill needed for a target IR:

$\text{IC}_{\text{required}} = \frac{\text{IR}_{\text{target}}}{\sqrt{\text{BR}}}$ .

GARP’s central example: a stock market timer trading just the aggregate market “has narrow breadth because there are few assets, sometimes just stocks and bonds, to trade”. With bets every quarter, the timer makes “only four bets a year” and needs an IC of 0.25 for an IR of 0.50. Note what counts as a bet: one allocation decision between stocks and bonds per period is one bet, not one per asset. Cross-sectional stock selectors, by contrast, have great breadth and can succeed with ICs of only 2% to 5%.

Manager X: BR = 1 decision per month × 12 = 12, $\sqrt{12} =$ 3.4641

$\text{IC}_{\text{X}} =$ 0.45/3.4641 = 0.1299 ≈ 0.130

Manager Y: BR = 25 × 12 = 300, $\sqrt{300} =$ 17.3205

$\text{IC}_{\text{Y}} =$ 0.45/17.3205 = 0.0260 ≈ 0.026

The timer needs five times the forecasting accuracy of the stock selector ($\sqrt{\text{300/12}} = \sqrt{25} =$ 5), which is the play well versus play often trade-off in numbers.

**Fragile fact.** A market timer’s bet is the decision, so one stocks-versus-bonds switch per period is one bet; and breadth is annual when the IR target is annual.

**Reference**

LO 85.d (Schweser R85, verbatim): “Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.”

GARP Part II Book 5 (RMIM), Chapter 3 “Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)”, Section 3.3 “Active Management”, subsection “Creating Alpha”, market timer and cross-sectional strategy examples. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Fundamental Law of Active Management”. Schweser’s version uses 200 bets and IC 0.035 for IR 0.50; GARP uses 400 bets and IC 0.025. Both are consistent with the law; the difference is the illustration chosen (likely a condensation or version difference).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 d, where it is Q4 of 14.

Switching between stocks and bonds is a single allocation decision; GARP counts the quarterly stocks-and-bonds timer as four bets a year, not eight. c.reason: X is right, but Y uses monthly breadth: 0.45/$\sqrt{25} =$ 0.090. C would be correct only if the target were a monthly IR of 0.45 for Y.

d.reason: Divides by breadth instead of its square root: 0.45/12 = 0.0375 and 0.45/300 = 0.0015. D would be correct only if IR were linear in BR.
