questions.question:
A member of the risk committee at a UK life insurer is comparing two equity managers using the fundamental law. Manager P runs a concentrated macro timing strategy; Manager Q runs a quantitative cross-sectional strategy that combines value and momentum signals.

| Manager | Independent bets per year | IC | Mandate size |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | 9 | 0.200 | GBP 300 million |
| Q | 576 | 0.025 | GBP 300 million |

Which of the following statements best describes the comparison under the law?

options.text: Both have a law-implied IR of 0.60: P plays well with narrow breadth while Q plays often with a small edge, and the law treats both routes to a high IR as valid.
Both have a law-implied IR of 0.60, but Q’s much larger breadth shows that Q is the more skillful forecaster of the two, so Q should be preferred.
P’s law-implied IR exceeds Q’s, because placing only nine bets a year reduces the chance of making mistakes and so raises expected performance.
Only P reaches an IR of 0.60, because under the law an IC as small as 0.025 cannot produce a useful information ratio, whatever the breadth.

questions.solution:
UK insurer risk committee: comparing a 9-bet macro timer (IC 0.20) with a 576-bet value and momentum manager (IC 0.025).

**Concept and theory**

The law shows a central trade-off in active management. Grinold and Kahn put it as: it is important “to play often (high breadth, BR) and to play well (high IC)”. GARP sums up: you can be very talented at forecasting and make few bets really count, or you can have a very small edge but make a lot of bets, and both lead to high information ratios. Cross-sectional strategies such as value, size and momentum have great breadth because hundreds of stocks can be traded, so ICs of 2% to 5% can be highly profitable. IC is the skill measure; BR is a count of independent opportunities, not a measure of skill.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{IR}_{\text{P}} =$ 0.200 $\times\sqrt{9} =$ 0.200 × 3 = 0.60

$\text{IR}_{\text{Q}} =$ 0.025 $\times\sqrt{576} =$ 0.025 × 24 = 0.60

The mandate sizes are equal and play no part. The two managers reach the same law-implied IR by opposite routes: P by high IC with narrow breadth, Q by high breadth with a small IC.

**Fragile fact.** IC measures skill; BR counts independent bets. A large BR says “plays often”, never “forecasts better”.

**Reference**

LO 85.d (Schweser R85, verbatim): “Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.”

GARP Part II Book 5 (RMIM), Chapter 3 “Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)”, Section 3.3 “Active Management”, subsection “Creating Alpha”, quotation from Grinold and Kahn (1999) and the cross-sectional strategies example. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Fundamental Law of Active Management” (“play smart” or “play often”). Schweser’s “play smart” is GARP’s “play well”; same idea.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 d, where it is Q5 of 14.

a.reason: A gets both numbers right and states GARP’s trade-off: playing well and playing often are alternative routes to the same IR.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** B gets the IRs right but attributes to breadth the property of IC. Forecasting skill is measured by IC, and P’s IC (0.200) is eight times Q’s (0.025). Q’s larger breadth reflects more bets, not more skill. B would be correct only if it said Q “plays more often” rather than “forecasts more skillfully”.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** Under the law IR rises with $\sqrt{\text{BR}}$; fewer bets lower the IR unless compensated by a higher IC. “Fewer bets, fewer mistakes, higher performance” reverses the law’s direction, and the IRs are in fact equal. C would be correct only if P’s IC were high enough to lift its IR above 0.60, for example an IC above 0.20 with nine bets.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D drops the breadth condition: a small IC is enough when breadth is large. GARP explicitly says cross-sectional strategies can have ICs of only 2% to 5% and be highly profitable. D would be correct only if Q’s breadth were small, for example nine bets a year (IR of 0.075).

questions.question: A model validation analyst at an Australian superannuation fund is reviewing an internal memo on the assumptions behind Grinold’s fundamental law, before the fund uses the law to set AUD information ratio targets for its external managers. Which of the following statements in the memo is NOT correct?

options.text: The law is derived under mean-variance utility, so the shortcomings of mean-variance utility also apply to it.
The framework assumes that all of the information available to the manager is used optimally.
The framework ignores higher-moment risks such as skewness, but it does capture downside risk because the IR scales alpha by tracking error.
The relationship IR $= \text{IC} \times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$ is itself an approximation within the mean-variance framework.

questions.solution:
Australian superannuation fund model validation: which memo statement about the law’s assumptions is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP states the law’s assumptions in one compact passage:

- It is derived under mean-variance utility, so all the shortcomings of mean-variance utility apply.
- In particular, using mean-variance utility, the framework ignores downside risk and other higher-moment risk, while assuming that all information is used optimally.
- A crucial assumption is that the forecasts are independent of each other.
- Footnote 3: the law is itself an approximation in the mean-variance framework; better approximations and extensions exist.

Why does mean-variance utility matter? A mean-variance investor cares only about expected return and variance. Tracking error is a standard deviation: it treats upside and downside deviations symmetrically and is silent on skewness and fat tails. So an IR built on it cannot distinguish a strategy with symmetric outcomes from one with rare, large losses. (This mechanism is an explanatory gloss; GARP states the conclusion, that the framework ignores downside and higher-moment risk, without spelling out the mechanism.)

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and D restate GARP’s assumptions. C splits “downside risk” from “higher-moment risk” and claims the IR captures the former through tracking error. GARP says the framework ignores both. Tracking error is a symmetric dispersion measure, so it does not isolate downside risk. C is the incorrect statement.

**Fragile fact.** The framework ignores both downside risk and higher-moment risk; tracking error is symmetric and does not rescue either.

**Reference**

LO 85.d (Schweser R85, verbatim): “Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.”

GARP Part II Book 5 (RMIM), Chapter 3 “Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)”, Section 3.3 “Active Management”, subsection “Creating Alpha”, paragraph beginning “Grinold’s fundamental law is derived under mean-variance utility”, and footnote 3. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Fundamental Law of Active Management”. Schweser mentions only “ignores downside risk” and independence; it omits mean-variance utility, optimal use of information and higher moments. GARP used; condensation, not a conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 d, where it is Q6 of 14.

a.reason: **Correct statement.** GARP: the law “is derived under mean-variance utility, and so all the shortcomings of mean-variance utility apply”. A would be the answer only if it said the law is derived under a utility function that rewards positive skewness, for example.

b.reason: **Correct statement.** GARP: the framework assumes “that all information is used optimally”. B would be the answer if it said the law allows for information being used inefficiently (that would be a polarity flip).

c.reason: GARP: “the Grinold-Kahn framework ignores downside risk and other higher moment risk”. C contradicts the first half of that sentence.

d.reason:
**Correct statement.** GARP footnote 3: “The fundamental law is itself an approximation in the mean-variance framework.” This is also why Schweser writes “approximately equal”. D would be the answer if it said the relationship holds exactly (an absolute-claim trap).

The answer C is built by a **scope or condition error**: it keeps half of GARP’s “ignores downside and higher-moment risk” and overextends tracking error into a downside measure.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a German insurer is reviewing a proposal for a EUR overlay mandate. The manager sells out-of-the-money equity index put options on many separate underlyings, collecting premiums in most months but facing occasional large losses. Using an estimated IC and the number of independent positions, the manager’s pitch shows a law-implied information ratio well above 1.0. Which concern about this use of the law is most directly grounded in the law’s own assumptions?

options.text: The law penalizes left-tail losses through the IC term, so the high IR shown in the pitch already reflects the occasional large losses.
The law is derived under mean-variance utility and ignores downside and higher-moment risk, so a high IR can overstate the appeal of a strategy with rare large losses.
Transactions costs on the options are understated, since the law builds these costs into the maximum information ratio it reports.
ICs fall as assets under management rise, and the law captures this by reducing the breadth input as the overlay grows.

German insurer CRO: a put-selling overlay pitched with a law-implied IR above 1.0; which concern rests on the law’s own assumptions?

**Concept and theory**

The law is built on mean-variance utility. Mean-variance preferences rank strategies by mean and variance only. A strategy that sells out-of-the-money puts earns small, steady premiums most of the time and suffers rare, large losses: its return distribution is negatively skewed with a fat left tail. Variance (and hence tracking error and IR) understates how unpleasant those rare losses are (an explanatory gloss on the source). GARP states that, by using mean-variance utility, the framework ignores downside risk and other higher-moment risk. A law-implied IR therefore cannot be read as evidence that such a strategy is attractive.

Two other features of the law are relevant only as distractors here: it ignores transactions costs (that is why its IR is a maximum), and its first limitation is that IC is assumed constant across BR even though ICs fall as AUM rise.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem describes the classic profile of a negatively skewed, left-tail-heavy strategy, and asks for the concern “most directly grounded in the law’s own assumptions”. The deciding fact is the mean-variance assumption and its consequence: downside and higher-moment risks are ignored. Nothing in the stem concerns asset growth or costs.

**Fragile fact.** Mean-variance utility means the law is blind to downside and higher-moment risk; it does not penalize them through IC, BR or tracking error.

**Reference**

LO 85.d (Schweser R85, verbatim): “Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.”

GARP Part II Book 5 (RMIM), Chapter 3 “Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)”, Section 3.3 “Active Management”, subsection “Creating Alpha”, paragraph on mean-variance utility. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Fundamental Law of Active Management” (“ignores downside risk”). Boundary: the false-alpha problem of nonlinear payoffs in regressions belongs to LO 85.g and is not tested here; this question tests only the law’s assumption.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 d, where it is Q7 of 14.

IC is a correlation of forecasts with returns and carries no tail information. A would be correct only for a framework built on a downside-sensitive utility, which the law is not.

b.reason: B names the assumption (mean-variance utility) and its stated consequence (ignores downside and higher-moment risk) and draws the right implication: a high IR can overstate the appeal of a strategy with rare large losses.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The law ignores transactions costs; that is precisely why it gives the maximum attainable IR. Saying it “builds these costs in” reverses its stated condition. C would be correct only for a cost-adjusted extension of the law. (Costs may well matter for an options overlay, but the option misstates what the law does.)

The limitation is that the law assumes IC is constant; it does not capture the decline. D would be correct only if it said “the law assumes IC is constant across BR, which overstates the IR as the overlay grows”, and even then it would not address the stem’s tail-risk profile.

The office proposes to grow the program’s assets from USD 0.5 billion to USD 5 billion by hiring additional external sub-managers, raising breadth to 400 independent bets per year. Due diligence confirms that the new sub-managers’ forecasts are uncorrelated with each other and with the existing bets. The office projects an information ratio of 1.60. Which of the following statements best evaluates the projection?

options.text: The projection is conservative, because a larger program can fund more research, which raises the IC above 0.08 and lifts the IR beyond 1.60.
The projection is sound, because IC and BR are properties of the strategy itself, and neither input is affected by the size of the program.
The projection understates the IR, because quadrupling breadth should quadruple the IR to 3.20 when the IC stays at 0.08.
The projection is likely overstated, because it assumes the IC stays at 0.08 across the added breadth, whereas ICs tend to fall as hiring widens and assets rise.

GARP names two very important limitations of the fundamental law. The first: ICs are assumed to be constant across BR. “The first manager whom you find may truly have a high IC, but the one hundredth manager whom you hire probably does not.” As assets under management increase, the ability to generate ICs diminishes. The empirical evidence shows decreasing returns to scale: as funds get bigger, performance deteriorates, in mutual funds, hedge funds and private equity. Thus ICs tend to fall as AUM rise. (The second limitation, correlated bets reducing BR, is ruled out in this stem by the due-diligence finding.)

Current: IR = 0.08 $\times\sqrt{100} =$ 0.08 × 10 = 0.80

Projection: IR = 0.08 $\times\sqrt{400} =$ 0.08 × 20 = 1.60

The arithmetic is right, but it holds the IC at 0.08 while quadrupling breadth through new hires and growing assets tenfold. That is exactly the first limitation: the added sub-managers are unlikely to match the original IC, and the larger program faces decreasing returns to scale. The projection is therefore likely to overstate the IR. Correlation is not the issue, because the stem rules it out.

**Fragile fact.** Limitation 1 is about IC (assumed constant, in fact falls with AUM and with more hires); limitation 2 is about BR (correlated bets). Do not cross them.

**Reference**

LO 85.d (Schweser R85, verbatim): “Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.”

GARP Part II Book 5 (RMIM), Chapter 3 “Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)”, Section 3.3 “Active Management”, subsection “Creating Alpha”, paragraph “There are two very important limitations of the fundamental law” and footnote 5. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Fundamental Law of Active Management”. Schweser lists pension funds and sovereign wealth funds in addition to mutual funds, hedge funds and private equity; GARP cites evidence for mutual funds, hedge funds and private equity. GARP used; likely a condensation difference.

d.reason: D identifies the hidden assumption (constant IC across the added breadth) and the source’s evidence against it (ICs tend to fall as hiring widens and assets rise).

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Chinese life insurer is reviewing a CNY fixed income manager-of-managers program. The program has hired 40 external bond managers; each was asked to beat its benchmark, and each has done so by buying illiquid, higher-yielding corporate bonds. The program’s annual report applies the fundamental law with breadth set equal to the total number of bond positions held across all 40 managers. Which statement best describes the problem with the report?

options.text: Because all 40 managers are reaching for yield, the program holds essentially a single bet on an illiquidity factor rather than many independent bets, so breadth and the IR are overstated.
Hiring 40 separate managers ensures that their forecasts are independent of each other, so the report’s breadth is correct and the IR it shows is reliable.
The common illiquidity exposure lowers each manager’s IC but leaves breadth unchanged, so only the IC input in the report needs to be revised.
Correlated forecasts matter for equity factor tilts such as value against growth, but not for bond portfolios, so the report’s breadth can stand.

Chinese life insurer: 40 bond managers all reaching for yield in illiquid bonds; report sets BR equal to total positions.

**Concept and theory**

The law’s crucial assumption is that forecasts are independent of each other. GARP’s second limitation: it is difficult to have truly independent forecasts in BR. Manager decisions tend to be correlated, and correlated bets reduce BR. GARP gives two illustrations:

- An equity manager overweight 1,000 value stocks and underweight 1,000 growth stocks has not placed 1,000 different bets, but just one bet on a value-growth factor.
- Hiring one hundred fixed income managers who are all “reaching for yield” by buying illiquid bonds gives not one hundred different bets but a single bet on an illiquidity factor.

Correlated factor bets tend to dominate at the overall portfolio level, which is why top-down factor investing matters.

**Applying it to this question**

The 40 managers have independently chosen the same exposure: illiquid, higher-yielding corporates. Their positions load on one common factor, illiquidity. Counting every position as a bet treats correlated decisions as independent, so the report’s BR (and therefore its IC $\times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$) is far too high. The effective breadth is close to a single factor bet.

**Fragile fact.** Correlation among bets shrinks breadth, not IC; many managers making the same factor bet count as roughly one bet.

**Reference**

LO 85.d (Schweser R85, verbatim): “Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.”

GARP Part II Book 5 (RMIM), Chapter 3 “Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)”, Section 3.3 “Active Management”, subsection “Creating Alpha”, “Second, it is difficult to have truly independent forecasts in BR”. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Fundamental Law of Active Management” (independence assumption; NBIM). Schweser does not give the value-growth or reaching-for-yield illustrations; GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 d, where it is Q9 of 14.

a.reason: A is GARP’s own fixed income example applied to this program: reaching for yield across many managers gives a single bet on an illiquidity factor, so breadth and the IR are overstated.

b.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** Separate mandates do not “ensure” independent forecasts; GARP’s point is precisely that many managers can end up making the same bet. B would be correct only if due diligence had shown the managers’ bets to be uncorrelated (as in Q8’s stem).

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** C moves the effect of correlation from BR to IC. GARP says correlated bets reduce BR; the individual managers’ forecasting quality is a different input. C would be correct only if the question concerned whether each manager’s forecasts were accurate, not whether they were independent.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D restricts the independence problem to equity tilts. GARP gives a fixed income example (reaching for yield) alongside the equity value-growth example. D would be correct only if the bond managers held unrelated exposures.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 d Q10
questions.question:
A junior quantitative analyst at a Frankfurt hedge fund is checking an external manager’s claimed information ratio on a EUR equity mandate. The manager holds 600 overweight positions in value stocks offset by 600 underweight positions in growth stocks, resets this tilt at each quarter-end, and counts every position at every reset as a separate bet.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Positions held (long plus short) | 1,200 |
| Resets per year | 4 |
| IC per bet (manager’s estimate) | 0.03 |
| Annual tracking error | 6.0% |
| Manager’s breadth (positions × resets) | 4,800 |
| Manager’s claimed IR | 2.08 |

The analyst finds that every position expresses the same value-growth tilt and that the four quarterly tilts are independent of each other. Assuming the IC of 0.03 applies to each independent bet, the law-implied maximum IR is closest to:
questions.solution:
Frankfurt hedge fund analyst: 1,200 value/growth positions reset quarterly, all one tilt; law-implied IR with IC 0.03 per independent bet.

**Concept and theory**

Breadth counts independent bets, and depends on how many securities can be traded and how frequently. When positions are correlated, they collapse into fewer bets. GARP: an equity manager overweight 1,000 value stocks offset by underweight positions in 1,000 growth stocks “has not placed 1,000 different bets; he’s placed just one bet on a value-growth factor”. The frequency dimension still applies: GARP’s quarterly market timer makes four bets a year. So one factor tilt, independently reset each quarter, is four bets a year. Note that the law gives

IR $= \text{IC} \times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$, BR = number of independent bets per year.

**Applying it to this question**

Manager’s count: BR = 1,200 × 4 = 4,800, IR = 0.03 $\times\sqrt{4{,}800} =$ 0.03 × 69.28 = 2.08

Independent bets: BR = 1 tilt × 4 resets = 4, $\sqrt{4} =$ 2

IR = 0.03 × 2 = 0.06

The 6.0% tracking error does not enter the law. The manager’s claimed IR is overstated by a factor of about 35, because 1,200 correlated positions are one factor bet.

**Fragile fact.** Count independent decisions, not positions: a long-short factor tilt is one bet per reset, however many names it spans.

**Reference**

LO 85.d (Schweser R85, verbatim): “Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.”

GARP Part II Book 5 (RMIM), Chapter 3 “Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)”, Section 3.3 “Active Management”, subsection “Creating Alpha”, value-growth example under the second limitation, and the quarterly market timer example. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Fundamental Law of Active Management”. The numerical combination (one tilt times four resets) is an application of GARP’s two statements; GARP gives no separate effective-breadth formula, and none is assumed here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 d, where it is Q10 of 14.

a.reason: The manager’s own figure, treating 4,800 correlated position-resets as independent bets. A would be correct only if the 1,200 positions were independent forecasts each quarter.

b.reason: 0.06 applies GARP’s value-growth example (one factor bet, not 1,200) together with the frequency dimension of breadth (four independent resets per year).

c.reason: 0.03 $\times\sqrt{1{,}200} =$ 1.039 counts every position as an independent bet but ignores the four resets. C would be correct only for 1,200 independent bets made once a year.

d.reason: 0.03 × 4 = 0.12 multiplies IC by breadth rather than its square root. D would be correct only if IR were linear in BR.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 d Q11
questions.question: A risk consultant is preparing a briefing for the board of a Dutch pension fund on what Grinold’s fundamental law can and cannot do for the fund’s EUR active equity program. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The law appears widely in the academic literature, because it links the information ratio to the economic sources of risk premiums.
The law identifies where positive risk-adjusted opportunities lie, so it serves chiefly as a tool for searching out high-IR strategies.
Under the law’s framing, alpha requires superior information; a superior ability to process public information is not enough to generate it.
The law is a statistical model devoid of economic content: it offers a systematic way to evaluate opportunities, not a way to locate them.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant’s board briefing: what the law can and cannot do; which statement is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

GARP is explicit about the nature of the law:

- The law is useful to frame the active management process: alpha begins with raw information, which is processed into forecasts, and then portfolios are constructed optimally to balance return forecasts against risk.
- The key to generating alpha is forecasting, which requires superior information or superior ability to process public information.
- Despite its influence in industry, the law makes only scant appearance in the academic literature, because it is a statistical model devoid of economic content. It says nothing about where positive risk-adjusted opportunities are; it only provides a method of systematically evaluating them.
- It was intended originally as a portfolio construction tool.

Schweser says the same in condensed form: the law “does not provide a tool for searching for high IR plays” but is “a good mechanism for systematically evaluating investment strategies”.

**Applying it to this question**

The board needs to know what the law can do (evaluate, frame the process, set skill or breadth requirements) and what it cannot (locate opportunities, explain risk premiums). The deciding fact is GARP’s “devoid of economic content . . . says nothing about where . . . opportunities are; it only provides a method of systematically evaluating them”.

**Fragile fact.** The law evaluates opportunities; it does not locate them, and its academic footprint is scant, not wide.

**Reference**

LO 85.d (Schweser R85, verbatim): “Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.”

GARP Part II Book 5 (RMIM), Chapter 3 “Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)”, Section 3.3 “Active Management”, subsection “Creating Alpha”, paragraphs beginning “Nevertheless, the fundamental law is useful” and “Despite its influence in industry”. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Fundamental Law of Active Management” (“does not provide a tool for searching for high IR plays”). Consistent; Schweser omits the academic-literature and economic-content points.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 d, where it is Q11 of 14.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says the law makes only scant appearance in the academic literature, precisely because it has no economic content. A flips both facts. A would be correct for an economic theory of risk premiums such as the CAPM or factor models.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** B attributes to the law the role of an economic theory of where alpha lies (what GARP turns to next, the risk anomaly). The law only evaluates opportunities. B would be correct for a model of the sources of returns, not for a statistical evaluation framework.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** GARP lists two routes to forecasting edge: superior information or superior ability to process public information. C drops the second condition. C would be correct only if the source required private information, which it does not.

d.reason: D restates GARP’s characterization directly: a statistical model with no economic content, useful for evaluating opportunities systematically, not for finding them.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 d Q12
questions.question: A trustee of a public pension fund in Asia is studying how Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), which manages the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund, applied Grinold’s fundamental law under its founding CEO, Knut Kjær. Which of the following best describes NBIM’s approach?

options.text: NBIM centralized all active decisions under a single chief investment officer, so that every forecast was consistent with one house view.
NBIM used the law mainly as a portfolio construction tool, applying it to compute the optimal security weights within each mandate.
NBIM used the law’s intuition as a management style, delegating active decisions widely to specialized groups acting as independently as possible.
NBIM delegated active decisions widely, but superiors reviewed and approved each decision so that the delegated groups stayed within their risk limits.

questions.solution:
Asian pension trustee studying NBIM under Knut Kjær: how did NBIM apply the law?

**Concept and theory**

Since alpha is created by finding many different forecasts that are independent, the law suggests seeking breadth through independence. GARP: while the law was intended originally as a portfolio construction tool, Knut Kjær, the founding CEO of NBIM, also used its intuition as a management style. His philosophy was to delegate widely to specialized managers and to ensure that they act as independently as possible. In his words (NBIM Annual Report 2007), decisions on active investments must be delegated to many different groups and individuals, and the delegation must be real, without intervention from superiors, provided the individual stays within the agreed structure and risk limits. The sense of ownership from responsibility and the absence of intervention is an important motivation.

| Law’s original purpose | Kjær’s use at NBIM |
|---|---|
| Portfolio construction tool | Management style: many independent decision makers to maximize independent breadth |

**Applying it to this question**

The trustee asks how NBIM applied the law. Three features decide it: intuition used as a management style; wide delegation to specialized groups; real independence without intervention from superiors (within agreed structure and risk limits).

**Fragile fact.** NBIM used the law’s intuition as a management style; independence came from no intervention by superiors, within agreed risk limits.

**Reference**

LO 85.d (Schweser R85, verbatim): “Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.”

GARP Part II Book 5 (RMIM), Chapter 3 “Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)”, Section 3.3 “Active Management”, subsection “Creating Alpha”, paragraph on Knut Kjær and footnote 4 (NBIM Annual Report, 2007, “Ten Years of NBIM”). Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Fundamental Law of Active Management”. Schweser says NBIM uses “a large list of entirely independent asset managers” to keep forecasts independent; GARP’s fuller account is used. Consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 d, where it is Q12 of 14.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Centralizing decisions under one house view would make forecasts correlated and shrink breadth, the opposite of Kjær’s aim. A would describe a top-down single-view manager, not NBIM.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** B attributes to NBIM’s use of the law its original purpose as a portfolio construction tool. GARP contrasts the two: the law was intended for portfolio construction, but Kjær used its intuition as a management style. B would be correct for the law’s original design, not for NBIM.

c.reason: C states the management-style use and the wide delegation to independent specialized groups, which is GARP’s description of Kjær’s philosophy.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** Right action (wide delegation), wrong actor in the control loop. Kjær insisted delegation be real, without intervention from superiors; the boundary was the agreed structure and risk limits, not superiors’ approval of each decision. D would be correct for an organization with a central sign-off on every trade, which is what NBIM rejected.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 d Q13
questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Singapore asset manager runs a stock selection strategy. The chief investment officer requires an annual information ratio of 0.60 under the fundamental law. The following data are available:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Information coefficient (IC) | 0.05 |
| Independent bets currently made each month | 8 |
| Target annual information ratio | 0.60 |
| Annual tracking error | 3.5% |
| Assets under management | SGD 1.2 billion |

Holding the IC constant, how many additional independent bets per month are needed to reach the target?
questions.solution:
Singapore portfolio manager: IC 0.05, 8 independent bets a month, target IR 0.60; additional bets per month needed.

**Concept and theory**

Rearranging the law for breadth:

2

IR $= \text{IC} \times\sqrt{\text{BR}} =\Rightarrow\text{BR}_{\text{required}} = \left( \frac{\text{IR}_{\text{target}}}{\text{IC}} \right)$ .

Because IR rises only with the square root of breadth, the required number of bets rises with the square of the IR-to-IC ratio. Breadth is annual for an annual IR (GARP’s examples: four bets a year, four hundred bets per year).

**Applying it to this question**

IR/IC = 0.60/0.05 = 12

$\text{BR}_{\text{required}} =$ $\text{12}^{2} =$ 144 independent bets per year

Per month: 144/12 = 12

Current: 8 per month (96 a year; IR = 0.05 $\times\sqrt{96} =$ 0.49)

Additional per month = 12 − 8 = 4

Tracking error and AUM do not enter the law. Raising monthly bets from 8 to 12 lifts the maximum IR from about 0.49 to 0.60, assuming the IC holds at 0.05.

**Fragile fact.** Required breadth is the square of IR/IC, and it is annual; convert to monthly before comparing with monthly bets.

**Reference**

LO 85.d (Schweser R85, verbatim): “Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.”

GARP Part II Book 5 (RMIM), Chapter 3 “Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)”, Section 3.3 “Active Management”, subsection “Creating Alpha”, Equation (3.5) and the examples that follow. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Fundamental Law of Active Management”. No GARP vs Schweser difference affects this calculation.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 d, where it is Q13 of 14.

a.reason: 144 − 96 = 48 is the additional bets per year, not per month. A would be correct if the question asked for additional annual bets.

b.reason: B squares the IR-to-IC ratio to get annual breadth, converts to a monthly rate, and subtracts the current bets.

c.reason: 12 is the total monthly breadth required (and, coincidentally, the IR-to-IC ratio). It omits the final subtraction of the 8 bets already made. C would be correct if the manager currently made no bets.

d.reason: 144 − 8 = 136 compares an annual requirement with a monthly count. D would be correct only if the target IR were defined monthly with 144 bets a month needed.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 d Q14
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Japanese trust bank is reviewing the record of an in-house JPY equity strategy whose assets under management have quadrupled over three years. The strategy widened its coverage as it grew, and an ex post study of its forecasts gives the following:

| Period | IC | Independent bets per year |
|---|---|---|
| Three years ago (before growth) | 0.10 | 64 |
| Latest year (after growth) | 0.06 | 100 |

Under the fundamental law, how did the strategy’s maximum attainable information ratio change?

options.text: It fell from 0.80 to 0.60.
It rose from 0.80 to 1.00.
It fell from 0.80 to 0.48.
It rose from 0.80 to 1.25.

questions.solution:
Japanese trust bank analyst: AUM quadrupled; IC fell from 0.10 to 0.06 while breadth rose from 64 to 100; change in maximum IR.

**Concept and theory**

The law takes IC as constant across BR, but GARP’s first limitation is that this is unrealistic: as assets under management increase, the ability to generate ICs diminishes, and the evidence on active management shows decreasing returns to scale. A growing fund may add breadth by covering more names, yet lose more through a lower IC than it gains from the extra bets, because IR is linear in IC but only rises with the square root of BR.

IR $= \text{IC} \times\sqrt{\text{BR}}$.

**Applying it to this question**

Before: IR = 0.10 $\times\sqrt{64} =$ 0.10 × 8 = 0.80

After: IR = 0.06 $\times\sqrt{100} =$ 0.06 × 10 = 0.60

Change = 0.60 − 0.80 = −0.20 (a fall of 25%)

Breadth rose by a factor of $\sqrt{\text{100/64}} =$ 1.25 in IR terms, but IC fell by a factor of 0.06/0.10 = 0.60, so the net effect is 1.25 × 0.60 = 0.75 of the original IR. Growth hurt: the strategy now has a lower ceiling despite more bets.

**Fragile fact.** IR is linear in IC but only rises with $\sqrt{\text{BR}}$, so a moderate IC decline can outweigh a large rise in breadth.

**Reference**

LO 85.d (Schweser R85, verbatim): “Describe Grinold’s fundamental law of active management, including its assumptions and limitations, and calculate the maximum attainable information ratio using this law.”

GARP Part II Book 5 (RMIM), Chapter 3 “Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly)”, Section 3.3 “Active Management”, subsection “Creating Alpha”, first limitation (“ICs are assumed to be constant across BR”; “ICs tend to fall as assets under management rise”). Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.1, “Fundamental Law of Active Management” (“as assets under management go up, the IC tends to decline”). Consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 d, where it is Q14 of 14.

a.reason: A uses the post-growth IC and post-growth breadth together, exactly as the law requires, and captures the decreasing-returns-to-scale effect GARP describes.

b.reason: 0.10 $\times\sqrt{100} =$ 1.00 applies the new breadth with the old IC, which is the law’s constant-IC assumption that the data in the stem disprove. B would be correct if the IC had stayed at 0.10.

c.reason: 0.06 $\times\sqrt{64} =$ 0.48 pairs the new IC with the old breadth. C would be correct if coverage had not widened.

d.reason: 0.80 × 100/64 = 1.25 scales the IR linearly with breadth and ignores the IC decline. D would be correct only if IR were proportional to BR and IC were constant.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 e Q1
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Brazilian insurer wants to build a passive portfolio that mimics the systematic return of an external equity fund, so that the fund’s alpha can be measured against it. A CAPM regression of the fund’s monthly excess returns over T-bills gives the following estimates.

|  | Coefficient | t-stat |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha (% per month) | 0.30 | 1.40 |
| Market loading | 1.25 | 9.80 |
| Adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ | 0.31 |  |

The analyst has BRL 40 million to allocate to the mimicking portfolio. Which of the following positions best describes the CAPM benchmark portfolio that replicates BRL 40 million invested in the fund?

options.text: BRL 40.0 million long in the market portfolio and no position in T-bills
BRL 50.0 million long in the market portfolio and BRL 10.0 million short in T-bills
BRL 50.0 million long in the market portfolio and BRL 10.0 million long in T-bills
BRL 32.0 million long in the market portfolio and BRL 8.0 million long in T-bills

questions.solution:
Brazilian insurer: CAPM beta of 1.25, BRL 40 million to put into the CAPM mimicking portfolio.

**Concept and theory**

The CAPM says E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} = \beta_{\text{i}} (\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )$. GARP rearranges this into a statement about money. With $\beta_{\text{i}} =$ 1.3:

$$\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) = \text{r}_{\text{f}} + 1.3\,\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}}) - 1.3\,\text{r}_{\text{f}} = \underbrace{-0.3\,\text{r}_{\text{f}} + 1.3\,\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}})}_{\text{\textdollar}1}.$$

The left side is \$1 in the asset; the right side is also \$1, made of a \$1.30 levered position in the market financed by a short position of \$0.30 in T-bills. The CAPM therefore implies a replicating (mimicking) portfolio, and the beta is a mimicking portfolio weight. The general rule is $\beta$ in the market and (1 $- \beta)$ in T-bills, so that the weights sum to one. When $\beta>$ 1, 1 $- \beta$ is negative: the benchmark borrows at the T-bill rate. When $\beta<$ 1, 1 $- \beta$ is positive: the benchmark lends (holds Tbills). Alpha is any expected return in excess of this benchmark, E$(\text{r}_{\text{i}}) = \alpha_{\text{i}} + [($1 $- \beta)\text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta\text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{m}})]$.

|  | $\beta<$ 1 (Berkshire, 0.51) | $\beta>$ 1 (GARP example, 1.3) |
|---|---|---|
| Market position per \$1 | +\$0.51 | +\$1.30 |
| T-bill position per \$1 | +\$0.49 (lend) | −\$0.30 (borrow) |
| Total | \$1 | \$1 |

**Applying it to this question**

With capital K = BRL 40 million, step by step:

Market position $= \beta\times\text{K} =$ 1.25 × 40 = BRL 50.0 million (long)

T-bill position = (1 $- \beta) \times\text{K} = ($1 − 1.25) × 40 = −BRL 10.0 million (short)

Check : 50.0 − 10.0 = BRL 40.0 million = K.

The alpha (0.30% per month), its t-statistic and the adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ are irrelevant to the positions: alpha is what the fund earns over the benchmark, not a holding in it.

**Fragile fact.** $\beta>$ 1 means the T-bill leg is short (borrowing); $\beta<$ 1 means it is long. The weights always sum to one.

**Reference**

LO 85.e: Apply a factor regression to construct a benchmark with multiple factors, measure a portfolio’s sensitivity to those factors, and measure alpha against that benchmark. GARP, Chapter 3 Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly), Section 3.4 Factor Benchmarks, subsection “CAPM Benchmark”, Equations (3.6) to (3.8). Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.2 (same \$1.30 long / \$0.30 short example). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 e, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Holding the capital in the market alone assumes a beta of 1.0. It ignores the estimated beta of 1.25 and would understate the systematic exposure. It would be correct only if the regression had returned $\beta=$ 1.

b.reason: GARP: applying the CAPM with $\beta=$ 1.3 “assumes that we can produce the same return as \$1 in asset i by holding a short position in T-bills of −\$0.30 and a levered position in the market of \$1.30”. Scaling to $\beta=$ 1.25 and BRL 40 million gives long BRL 50 million in the market and short BRL 10 million in T-bills.

c.reason: **Sign error.** The analyst takes \|1 $- \beta|$ and puts BRL 10 million long in T-bills. The portfolio then costs BRL 60 million, not 40, so it no longer replicates BRL 40 million in the fund. It would be correct only for $\beta=$ 0.75 with BRL 40 million (BRL 30 million market, BRL 10 million T-bills), not for these numbers.

d.reason: **Inverse-weight error.** The analyst divides by beta: 40/1.25 = 32 in the market and the remaining 8 in T-bills. This scales exposure down when the fund is more volatile than the market. It would be correct only if the beta were 0.80 (0.80 × 40 = 32).

questions.loText: Apply a factor regression to construct a benchmark with multiple factors, measure a portfolio’s sensitivity to those factors, and measure alpha against that benchmark.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 e Q2
questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Canadian asset manager is setting up a CAD 25 million factor benchmark portfolio for a client’s equity mandate. Regressing the mandate’s monthly excess returns on the market, SMB, HML and UMD factors gives the loadings below.

|  | Coefficient | t-stat |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha (% per month) | 0.15 | 1.10 |
| Market loading | 0.85 | 14.20 |
| SMB loading | 0.30 | 4.10 |
| HML loading | −0.45 | −5.60 |
| UMD loading | 0.20 | 3.30 |

Which of the following correctly describes the T-bill, size and value legs of the mimicking portfolio?

options.text: T-bills: CAD 3.75 million short; size: long CAD 7.50 million small caps, short CAD 7.50 million large caps; value: long CAD 11.25 million growth stocks, short CAD 11.25 million value stocks
T-bills: CAD 3.75 million long; size: long CAD 7.50 million small caps, short CAD 7.50 million large caps; value: long CAD 11.25 million value stocks, short CAD 11.25 million growth stocks
T-bills: CAD 2.50 million long; size: long CAD 7.50 million small caps, short CAD 7.50 million large caps; value: long CAD 11.25 million growth stocks, short CAD 11.25 million value stocks
T-bills: CAD 3.75 million long; size: long CAD 7.50 million small caps, short CAD 7.50 million large caps; value: long CAD 11.25 million growth stocks, short CAD 11.25 million value stocks

questions.solution:
Canadian asset manager: CAD 25 million factor benchmark with market, SMB, HML and UMD loadings; identify the T-bill, size and value legs.

**Concept and theory**

Fama and French (1993) extended the CAPM benchmark with a size factor and a value factor; Carhart (1997) added momentum. GARP stresses that SMB, HML and UMD are long-short factors: mimicking portfolios made of simultaneous \$1 long and \$1 short positions.

SMB = \$1 in small caps − \$1 in large caps,

HML = \$1 in value stocks − \$1 in growth stocks,

UMD = \$1 in past winners (up) − \$1 in past losers (down).

Because each long-short factor is self-financing, it uses no net capital. The only legs that use capital are the market and T-bills, so the T-bill weight is 1 $- \beta$, exactly as in the CAPM benchmark. A loading multiplies the long-short pair: a loading of +x means long x in the first leg and short x in the second; a loading of −x reverses both. GARP’s Berkshire benchmark shows this: (1 − 0.67) = \$0.33 in T-bills, +\$0.67 in the market, −\$0.50 in small caps +\$0.50 in large caps, +\$0.38 in value −\$0.38 in growth, and it “still represents \$1 of capital allocated between factor portfolios”.

**Applying it to this question**

With capital K = CAD 25 million:

Market = 0.85 × 25 = CAD 21.25 million long

T-bills = (1 − 0.85) × 25 = CAD 3.75 million long

Size leg = 0.30 × 25 = 7.50 : long CAD 7.50m small caps, short CAD 7.50m large caps Value leg = −0.45 × 25 = −11.25 : short CAD 11.25m value, long CAD 11.25m growth

Momentum leg = 0.20 × 25 = 5.00 : long CAD 5m past winners, short CAD 5m past losers

Net capital = 21.25 + 3.75 + 0 + 0 + 0 = CAD 25 million.

The alpha, its t-statistic and the momentum leg are not needed to answer the question.

**Fragile fact.** T-bill weight = 1 $- \beta$ only; the long-short loadings never enter it. The sign of each loading decides which side of the pair is long.

**Reference**

LO 85.e: Apply a factor regression to construct a benchmark with multiple factors, measure a portfolio’s sensitivity to those factors, and measure alpha against that benchmark. GARP, Chapter 3, Section 3.4, subsections “Size and Value-Growth Benchmarks” and “Adding Momentum” (Berkshire benchmarks after Equations (3.10) and (3.11)). Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.2 (“The factors SMB and HML are long-short factors”; “All of the factor weights in this formula sum to 1.0”). No conflict. questions.question:
A risk consultant hired by an Australian superannuation fund is reviewing three external equity managers. For each manager she regresses monthly excess returns on the market, SMB, HML and UMD factors. The size, value and momentum loadings (t-statistics in brackets) are:

| Manager | SMB loading s | HML loading h | UMD loading u |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | 0.42 (6.1) | −0.35 (−4.8) | 0.02 (0.3) |
| Y | −0.03 (−0.4) | 0.55 (7.9) | 0.28 (4.2) |
| Z | −0.48 (−5.5) | 0.01 (0.1) | −0.25 (−3.6) |

Which of the following statements in her draft report is most accurate?

options.text: Manager X behaves like a small-cap growth investor and shows no meaningful momentum exposure.
Manager Y holds mainly large-cap stocks, since its SMB loading is not positive.
Manager Z is a momentum investor that tends to co-move with stocks that have gone up.
Manager Z is less value oriented than the market, since the market itself has a positive HML loading.

questions.solution:
Australian superannuation fund: read the size, value and momentum loadings of three managers.

**Concept and theory**

A factor loading is a sensitivity: how much the asset co-moves with the factor. GARP explains each sign:

| Loading | Positive | Zero | Negative |
|---|---|---|---|
| s (SMB) | co-moves with small stocks | medium-size stock | co-moves with large stocks |
| h (HML) | value orientation | neither value nor growth | acts like a growth stock |
| u (UMD) | co-moves with past winners | no momentum exposure | co-moves with past losers |

GARP adds that “the market itself is neither small nor big and neither value nor growth, so the market has zero s and h loadings”. A loading counts as a real exposure only if it is statistically significant (absolute t-statistic above about two).

**Applying it to this question**

Manager X: s = 0.42 (t = 6.1), small-cap; h = −0.35 (t = −4.8), growth; u = 0.02 (t = 0.3), no momentum. So X is a small-cap growth manager without momentum exposure. Manager Y: s ≈ 0 (t = −0.4), medium size; h = 0.55, value; u = 0.28, momentum. Manager Z: s = −0.48, large-cap; h ≈ 0, neither value nor growth; u = −0.25 (t = −3.6), co-moves with past losers.

**Fragile fact.** Zero s means medium size, not large; negative u means co-moving with past losers. The market has s $= \text{h} =$ 0.

**Reference**

LO 85.e: Apply a factor regression to construct a benchmark with multiple factors, measure a portfolio’s sensitivity to those factors, and measure alpha against that benchmark. GARP, Chapter 3, Section 3.4, subsections “Size and Value-Growth Benchmarks” and “Adding Momentum”. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.2 (signs of the SMB, HML and UMD betas). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 e, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: Positive significant s means co-movement with small stocks; negative significant h means “the stock is acting like a growth stock”; an insignificant u near zero means no momentum exposure, as with Berkshire’s u = −0.04 (t = −0.66), which GARP reads as consistent with Buffett’s “avowed eschewal of momentum investing”.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** An SMB loading of zero does not mean large-cap. GARP: if a stock co-moves with neither small nor large stocks “it’s a medium-size stock, and s would be zero”. B would be correct if Y’s s were significantly negative.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** A negative UMD loading means the manager co-moves with stocks that have gone down, not up. C would be correct if Z’s u were significantly positive, like Y’s.

d.reason: **Sibling swap of the market’s property.** The market is the neutral reference: its s and h loadings are zero, not positive. Z’s h ≈ 0 makes it as value-neutral as the market. D would be correct only if the market had a positive HML loading, which GARP rules out.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a UK university endowment is measuring the alpha of an equity manager against a Fama-French three-factor benchmark (market, SMB and HML). The regression loadings and the sample averages of monthly returns are shown below.

| Average monthly return | % | Loading | Estimate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Manager total return | 1.35 | Market loading $\beta$ | 0.90 |
| T-bill return | 0.25 | SMB loading s | −0.40 |
| Market excess return | 0.60 | HML loading h | 0.80 |
| SMB factor return | 0.25 |  |  |
| HML factor return | 0.35 |  |  |
| UMD factor return | 0.50 |  |  |

What is the manager’s annualized alpha relative to the Fama-French benchmark, using simple multiplication by 12?
questions.solution:
UK endowment: compute annualized alpha against a Fama-French three-factor benchmark from loadings and average factor returns.

**Concept and theory**

Once the loadings are estimated, the factor benchmark is a portfolio, and its return can be computed each period. GARP defines the excess return relative to the benchmark as $\text{r}^{\text{ex}} = \text{r}_{\text{i}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}$, and “the average of the excess returns is the alpha”. In the Fama-French case, with returns measured in excess of T-bills,

$\alpha= \overline{(\text{r}_{\text{i}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )} - \left[\beta\overline{(\text{r}_{\text{m}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )} + \text{s} \overline{\text{SMB}} + \text{h} \overline{\text{HML}}\right]$ .

Each factor contributes its loading times its average return. A loading on a factor with a positive average return raises the benchmark and lowers alpha; a negative loading on such a factor does the opposite. GARP notes that Berkshire’s negative SMB loading means “being large counts against Buffett’s outstanding performance”, and that its positive HML loading is what mainly lowers its Fama-French alpha below its CAPM alpha. Monthly alpha is annualized by multiplying by 12 (GARP: 0.72% × 12 = 8.6%).

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then one step per line:

Manager excess return = 1.35% − 0.25% = 1.10%

Market term = 0.90 × 0.60% = 0.54%

Size term = −0.40 × 0.25% = −0.10%

Value term = 0.80 × 0.35% = 0.28%

Benchmark excess return = 0.54 − 0.10 + 0.28 = 0.72%

$\alpha_{\text{monthly}} =$ 1.10 − 0.72 = 0.38%

$\alpha_{\text{annual}} =$ 12 × 0.38% = 4.56%

The UMD factor return (0.50%) is irrelevant: the benchmark is the three-factor model, which has no UMD loading. The manager earns 4.56% a year more than a passive portfolio with the same market, size and value exposures.

**Fragile fact.** Each factor’s contribution is loading times factor return, sign included; a negative SMB loading with a positive SMB premium raises alpha.

**Reference**

LO 85.e: Apply a factor regression to construct a benchmark with multiple factors, measure a portfolio’s sensitivity to those factors, and measure alpha against that benchmark. GARP, Chapter 3, Section 3.4, subsections “Factor Regressions” $\text{(r}^{\text{ex}} = \text{r}_{\text{i}} - \text{r}^{\text{bmk}}$, “The average of the excess returns is the alpha”) and “Size and Value-Growth Benchmarks”. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.2. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 e, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: Treating s = −0.40 as +0.40 makes the size term +0.10%, the benchmark 0.92%, monthly alpha 0.18%, and 12 × 0.18 = 2.16%. Correct only if the manager had a small-cap tilt of +0.40.

b.reason: Using only the market term: 1.10 − 0.54 = 0.56%, ×12 = 6.72%. This is an alpha against a CAPM-style benchmark that happens to use the three-factor beta, and ignores the size and value legs. Correct only if the question asked for alpha with s $= \text{h} =$ 0.

c.reason: It is the average return in excess of the Fama-French mimicking portfolio, exactly GARP’s definition of alpha against a factor benchmark, annualized by 12.

d.reason: Using the manager’s total return instead of its excess return: 1.35 − 0.72 = 0.63%, ×12 = 7.56%. The regression is on excess returns, so the T-bill return must be subtracted. Correct only if the T-bill return were zero.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a German bank is reviewing a model validation report on a fund that the bank’s wealth unit distributes. The report compares three regressions of the fund’s monthly excess returns.

|  | CAPM | Fama-French | Fama-French + UMD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alpha (% per month) | 0.41 | 0.33 | 0.35 |
| Market loading | 0.62 | 0.78 | 0.77 |
| UMD loading (t-stat) | n/a | n/a | 0.03 (0.4) |
| Adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ | 0.12 | 0.25 | 0.25 |

The report makes four claims:

I. The rise in the market loading from 0.62 to 0.78 indicates that SMB and HML help explain the fund’s returns.

II. Because adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ is unchanged when UMD is added, the momentum factor does not improve the fit.

III. Because adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ rises from 0.12 to 0.25, the Fama-French alpha of 0.33% is statistically significant.

IV. Because the UMD loading is insignificant, the alpha must be identical in the last two regressions.

Which of the claims are correct?

options.text: I only
I and III only
II and IV only
I and II only

questions.solution:
German bank audit: which of four claims about CAPM, Fama-French and Fama-French + UMD regressions are correct.

**Concept and theory**

GARP reads three diagnostics when factors are added to a regression.

- Market loading shift. Berkshire’s market beta rose from 0.51 (CAPM) to 0.67 (Fama-French). GARP: “This is an indication that adding the SMB and HML factors is doing something; the market beta would stay the same only if the SMB and HML factors would have no ability to explain Buffett’s returns.”
- Adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$. It rose from 14% to 27% with SMB and HML (better fit), and stayed at 27% with UMD, “implying that adding the momentum factor has not improved the fit”.
- Alpha. Alpha moves as factors are added: Berkshire’s went from 0.72% to 0.65% to 0.68% per month. Significance of alpha is judged by its own t-statistic, not by $\text{R}^{2}$.

**Applying it to this question**

I: market loading 0.62 to 0.78, a shift, so SMB and HML are doing something. True. II: adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ 0.25 to 0.25 when UMD is added, so no improvement in fit. True. III: $\text{R}^{2}$ measures how much return variation the benchmark explains; it says nothing about whether alpha differs from zero. No alpha t-statistic is given. False. IV: alpha moved from 0.33% to 0.35% even with an insignificant UMD loading, as in GARP (0.65% to 0.68%). False. Correct: I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** A change in the market loading signals the new factors matter; an unchanged adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ signals they add no fit; neither says anything about alpha’s significance.

**Reference**

LO 85.e: Apply a factor regression to construct a benchmark with multiple factors, measure a portfolio’s sensitivity to those factors, and measure alpha against that benchmark. GARP, Chapter 3, Section 3.4, subsections “Size and Value-Growth Benchmarks” and “Adding Momentum”. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.2 (“the market beta rose from 0.51 to 0.67”; “adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ also rose from 0.14 to 0.27, which suggests that SMB and HML do add value”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 e, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: **I only, polarity on claim II.** It rejects II, treating an unchanged adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ as an improvement or as uninformative. GARP reads the unchanged 27% as no improvement. A would be right if adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ had fallen and II claimed it was unchanged.

b.reason: **I and III, fit confused with significance: sibling swap.** III attributes to $\text{R}^{2}$ the job of the alpha t-statistic. B would be right only if the report showed an alpha t-statistic above two.

c.reason: **II and IV, absolute claim.** IV promises that alpha must be identical, but the table itself shows it changing. C would be right only if the UMD factor had a loading of exactly zero in the sample.

d.reason: Claims I and II restate GARP’s own readings of the Berkshire regressions; III and IV do not follow.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 e Q6
questions.question:
A CRO at a Japanese regional bank is reviewing a fund in the bank’s securities portfolio. A Fama-French regression of the fund’s monthly excess returns gives the output below. The bank uses the conventional two-sided 95% confidence level.

|  | Coefficient | Standard error |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha (% per month) | 0.42 | 0.25 |
| Market loading | 1.15 | 0.05 |
| SMB loading | 0.10 | 0.08 |
| HML loading | −0.30 | 0.09 |

Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: Alpha is not significant, the fund has a significant growth tilt, and its size exposure is not significant.
Alpha is significant because its t-statistic exceeds 1.645, and the fund has a significant growth tilt.
Alpha is not significant, the fund has a significant value tilt, and its size exposure is not significant.
Alpha is not significant, the fund has a significant growth tilt, and it has a significant small-cap tilt.

questions.solution:
Japanese bank CRO: judge significance of alpha and loadings from coefficients and standard errors.

**Concept and theory**

A regression coefficient is an estimate. Its t-statistic is the coefficient divided by its standard error, t $= \hat{\theta}$/SE$(\hat{\theta}$), and measures how many standard errors the estimate lies from zero. GARP: Berkshire’s alpha “is also statistically significant, with a high t-statistic above two. The cutoff level of two corresponds to the 95% confidence level”. GARP also stresses that “most factor regressions do not produce significant alpha estimates”. The same test applies to loadings: a loading is a reliable sensitivity only if \|t\| > 2.

**Applying it to this question**

Each t-statistic is the coefficient divided by its standard error:

$\text{t}_{\alpha} =$ 0.42/0.25 = 1.68 ⇒ \|t\| \< 2, alpha not significant

$\text{t}_{\beta} =$ 1.15/0.05 = 23.0 ⇒ market loading significant

$\text{t}_{\text{s}} =$ 0.10/0.08 = 1.25 ⇒ \|t\| \< 2, no significant size exposure

$\text{t}_{\text{h}} = -$0.30/0.09 = −3.33 ⇒ \|t\| > 2, h \< 0, significant growth tilt

The fund looks like a levered market play with a growth tilt, and its 0.42% monthly alpha cannot be distinguished from zero.

**Fragile fact.** Significance is \|coefficient/SE\| > 2 at 95%; it is the t-statistic of the coefficient itself that matters, not its size.

**Reference**

LO 85.e: Apply a factor regression to construct a benchmark with multiple factors, measure a portfolio’s sensitivity to those factors, and measure alpha against that benchmark. GARP, Chapter 3, Section 3.4, subsections “Factor Regressions” (cutoff of two, most alphas insignificant) and “Size and Value-Growth Benchmarks”. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.2 (“statistically significant at a 95% confidence level due to the absolute value of the t-statistic being greater than 2.0”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 e, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: All three parts match the t-statistics against GARP’s cutoff of two: insignificant alpha, significantly negative h (growth), insignificant s.

b.reason: **Wrong percentile.** 1.645 is the one-sided 95% (two-sided 90%) critical value. The stem specifies a two-sided 95% test, whose cutoff GARP gives as two. B would be correct under a one-sided 95% or two-sided 90% test.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** A negative HML loading means the fund acts like growth stocks, not value. C would be correct if h were +0.30.

d.reason: **Significance condition dropped.** A positive SMB point estimate is not a significant tilt when t = 1.25. D would be correct if the SMB standard error were below 0.05.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 e Q7
questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a Swiss family office is reading a briefing note on factor regressions used to evaluate the office’s managers and single-stock holdings. Which of the following statements in the note is least accurate?

options.text: A CAPM regression adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ of 14% for an individual stock is relatively high, since most stocks have CAPM $\text{R}^{2}$s below 10%.
CAPM regressions on individual stocks tend to have low $\text{R}^{2}$s because idiosyncratic risk is large in stock returns.
A high adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ in a factor regression shows that the manager is adding value relative to the factor benchmark.
If added factors had no ability to explain a fund’s returns, its market loading would stay the same as in the CAPM regression.

questions.solution:
Swiss family office: find the least accurate statement about $\text{R}^{2}$ in factor regressions.

**Concept and theory**

Adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ measures the share of an asset’s return variation that the factor benchmark explains, adjusted for the number of factors. It measures fit, not performance. GARP gives three anchors.

- Berkshire’s CAPM adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ of 14% “is also relatively high. For most stocks, CAPM regressions produce $\text{R}^{2}$s of less than 10%.”
- The reason (footnote 7): “CAPM regressions tend to produce low $\text{R}^{2}$s because idiosyncratic risk is large in stock returns.”
- CalPERS: adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ of 90% against a 32% bond / 68% stock benchmark, yet alpha was −1.11% per year (t = −1.16). A near-perfect fit coexisted with no evidence of value added.

GARP also notes that the market beta “would stay the same only if the SMB and HML factors would have no ability to explain” the returns.

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and D restate GARP. C claims that high $\text{R}^{2}$ shows value added. Value added is measured by alpha and its t-statistic; a high $\text{R}^{2}$ just means the fund behaves very like its passive mimicking portfolio.

**Fragile fact.** High $\text{R}^{2}$ means close tracking of the benchmark, which is compatible with zero or negative alpha.

**Reference**

LO 85.e: Apply a factor regression to construct a benchmark with multiple factors, measure a portfolio’s sensitivity to those factors, and measure alpha against that benchmark. GARP, Chapter 3, Section 3.4, subsections “Factor Regressions” (footnote 7), “Size and Value-Growth Benchmarks” and “Doing without Risk-Free Assets” (CalPERS). Schweser does not cover CalPERS (condensed source); GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 e, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: restates GARP’s comparison with typical stocks. It would be inaccurate only if typical CAPM $\text{R}^{2}$s were above 14%.

b.reason: restates footnote 7. It would be inaccurate only if it were applied to diversified portfolios, whose idiosyncratic risk is small.

c.reason: It confuses fit with skill. CalPERS is the direct counter-example: 90% adjusted $\text{R}^{2}$ with a negative, insignificant alpha.

d.reason:
restates GARP’s reading of the beta shift. It would be inaccurate if it claimed the reverse, that an unchanged beta proves the new factors matter.

The wrong (least accurate) statement C was built by a sibling swap: it gives $\text{R}^{2}$ the role that alpha plays.

questions.loText: Apply a factor regression to construct a benchmark with multiple factors, measure a portfolio’s sensitivity to those factors, and measure alpha against that benchmark.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 e Q8
questions.question: A consultant to a Dutch pension fund wants a low-cost passive benchmark for the fund’s total portfolio. She proposes regressing the fund’s annual gross returns (not net of the risk-free rate) on the gross returns of a stock index and a bond index, with no T-bill position in the benchmark. Which of the following best describes how she can turn the regression into a valid benchmark portfolio?

options.text: She cannot: a benchmark portfolio requires a risk-free asset, so the regression must use returns in excess of T-bills.
She should restrict the stock and bond loadings to sum to one, so that EUR 1 in the fund is matched by EUR 1 in stocks and bonds plus alpha.
She should leave the loadings unrestricted, since the intercept absorbs any difference between the loadings’ sum and one.
She should restrict the stock and bond loadings to sum to zero, so that the benchmark is self-financing like SMB and HML.

questions.solution:
Dutch pension fund: build a benchmark from gross stock and bond returns without a risk-free asset.

**Concept and theory**

GARP: “Benchmark portfolios need not include risk-free assets.” For CalPERS, GARP proposes a cheap passive stock-bond benchmark like the Canada Pension Plan’s Reference Portfolio. The regression uses gross returns (Equation (3.12)):

$\text{r}_{\text{it}} = \alpha+ \beta_{\text{s}}\text{r}_{\text{st}} + \beta_{\text{b}}\text{r}_{\text{bt}} + \epsilon_{\text{it}}$, $\beta_{\text{s}} + \beta_{\text{b}} =$ 1.

The restriction makes the loadings portfolio weights: \$1 in the fund on the left equals \$1 in stocks and bonds on the right, plus any alpha.

|  | Excess-return benchmark | Gross-return benchmark |
|---|---|---|
| Dependent variable | $\text{r}_{\text{i}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ | $\text{r}_{\text{i}}$ |
| Residual weight | T-bills, 1 $- \beta$ | none |
| Restriction | none needed | loadings sum to one |

**Applying it to this question**

Gross returns and no T-bills: the loadings must be restricted to sum to one, as for CalPERS (0.68 stocks +0.32 bonds = 1).

**Fragile fact.** Gross returns: loadings sum to one. Excess returns: T-bills take 1 $- \beta$. Long-short factors: each pair nets to zero.

**Reference**

LO 85.e: Apply a factor regression to construct a benchmark with multiple factors, measure a portfolio’s sensitivity to those factors, and measure alpha against that benchmark. GARP, Chapter 3, Section 3.4, subsection “Doing without Risk-Free Assets” (CalPERS, Equation (3.12)). Schweser Reading 85 does not cover this case; content from GARP. Note: GARP’s Figure 3.3 caption says “32% stocks/68% bonds”, reversing its own regression (0.32 bonds, 0.68 stocks); the regression is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 e, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** It says a risk-free asset is always required. GARP states the opposite. A would be correct only for an unrestricted excess-return regression, where T-bills fill the gap.

b.reason: GARP: “To obtain a benchmark portfolio, we require the restriction that \[the loadings sum to one\]. That is, the portfolio weights must sum to one.”

c.reason: **Condition dropped.** Without the restriction the loadings need not sum to one, so they are not portfolio weights and the right side no longer represents \$1 of capital. C would be correct only for an excess-return regression where T-bills take 1 $- \beta$.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Summing to zero is the property of the self-financing long-short factors (SMB, HML), not of a fully invested stock-bond benchmark. A zero-sum benchmark cannot replicate \$1 in the fund. D would describe how a single long-short factor such as SMB is built.

questions.loText: Apply a factor regression to construct a benchmark with multiple factors, measure a portfolio’s sensitivity to those factors, and measure alpha against that benchmark.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 e Q9
questions.question: A risk consultant is advising the investment committee of a Singapore insurer that measures its equity managers’ alphas against Fama-French factor benchmarks. Which of the following statements in her memo is most accurate?

options.text: Every factor regression assumes the factor benchmark can be created; since SMB and HML cannot be traded directly, the factors chosen can strongly influence the measured alpha.
Fama and French created SMB and HML indices that can be bought directly, so the main difficulty with the model lies in estimating the loadings rather than replicating the factors.
Adding further factors to a benchmark always lowers the measured alpha, since each extra factor explains part of the return that was previously counted as alpha.
Since the benchmark’s factor weights sum to one, larger SMB and HML loadings reduce the amount of capital the benchmark can hold in T-bills.

questions.solution:
Singapore insurer: most accurate statement about the tradeability of factors and how factor choice affects alpha.

**Concept and theory**

A factor benchmark is meant to be an investable alternative: the return an investor could have earned passively with the same exposures. GARP: “Every time we run a factor regression, we are assuming that we can create a factor benchmark portfolio.” Schweser makes the practical point: Fama and French created SMB and HML indices “but there is no way to directly trade an SMB or HML portfolio. These indices are conceptual and not directly tradeable. It is important to include only tradeable factors because the factors chosen will greatly influence the calculated alpha.” Also, adding factors changes alpha in either direction: Berkshire’s alpha fell from 0.72% to 0.65% when SMB and HML were added, then rose to 0.68% when UMD was added. (Using tradeable ETFs instead is style analysis, LO 85.f.)

**Applying it to this question**

The memo statement must combine the assumption behind every factor regression with the consequence of non-tradeable factors. Only A does so.

**Fragile fact.** SMB and HML are self-financing but not directly tradeable; adding factors can move alpha up or down.

**Reference**

LO 85.e: Apply a factor regression to construct a benchmark with multiple factors, measure a portfolio’s sensitivity to those factors, and measure alpha against that benchmark. GARP, Chapter 3, Section 3.4, subsections “Size and Value-Growth Benchmarks” (“Every time we run a factor regression, we are assuming that we can create a factor benchmark portfolio”) and “Adding Momentum”. Schweser Reading 85, Module 85.2, final paragraph (tradeability). Boundary: GARP’s own discussion of non-tradeable Fama-French portfolios sits in “Time-Varying Factor Exposures” (LO 85.f); Schweser places the warning under LO 85.e, so only the warning is tested here, not the ETF remedy.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 e, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: It joins GARP’s assumption (the benchmark can be created) with Schweser’s warning (SMB and HML are not directly tradeable, and factor choice greatly influences alpha).

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It turns “not directly tradeable” into “can be bought directly”. It would be correct for tradeable factor proxies such as index ETFs (the LO 85.f approach), not for the Fama-French indices.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** “Always lowers” is contradicted by GARP: adding UMD raised Berkshire’s alpha from 0.65% to 0.68%. Alpha falls only when the fund loads on a factor with a positive average return in the direction that raises the benchmark. C would be correct with “can lower”.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It gives the long-short legs the capital-using property of the market leg. SMB and HML are \$1 long and \$1 short, so the T-bill weight is 1 $- \beta$ regardless of s and h (Berkshire: 1 − 0.67 = 0.33 with s = −0.50, h = 0.38). D would be correct only if SMB and HML were long-only funded portfolios.
