questions.question: A board member of a Singapore sovereign wealth fund receives two research reports. Report X sorts U.S. stocks into quintiles on lagged idiosyncratic volatility; Report Y sorts them on lagged beta. Both cover September 1963 to December 2011, and both find that the riskiest quintile has the lowest Sharpe ratio. The board member asks the CRO how the two anomalies differ. Which response by the CRO best describes the difference?

options.text: Both anomalies show up in raw average returns as well as in Sharpe ratios, so a simple long-low, short-high return spread captures either anomaly equally well.
The volatility anomaly shows up in both raw average returns and Sharpe ratios, whereas raw average returns are roughly flat across beta quintiles and the beta anomaly appears in Sharpe ratios.
The beta anomaly shows up in both raw average returns and Sharpe ratios, whereas raw average returns are roughly flat across volatility quintiles and the volatility anomaly appears in Sharpe ratios.
Neither anomaly shows up in raw average returns; both appear only after adjusting for risk, since the riskiest stocks in each sort earn roughly the same raw returns as the safest.

questions.solution:
CRO explaining to a board member how the volatility anomaly and the beta anomaly differ.

**Concept and theory**

The two anomalies share one conclusion and differ in how it appears.

|  | Volatility anomaly | Beta anomaly |
|---|---|---|
| Sort variable | Lagged idiosyncratic (or total) volatility | Lagged beta |
| Raw average returns | Fall sharply: above 10%, 6.8%, | Roughly flat: about 15%, then |
|  | 0.1% | 12.7% |
| Raw Sharpe ratios | 0.8 to 0.0 | 0.9 to 0.4 |
| Why Sharpe falls | Numerator falls and denominator rises | Mainly the denominator rises |
| Factor | VOL, Sharpe 0.6 | BAB, Sharpe 0.5 |

Schweser’s Key Concept states the common ground: both say that stocks with higher risk, by standard deviation or by beta, “produce lower risk-adjusted returns.” GARP adds the difference: high-volatility stocks have “abysmally low” raw returns, whereas the beta anomaly “is not that stocks with high betas have low returns; they don’t.” The consequence for factor building: differences in average returns across beta quintiles “are tiny,” so the beta anomaly cannot be traded by a simple return spread, whereas volatility quintiles show “pronounced differences in expected returns.”

**Applying it to this question**

Both reports agree on the shared fact (lowest Sharpe ratio in the riskiest quintile), so the difference must lie in raw returns. The deciding fact: the volatility sort shows the anomaly in raw returns and Sharpe ratios; the beta sort shows it in Sharpe ratios with flat raw returns.

**Fragile fact.** “Both anomalies mean lower risk-adjusted returns” is true; “both mean flat raw returns” is false. Only beta is flat in raw returns.

**Reference**

LO 85.h: Compare the volatility anomaly and the beta anomaly and analyze evidence of each anomaly. GARP FRM Part II, Risk Management and Investment Management (2025 edition), Chapter 3, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly), Section 3.5 Low Risk Anomaly, subsections “Lagged Volatility and Future Returns,” “Lagged Beta and Future Returns” and “Betting against Beta.” Schweser Key Concepts LO 85.h states only the shared conclusion; the raw-return contrast comes from GARP and from Schweser’s 85.h text.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 h, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: **Scope error: overextension.** A extends the volatility anomaly’s raw-return property to the beta anomaly. Because beta-quintile returns are nearly flat, a raw return spread captures little; that is why BAB must scale its legs by beta. A would be true only for the volatility sort.

b.reason: B matches GARP’s quintile results for both sorts, and Schweser’s “This beta anomaly does not suggest that stocks with higher betas have low returns because they do not.”

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** C swaps the attributions: it gives the beta anomaly the falling raw returns and the volatility anomaly the flat raw returns. It would be correct only if the labels on Reports X and Y were exchanged.

d.reason: **Scope error from the shared Key Concept.** The shared statement, “lower risk-adjusted returns,” is true for both, but D overextends it to say neither shows up in raw returns. Volatility-sorted raw returns fall from above 10% to 0.1%. D would be right only for the beta sort.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a UK asset manager is reviewing a research note that supports the launch of the firm’s low-volatility equity fund. Which of the following statements in the note is least accurate?

options.text: Clientele models, in which some agents cannot diversify, predict the negative relation between idiosyncratic volatility and future returns that later empirical work documented.
Under the CAPM and its multifactor extensions, idiosyncratic volatility should be unrelated to expected returns, which depend on how assets covary with factor risks.
The negative relation survived controls for size, value, liquidity risk, co-skewness, analyst forecast dispersion and momentum, and aggregate volatility risk did not explain it.
Follow-up work found the volatility effect in each G7 country and across all developed stock markets, and skewness did not explain the puzzle.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor reviewing the theory and robustness claims in a low-volatility fund’s research note.

**Concept and theory**

Should volatility matter at all? GARP sets out three theoretical positions before showing the evidence.

| Framework | Prediction for idiosyncratic volatility and expected returns |
|---|---|
| CAPM and multifactor extensions | No relation: expected returns depend on covariance with factor risks; idiosyncratic volatility (tracking error) should not matter |
| Clientele models (segmented markets, some agents cannot diversify) | Positive: agents must be paid for bearing idiosyncratic risk |
| Noise-trader models | Positive: higher volatilities associated with higher risk premiums |
| Ang et al. (2006) evidence | Negative: “exactly the opposite” |

Robustness of the evidence. The negative relation holds for both idiosyncratic and total volatility, after controls for size, value, leverage, liquidity risk, volume, turnover, bid-ask spreads, co-skewness risk, dispersion in analysts’ forecasts and momentum. Aggregate volatility risk does not explain it. Ang et al. (2009) find it in each G7 country and across all developed markets, with controls for private information, transaction costs, analyst coverage, institutional ownership and delay measures; skewness did not explain the puzzle.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the least accurate statement, so three statements must match GARP and one must corrupt it. The deciding fact is the sign predicted by clientele models.

**Fragile fact.** Three predictions, three signs: CAPM zero, clientele and noise-trader models positive, data negative.

**Reference**

LO 85.h: Compare the volatility anomaly and the beta anomaly and analyze evidence of each anomaly. GARP FRM Part II, Risk Management and Investment Management (2025 edition), Chapter 3, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly), Section 3.5 Low Risk Anomaly, subsection “Volatility Anomaly” (and its footnotes 24 and 25). Schweser 85.h lists only some controls (leverage, volume, bid-ask spreads, analyst dispersion, momentum) and does not discuss clientele or noise-trader models; the theory and international evidence are GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 h, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: GARP: in markets segmented by clientele effects, “idiosyncratic volatility should be positively related to returns.” A says clientele models predict the negative relation, a polarity flip. The negative relation is what the data show, against both the CAPM (no relation) and clientele models (positive).

b.reason: **Accurate.** GARP: under the CAPM and its extensions, stock return volatility “itself should not matter”; expected returns depend on covariance with factor risks. This option would be false if it claimed the CAPM predicts a negative relation (a polarity trap on the CAPM).

c.reason: **Accurate.** The listed controls are in GARP’s list, and aggregate volatility risk “did not explain” the result. This option would become false if it said aggregate volatility risk explained the anomaly (a misreading of the fact that volatility risk is a pervasive factor).

d.reason: **Accurate.** GARP: the effect “existed in each G7 country and across all developed stock markets” and “Skewness did not explain the puzzle.” This option would be false if it restricted the effect to the U.S. (scope error).

questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 h Q6
questions.question:
A risk consultant advising a Swiss private bank on its CHF equity mandates is reviewing four statements in a client presentation on contemporaneous and lagged risk measures.

I. When portfolios are formed at the end of a period on volatilities realized over that period, volatility and returns over that same period are still negatively related.

II. When portfolios are formed at the end of a period on betas realized over that period, betas and returns over that same period are positively related, as the CAPM predicts.

III. The CAPM predicts that betas estimated over the past quarter should be positively related to stock returns over the following quarter.

IV. Because the contemporaneous volatility relation is negative, an investor can trade it directly by forming portfolios on volatilities realized over the same period.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
II and IV only
I and II only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Risk consultant auditing four statements on contemporaneous and lagged risk-return relations.

**Concept and theory**

Lagged sorts rank stocks on a risk measure estimated over a past window and then measure returns over a future window: they are predictive and tradeable. Contemporaneous sorts form portfolios at the end of a period on risk realized over that period and compare with returns over the same period: GARP stresses that “these are not tradeable portfolios.”

|  | Volatility | Beta |
|---|---|---|
| Lagged (predictive) | Negative (volatility anomaly) | Flat raw returns, falling Sharpe (beta anomaly) |
| Contemporaneous | Still negative | Positive, as the CAPM predicts |
| CAPM prediction | Idiosyncratic volatility irrelevant | Contemporaneous relation positive; no prediction for lagged betas |

For volatility, the most volatile stocks “currently lose money (which we cannot forecast), and they also tend to lose money in the future as well (which is predictable).” For beta, the CAPM “does not predict that lagged betas should lead to higher returns”; it predicts a contemporaneous relation, and the data show a positive one (“exactly what the CAPM predicts”).

**Applying it to this question**

I: contemporaneous volatility relation is still negative: true. II: contemporaneous beta relation is positive, as the CAPM predicts: true. III: the CAPM makes no lagged-beta prediction: false. IV: contemporaneous portfolios are not tradeable: false. Correct set: I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Contemporaneous: volatility negative, beta positive. The CAPM speaks to the contemporaneous beta relation, not the lagged one.

**Reference**

LO 85.h: Compare the volatility anomaly and the beta anomaly and analyze evidence of each anomaly. GARP FRM Part II, Risk Management and Investment Management (2025 edition), Chapter 3, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly), Section 3.5 Low Risk Anomaly, subsections “Contemporaneous Volatility and Returns” and “Contemporaneous Beta and Returns.” Schweser 85.h covers the CAPM’s contemporaneous versus lagged prediction for beta; the contemporaneous volatility result and the non-tradeability point are GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 h, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: **I and III only.** Accepts III, a scope or condition error that moves the CAPM’s prediction from the contemporaneous window to the lagged window, and rejects the true II. A would be right if the CAPM were a forecasting model for next-period returns from past betas, which GARP says it is not.

b.reason: **II and IV only.** Accepts IV, a condition error: contemporaneous portfolios use information only known at the end of the period, so they cannot be traded. B would be right only if the sort used volatility estimated before the return window, which is the lagged, tradeable sort.

c.reason: Statements I and II restate GARP’s “Contemporaneous Volatility and Returns” and “Contemporaneous Beta and Returns” findings; III and IV each contradict a specific GARP sentence.

d.reason: **I, II and III only.** Contains both true statements but adds III. It is the most tempting distractor because it sounds like textbook CAPM; D would be right only if “past betas” were replaced by “betas over the same period.”

questions.question: A member of the risk committee at a Japanese life insurer reviews a backtest of the insurer’s JPY equity sleeve. Stocks were grouped at the end of each quarter by betas realized during that quarter, and the highest-beta group earned the highest average return over that same quarter. The member argues that this contradicts the beta anomaly cited in a proposal to tilt the sleeve toward low-beta stocks. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: The member is right: the beta anomaly states that high-beta stocks earn low raw returns in every period, so any positive same-period relation refutes it.
The member is not right: the CAPM predicts a positive same-period relation, which the data confirm; the anomaly concerns past betas, which predict future betas poorly.
The member is not right: the same-period relation between beta and returns is also negative in the data, so the backtest is most likely mis-specified.
The member is right: the result shows that past betas forecast future betas accurately, so a sort on past betas should also deliver higher future returns.

questions.solution:
Risk committee member claiming that a positive same-quarter beta-return relation refutes the beta anomaly.

**Concept and theory**

The CAPM is a statement about expected returns and the beta that applies over the same period. GARP: the CAPM “states that there should be a contemporaneous relation between beta and expected returns. That is, stocks with higher betas should have higher average returns over the same periods used to measure the betas and the returns.” Forming portfolios at the end of each three-month period on realized betas, GARP finds “a positive contemporaneous relation between beta and returns. This is exactly what the CAPM predicts!”

How can a positive contemporaneous relation coexist with a negative relation between past betas and future returns? “If we could find the future beta, future betas line up with future returns in keeping with what the CAPM tells us.” The problem is forecasting: “Past betas do a lousy job at predicting future betas.” Schweser: the contemporaneous relation is “a confirming, not a predictive, metric.”

**Applying it to this question**

The backtest groups stocks by betas realized during the quarter and measures returns over that same quarter. That is a contemporaneous test, not the lagged sort that defines the beta anomaly. The positive result is expected and does not contradict the anomaly.

**Fragile fact.** Same-period beta relation: positive (CAPM works). Past-beta to future-return relation: the anomaly. The bridge is beta prediction.

**Reference**

LO 85.h: Compare the volatility anomaly and the beta anomaly and analyze evidence of each anomaly. GARP FRM Part II, Risk Management and Investment Management (2025 edition), Chapter 3, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly), Section 3.5 Low Risk Anomaly, subsections “Contemporaneous Beta and Returns” and “Lagged Beta and Future Returns.” Schweser 85.h: CAPM “does not predict that lagged betas. . . should produce higher returns” and “historical betas are not good predictors of future betas.”

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 h, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** The beta anomaly does not say high-beta stocks earn low raw returns “in every period”; it says high lagged betas go with lower future risk-adjusted returns, and raw returns across lagged-beta quintiles are roughly flat. A would hold only if the anomaly were a universal negative raw-return relation, which no source states.

b.reason: B identifies the test as contemporaneous, states that the CAPM predicts the positive result, and places the anomaly where GARP does: in the poor predictive power of past betas for future betas.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** “Also negative in the same period” is the contemporaneous volatility result. For beta the contemporaneous relation is positive, so the backtest is consistent with the data. C would be correct if the committee had sorted on realized volatility.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says past betas predict future betas poorly (“lousy job”). D flips this to “accurately,” and then wrongly infers that a past-beta sort should produce higher future returns. D would be right only in a world without beta estimation noise and time variation.

questions.question:
A model validation analyst at the asset management unit of a U.S. bank reviews a beta-sorting study. Stocks are ranked into quintiles on betas estimated over the previous three months (pre-ranking betas); post-ranking betas are the realized betas over the three months after formation.

|  | Q1 (low) | Q2 | Q3 | Q4 | Q5 (high) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Average pre-ranking beta | 0.05 | 0.55 | 0.95 | 1.40 | 2.25 |
| Average post-ranking beta | 0.50 | 0.75 | 0.95 | 1.20 | 1.65 |

Which conclusion is most consistent with the table and with the evidence on the beta anomaly?

options.text: The post-ranking betas are so much flatter that the beta spread across the quintiles effectively vanishes, so a sort on past betas carries no information about future betas.
The flattening comes from estimation noise in the highest-beta quintile only, since the betas of low-beta stocks are estimated precisely from past daily returns.
Past betas predict future betas well, so the weak relation between past betas and future returns shows that beta fails even when future betas are known.
Past betas predict future betas poorly because of noise at both ends, and betas estimated from option prices or accounting data yield a positive beta-return relation.

questions.solution:
Model validation analyst interpreting pre-ranking versus post-ranking betas from a beta-sorting study.

**Concept and theory**

The pre-ranking beta is the beta over the previous three months, used to rank stocks into portfolios. The post-ranking beta is the realized beta over the next three months after formation. If betas were measured without error and stable, the two lines would coincide. GARP’s Figure 3.10 Panel B shows “considerable noise in estimating betas at both ends, which is why the post-ranking beta line is much flatter than the pre-ranking betas. Betas are noisy!” Extreme estimates are partly noise, so they regress toward the middle. Yet there is “still a large spread in post-ranking betas of over 1.0 between the highest and lowest beta portfolios.”

The implication: “the real mystery in the low-beta anomaly is actually not so much that beta does not work; it is that we have such difficulty in predicting future betas, especially with past betas.” Studies using other information find positive risk relations: Buss and Vilkov (2012) estimate betas from options and find them better predictors of future betas, giving a positive risk-return relation; Cosemans et al. (2012) combine accounting valuation information with past returns and also find a positive relation.

**Applying it to this question**

From the table:

Pre-ranking spread = 2.25 − 0.05 = 2.20

Post-ranking spread = 1.65 − 0.50 = 1.15

The post-ranking line is flatter at both ends (quintile 1 rises from 0.05 to 0.50; quintile 5 falls from 2.25 to 1.65), but the spread remains above 1.0. This matches GARP’s description and supports D.

**Fragile fact.** Post-ranking betas are flatter at both ends, but the spread is still over 1.0. The puzzle is beta prediction, not beta itself.

**Reference**

LO 85.h: Compare the volatility anomaly and the beta anomaly and analyze evidence of each anomaly. GARP FRM Part II, Risk Management and Investment Management (2025 edition), Chapter 3, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly), Section 3.5 Low Risk Anomaly, subsection “Lagged Beta and Future Returns” (Figure 3.10 Panel B) and the passage after “Contemporaneous Beta and Returns.” Schweser 85.h mentions Buss and Vilkov (2012) and the beta prediction challenge; pre-and post-ranking betas and Cosemans et al. (2012) are GARP only. Table values are illustrative.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 h, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** The spread shrinks but does not vanish: 1.15 in the table, “over 1.0” in GARP. Past betas carry some information, just not enough. A would be right only if post-ranking betas were roughly equal across quintiles.

b.reason: **Scope error.** GARP locates the noise “at both ends.” The table confirms it: quintile 1’s beta rises by 0.45 and quintile 5’s falls by 0.60. B would be correct only if quintile 1’s post-ranking beta stayed near 0.05.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C reverses “past betas do a lousy job at predicting future betas” and then reverses the conclusion: GARP says that when future betas are known they “line up with future returns.” C would hold only if post-ranking betas tracked pre-ranking betas one for one.

d.reason: D captures both halves of GARP’s argument: noise at both ends means past betas predict future betas poorly, and betas estimated from option-implied or accounting information yield a positive beta-return relation.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Chinese fund management company that runs CNY equity products is preparing a report on the history of the evidence on risk and return, and must choose one statement to include. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Friend and Blume (1970) found that risk-adjusted performance was inversely and highly significantly related to risk, measured by both CAPM beta and volatility.
Fama and French (1992) found the relation between beta and average returns to be positive but “too flat” compared with what the CAPM predicted.
Haugen and Heins (1975), using data from 1926 to 1971, found that portfolios with greater variance in monthly returns earned greater average returns.
The first studies showing a negative relation between risk and returns appeared only after Ang, Hodrick, Xing and Zhang published their 2006 paper.

questions.solution:
Junior risk analyst choosing an accurate statement on the history of risk-return evidence.

**Concept and theory**

GARP: the negative relation between risk (beta and volatility) and returns “has a long history,” with the first studies in the late 1960s and early 1970s; these results were largely forgotten and “recently have come roaring back” after Ang et al. (2006).

| Study | Finding |
|---|---|
| Friend and Blume (1970), | Risk-adjusted performance depends on risk (beta and |
| 1960 to 1968 | volatility); the relation is “inverse and highly significant” |
| Black, Jensen and Scholes (1972) | Beta-return relation positive but “too flat” compared with the CAPM |
| Haugen and Heins (1975), | Portfolios with lesser variance in monthly returns had |
| 1926 to 1971 | greater average returns |
| Fama and MacBeth (1973) | Volatility carries an insignificant coefficient |
| Fama and French (1992) | “Beta shows no power to explain average returns”; insignificant, negative point estimates |

**Applying it to this question**

Each option names a study and a finding. Check author against finding and direction against the source. Only A matches on both.

**Fragile fact.** “Too flat” belongs to Black, Jensen and Scholes (1972); “no power” belongs to Fama and French (1992).

**Reference**

LO 85.h: Compare the volatility anomaly and the beta anomaly and analyze evidence of each anomaly. GARP FRM Part II, Risk Management and Investment Management (2025 edition), Chapter 3, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly), Section 3.5 Low Risk Anomaly, subsections “History” and “Beta Anomaly,” plus footnote 24. Schweser 85.h cites only Haugen and Heins (1975) and says first CAPM tests in the 1970s found a positive relation; Friend and Blume, Black, Jensen and Scholes, and Fama and French (1992) are GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 h, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: GARP quotes Friend and Blume (1970), who used beta and volatility: “In all cases risk-adjusted performance is dependent on risk. The relationship is inverse and highly significant.”

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** “Positive but too flat” is Black, Jensen and Scholes (1972). Fama and French (1992) found beta has “no power to explain average returns” and an insignificant, negatively signed relation. B would be right with Black, Jensen and Scholes named.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** Haugen and Heins found portfolios with lesser variance earned greater average returns. C reverses the direction. C would describe what the conventional hypothesis predicted, which their results did not support.

d.reason: **Scope error: wrong time frame.** The first studies showing a negative relation appeared in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Ang et al. (2006) helped relaunch the literature. D would be right only if “first” were replaced by “the modern revival of.”

questions.loText: Compare the volatility anomaly and the beta anomaly and analyze evidence of each anomaly.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 h Q10
questions.question: A quantitative analyst at a Brazilian asset manager is building BRL-hedged versions of the betting-against-beta (BAB) and volatility (VOL) factors described in the reading. Which statement about the construction of the two factors is most accurate?

options.text: BAB can be formed simply as the return difference between the lowest-beta and highest-beta quintiles, since average returns differ sharply across beta quintiles.
BAB scales its long and short legs to a 15% target volatility, while VOL scales its long and short legs by their pre-ranking betas to unit beta.
BAB can use all five beta quintiles, because levering up the lowest-beta quintile, whose pre-ranking beta is close to zero, needs only a modest position.
Volatility portfolios can be traded without the risk-free asset because expected returns differ markedly across volatility quintiles, unlike returns across beta quintiles.

questions.solution:
Quantitative analyst building the BAB and VOL factors.

**Concept and theory**

Why BAB cannot be a simple spread. Across beta quintiles “the differences in average returns. . . are tiny; what’s large are the differences in Sharpe ratios.” So Frazzini and Pedersen form BAB by scaling each leg by its pre-ranking beta:

$\text{BAB}_{\text{t}+1} = \frac{\text{r}_{\text{L,t}}+_{1} - \text{r}_{\text{f}}}{\beta_{\text{L,t}}} - \frac{\text{r}_{\text{H,t}}+_{1} - \text{r}_{\text{f}}}{\beta_{\text{H,t}}}$

where $\text{r}_{\text{L,t}}+_{1}$, $\text{r}_{\text{H,t}}+_{1}$ are next-period returns of the low- and high-beta portfolios and $\beta_{\text{L,t}}$, $\beta_{\text{H,t}}$ their pre-ranking betas. The long leg levers up the low-beta portfolio; the short leg combines the high-beta portfolio with the risk-free asset. “In effect, the Long and Short portfolios are unit beta positions.”

Why only two or three portfolios. The lowest pre-ranking beta quintile has a beta close to zero; levering it to unit beta “results in a position close to infinity.” So BAB uses two (at most three) portfolios.

The VOL factor. GARP’s analog scales to a target volatility:

$\text{VOL}_{\text{t}}+_{1} = \sigma_{\text{target}} \times\left( \frac{\text{r}_{\text{L,t}}+_{1} - \text{r}_{\text{f}}}{\sigma_{\text{L,t}}} - \frac{\text{r}_{\text{H,t}}+_{1} - \text{r}_{\text{f}}}{\sigma_{\text{H,t}}} \right)$ , $\sigma_{\text{target}} =$ 15%,

using the first and fifth volatility quintiles, with $\sigma_{\text{L,t}}$, $\sigma_{\text{H,t}}$ the pre-ranking volatilities. “One advantage of the volatility portfolios is that they can be directly traded without using the risk-free asset because there are pronounced differences in expected returns, not only volatilities, across the volatility quintiles.”

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are the scaling rule of each factor and why volatility portfolios do not need the risk-free asset. Only D is consistent with both.

**Fragile fact.** BAB: divide by pre-ranking $\beta$, unit beta, two portfolios. VOL: divide by pre-ranking $\sigma$, times 15%, quintiles 1 and 5.

**Reference**

LO 85.h: Compare the volatility anomaly and the beta anomaly and analyze evidence of each anomaly. GARP FRM Part II, Risk Management and Investment Management (2025 edition), Chapter 3, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly), Section 3.5 Low Risk Anomaly, subsections “Risk Anomaly Factors,” “Betting against Beta” and “Volatility Factor” (equations 3.17 and 3.18). The extraction of equation 3.17 is incomplete; the full BAB form above is reconstructed from the surviving numerator over $\beta_{\text{L,t}}$, the text (“scaling the low- and high-beta portfolios by their betas,” unit-beta Long and Short legs, pre-ranking betas) and the parallel VOL formula 3.18. Schweser does not cover the factor construction.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 h, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Average returns across beta quintiles differ only slightly, which is why BAB cannot be built “just by taking differences of the portfolios.” A would be true for volatility quintiles, where raw returns differ sharply.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** B swaps the scaling rules: BAB scales by pre-ranking betas to unit beta, VOL by pre-ranking volatilities to a 15% target. B would be correct with the factor labels exchanged.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** A pre-ranking beta near zero makes the required leverage close to infinite, not modest; that is why BAB uses two or three portfolios at most. C would hold only if the lowest-beta quintile had a beta well away from zero.

d.reason: D restates GARP’s “one advantage” sentence and the contrast with the tiny return differences across beta quintiles.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-3 h Q11
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at the asset management subsidiary of a French bank computes one month’s return on a two-portfolio BAB factor built as in the reading (Frazzini and Pedersen). The monthly data, in EUR terms, are below.

|  | Low-beta portfolio High-beta portfolio |
|---|---|
| Return over the month (%) | 1.10 1.45 |
| Pre-ranking beta (start of month) | 0.50 1.70 |
| Post-ranking beta (realized over the month) | 0.70 1.40 |
| Risk-free rate for the month (%) | 0.25 |

What is the BAB factor return for the month?
questions.solution:
Treasury analyst computing one month’s BAB factor return from portfolio returns, betas and the risk-free rate.

**Concept and theory**

BAB goes long the low-beta portfolio levered to unit beta and short the high-beta portfolio de-levered to unit beta (combined with the risk-free asset). Each leg’s excess return is divided by its pre-ranking beta, the beta known at the start of the period when the position is set:

$\text{BAB}_{\text{t}+1} = \frac{\text{r}_{\text{L,t}}+_{1} - \text{r}_{\text{f}}}{\beta_{\text{L,t}}} - \frac{\text{r}_{\text{H,t}}+_{1} - \text{r}_{\text{f}}}{\beta_{\text{H,t}}}$ .

Because the beta anomaly shows up as flat raw returns but large Sharpe ratio differences, scaling by beta is what turns “similar returns at very different risk” into a positive factor return. Post-ranking betas are measured after the fact, so they cannot be used to size a tradeable position.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then one step per line:

Low-beta excess return = 1.10% − 0.25% = 0.85%

Long leg (unit beta) = 0.85%/0.50 = 1.700%

High-beta excess return = 1.45% − 0.25% = 1.20%

Short leg (unit beta) = 1.20%/1.70 = 0.706%

BAB = 1.700% − 0.706% = 0.994% ≈ 0.99%

Meaning: although the high-beta portfolio earned more in raw terms (1.45% versus 1.10%), per unit of beta the low-beta portfolio earned far more, so the BAB position, which is beta neutral on pre-ranking betas, gained about 0.99% in the month. Post-ranking betas are an irrelevant input.

**Fragile fact.** Subtract $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ first, then divide by the pre-ranking beta; the low-beta leg is levered up (divide by a beta below 1), the high-beta leg scaled down.

**Reference**

LO 85.h: Compare the volatility anomaly and the beta anomaly and analyze evidence of each anomaly. GARP FRM Part II, Risk Management and Investment Management (2025 edition), Chapter 3, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly), Section 3.5 Low Risk Anomaly, subsection “Betting against Beta” (equation 3.17, reconstructed as noted in Solution 10; footnote 28 confirms the use of pre-ranking portfolio betas). Schweser does not cover BAB construction; this is GARP-only content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 h, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: 0.85/0.70 = 1.214%, 1.20/1.40 = 0.857%, difference 0.357% ≈ 0.36%. Post-ranking betas are realized after formation and are not known when the position is set. A would be right only if the factor were defined on ex post betas.

b.reason: −0.35**% (dropped term: no beta scaling).** (1.10 − 0.25) − (1.45 − 0.25) = −0.35%, a simple long-low, short-high spread. This is exactly what GARP says cannot capture the beta anomaly, because raw return differences across beta portfolios are tiny. B would be the answer if the question asked for the unscaled return spread.

c.reason: C applies the reading’s BAB construction with pre-ranking betas and excess returns, giving 0.99%.

d.reason: 1.10/0.50 = 2.200%, 1.45/1.70 = 0.853%, difference 1.347% ≈ 1.35%. Dividing raw returns by beta ignores the financing of the levered long leg and the risk-free component of the short leg. D would be right only with $\text{r}_{\text{f}} =$ 0.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Hong Kong insurer reviews the reading’s Fama-French plus momentum regression of the BAB and VOL factors, estimated on monthly returns from October 1963 to December 2011. The correlation between the two factors over the sample is −9%.

|  | $\frac{\text{BAB factor}}{\text{Coeff. t-stat}}$ | $\frac{\text{VOL factor}}{\text{Coeff. t-stat}}$ |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha (% per month) | 0.33 1.89 | 0.42 4.37 |
| MKT loading | −0.17 −4.13 | 0.87 38.80 |
| SMB loading | 0.29 5.20 | −0.63 −20.30 |
| HML loading | 0.48 7.85 | 0.20 5.73 |
| UMD loading | 0.09 2.35 | 0.13 6.00 |

Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: BAB’s alpha is significant at the 95% level because its t-statistic exceeds the one-tailed critical value of 1.65, so both factors earn significant alphas.
VOL’s alpha is strongly significant while BAB’s is only borderline at the 95% level, and both factors carry significant value and momentum tilts.
Because both factors load positively on HML and UMD, the two anomalies are largely one value and momentum effect, so holding either factor alone is sufficient.
BAB’s alpha is strongly significant while VOL’s is only borderline at the 95% level, and both factors carry significant value and momentum tilts.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst interpreting the Fama-French plus momentum regression of the BAB and VOL factors.

**Concept and theory**

Regressing a factor’s returns on the Fama-French factors plus momentum asks whether the factor earns a return (alpha) not explained by market, size (SMB), value (HML) and momentum (UMD) exposures. A t-statistic tests whether a coefficient differs from zero; at the standard 95% level (two-sided) the critical value is about 1.96, so \|t\| = 1.89 corresponds to a p-value of about 0.06. GARP’s reading of the table:

|  | BAB | VOL |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha | 0.33% per month (4% per year), t = 1.89, p = 0.06: borderline | 0.42% per month (5% per year), t = 4.37: strongly significant |
| HML, UMD | Positive and significant: value and momentum tilts | Positive and significant: value and momentum tilts |
| SMB | Positive (0.29): beta anomaly manifests more in small stocks | Negative (−0.63): volatility anomaly more pervasive in large, liquid stocks |

Separately, the factors have Sharpe ratios of 0.6 (VOL) and 0.5 (BAB) and a correlation of −9%: the two anomalies are distinct, and GARP’s advice is “do both.”

**Applying it to this question**

Read each row. Alpha: VOL t = 4.37 > 1.96, strongly significant; BAB t = 1.89 \< 1.96, borderline (p about 0.06). HML: t = 7.85 and 5.73; UMD: t = 2.35 and 6.00, all above 1.96 and positive. So both have significant value and momentum tilts. The conclusion in B follows.

**Fragile fact.** 95% two-sided means about 1.96, so BAB at 1.89 is borderline. Positive SMB means small-stock exposure: BAB; negative SMB means large-stock exposure: VOL.

**Reference**

LO 85.h: Compare the volatility anomaly and the beta anomaly and analyze evidence of each anomaly. GARP FRM Part II, Risk Management and Investment Management (2025 edition), Chapter 3, Alpha (and the Low-Risk Anomaly), Section 3.5 Low Risk Anomaly, subsection “Betting-against-Beta and Volatility Factors” (regression table). GARP internal inconsistency: one sentence says “the BAB factor carries a negative SMB loading, whereas it is positive for the VOL factor,” which contradicts its own table (BAB +0.29, VOL −0.63) and its own conclusion (beta anomaly more in small stocks, volatility anomaly more in large stocks). The table and conclusion are used here; the question does not depend on the sentence. Schweser does not cover this regression.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-3 h, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: **Wrong percentile.** 1.65 is the one-tailed 95% critical value (equivalently the two-tailed 90% value). The standard two-sided 95% test needs about 1.96, which 1.89 does not reach. A would be right only for a one-sided test or a 90% two-sided test.

b.reason: B matches GARP: BAB’s alpha “is borderline statistically significant at the standard 95% level,” VOL’s is “much more statistically significant,” and “both BAB and VOL have significant value tilts (positive HML loadings) and momentum tilts (positive UMD loadings).”

c.reason: **Scope error: overextended inference.** Sharing positive HML and UMD tilts does not make the factors one effect: they still earn alpha after controlling for HML and UMD (strongly so for VOL), their size loadings have opposite signs, and their correlation is −9%. GARP concludes they are distinct and advises doing both. C would be closer to right only if the alphas were zero and the factors highly positively correlated.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** D swaps the significance verdicts of the two factors. It would be correct only if the t-statistics were exchanged.
