questions.loText: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-4 d Q2
questions.question: The chief risk officer of a Canadian public pension plan is reviewing a consultant’s memo on the plan’s CAD equity optimizer. The memo ranks how much the plan would gain from better information on each optimizer input. Which of the following statements in the memo is most accurate?

options.text: Transaction cost estimates are uncertain, though less so than alpha forecasts, so perfect information on returns would be worth much more than perfect information on transaction costs.
Transaction cost estimates are more uncertain than alpha forecasts, so perfect information on transaction costs would be worth much more than perfect information on returns.
Accurate estimation of transaction costs is just as important as accurate forecasts of exceptional return, because both remove the same amount of uncertainty from value added.
Transaction cost estimates are less uncertain than alpha forecasts, so they are a minor input whose inclusion does not change how precisely the alphas must be estimated.

questions.solution:
CRO reviews a consultant’s memo ranking the value of better information on each optimizer input.

**Concept and theory**

Every optimizer input except the current portfolio is an estimate, so a natural question is which estimate deserves the most effort. GARP addresses it directly in Section 4.4: “It has been said that accurate estimation of transactions costs is just as important as accurate forecasts of exceptional return. That is an overstatement, but it does point out the crucial role transactions costs play.” Footnote 5 explains why it is an overstatement: perfect information about returns is much more valuable than perfect information about costs, because returns are much less certain than costs, so accurate estimation of returns removes far more uncertainty.

Schweser condenses the same idea: costs are “uncertain, although typically less so than alphas,” and because they reduce active return and are uncertain, “transaction costs are an important input.”

|  | Alpha (returns) | Transaction costs |
|---|---|---|
| Uncertainty | Much higher | Lower, but not zero |
| Value of perfect information | Much higher | Lower |
| Importance in construction | Most important input | Important; “crucial role” |

**Applying it to this question**

The memo ranks the gain from better information. The deciding facts are two directions: costs are less uncertain than alphas, and so perfect return information is worth more. A also keeps the qualifier that costs remain uncertain, which matches both sources.

**Fragile fact.** Costs are less uncertain than alphas, yet still important; “just as important as return forecasts” is GARP’s example of an overstatement.

**Reference**

LO 86.d: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction. GARP Chapter 4, Portfolio Construction (Grinold and Kahn), Section 4.4 “Transactions Costs” (lines 5105 to 5114) and footnote 5 (lines 5170 to 5173); Section 4.1 “Introduction” (lines 4784 to 4794). Schweser Reading 86, “Transaction Costs”, first paragraph. No conflict between the sources.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 d, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: It restates GARP footnote 5 (“Perfect information regarding returns is much more valuable than perfect information regarding transactions costs. The returns are much less certain than the transactions costs.”) and Schweser’s “uncertain, although typically less so than alphas.”

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses both directions: it makes costs the more uncertain input and cost information the more valuable. B would be correct only if alphas were measured more precisely than costs; the source says the opposite.

c.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** This is the claim GARP quotes and then calls “an overstatement.” Equal importance and an equal reduction in uncertainty are exactly what footnote 5 denies. C would be right only as a description of what “has been said,” not of what is true.

d.reason: **Scope error.** It starts from a true premise (costs are less uncertain) and stretches it to a false conclusion (costs are minor and do not affect how precisely alphas must be estimated). GARP says costs play a “crucial role” and “force greater precision on our estimates of alpha”; Schweser says including them “increases the importance of both precision in estimating alphas and of the choice of scale.” D would fit a world with negligible costs.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-4 d Q3
questions.question: An internal auditor at a UK life insurer’s asset management arm is reviewing the methodology document for the optimizer that runs its GBP active equity mandate. The document contains the four statements below on the treatment of transaction costs. Which of the statements is NOT correct?

options.text: The objective of portfolio construction is to maximize risk-adjusted annual active return.
Transaction costs are incurred at the point in time when the portfolio is rebalanced, while the alphas and the active risk are realized over the investment horizon.
Each trade’s cost is amortized so that it can be compared with the annual rate of gain from alpha and the annual rate of loss from active risk.
Because alphas are forecast over a one-year horizon, every trade’s cost should be amortized at the same rate, whatever the anticipated holding period of the position.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor checks four methodology statements on how a GBP optimizer treats transaction costs; find the false one.

**Concept and theory**

The second complication that costs bring is a mismatch of timing. GARP 4.1 warns: “We must be careful to compare transactions costs incurred at a point in time with returns and risk realized over a period of time.” Section 4.4 sets out the fix in four steps:

1. The objective is to maximize risk-adjusted annual active return.
2. Rebalancing incurs costs at that point in time, while alphas and active risk are expected over the next year.
3. A rule is needed to allocate the costs over the one-year period: the costs are amortized so that they can be compared with the annual rate of gain from alpha and the annual rate of loss from active risk.
4. “The rate of amortization will depend on the anticipated holding period.”

The general rule that follows from GARP’s example is

$\text{TC}_{\text{ann}} = \frac{\text{TC}_{\text{RT}}}{\text{h}}$ .

A 6-month holding period doubles the round-trip cost per year; a 24-month holding period halves it. Schweser adds that holding periods are uncertain, which raises the question of over what period costs should be amortized.

**Applying it to this question**

A NOT-correct question: three statements must match the source and one must contradict it. A, B and C are steps 1 to 3 above. D keeps the one-year comparison period (true: costs are allocated over the year) but then assigns one amortization rate to every trade, which cuts the link to the anticipated holding period (step 4).

**Fragile fact.** Costs are allocated to a one-year comparison period, but the rate of amortization is set by each trade’s anticipated holding period.

**Reference**

LO 86.d: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction. GARP Chapter 4, Portfolio Construction (Grinold and Kahn), Section 4.4 “Transactions Costs” (lines 5138 to 5149, 5120 to 5132) and Section 4.1 “Introduction” (lines 4816 to 4818). Schweser Reading 86, “Transaction Costs”, second paragraph, and Key Concepts LO 86.d. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 d, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: **True statement.** GARP 4.4 verbatim: “The objective in portfolio construction is to maximize risk-adjusted annual active return.” It would become false under a polarity flip (for example “minimize”) or a sibling swap (for example “maximize total return”).

b.reason: **True statement.** GARP 4.4: rebalancing incurs costs “at that point in time,” while alphas and active risk are “expected over the next year.” It would be false if the timing were reversed (costs over time, benefits at a point), a polarity flip.

c.reason: **True statement.** GARP 4.4: “We must amortize the transactions costs to compare them to the annual rate of gain from the alpha and the annual rate of loss from the active risk.” It would be false if it said costs need no adjustment before comparison, a scope error.

d.reason: GARP: “The rate of amortization will depend on the anticipated holding period.” Two trades with the same round-trip cost but holding periods of 6 and 24 months are charged 2 and 0.5 times their round-trip cost per year, not the same rate. D therefore contradicts the source. Its corruption is a scope or condition error: it drops the holding-period condition and lets the one-year forecast horizon set the rate.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-4 d Q4
questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Tokyo asset manager is choosing between two ideas for the same slot in a TOPIX-benchmarked JPY fund. Assume perfect certainty, no difference in active risk, and that Idea X can be replaced every three months by a similar stock with the same profile.

| Item | Idea X | Idea Y |
|---|---|---|
| Expected alpha (% per year) | 5.00 | 3.60 |
| Cost of each purchase or each sale (% of value) | 0.45 | 0.60 |
| Anticipated holding period (months) | 3 | 18 |
| Position size (JPY billion) | 2.0 | 2.0 |

Which of the following best describes the annual alpha of each idea net of amortized transaction costs?

options.text: Idea X: 3.20%; Idea Y: 3.20%
Idea X: 1.40%; Idea Y: 2.80%
Idea X: 4.10%; Idea Y: 2.40%
Idea X: 4.78%; Idea Y: 1.80%

questions.solution:
Tokyo PM compares a 3-month rotation idea with an 18-month hold, net of amortized costs; position size is irrelevant.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s example sets up two stocks, each with an annual alpha of 4%, each priced at \$100 and costing \$0.75 to buy and \$0.75 to sell. Stock 1 gains \$2 in 6 months and can then be replaced by a similar stock; stock 2 gains \$8 over 24 months. Over 2 years the stock 1 sequence pays costs of \$0.75, \$1.50, \$1.50, \$1.50 and \$0.75 (total \$6), for a 1% annual return; stock 2 pays \$1.50 in total, for 3.25% a year. The annualized cost is 3% for stock 1 and 0.75% for stock 2. The general rule:

$\text{TC}_{\text{ann}} = \frac{\text{TC}_{\text{RT}}}{\text{h}}$ , net alpha $= \alpha- \text{TC}_{\text{ann}}$.

Three details trip people up: (i) the round trip is purchase plus sale; (ii) h is in years; (iii) the cost is divided by h, so short holding periods multiply the cost.

**Applying it to this question**

Round-trip costs:

$\text{TC}^{\text{X}}_{\text{RT}} =$ 0.45% + 0.45% = 0.90%, $\text{TC}^{\text{Y}}_{\text{RT}} =$ 0.60% + 0.60% = 1.20%.

Holding periods in years: $\text{h}_{\text{X}} =$ 3/12 = 0.25, $\text{h}_{\text{Y}} =$ 18/12 = 1.5.

$\text{TC}^{\text{X}}_{\text{ann}} =$ 0.90%/0.25 = 3.60% per year, $\text{TC}^{\text{Y}}_{\text{ann}} =$ 1.20%/1.5 = 0.80% per year.

$\text{Net}_{\text{X}} =$ 5.00% − 3.60% = 1.40%, $\text{Net}_{\text{Y}} =$ 3.60% − 0.80% = 2.80%.

Meaning: although X has the higher gross alpha, its cost is paid four times a year, so Y adds twice as much alpha after costs. The JPY 2.0 billion position size is irrelevant because both alpha and cost are percentages of value.

**Fragile fact.** Divide the round-trip cost by the holding period in years: a 3-month hold multiplies the round trip by 4.

**Reference**

LO 86.d: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction. GARP Chapter 4, Portfolio Construction (Grinold and Kahn), Section 4.4 “Transactions Costs”, stock 1 and stock 2 example and general rule (lines 5105 to 5132 and 5152 to 5162). Schweser Reading 86, “Transaction Costs”, second paragraph. Schweser’s illustration is simpler (2% per 6 months vs 4% per year with a 1% cost, giving about 2% and 3% a year) and states the cost directly as a round trip; same rule, different numbers. GARP’s example is used here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 d, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **Wrong input twin: one-way cost used as the round trip.** 5.00 − 0.45/0.25 = 5.00 − 1.80 = 3.20% and 3.60 − 0.60/1.5 = 3.60 − 0.40 = 3.20%. Using one leg halves each cost. A would be correct if the table showed the round-trip cost (0.45% and 0.60%) rather than the cost of each purchase or each sale.

b.reason: It applies GARP’s rule (“the annualized transactions cost is the round-trip cost divided by the holding period in years”) with the round trip built from both legs, exactly as GARP’s example charges \$0.75 on entry and \$0.75 on exit.

c.reason: **Dropped term: no amortization.** 5.00 − 0.90 = 4.10% and 3.60 − 1.20 = 2.40%. The round trip is charged once a year regardless of how often it is paid, which is the mistake GARP’s stock 1 sequence is built to expose. C would be correct only if both holding periods were exactly one year.

d.reason: **Unit slip: multiplied by the holding period instead of dividing.** 5.00 − 0.90 × 0.25 = 4.775 ≈ 4.78% and 3.60 − 1.20 × 1.5 = 1.80%. Multiplying rewards short holding periods, the opposite of the rule. There is no stem under which D is correct, since cost per year always falls as the holding period lengthens.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Singapore bank is assessing a single SGD stock idea for the bank’s active equity book. The alpha accrues at a constant annual rate while the position is held, and the position will return to cash at the end of its holding period with no successor trade.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Expected alpha (% per year) | 2.40 |
| Purchase cost (% of value) | 0.40 |
| Sale cost (% of value) | 0.50 |
| Residual volatility (% per year) | 28.00 |
| Information coefficient | 0.06 |

Ignoring active risk, what is the minimum anticipated holding period for which the expected alpha at least covers the annualized transaction cost?

options.text: 4.5 months
2.0 months
32 months
9 months

questions.solution:
Singapore analyst finds the break-even holding period for a single stock idea; volatility and IC are irrelevant.

**Concept and theory**

Because a trade’s cost is paid at one moment while its alpha accrues over time, the same trade can be worth doing or not depending on how long the position is held. GARP’s rule turns this into a break-even condition. The trade is worthwhile (ignoring active risk) when annual alpha at least covers annualized cost:

$\alpha\ge\frac{\text{TC}_{\text{RT}}}{\text{h}} \Leftarrow\Rightarrow$ h $\ge\text{h}^{*} = \frac{\text{TC}_{\text{RT}}}{\alpha}$ .

$\text{h}^{*}$ is the break-even holding period in years: hold for less and the costs, paid at a faster annual rate, exceed the alpha; hold for longer and the trade adds value. The condition works because GARP amortizes costs at a rate that “will depend on the anticipated holding period.”

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{TC}_{\text{RT}} =$ 0.40% + 0.50% = 0.90%

$\text{h}^{*} =$ 0.90%/2.40% = 0.375 years

$\text{h}^{*} =$ 0.375 × 12 = 4.5 months

Check: at 4.5 months the annualized cost is 0.90%/0.375 = 2.40%, equal to the alpha. Meaning: the analyst should support the idea only if the position is expected to stay on the book for at least 4.5 months. The residual volatility and information coefficient would matter for scaling the alpha, but the stem gives the alpha directly and asks to ignore active risk, so they play no role.

**Fragile fact.** Break-even $\text{h}^{*} = \text{TC}_{\text{RT}}$/$\alpha$ in years; a shorter anticipated hold than $\text{h}^{*}$ makes the trade value-destroying.

**Reference**

LO 86.d: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction. GARP Chapter 4, Portfolio Construction (Grinold and Kahn), Section 4.4 “Transactions Costs”, general rule and amortization paragraph (lines 5126 to 5149). Schweser Reading 86, “Transaction Costs”. The break-even rearrangement is algebra on GARP’s stated rule; GARP does not present it as a separate formula.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 d, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: It solves GARP’s rule, annualized cost equals round-trip cost divided by holding period in years, for the holding period at which the annualized cost equals the annual alpha, with the round trip built from both legs.

b.reason: **Wrong input twin: purchase cost used as the round trip.** 0.40/2.40 = 0.1667 years = 2.0 months. Dropping the sale leg understates the cost. B would be correct if the purchase cost were the only cost, for example a position that is never sold.

c.reason: **Inverted ratio.** 2.40/0.90 = 2.667 years = 32 months. Dividing alpha by cost gives a number of years with no meaning in the rule. There is no stem under which this is the break-even period.

d.reason: **Double counting the round trip.** 2 × 0.90/2.40 = 0.75 years = 9 months. This charges the full round trip on entry and again on exit. D would be correct if the round-trip cost were 1.80%, that is, if 0.40% and 0.50% were the costs per leg on each of two separate trades.

questions.question: The chief investment officer of a Brazilian pension fund oversees two external managers, P and Q, who hold the same stock in their BRL mandates and receive the same upgrade to its alpha forecast. For each manager, moving the position to the new optimum would add 1.2% per year of expected alpha on the position, and the round-trip cost of the trade is 0.9%. Manager P expects to revise the position again in 6 months; Manager Q expects to hold it for 18 months. Ignoring changes in active risk, which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Both managers should trade, because the 1.2% expected annual alpha gain exceeds the 0.9% round-trip cost.
Manager P should trade and Manager Q should not, because the longer holding period exposes Q to more transaction costs.
Manager Q should trade and Manager P should not, even though both managers have received the same new information.
Neither manager should trade, because new information about alpha never justifies incurring transaction costs.

questions.solution:
Brazilian CIO compares two managers with the same alpha upgrade but different anticipated holding periods.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser’s Key Concepts list the first implication of transaction costs: they “may make it optimal not to rebalance even with the arrival of new information.” The reason is the timing mismatch. New information raises the expected annual alpha of a position, but acting on it means paying a cost now. Whether the gain covers the cost depends on how long the revised position will be held, because the cost is amortized at a rate set by the anticipated holding period (GARP 4.4). Schweser’s Key Concepts say this explicitly: the point-in-time cost and over-the-horizon benefit make “rebalancing decisions dependent on the estimated holding period of portfolio assets.”

trade if $\Delta\alpha> \frac{\text{TC}_{\text{RT}}}{\text{h}}$ , otherwise stay put.

**Applying it to this question**

Manager P: h = 0.5, $\text{TC}_{\text{ann}} =$ 0.9%/0.5 = 1.8% > 1.2% ⇒ do not trade

Manager Q: h = 1.5, $\text{TC}_{\text{ann}} =$ 0.9%/1.5 = 0.6% \< 1.2% ⇒ trade

The new information and the cost are identical; only the anticipated holding period differs, and it reverses the decision. For P, not rebalancing is optimal despite the arrival of new information.

**Fragile fact.** Longer anticipated holding period means lower annualized cost, so the longer-horizon manager is the one who trades.

**Reference**

LO 86.d: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction. Schweser Reading 86, Key Concepts LO 86.d. GARP Chapter 4, Portfolio Construction (Grinold and Kahn), Section 4.4 “Transactions Costs” (lines 5138 to 5149, amortization at a rate set by the anticipated holding period). GARP Section 4.4 does not use Schweser’s phrase “optimal not to rebalance”; it follows from GARP’s amortization rule, and GARP Section 4.6 makes the same point about trading on new information, which belongs to LO 86.f and is not tested here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 d, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: **Dropped term: no amortization.** Comparing an annual gain (1.2%) with an unamortized one-off cost (0.9%) ignores that P pays the cost twice a year in annual terms. A would be correct if both managers expected to hold the position for exactly one year or longer.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** A longer holding period spreads the same round trip over more years and lowers the annual cost; it does not expose Q to more cost. B reverses the direction of the holding-period effect. It would be correct if the round trip were multiplied by the holding period, which is not GARP’s rule.

c.reason: It reflects both halves of the Key Concept: costs can make it optimal not to act on new information (P), and the decision depends on the estimated holding period (P vs Q).

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** Costs “may” make rebalancing suboptimal; they do not always do so. Q’s trade clears its amortized cost. D would be correct only if every possible trade had an annualized cost above its alpha gain.

questions.question: A risk consultant is validating the optimizer of a USD active equity manager. The manager’s raw alphas have a cross-sectional standard deviation twice the scale implied by its information coefficient and residual volatility. Before transaction costs were modeled, the manager compensated by doubling active risk aversion, and the optimizer then produced the intended active holdings. Transaction costs have now been added to the optimizer, but the alphas are still unrescaled and risk aversion is still doubled. Which of the following best describes the consultant’s finding?

options.text: The doubled risk aversion restores the alpha versus active risk balance, but the inflated alphas understate trade benefits relative to costs, so the manager will trade too little until the alphas are rescaled.

The doubled risk aversion restores the alpha versus active risk balance, but the inflated alphas overstate trade benefits relative to costs, so the manager will trade too much until the alphas are rescaled.
The doubled risk aversion restores both the alpha versus active risk and the alpha versus cost balances, because a scale error can always be offset by adjusting active risk aversion.
The doubled risk aversion restores the balance between transaction costs and active risk, which is the only new trade-off that costs introduce, so no rescaling of the alphas is needed.

questions.solution:
Consultant validates a USD optimizer that offset over-scaled alphas with doubled risk aversion, then added costs.

**Concept and theory**

GARP 4.4 explains why costs force precision on the alpha scale. Without costs, the optimizer maximizes $\text{h}^{\top}\alpha- \lambda_{\text{A}} \text{h}^{\top}$Vh over active holdings h (GARP footnote 1), where V is the covariance matrix. Its first-order condition gives

$\text{h}^{*} = \frac{\text{V}^{-1}\alpha}{2\lambda_{\text{A}}}$ .

Doubling every alpha and doubling $\lambda_{\text{A}} \text{leaves h}^{*}$ unchanged. That is GARP’s “single knob”: “we can offset any problem in setting the scale of the alphas by increasing or decreasing the active risk aversion.” The problem is one-dimensional.

Transaction costs add a term that does not scale with alpha:

$\text{m}_{\text{h}}\text{ax h}^{\top}\alpha- \lambda_{\text{A}} \text{h}^{\top}$Vh $- \text{TC}(\text{h})$.

With alphas at 2$\alpha_{0}$ and risk aversion at 2$\lambda_{0}$ the objective is

2 $\left[\text{h}^{\top}\alpha_{0} - \lambda_{0} \text{h}^{\top}\text{Vh}\right] - \text{TC}(\text{h}) =$ 2 $[\text{h}^{\top}\alpha_{0} - \lambda_{0} \text{h}^{\top}$Vh $- \frac{1}{2}$ TC$(\text{h})]$ ,

which is the correctly scaled problem with costs at half their true size. GARP: “Transactions costs make this a two-dimensional problem. The trade-off between alpha and active risk remains, but now there is a new trade-off between the alpha and the transactions costs. We therefore must be precise in our choice of scale.” (The algebra above is derived from GARP’s stated objective; GARP states the conclusion in words.)

**Applying it to this question**

The manager fixed the alpha versus risk knob, so holdings would be right if trading were free. But the inflated alphas make every trade’s benefit look twice as large relative to its cost, so the optimizer trades more than it should. The cure is to rescale the alphas, not to turn the risk aversion knob again.

**Fragile fact.** One knob (risk aversion) fixes alpha versus risk; it cannot also fix alpha versus costs. Over-scaled alphas with costs mean too much trading.

**Reference**

LO 86.d: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction. GARP Chapter 4, Portfolio Construction (Grinold and Kahn), Section 4.4 “Transactions Costs” (lines 5112 to 5136) and footnote 1 (lines 4914 to 4920). Schweser Reading 86, “Transaction Costs”: including costs “increases the importance of both precision in estimating alphas and of the choice of scale”. How the alpha scale is set (volatility times IC) is LO 86.b and is not tested; the stem gives the scale error directly.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 d, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Over-scaled alphas make trades look more attractive against costs, not less. A would be correct if the raw alphas had half the proper scale and risk aversion had been halved to compensate.

b.reason: It keeps the true part of the one-knob result (the alpha versus active risk balance is restored), and it states the consequence of the second dimension: with over-scaled alphas, trade benefits are overstated against costs, so turnover is too high until the scale is fixed.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** “A scale error can always be offset by adjusting active risk aversion” is true only “when we consider only alphas and active risk” (GARP). Extending it to a problem with costs drops that condition. C would be correct for a manager with zero transaction costs.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** The new trade-off that costs bring is between alpha and costs, not between costs and active risk. D swaps in the wrong partner for the cost term and then concludes no rescaling is needed. It would be correct only if the cost term scaled with the risk penalty, which it does not.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Frankfurt asset manager runs a EUR equity rotation strategy in which each position is held for 3 months and then replaced by a similar one. The latest attribution report shows the following.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Gross expected alpha (% per year) | 5.00 |
| Alpha net of amortized transaction costs (% per year) | 2.60 |
| Tracking error (% per year) | 3.50 |
| Assets under management (EUR million) | 400.00 |

The manager proposes to hold each position for 9 months instead, with the same round-trip cost per trade and, by assumption, the same gross expected alpha of 5.00% per year. The annual alpha net of amortized transaction costs under the proposal is closest to:
questions.solution:
Frankfurt PM backs out the round-trip cost of a 3-month rotation and re-applies it to a 9-month hold.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s rule links three quantities: round-trip cost, holding period and annualized cost, $\text{TC}_{\text{ann}} =$ $\text{TC}_{\text{RT}}$/h. The round trip is a property of the trade (what it costs to get in and out); the annualized cost is a property of the trade and the holding period. When a report gives only gross and net alpha, the annualized cost is their difference, and the round trip can be recovered by multiplying back by the holding period:

$\text{TC}_{\text{ann}} = \alpha_{\text{gross}} - \alpha_{\text{net}}$, $\text{TC}_{\text{RT}} = \text{TC}_{\text{ann}} \times$ h.

The recovered round trip can then be amortized over any other holding period. This is GARP’s stock 1 versus stock 2 contrast run in reverse.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{TC}^{(\text{3m})}_{\text{ann}} =$ 5.00% − 2.60% = 2.40% per year

$\text{TC}_{\text{RT}} =$ 2.40% × 0.25 = 0.60% per trade

$\text{TC}^{(\text{9m})}_{\text{ann}} =$ 0.60%/0.75 = 0.80% per year

$\alpha^{(\text{9m})}_{\text{net}} =$ 5.00% − 0.80% = 4.20% per year

Meaning: tripling the holding period cuts the annual cost burden to a third, lifting net alpha by 1.60 percentage points, provided the gross alpha really holds up over the longer hold (an assumption given in the stem; whether alpha decays with horizon is LO 86.f). Tracking error and AUM are irrelevant inputs.

**Fragile fact.** Net minus gross gives the annualized cost, not the round trip; multiply by the old holding period to get the round trip before re-amortizing.

**Reference**

LO 86.d: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction. GARP Chapter 4, Portfolio Construction (Grinold and Kahn), Section 4.4 “Transactions Costs”, example and general rule (lines 5117 to 5132). Schweser Reading 86, “Transaction Costs”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 d, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: **Wrong input twin: annualized cost used as the round trip.** 5.00 − 2.40/0.75 = 5.00 − 3.20 = 1.80%. The 2.40% is already a per-year figure; dividing it by the holding period again amortizes twice. A would be correct if the report had shown a 2.40% round-trip cost per trade.

b.reason: **Dropped term: no amortization.** 5.00 − 0.60 = 4.40%. The round trip is charged once a year, which is right only for a 12-month hold. B would be correct if the proposal were to hold each position for exactly one year.

c.reason: **Unit slip: multiplied by the holding period.** 5.00 − 0.60 × 0.75 = 5.00 − 0.45 = 4.55%. Multiplying instead of dividing understates the annual cost of any hold shorter than a year. No stem makes this correct under GARP’s rule.

d.reason: It recovers the per-trade round trip and re-amortizes it over 0.75 years, applying GARP’s rule that the rate of amortization depends on the anticipated holding period.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a Chinese insurer’s asset management company is reviewing a CNY A-share manager whose optimizer amortizes every trade’s round-trip cost over a fixed one-year period. The book holds tactical trades, each held for about 3 months, and core holdings, each held for about 2 years; every round trip costs 0.8% of value. Which of the following is the most likely consequence of this amortization rule?

options.text: The optimizer understates the annual cost of the tactical trades and overstates that of the core holdings, tilting the portfolio toward short-horizon trades.
The optimizer overstates the annual cost of the tactical trades and understates that of the core holdings, tilting the portfolio toward long-horizon holdings.
The optimizer measures both kinds of trade correctly, because a trade’s round-trip cost is the same whatever period it is amortized over.
The optimizer misstates active risk rather than costs, because the amortization period affects only the penalty for active risk.

questions.solution:
Risk committee member reviews a CNY optimizer that amortizes every round trip over a fixed one year.

**Concept and theory**

GARP requires costs to be allocated over the one-year comparison period, and adds that “the rate of amortization will depend on the anticipated holding period.” Its example shows the two directions: “For a 6-month holding period, we double the round-trip transactions cost to get the annual transactions cost, and for a 24-month holding period, we halve the round-trip transactions cost.” A rule that charges every round trip once per year is right only for one-year holds:

| Holding period | Correct $\text{TC}_{\text{ann}}$ (%) | One-year rule (%) | Error |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 months (h = 0.25) | 3.20 | 0.80 | understated, factor 4 |
| 2 years (h = 2) | 0.40 | 0.80 | overstated, factor 2 |

**Applying it to this question**

With a 0.8% round trip: tactical trades should carry 0.8%/0.25 = 3.2% a year but are charged 0.8%; core holdings should carry 0.8%/2 = 0.4% but are charged 0.8%. The optimizer therefore sees short-horizon trades as cheaper than they are and long-horizon holdings as dearer than they are, so it leans toward short-horizon turnover that may not cover its true cost.

**Fragile fact.** Holding shorter than a year: true annual cost is higher than the round trip; longer than a year: lower.

**Reference**

LO 86.d: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction. GARP Chapter 4, Portfolio Construction (Grinold and Kahn), Section 4.4 “Transactions Costs” (lines 5122 to 5149). Schweser Reading 86, “Transaction Costs”, second paragraph. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 d, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: It gets both directions right and draws the resulting tilt, applying GARP’s doubling and halving logic to 3-month and 2-year horizons.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses both errors: charging 0.8% a year is too little for a round trip paid four times a year and too much for one paid every two years. B would be correct if the holding periods were swapped, that is, if the tactical trades were held for more than a year and the core holdings for less than a year.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The round-trip cost is indeed the same, but the annual cost depends on how often that round trip is paid, which is the whole point of amortization. C would be correct only if every position were held for exactly one year.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** The amortization rule concerns how costs are compared with annual alpha; it does not enter the active risk penalty. D would be correct only if the stem described an error in the covariance estimates or the risk aversion.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a US university endowment is reading a report from the endowment’s USD equity manager explaining why modeling transaction costs forces the manager to be more precise about its alphas. Which of the following statements in the report is LEAST accurate?

options.text: When only alpha and active risk are considered, a mis-scaled set of alphas can be offset by raising or lowering active risk aversion.
Once transaction costs are included, precision matters most in the covariance estimates, because costs are traded off against active risk rather than against alpha.
Once transaction costs are included, a second trade-off, between alpha and transaction costs, sits alongside the trade-off between alpha and active risk.
Including transaction costs increases the importance of both precise alpha estimates and the correct choice of alpha scale.

questions.solution:
Endowment board member checks a manager’s report on why costs force alpha precision; find the least accurate statement.

**Concept and theory**

GARP 4.4 gives the reasoning in three steps. First, with only alphas and active risk, “we can offset any problem in setting the scale of the alphas by increasing or decreasing the active risk aversion”; it is a one-dimensional problem with a single knob. Second, “transactions costs make this a two-dimensional problem. The trade-off between alpha and active risk remains, but now there is a new trade-off between the alpha and the transactions costs.” Third, “we therefore must be precise in our choice of scale, to correctly trade off between the hypothetical alphas and the inevitable transactions costs”; costs “force greater precision on our estimates of alpha.” Schweser: including costs “increases the importance of both precision in estimating alphas and of the choice of scale.”

|  | Without costs | With costs |
|---|---|---|
| Trade-offs | Alpha vs active risk | Alpha vs active risk, and alpha vs costs |
| Fix for a scale error | Adjust risk aversion | Rescale the alphas |
| Precision demanded | Alpha scale can be loose | Alpha estimates and scale must be precise |

**Applying it to this question**

LEAST accurate: three options restate the three steps (A, C, D). B names a different input, covariances, and a different partner for the cost term, active risk.

**Fragile fact.** The new trade-off pairs costs with alpha, so the precision demanded is in alpha estimates and alpha scale.

**Reference**

LO 86.d: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction. GARP Chapter 4, Portfolio Construction (Grinold and Kahn), Section 4.4 “Transactions Costs” (lines 5111 to 5136). Schweser Reading 86, “Transaction Costs”, first paragraph, and Key Concepts LO 86.d. Covariance precision belongs to the quadratic programming discussion in GARP Section 4.7 (LO 86.h) and is excluded here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 d, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: **True statement.** GARP’s single-knob result, verbatim in substance. It would become false through a scope error if extended to a problem with costs.

b.reason: The new trade-off is “between the alpha and the transactions costs,” and the precision it demands is in the alphas and their scale. B replaces both with their siblings (covariances, active risk). Covariance precision matters a great deal for quadratic programming (LO 86.h), but that is not the implication of transaction costs that this LO describes. The corruption is a sibling swap.

c.reason: **True statement.** GARP’s “new trade-off between the alpha and the transactions costs.” It would become false under a sibling swap of the cost term’s partner, which is what B does.

d.reason: **True statement.** Schweser’s sentence on precision in alphas and the choice of scale. It would become false under a polarity flip (“decreases the importance”), as in statement IV of Q12.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a London multi-manager firm has capital for one more GBP position in a FTSE 350 mandate. All four candidates have the same marginal contribution to active risk, and each can be replaced at the end of its holding period by a similar successor, so each annualized figure applies throughout the year.

| Trade | Alpha (% per year) | Round-trip cost (%) | Holding (months) | Free float (GBP bn) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| K | 6.80 | 2.40 | 3 | 4.1 |
| L | 5.40 | 0.90 | 3 | 12.6 |
| M | 4.00 | 1.20 | 24 | 2.3 |
| N | 2.60 | 0.30 | 9 | 18.9 |

Which trade adds the most annual alpha net of amortized transaction costs?

options.text: Trade K
Trade L
Trade M
Trade N

questions.solution:
London PM ranks four GBP trades by alpha net of amortized costs; free float is irrelevant.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s two-stock example makes one point that this question generalizes: the best trade is not the one with the highest alpha or the lowest cost, but the one with the highest alpha net of annualized cost, because the annual cost depends on how often the round trip is paid. In GARP’s example both stocks have the same 4% annual alpha, yet the 24-month hold earns 3.25% a year and the 6-month rotation only 1%. With equal marginal contributions to active risk, ranking by

$\alpha- \frac{\text{TC}_{\text{RT}}}{\text{h}}$

is the right comparison, and it is where the alpha versus cost trade-off of GARP 4.4 becomes concrete.

**Applying it to this question**

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Shanghai fund management company is drafting a training note for the firm’s CNY equity desk on the implications of transaction costs for portfolio construction. The draft contains four statements.

I. Transaction costs may make it optimal not to rebalance even when new information about alphas arrives.

II. Transaction costs increase the importance of robust alpha estimates.

III. Because costs are paid at a point in time while the benefits accrue over the investment horizon, rebalancing decisions depend on the estimated holding period of the assets.

IV. Transaction costs make the choice of alpha scale less important, because the alpha versus cost trade-off can be balanced by adjusting active risk aversion.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I, II, III and IV
II and III only
I and III only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Shanghai junior analyst’s training note lists four implications of transaction costs; pick the correct set.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser’s Key Concepts for LO 86.d summarize the LO’s implications in three sentences:

1. Transaction costs “may make it optimal not to rebalance even with the arrival of new information.”
2. They “increase the importance of robust alpha estimates.”
3. Because costs “occur at a point in time while the benefits of the portfolio adjustments occur over the investment horizon,” analysis is complicated and it “makes rebalancing decisions dependent on the estimated holding period of portfolio assets.”

GARP supplies the reasons: costs force “greater precision on our estimates of alpha”; they turn a one-knob problem into a two-dimensional one, so “we therefore must be precise in our choice of scale”; and costs must be amortized at a rate that “will depend on the anticipated holding period.”

**Applying it to this question**

Statements I, II and III restate the three Key Concepts. Statement IV reverses the scale implication and borrows the no-cost single-knob argument for a setting with costs.

**Fragile fact.** Costs make alpha precision and alpha scale more important; risk aversion fixes only the alpha versus risk balance.

**Reference**

LO 86.d: Explain the implications of transaction costs on portfolio construction. Schweser Reading 86, Key Concepts LO 86.d. GARP Chapter 4, Portfolio Construction (Grinold and Kahn), Section 4.4 “Transactions Costs” (lines 5111 to 5149). The “optimal not to rebalance” phrasing is Schweser’s summary; GARP reaches the same point through the amortization rule. No conflict on content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 d, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: **Accepts IV: polarity flip.** Statement IV flips “increases the importance of the choice of scale” to “less important” and then applies the single-knob fix outside its condition. Accepting it is the error. A would be correct if IV read “more important, because risk aversion can no longer offset a scale error.”

b.reason: **Rejects I: absolute-claim error.** Rejecting I amounts to believing that new information should always trigger a rebalance. That holds only with zero costs; with costs, rebalancing is worthwhile only when the gain covers the amortized cost (see Q6). B would be correct if I said costs always make rebalancing suboptimal.

c.reason: **Rejects II: scope error.** Rejecting II treats costs as a separate deduction with no effect on how alphas must be estimated. GARP says costs “force greater precision on our estimates of alpha.” C would be correct if II said costs reduce the need for precise alphas.

d.reason: I, II and III match the source; IV contradicts GARP 4.4 (costs make the choice of scale more important, and risk aversion cannot balance the alpha versus cost trade-off). So the correct set is I, II and III only.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Paris-based asset manager is presenting the firm’s rebalancing framework to newly hired analysts. She introduces stock n’s marginal contribution to value added, $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$, where value added is risk-adjusted alpha. Which of the following statements should she present as most accurate?

options.text: $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} = \alpha_{\text{n}} -$ 2$\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}} \text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$, measured as the holding of stock n rises with an offsetting pro rata cut in the other stocks, so the cash position is unchanged.

$\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} = \alpha_{\text{n}} +$ 2$\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}} \text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$, so adding a stock with a positive marginal contribution to active risk raises value added by more than its alpha.

$\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} = \alpha_{\text{n}} -$ 2$\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}} \text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$, so a stock with a positive alpha can still have a negative $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ if its marginal contribution to active risk is large enough.

$\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} = \alpha_{\text{n}} -$ 2$\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}} \text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$, so whenever $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ is positive the manager should add to stock n, whatever the cost of buying it.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst in Paris introduces $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ to new analysts; which statement is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Portfolio construction maximizes value added, risk-adjusted active return: VA $= \alpha_{\text{P}} - \lambda_{\text{A}}\psi^{2}_{\text{P}}$, where $\alpha_{\text{P}}$ is the portfolio’s alpha, $\psi_{\text{P}}$ its active risk and $\lambda_{\text{A}}$ the active risk aversion. To decide whether a single position should change, GARP asks a marginal question: if I hold a little more of stock n and a little less cash, how fast does value added change? That rate is the **marginal** **contribution to value added**, $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$.

Two forces move it. First, the extra holding adds alpha at the rate $\alpha_{\text{n}}$ (GARP: “$\alpha_{\text{n}}$ measures the effect on portfolio alpha”). Second, the extra holding changes active risk at the rate $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$, and because the penalty is $\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi^{2}_{\text{P}}$, the penalty changes at the rate 2$\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}} \cdot\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ (the derivative of $\psi^{2}_{\text{P}}$ is 2$\psi_{\text{P}}$ times the change in $\psi_{\text{P}}$). GARP says the loss in value added from the change in active risk “will be proportional to $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$”. Hence

$$\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} = \underbrace{\alpha_{\text{n}}}_{\text{alpha gained}} - \underbrace{2\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}}\,\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}}_{\text{risk penalty incurred}}.$$

| Element | Meaning in GARP |
|---|---|
| Experiment | Holding of stock n up, cash position down by the same amount |
| $\alpha_{\text{n}}$ | Effect on portfolio alpha of the extra holding |
| $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ | Rate at which active risk changes as stock n is added |
| 2$\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}}\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ | Rate of loss in value added from the extra active risk |
| Trade rule | Buy only if $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} > \text{PC}_{\text{n}}$; sell only if $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} < -\text{SC}_{\text{n}}$ |

**Applying it to this question**

Three options share the correct formula, so the discriminating content is the qualifier after it. The only conclusion that follows from the formula alone is that a positive $\alpha_{\text{n}}$ can be outweighed by a large positive $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$: for example $\alpha_{\text{n}} =$ 0.30%, $\lambda_{\text{A}} =$ 0.10, $\psi_{\text{P}} =$ 3%, $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}} =$ 1.0 gives $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} =$ 0.30 − 0.60 = −0.30%.

**Fragile fact.** The risk term is subtracted and carries the factor 2 (and $\psi_{\text{P}}$); the experiment is “stock up, cash down”.

**Reference**

LO 86.g: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs. GARP Chapter 4 (Portfolio Construction), Section 4.6 “Portfolio Revisions” (Eq. 4.7 and the paragraph before it); objective in Section 4.2 “Alphas and Portfolio Construction”, footnote 1. Schweser Reading 86, Module 86.2, “Portfolio Revisions and Rebalancing”. Equations (4.7) and (4.9) are partly garbled in the project’s GARP text extraction; the forms used here are pinned down by the visible fragments of Eq. (4.9), by Eq. (4.8), by GARP’s worked numbers and by the objective in Section 4.2, footnote 1. No conflict on this point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 g, where it is Q1 of 11.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The formula is right but the experiment is wrong. GARP defines $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ for an increase in stock n “with an offsetting decrease in the cash position”, not a pro rata cut in other stocks. Funding from other stocks would add their own alpha and risk effects. A would be right only if the stem defined a different, stock-funded marginal measure.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** The sign of the risk term is reversed. Extra active risk is penalized, so a positive $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ lowers value added. The nearest true statement would concern a stock with a negative $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ (adding it reduces active risk): its $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ does exceed its alpha.

c.reason: GARP: “Stock n’s marginal contribution to value added depends on its alpha and marginal contribution to active risk”, with the risk loss proportional to $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ and subtracted. Since the subtraction can exceed $\alpha_{\text{n}}$, a positive-alpha stock can carry a negative $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** “Whenever positive . . . whatever the cost” ignores the hurdle. GARP: a purchase yields a net benefit only if $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ exceeds the purchase cost (0.80% − 0.50% in GARP’s example). D would be right only with zero transaction costs.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at an Australian superannuation fund runs an AUD 1.4 billion active equity mandate. After new research she revises the alpha of stock K. The portfolio was optimal before the revision, with no limits on holdings or cash and no other constraints. Her inputs are:

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Revised alpha of K, $\alpha_{\text{K}}$ (%) | 2.10 |
| Active risk aversion, $\lambda_{\text{A}}$ | 0.06 |
| Portfolio active risk, $\psi_{\text{P}}$ (%) | 4.00 |
| Marginal contribution of K to active risk, $\text{MCAR}_{\text{K}}$ | 1.50 |
| Purchase cost, $\text{PC}_{\text{K}}$ (%) | 0.60 |
| Sales cost, $\text{SC}_{\text{K}}$ (%) | 0.85 |
| Benchmark weight of K (%) | 3.20 |

Which of the following gives the correct action on stock K and its net benefit at the margin?

options.text: Buy more of K; the net benefit at the margin is 0.78%.
Buy more of K; the net benefit at the margin is 0.53%.
Buy more of K; the net benefit at the margin is 1.38%.
Buy more of K; the net benefit at the margin is 1.14%.

questions.solution:
Australian superannuation PM revises stock K’s alpha; correct action and net benefit at the margin?

**Concept and theory**

Transaction costs create a gap between “worth holding more” and “worth paying to hold more”. Buying stock n costs $\text{PC}_{\text{n}}$ per unit traded; the benefit per unit is $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$. So a purchase is justified only if $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} > \text{PC}_{\text{n}}$, and its net benefit at the margin is $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} - \text{PC}_{\text{n}}$. Symmetrically, selling saves $-\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ per unit and costs $\text{SC}_{\text{n}}$, so a sale is justified only if $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} < -\text{SC}_{\text{n}}$, with net benefit $-\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} - \text{SC}_{\text{n}}$. Between those limits the manager does nothing (Eq. 4.8). GARP’s own example: $\text{PC}_{\text{n}} =$ 0.50%, $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} =$ 0.80% gives a net benefit of 0.30%.

**Applying it to this question**

Working, one step per line:

Formula: $\text{MCVA}_{\text{K}} = \alpha_{\text{K}} -$ 2$\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}} \text{MCAR}_{\text{K}}$

Risk penalty: 2 × 0.06 × 4.00 × 1.50 = 0.72%

$\text{MCVA}_{\text{K}}$ : 2.10 − 0.72 = 1.38%

Test: 1.38% $> \text{PC}_{\text{K}} =$ 0.60% ⇒ buy

Net benefit: 1.38 − 0.60 = 0.78%

Meaning: each marginal unit of K bought adds 0.78% of risk-adjusted value after paying the purchase cost, so she should keep buying until $\text{MCVA}_{\text{K}}$ falls to $\text{PC}_{\text{K}}$. The benchmark weight (3.20%) is irrelevant: the decision uses only alpha, the risk penalty and the cost.

**Fragile fact.** Buy hurdle $= \text{PC}_{\text{n}}$, sell hurdle $= -\text{SC}_{\text{n}}$; the net benefit is measured at the margin against the cost of the trade in that direction.

**Reference**

LO 86.g: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs. GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.6 “Portfolio Revisions” (Eq. 4.7, Eq. 4.8 and the 0.80%/0.50% example). Schweser Reading 86, “Portfolio Revisions and Rebalancing”. Forms of Eq. (4.7) and (4.9) reconstructed from a garbled extraction; see “Core framework”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 g, where it is Q2 of 11.

a.reason: GARP: “If it exceeded the purchase cost . . . then a purchase of stock n would yield a net benefit of” $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} - \text{PC}_{\text{n}}$. Here 1.38 − 0.60 = 0.78%.

b.reason: **Wrong input twin.** 1.38 − 0.85 = 0.53% deducts the sales cost from a purchase. SC is the hurdle for a sale. B would be right if the stem’s purchase cost were 0.85%.

c.reason: **Intermediate result.** 1.38% is $\text{MCVA}_{\text{K}}$ itself, before deducting the cost of buying. It would be right only if trading were costless.

d.reason: **Dropped term.** 2.10 − 0.06 × 4.00 × 1.50 − 0.60 = 2.10 − 0.36 − 0.60 = 1.14% drops the factor 2 in the risk penalty. D would be right only if value added were defined with a penalty whose marginal rate were $\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}}\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$.

questions.question:
The chief risk officer of a Frankfurt-based asset manager is reviewing a EUR equity portfolio after an alpha update. The portfolio was optimal before the update, there are no limits on holdings or cash, active risk aversion is $\lambda_{\text{A}} =$ 0.08 and portfolio active risk is $\psi_{\text{P}} =$ 3.0%. For four holdings:

| Stock | Updated $\alpha_{\text{n}}$ (%) | $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ | $\text{PC}_{\text{n}}$ (%) | $\text{SC}_{\text{n}}$ (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| W | −0.40 | 1.00 | 0.55 | 0.70 |
| X | 0.30 | 2.50 | 0.80 | 1.00 |
| Y | 0.20 | 2.00 | 0.50 | 0.60 |
| Z | −1.10 | −1.00 | 0.70 | 0.65 |

Which of these holdings should the manager reduce?

options.text: W, X, Y and Z
W, X and Y only
W, Y and Z only
W and Y only

questions.solution:
Frankfurt CRO screens four holdings after an alpha update; which should be reduced?

**Concept and theory**

After new information each holding is tested separately against Eq. (4.8). Selling stock n lowers the holding, so the value added changes by $-\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ per unit sold; the sale costs $\text{SC}_{\text{n}}$. A sale is therefore justified only when $-\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} > \text{SC}_{\text{n}}$, i.e. $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} < -\text{SC}_{\text{n}}$. A negative $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ alone is not enough: it must be negative by more than the sales cost. GARP’s example: $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} = -$1.30% with $\text{SC}_{\text{n}} =$ 0.75% gives a net benefit of 0.55% from selling. Note also that $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ can be negative (adding the stock reduces active risk), in which case the risk term adds to $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$.

**Applying it to this question**

Common factor: 2$\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}} =$ 2 × 0.08 × 3.0 = 0.48, so $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} = \alpha_{\text{n}} -$ 0.48 $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$.

| Stock | $\alpha_{\text{n}}$ | 0.48 $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ | $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ | $-\text{SC}_{\text{n}}$ | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| W | −0.40 | 0.48 | −0.88 | −0.70 | Sell (net 0.18%) |
| X | 0.30 | 1.20 | −0.90 | −1.00 | Hold |
| Y | 0.20 | 0.96 | −0.76 | −0.60 | Sell (net 0.16%) |
| Z | −1.10 | −0.48 | −0.62 | −0.65 | Hold |

None has $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} > \text{PC}_{\text{n}}$, so there are no purchases. Reduce W and Y only. Note Y has a positive alpha yet is sold (heavy risk contribution), and Z has the most negative alpha yet is held (its negative MCAR softens the penalty, and its MCVA of −0.62% does not clear −0.65%).

**Fragile fact.** Sell only if $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} < -\text{SC}_{\text{n}}$; a negative $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}} \text{raises MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ because the penalty is subtracted.

**Reference**

LO 86.g: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs. GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.6 “Portfolio Revisions” (Eq. 4.8 and the −1.30%/0.75% sale example). Schweser Reading 86, “Portfolio Revisions and Rebalancing”. Forms of Eq. (4.7) and (4.9) reconstructed from a garbled extraction; see “Core framework”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 g, where it is Q3 of 11.

b.reason: **Wrong input twin.** Testing $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} < -\text{PC}_{\text{n}}$ uses the purchase cost for a sale: X becomes a sale (−0.90 \< −0.80) and Z stays held (−0.62 > −0.70), giving W, X and Y. B would be right if X’s sales cost were 0.80%.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a São Paulo asset manager is preparing a rebalancing report for a BRL equity fund and must state the alpha no-trade band for stock M, a current holding. The fund’s portfolio is optimal, with no limits on holdings or cash. The inputs are:

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Active risk aversion, $\lambda_{\text{A}}$ | 0.04 |
| Portfolio active risk, $\psi_{\text{P}}$ (%) | 6.00 |
| Marginal contribution of M to active risk, $\text{MCAR}_{\text{M}}$ | 1.25 |
| Purchase cost, $\text{PC}_{\text{M}}$ (%) | 0.45 |
| Sales cost, $\text{SC}_{\text{M}}$ (%) | 0.70 |
| Total return volatility of M (%) | 31.00 |

Which of the following is the no-trade band for the alpha of stock M?

options.text: 0.15% $\le\alpha_{\text{M}} \le$ 1.30%

questions.solution:
BRL fund junior analyst states the alpha no-trade band for stock M.

Eq. (4.8) is a band on $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$. Substituting $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} = \alpha_{\text{n}} -$ 2$\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}}\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ and adding the risk term to every part converts it into a band on the alpha itself (Eq. 4.9):

$$\underbrace{2\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}}\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}} - \text{SC}_{\text{n}}}_{\text{lower bound}} \le \alpha_{\text{n}} \le \underbrace{\text{PC}_{\text{n}} + 2\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}}\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}}_{\text{upper bound}}.$$

GARP: while the alpha stays inside the band the portfolio remains optimal and new information should not trigger a trade. The sales cost sits on the lower side (alpha must fall far enough to justify selling) and the purchase cost on the upper side.

**Applying it to this question**

Working, one step per line:

Risk term: 2 × 0.04 × 6.00 × 1.25 = 0.60%

Lower bound: 0.60 $- \text{SC}_{\text{M}} =$ 0.60 − 0.70 = −0.10%

Upper bound: 0.60 $+ \text{PC}_{\text{M}} =$ 0.60 + 0.45 = 1.05%

Check width: 1.05 − (−0.10) = 1.15% $= \text{PC}_{\text{M}} + \text{SC}_{\text{M}}$

Meaning: any revised alpha for M between −0.10% and 1.05% leaves the portfolio optimal net of costs; no trade. The stock’s total volatility (31%) is irrelevant: risk enters only through its marginal contribution to active risk.

**Fragile fact.** Lower bound uses SC, upper bound uses PC; the risk term is added to both.

**Reference**

LO 86.g: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs. GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.6 “Portfolio Revisions” (band paragraph, Eq. 4.9). Schweser Reading 86, “Portfolio Revisions and Rebalancing” (“Rearranging this relationship with respect to alpha gives a no-trade region for alpha”). Forms of Eq. (4.7) and (4.9) reconstructed from a garbled extraction; see “Core framework”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 g, where it is Q4 of 11.

c.reason: **Wrong input twin: PC and SC swapped.** 0.60 − 0.45 = 0.15% to 0.60 + 0.70 = 1.30% puts the purchase cost on the sell side and the sales cost on the buy side. It would be right if $\text{PC}_{\text{M}} =$ 0.70% and $\text{SC}_{\text{M}} =$ 0.45%.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Toronto pension plan runs the CAD equity sleeve. He has no intuitive feel for active risk aversion, but he expects an information ratio of 0.60 and targets 4.0% active risk; the sleeve currently runs at exactly that active risk and is otherwise optimal, with no limits on holdings or cash. He receives a revised alpha for stock R.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Information ratio, IR | 0.60 |
| Target (and current) active risk, $\psi_{\text{P}}$ (%) | 4.00 |
| Marginal contribution of R to active risk, $\text{MCAR}_{\text{R}}$ | 0.90 |
| Purchase cost, $\text{PC}_{\text{R}}$ (%) | 0.40 |
| Sales cost, $\text{SC}_{\text{R}}$ (%) | 0.55 |
| Benchmark weight of R (%) | 1.80 |
| Revised alpha of R, $\alpha_{\text{R}}$ (%) | 1.10 |

Which statement about stock R’s alpha no-trade band and the right response is correct?

options.text: The band is −0.01% to 0.94%; the revised alpha calls for buying more of R.
The band is 0.53% to 1.48%; the revised alpha calls for no trade in R.
The band is 0.14% to 1.09%; the revised alpha calls for buying more of R.
The band is −0.55% to 0.40%; the revised alpha calls for buying more of R.

questions.solution:
Toronto pension PM backs out $\lambda_{\text{A}}$ from IR and active risk, then sets stock R’s band and decides.

**Concept and theory**

Managers rarely have intuition about $\lambda_{\text{A}}$, but they do about their information ratio and desired active risk. GARP’s optimality relationship (Eq. 4.3, Section 4.5) translates these:

$\lambda_{\text{A}} = \frac{\text{IR}}{2 \psi_{\text{P}}}$ ,

with $\psi_{\text{P}}$ in percent (GARP: IR 0.5 and 5% active risk give $\lambda_{\text{A}} =$ 0.05; “verify that our optimizer is using percents and not decimals”). That $\lambda_{\text{A}}$ then feeds the risk term of the alpha band, Eq. (4.9).

**Applying it to this question**

Working, one step per line:

$\lambda_{\text{A}} =$ 0.60/(2 × 4.00) = 0.075

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Shanghai fund management company is reviewing the rebalancing policy of a CNY equity fund. The policy applies GARP’s alpha no-trade band, derived from the marginal contribution to value added, to every holding. Which of the following statements in the policy’s commentary is most accurate?

options.text: A higher active risk aversion widens each stock’s band in proportion, so a more risk-averse manager will trade less often in every stock.

The transaction costs $\text{PC}_{\text{n}} \text{and SC}_{\text{n}}$ fix where each stock’s band sits, while the risk term 2$\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}} \text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ fixes how wide the band is.

The band’s width equals $\text{PC}_{\text{n}} + \text{SC}_{\text{n}}$, and a larger risk term 2$\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}} \text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ raises both the lower and the upper bound by the same amount.

The band’s width equals $\text{PC}_{\text{n}} + \text{SC}_{\text{n}}$, and a larger risk term 2$\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}} \text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ lowers both the lower and the upper bound by the same amount.

questions.solution:
Shanghai internal auditor reviews commentary on the alpha no-trade band; most accurate statement?

**Concept and theory**

Write the band as $[ \text{R}_{\text{n}} - \text{SC}_{\text{n}}$, $\text{R}_{\text{n}} + \text{PC}_{\text{n}} ] \text{with R}_{\text{n}} =$ 2$\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}}\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$. Two separate levers act on it:

| Lever | Effect on the alpha band |
|---|---|
| Costs $\text{PC}_{\text{n}}$, $\text{SC}_{\text{n}}$ | Set the **width**: $(\text{R}_{\text{n}} + \text{PC}_{\text{n}}) - (\text{R}_{\text{n}} - \text{SC}_{\text{n}}) = \text{PC}_{\text{n}} + \text{SC}_{\text{n}}$ |
| Risk term $\text{R}_{\text{n}}$ ($\lambda_{\text{A}}$, $\psi_{\text{P}}$, $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$) | Sets the **location**: moves both bounds by the same amount |

GARP states that the bandwidth is the sum of the sale and purchase costs (0.50% + 0.75% = 1.25% in its example). Intuitively, the risk term tells you how much alpha a stock needs merely to justify its current risk contribution; the costs tell you how far alpha must move from that level before a trade pays.

**Applying it to this question**

The question turns on width versus location. A higher $\text{R}_{\text{n}}$ (higher $\lambda_{\text{A}}$, $\psi_{\text{P}}$ or positive $\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$) raises both bounds equally; the width stays $\text{PC}_{\text{n}} + \text{SC}_{\text{n}}$. Numerical check: with PC = 0.50, SC = 0.75, R = 0.40 the band is −0.35 to 0.90; with R = 0.80 it is 0.05 to 1.30. Both widths are 1.25%.

**Fragile fact.** Costs → width; risk term → location, and a larger risk term moves the band up.

**Reference**

LO 86.g: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs. GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.6 “Portfolio Revisions” (bandwidth sentence, Eq. 4.9). Schweser Reading 86, “Portfolio Revisions and Rebalancing”. **Conflict:** Schweser Module Quiz 86.2 Q1 keys risk aversion and MCAR as factors that “increase the no-trade region for the alpha”; GARP’s Eq. (4.9) and bandwidth sentence show they shift the band, with width $\text{PC}_{\text{n}} + \text{SC}_{\text{n}}$. GARP used. This looks like Schweser loosely reading “determined by” as “larger”, not a version difference. Forms of Eq. (4.7) and (4.9) reconstructed from a garbled extraction; see “Core framework”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 g, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attributes the cost lever’s property (width) to the risk lever. Risk aversion shifts the band; it does not widen it. This is the trap embedded in Schweser’s Module Quiz 86.2 Q1 key (see (f)). A would be right only for Leland’s allocation-space region, whose size does depend on risk aversion, not for the Eq. (4.9) alpha band.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** The roles are reversed: costs fix the width and the risk term fixes the location. B would be right only if the band were defined as $\text{PC}_{\text{n}} \pm\text{R}_{\text{n}}$, which it is not.

c.reason: Directly from Eq. (4.9) and GARP’s bandwidth sentence: width $\text{PC}_{\text{n}} + \text{SC}_{\text{n}}$, and the risk term is added to both bounds.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** The risk term is added to both bounds (the alpha needed to justify a holding rises with the risk it adds), so a larger term raises them. D would be right only if the risk term were subtracted, as it is in $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ itself.

questions.question:
A quantitative analyst at a US university endowment monitors a USD equity portfolio that was optimal, with no limits on holdings or cash. A volatility spike leads to a re-estimate of risk, but no new alpha information arrives: stock T’s alpha stays at 0.30%. Active risk aversion is $\lambda_{\text{A}} =$ 0.10, $\text{PC}_{\text{T}} =$ 0.35% and $\text{SC}_{\text{T}} =$ 0.50%.

| Input | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Portfolio active risk, $\psi_{\text{P}}$ (%) | 3.00 | 4.00 |
| Marginal contribution of T to active risk, $\text{MCAR}_{\text{T}}$ | 0.80 | 1.10 |
| Alpha of T, $\alpha_{\text{T}}$ (%) | 0.30 | 0.30 |

Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The new band is 0.38% to 1.23%; hold T, because with no new alpha information there is nothing to trade on.
The new band is 0.38% to 1.23%; reduce T, because its unchanged alpha now lies below the lower bound.
The new band is −0.02% to 1.23%; hold T, because its unchanged alpha still lies inside the band.
The new band is 0.53% to 1.38%; reduce T, because its unchanged alpha now lies below the lower bound.

questions.solution:
US endowment analyst: risk re-estimate with unchanged alpha; new band and action for stock T.

**Concept and theory**

The band in Eq. (4.9) is built from current inputs. “New information” that moves the band can arrive through the risk side as well as the alpha side: if $\psi_{\text{P}} \text{or MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ rises, the alpha a stock needs merely to justify its holding rises, and the whole band shifts up by the change in 2$\lambda_{\text{A}}\psi_{\text{P}}\text{MCAR}_{\text{n}}$. If the alpha is unchanged but the band moves above it, the stock’s $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ has fallen below $-\text{SC}_{\text{n}}$ and Eq. (4.8) calls for a sale, even though nothing about expected return has changed.

**Applying it to this question**

Working, one step per line:

Old risk term: 2 × 0.10 × 3.00 × 0.80 = 0.48% ⇒ band −0.02% to 0.83%

New risk term: 2 × 0.10 × 4.00 × 1.10 = 0.88%

New lower bound: 0.88 − 0.50 = 0.38%

New upper bound: 0.88 + 0.35 = 1.23%

Test: $\alpha_{\text{T}} =$ 0.30% \< 0.38% ⇒ reduce T

Check via MCVA : 0.30 − 0.88 = −0.58% $< -\text{SC}_{\text{T}} = -$0.50%, net benefit 0.58 − 0.50 = 0.08% Meaning: the band moved up by 0.40% (width still 0.85%), and the unchanged alpha no longer pays for T’s larger risk contribution net of the sales cost.

**Fragile fact.** A higher risk term moves the whole band up; an unchanged alpha can fall out of the bottom and trigger a sale.

**Reference**

LO 86.g: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs. GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.6 “Portfolio Revisions” (Eq. 4.8, Eq. 4.9). Schweser Reading 86, “Portfolio Revisions and Rebalancing”; Key Concepts LO 86.g (region determined by risk aversion, the portfolio’s active risk, the marginal contribution to active risk and transaction costs). Forms of Eq. (4.7) and (4.9) reconstructed from a garbled extraction; see “Core framework”. Same Schweser quiz conflict as Q6 (GARP used).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 g, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The band is right but the conclusion restricts “new information” to alpha. Eq. (4.8) depends on $\psi_{\text{P}} \text{and MCAR}_{\text{n}}$ too. A would be right only if the risk inputs were unchanged.

b.reason: The new band is 0.38% to 1.23% and $\alpha_{\text{T}}$ is below its lower bound, so $\text{MCVA}_{\text{T}} < -\text{SC}_{\text{T}}$: GARP’s sale condition.

c.reason: **Sibling swap: widen versus shift.** Keeping the old lower bound (−0.02%) and taking the new upper bound treats the higher risk term as widening the band (width 1.25% instead of 0.85%). It would be right only if the risk term affected the upper bound alone.

d.reason: **Wrong input twin: PC and SC swapped.** 0.88 − 0.35 = 0.53% and 0.88 + 0.50 = 1.38% put PC on the sell side and SC on the buy side. The action matches but the band is wrong. It would be right if $\text{PC}_{\text{T}} =$ 0.50% and $\text{SC}_{\text{T}} =$ 0.35%.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at the asset management arm of a London insurer runs a GBP equity mandate with no limits on holdings or cash. After a positive alpha revision on stock V, she bought V until a further purchase would no longer add value net of cost. For V, $\text{PC}_{\text{V}} =$ 0.40% and $\text{SC}_{\text{V}} =$ 0.60%. Assume $\lambda_{\text{A}}$, $\psi_{\text{P}} \text{and MCAR}_{\text{V}}$ stay unchanged from this point on. Which statement best describes stock V’s position immediately after the purchase?

options.text: $\text{MCVA}_{\text{V}} =$ 0, since she bought until marginal value added was exhausted; the alpha must fall by 0.60% before she would sell any V.
$\text{MCVA}_{\text{V}} = -\text{SC}_{\text{V}}$ , at the lower end of the band; any further decrease in the alpha of V would lead her to sell some V.
$\text{MCVA}_{\text{V}} = \text{PC}_{\text{V}}$ , at the upper end of the band; the alpha must fall by 0.60% before she would sell any V.
$\text{MCVA}_{\text{V}} = \text{PC}_{\text{V}}$ , at the upper end of the band; the alpha must fall by 1.00% before she would sell any V.

questions.solution:
London insurer PM has just bought stock V to the point of no further net value; where is V in its band?

**Concept and theory**

With costs, a manager buys only while the marginal benefit exceeds the cost: while $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} > \text{PC}_{\text{n}}$. Each purchase raises active risk in n’s direction and so lowers $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$; buying stops exactly when $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} = \text{PC}_{\text{n}}$. That is the upper edge of the band in Eq. (4.8). To reach the lower edge, where a sale pays, $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ must fall to $-\text{SC}_{\text{n}}$, a distance of $\text{PC}_{\text{n}} + \text{SC}_{\text{n}}$. With risk inputs unchanged, a fall in $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ comes one for one from a fall in $\alpha_{\text{n}}$. GARP makes exactly this point: just after a purchase, $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}}$ equals the purchase cost and the stock sits at the upper end of the band; any rise in alpha means further buying, and in GARP’s example alpha must fall by the full 1.25% before a sale is considered.

Without costs the first-order condition would be $\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} =$ 0; costs replace that single point by a band.

**Applying it to this question**

Working, one step per line:

After buying: $\text{MCVA}_{\text{V}} = \text{PC}_{\text{V}} =$ 0.40% $(\text{upper end})$

Sell trigger: $\text{MCVA}_{\text{V}} < -\text{SC}_{\text{V}} = -$0.60%

Required fall in $\text{MCVA}_{\text{V}} (= \text{fall in} \alpha_{\text{V}} )$ : 0.40 − (−0.60) = 1.00% $= \text{PC}_{\text{V}} + \text{SC}_{\text{V}}$

**Fragile fact.** Just bought $\Rightarrow\text{MCVA} =$ PC (top of band); the alpha must fall by PC + SC, the full width, before selling.

**Reference**

LO 86.g: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs. GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.6 “Portfolio Revisions” (band paragraph before Eq. 4.8). Schweser Reading 86, “Portfolio Revisions and Rebalancing” (Schweser omits this paragraph; content from GARP). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 g, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** $\text{MCVA}_{\text{V}} =$ 0 is the stopping condition without transaction costs; with costs, buying stops when $\text{MCVA}_{\text{V}} \text{reaches PC}_{\text{V}}$ . The 0.60% would then be the distance from 0 to $-\text{SC}_{\text{V}}$ . A would be right only if $\text{PC}_{\text{V}} =$ 0.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It places V at the wrong end. The lower end is where a manager sits just after a sale; any further fall in alpha would then trigger more selling. B would be right if the stem said she had just sold V.

c.reason: **Dropped term.** The location is right but the distance omits $\text{PC}_{\text{V}}$ : from +0.40% to −0.60% is 1.00%, not 0.60%. C would be right only if $\text{PC}_{\text{V}}$ were zero.

d.reason: It states both GARP facts: the position sits at the upper end with $\text{MCVA}_{\text{V}} = \text{PC}_{\text{V}}$ , and alpha must fall by the full bandwidth, 0.40% + 0.60% = 1.00%, before a sale.

questions.question: A risk consultant is validating the rebalancing engine of a Milan-based asset manager’s EUR equity fund. The engine applies the rule $-\text{SC}_{\text{n}} \le\text{MCVA}_{\text{n}} \le\text{PC}_{\text{n}}$ to each holding and trades only the stocks that breach it. Which statement about the assumptions and simplifications behind this rule is most accurate?

options.text: It takes the current portfolio as optimal with no limits on holdings or cash, and it folds the amortization horizon into the costs $\text{PC}_{\text{n}} \text{and SC}_{\text{n}}$.
It takes the current portfolio as optimal with no limits on holdings or cash, and it fully solves the dynamic problem of alphas, risks and costs over time.
It holds only when there are no limits on holdings or cash; adding any such constraint makes the band analysis essentially different and unusable.
It holds only when the purchase cost and the sales cost of each stock are equal, since otherwise the band could not be placed around the alpha.

questions.solution:
Consultant validates a Milan fund’s rebalancing engine; which statement on the rule’s assumptions is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s band rests on stated assumptions and simplifications:

| Assumption or simplification | GARP’s wording (Section 4.6) |
|---|---|
| Current portfolio is optimal | The band holds “if the current portfolio is optimal” |
| No limits (footnote 6) | No limits on holdings or cash and no other constraints; with them the analysis is more complicated “but not essentially different” |
| Amortization | The amortization horizon is subsumed into SC and PC |
| Static, not dynamic | A full treatment needs the dynamic problem of alphas, risks and costs over time |

Costs are paid at once while alpha accrues over time, so $\text{PC}_{\text{n}} \text{and SC}_{\text{n}}$ here are read as already amortized (the calculation is LO 86.d).

**Applying it to this question**

The correct statement must keep the optimality and no-limits assumptions and treat amortization as a simplification, without claiming a dynamic solution, overstating constraints or adding a condition GARP never imposes.

**Fragile fact.** Amortization is folded into PC and SC (a simplification); constraints make it “more complicated, but not essentially different”.

**Reference**

LO 86.g: Determine the optimal no-trade region for rebalancing with transaction costs. GARP Chapter 4, Section 4.6 “Portfolio Revisions” (footnote 6; paragraph after Eq. 4.9). Schweser Reading 86 omits these assumptions; content from GARP. Amortization arithmetic (LO 86.d) not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-4 g, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: It matches GARP’s footnote 6 and its remark that the analysis is simplified by subsuming the amortization horizon into SC and PC.

b.reason: **Scope error.** The first half is right, but GARP says the band simplifies the problem; the full dynamic problem is only solved in very simple cases (one or two assets, such as Leland). B would describe a fully dynamic multi-period model, not this rule.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** GARP says adding limits makes the analysis more complicated but “not essentially different”. C would be right only if GARP said the analysis breaks down under constraints.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** GARP imposes no equal-cost condition; its own example uses PC = 0.50% and SC = 0.75%. Unequal costs merely make the band asymmetric about the risk term. D would be right only if the rule were defined as a symmetric band, such as ± a single cost.
