questions.question:
A treasury analyst at an Australian bank receives the morning delta-normal VaR run (95%, $\alpha=$ 1.65) for a book exposed to three risk factors. The current portfolio VaR is AUD 5.117 million.

| Risk factor | Position (AUD m) | Volatility (%) | Marginal VaR |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 20 | 10 | 0.1468 |
| 2 | 12 | 12 | 0.1634 |
| 3 | 8 | 5 | 0.0275 |

A trader proposes a trade that adds AUD 4 million of exposure to factor 1 and reduces the exposure to factor 2 by AUD 5 million, leaving factor 3 unchanged. Using the marginal VaR shortcut, which of the following best describes the incremental VaR of the trade?

options.text: +AUD 1.404 million; the trade is risk-increasing
+AUD 0.587 million; the trade is risk-increasing
−AUD 0.230 million; the trade is risk-reducing
−AUD 0.330 million; the trade is risk-reducing

questions.solution:
AUD three-factor book: shortcut incremental VaR of +4 in factor 1 and −5 in factor 2.

**Concept and theory**

Incremental VaR is the change in VaR owing to a new position: ideally $\text{VaR}_{\text{p}}+_{\text{a}} - \text{VaR}_{\text{p}}$ from a full revaluation (Equation 5.21), where a is the vector of new exposures, possibly in several risk factors. Expanding in a series around the current point, $\text{VaR}_{\text{p}}+_{\text{a}} = \text{VaR}_{\text{p}} + (\Delta\text{VaR})^{'}$ a + . . . (5.22), and ignoring second-order terms gives the shortcut

Incremental VaR $\approx(\Delta\text{VaR})^{'} \text{a} = \sum_{\text{i}} \Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} \text{a}_{\text{i}} ($5.23).

The signs of $\text{a}_{\text{i}}$ matter: reducing an exposure $\text{(a}_{\text{i}} <$ 0) in a factor with positive marginal VaR lowers VaR. If VaR falls, the trade is risk-reducing, a hedge; otherwise it is risk-increasing.

**Applying it to this question**

a = (+4, −5, 0) in AUD millions; marginal VaRs (0.1468, 0.1634, 0.0275).

$\Delta\text{VaR}_{1}\text{a}_{1} =$ 0.1468 × 4 = +0.5872

$\Delta\text{VaR}_{2}\text{a}_{2} =$ 0.1634 × (−5) = −0.8170

$\Delta\text{VaR}_{3}\text{a}_{3} =$ 0.0275 × 0 = 0

$(\Delta\text{VaR})^{'} \text{a} =$ 0.5872 − 0.8170 = −0.2298

The shortcut estimates that VaR falls by about AUD 0.23 million, so the trade is risk-reducing. (For comparison, a full revaluation with the underlying correlations, $\rho_{12} =$ 0.5, $\rho_{13} =$ 0.1, $\rho_{23} =$ 0.3, gives a new VaR of 4.960 and an exact change of −0.158: the trade is 20 to 42% of the existing exposures, so second-order terms are not negligible, but the sign is the same.)

**Reference**

LO 87.a. GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2 VaR Tools, Incremental VaR (Equations 5.21 to 5.23, Figures 5.2 and 5.3, Incremental VaR box) and Example 5.1 continued (\$528 shortcut against \$529 exact). Schweser Module 87.1, Incremental VaR (Steps 1 to 3, cross product of the risk-factor vector with marginal VaRs). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 a, where it is Q7 of 13.

b.reason: **Dropped term.** 0.5872 keeps only the factor 1 leg. It would be correct if the trade changed factor 1 alone.

It ignores covariances; since $\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} = \alpha\rho_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$, it would be correct only if each factor were perfectly correlated with the portfolio ($\rho_{\text{i}} =$ 1).

questions.source: High quality paper IM-5 a Q8
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a US dealer bank supports a trading desk whose book holds about 120,000 trades; a full VaR run takes 12 minutes. A client proposes a trade whose exposures to two risk factors are each about 35% of the desk’s current exposure to those factors. The head of trading wants to quote within a minute and proposes to estimate the trade’s incremental VaR as $(\Delta\text{VaR})^{'} \times$ a, using the marginal VaR vector from the last run. Which of the following comments by the analyst is most accurate?

options.text: The shortcut gives the exact incremental VaR for a trade of any size, because the marginal VaR vector is the derivative of VaR at the current positions.

The shortcut reuses the marginal VaR vector from the last run and trades accuracy for speed; it suits small trades, but a trade this large needs a before-and-after revaluation, as VaR changes nonlinearly.
The shortcut is most valuable for small books, because a full revaluation of a small book requires the largest number of computations.
The trade can be classed as a hedge without either method if its own individual VaR is smaller than the desk’s current portfolio VaR.

questions.solution:
US dealer, 120,000 trades, 12-minute VaR run, large client trade: is the $(\Delta\text{VaR})^{'}$ a shortcut appropriate?

**Concept and theory**

GARP contrasts two ways to measure incremental VaR:

|  | Full revaluation | Marginal VaR shortcut |
|---|---|---|
| Formula | $\text{VaR}_{\text{p}}+_{\text{a}} - \text{VaR}_{\text{p}}$ | $(\Delta\text{VaR})^{'}$ a |
| Inputs | A second VaR run with the trade | Marginal VaR vector, a by-product of the last run |
| Speed | Slow; operations grow with the square of the number of risk factors | Fast; allows real-time trading limits |
| Accuracy | Exact; captures the nonlinear response of VaR | First-order; good when the trade is small relative to the portfolio |

GARP’s own illustration is a bank with 100,000 trades and a 10-minute VaR run: waiting for a revaluation is “most likely too long”, so one accepts an approximation, “trading off faster computation time against accuracy”. The shortcut is “especially useful for large portfolios” and a good approximation when “a proposed trade is likely to be small relative to the outstanding portfolio”. The incremental VaR box adds that the amount can be large, “in which case VaR changes in a nonlinear fashion”.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem is built to switch the trade-off: the trade is about 35% of the relevant exposures, so it is not small, and the linear approximation will miss the curvature of VaR. Speed favours the shortcut; size favours revaluation. The accurate comment must name both sides.

**Fragile fact.** Shortcut: faster and less accurate; best for large portfolios and small trades. Full revaluation: slower and exact.

**Reference**

LO 87.a. GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2 VaR Tools, Incremental VaR (Equations 5.21 to 5.23, the 100,000-trade illustration, Incremental VaR box). Schweser Module 87.1 Incremental VaR and Module Quiz 87.1 Q3 (full revaluation “more costly, but also more accurate”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 a, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** The derivative is exact only for an infinitesimal change; Equation 5.22 drops second-order terms that grow with the trade. A would be correct if “for a trade of any size” were replaced by “approximately, for small trades”.

b.reason: B states the speed-for-accuracy trade, the source of the speed (the marginal VaR vector from the last run), the condition (small trades) and the reason it fails here (nonlinearity for large trades).

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says the shortcut is especially useful for large portfolios, where full revaluation needs many computations (operations rise with the square of the number of risk factors). C would be correct with “small” and “largest” reversed.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Whether a trade is a hedge depends on the change in portfolio VaR, not on the trade’s own individual VaR compared with the portfolio VaR; a small but positively correlated trade still raises VaR. D would be correct if it referred to the sign of the incremental VaR.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-5 a Q9
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Chinese securities firm reviews a two-position book. Position 1 is CNY 50 million with annual volatility 16%; Position 2 is CNY 30 million with annual volatility 25%. The correlation between the two positions is 0.30, and the firm uses annual VaR at 95% ($\alpha=$ 1.65). The head of the desk is considering closing Position 2 entirely. Which of the following correctly gives the component VaR of Position 2 and the exact reduction in portfolio VaR if Position 2 is closed?

options.text: Component VaR CNY 9.801 million; exact reduction CNY 7.425 million
Component VaR CNY 9.801 million; exact reduction CNY 9.801 million
Component VaR CNY 12.375 million; exact reduction CNY 7.425 million
Component VaR CNY 9.801 million; exact reduction CNY 8.250 million

questions.solution:
Two-position CNY book: component VaR of Position 2 against the exact VaR reduction from closing it.

**Concept and theory**

Component VaR, $\text{CVaR}_{\text{i}} = \Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} \text{x}_{\text{i}}$, takes the slope of VaR at the current holding and extends it linearly over the whole position. It therefore only approximates the effect of deleting the position; “the quality of this linear approximation improves when the VaR components are small”. The exact effect of deleting position i is an incremental VaR: the full portfolio VaR minus the VaR of the portfolio without i. In a two-asset book, the portfolio without position 2 is position 1 alone, whose VaR is its individual VaR. GARP’s two-currency example shows the gap: component VaR of the EUR \$152,108 against an exact deletion change of \$92,738.

**Applying it to this question**

CNY millions, $\alpha=$ 1.65, x = (50, 30).

$\text{x}_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$ : 50(0.16) = 8.0, 30(0.25) = 7.5

$\sigma^{2}_{\text{p}}\text{W}^{2} =$ $\text{8.0}^{2} +$ $\text{7.5}^{2} +$ 2(0.30)(8.0)(7.5) = 64 + 56.25 + 36 = 156.25, $\sigma_{\text{p}}\text{W} =$ 12.5

$\text{VaR}_{\text{p}} =$ 1.65 × 12.5 = 20.625

$(\Sigma\text{x})_{2} =$ 0.30(0.16)(0.25)(50) + $\text{0.25}^{2}($30) = 0.600 + 1.875 = 2.475

$\Delta\text{VaR}_{2} =$ 1.65 × 2.475/12.5 = 0.3267, $\text{CVaR}_{2} =$ 0.3267 × 30 = 9.801

$\text{VaR}^{\text{ind}}_{1} =$ 1.65 × 8.0 = 13.200

Exact reduction = 20.625 − 13.200 = 7.425

Check: $\text{CVaR}_{1} =$ 1.65 × (0.0256 × 50 + 0.012 × 30)/12.5 × 50 = 10.824, and 10.824 + 9.801 = 20.625. Closing Position 2 would lower VaR by CNY 7.425 million, less than the CNY 9.801 million that the linear decomposition attributes to it, because Position 2 is large relative to the book.

**Fragile fact.** Deleting position i leaves the other position: subtract the remaining position’s VaR, not the deleted one’s.

**Reference**

LO 87.a. GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2 VaR Tools, Component VaR (Equations 5.27 and 5.28, Component VaR box) and Example 5.1 continued (EUR deletion \$92,738 against component \$152,108); Section 5.3 Summary and Figure 5.4. Schweser’s examples describe component VaR as the amount by which VaR “will decrease” if a position is removed; GARP is explicit that this is approximate, and GARP is followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 a, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: It pairs the component VaR (marginal VaR times position, Equation 5.27) with the exact before-and-after change, the incremental VaR of the deletion.

b.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** It treats the component VaR as the exact deletion effect. It would be correct only for a very small position, where the linear approximation is close.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** 12.375 = 1.65 × 7.5 is the individual VaR of Position 2, which ignores diversification. It would be correct as a component VaR only if Position 2 were perfectly correlated with the portfolio ($\rho_{2} =$ 1; here $\rho_{2} =$ 0.792).

d.reason: **Wrong input twin.** 8.250 = 20.625 − 12.375 subtracts Position 2’s own individual VaR, which is the exact change from deleting Position 1, not Position 2. It would be correct if the question asked about closing Position 1.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-5 a Q10
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Canadian pension plan is preparing a risk-contribution report at 99% ($\alpha=$ 2.33). The diversified VaR of the portfolio is CAD 25.134 million and its undiversified VaR is CAD 34.368 million.

| Asset | Position (CAD m) | Volatility (%) | Correlation with portfolio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Equities | 60 | 14 | 0.891 |
| 2 Credit | 25 | 20 | 0.724 |
| 3 Gold overlay | 15 | 9 | −0.233 |

Which of the following best describes the percent contribution to VaR of Asset 3?

options.text: +9.2%; the overlay uses 9.2% of the portfolio’s risk
+2.9%; the overlay adds to the portfolio’s risk
−2.9%; the overlay acts as a hedge for the rest of the portfolio
−2.1%; the overlay acts as a hedge for the rest of the portfolio

questions.solution:
CAD pension plan risk-contribution report: percent contribution of a gold overlay with $\rho= -$0.233 to the portfolio.

**Concept and theory**

Adding up individual VaRs and expressing each as a percentage “is not useful because it completely ignores diversification effects”. What is needed is an additive decomposition. Component VaR provides it, and Equation 5.29 gives the most direct form:

$\text{CVaR}_{\text{i}} = \text{VaR w}_{\text{i}} \beta_{\text{i}} = (\alpha\sigma_{\text{p}}\text{W}) \text{w}_{\text{i}} \frac{\rho_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{i}}}{\sigma_{\text{p}}} = (\alpha\sigma_{\text{i}}\text{w}_{\text{i}}\text{W})\rho_{\text{i}} = \text{VaR}_{\text{i}} \rho_{\text{i}}$,

“This conveniently transforms the individual VaR into its contribution to the total portfolio simply by multiplying it by the correlation coefficient.” Normalising by the diversified VaR gives the percent contribution $\text{CVaR}_{\text{i}}$/VaR $= \text{w}_{\text{i}} \beta_{\text{i}}$ (Equation 5.30). A negative component means the position hedges the rest of the portfolio.

**Applying it to this question**

Equation 5.29 gives the component directly from the table, without the covariance matrix:

$\text{VaR}^{\text{ind}}_{3} =$ 2.33 × 0.09 × 15 = 3.1455

$\text{CVaR}_{3} = \text{VaR}^{\text{ind}}_{3} \times\rho_{3} =$ 3.1455 × (−0.233) = −0.7329

Percent contribution $= \text{CVaR}_{3}$/VaR$_{\text{p}} = -$0.7329/25.134 = −2.92%

The overlay reduces portfolio VaR by about 2.9% of its total, so it is a net hedge. (Full precision gives −2.91%; the other two contributions are +69.4% and +33.5%, and the three sum to 100%.)

**Fragile fact.** Percent contribution divides by the diversified VaR; the correlation used is with the portfolio, and its sign carries through.

**Reference**

LO 87.a. GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2 VaR Tools, Component VaR (Equations 5.27 to 5.30). Schweser Module 87.1, Component VaR (Example 2, Part 2, percent of contribution). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 a, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** 3.1455/34.368 = 9.2% is the naive individual-VaR share that GARP rejects; it ignores the overlay’s negative correlation. It would be correct only if all correlations were +1, when individual and component VaRs coincide.

b.reason: **Sign error.** +2.9% uses $|\rho_{3}|$. It would be correct if the overlay were positively correlated with the portfolio ($\rho_{3} = +$0.233).

c.reason: It uses $\text{VaR}_{\text{i}}\rho_{\text{i}}$ divided by the diversified VaR and reads the negative sign as GARP does: “components with a negative sign act as a hedge”.

d.reason: **Wrong input twin.** −0.7329/34.368 = −2.1% divides by the undiversified VaR. Component VaRs sum to the diversified VaR, so that is the denominator. D would be correct only if diversified and undiversified VaR were equal.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-5 a Q11
questions.question:
A bank regulator reviewing a firm’s internal risk-decomposition framework reads four statements about component VaR in a delta-normal setting.

I. The component VaRs of all positions add up exactly to the diversified portfolio VaR, because the weighted sum of the betas, $\sum_{\text{i}} \text{w}_{\text{i}} \beta_{\text{i}}$, equals one.

II. A position’s component VaR equals its individual VaR multiplied by its correlation with the portfolio, so its absolute value cannot exceed its individual VaR.

III. Component VaR approximates the change in VaR from deleting a position most closely in portfolios made up of a few large positions.

IV. Expressing each position’s individual VaR as a share of the undiversified VaR gives the same percent contributions as component VaR, even when correlations are below one.

Which of these statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I, II and III only
II and IV only
I and II only

questions.solution:
Regulator review: four statements about component VaR.

**Concept and theory**

Three properties of component VaR matter here.

1. Additivity. $\sum_{\text{i}} \text{CVaR}_{\text{i}} = \text{VaR} \sum_{\text{i}} \text{w}_{\text{i}} \beta_{\text{i}} =$ VaR, because $\sum_{\text{i}} \text{w}_{\text{i}} \beta_{\text{i}}$ is the beta of the portfolio with itself, which is one (Equation 5.28).
2. Bound. $\text{CVaR}_{\text{i}} = \text{VaR}_{\text{i}}\rho_{\text{i}}$ (Equation 5.29) and $|\rho_{\text{i}}| \le$ 1, so $|\text{CVaR}_{\text{i}}| \le\text{VaR}_{\text{i}}$; Schweser: component VaR “will generally be less than” stand-alone VaR because of diversification.
3. Approximation quality. As an estimate of the deletion effect, the linear approximation “improves when the VaR components are small. Hence this decomposition is more useful with large portfolios, which tend to have many small positions.”

**Applying it to this question**

I is property 1, true. II is property 2, true. III reverses property 3, false. IV is the naive individual-VaR decomposition that GARP calls “not useful”, false whenever correlations are below one.

**Fragile fact.** Additivity is exact; the deletion interpretation is approximate and best for many small positions.

**Reference**

LO 87.a. GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2 VaR Tools, Component VaR (Equations 5.27 to 5.30, box, footnote on $\sum\text{w}_{\text{i}} \beta_{\text{i}} =$ 1, comment on the two-asset approximation). Schweser Module 87.1, Component VaR. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 a, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: **Rejects II: a true bound treated as false.** II follows directly from Equation 5.29 with $|\rho_{\text{i}}| \le$ 1; rejecting it implies a component could carry more risk than the position has on its own. A would be correct if statement II had instead claimed that a component VaR can never be negative (false: a hedge has a negative component).

b.reason: **Accepts III: polarity flip.** GARP says the approximation is better with many small positions and worse with a few large ones (its own two-asset example is “not as good”). III would be true with “few large” replaced by “many small”.

c.reason: **Rejects I, accepts IV: sibling swap.** IV substitutes individual VaR shares for component VaR shares. With correlations below one they differ (compare Q10: 9.2% against −2.9%). IV would be true only if all correlations were +1; rejecting I denies the defining additive property.

d.reason: Only statements I and II are correct.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a UK multi-strategy fund cannot treat portfolio returns as elliptical because the desks hold large option positions. She runs a historical simulation with 200 daily scenarios and takes the 95% VaR as the 10th-worst portfolio P&L, a loss of GBP 4.80 million. To estimate component VaRs she averages each desk’s P&L over a window running from the 8th-worst to the 12th-worst portfolio outcome. The desks’ capital allocations are 50% (A), 30% (B) and 20% (C).

| Rank (worst first) | Portfolio P&L | Desk A | Desk B | Desk C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | −5.02 | −3.10 | −1.20 | −0.72 |
| 8 | −4.95 | −2.60 | −1.65 | −0.70 |
| 9 | −4.88 | −3.35 | −0.80 | −0.73 |
| 10 | −4.80 | −2.65 | −1.45 | −0.70 |
| 11 | −4.74 | −3.04 | −0.95 | −0.75 |
| 12 | −4.69 | −2.94 | −0.65 | −1.10 |
| 13 | −4.61 | −2.30 | −1.70 | −0.61 |

All figures in GBP million.

The component VaR of Desk B, expressed as a positive loss, is closest to:

options.text: GBP 1.45 million
GBP 1.10 million
GBP 1.39 million
GBP 0.33 million

questions.solution:
Option-heavy UK fund, 200 historical scenarios: component VaR of Desk B by averaging over the 8th to 12th worst outcomes.

**Concept and theory**

The beta-based formulas hold for normal and, more generally, elliptical distributions. When the distribution has an irregular shape, for example “owing to option positions”, GARP uses Euler’s theorem. The portfolio return is homogeneous of degree one in the positions, $\text{R}_{\text{p}} = \sum_{\text{i}}(\partial\text{R}_{\text{p}}$/$\partial\text{w}_{\text{i}}) \text{w}_{\text{i}}$ (Equation 5.32); applying this at the VaR realisation gives VaR $= \sum_{\text{i}} \Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} \text{x}_{\text{i}}$ (5.33) and

$\text{R}^{*}_{\text{p}} = \sum_{\text{i}} \text{E}(\text{R}_{\text{i}} | \text{R}_{\text{p}} = \text{R}^{*}_{\text{p}}) \text{w}_{\text{i}} ($5.34),

so each component VaR is the expected contribution of component i given that the portfolio loss equals VaR. Estimating it from the single scenario at the VaR is “less reliable because \[it is\] based on one data point only”; GARP’s remedy is “to examine a window of observations around $\text{R}^{*}_{\text{p}}$ and to average the realized values of each component over this window”.

**Applying it to this question**

Desk P&L is already in currency, so E$(\text{R}_{\text{i}} | \cdot) \text{w}_{\text{i}}$W is read directly from the Desk B column; the capital allocations are not needed.

Desk B, ranks 8 to 12 : −1.65, −0.80, −1.45, −0.95, −0.65

Sum = −5.50, Average = −5.50/5 = −1.10

$\text{CVaR}_{\text{B}} =$ 1.10 (as a positive loss)

Check: the window averages for A and C are −2.916 and −0.796; the three components sum to 4.812, the window average of the portfolio loss, close to the VaR of 4.80. Desk B accounts for about 23% of the tail loss, even though its worst day in the table (−1.70, rank 13) is not in the window.

**Fragile fact.** Condition on the portfolio’s tail rows, not the desk’s own worst rows; currency P&L already includes the weight.

**Reference**

LO 87.a. GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.5 VaR Tools for General Distributions (Equations 5.32 to 5.34 and the window-averaging remedy). Schweser Module 87.1 (Steps 1 to 4 for non-elliptical distributions, and averaging returns “slightly above and below” $\text{R}_{\text{P}}(\text{VaR})$). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 a, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** 1.45 is Desk B’s P&L in the single 10th-worst scenario, the one-data-point estimate of Equation 5.34 that GARP calls less reliable; the stem specifies the window. It would be correct if the analyst used only the scenario at the VaR.

b.reason: It conditions on the portfolio outcome (rows near the VaR) and averages Desk B’s realised P&L over the stated window, as in GARP Section 5.5.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** 1.39 is the average of Desk B’s own five worst values in the table (−1.70, −1.65, −1.45, −1.20, −0.95). Sorting the desk’s own P&L measures its stand-alone tail, not its contribution when the portfolio is at its VaR. It would be correct for a stand-alone tail measure of Desk B.

d.reason: **Unit error: weight counted twice.** 1.10 × 0.30 = 0.33 multiplies by the capital weight again, although the P&L is already in currency. It would be correct only if the table gave Desk B’s returns per unit of portfolio value rather than currency P&L.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a US university endowment is shown a chart that plots portfolio VaR (vertical axis) against the amount held in one currency position (horizontal axis), with all other positions fixed. A straight line is drawn tangent to the VaR curve at the current holding. Which of the following statements comparing the VaR measures shown on this chart is most accurate?

options.text: Marginal VaR is the slope of the tangent line at the current holding; the incremental VaR of deleting the position is measured along the curve, and component VaR, measured along the tangent line, only approximates it.
Component VaR is measured along the curve and is therefore the exact change in VaR from deleting the position, while incremental VaR is the tangent-line approximation of that change.
Marginal VaR and incremental VaR coincide at every holding size, because both are read from the same VaR curve and both measure the effect of the position on portfolio VaR.
Because component VaR is read from the tangent line rather than the curve, it can exceed the position’s individual VaR when the position is imperfectly correlated with the portfolio.

questions.solution:
Chart of portfolio VaR against one position with a tangent line: comparing marginal, incremental, component and individual VaR.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Figure 5.4 plots the two-currency portfolio’s VaR against the amount held in the euro. At the current holding of \$1 million the VaR is \$257,738.

| Measure |  | Where it sits on the chart | EUR value (Table 5.1) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Marginal VaR |  | Slope of the tangent line at the current holding | 0.1521 |
| Incremental (delete EUR) | VaR | Drop in VaR measured along the curve, from \$1 million to zero | \$92,738 |
| Component VaR |  | Drop measured along the tangent line: slope times holding | \$152,108 |
| Individual VaR |  | VaR of the EUR alone, $\alpha\sigma_{\text{i}} \text{x}_{\text{i}}$ | \$198,000 |

“The graph illustrates that the component VaR is only an approximation of the incremental VaR.” Component VaRs add up to total VaR, which gives a quick decomposition, while $\text{CVaR}_{\text{i}} = \text{VaR}_{\text{i}}\rho_{\text{i}}$ keeps each component at or below its individual VaR.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option is a claim about where a measure lives on the chart. The tangent line gives the slope (marginal VaR) and its linear extension (component VaR); the curve gives exact changes (incremental VaR). Only A places all three correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Curve: incremental VaR (exact). Tangent: marginal VaR (slope) and component VaR (slope times holding, approximate).

**Reference**

LO 87.a. GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.3 Summary, Figure 5.4 and Table 5.1; Section 5.2 Component VaR. Erratum in the GARP text: Section 5.3 gives the EUR marginal VaR as 0.0528, but Table 5.1 and Example 5.1 show 0.0528 is the CAD figure and the EUR figure is 0.1521 (\$152,108 / \$1 million); this looks like a typesetting slip, not a version difference. Schweser does not discuss the chart.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 a, where it is Q13 of 13.

a.reason: It restates GARP Section 5.3: marginal VaR is the slope of the tangent at the current value, incremental VaR is measured along the curve, and component VaR, measured along the tangent, only approximates it.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It exchanges the roles of component and incremental VaR. It would be correct with the two names swapped.

c.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** Marginal VaR is a per-unit slope and incremental VaR a finite change along a curved function; they agree (after scaling by the trade size) only for very small trades. C would be correct with “at every holding size” replaced by “approximately, for small changes”.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** Component VaR equals individual VaR times the correlation with the portfolio, so imperfect correlation makes it smaller, not larger (EUR: \$152,108 against \$198,000). D would be correct with “exceed” replaced by “fall below”.

questions.question: A risk consultant engaged by a Dutch pension fund is presenting to newly hired analysts on why the fund’s risk system reports marginal VaR alongside individual (stand-alone) VaR when portfolio managers decide which positions to change. Which of the following statements made in the presentation is most accurate?

options.text: Ranking positions by individual VaR is sufficient to decide which position to trim, since the position with the highest stand-alone volatility always contributes most to portfolio risk.
Marginal VaR requires a separate full revaluation of the portfolio for each position, so it is mainly suited to overnight analysis rather than to decisions taken during the trading day.

Because portfolios are typically traded incrementally owing to transaction costs, the decision-relevant measure is how a small change in each position alters portfolio VaR, which is what marginal VaR captures.
Marginal VaR measures the change in portfolio VaR from deleting a position in its entirety, which makes it the preferred tool for deciding whether to liquidate a holding completely.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant explains to new analysts why the risk system reports marginal VaR when managers decide which positions to change.

**Concept and theory**

A VaR number tells a manager how much the whole portfolio could lose; it does not by itself tell the manager what to do. GARP opens Section 5.2 with exactly that question: “Which position should I alter to modify my VaR most effectively?” Two facts make marginal VaR the answer.

First, individual VaRs are not sufficient. Volatility measures the uncertainty of an asset taken in isolation, but once the asset sits in a portfolio what matters is its contribution to portfolio risk, which depends on its covariance with the rest of the portfolio. Second, portfolios are traded incrementally owing to transaction costs. Managers rarely delete whole positions; they nudge them. The relevant question is therefore the slope of portfolio VaR with respect to each position:

$\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} = \frac{\partial\text{VaR}}{\partial\text{x}_{\text{i}}} = \alpha\frac{\text{cov}(\text{R}_{\text{i}}\text{, R}_{\text{p}})}{\sigma_{\text{p}}} = \frac{\text{VaR}}{\text{W}} \beta_{\text{i}}$,

where $\beta_{\text{i}} = \text{cov}(\text{R}_{\text{i}}$, $\text{R}_{\text{p}})$/$\sigma^{2}_{\text{p}}$ is the beta of position i to the portfolio (GARP Eq. 5.17 and 5.20). GARP adds that the vector $\Sigma$w needed for $\beta$ is already an intermediate step of the VaR computation, so $\beta$ and marginal VaR “can be derived easily once VaR has been calculated”.

| Measure | What it answers | Decision use |
|---|---|---|
| Individual VaR | Risk of the position alone | Not sufficient for portfolio decisions |
| Marginal VaR | Change in portfolio VaR per extra unit of the position | Ranking small changes, choosing what to cut or add |
| Incremental / component VaR | Change from a whole new trade, or from deleting a position | Larger changes (approximate for deletions) |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks why marginal VaR, not individual VaR, is reported for position-change decisions. The deciding facts are the two GARP reasons above: contribution, not isolation, matters; and trades are incremental, so the derivative is the relevant quantity. Only statement C states both correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Marginal VaR is a per-unit slope for a small change; deleting a whole position is an incremental or component VaR question.

**Reference**

LO 87.c (Schweser Reading 87, Module 87.2): “Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.”

GARP Chapter 5, Portfolio Risk: Analytical Methods, Section 5.2 VaR Tools: Marginal VaR (Eq. 5.15 to 5.20). Schweser and GARP agree; Schweser omits the transaction-cost motivation.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 c, where it is Q1 of 11.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** It promises that the highest stand-alone volatility “always” means the largest contribution. GARP says individual VaRs are not sufficient precisely because contribution depends on covariance with the portfolio; a volatile asset with low or negative correlation can contribute little. A would be correct only if all assets were perfectly correlated with the portfolio, so that $\beta_{\text{i}} \propto\sigma_{\text{i}}$.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the computational fact. Marginal VaR is a by-product of the VaR run, which is why GARP says the shortcut “allows real-time trading limits”. B would describe incremental VaR by full revaluation, which does require re-running VaR for each proposed trade.

c.reason: GARP: “portfolios typically are traded incrementally owing to transaction costs. This is the purpose of VaR tools”, and marginal VaR is “the change in portfolio VaR resulting from taking an additional dollar of exposure to a given component”. C restates this.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attributes to marginal VaR the property of incremental VaR or component VaR. GARP: component VaR “indicates how the portfolio VaR would change approximately if the component was deleted”; incremental VaR is the change from a whole new position. D would be correct if “marginal VaR” were replaced by “incremental VaR from a full revaluation”.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-5 c Q2
questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Japanese asset manager runs a JPY 50 billion multi-asset portfolio with a one-month 95% VaR of JPY 2.0 billion. She must reduce exactly one position by JPY 1 billion, with the proceeds held in riskless cash, and wants the largest reduction in portfolio VaR. The risk system reports:

| Position | Weight (%) | Annualized volatility (%) | Beta to portfolio |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | 40 | 14 | 0.80 |
| Q | 25 | 22 | 1.10 |
| R | 20 | 18 | 1.35 |
| S | 15 | 10 | 0.90 |

Which position should she reduce, and what is the approximate reduction in portfolio VaR?

options.text: Position R; portfolio VaR falls by about JPY 54 million.
Position Q; portfolio VaR falls by about JPY 44 million.
Position R; portfolio VaR falls by about JPY 540 million.
Position P; portfolio VaR falls by about JPY 32 million.

questions.solution:
JPY 50 billion portfolio, VaR JPY 2.0 billion; cut one position by JPY 1 billion using betas to the portfolio.

**Concept and theory**

Marginal VaR converts a position’s beta to the portfolio into a currency sensitivity. Because VaR $= \alpha\sigma_{\text{p}}$W and $\beta_{\text{i}} = \text{cov}(\text{R}_{\text{i}}$, $\text{R}_{\text{p}})$/$\sigma^{2}_{\text{p}}$,

$\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} = \alpha\frac{\text{cov}(\text{R}_{\text{i}}\text{, R}_{\text{p}})}{\sigma_{\text{p}}} = \alpha\sigma_{\text{p}} \beta_{\text{i}} = \frac{\text{VaR}}{\text{W}} \beta_{\text{i}}$.

$\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}}$ is unitless: JPY of VaR per JPY of position. For a small change $\Delta\text{x}_{\text{i}}$ the first-order change in VaR is $\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} \times\Delta\text{x}_{\text{i}}$. GARP’s decision rule: an investor who must reduce one position by a fixed amount “should rank all marginal VaR numbers and pick the asset with the largest ∆VaR because it will have the greatest hedging effect”. Weight, stand-alone volatility and even total contribution are not the ranking criterion.

**Applying it to this question**

Scale factor from the report:

$\frac{\text{VaR}}{\text{W}} = \frac{2.0}{50} =$ 0.040

$\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{P}} =$ 0.040 × 0.80 = 0.032 $\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{Q}} =$ 0.040 × 1.10 = 0.044

$\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{R}} =$ 0.040 × 1.35 = 0.054 $\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{S}} =$ 0.040 × 0.90 = 0.036

Largest marginal VaR: R. First-order VaR change from cutting R by JPY 1,000 million:

∆VaR ≈ −0.054 × 1,000 m = −JPY 54 million $(\text{new VaR} \approx$ JPY 1,946 million).

Check: $\sum\text{w}_{\text{i}} \beta_{\text{i}} =$ 0.32 + 0.275 + 0.27 + 0.135 = 1.000, as GARP requires. The volatility column is an irrelevant input for this decision. The cut is 2% of the portfolio, small enough for the linear approximation.

**Fragile fact.** Multiply VaR/W by beta to get marginal VaR, then by the trade size, not by the whole position.

**Reference**

LO 87.c (Schweser Reading 87, Module 87.2): “Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.”

GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2 VaR Tools: Marginal VaR (Eq. 5.17, 5.20 and the “rank all marginal VaR numbers” paragraph); Section 5.3 Summary, Table 5.1 commentary. No GARP and Schweser conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 c, where it is Q2 of 11.

a.reason: R has the highest beta, so the highest marginal VaR (0.054). Cutting it by JPY 1 billion lowers VaR by about JPY 54 million, more than any other single cut.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: stand-alone risk.** Q has the highest volatility (22%), so ranking by standalone risk picks Q: 0.044 × 1,000 = 44 million. GARP: individual risk is not sufficient; Q’s lower correlation with the portfolio gives it a lower beta than R. B would be right if betas were proportional to volatilities (all correlations to the portfolio equal).

c.reason: **Scope error: component VaR used for a partial trade.** 0.054 × 10,000 m = 540 million is R’s component VaR, the approximate VaR change from deleting the whole JPY 10 billion position. The trade is JPY 1 billion, so the effect is one tenth of that. C would be the approximate answer if the question asked about eliminating R entirely (and even then only approximately).

d.reason: **Scope error: size instead of marginal risk.** P is the largest position (40%) and in fact has the largest component VaR (0.032 × 20,000 = 640 million), but it has the lowest marginal VaR, so cutting it by JPY 1 billion saves only 0.032 × 1,000 = 32 million. Size and total contribution are not the fixed-cut criterion. D would be right only if the question asked which position carries the most total risk.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-5 c Q3
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at the asset management arm of a Brazilian bank oversees a fully invested BRL portfolio with a portfolio VaR of BRL 65.75 million. The mandate requires the portfolio to remain fully invested, so any sale must be matched by an equal purchase. The analyst may move BRL 20 million from one position to another.

| Position | Position (BRL m) | Individual VaR (BRL m) | Marginal VaR |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equities | 250 | 52.0 | 0.118 |
| Corporate bonds | 300 | 21.5 | 0.061 |
| Government bonds | 400 | 18.0 | 0.034 |
| Infrastructure | 50 | 9.4 | 0.087 |

Which switch produces the largest first-order reduction in portfolio VaR, and what is that reduction closest to?

options.text: Sell equities and buy infrastructure; portfolio VaR falls by about BRL 0.62 million.
Sell equities and hold the proceeds; portfolio VaR falls by about BRL 2.36 million.
Sell government bonds and buy equities; portfolio VaR falls by about BRL 1.68 million.
Sell equities and buy government bonds; portfolio VaR falls by about BRL 1.68 million.

questions.solution:
Fully invested BRL portfolio; move BRL 20 million between positions with given marginal VaRs.

**Concept and theory**

When the portfolio must stay fully invested, a cut is only half a trade. GARP Section 5.6: positions “should be cut first where the marginal VaR is the greatest, keeping portfolio constraints satisfied. For example, if the portfolio needs to be fully invested, some other position, with the lowest marginal VaR, should be added to make up for the first change.” Schweser 87.c states the same: lower allocations to the highest marginal VaR and, with capital constant, increase allocations to positions with lower marginal VaR.

For a switch of a from position j to position k, the first-order VaR change is the sum of the two legs:

∆VaR $\approx\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{k}}(+\text{a}) + \Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{j}}(-\text{a}) = \text{a} (\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{k}} - \Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{j}})$.

The largest reduction comes from the largest gap: sell the highest marginal VaR, buy the lowest.

**Applying it to this question**

Highest ∆VaR: equities (0.118). Lowest ∆VaR: government bonds (0.034).

∆VaR ≈ 20 × (0.034 − 0.118)

= 20 × (−0.084) = −BRL 1.68 million.

The individual VaR column and the portfolio VaR of BRL 65.75 million are irrelevant inputs. The switch is 2% of the portfolio, so the linear approximation is reasonable.

**Fragile fact.** Fully invested: the VaR change is the gap between the two marginal VaRs times the amount switched, not the sale leg alone.

**Reference**

LO 87.c (Schweser Reading 87, Module 87.2): “Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.”

GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.6 From VaR to Portfolio Management: From Risk Measurement to Risk Management. Schweser Module 87.2 (LO 87.c) states the same rule. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 c, where it is Q3 of 11.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: individual VaR for the purchase leg.** Infrastructure has the smallest individual VaR (BRL 9.4 million, a small position), so ranking by stand-alone VaR picks it as the asset to add: 20 × (0.087 − 0.118) = −0.62 million. Its marginal VaR is second highest. A would be correct if infrastructure had the lowest marginal VaR.

b.reason: **Dropped term: constraint ignored.** −0.118 × 20 = −2.36 million counts only the sale and drops the offsetting purchase that the fully invested mandate requires. B would be right if the proceeds could be held in riskless cash, as in Q2.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the direction: selling government bonds and buying equities changes VaR by 20 × (0.118 − 0.034) = +1.68 million, an increase. The magnitude is right but the sign is wrong. C would describe the trade if the goal were to raise risk.

d.reason: D sells the highest marginal VaR and buys the lowest, giving the largest first-order reduction of BRL 1.68 million while keeping the portfolio fully invested, as GARP Section 5.6 prescribes.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-5 c Q4
questions.question:
The CRO of a Singapore family office is reviewing a junior analyst’s report on an SGD 400 million fully invested portfolio. Over several rounds the analyst repeatedly cut the position with the highest marginal VaR and added to the position with the lowest marginal VaR. The final round shows:

| Position | Weight (%) | Marginal VaR | Beta | Component VaR (SGD m) | Expected excess return (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Asia equities | 52 | 0.0645 | 1.000 | 13.42 | 6.0 |
| Global bonds | 31 | 0.0645 | 1.000 | 8.00 | 4.5 |
| Hedge funds | 17 | 0.0645 | 1.000 | 4.39 | 8.0 |

Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: The portfolio now maximizes expected excess return relative to VaR, because no position offers a lower marginal VaR than any other.
The portfolio has reached its global minimum-risk allocation, and no small fully invested reallocation can lower its VaR to a first order.
VaR can still be lowered by cutting the position with the largest component VaR and adding to the position with the smallest component VaR.
The portfolio cannot be at its global minimum-risk allocation unless the component VaRs of all three positions are also equal.

questions.solution:
CRO reviews an SGD portfolio after iterative cut-highest, add-lowest reallocation; all marginal VaRs equal 0.0645.

**Concept and theory**

The cut-highest, add-lowest process of Q3 can be repeated. Each round lowers VaR as long as marginal VaRs differ. GARP Section 5.6: “This process can be repeated up to the point where the portfolio risk has reached a global minimum. At this point, all the marginal VaRs, or the portfolio betas, must be equal”:

$\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} = \frac{\text{VaR}}{\text{W}} \beta_{\text{i}} =$ constant for all i.

Intuition: if two marginal VaRs differed, moving a small amount from the higher to the lower would still reduce VaR, so the portfolio could not be at the minimum. Because $\sum_{\text{i}} \text{w}_{\text{i}} \beta_{\text{i}} =$ 1, equal betas must all equal 1. Schweser Key Concepts for LO 87.c: “Portfolio risk will be at a global minimum where all the marginal VaRs are equal.” GARP’s Table 5.4 shows the CAD/EUR example ending with both marginal VaRs at 0.0762 and both betas at 1.000.

| Portfolio | Condition at the optimum |
|---|---|
| Global minimum-risk | All $\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}}$ (equivalently all $\beta_{\text{i}}$) equal |
| Best return-to-risk (optimal) | All $\text{E}_{\text{i}}$/$\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}}$ (equivalently $\text{E}_{\text{i}}$/$\beta_{\text{i}}$) equal |

**Applying it to this question**

All three marginal VaRs are 0.0645 and all betas are 1.000. Check: VaR/W $\times\beta=$ VaR/400 × 1 = 0.0645 implies VaR = SGD 25.8 million, which equals the sum of component VaRs 13.42 + 8.00 + 4.39 = 25.81. The minimum-risk condition is met. The expected excess returns give ratios $\text{E}_{\text{i}}$/$\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}}$ of 0.93, 0.70 and 1.24, which are unequal, so the portfolio is not the return-to-risk optimum. That column is a deliberate trap.

**Fragile fact.** Equal marginal VaRs means minimum risk; equal excess return per marginal VaR means best return to risk. Do not swap them.

**Reference**

LO 87.c (Schweser Reading 87, Module 87.2): “Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.”

GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.6 From VaR to Portfolio Management: From Risk Measurement to Risk Management (Eq. 5.35, Table 5.4). Schweser Module 87.2 and Key Concepts LO 87.c. Schweser places the same equal-MVaR statement under LO 87.d’s Key Concepts as well; this paper tests only recognising and applying the stopping rule, not solving for the minimum-risk weights (LO 87.d).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 c, where it is Q4 of 11.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: minimum risk versus optimal portfolio.** Maximizing expected excess return to VaR requires equal $\text{E}_{\text{i}}$/$\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}}$ (GARP Eq. 5.38, LO 87.d/87.e), not equal $\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}}$. Here the ratios are 0.93, 0.70 and 1.24. A would be right if the table showed equal ratios of expected excess return to marginal VaR.

b.reason: Equal marginal VaRs (equal betas) is GARP’s and Schweser’s condition for the global minimum-risk portfolio. With every slope equal, any small fully invested switch a$(\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{k}} - \Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{j}})$ has a first-order effect of zero.

c.reason: **Sibling swap: component VaR as the ranking variable.** Component VaR is $\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} \times\text{x}_{\text{i}}$; it differs here only because the positions differ in size. Ranking by component VaR confuses total contribution with marginal effect. With equal marginal VaRs, switching from the largest to the smallest component has a zero first-order effect. C would be right only if marginal VaRs differed in the same order.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error: extra condition added.** The minimum requires equal marginal VaRs, not equal component VaRs. Equal component VaRs would also need equal position sizes, which is not part of GARP’s condition. D would be correct only if the positions had equal weights.

questions.loText: Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-5 c Q5
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a UK bank is reviewing a trading desk that holds long FTSE index futures and short gilt futures. The desk describes the gilt leg as a hedge. Stock and gilt returns are negatively correlated ($\rho= -$0.15). The monthly 95% VaR report shows:

| Leg | Position (GBP m) | Monthly volatility (%) | Marginal VaR (per GBP 1) |
|---|---|---|---|
| FTSE futures | 5,000 | 5.5 | 0.0818 |
| Gilt futures | −12,000 | 1.2 | −0.0111 |

Which conclusion should the auditor report?

options.text: The gilt leg is hedging the equity leg, since its marginal VaR is negative, so enlarging the short gilt position would reduce the desk’s VaR.
Buying back GBP 1,000 million of the short gilt position would increase the desk’s VaR by about GBP 11 million.
The gilt leg contributes about GBP 133 million of component VaR and adds to risk; buying back part of the short would lower the desk’s VaR.
Selling GBP 1,000 million of FTSE futures would lower the desk’s VaR by about GBP 409 million.

questions.solution:
Auditor reviews a desk long FTSE futures and short gilt futures that calls the gilt leg a hedge.

**Concept and theory**

Marginal VaR is a derivative with respect to the signed position $\text{x}_{\text{i}}$. A negative $\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}}$ means that increasing $\text{x}_{\text{i}}$ (buying) lowers VaR. Whether a leg hedges or adds risk depends on the product of the slope and the position, the component VaR:

$\text{CVaR}_{\text{i}} = \Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} \times\text{x}_{\text{i}}$, $\sum_{\text{i}} \text{CVaR}_{\text{i}} =$ VaR.

GARP: “Components with a negative sign act as a hedge against the remainder of the portfolio. In contrast, components with a positive sign increase the risk of the portfolio.” Barings is GARP’s worked case. Leeson was long Nikkei futures and short JGB futures. With negative stock-bond correlation, “a hedged position typically would be long the two assets”. The JGB marginal VaR was negative, the position was short, and the component VaR was positive: “the bond position, instead of hedging, made things even worse”.

| Sign of $\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}}$ | Sign of $\text{x}_{\text{i}}$ | Sign of $\text{CVaR}_{\text{i}}$ | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| + | long | + | adds risk; cutting lowers VaR |
| − | long | − | hedge; buying more lowers VaR |
| − | short | + | adds risk; buying back lowers VaR |

**Applying it to this question**

Component VaRs from the report (marginal VaR times signed position):

$\text{CVaR}_{\text{gilt}} = (-$0.0111) × (−12,000) = +GBP 133.2 million

$\text{CVaR}_{\text{FTSE}} =$ 0.0818 × 5,000 = GBP 409 million

VaR ≈ 409 + 133 = GBP 542 million.

Buying back GBP 1,000 million of the short is $\Delta\text{x}_{\text{gilt}} = +$1,000:

∆VaR ≈ (−0.0111) × (+1,000) = −GBP 11.1 million.

The gilt leg adds about a quarter of the desk’s VaR. It is not a hedge.

**Fragile fact.** Negative marginal VaR on a short leg means the leg adds risk: the hedge is to buy, not to sell more.

**Reference**

LO 87.c (Schweser Reading 87, Module 87.2): “Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.”

GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.4 Examples: Barings: An Example in Risks (Table 5.3); Section 5.2 Component VaR (sign interpretation, Eq. 5.27, 5.28). Schweser does not cover Barings; GARP is the content basis.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 c, where it is Q5 of 11.

a.reason: **Sign error: slope read without the position.** A negative marginal VaR means buying the asset reduces risk. It does not make a short position a hedge. Enlarging the short (∆x \< 0) gives ∆VaR ≈ (−0.0111$)(\Delta\text{x}) >$ 0, so VaR rises. A would be right if the desk were long gilts, the hedge GARP says a negative correlation calls for.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** The magnitude, 0.0111 × 1,000 = 11.1 million, is right but the direction is reversed: buying back the short is a positive ∆x times a negative slope, so VaR falls. B would be right if the gilt marginal VaR were +0.0111.

c.reason: The gilt component VaR is positive (about GBP 133 million), so the leg increases risk, and the negative slope means buying back the short lowers VaR. This is GARP’s Barings diagnosis.

d.reason: **Scope error: component VaR used for a partial trade.** GBP 409 million is the component VaR of the whole GBP 5,000 million FTSE leg. Selling GBP 1,000 million lowers VaR by about 0.0818 × 1,000 = 81.8 million. D would approximate the effect of closing the entire equity leg.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-5 c Q6
questions.question: A senior trader at a Canadian dealer bank receives a client request to sell the bank CAD 25 million of a corporate bond, which would add a CAD 25 million long position to the bank’s book. The bank’s CAD 12 billion book has a one-day 99% VaR of CAD 180 million computed this morning; a full revaluation takes 15 minutes. In the morning run, the marginal VaR of this bond’s risk factor is −0.012 per CAD of long exposure, and its stand-alone annualized volatility is 20%. Which response best describes how the trader should use this information?

options.text: Decline to quote until a full revaluation is run, because marginal VaR cannot indicate whether a proposed trade will raise or lower the bank’s VaR.
Widen the bid-offer spread to discourage the trade, because the trade would raise the bank’s VaR by about CAD 0.30 million.
Leave the quote unchanged and refer the trade to the independent risk unit, because judging whether a client trade adds risk is a task for risk managers rather than traders.
Adjust the quote to make the trade more attractive to the client, because the trade would lower the bank’s VaR by about CAD 0.30 million.

questions.solution:
Dealer-bank trader prices a client trade that adds a CAD 25 million long position with marginal VaR −0.012.

**Concept and theory**

The marginal VaR vector comes out of the morning VaR run. A full revaluation of a client’s trade takes too long to wait for: GARP’s example is 10 minutes, and “most likely, this will be too long to wait to take action”. The shortcut

∆VaR $\approx(\Delta\text{VaR})^{'}$ a

is instant, accurate when the trade is small relative to the book, and “allows real-time trading limits”. In its Conclusions, GARP describes exactly this job: “a bank trader who has to evaluate whether a proposed trade with a client will increase or decrease the risk of the existing portfolio. Marginal VaR provides useful information to control the risk profile throughout the day. If the trade is risk-decreasing, then the trader should adjust the bid-offer spread to increase the probability that the client will do the trade. On the other hand, a trade that increases risk should be discouraged.”

**Applying it to this question**

The bank’s position change is a = +25 million (it buys the bond from the client).

∆VaR ≈ (−0.012) × (+25) = −CAD 0.30 million.

The trade is risk-reducing, and at 0.2% of the CAD 12 billion book it is small enough for the linear shortcut. The 20% stand-alone volatility, the CAD 180 million VaR and the 15-minute revaluation time are not needed to make the decision.

**Fragile fact.** Sign of the trade times sign of the marginal VaR: the bank buying an asset with negative marginal VaR reduces risk, so the trader improves the price.

**Reference**

LO 87.c (Schweser Reading 87, Module 87.2): “Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.”

GARP Chapter 5, Conclusions; Section 5.2 VaR Tools: Incremental VaR (shortcut Eq. 5.22, 5.23 and real-time trading limits). Schweser does not include the trader pricing application; GARP is the basis.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 c, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** It claims marginal VaR “cannot” show the direction of a trade’s effect. GARP says the opposite: the shortcut gives the direction and approximate size instantly, which is why it supports real-time limits. Waiting for a full revaluation is the slow method GARP warns against. A would be reasonable only for a trade that is large relative to the book.

b.reason: **Sign error.** (−0.012) × (+25) is −0.30, not +0.30. B treats the bank as going short the bond, or ignores the minus sign. B would be right if the client were buying the bond from the bank (a = −25 million), making the trade risk-increasing and one to discourage.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** GARP gives the evaluation to the trader, using marginal VaR in real time. C moves that task to the risk unit. C would describe a trade that breaches a limit and needs escalation, which the stem does not describe.

d.reason: The trade lowers VaR, so GARP says the trader should adjust the bid-offer spread to raise the chance that the client deals.

questions.loText: Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-5 c Q7
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a German insurer is evaluating a proposed rebalancing of a EUR 2 billion investment portfolio. The trade buys EUR 30 million of factor A and sells EUR 20 million of factor B and EUR 10 million of factor C, leaving factor D unchanged. The risk system reports, per EUR 1 of exposure:

| Risk factor | Trade (EUR m) | Marginal VaR | Individual VaR per EUR 1 ($\alpha\sigma_{\text{i}}$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A: euro government bonds | 30 | 0.041 | 0.120 |
| B: euro IG credit | −20 | 0.067 | 0.105 |
| C: euro equities | −10 | 0.095 | 0.160 |
| D: real estate | 0 | 0.052 | 0.090 |

Using the marginal VaR shortcut, the change in portfolio VaR from the trade is closest to:

options.text: A decrease of about EUR 1.06 million.
An increase of about EUR 1.06 million.
A decrease of about EUR 2.29 million.
A decrease of about EUR 0.10 million.

questions.solution:
German insurer’s three-leg rebalancing evaluated with the marginal VaR shortcut.

**Concept and theory**

A proposed trade is a vector a of changes in exposures to the risk factors. GARP expands the new VaR around the current portfolio:

$\text{VaR}_{\text{p}}+_{\text{a}} = \text{VaR}_{\text{p}} + (\Delta\text{VaR})^{'}$ a + · · · =⇒ Incremental VaR $\approx(\Delta\text{VaR})^{'} \text{a} = \sum_{\text{i}} \Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} \text{a}_{\text{i}}$

(Eq. 5.22, 5.23). Second-order terms are ignored, which is acceptable when a is small relative to the portfolio. Sales enter with a negative sign. The slopes are marginal VaRs, not stand-alone risk per unit ($\alpha\sigma_{\text{i}}$), because each leg’s effect on portfolio risk depends on its covariance with the portfolio.

**Applying it to this question**

Signed trade vector times marginal VaRs:

$(\Delta\text{VaR})^{'} \text{a} =$ 0.041(+30) + 0.067(−20) + 0.095(−10) + 0.052(0)

= 1.23 − 1.34 − 0.95 + 0

= −1.06 EUR million.

The trade is 3% of the EUR 2 billion portfolio, so the first-order estimate is reliable. The individual-VaR column is an irrelevant input. The rebalancing lowers risk: buying the low-marginal-VaR factor and selling the two higher ones.

**Fragile fact.** Each leg carries its own sign, and the slopes are marginal VaRs: ∆VaR $\approx\sum\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} \text{a}_{\text{i}}$.

**Reference**

LO 87.c (Schweser Reading 87, Module 87.2): “Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.”

GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2 VaR Tools: Incremental VaR (Eq. 5.21 to 5.23, Figures 5.2 and 5.3). Schweser LO 87.a describes the same three-step shortcut; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 c, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: Summing marginal VaR times signed trade size gives −1.06 million: VaR falls by about EUR 1.06 million.

b.reason: **Sign error.** +1.06 reverses the sign of the net result, for example by treating sales as positive and the purchase as negative. B would be right for the reverse trade (sell A, buy B and C).

c.reason: **Dropped term.** −1.34 − 0.95 = −2.29 counts the two sales and drops the EUR 30 million purchase of A, which adds +1.23. C would be right if the sale proceeds were held in riskless cash.

d.reason: **Wrong input twin.** Using individual VaR per unit instead of marginal VaR: 0.120(30) − 0.105(20) − 0.160(10) = 3.60 − 2.10 − 1.60 = −0.10. Stand-alone risk ignores correlation with the portfolio. D would be right only if every factor were perfectly correlated with the portfolio, so that $\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} = \alpha\sigma_{\text{i}}$.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-5 c Q8
questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a Chinese asset manager is reviewing a draft investment policy that sets out how portfolio managers of a CNY 10 billion fund may use marginal VaR. Which proposed use is least appropriate?

options.text: Ranking positions by marginal VaR when choosing which single position to trim by a fixed CNY 50 million in order to lower portfolio VaR.
Treating marginal VaR times position size as a precise estimate of the VaR reduction from fully liquidating the largest holding, which is 45% of the fund.
Screening proposed trades during the day with the marginal VaR shortcut, while recomputing the full portfolio VaR at the scheduled daily run.
Adding to the position with the lowest marginal VaR when proceeds from a cut must be reinvested to keep the fund fully invested.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee member reviews proposed policy uses of marginal VaR at a CNY 10 billion fund.

**Concept and theory**

Marginal VaR is a slope: the tangent to the VaR curve at the current position. It is exact for infinitesimal changes and a good approximation for small ones. GARP Section 5.6: “Marginal VaR and component VaR are useful tools, best suited to small changes in the portfolio.” For large changes VaR moves nonlinearly, and GARP’s incremental VaR definition notes that “the amount added or subtracted can be large, in which case VaR changes in a nonlinear fashion”. Component VaR, $\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} \times\text{x}_{\text{i}}$, approximates the effect of deleting a position, but “the quality of this linear approximation improves when the VaR components are small”.

GARP’s own example shows the gap. In the CAD/EUR portfolio, deleting the EUR position (one third of the portfolio) actually lowers VaR by \$92,738, while the component VaR is \$152,108. GARP: “The approximation is not as good as before because there are only two assets in the portfolio, which individually account for a large proportion of the total VaR.”

**Applying it to this question**

A (fixed small cut), C (intraday shortcut with periodic full runs) and D (fully invested add-lowest) are all small-change uses that GARP endorses. B applies the linear tool to liquidating 45% of the fund and calls the result “precise”. That is a large, nonlinear change requiring full revaluation.

**Fragile fact.** The linear tool is only as good as the change is small: whole or large deletions need full revaluation (GARP example: \$92,738 actual versus \$152,108 component).

**Reference**

LO 87.c (Schweser Reading 87, Module 87.2): “Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.”

GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.6 From VaR to Portfolio Management: From Risk Measurement to Risk Management; Section 5.2 Component VaR and Example 5.1 (continued); Section 5.3 Summary. Schweser notes that full revaluation is more costly but more accurate (Module Quiz 87.1, tagged LO 87.a); no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 c, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: **Appropriate.** GARP: to reduce positions by a fixed amount, “rank all marginal VaR numbers and pick the asset with the largest ∆VaR”. It would become inappropriate only if the fixed amount were large relative to the positions.

b.reason: Liquidating a 45% holding is not a small change, so marginal VaR times position gives only a rough estimate that can be badly wrong. In GARP’s two-currency example the component VaR overstates the true deletion effect by about 64% (152,108 against 92,738). A full revaluation, $\text{VaR}_{\text{p}}+_{\text{a}} - \text{VaR}_{\text{p}}$, is needed.

c.reason: **Appropriate.** GARP: the shortcut is “much faster to implement” because ∆VaR is a by-product of the VaR run, and it “allows real-time trading limits”. Periodic full revaluation keeps the slopes current. It would be inappropriate if the shortcut replaced full VaR runs permanently while the book changed a lot.

d.reason: **Appropriate.** GARP: if the portfolio must be fully invested, “some other position, with the lowest marginal VaR, should be added”. It would be inappropriate if the reinvestment went to the highest marginal VaR.

questions.loText: Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-5 c Q9
questions.question:
A risk analyst at a US public pension fund reviews the VaR report for a USD 1 billion multi-asset mandate. The investment committee asks which single sleeve to cut by USD 10 million, into riskless cash, to achieve the largest VaR reduction.

| Sleeve | Position (USD m) | Marginal VaR | Component VaR (USD m) | Contribution (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| US large cap | 450 | 0.060 | 27.00 | 51.1 |
| Japan equity | 150 | 0.075 | 11.25 | 21.3 |
| Emerging markets | 100 | 0.110 | 11.00 | 20.8 |
| Global bonds | 300 | 0.012 | 3.60 | 6.8 |
| Total | 1,000 |  | 52.85 | 100.0 |

Which recommendation is most appropriate?

options.text: Cut US large cap; portfolio VaR becomes about USD 52.25 million.
Cut emerging markets; portfolio VaR becomes about USD 41.85 million.
Cut global bonds; portfolio VaR becomes about USD 52.73 million.
Cut emerging markets; portfolio VaR becomes about USD 51.75 million.

questions.solution:
USD 1 billion mandate; committee asks which sleeve to cut by USD 10 million for the largest VaR reduction.

**Concept and theory**

A VaR report gives two different kinds of information. Component VaR and percentage contribution, $\text{CVaR}_{\text{i}}$/VaR $= \text{w}_{\text{i}} \beta_{\text{i}}$, show where the risk is now. They are useful for drill-down, and GARP notes that the largest contributors need not be the largest positions. Marginal VaR shows how fast VaR changes per unit of each position, and it is what decides a fixed-size cut. GARP on Table 5.1: “the marginal VaR column can be used to determine how to reduce risk. Since the marginal VaR for the EUR is three times as large as that for the CAD, cutting the position in the EUR will be much more effective than cutting the CAD position by the same amount.”

**Applying it to this question**

For a USD 10 million cut into cash, ∆VaR $\approx-\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} \times$ 10:

| Sleeve | $\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}}$ | VaR reduction (USD m) | New VaR (USD m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| US large cap | 0.060 | 0.60 | 52.25 |
| Japan equity | 0.075 | 0.75 | 52.10 |
| Emerging markets | 0.110 | 1.10 | 51.75 |
| Global bonds | 0.012 | 0.12 | 52.73 |

Emerging markets gives the largest reduction, even though it has the third-largest contribution.

**Fragile fact.** Biggest contributor is not the same as best cut: rank by marginal VaR, not by percentage contribution.

**Reference**

LO 87.c (Schweser Reading 87, Module 87.2): “Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.”

GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.3 Summary (Table 5.1 commentary); Section 5.4 Examples: A Global Portfolio Equity Report; Section 5.2 VaR Tools: Marginal VaR. No conflict with Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 c, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: contribution instead of marginal VaR.** US large cap has the largest component VaR (51.1%) because it is the largest sleeve, but its marginal VaR is only 0.060: 52.85 − 0.60 = 52.25. A answers a different question, which sleeve carries the most risk today, not which fixed cut lowers VaR most.

b.reason: **Scope error: deletes the whole component.** 52.85 − 11.00 = 41.85 subtracts the entire emerging-market component VaR, as if the whole USD 100 million sleeve were sold (and even that would be only an approximation). The trade is USD 10 million. B would be the component-VaR estimate of closing the sleeve.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** Global bonds has the lowest marginal VaR. That is the sleeve to add to in a fully invested switch, not the one to cut: 52.85 − 0.12 = 52.73, the smallest reduction. C would be right if the goal were to keep VaR as unchanged as possible.

d.reason: Emerging markets has the highest marginal VaR (0.110). Cutting it by USD 10 million lowers VaR by about USD 1.10 million to about USD 51.75 million.

questions.loText: Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-5 c Q10
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at an Australian family office reviews a fully invested AUD 9 million portfolio of two assets. Returns are normal and VaR uses $\alpha=$ 1.65. The manager wants to lower VaR by shifting a small amount between the assets.

| Asset | Position (AUD m) | Volatility (%) | Expected return (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | 8 | 10 | 7 |
| Y | 1 | 16 | 9 |

The correlation between X and Y is 0.20. Which recommendation, with its supporting reason, is correct?

options.text: Shift from Y to X, because Y’s marginal VaR is about 0.264 against about 0.165 for X.
Make no change, because portfolio VaR (about AUD 1.40 million) is already below undiversified VaR (about AUD 1.58 million).
Shift from X to Y, because X’s marginal VaR is about 0.162 against about 0.100 for Y.
Shift from Y to X, because X’s marginal VaR is about 0.162 against about 0.100 for Y.

questions.solution:
Two-asset AUD portfolio (X: AUD 8m at 10%, Y: AUD 1m at 16%, $\rho=$ 0.20); which way to shift to lower VaR.

**Concept and theory**

With dollar positions x and covariance matrix $\Sigma$, the dollar variance is $\sigma^{2}_{\text{p}}\text{W}^{2} = \text{x}^{'}\Sigma$x (GARP Eq. 5.6). Each element of $\Sigma$x is the covariance of a position with the portfolio in dollar terms, so

$\Delta\text{VaR} = \alpha\frac{\Sigma\text{x}}{\sqrt{\text{x}^{'}\Sigma\text{x}}}$ .

This is GARP’s Example 5.1 calculation, $\Delta\text{VaR} =$ 1.65 × \[0.0050, 0.0144\]/0.156. A large, low-volatility position can have a higher marginal VaR than a small, high-volatility one, because it dominates the portfolio and so co-moves strongly with it. In a fully invested portfolio, VaR falls by moving from the higher marginal VaR to the lower one (GARP Section 5.6).

**Applying it to this question**

Covariance, dollar variance and marginal VaRs:

$\sigma_{\text{XY}} =$ 0.20 × 0.10 × 0.16 = 0.0032

$\Sigma$ 0.01 × 8 + 0.0032 × 1 0.0832

x $= \left[ \right] = \left[ \right]$

0.0032 × 8 + 0.0256 × 1 0.0512

$\text{x}^{'}\Sigma\text{x} =$ 8(0.0832) + 1(0.0512) = 0.7168, $\sqrt{0.7168} =$ 0.8466

$\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{X}} =$ 1.65 × 0.0832/0.8466 = 0.162

$\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{Y}} =$ 1.65 × 0.0512/0.8466 = 0.100

VaR = 1.65 × 0.8466 = AUD 1.397 million.

Since $\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{X}} > \Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{Y}}$, shift from X to Y. Check by full revaluation: moving AUD 0.1 million from X to Y gives VaR of AUD 1.391 million, a fall of about AUD 6,000, close to 0.1 × (0.100 − 0.162) = −0.0062. The risk minimum lies at about AUD 6.9 million in X, so X is overweight from a risk standpoint. Expected returns are irrelevant to a VaR-reduction decision.

**Fragile fact.** Marginal VaR depends on position size and covariance with the portfolio: the low-volatility asset can be the one to cut.

**Reference**

LO 87.c (Schweser Reading 87, Module 87.2): “Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.”

GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2 VaR Tools: Marginal VaR (Eq. 5.17) and Example 5.1 (continued); Section 5.6 From Risk Measurement to Risk Management. Schweser Module 87.2 worked example (\$4m/\$2m moved to \$5m/\$1m, VaR from \$608,490 to \$546,247) applies the same rule; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 c, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: **Wrong input twin: individual VaR per unit used as marginal VaR.** 1.65 × 0.16 = 0.264 and 1.65 × 0.10 = 0.165 are stand-alone VaRs per dollar, $\alpha\sigma_{\text{i}}$, which ignore covariance with the portfolio. They reverse the ranking. A would be right only if both assets were perfectly correlated with the portfolio.

b.reason: **Condition error.** Diversified VaR (1.397) below undiversified VaR (1.65(0.8 + 0.16) = 1.584) only shows a diversification benefit. The minimum requires equal marginal VaRs, and 0.162 is not 0.100. B would be right if the marginal VaRs were equal.

c.reason: X’s marginal VaR (0.162) exceeds Y’s (0.100), so moving funds from X to Y lowers VaR to a first order, even though Y is the more volatile asset.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** The marginal VaRs are right but the action is reversed: moving from Y to X adds to the higher marginal VaR and raises VaR. D would be right if the goal were to increase risk, or if the marginal VaRs were the other way round.

questions.loText: Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-5 c Q11
questions.question:
The treasurer of a Swiss foundation’s CHF 800 million endowment will add CHF 5 million to exactly one of four assets not currently held, and wants the smallest increase in the portfolio’s annual 99% VaR ($\alpha=$ 2.33), currently CHF 150 million. All four candidates have the same expected return.

| Candidate | Annual volatility (%) | Correlation with current portfolio |
|---|---|---|
| K | 10 | 0.20 |
| L | 16 | 0.45 |
| M | 40 | 0.08 |
| N | 5 | 0.85 |

Which candidate should the treasurer choose, and what is the approximate increase in VaR?

options.text: Candidate K; VaR rises by about CHF 0.23 million.
Candidate N; VaR rises by about CHF 0.50 million.
Candidate M; VaR rises by about CHF 0.37 million.
Candidate K; VaR rises by about CHF 0.17 million.

questions.solution:
Swiss endowment adds CHF 5 million to one of four new assets; smallest increase in 99% VaR.

**Concept and theory**

For an asset not yet held, the marginal VaR at zero position is still $\alpha\text{cov}(\text{R}_{\text{i}}$, $\text{R}_{\text{p}})$/$\sigma_{\text{p}}$. Writing cov$(\text{R}_{\text{i}}$, $\text{R}_{\text{p}}) = \rho_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{p}}$, or equivalently $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{p}}$ (GARP, Component VaR discussion before Eq. 5.29):

$\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} = \alpha\frac{\rho_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{p}}}{\sigma_{\text{p}}} = \alpha\rho_{\text{i}} \sigma_{\text{i}}$, ∆VaR $\approx\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} \times$ a.

With equal expected returns, the best addition is the one with the lowest marginal VaR, which is the lowest product $\rho_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$. Neither volatility alone nor correlation alone is the right ranking. GARP Eq. 5.29 makes the same point for component VaR: individual VaR times correlation gives the contribution.

**Applying it to this question**

| Candidate | $\rho_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$ | $\Delta\text{VaR}_{\text{i}} =$ 2.33$\rho_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$ | ∆VaR for CHF 5m (CHF m) |
|---|---|---|---|
| K | 0.0200 | 0.0466 | 0.233 |
| L | 0.0720 | 0.1678 | 0.839 |
| M | 0.0320 | 0.0746 | 0.373 |
| N | 0.0425 | 0.0990 | 0.495 |

K has the lowest marginal VaR. Its addition raises VaR by about CHF 0.23 million. The CHF 150 million VaR and CHF 800 million value give $\sigma_{\text{p}} =$ 150/(2.33 × 800) = 8.05%, which is not needed because $\sigma_{\text{p}}$ cancels. The CHF 5 million addition is 0.6% of the portfolio, so the linear approximation holds.

**Fragile fact.** Marginal VaR of an addition is $\alpha\rho_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$: rank by the product, not by volatility or correlation alone, and use the stated confidence level.

**Reference**

LO 87.c (Schweser Reading 87, Module 87.2): “Apply the concept of marginal VaR in making portfolio management decisions.”

GARP Chapter 5, Section 5.2 VaR Tools: Marginal VaR (Eq. 5.17, 5.18, 5.20) and Component VaR (Eq. 5.29, $\beta_{\text{i}} = \rho_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$/$\sigma_{\text{p}}$). Schweser gives the same beta identity (“$\beta_{\text{i}} = (\rho_{\text{i}} \times\sigma_{\text{i}})$/$\sigma_{\text{P}}$”); no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-5 c, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: K has the smallest $\rho_{\text{i}}\sigma_{\text{i}}$ (0.020), hence the lowest marginal VaR (0.0466). 0.0466 × 5 = 0.233: about CHF 0.23 million.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: stand-alone volatility.** N has the lowest volatility (5%), but its high correlation (0.85) gives $\rho\sigma=$ 0.0425 and $\Delta\text{VaR} =$ 2.33 × 0.0425 × 5 = 0.50 million. B would be right if all candidates had the same correlation with the portfolio.

c.reason: **Correlation misuse: correlation alone.** M has the lowest correlation (0.08), but its 40% volatility gives $\rho\sigma=$ 0.032 and $\Delta\text{VaR} =$ 2.33 × 0.032 × 5 = 0.37 million. C would be right if all candidates had the same volatility.

d.reason: **Wrong percentile.** 1.65 × 0.020 × 5 = 0.165 ≈ 0.17 uses the 95% deviate instead of the 99% deviate (2.33) stated in the stem. The asset is right but the number is wrong. D would be right for a 95% VaR.
