questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a US online wealth platform handles a complaint. The platform shows each client a “personal return” (the dollar-weighted return of the client’s own account) next to the “fund return” (the fund’s time-weighted return). One client’s personal return over the year is 3.1%, while the fund return is 7.4%. She made one large deposit during the year and alleges misreporting. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: The platform should replace the fund return with the dollar-weighted return of all clients, because the time-weighted return is always the higher of the two when returns vary.
Her large deposit came before the weaker part of the year; her personal return reflects that timing, which she controls, while the fund return measures the manager.
Her personal return is lower because the dollar-weighted return excludes the dividends that the fund reinvested, whereas the fund return includes them.
Her large deposit came before the strongest part of the year; the dollar-weighted return penalises money that arrives before a strong period.

questions.solution:
Q12: US wealth platform; client’s personal (dollar-weighted) return below the fund’s time-weighted return.

**Concept and theory**

The two numbers answer different questions. The fund’s time-weighted return measures the manager’s ability to select investments and is unaffected by any client’s flow timing. The client’s dollar-weighted return measures how her own money grew, so it reflects her timing; Schweser notes that the dollar-weighted return may be more appropriate when the investor controls the flows, and that contributions just before relatively poor performance depress it.

**Applying it to this question**

Her DWR (3.1%) is below the fund’s TWR (7.4%), so by GARP’s rule her large deposit was invested during the weaker part of the year. There is no misreporting; each figure is the appropriate measure for its purpose.

**Fragile fact.** DWR below TWR: the investor’s money was concentrated in the weaker period. The TWR is not always higher.

**Reference**

LO 89.a (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.1, “Time-Weighted and Dollar-Weighted Returns”): “Differentiate between the time-weighted and dollar-weighted returns of a portfolio and describe their appropriate uses.” Schweser 89.a; GARP Chapter 8, 8.1, Time-Weighted Returns versus Dollar-Weighted Returns, and Problem 10. GARP and Schweser agree.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 a, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** The TWR is not always the higher measure: here it is higher, but in Q7 and Q11 the DWR is higher, and GARP’s own example gives the reverse ordering only because of which year held more money. GARP Problem 10 offers “when the rate of return varies, the time-weighted return is higher” as a candidate reason; the reason that holds is that the TWR is unaffected by the timing of contributions and withdrawals. A would be correct only if every client had made a single deposit at the start of the year, in which case each DWR would equal the TWR and a restatement would change nothing.

b.reason: It gives the correct direction (deposit before the weaker part) and the correct use of each measure.

c.reason: **Scope error.** Both measures include income: dividends are cash flows in the IRR and part of each HPR. Correct only if the platform’s personal return were a price-only figure.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** Money arriving before a strong period raises the DWR above the TWR; her DWR is lower. Correct only if her personal return had been above 7.4%.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 b Q1
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Swiss private bank is presenting the Sharpe ratio to newly hired analysts, in the context of clients who place their entire risky wealth in a single actively managed CHF portfolio. Which of the following statements in the presentation is most accurate?

options.text: The Sharpe ratio divides the portfolio’s average excess return by its beta, so it measures the reward earned per unit of the systematic risk borne by the client.
The Sharpe ratio is the relevant measure when the portfolio is one of many subportfolios combined into a larger fund, because each subportfolio’s nonsystematic risk is then retained in full.

Because a client can always choose a passive indexed equity fund instead, an active portfolio held as the entire risky portfolio must offer a higher Sharpe ratio than the market index to be an acceptable candidate.
Moving part of the portfolio into T-bills raises its Sharpe ratio, because mixing with the risk-free asset lowers volatility by proportionally more than it lowers excess return.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst at a Swiss private bank presents the Sharpe ratio for clients holding one active portfolio as their entire risky wealth.

**Concept and theory**

The Sharpe ratio is the oldest reward-to-volatility measure. GARP defines it as

$\text{S}_{\text{P}} = \frac{\bar{r}_{\text{P}} - \bar{r}_{\text{f}}}{\sigma_{\text{P}}}$ ,

where $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{P}}$ is the average portfolio return over the sample, $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}}$ the average risk-free rate (a sample average because the rate may move), and $\sigma_{\text{P}}$ the standard deviation of portfolio returns over the same period. The numerator is the reward for bearing risk; the denominator is total risk, systematic plus nonsystematic.

Why total risk? GARP’s section “The Sharpe Ratio for Overall Portfolios” starts from mean-variance utility U $= \text{E}(\text{r}_{\text{P}}) - \frac{1}{2}$ A$\sigma^{2}_{\text{P}}$. An investor with such preferences wants the risky portfolio with the highest possible Sharpe ratio, because the Sharpe ratio is the slope of the capital allocation line (CAL): the increase in expected return per unit of extra volatility as the investor mixes the risky portfolio with bills. When the portfolio is the investor’s whole risky position, nothing else diversifies its idiosyncratic risk, so all of its volatility matters.

The benchmark follows directly: the investor can always buy an indexed equity fund, whose Sharpe ratio is the market’s. An active portfolio therefore has to beat the market’s Sharpe ratio to deserve a place as the optimal risky portfolio.

| Measure | Risk in denominator | Most relevant when |
|---|---|---|
| Sharpe | Total SD $\sigma_{\text{P}}$ | Portfolio is the entire risky fund |
| Treynor | Beta $\beta_{\text{P}}$ | Portfolio is one of many subportfolios |
| Information ratio | Residual SD $\sigma(\text{e}_{\text{P}})$ | Active portfolio mixed with a passive index |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem fixes the role: the client puts the entire risky wealth into one portfolio. The deciding fact is that the hurdle for such a portfolio is the market index’s Sharpe ratio, because the passive index fund is always available. Only C states that.

**Fragile fact.** Sharpe uses total risk and its hurdle is the market index’s Sharpe ratio, not zero.

**Reference**

LO 89.b (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.2): “Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.”

GARP Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.1: Risk-Adjusted Performance Measures (item 1, Sharpe ratio) and The Sharpe Ratio for Overall Portfolios. Schweser (Sharpe Ratio) agrees on definition; it does not state the market-Sharpe hurdle explicitly.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 b, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Dividing excess return by beta is Treynor’s measure, which uses systematic risk. Sharpe divides by total standard deviation. A would be correct if “Sharpe ratio” were replaced by “Treynor measure”.

b.reason: **Sibling swap of circumstance, with a polarity flip in the reason.** When a portfolio is one of many subportfolios, GARP says the nonsystematic risk of each “will be largely diversified away, so only systematic risk is relevant”, which makes Treynor the right measure. B attaches Treynor’s circumstance to Sharpe and reverses what happens to nonsystematic risk. B would be correct for a portfolio held on its own, not as one of many.

c.reason: GARP: the benchmark for acceptable performance “is the Sharpe ratio of the market index because the investor can easily opt for a passive strategy by investing in an indexed equity mutual fund. The actively managed portfolio therefore must offer a higher Sharpe ratio than the market index if it is to be an acceptable candidate for the investor’s optimal risky portfolio.”

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** Mixing a risky portfolio with bills moves the investor along the same CAL, whose slope is the Sharpe ratio. Excess return and standard deviation both scale by the same fraction y, so the Sharpe ratio is unchanged, not higher. D would be correct only if the claim were “leaves its Sharpe ratio unchanged”.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 b Q2
questions.question:
The CIO of a Canadian public pension plan must choose a performance measure for each of three decisions:

I. Selecting one balanced fund that will hold the entire risky allocation of a small supplementary plan.

II. Ranking twelve external equity managers, each of which will run one sleeve of the main plan’s multi-manager risky portfolio.

III. Selecting a hedge fund to add as an active position alongside the main plan’s largely passive, indexed equity core.

Which assignment of measures to decisions I, II and III, respectively, is most appropriate?

options.text: Sharpe ratio; Treynor measure; information ratio.
Treynor measure; Sharpe ratio; information ratio.
Sharpe ratio; information ratio; Treynor measure.
Sharpe ratio; Treynor measure; Jensen’s alpha.

questions.solution:
Canadian pension CIO assigns a measure to three decisions: entire risky fund, one sleeve of many, hedge fund added to indexed core.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s central message for this LO is that “the appropriate performance measure depends on the role of the portfolio to be evaluated”. Each measure uses the risk that actually matters to the investor in that role.

- **Entire investment fund.** All of the portfolio’s volatility is borne; nothing else diversifies it. Use the Sharpe ratio, ($\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{P}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} )$/$\sigma_{\text{P}}$.
- **One subportfolio of many.** When a sponsor such as CalPERS parcels assets out to many managers, each manager’s nonsystematic risk is largely diversified away across the managers, “so only systematic risk is relevant”. Use the Treynor measure, ($\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{P}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} )$/$\beta_{\text{P}}$.
- **Active portfolio optimally mixed with a passive index.** The active position earns alpha but tilts the whole portfolio away from the index, adding diversifiable risk. GARP shows the improvement in the overall Sharpe ratio is determined by the active portfolio’s information ratio, $\alpha_{\text{P}}$/$\sigma(\text{e}_{\text{P}})$ (Eq. 8.2).
- **Jensen’s alpha.** GARP notes that it has “not encountered a situation in which alpha is the criterion used to choose one fund over another”; positive alpha is required for every measure to beat the index, but alpha alone is not the selection rule.

**Applying it to this question**

Decision I is an entire risky allocation: Sharpe. Decision II is one sleeve among twelve managers: Treynor. Decision III adds an active hedge fund to a largely passive indexed core, which is exactly GARP’s university-plus-hedge-fund illustration: information ratio.

**Fragile fact.** Many sleeves: Treynor. One active satellite to a passive core: information ratio. Do not swap them.

**Reference**

LO 89.b (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.2): “Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.1: The Treynor Ratio; The Information Ratio; the summary table of measures and applications; Summary item 2. Schweser lists the measures but gives less on circumstances; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 b, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: It reproduces GARP’s summary table: Sharpe “when choosing among portfolios competing for the overall risky portfolio”, Treynor “when ranking many portfolios that will be mixed to form the overall risky portfolio”, information ratio “when evaluating a portfolio to be mixed with the benchmark portfolio”.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It exchanges the Sharpe and Treynor circumstances between I and II. A standalone fund’s diversifiable risk is not washed out, so beta understates its risk; a sleeve’s diversifiable risk is washed out, so total SD overstates it. B would be correct if decision I were a sleeve and decision II a stand-alone fund.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It exchanges the Treynor and IR circumstances between II and III. The IR is for one active bet combined with a passive core; with many sleeves together forming the portfolio, residual risks diversify across sleeves and beta is what remains. C would be correct if decision II were adding a single active fund to an index fund and decision III were ranking sleeves.

d.reason: **Sibling swap: alpha as the criterion.** Alpha ignores the cost of the diversifiable risk the hedge fund adds. GARP: positive alpha is necessary but “not sufficient”; the IR scales alpha by the residual risk taken to earn it. D would be correct only if all candidates had identical residual risk, in which case IR and alpha rank them the same way.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 b Q3
questions.question:
A senior investment analyst at an Australian superannuation fund uses a fund-of-funds approach: the AUD 40 billion risky portfolio is spread across many external managers, so each manager’s nonsystematic risk is largely diversified away. She must choose one of two finalists for a new sleeve. Over the evaluation period the average risk-free rate was 4.0% and the market index returned 12.0% with a standard deviation of 18%.

| Manager | Average return (%) | Beta | Standard deviation (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kestrel | 19.2 | 1.40 | 26 |
| Lyre | 13.4 | 0.75 | 24 |

Which manager should she select, and on what basis?

options.text: Kestrel, because its Jensen’s alpha of 4.0% exceeds Lyre’s alpha of 3.4%.
Lyre, because its Treynor measure of 12.53% exceeds Kestrel’s Treynor measure of 10.86%.
Kestrel, because its Sharpe ratio of 0.58 exceeds Lyre’s Sharpe ratio of 0.39.
Lyre, because its Treynor measure of 17.87% exceeds Kestrel’s Treynor measure of 13.71%.

questions.solution:
Australian superannuation fund, fund-of-funds structure, chooses between two managers for a new sleeve.

**Concept and theory**

In a multi-manager structure each manager’s idiosyncratic risk is diversified across the other managers. What survives in the total portfolio is each sleeve’s systematic risk, so the right reward-to-risk ratio is Treynor’s:

$\text{T}_{\text{P}} = \frac{\bar{r}_{\text{P}} - \bar{r}_{\text{f}}}{\beta_{\text{P}}}$ .

GARP’s Table 8.1 makes the point that this need not agree with alpha: portfolio Q had the higher alpha (3.5% vs 3.0%), yet U was preferred because its Treynor ratio (the slope of its line in return-beta space) was steeper. A high-beta portfolio can earn a large alpha in absolute terms while offering less excess return per unit of beta. The market’s Treynor ratio is simply the market risk premium, ($\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{M}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} )$/1.

**Applying it to this question**

Treynor measures:

$\text{T}_{\text{Kestrel}} = \frac{19.2 - 4.0}{1.40} = \frac{15.2}{1.40} =$ 10.86%

$\text{T}_{\text{Lyre}} = \frac{13.4 - 4.0}{0.75} = \frac{9.4}{0.75} =$ 12.53%

$\text{T}_{\text{M}} = \frac{12.0 - 4.0}{1.00} =$ 8.00%

Alphas (for the distractor): $\alpha_{\text{K}} =$ 19.2 − \[4.0 + 1.40(8.0)\] = 4.0%, $\alpha_{\text{L}} =$ 13.4 − \[4.0 + 0.75(8.0)\] = 3.4%. The standard deviations are irrelevant to the sleeve decision. Lyre delivers more excess return per unit of beta, so it is preferred even though its alpha is lower.

**Fragile fact.** Higher alpha does not mean higher Treynor: $\text{T}_{\text{P}} - \text{T}_{\text{M}} = \alpha_{\text{P}}$/$\beta_{\text{P}}$, so a large beta dilutes alpha.

**Reference**

LO 89.b (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.2): “Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.1: The Treynor Ratio (Table 8.1, Figure 8.3). Schweser (Treynor Measure) agrees.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 b, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: alpha as the criterion.** Kestrel’s alpha is higher (4.0% vs 3.4%), but GARP’s Q versus U example shows the higher-alpha portfolio can be inferior when beta is the relevant risk, because alpha is not scaled by beta. A would be correct only if both managers had the same beta.

b.reason: The stem states that nonsystematic risk is largely diversified away across managers, which is GARP’s exact condition for the Treynor measure; Lyre’s Treynor of 12.53% beats Kestrel’s 10.86%.

c.reason: **Scope error.** The Sharpe ratios are computed correctly, 15.2/26 = 0.58 and 9.4/24 = 0.39, but total risk is the wrong denominator for a sleeve whose idiosyncratic risk washes out. C would be correct if the chosen manager were to hold the fund’s entire risky portfolio.

d.reason: **Dropped term.** The risk-free rate was not subtracted: 19.2/1.40 = 13.71 and 13.4/0.75 = 17.87. It happens to pick the same manager, but the measure is misstated. D would be correct only if the risk-free rate were zero.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 b Q4
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Singapore asset manager is reviewing the firm’s methodology note on Jensen’s alpha before it is circulated to SGD fund clients. Which of the following statements in the note is most accurate?

options.text: Jensen’s alpha is meaningful only when a portfolio’s ratio of excess return to risk is ranked against a peer group, so it cannot be interpreted for a single portfolio in isolation.
Like the Sharpe ratio, Jensen’s alpha penalizes nonsystematic risk, so a poorly diversified portfolio will show a lower alpha than an otherwise identical well-diversified portfolio.
Any positive estimated alpha identifies a superior manager, regardless of the statistical significance of the estimate or the length of the sample period.
Under the Fama-French three-factor model, alpha is the portfolio’s return left after subtracting the risk-free rate and the returns explained by its loadings on the market, SMB and HML factors.

questions.solution:
Singapore internal auditor reviews a methodology note on Jensen’s alpha.

**Concept and theory**

Jensen’s alpha is the average return earned over and above the return the CAPM requires for the portfolio’s beta:

$\alpha_{\text{P}} =$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{P}} - [\bar{\text{r}}$$_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{P}}(\bar{\text{r}}$$_{\text{M}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} )]$.

Its properties, from the two sources:

- It is a direct measure: it is a return difference in percent, so a single portfolio can be judged without ranking it against others (Schweser).
- It uses only systematic risk (beta). Like Treynor, it “gives no indication of the diversification in the portfolio” (Schweser).
- A superior manager has a statistically significant and positive alpha (Schweser); testing that significance is LO 89.d.
- When performance is evaluated against a multifactor model, alpha is the residual after all factor exposures. GARP’s footnote gives the Fama-French version: $\alpha_{\text{P}} =$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{P}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} - \beta_{\text{P}}(\bar{\text{r}}$$_{\text{M}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} ) - \text{s}_{\text{P}} \text{r}_{\text{SMB}} - \text{h}_{\text{P}} \text{r}_{\text{HML}}$, where $\text{s}_{\text{P}} \text{and h}_{\text{P}}$ are the loadings on the size (SMB) and value (HML) portfolios.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding fact is GARP’s footnote 6, the multifactor form. Statement D describes it exactly; the other three each corrupt a true property listed above.

**Fragile fact.** Alpha is blind to diversification (systematic risk only), like Treynor; Sharpe is the one that sees nonsystematic risk.

**Reference**

LO 89.b (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.2): “Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.1: Risk-Adjusted Performance Measures, item 3 (Jensen’s alpha) and footnote 6. Schweser (Jensen’s Alpha) supplies “direct measure”, “statistically significant” and “no indication of the diversification”; GARP and Schweser are consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 b, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Schweser says Jensen’s alpha “is a direct measure of performance (i.e., it yields the performance measure without being compared to other portfolios)”. A reverses this. A would describe the Sharpe or Treynor ratio, whose raw values are meaningful mainly in comparison (against the market’s ratio or peers).

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Penalizing nonsystematic risk is a Sharpe property. Alpha depends only on beta, so two portfolios with the same return and beta have the same alpha whatever their residual risk. B would be correct with “Jensen’s alpha” replaced by “the Sharpe ratio”.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops Schweser’s condition that a superior manager has a statistically significant positive alpha, and GARP’s warning that reliable measures need a long sample. C would be correct only if the alpha estimate were measured without noise.

d.reason: GARP footnote 6: “when the Fama-French 3-factor model is used, Jensen’s alpha will be $\alpha_{\text{P}} =$ $\text{r}_{\text{P}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} - \beta_{\text{P}}(\text{r}_{\text{M}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) - \text{s}_{\text{P}}\text{r}_{\text{SMB}} - \text{h}_{\text{P}}\text{r}_{\text{HML}}$”. D restates that alpha is what remains after the risk-free rate and all three factor-explained returns are removed.

questions.loText: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 b Q5
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a German insurer is evaluating an external EUR equity mandate over the past five years. She has collected the following averages:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Mandate average return (%) | 11.60 |
| Mandate beta | 1.25 |
| Mandate standard deviation (%) | 21.00 |
| Mandate residual standard deviation (%) | 9.00 |
| Market index average return (%) | 8.80 |
| Average T-bill rate (%) | 2.40 |

Which of the following is closest to the mandate’s Jensen’s alpha?
questions.solution:
German insurer’s analyst computes Jensen’s alpha for an EUR equity mandate from five-year averages.

**Concept and theory**

Alpha compares what the portfolio earned with what the CAPM says it should have earned given its systematic risk. The required return is the risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium. Total and residual standard deviations play no part, because alpha prices only beta risk.

$\alpha_{\text{P}} =$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{P}} - [\bar{\text{r}}$$_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{P}}(\bar{\text{r}}$$_{\text{M}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} )]$

**Applying it to this question**

Market risk premium = $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{M}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} =$ 8.8 − 2.4 = 6.4%

CAPM required return = 2.4 + 1.25 × 6.4 = 2.4 + 8.0 = 10.4%

$\alpha_{\text{P}} =$ 11.6 − 10.4 = 1.2%

The mandate earned 1.2 percentage points a year more than its beta of 1.25 required. The 21.0% total and 9.0% residual standard deviations are irrelevant inputs.

**Fragile fact.** Beta multiplies the market premium ($\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{M}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} )$, and $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}}$ is then added back.

**Reference**

LO 89.b (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.2): “Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.1: Risk-Adjusted Performance Measures, item 3; Concept Check 8.2 solution. Schweser (Jensen’s Alpha) agrees.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 b, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: 1.2% is the actual return minus the CAPM return for the mandate’s beta, which is GARP’s definition.

b.reason: **Dropped term.** −1.8% comes from multiplying beta by the market return rather than the market risk premium: 2.4 + 1.25 × 8.8 = 13.4, then 11.6 − 13.4 = −1.8. B would be correct only if the risk-free rate were zero inside the bracket.

c.reason: **Dropped term: beta ignored.** 2.8% is 11.6 − 8.8, the return over the market. It treats beta as 1. C would be correct for a beta of exactly 1.00.

d.reason: **Dropped term: risk-free rate omitted.** 3.6% is 11.6 − 1.25 × 6.4 = 11.6 − 8.0, forgetting to add $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}}$ back into the required return. D would be correct if the risk-free rate were zero.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a US university endowment is briefing the investment committee on how to evaluate a hedge fund that would be added to the endowment’s core holdings, which closely resemble an indexed, well-diversified equity fund. Which of the following statements in the briefing is most accurate?

options.text: The relevant ratio is the hedge fund’s excess return over the T-bill rate divided by its total standard deviation, because total volatility is what the endowment bears from the addition.
Because the hedge fund will sit alongside a diversified core, its nonsystematic risk is irrelevant to the decision, so the fund should be chosen on its Treynor measure.

The relevant ratio is the hedge fund’s alpha divided by the standard deviation of its residual returns, which quantifies the trade-off between the alpha gained and the diversifiable risk added by tilting away from the index.
A lower information ratio is preferable, because it signals that the hedge fund delivers its alpha while adding less residual risk to the endowment’s overall portfolio.

questions.solution:
US endowment analyst briefs the committee on evaluating a hedge fund added to an indexed, diversified core.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s third situation: a fund with a largely passive, well-diversified position adds an active portfolio (its example is a university adding a hedge fund to traditional core holdings). The active position offers alpha, the return above the risk premium for its systematic risk. But it tilts the total risky portfolio away from the index, which exposes the fund to risk that could in principle be diversified. GARP’s Eq. 8.2 shows that, when the active position is combined optimally with the indexed core, the improvement in the overall Sharpe ratio is determined by the information ratio

$\text{IR}_{\text{P}} = \frac{\alpha_{\text{P}}}{\sigma(\text{e}_{\text{P}})}$ ,

where $\sigma(\text{e}_{\text{P}})$ is the standard deviation of the residual (nonsystematic) returns, called “tracking error” in the industry. A higher IR means more alpha per unit of diversifiable risk added, so candidates with the best IRs are preferred.

Terminology note (GARP): some writers define the information ratio as excess return, rather than alpha, per unit of nonsystematic risk and use “appraisal ratio” for alpha over nonsystematic risk. Schweser’s main formula is benchmark-relative surplus return over its standard deviation, with alpha over unsystematic risk given as an alternative.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem describes GARP’s university-and-hedge-fund case exactly. The deciding fact is that the reward is alpha and the risk is residual standard deviation, the diversifiable risk the tilt introduces.

**Fragile fact.** In GARP the IR numerator is alpha and the denominator residual SD; check which definition a question gives.

**Reference**

LO 89.b (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.2): “Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.1: Risk-Adjusted Performance Measures (item 4) and The Information Ratio (Eq. 8.2; the equation itself is not in the text extraction and is not used numerically). Conflict: Schweser’s main definition is benchmark surplus return over its standard deviation; GARP uses alpha over residual SD and notes industry terminology varies. Resolved from GARP; looks like a presentation difference rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 b, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Excess return over total SD is the Sharpe ratio, which suits a portfolio held as the entire risky fund. Here the hedge fund is a satellite whose systematic part overlaps with the core. A would be correct if the endowment were to replace its whole core with the hedge fund.

b.reason: **Scope error.** Nonsystematic risk is precisely what the active tilt adds to an otherwise indexed portfolio, so it is not irrelevant; the Treynor case needs many sleeves whose residual risks diversify each other. B would be correct if the hedge fund were one of many active sleeves together forming the risky portfolio.

c.reason: GARP: the information ratio “divides the alpha of the portfolio by the nonsystematic risk of the portfolio” and “quantifies the trade-off between alpha and diversifiable risk”; it is the appropriate measure for the hedge fund added to an indexed position.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** Schweser: “A higher information ratio indicates better performance.” A lower IR means less alpha per unit of residual risk. D would be correct with “lower” replaced by “higher”.

questions.question:
A portfolio analyst at a Japanese life insurer has estimated the following annualized statistics for two internal JPY equity portfolios, G and H, from index-model regressions. The market index had an average excess return of 8.0% and a standard deviation of 20.0%. The information ratio is defined as alpha divided by residual standard deviation.

| Portfolio | Avg. excess return (%) | Std. deviation (%) | Beta | Residual std. dev. (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| G | 9.0 | 16.8 | 0.80 | 5.0 |
| H | 15.0 | 26.1 | 1.10 | 14.0 |

Which portfolio is preferred in each of three roles: (i) the investor’s entire risky fund, (ii) one of many sleeves of a multi-manager fund, and (iii) an active position to be optimally mixed with a passive index holding?

options.text: H in all three roles.
G in role (i), H in role (ii), and G in role (iii).
H in role (i), G in role (ii), and G in role (iii).
H in role (i), H in role (ii), and G in role (iii).

questions.solution:
Japanese insurer’s analyst chooses between portfolios G and H for three different roles using index-model statistics.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s worked example (Tables 8.2 and 8.3) shows that the same two portfolios can rank differently depending on the role: Q was preferred as the entire fund (higher Sharpe) and as a subportfolio (higher Treynor), while P was preferred as an active portfolio to be mixed with the index (higher IR). The rule is:

(i) $\text{S}_{\text{P}} = \frac{\bar{r}_{\text{P}} - \bar{r}_{\text{f}}}{\sigma_{\text{P}}}$ , (ii) $\text{T}_{\text{P}} = \frac{\bar{r}_{\text{P}} - \bar{r}_{\text{f}}}{\beta_{\text{P}}}$ , (iii) $\text{IR}_{\text{P}} = \frac{\alpha_{\text{P}}}{\sigma(\text{e}_{\text{P}})}$ , $\alpha_{\text{P}} = (\bar{\text{r}}$$_{\text{P}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} ) - \beta_{\text{P}}(\bar{\text{r}}$$_{\text{M}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} )$.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{S}_{\text{G}} =$ 9.0/16.8 = 0.536, $\text{S}_{\text{H}} =$ 15.0/26.1 = 0.575 ⇒ (i) H

$\text{T}_{\text{G}} =$ 9.0/0.80 = 11.25%, $\text{T}_{\text{H}} =$ 15.0/1.10 = 13.64% ⇒ (ii) H

$\alpha_{\text{G}} =$ 9.0 − 0.80 × 8.0 = 2.6%, $\alpha_{\text{H}} =$ 15.0 − 1.10 × 8.0 = 6.2%

$\text{IR}_{\text{G}} =$ 2.6/5.0 = 0.52, $\text{IR}_{\text{H}} =$ 6.2/14.0 = 0.44 ⇒ (iii) G

Both beat the market $\text{(S}_{\text{M}} =$ 0.40, $\text{T}_{\text{M}} =$ 8.0%). H is more aggressive, with a much larger residual risk; G is better diversified and earns more alpha per unit of residual risk.

**Fragile fact.** The better-diversified portfolio (lower residual SD) can win on IR while losing on both Sharpe and Treynor.

**Reference**

LO 89.b (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.2): “Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.1: Implementing Performance Measurement: An Example (Tables 8.2 and 8.3) and the summary table. The IR is defined in the stem as alpha over residual SD (GARP’s definition), avoiding Schweser’s benchmark-relative version.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 b, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: alpha as the criterion.** H has the higher alpha (6.2% vs 2.6%), but for role (iii) alpha must be scaled by the residual risk it costs; H’s 14% residual SD makes its IR lower. A would be correct if the two portfolios had equal residual SDs.

b.reason: **Sibling swap of circumstance in role (i).** It judges the entire-fund role by IR (G 0.52) instead of Sharpe (H 0.575). B would be correct if role (i) were an active addition to an index holding.

c.reason: **Sibling swap of circumstance in role (ii).** It judges the sleeve role by IR instead of Treynor (H 13.64% vs G 11.25%). C would be correct if role (ii) were a single active satellite rather than one of many sleeves.

d.reason: H wins on Sharpe and Treynor, G wins on the information ratio, exactly the pattern of GARP’s example, where “the appropriate way to evaluate a portfolio depends in large part on how the portfolio fits into the investor’s overall investment plan”.

questions.loText: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 b Q8
questions.question: A risk consultant reviewing a UK pension scheme’s manager report notices that one GBP equity fund ranks 2nd of 8 peer funds on the Treynor measure but 7th of 8 on the Sharpe ratio, over the same period and with the same risk-free rate. Which conclusion should the consultant draw?

options.text: The fund’s beta must have been mismeasured, because the two measures share the same numerator and therefore always rank funds identically.
The fund carries substantial unsystematic risk relative to its peers; the rank gap signals poor diversification, although it is not an absolute measure of how undiversified the fund is.
The fund is better diversified than its peers, because diversifiable risk lowers a fund’s Treynor measure while leaving its Sharpe ratio unaffected.
The rank gap arises because the Sharpe ratio subtracts the risk-free rate in its numerator while the Treynor measure subtracts the market return.

questions.solution:
UK consultant sees a fund rank 2nd on Treynor but 7th on Sharpe among eight peers.

**Concept and theory**

Sharpe and Treynor share the same numerator, average excess return over the risk-free rate. They differ only in the risk denominator: total SD for Sharpe, beta for Treynor. Total risk equals systematic plus unsystematic risk. For a well-diversified portfolio unsystematic risk is small, total and systematic risk are close, and the two measures rank portfolios almost identically. Schweser: for a less well-diversified portfolio, “the difference in rankings based on the two measures is likely due to the amount of diversification”. A fund that ranks high on Treynor but low on Sharpe has a low beta relative to its total risk, so much of its volatility is diversifiable. Schweser adds two limits: we “do not get an absolute measure of the lack of diversification”, but “the greater the difference in rankings, the less diversified the portfolio”.

**Applying it to this question**

Same period, same risk-free rate, so the numerators are comparable. The jump from 2nd (beta-based) to 7th (total-risk-based) means the fund’s total risk is large relative to its beta: substantial unsystematic risk, that is, poor diversification relative to peers.

**Fragile fact.** High Treynor rank with low Sharpe rank means less diversified, and the gap is a signal, not a measurement.

**Reference**

LO 89.b (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.2): “Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.”

Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.2, Treynor Measure section (diversification and rankings). GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.1, items 1 and 2, and the Table 8.3 discussion (P better diversified, lower residual SD) support the same logic. No conflict; the “not an absolute measure” wording is Schweser’s.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 b, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** The two measures rank identically only if every fund’s total risk is proportional to its beta, which requires equal diversification across funds. A would be correct only if all eight funds were perfectly diversified.

b.reason: B states both halves of Schweser’s point: the rank change “shows the presence of unsystematic risk”, but it is not an absolute measure of the lack of diversification.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** Diversifiable risk enters the Sharpe denominator, not Treynor’s; it lowers Sharpe and leaves Treynor untouched. Ranking better on Treynor than on Sharpe signals worse diversification. C would be correct if the ranks were reversed (2nd on Sharpe, 7th on Treynor) and the reason restated.

d.reason: **Sibling swap of the numerator.** Both measures subtract the risk-free rate; subtracting the benchmark return is the numerator of Schweser’s benchmark-based information ratio. D would be correct if it described the Sharpe ratio versus the information ratio.

questions.loText: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 b Q9
questions.question:
The CRO of a Brazilian asset manager is assessing a BRL 2 billion equity fund that a client intends to hold as the client’s entire risky portfolio. Over the evaluation period:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Fund Jensen’s alpha (%) | 1.50 |
| Fund standard deviation (%) | 24.00 |
| Correlation of fund with market | 0.70 |
| Market standard deviation (%) | 20.00 |
| Market Sharpe ratio | 0.40 |

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The fund’s Sharpe ratio exceeds the market’s by about 0.063, and its Treynor measure exceeds the market’s by about 1.79 percentage points.
The fund’s Sharpe ratio is below the market’s by about 0.120, and its Treynor measure exceeds the market’s by about 1.79 percentage points.
The fund’s Sharpe ratio is below the market’s by about 0.058, and its Treynor measure exceeds the market’s by about 1.79 percentage points.
The fund’s Sharpe ratio is below the market’s by about 0.058, and its Treynor measure is below the market’s by about 1.79 percentage points.

questions.solution:
Brazilian CRO checks whether a fund with positive alpha beats the market on Sharpe and Treynor.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s section “The Role of Alpha in Performance Measures” links every ratio to alpha. Writing excess return as $\alpha_{\text{P}} + \beta_{\text{P}}(\bar{\text{r}}$$_{\text{M}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} )$ and using $\beta_{\text{P}} = \rho\sigma_{\text{P}}$/$\sigma_{\text{M}}$:

$\text{T}_{\text{P}} = \frac{\alpha_{\text{P}}}{\beta_{\text{P}}} + \text{T}_{\text{M}}$, $\text{S}_{\text{P}} = \frac{\alpha_{\text{P}}}{\sigma_{\text{P}}} + \rho\text{S}_{\text{M}}$,

so

$\text{T}_{\text{P}} - \text{T}_{\text{M}} = \frac{\alpha_{\text{P}}}{\beta_{\text{P}}}$ , $\text{S}_{\text{P}} - \text{S}_{\text{M}} = \frac{\alpha_{\text{P}}}{\sigma_{\text{P}}} - ($1 $- \rho) \text{S}_{\text{M}}$.

Positive alpha is necessary to beat the index on every measure, which is why alpha is so widely used. But it is not sufficient for Sharpe: exploiting mispricing means departing from full diversification, and when $\rho<$ 1 the term (1 $- \rho)\text{S}_{\text{M}}$ is the cost of the extra nonsystematic risk. GARP: a fund “can achieve a positive alpha, yet, at the same time, its volatility may increase to a level at which its Sharpe ratio will actually fall”.

**Applying it to this question**

$\frac{\alpha_{\text{P}}}{\sigma_{\text{P}}} = \frac{1.50}{24.0} =$ 0.0625

(1 $- \rho)\text{S}_{\text{M}} = ($1 − 0.70) × 0.40 = 0.1200

$\text{S}_{\text{P}} - \text{S}_{\text{M}} =$ 0.0625 − 0.1200 = −0.0575

$\beta_{\text{P}} = \rho\sigma_{\text{P}}$/$\sigma_{\text{M}} =$ 0.70 × 24/20 = 0.84

$\text{T}_{\text{P}} - \text{T}_{\text{M}} = \alpha_{\text{P}}$/$\beta_{\text{P}} =$ 1.50/0.84 = 1.79 percentage points

Check directly: market excess return = 0.40 × 20 = 8.0%; fund excess return = 1.50 + 0.84 × 8.0 = 8.22%; $\text{S}_{\text{P}} =$ 8.22/24 = 0.3425 against 0.40; $\text{T}_{\text{P}} =$ 8.22/0.84 = 9.79% against 8.00%. Since the client holds the fund as the entire risky portfolio, the Sharpe comparison is the decision-relevant one, and the fund fails it despite its positive alpha. The BRL 2 billion size is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Positive alpha guarantees beating the market on Treynor, but not on Sharpe when $\rho<$ 1.

**Reference**

LO 89.b (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.2): “Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.1: The Role of Alpha in Performance Measures (table of relations to alpha). Schweser does not present this table; it states that a large share of unsystematic risk lowers Sharpe but leaves Treynor unaffected, which is consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 b, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: **Dropped term.** +0.063 is $\alpha_{\text{P}}$/$\sigma_{\text{P}}$ alone; it omits −(1 $- \rho)\text{S}_{\text{M}}$, the cost of imperfect correlation. A would be correct only if $\rho=$ 1 (a perfectly diversified fund).

b.reason: **Intermediate result.** 0.120 is (1 $- \rho)\text{S}_{\text{M}}$, one piece of the calculation, reported as the shortfall. B would be correct only if alpha were zero.

c.reason: It gives both the correct Sharpe shortfall (−0.058) and the correct Treynor excess (+1.79 points), illustrating GARP’s “necessary but not sufficient” point.

d.reason: **Sign error.** Treynor’s improvement $\alpha_{\text{P}}$/$\beta_{\text{P}}$ has the sign of alpha, so with positive alpha it must be positive. D would be correct only if alpha were −1.50%, which would also change the Sharpe figure.

questions.loText: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.

questions.question: A board member of a UK charity is reviewing a consultant’s report. Over three years, the charity’s high-yield bond manager had the 8th-best return among 80 funds in the consultant’s high-yield comparison universe, and the consultant calls this “90th percentile performance, clearly justifying the fees”. Which criticism of the consultant’s conclusion is most valid?

options.text: The universe median is not an investable strategy, so the ranking does not show whether the manager beat what a passive investor could have earned, and durations may differ across funds in the universe.
The ranking ignores investment style, because comparison universes pool all fixed-income funds together regardless of their credit quality or risk characteristics.
The 8th-best fund out of 80 is a 10th percentile manager, so the consultant has overstated the manager’s standing relative to the comparison universe.
Universe rankings are based on dollar-weighted returns, so this ranking is distorted mainly by the timing of the charity’s contributions to and withdrawals from the fund.

questions.solution:
UK charity board member reviews a consultant’s “90th percentile” universe ranking of a high-yield manager.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens “Adjusting Returns for Risk” with the simplest risk adjustment: compare a fund with other funds of similar risk. Funds are grouped into comparison universes (high-yield bonds, growth equity and so on); their (usually time-weighted) average returns are ordered and each manager gets a percentile rank. The ninth-best of 100 is the 90th percentile manager: better than 90% of competitors.

GARP names the weaknesses. (1) Within a universe, managers may concentrate on subgroups, so portfolios are not truly comparable: in equity some hold high-beta or aggressive growth stocks, in fixed income “durations can vary across managers”. Schweser: the method “will fail if risk differences remain across the funds within a given style”. (2) More fundamentally, “the benchmark performance is not an investable strategy”: the median fund cannot be known in advance, so a passive investor cannot lock in the median return. To ask whether a manager justified fees, we want comparison with what a passive investor could have earned, such as an index fund. These problems motivate the formal risk-adjusted measures.

**Applying it to this question**

8th best of 80 beats 72 of 80 funds, so the percentile label (90th) is right. The flaw is in the conclusion about fees: the ranking says nothing about beating an investable passive alternative, and high-yield managers in the universe may run different durations.

**Fragile fact.** The universe median is not investable; that is the fundamental objection, not the percentile arithmetic.

**Reference**

LO 89.b (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.2): “Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.1: Adjusting Returns for Risk (Figure 8.1). Schweser, Module 89.2, Universe Comparisons. Boundary call: Schweser places universe comparisons inside the LO 89.b/89.c section ahead of the Sharpe ratio, and GARP uses it to motivate the risk-adjusted measures, so it is treated as part of 89.b.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 b, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: It states both of GARP’s criticisms that bear on “justifying the fees”.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Comparison universes exist precisely to group funds of similar style and risk, such as high-yield bonds. B would be correct only for a ranking against all fixed-income funds pooled together.

c.reason: **Convention flip.** GARP’s convention ranks the better performers at the higher percentile: 8th of 80 beats 90% of the universe, so “90th percentile” is right. C would be correct only if the scale counted from the top.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** GARP says the universe orders “(usually time-weighted) average returns”, which remove the effect of client cash-flow timing; dollar-weighting is the LO 89.a alternative. D would be correct if the consultant had used IRRs.

questions.loText: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 b Q11
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Chinese asset manager is validating the process used to produce risk-adjusted performance reports on its CNY equity managers. Which of the following recommendations is most appropriate?

options.text: Compute each manager’s Treynor measure with the beta estimated over the five years before the evaluation period, since beta is stable and a pre-period estimate is the most reliable input.
Rely on 12 months of returns provided the period was a bull market, since the measures need only one representative market environment to be reliable.
Report one composite score for each manager, since the Sharpe, Treynor, Jensen and information ratio measures always rank managers consistently.
Estimate beta by regressing returns on market returns over the measurement period itself, and rely on results only after a long, consistent history spanning bull and bear markets.

questions.solution:
Chinese internal auditor validates the process behind risk-adjusted performance reports.

**Concept and theory**

Risk-adjusted measures are only as good as their inputs and samples. Three source points:

- **Beta for Treynor (and alpha).** Schweser’s Professor’s Note: ideally use the portfolio’s actual beta over the measurement period. Beta changes as covariance with the market varies, so a pre-measurement-period beta “may not yield reliable results”. Estimate it by regressing the portfolio’s returns on market returns over the period.
- **Sample requirements.** GARP: reliability “requires quite a long history of consistent management with a steady level of performance and a representative sample of investment environments: bull as well as bear markets”.
- **Consistency across measures.** GARP: the measures “do not necessarily provide consistent assessments of performance because the risk measures used to adjust returns differ substantially”.

**Applying it to this question**

The auditor needs the recommendation that agrees with all three points. D uses a measurement-period regression beta and requires a long, consistent, bull-and-bear history.

**Fragile fact.** Use the beta of the measurement period, estimated by regression, not a historical pre-period beta.

**Reference**

LO 89.b (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.2): “Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.1: Risk-Adjusted Performance Measures (opening paragraphs). Schweser, Module 89.2, Treynor Measure, Professor’s Note. The beta guidance is Schweser-only content (GARP’s text does not discuss it), from a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 b, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip on the beta guidance.** Schweser warns that beta is not stable and the pre-measurement-period beta may be unreliable. A would be correct only if beta were genuinely constant over time.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** GARP requires a representative sample covering bull and bear markets and a long history; 12 months of a bull market fails both. B would be correct for neither source.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** The measures adjust for different risks (total, systematic, residual) and can rank managers differently, as Concept Check 8.2 and Table 8.3 show. C would be correct only if every manager were fully diversified and the roles identical.

d.reason: It combines Schweser’s beta guidance with GARP’s reliability conditions.

questions.loText: Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 b Q12
questions.question:
A private wealth adviser in Hong Kong has a client who will place the client’s entire risky HKD portfolio in exactly one of three actively managed funds, or else in a passive market index fund. Over the evaluation period the risk-free rate was 3.0%.

| Fund | Average return (%) | Standard deviation (%) | Beta |
|---|---|---|---|
| R | 16.0 | 26.0 | 1.10 |
| S | 10.0 | 14.5 | 0.60 |
| T | 12.0 | 24.0 | 0.70 |
| Market index | 10.0 | 16.0 | 1.00 |

Which recommendation is most appropriate?

options.text: Fund T, because its Treynor measure of 12.86% is the highest of the three funds.
Fund R, because its Sharpe ratio of 0.50 is the highest of the three and exceeds the market’s 0.44.
Fund S, because its Sharpe ratio of 0.69 is the highest of the three and exceeds the market’s 0.63.
The index fund, because none of the three funds has a Sharpe ratio above the market’s 0.63.

questions.solution:
Hong Kong adviser picks one fund as a client’s entire risky portfolio, or the index fund.

**Concept and theory**

When one fund will be the client’s entire risky portfolio, total volatility is borne in full, so the Sharpe ratio is the relevant measure. GARP: the hurdle is the market index’s Sharpe ratio, since a passive index fund is always available. The decision rule is therefore: pick the fund with the highest Sharpe ratio, provided it exceeds the market’s; otherwise pick the index fund.

$\text{S}_{\text{P}} = \frac{\bar{r}_{\text{P}} - \bar{r}_{\text{f}}}{\sigma_{\text{P}}}$

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{S}_{\text{R}} = ($16.0 − 3.0)/26.0 = 0.500

$\text{S}_{\text{S}} = ($10.0 − 3.0)/14.5 = 0.483

$\text{S}_{\text{T}} = ($12.0 − 3.0)/24.0 = 0.375

$\text{S}_{\text{M}} = ($10.0 − 3.0)/16.0 = 0.4375

Fund R has the highest Sharpe ratio and beats the market’s 0.44, so R is the recommendation. Beta is irrelevant here (Treynor values for reference: R 11.82%, S 11.67%, T 12.86%, market 7.00%).

**Fragile fact.** Compare with the market’s Sharpe ratio computed the same way (with $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}}$ subtracted), not with zero or with a raw return-to-risk ratio.

**Reference**

LO 89.b (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.2): “Describe risk-adjusted performance measures, such as Sharpe’s measure, Treynor’s measure, Jensen’s measure (Jensen’s alpha), and the information ratio, and identify the circumstances under which the use of each measure is most relevant.”

GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.1: Risk-Adjusted Performance Measures (item 1) and The Sharpe Ratio for Overall Portfolios; Summary item 2(a). Schweser agrees.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 b, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** T has the highest Treynor measure, 9.0/0.70 = 12.86%, but Treynor ignores T’s large unsystematic risk (total SD 24% with beta 0.70), which the client would bear in full. A would be correct if the fund were one of many sleeves.

b.reason: R is the only fund that is both best among the funds on the measure appropriate for an entire risky portfolio and better than the passive alternative on that measure.

c.reason: **Dropped term.** Forgetting the risk-free rate gives 10.0/14.5 = 0.69 for S, 16.0/26.0 = 0.62 for R and 10.0/16.0 = 0.63 for the market; the omission favours low-volatility funds. C would be correct only if the risk-free rate were zero.

d.reason: **Dropped term in the benchmark only.** The funds’ Sharpe ratios are computed correctly but the market’s is computed without subtracting $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}}$ (10.0/16.0 = 0.63), so no fund appears to clear the hurdle. D would be correct only if the market’s true Sharpe ratio were above 0.50.

questions.loText: Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 c Q1
questions.question: The chief investment officer of a Canadian public-sector pension plan runs a fund-of-funds structure: plan assets are split across 14 external equity managers, and the combined portfolio is well diversified. She must choose between two candidate managers for one of the 14 mandates and asks her team which performance measure should drive the comparison. Which recommendation is most accurate?

options.text: Use the $\text{M}^{2}$ measure, because mixing each candidate with T-bills to the index’s standard deviation allows the candidates’ returns to be compared directly at equal total risk.
Use the Treynor measure (or equivalently $\text{T}^{2}$), because each manager’s nonsystematic risk will be largely diversified away across the plan, so beta is the relevant risk.
Use the Treynor measure, because it penalises each manager’s nonsystematic risk, which would otherwise accumulate across the 14 mandates of the plan.
Use the $\text{M}^{2}$ measure, because when many managers are combined each manager’s beta is diversified away, so standard deviation is the relevant risk.

questions.solution:
Pension CIO with 14 external managers choosing one manager for one mandate; which measure should drive the comparison.

**Concept and theory**

Every risk-adjusted measure divides (or adjusts) a reward by a risk, and the right risk depends on what risk the investor will actually bear once the portfolio is in place. GARP makes the point through two settings:

| Setting | Risk that survives | Measure |
|---|---|---|
| Portfolio is the investor’s entire risky fund | Total volatility (systematic plus nonsystematic) | Sharpe ratio, or its return-unit version $\text{M}^{2}$ |
| Portfolio is one of many subportfolios mixed together | Systematic risk only (nonsystematic risk diversifies away across managers) | Treynor measure, or its return-unit version $\text{T}^{2}$ |

The Treynor measure is $\text{T}_{\text{P}} = (\bar{\text{r}}$$_{\text{P}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{f}} )$/$\beta_{\text{P}}$: excess return per unit of beta. GARP’s example is CalPERS, which parcels assets out to many professional managers. “When employing a number of managers, the nonsystematic risk of each manager will be largely diversified away, so only systematic risk is relevant.”

**Applying it to this question**

The stem says the plan uses 14 managers and the combined portfolio is well diversified. The candidate fills one mandate, so it is a component of the full risky portfolio. Its idiosyncratic risk will be washed out by the other 13 managers; only its beta adds to plan risk. The deciding fact is therefore the role of the portfolio: a component, not the whole.

**Fragile fact.** Many managers: nonsystematic risk disappears, so beta-based Treynor or $\text{T}^{2}$. One fund that is the whole portfolio: total risk, so Sharpe or $\text{M}^{2}$.

**Reference**

LO 89.c (Schweser Reading 89): “Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.” GARP: Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.1 The Conventional Theory of Performance Evaluation, subsection The Treynor Ratio. Also the summary table of measures (Treynor: “when ranking many portfolios that will be mixed to form the overall risky portfolio”). Schweser covers $\text{M}^{2}$ but treats Treynor’s use mainly under LO 89.b; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 c, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: $^{2}$ **for Treynor).** The mechanics in A are a correct description of $\text{M}^{2}$, but $\text{M}^{2}$ is built on total volatility and suits a portfolio that is the investor’s entire risky fund. A would be correct if the stem said the chosen manager would run the whole plan.

b.reason: GARP: “The appropriate performance metric when evaluating components of the full risky portfolio is now the Treynor measure,” and “We can use either the $\text{T}^{2}$ or the Treynor measure to rank portfolios when beta is the relevant measure of risk.” B gives both the measure and the correct reason.

c.reason: **Polarity flip: “penalises” for “ignores”.** Treynor divides by beta, so it ignores nonsystematic risk, and the reason it fits here is that nonsystematic risk does not accumulate: it diversifies away. C reverses both the property and the mechanism. It would describe the Sharpe ratio (which does penalise nonsystematic risk) in a single-manager setting.

d.reason: **Polarity flip: which risk diversifies.** Combining managers diversifies away nonsystematic risk, never beta; betas add up as a weighted average. D reverses this and so reaches the wrong measure. No stem makes D right: beta is never diversified away by combining long portfolios.

questions.loText: Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 c Q2
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Singapore wealth manager is preparing a quarterly review, in SGD, of an actively managed equity fund against its market index. She has the following annual data:

|  | Fund P | Index M |
|---|---|---|
| Average return (%) | 14.6 | 10.4 |
| Standard deviation (%) | 32.0 | 20.0 |
| Beta | 1.15 | 1.00 |
| Tracking error (%) | 15.0 | 0.0 |
| T-bill rate (%) |  | 2.8 |

Using $\text{M}^{2}$ defined as the return on the risk-adjusted portfolio minus the return on the index, the $\text{M}^{2}$ of Fund P is closest to:
questions.solution:
SGD equity fund versus index; compute $\text{M}^{2}$ with beta and tracking error supplied as irrelevant inputs.

**Concept and theory**

A Sharpe ratio difference is hard to interpret. $\text{M}^{2}$ (Modigliani-squared, popularised by Leah and Franco Modigliani) turns it into a return difference. Imagine mixing the active portfolio P with T-bills (or borrowing) so that the adjusted portfolio P\* has exactly the index’s standard deviation. Two portfolios with equal volatility can be compared simply by their returns:

$\text{w}_{\text{P}} = \frac{\sigma_{\text{M}}}{\sigma_{\text{P}}}$ , $\text{r}_{\text{P}}* = \text{w}_{\text{P}} \text{r}_{\text{P}} + ($1 $- \text{w}_{\text{P}}) \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ , $\text{M}^{2} = \text{r}_{\text{P}}* - \text{r}_{\text{M}}$.

Here $\text{w}_{\text{P}}$ is the weight in P, 1 $- \text{w}_{\text{P}}$ the weight in T-bills (negative means borrowing), $\sigma$ the standard deviations, $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ the T-bill rate and $\text{r}_{\text{M}}$ the index return. Equivalently $\text{M}^{2} = \sigma_{\text{M}}(\text{S}_{\text{P}} - \text{S}_{\text{M}})$, where S is the Sharpe ratio. Only standard deviations enter; beta and tracking error play no part.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{w}_{\text{P}} =$ 20.0/32.0 = 0.625 (62.5% in P, 37.5% in T-bills)

$\text{r}_{\text{P}}* =$ 0.625(14.6%) + 0.375(2.8%) = 9.125% + 1.050% = 10.175%

$\text{M}^{2} =$ 10.175% − 10.4% = −0.225% ≈ −0.23%

Check: $\text{S}_{\text{P}} = ($14.6 − 2.8)/32 = 0.36875, $\text{S}_{\text{M}} = ($10.4 − 2.8)/20 = 0.380

$\text{M}^{2} =$ 20% × (0.36875 − 0.380) = −0.225%

Meaning: P beat the index by 4.2 points in raw terms, but at the index’s volatility it would have lagged by about 0.23 points.

**Fragile fact.** The weight is $\sigma_{\text{M}}$/$\sigma_{\text{P}}$ (index over portfolio); a portfolio more volatile than the index is diluted with bills, not levered.

**Reference**

LO 89.c (Schweser Reading 89): “Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.” GARP: Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.1 The Conventional Theory of Performance Evaluation, subsection The $\text{M}^{2}$ Measure and the Sharpe Ratio (Example 8.1). GARP’s Equation 8.1 is lost in the text extraction; it is pinned down by the worked example (26.7% − 28% = −1.3%) and the key equation $\text{M}^{2} = \sigma_{\text{M}}(\text{S}_{\text{P}} - \text{S}_{\text{M}})$. Schweser agrees $\text{(P}^{'}$ notation).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 c, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: **Dropped adjustment: raw return gap.** 14.6 − 10.4 = 4.20% compares returns at very different risk levels (32% versus 20% volatility). A would be right only if P had the index’s standard deviation.

b.reason: $^{2}$**).** Re-scaling to beta 1: 2.8 + 11.8/1.15 = 13.06%, minus 10.4 gives 2.66%. This is the $\text{T}^{2}$ measure, using the irrelevant beta. It would be correct if the stem asked for $\text{T}^{2}$.

c.reason: **Inverted weight.** Using 32/20 = 1.6: 1.6(14.6) − 0.6(2.8) = 21.68%, minus 10.4 gives 11.28%. This levers up a portfolio that is already more volatile than the index, moving away from the target. It would be the right weight only if $\sigma_{\text{P}}$ were 12.5% (so that $\sigma_{\text{M}}$/$\sigma_{\text{P}} =$ 1.6).

d.reason: GARP Example 8.1: P\* is formed by mixing P with bills so that it “has exactly the same standard deviation as the market index”, and “$\text{M}^{2}$ is the vertical distance between points M and P\*”. The calculation above gives −0.23%.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 c Q3
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a US asset manager is presenting to newly hired analysts a chart of average return (vertical axis) against standard deviation (horizontal axis). It shows the capital market line (CML) drawn from the risk-free rate through the market index M, and the capital allocation line (CAL) drawn from the risk-free rate through an active portfolio P. Portfolio P has a higher average return and a higher standard deviation than M, and its CAL is flatter than the CML. Which statement about the chart is most accurate?

options.text: The risk-adjusted portfolio P\* lies on P’s CAL at the standard deviation of M; $\text{M}^{2}$ is the vertical distance between M and P\*, and it is negative here because P\* lies below M.
The risk-adjusted portfolio is found by moving along the CML until its standard deviation equals that of P; $\text{M}^{2}$ is the vertical distance between P and that point.
Because P’s average return is higher than that of M, P\* lies above M and $\text{M}^{2}$ is positive, even though P’s CAL is flatter than the CML.
P\* is found by moving up P’s CAL, borrowing at the risk-free rate, until its standard deviation matches that of M; $\text{M}^{2}$ is the vertical distance between M and P\*.

questions.solution:
New-hire presentation of the return versus standard deviation chart; which statement about P\*, the CAL and $\text{M}^{2}$ is right.

**Concept and theory**

On a chart of average return against standard deviation, every mix of the risk-free asset and a risky portfolio lies on a straight line from $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ through that portfolio: the CAL. For the market index this line is the CML. The slope of each line is the portfolio’s Sharpe ratio. Mixing P with T-bills moves you down P’s CAL towards $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ ; borrowing to buy more P moves you up and out along it. $\text{M}^{2}$ picks the point on P’s CAL directly above or below M (same standard deviation) and measures the vertical gap.

| Feature of the chart | Meaning |
|---|---|
| CAL of P flatter than CML | $\text{S}_{\text{P}} < \text{S}_{\text{M}}$, so $\text{M}^{2} <$ 0 |
| P to the right of M ($\sigma_{\text{P}} > \sigma_{\text{M}}$) | Move down P’s CAL (add T-bills) to reach P\* |
| P to the left of M ($\sigma_{\text{P}} < \sigma_{\text{M}}$) | Move up P’s CAL (borrow) to reach P\* |
| Vertical distance M to P\* | $\text{M}^{2}$ |

**Applying it to this question**

P has higher return and higher standard deviation than M, and its CAL is flatter. To reach M’s standard deviation we move down P’s CAL, mixing in bills. Because the CAL is flatter than the CML, at the same standard deviation it sits lower than the CML, so P\* is below M and $\text{M}^{2}$ is negative.

**Fragile fact.** Direction along the CAL: P to the right of M means move down (add bills); P to the left means move up (borrow). The sign of $\text{M}^{2}$ follows the slope comparison, not the raw return.

**Reference**

LO 89.c (Schweser Reading 89): “Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.” GARP: Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.1 The Conventional Theory of Performance Evaluation, subsection The $\text{M}^{2}$ Measure and the Sharpe Ratio, Example 8.1 and Figure 8.2. Schweser Figure 89.2 shows the same CML/CAL picture $\text{(P}^{'}$ notation). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 c, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: GARP Example 8.1: “Portfolio P’s CAL is less steep than the CML, consistent with its lower Sharpe ratio. . . P\* is formed by moving down portfolio P’s capital allocation line (by mixing P with T-bills) until we reduce the standard deviation by just enough to match that of the market index. $\text{M}^{2}$ is the vertical distance between points M and P\*.” The figure caption notes that the $\text{M}^{2}$ of P is negative even though its average return was greater than that of M.

b.reason: **Role misassignment: the index is adjusted instead of P.** $\text{M}^{2}$ adjusts the active portfolio to the index’s risk, not the index to the portfolio’s risk, and the comparison point is M, not P. B would describe a different (non-GARP) construction that levers the benchmark up to P’s volatility.

c.reason: **Polarity flip on the sign, driven by raw return.** Raw return does not set the sign of $\text{M}^{2}$; the relative slopes do. A flatter CAL means lower return at every standard deviation, so P\* is below M. C would be right only if P’s CAL were steeper than the CML.

d.reason: **Condition error: borrowing used when diluting is required.** Borrowing moves up the CAL and raises volatility further. It is the right step only when $\sigma_{\text{P}} < \sigma_{\text{M}}$, the case GARP mentions in parentheses. D would be correct for a portfolio plotted to the left of M.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 c Q4
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Japanese life insurer is evaluating, in JPY terms, an equity sleeve U that is one of several sleeves making up the insurer’s diversified equity allocation. He has the following data for the year:

|  | Sleeve U Index M |
|---|---|
| Average return (%) | 9.40 8.00 |
| Beta | 0.75 1.00 |
| Standard deviation (%) | 18.00 16.00 |
| Risk-free rate (%) | 0.60 |

Defining $\text{T}^{2}$ as the return on U after it is combined with the risk-free asset to have the market’s beta, minus the market return, the $\text{T}^{2}$ measure of Sleeve U is closest to:
questions.solution:
JPY sleeve with beta 0.75; compute $\text{T}^{2}$ (leverage needed), with standard deviations supplied as irrelevant inputs.

**Concept and theory**

$\text{T}^{2}$ is the beta-based twin of $\text{M}^{2}$. Since a component portfolio’s relevant risk is beta, we adjust it to the market’s beta of 1 by mixing with T-bills, then compare returns directly:

$\text{w}_{\text{U}} = \frac{\beta_{\text{M}}}{\beta_{\text{U}}} = \frac{1}{\beta_{\text{U}}}$ , $\text{r}_{\text{U}}* = \text{w}_{\text{U}} \text{r}_{\text{U}} + ($1 $- \text{w}_{\text{U}} ) \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ , $\text{T}^{2} = \text{r}_{\text{U}}* - \text{r}_{\text{M}} = \text{T}_{\text{U}} - \text{T}_{\text{M}}$.

$\text{T}_{\text{U}} = (\text{r}_{\text{U}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )$/$\beta_{\text{U}}$ is the Treynor measure and $\text{T}_{\text{M}} = \text{r}_{\text{M}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ is the market’s. If $\beta_{\text{U}} <$ 1, $\text{w}_{\text{U}} >$ 1 and 1 $- \text{w}_{\text{U}} <$ 0: the adjusted portfolio borrows at the risk-free rate. GARP: “This measure is analogous to the $\text{M}^{2}$ measure, but it extends the Treynor rather than the Sharpe measure.”

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{w}_{\text{U}} =$ 1/0.75 = 1.3333 (133.3% in U, borrow 33.3%)

$\text{r}_{\text{U}}* =$ 1.3333(9.40%) − 0.3333(0.60%) = 12.533% − 0.200% = 12.333%

$\text{T}^{2} =$ 12.333% − 8.00% = 4.33%

Check: $\text{T}_{\text{U}} = ($9.40 − 0.60)/0.75 = 11.733%, $\text{T}_{\text{M}} =$ 8.00 − 0.60 = 7.40%, $\text{T}_{\text{U}} - \text{T}_{\text{M}} =$ 4.33%

Meaning: levered to the market’s beta, the sleeve would have beaten the index by about 4.33 points. The standard deviations play no role.

**Fragile fact.** Beta below 1: the weight in U is 1/$\beta>$ 1, and the borrowing term is subtracted ($-(\text{w} -$ 1$)\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ ).

**Reference**

LO 89.c (Schweser Reading 89): “Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.” GARP: Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.1 The Conventional Theory of Performance Evaluation, subsection The Treynor Ratio, Example 8.2 Equalizing Beta and the $\text{T}^{2}$ Measure. Schweser does not present $\text{T}^{2}$; content is from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 c, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: Jensen’s alpha, not rescaled.** 9.40 − \[0.60 + 0.75(7.40)\] = 3.25%. Alpha is measured at the sleeve’s own beta of 0.75; $\text{T}^{2}$ rescales it to beta 1, i.e. $\text{T}^{2} = \alpha$/$\beta=$ 3.25/0.75 = 4.33%. A would be correct if the question asked for Jensen’s alpha.

b.reason: $^{2}$**, using the irrelevant standard deviations).** Weight 16/18 = 0.8889: 0.8889(9.40) + 0.1111(0.60) = 8.42%, minus 8.00 gives 0.42%. This matches total risk, which is the wrong risk for a sleeve within a diversified allocation. B would be right if the question asked for $\text{M}^{2}$.

c.reason: GARP Example 8.2 (portfolio U, beta 0.8): “we will need to use leverage to increase systematic risk to match that of the market index. . . The return on the adjusted portfolio U\* is 1.25 × 17 − .25 × 6 = 19.75%, which beats the market’s return by 3.75%.” The same procedure gives 4.33% here.

d.reason: **Sign error on the borrowing term.** 1.3333(9.40) + 0.3333(0.60) = 12.73%, minus 8.00 gives 4.73%. Borrowing costs the risk-free rate, so the −0.3333 weight must subtract $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ . D would be the answer only if the extra 33.3% earned rather than cost the risk-free rate, which is impossible when the total weight in U already exceeds 100%.
