questions.loText: Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 c Q5
questions.question: A risk consultant to a Brazilian family office reports that Fund X has a Sharpe ratio of 0.62, Fund Y has 0.58 and the market index has 0.55, with an index standard deviation of 22%. The client asks whether a Sharpe ratio gap of a few hundredths is economically meaningful, so the consultant converts the figures into $\text{M}^{2}$ measures. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Fund X’s $\text{M}^{2}$ is 7.00%, the Sharpe ratio gap of 0.07 expressed in percentage points, and X ranks above Y under both measures.
Fund X’s $\text{M}^{2}$ is 1.54%, but X and Y could rank differently under $\text{M}^{2}$ than under the Sharpe ratio if their standard deviations differ.
Fund X’s $\text{M}^{2}$ is 1.54%, and $\text{M}^{2}$ is preferred to the Sharpe ratio because it adjusts for beta, which the Sharpe ratio ignores.
Fund X’s $\text{M}^{2}$ is 1.54%: scaled to the index’s volatility it would have beaten the index by 1.54 percentage points, and X and Y rank the same under $\text{M}^{2}$ and Sharpe.

questions.solution:
Sharpe ratios 0.62, 0.58 and 0.55 with index volatility 22%; convert to $\text{M}^{2}$ and interpret.

**Concept and theory**

GARP raises the problem $\text{M}^{2}$ solves: in Concept Check 8.2, $\text{S}_{\text{P}} =$ 0.69 and $\text{S}_{\text{M}} =$ 0.73, “But is a difference of .04 in the Sharpe ratio economically meaningful?” Sharpe ratios are hard to interpret. $\text{M}^{2}$ uses the same risk (total volatility) as the Sharpe ratio, “but its risk adjustment leads to an easy-to-interpret differential return relative to the benchmark index.” Since P\* lies on P’s CAL at $\sigma_{\text{M}}$, its excess return is $\text{S}_{\text{P}}\sigma_{\text{M}}$ and the market’s is $\text{S}_{\text{M}}\sigma_{\text{M}}$, so

$\text{M}^{2} = \text{r}_{\text{P}}* - \text{r}_{\text{M}} = \sigma_{\text{M}} (\text{S}_{\text{P}} - \text{S}_{\text{M}})$.

With $\sigma_{\text{M}}$ fixed for all funds, $\text{M}^{2}$ is an increasing linear function of $\text{S}_{\text{P}}$, so it always ranks funds in the same order as the Sharpe ratio. Schweser: “$\text{M}^{2}$ will produce the same conclusions as the Sharpe ratio.”

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{M}^{2}_{\text{X}} =$ 22% × (0.62 − 0.55) = 22% × 0.07 = 1.54%

$\text{M}^{2}_{\text{Y}} =$ 22% × (0.58 − 0.55) = 22% × 0.03 = 0.66%

X ranks above Y under both measures. The gap of 0.04 in Sharpe ratio is worth 22% × 0.04 = 0.88 percentage points of return at index volatility.

**Fragile fact.** $\text{M}^{2} = \sigma_{\text{M}}(\text{S}_{\text{P}} - \text{S}_{\text{M}})$: multiply by the index’s volatility, not the fund’s.

**Reference**

LO 89.c (Schweser Reading 89): “Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.” GARP: Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.1 The Conventional Theory of Performance Evaluation, subsection The $\text{M}^{2}$ Measure and the Sharpe Ratio; Key Equations. Schweser $\text{M}^{2}$ section agrees (“same conclusions as the Sharpe ratio”).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 c, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: $\sigma_{\text{M}}$ **dropped).** 0.07 read as 7% omits the multiplication by $\sigma_{\text{M}} =$ 0.22. A would be right only if the index standard deviation were 100%.

b.reason: **Absolute claim reversed: ranking can never differ.** With one benchmark, $\text{M}^{2}$ and Sharpe rankings are identical whatever the funds’ own standard deviations, because $\sigma_{\text{M}}$ is a common positive scale. B would be true of $\text{M}^{2}$ versus Treynor, not $\text{M}^{2}$ versus Sharpe.

c.reason: $^{2}$**).** $\text{M}^{2}$, like Sharpe, “focuses on total volatility as a measure of risk”. Adjusting for beta is the $\text{T}^{2}$ measure. C would be correct if it described $\text{T}^{2}$ against the Sharpe ratio.

d.reason: D gives the right number, the right interpretation (return advantage at the index’s volatility) and the correct ranking property.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 c Q6
questions.question: An internal auditor at an Australian superannuation fund is validating a chart in the manager-selection pack. It plots average return (vertical axis) against beta (horizontal axis) and shows the security market line (SML) from the risk-free rate through the market index M, plus a T-line for each of two equity sleeves, Q and U, each drawn from the risk-free rate through the sleeve’s point. Which statement in the pack is most accurate?

options.text: The slope of the SML is the market’s Sharpe ratio, and a sleeve is preferred if its T-line lies above the SML at the sleeve’s own standard deviation.
The sleeve with the steeper T-line is preferred, because for any beta it offers the higher return; its $\text{T}^{2}$ is the vertical gap at a beta of 1.0 between its T-line and M.
The sleeve whose point lies farther above the SML at its own beta is always preferred, because that vertical distance is the correct basis for ranking sleeves.
Each T-line starts at M and its slope equals the sleeve’s Jensen’s alpha, so the sleeve with the higher alpha always has the steeper T-line and is preferred.

questions.solution:
Auditor validating a return versus beta chart with the SML and T-lines for sleeves Q and U.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Figure 8.3 is the beta version of the CAL chart. Risk is measured by beta. The SML runs from the risk-free rate through M; “Its slope is the market’s Treynor ratio”. For a portfolio Q, “the line through point Q shows us all the beta-return combinations that can be achieved by mixing bills with portfolio Q. The slope of this line is portfolio Q’s Treynor ratio”: the T-line. Steeper T-line means more return per unit of beta at every beta level. The adjusted portfolio Q\* is the point on Q’s T-line at beta 1, so $\text{T}^{2} = \text{r}_{\text{Q}}* - \text{r}_{\text{M}}$ is the vertical gap at beta 1 between the T-line and M.

|  | Total-risk chart $\text{(M}^{2}$) | Beta chart $\text{(T}^{2}$) |
|---|---|---|
| Horizontal axis | Standard deviation | Beta |
| Market line | CML, slope $\text{S}_{\text{M}}$ | SML, slope $\text{T}_{\text{M}}$ |
| Portfolio line | CAL, slope $\text{S}_{\text{P}}$ | T-line, slope $\text{T}_{\text{P}}$ |
| Measure | Gap at $\sigma_{\text{M}}$ | Gap at $\beta=$ 1 |

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are what the slopes mean (Treynor ratios) and the ranking rule (steepest T-line). In GARP’s example, Q has the higher alpha (3.5% versus 3%), i.e. it lies farther above the SML at its own beta, yet U is preferred because its T-line is steeper.

**Fragile fact.** Slope of a line on the beta chart equals the Treynor ratio; height above the SML at the sleeve’s own beta equals alpha. They can rank sleeves differently.

**Reference**

LO 89.c (Schweser Reading 89): “Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.” GARP: Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.1 The Conventional Theory of Performance Evaluation, subsection The Treynor Ratio, Table 8.1 and Figure 8.3. The $\text{T}^{2}$ gap at beta 1 is read from GARP’s construction of Q\*, not stated in words. Schweser does not cover the T-line chart.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 c, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: Sharpe and standard deviation on a beta chart.** The SML slope is the market’s Treynor ratio, and standard deviation is not on this chart. A would describe the CML chart used for $\text{M}^{2}$.

b.reason: GARP: “When we measure risk using beta, that will be the portfolio with the steepest T-line, or, equivalently, the portfolio with the highest Treynor ratio. . . For any level of risk (beta), it provides the higher return.” The $\text{T}^{2}$ gap at beta 1 follows from the construction of Q\*.

c.reason: **Absolute claim: vertical distance at own beta is alpha.** The vertical distance above the SML at the portfolio’s own beta is Jensen’s alpha. GARP shows that “despite its lower alpha, portfolio U actually will be preferred to portfolio Q.” C would hold only if both sleeves had the same beta.

d.reason: **Role misassignment and sibling swap: start point and slope.** T-lines start at the risk-free rate (they are mixes of bills and the sleeve), not at M, and their slope is the Treynor ratio, not alpha. D would be correct only if all sleeves had equal betas, in which case the alpha ranking and the slope ranking coincide.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 c Q7
questions.question:
The chief risk officer of a UK multi-manager firm receives security characteristic line (SCL) regression output, in GBP terms, for three sleeves that will each form a small part of a diversified client portfolio. The market’s average excess return over the period was 6.0%.

|  | Sleeve X | Sleeve Y | Sleeve Z |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alpha (%) | 2.40 | 1.80 | 2.10 |
| Beta | 1.50 | 0.90 | 1.20 |
| Residual standard deviation (%) | 6.10 | 3.40 | 4.80 |

Which sleeve has the highest $\text{T}^{2}$ measure, and what is that $\text{T}^{2}$?

options.text: Sleeve X, 2.40%
Sleeve X, 3.60%
Sleeve Y, 2.00%
Sleeve Y, 8.00%

questions.solution:
UK multi-manager CRO with SCL alpha and beta for three sleeves; find the highest $\text{T}^{2}$.

**Concept and theory**

Jensen’s alpha is $\alpha_{\text{P}} = \text{r}_{\text{P}} - [\text{r}_{\text{f}} + \beta_{\text{P}}(\text{r}_{\text{M}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )]$. Dividing by $\beta_{\text{P}}$:

$\frac{\alpha_{\text{P}}}{\beta_{\text{P}}} = \frac{\text{r}_{\text{P}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}}}{\beta_{\text{P}}} - (\text{r}_{\text{M}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} ) = \text{T}_{\text{P}} - \text{T}_{\text{M}} = \text{T}^{2}_{\text{P}}$.

GARP’s table on the role of alpha gives this “improvement compared to market index”: $\text{T}_{\text{P}} - \text{T}_{\text{M}} =$ $\alpha_{\text{P}}$/$\beta_{\text{P}}$. So alpha is necessary for a positive $\text{T}^{2}$, but the ranking of sleeves by $\text{T}^{2}$ is by alpha per unit of beta, not by alpha. A sleeve that earns a large alpha by taking a lot of beta can rank below a smaller-alpha, lower-beta sleeve.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{T}^{2}_{\text{X}} =$ 2.40/1.50 = 1.60%

$\text{T}^{2}_{\text{Y}} =$ 1.80/0.90 = 2.00%

$\text{T}^{2}_{\text{Z}} =$ 2.10/1.20 = 1.75%

Ranking by $\text{T}^{2}$: Y, Z, X, exactly the reverse of the alpha ranking (X, Z, Y). Check with Treynor ratios: $\text{T}_{\text{Y}} = ($1.80 + 0.90 × 6)/0.90 = 8.00%, $\text{T}_{\text{M}} =$ 6.00%, so $\text{T}^{2}_{\text{Y}} =$ 2.00%. The residual standard deviations are irrelevant to $\text{T}^{2}$ (they would matter for the information ratio).

**Fragile fact.** $\text{T}^{2} = \alpha$/$\beta$: divide alpha by beta. Higher alpha does not mean higher $\text{T}^{2}$.

**Reference**

LO 89.c (Schweser Reading 89): “Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.” GARP: Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.1 The Conventional Theory of Performance Evaluation, subsection The Treynor Ratio (Table 8.1) and The Role of Alpha in Performance Measures. Conflict: Schweser states that “Jensen’s alpha will produce the same conclusions as the Treynor measure.” That is true for the sign versus the market (alpha positive exactly when $\text{T}_{\text{P}} > \text{T}_{\text{M}}$, since $\beta_{\text{P}} >$ 0) but not for rankings between portfolios with different betas, as GARP’s Q and U show. GARP is used; this looks like a Schweser simplification rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 c, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: $^{2}$**).** X has the largest alpha, 2.40%, but alpha is not scaled for beta. A would be correct if all three sleeves had a beta of 1.0, when $\text{T}^{2} = \alpha$.

b.reason: **Calculation slip: multiplied instead of divided.** 2.40 × 1.50 = 3.60% rewards beta rather than adjusting for it. No consistent definition produces this; it would match only if $\text{T}^{2}$ were defined as $\alpha\beta$.

c.reason: Sleeve Y has the highest alpha per unit of beta, hence the steepest T-line and the highest $\text{T}^{2}$ of 2.00%. This mirrors GARP Table 8.1, where Q has the higher alpha but U the higher Treynor and $\text{T}^{2}$.

d.reason: **Intermediate result: Treynor ratio, market not subtracted.** 8.00% is Y’s Treynor ratio $\text{T}_{\text{Y}}$. $\text{T}^{2}$ requires subtracting $\text{T}_{\text{M}} =$ 6.00%. D would be the answer if the question asked for the Treynor measure.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Chinese asset manager runs a low-volatility equity fund P that is sold as a stand-alone, entire-portfolio product, so the firm evaluates it on total risk. Over the year, in CNY terms, Fund P returned 7.2% with a standard deviation of 9%, the market index returned 8.5% with a standard deviation of 15%, and the risk-free rate was 2.1%. Which of the following correctly states Fund P’s $\text{M}^{2}$ and the composition of the risk-adjusted portfolio P\*?

options.text: $\text{M}^{2} = +$2.10%; P\* invests 166.7% of capital in Fund P, financed by borrowing 66.7% at the risk-free rate.
$\text{M}^{2} = -$1.30%; P\* is Fund P itself, since its return can be compared directly with the index return.
$\text{M}^{2} = +$4.90%; P\* invests 166.7% of capital in Fund P and a further 66.7% in T-bills.
$\text{M}^{2} = -$3.34%; P\* invests 60% of capital in Fund P and 40% in T-bills.

questions.solution:
CNY low-volatility fund (9% versus index 15%); compute $\text{M}^{2}$ and describe P\*.

**Concept and theory**

The $\text{M}^{2}$ recipe works in both directions. GARP: “(If the active portfolio had lower standard deviation than the index, it would be leveraged by borrowing money and investing the proceeds in the portfolio.)” With $\text{w}_{\text{P}} = \sigma_{\text{M}}$/$\sigma_{\text{P}} >$ 1, the T-bill weight 1 $- \text{w}_{\text{P}}$ is negative, meaning a loan at the risk-free rate:

$\text{r}_{\text{P}}* = \text{w}_{\text{P}} \text{r}_{\text{P}} - (\text{w}_{\text{P}} -$ 1$) \text{r}_{\text{f}}$ , $\text{M}^{2} = \text{r}_{\text{P}}* - \text{r}_{\text{M}}$.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{w}_{\text{P}} =$ 15/9 = 1.6667 (166.7% in P, borrow 66.7%)

$\text{r}_{\text{P}}* =$ 1.6667(7.2%) − 0.6667(2.1%) = 12.0% − 1.4% = 10.6%

$\text{M}^{2} =$ 10.6% − 8.5% = +2.10%

Check: $\text{S}_{\text{P}} = ($7.2 − 2.1)/9 = 0.5667, $\text{S}_{\text{M}} = ($8.5 − 2.1)/15 = 0.4267, 15% × 0.14 = 2.10%

Meaning: the fund lagged the index by 1.3 points in raw terms, but levered to the index’s volatility it would have beaten the index by 2.1 points.

**Fragile fact.** $\sigma_{\text{P}} < \sigma_{\text{M}}$: weight above 1, borrow, subtract $(\text{w} -$ 1$)\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ . A low-volatility fund can lose on raw return yet win on $\text{M}^{2}$.

**Reference**

LO 89.c (Schweser Reading 89): “Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.” GARP: Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.1 The Conventional Theory of Performance Evaluation, subsection The $\text{M}^{2}$ Measure and the Sharpe Ratio. Schweser’s worked example only covers the de-levering case (50/50 with the risk-free asset); the leverage case is from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 c, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: A gives the correct $\text{M}^{2}$ and the correct composition: 166.7% in P funded by borrowing 66.7% at the risk-free rate, as GARP’s parenthetical prescribes.

b.reason: **Scope error: no risk adjustment.** 7.2 − 8.5 = −1.30% compares a 9%-volatility fund with a 15%-volatility index. B would be right only if $\sigma_{\text{P}} = \sigma_{\text{M}}$.

c.reason: **Sign error on the borrowing leg.** 1.6667(7.2) + 0.6667(2.1) = 13.4%, minus 8.5 gives 4.90%. The extra 66.7% is borrowed, so it costs $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ ; you cannot hold 166.7% in P and also 66.7% in bills with 100% of capital. C would need 233% of capital.

d.reason: **Inverted weight.** 9/15 = 0.6 gives 0.6(7.2) + 0.4(2.1) = 5.16% and $\text{M}^{2} = -$3.34%. This de-levers a portfolio that is already less volatile, producing a 5.4% volatility portfolio. D’s weights would be right only if $\sigma_{\text{P}}$ were 25%.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 c Q9
questions.question:
A member of the investment committee of a German charitable foundation reviews a consultant’s report, in EUR terms. The foundation will place its entire risky allocation in a single vehicle: either active Fund P or an index fund tracking M. The risk-free rate was 2.0%.

|  | Fund P | Index M |
|---|---|---|
| Average return (%) | 13.4 | 11.0 |
| Beta | 1.10 | 1.00 |
| Standard deviation (%) | 30.0 | 20.0 |
| Residual standard deviation (%) | 17.0 | 0.0 |

Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: Choose Fund P: its $\text{T}^{2}$ of +1.36% shows it beats the index at equal systematic risk, and Treynor is the relevant measure for an entire risky portfolio.
Choose the index fund: P’s $\text{M}^{2}$ of −1.40% shows it lags at equal total risk; P’s positive $\text{T}^{2}$ ignores its large nonsystematic risk, which a stand-alone holding keeps.
Choose the index fund: P’s $\text{M}^{2}$ of −1.40% shows it lags at equal total risk, and P’s $\text{T}^{2}$ must also be negative, since $\text{M}^{2} \text{and T}^{2}$ always agree in sign.
Choose Fund P: its $\text{M}^{2}$ is +2.40%, the gap between its return and the index return, since both measures are expressed as return differences.

questions.solution:
German foundation choosing one vehicle for its whole risky allocation; Fund P wins on Treynor but loses on $\text{M}^{2}$.

**Concept and theory**

$\text{M}^{2} \text{and T}^{2}$ can disagree because they use different risks. A fund with a lot of nonsystematic (residual) risk has a total volatility much larger than its beta implies. Beta-based measures do not see that residual risk; total-risk measures do. GARP’s Concept Check 8.2 is the template: portfolio P has $\text{T}_{\text{P}} =$ 24.2 $> \text{T}_{\text{M}} =$ 22 and positive alpha, yet $\text{S}_{\text{P}} =$ 0.69 $< \text{S}_{\text{M}} =$ 0.73 and $\text{M}^{2} = -$1.3%, with residual risk of 18%. Schweser: a discrepancy “could occur if the manager takes on a large proportion of unsystematic risk relative to systematic risk. This would lower the Sharpe ratio but leave the Treynor measure unaffected.” Which conclusion counts depends on the portfolio’s role. GARP’s summary: Sharpe “when the portfolio represents the entire investment fund”; Treynor “when the portfolio represents one subportfolio of many”.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{T}_{\text{P}} = ($13.4 − 2.0)/1.10 = 10.364%, $\text{T}_{\text{M}} =$ 11.0 − 2.0 = 9.0%, $\text{T}^{2}_{\text{P}} = +$1.36%

$\text{S}_{\text{P}} =$ 11.4/30 = 0.380, $\text{S}_{\text{M}} =$ 9.0/20 = 0.450

$\text{M}^{2}_{\text{P}} =$ 20% × (0.380 − 0.450) = −1.40%

The foundation will hold P on its own, so P’s 17% residual risk is not diversified away. Total risk is relevant: $\text{M}^{2}$ decides, and P underperforms.

**Fragile fact.** High residual risk: Treynor and $\text{T}^{2}$ look good, Sharpe and $\text{M}^{2}$ look bad. A stand-alone holding is judged on total risk.

**Reference**

LO 89.c (Schweser Reading 89): “Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.” GARP: Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.1 The Conventional Theory of Performance Evaluation, subsection The $\text{M}^{2}$ Measure and the Sharpe Ratio; The Treynor Ratio; summary table of measures (Concept Check 8.2). Schweser $\text{M}^{2}$ section agrees on the cause of discrepancy.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 c, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap and role misassignment: Treynor for the whole fund.** The $\text{T}^{2}$ number is right, but Treynor suits a subportfolio of many. A would be correct if P were one of many sleeves in a diversified portfolio.

b.reason: B picks the right measure for the role, gets the number right, and explains the positive $\text{T}^{2}$ correctly: beta ignores the residual risk that a stand-alone holding keeps.

c.reason: $^{2} \text{and T}^{2}$ **always agree).** They agree in sign only if both Sharpe and Treynor beat the market. Here $\text{T}^{2} = +$1.36% while $\text{M}^{2} = -$1.40%. C would hold only for a fully diversified portfolio (residual risk near zero), where total and systematic risk nearly coincide.

d.reason: $^{2}$**).** 13.4 − 11.0 = 2.40% is the unadjusted difference; $\text{M}^{2}$ first matches volatilities. D would be right only if P’s standard deviation equalled the index’s 20%.

questions.question: A junior analyst at a French insurer’s asset management arm is drafting a glossary entry on the Modigliani-squared measure for the performance committee. Which of the following statements should NOT be included because it is incorrect?

options.text: The “squared” refers to the measure’s two originators, Leah and Franco Modigliani; the calculation itself contains no squared terms.
Some sources define $\text{M}^{2}$ as the return on the risk-adjusted portfolio itself rather than that return minus the market return; both versions rank portfolios identically.
If the active portfolio has a lower standard deviation than the index, the risk-adjusted portfolio is formed by borrowing at the risk-free rate and investing the proceeds in the portfolio.
Because $\text{M}^{2}$ adjusts the active portfolio to the index’s beta before returns are compared, it always ranks portfolios in the same order as the Treynor measure.

questions.solution:
Glossary entry on $\text{M}^{2}$; identify the statement that is NOT correct.

**Concept and theory**

Key facts about $\text{M}^{2}$ and how it differs from its beta-based twin:

| Fact | Source |
|---|---|
| Name | “M-squared” refers to Leah and Franco Modigliani; no squared terms (Schweser Professor’s Note; GARP “dubbed the $\text{M}^{2}$ mea- |
| Definition variants | sure (for Modigliani-squared)”) Sometimes $\text{M}^{2}$ is the return on $\text{P}^{'}$ itself; rankings identical either |
| Leverage case | way (Schweser Professor’s Note) If $\sigma_{\text{P}} < \sigma_{\text{M}}$, borrow and invest in P (GARP) |
| Risk used $\text{T}^{2}$ | Total volatility, matched to the index’s standard deviation; ranks like Sharpe (GARP, Schweser) Matches the index’s beta; ranks like Treynor (GARP) |

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and C each restate a source fact. D describes the $\text{T}^{2}$ construction (matching beta) and claims $\text{M}^{2}$ ranks like Treynor, which contradicts the fact that $\text{M}^{2}$ ranks like Sharpe.

**Fragile fact.** $\text{M}^{2}$ matches standard deviation (Sharpe family); $\text{T}^{2}$ matches beta (Treynor family). Do not cross them.

**Reference**

LO 89.c (Schweser Reading 89): “Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.” GARP: Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.1 The Conventional Theory of Performance Evaluation, subsection The $\text{M}^{2}$ Measure and the Sharpe Ratio. Statements A and B rest on Schweser’s Professor’s Notes; GARP has no equivalent note on the alternative definition (GARP defines $\text{M}^{2} \text{as r}_{\text{P}}* - \text{r}_{\text{M}}$ only). No content conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 c, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: **True; would be wrong under a polarity flip.** Schweser: “There are no squared terms in the M-squared calculation.” It would be wrong if it claimed the measure squares a return difference.

b.reason: **True; would be wrong under an absolute claim of different rankings.** Schweser notes the two definitions “provide identical portfolio performance rankings” because subtracting the same $\text{r}_{\text{M}}$ from every $\text{P}^{'}$ return does not change the order.

c.reason: **True; would be wrong under a condition flip.** GARP’s parenthetical prescribes borrowing when the active portfolio is less volatile. It would be wrong if it said “higher standard deviation”.

d.reason: GARP: $\text{M}^{2}$ mixes P with T-bills so that “the resulting ‘adjusted’ portfolio matches the volatility of a passive market index”; it “focuses on total volatility as a measure of risk”. Rankings by $\text{M}^{2}$ and Treynor can differ (Questions 9 and 11).

questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 c Q11
questions.question:
The chief investment officer of an Ontario university endowment is assessing two equity funds, J and K, in CAD terms. In Scenario 1 the chosen fund would hold the endowment’s entire risky allocation. In Scenario 2 it would be one of 20 sleeves in an already diversified portfolio. The risk-free rate was 3.0%.

|  | Fund J | Fund K | Index M |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average return (%) | 12.0 | 15.5 | 10.0 |
| Standard deviation (%) | 18.0 | 30.0 | 16.0 |
| Beta | 1.20 | 1.10 | 1.00 |

Which choice is best supported by the data?

options.text: Fund J in both scenarios, because J has the higher $\text{M}^{2}$ (+1.00% versus −0.33%).
Fund K in Scenario 1 and Fund J in Scenario 2, matching each fund to the measure it ranks best on.
Fund J in Scenario 1 $\text{(M}^{2}$ of +1.00% versus −0.33%) and Fund K in Scenario 2 $\text{(T}^{2}$ of +4.36% versus +0.50%).
Fund K in both scenarios, because K has the higher average return and the higher $\text{T}^{2}$.

questions.solution:
Ontario endowment choosing between Funds J and K as the entire risky allocation and as one of 20 sleeves.

**Concept and theory**

The same pair of funds can deserve different choices in different roles. If the fund is the entire risky allocation, total risk matters and $\text{M}^{2}$ (Sharpe) ranks them. If it is one of many sleeves, nonsystematic risk diversifies away and $\text{T}^{2}$ (Treynor) ranks them. GARP’s Table 8.3 discussion: “the appropriate way to evaluate a portfolio depends in large part on how the portfolio fits into the investor’s overall investment plan.”

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{M}^{2}_{\text{J}} =$ 3.0 $+ \frac{16}{18} ($12.0 − 3.0) − 10.0 = 3.0 + 8.00 − 10.0 = +1.00%

$\text{M}^{2}_{\text{K}} =$ 3.0 $+ \frac{16}{30} ($15.5 − 3.0) − 10.0 = 3.0 + 6.667 − 10.0 = −0.33%

$\text{T}^{2}_{\text{J}} = \frac{12.0-3.0}{1.20} - ($10.0 − 3.0) = 7.50 − 7.00 = +0.50%

$\text{T}^{2}_{\text{K}} = \frac{15.5-3.0}{1.10} -$ 7.00 = 11.364 − 7.00 = +4.36%

J wins on total risk; K wins on systematic risk. K’s 30% volatility with a beta of only 1.10 signals large residual risk, which hurts it as a stand-alone holding but diversifies away as one of 20 sleeves.

**Fragile fact.** Entire fund: $\text{M}^{2}$ (total risk). One sleeve of many: $\text{T}^{2}$ (beta). A fund with high volatility but modest beta carries large residual risk.

**Reference**

LO 89.c (Schweser Reading 89): “Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.” GARP: Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.1 The Conventional Theory of Performance Evaluation, subsection Implementing Performance Measurement: An Example (Tables 8.2 and 8.3) and the summary table of measures. Schweser agrees that $\text{Sharpe/M}^{2}$ and Treynor rankings can swap when unsystematic risk differs (Figure 89.3 discussion).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 c, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error: one measure applied to both roles.** $\text{M}^{2}$ is correct only for Scenario 1. A would be right if $\text{T}^{2}$ also favoured J, as it would if K’s beta were above about 1.67.

b.reason: **Role misassignment: measures swapped between scenarios.** B picks each fund by the measure that suits the other role. It would be right only if the entire-fund case called for beta-based measures, which contradicts GARP’s summary.

c.reason: Scenario 1 (entire fund): $\text{M}^{2}$ favours J. Scenario 2 (one of 20 sleeves): $\text{T}^{2}$ favours K. C matches each role to its measure.

d.reason: **Scope error with raw return.** K’s higher $\text{T}^{2}$ is right for Scenario 2, but its higher average return is not a risk-adjusted basis, and in Scenario 1 its $\text{M}^{2}$ is negative. D would be right only if K also had the higher Sharpe ratio.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 c Q12
questions.question:
A regulator reviewing the manager-selection policy of a US state pension plan, which allocates assets across many external managers, reads the following statements in the policy document:

I. When beta is the relevant measure of risk, ranking candidate portfolios by $\text{T}^{2}$ or by the Treynor measure gives the same ordering.

II. To form the beta-adjusted portfolio for a candidate with a beta of 1.60, the evaluator invests 62.5% in the candidate and 37.5% in T-bills.

III. A candidate with a beta below 1.0 can have a positive $\text{T}^{2}$ only if its alpha exceeds the market’s excess return.

IV. $\text{T}^{2}$ is the preferred measure when the candidate portfolio will form the investor’s entire risky portfolio.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I and IV only
II and III only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Regulator reviewing four policy statements on $\text{T}^{2}$ and Treynor in a multi-manager pension plan.

**Concept and theory**

$\text{T}^{2} = \text{T}_{\text{P}} - \text{T}_{\text{M}}$ (with $\beta_{\text{M}} =$ 1). Since $\text{T}_{\text{M}}$ is the same for every candidate, $\text{T}^{2}$ is the Treynor ratio shifted by a constant, so the two always rank candidates identically. GARP: “We can use either the $\text{T}^{2}$ or the Treynor measure to rank portfolios when beta is the relevant measure of risk.” The beta-adjusted portfolio uses w = 1/$\beta_{\text{P}}$ in the candidate and 1 − w in T-bills. Because $\text{T}^{2} = \alpha_{\text{P}}$/$\beta_{\text{P}}$ and $\beta_{\text{P}} >$ 0, $\text{T}^{2}$ is positive whenever alpha is positive, whatever the beta.

**Applying it to this question**

- I: true, as above.
- II: w = 1/1.60 = 0.625, so 62.5% in the candidate and 37.5% in T-bills; beta = 0.625 × 1.60 = 1.0. True.
- III: false. $\text{T}^{2} = \alpha$/$\beta>$ 0 iff $\alpha>$ 0. A beta of 0.8 with alpha of 1% gives $\text{T}^{2} =$ 1.25%, though alpha is far below a typical market excess return.
- IV: false. For an entire risky portfolio, total risk matters, so Sharpe or $\text{M}^{2}$ applies; $\text{T}^{2}$ suits a subportfolio of many.

**Fragile fact.** Beta-adjusted weight is 1/$\beta$ (62.5% for beta 1.60; above 100% and borrowing for beta below 1). Positive alpha means positive $\text{T}^{2}$.

**Reference**

LO 89.c (Schweser Reading 89): “Describe the uses for the Modigliani-squared and Treynor’s measure in comparing two portfolios and the graphical representation of these measures.” GARP: Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.1 The Conventional Theory of Performance Evaluation, subsection The Treynor Ratio (Example 8.2) and The Role of Alpha in Performance Measures. Schweser does not present $\text{T}^{2}$; content from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 c, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: Only I and II are correct, so the answer is “I and II only”.

b.reason: **Includes IV: role misassignment.** IV assigns the beta-based measure to the entire-fund role. B would be correct if IV said “one of many subportfolios”.

c.reason: **Includes III, excludes I: condition error.** III invents a condition (alpha above the market excess return) that $\text{T}^{2} = \alpha$/$\beta$ does not need, and C drops the true statement I. C would need III to be true and I false.

d.reason: **Includes III: condition error.** I and II are right, but III is false as shown. D would be correct only if $\text{T}^{2}$ were defined as $\alpha- (\text{r}_{\text{M}} - \text{r}_{\text{f}} )$, which is not GARP’s definition.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe style analysis.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 e Q1
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Singapore public pension fund is preparing an induction session for newly hired analysts on how the fund describes the investment style of its external managers. She wants one slide that explains where style analysis comes from and what it measures. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Style analysis can be viewed as a generalization of the market timing regression, in which a dummy variable for up markets is added to the single-index model.
Style analysis can be viewed as a generalization of the index model, in which each exposure of a portfolio to a segment of the market is treated as an implicit asset allocation decision.
In the single-index version of this idea, portfolios with low betas are described as cyclical or aggressive, while portfolios with high betas are described as defensive.
The study that popularised the concept showed that asset allocation explains all of the variation in fund returns, and later studies have confirmed this exact interpretation without dispute.

questions.solution:
Singapore pension analyst: which statement correctly explains the origin and purpose of style analysis?

**Concept and theory**

The single-index model already describes a facet of a manager’s style: its beta. GARP notes that portfolios with high betas are called cyclical or aggressive because they respond strongly to economy-wide developments, and low-beta portfolios are called defensive. Multifactor models generalize this: a portfolio has exposures to several risk factors or segments of the market, and each exposure can be viewed as an implicit asset allocation decision. William Sharpe introduced style analysis as a tool to systematically measure these exposures. The chapter introduction says style analysis “may be viewed as a generalization of the index model and the alpha statistic that it generates”.

Its popularity was helped by a study (Brinson, Singer and Beebower) concluding that most of the variation in returns of 82 funds could be explained by their asset allocation to bills, bonds and stocks. Later studies took issue with the exact interpretation, but there is widespread agreement that asset allocation is responsible for a high proportion of the variation in investment performance across funds.

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Single-index model | One exposure (beta): high beta cyclical or aggressive, low beta defensive |
| Style analysis | Many exposures (asset class indexes), each an implicit allocation; intercept plays the role of alpha |

**Applying it to this question**

The analyst wants the lineage and the purpose. The deciding fact is GARP’s description of style analysis as a generalization of the index model, with each exposure read as an implicit asset allocation decision.

**Fragile fact.** High beta is cyclical or aggressive; low beta is defensive. Asset allocation explains a high proportion, not all, of return variation.

**Reference**

LO 89.e (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.3, “Style Analysis”): “Describe style analysis.” GARP Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.2, Style Analysis (opening paragraphs) and the chapter introduction. Schweser: Module 89.3, Style Analysis, steps 1 and 3. No conflict: Schweser does not discuss the index-model lineage; content from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 e, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** The up-market dummy variable belongs to the market timing regression (LO 89.h), not to style analysis. It would be correct if the stem asked how the index model is extended to test market timing ability.

b.reason: B restates GARP 8.2 directly: multifactor exposures to segments of the market are “an implicit sort of asset allocation decision”, and style analysis measures these exposures as a generalization of the index model.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** The labels are reversed: high beta means cyclical or aggressive, low beta means defensive. Swap “low” and “high” and the statement is correct.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** The study found that most of the variation was explained by asset allocation, and later studies took issue with the exact interpretation; only the broad conclusion (a high proportion) is widely agreed. With “most” and “widespread agreement on a high proportion”, D would be correct.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe style analysis.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 e Q2
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Shanghai fund management company is validating the documentation of the firm’s returns-based style analysis model, which is applied to its long-only CNY equity and bond mutual funds. The documentation contains the following statements:

I. The fund’s returns are regressed on the returns of indexes representing a range of asset classes, and the coefficient on each index measures the fund’s implicit allocation to that style.

II. The coefficients are constrained to be zero or positive, because the funds analysed are barred from taking short positions.

III. The coefficients are constrained to sum to 100%, so that together they represent a complete asset allocation.

IV. The intercept is constrained to equal zero, so that all of the fund’s average return is attributed to its style exposures.

Which of the statements are consistent with Sharpe’s style analysis?

options.text: I and II only
I and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Shanghai auditor: which four documentation statements about style analysis are consistent with Sharpe’s method?

**Concept and theory**

Sharpe’s idea was to regress fund returns on indexes representing a range of asset classes (Schweser: an exhaustive and mutually exclusive set of asset class indices). The regression coefficient on each index measures the fund’s implicit allocation to that “style”. Because the funds are barred from short positions, the coefficients are constrained to be zero or positive and to sum to 100%, so that they represent a complete asset allocation. The intercept is not constrained away: it measures the average return from security selection of the fund portfolio, tracking the average success of selection over the sample.

| Output | Meaning in GARP 8.2 |
|---|---|
| Coefficient $\beta_{\text{j}}$ | Implicit allocation to style j; $\beta_{\text{j}} \ge$ 0, $\sum\beta_{\text{j}} =$ 1 |
| R-square | Share of return variability due to style choice |
| Intercept $\alpha$ | Average return from security selection |

**Applying it to this question**

I: true (regressors are asset class indexes; coefficients are implicit allocations). II: true (no shorting, so zero or positive). III: true (sum to 100%, a complete allocation). IV: false, because the intercept is estimated freely and is precisely where average selection return appears. So I, II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** The constraints apply to the coefficients, never to the intercept. Reason for nonnegativity: funds are barred from short positions.

**Reference**

LO 89.e (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.3, “Style Analysis”): “Describe style analysis.” GARP Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.2, Style Analysis (Sharpe’s regression, constraints, R-square and intercept). Schweser: Module 89.3, Style Analysis, steps 1 and 3. Schweser adds the wording “exhaustive and mutually exclusive” for the regressors; not a conflict, and not the deciding fact here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 e, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error, drops III.** Omitting III treats the sum-to-100% constraint as optional; without it the coefficients would not form a complete allocation. A would be right only if the model allowed leverage or partial investment, which Sharpe’s method does not.

b.reason: **Role misassignment, includes IV.** It gives the intercept a role it does not have (forced to zero) and assigns all return to style. B would be right only for a model that, unlike Sharpe’s, suppresses the intercept.

c.reason: **Condition error, drops I, adds IV.** Omitting I loses the definition of the coefficients as implicit allocations, and IV is false as above. C would require a method in which coefficients are not allocations and the intercept is suppressed.

d.reason:
GARP: coefficients “constrained to be either zero or positive and to sum to 100%, so as to represent a complete asset allocation”; “the intercept measures the average return from security selection”.

Statement IV contradicts the second sentence.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe style analysis.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 e Q3
questions.question:
A risk consultant at an Australian superannuation fund is preparing a report on an AUD multi-asset manager. She runs Sharpe’s style analysis on 60 monthly returns and obtains the output below. The fund’s annualised volatility over the same period was 14.0%.

| Style portfolio | Coefficient (%) |
|---|---|
| Cash | 10 |
| Australian large cap | 55 |
| Australian small cap | 15 |
| Growth (high P/E) | 20 |
| Total | 100 |
| R-square | 88 |

Which of the following sentences should she include in the report?

options.text: 88% of the variability of the fund’s returns is attributable to style choice, and the remaining 12% to security selection within asset classes and to timing that shows up as periodic changes in allocation.
88% of the variability of the fund’s returns is attributable to security selection within asset classes and to timing, and the remaining 12% is attributable to the fund’s style choice.
55% of the variability of the fund’s returns is attributable to style choice, because the largest coefficient gives the share of return variability that is explained by asset allocation.
88% of the variability of the fund’s returns is attributable to style choice, and the remaining 12% solely to security selection, because any timing is captured entirely by the style coefficients.

questions.solution:
Australian super fund consultant: how to word the reading of R-square 88% from a style regression.

**Concept and theory**

The R-square of the style regression measures the percentage of return variability attributable to style choice rather than security selection. The rest, 1 $- \text{R}^{2}$, is the proportion of return variability not explained by asset allocation. GARP attributes it to two things: security selection within asset classes, and timing that shows up as periodic changes in allocation (because the regression fits one fixed set of weights, any switching between asset classes over the sample appears in the residual). For Magellan, residual variability was 100 − 97.5 = 2.5%.

Share due to style $= \text{R}^{2}$, Share due to selection and timing = 1 $- \text{R}^{2}$.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{R}^{2} =$ 0.88 $\Rightarrow\text{style share} =$ 88%, 1 $- \text{R}^{2} =$ 1 − 0.88 = 0.12 = 12%.

The 12% is split between selection within asset classes and timing. The coefficients (10, 55, 15, 20) are allocations, not variance shares, and the 14.0% volatility is irrelevant to the attribution of variability.

**Fragile fact.** 1 $- \text{R}^{2}$ is selection and timing, not selection alone; and it is a share of variability, not of return.

**Reference**

LO 89.e (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.3, “Style Analysis”): “Describe style analysis.” GARP Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.2, Style Analysis (R-square paragraph and “The proportion of return variability not explained by asset allocation. . . ”). Schweser: Module 89.3, Style Analysis, steps 1 and 3. Schweser states “percentage attributable to selection = 1 $- \text{R}^{2}$” with selection including market timing; consistent with GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 e, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: A matches GARP word for word in substance: R-square is the share due to style choice; the remainder is selection within asset classes plus timing that shows up as periodic changes in allocation.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It swaps the two shares: R-square is the style share, not the selection share. B would be correct only if the stem gave $\text{R}^{2} =$ 12%.

c.reason: **Wrong input twin.** It reads the largest coefficient (55%) as a variance share. Coefficients are implicit allocations; the share of variability is the R-square. C would describe the fund’s largest effective allocation, not its variance attribution.

d.reason: **Scope error, drops a condition.** It drops timing from the residual. Because the weights are estimated as constant, timing that changes allocation over time is not captured by the coefficients and falls in the residual. D would be correct only for a manager known never to change allocations.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe style analysis.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 e Q4
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a São Paulo asset manager is reviewing a vendor report on a long-only BRL equity fund that, under its regulations, cannot sell short. The vendor ran an ordinary unconstrained regression of the fund’s monthly returns on four style indexes.

| Regressor | Coefficient |
|---|---|
| Cash (CDI) | −0.12 |
| Large cap index | 0.78 |
| Small cap index | 0.46 |
| Value index | −0.12 |
| Sum of coefficients | 1.00 |
| Intercept (% per month) | 0.04 |
| R-square | 0.97 |

Which of the following statements about the vendor output is most accurate?

options.text: It is a valid Sharpe style analysis, because the coefficients sum to 100% and so represent a complete asset allocation of the fund.
It is a valid Sharpe style analysis, because the negative coefficients simply capture the fund’s short positions in cash and in value stocks.
It is not a valid Sharpe style analysis, because for a fund barred from short positions the coefficients must be zero or positive as well as sum to 100%.
It is not a valid Sharpe style analysis, because each coefficient must also equal the fund’s reported holding weight in that asset class at period end.

questions.solution:
São Paulo analyst: is an unconstrained regression with two negative coefficients a valid style analysis of a no-short fund?

**Concept and theory**

Sharpe’s style analysis is a constrained regression. The coefficients are meant to be read as the fund’s effective asset allocation, so they must look like a real allocation of a long-only fund: each between zero and one and together summing to one. GARP gives the reason explicitly: “Because funds are barred from short positions, the regression coefficients are constrained to be either zero or positive and to sum to 100%.” Only under both constraints do the coefficients form a complete allocation that can be used to build a passive tracking portfolio.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each constraint on the vendor output:

$\sum_{\beta_{\text{j}}} = -_{0.12} +_{0.78} +_{0.46} -_{0.12} =_{1.00 \text{(sum constraint met)}}$

$\beta_{\text{cash}} = -$0.12 \< 0, $\beta_{\text{value}} = -$0.12 \< 0 (nonnegativity violated)

So the output fails one of the two constraints. The R-square (0.97) and intercept (0.04% per month) are irrelevant to the validity question.

**Fragile fact.** Two constraints, both required: $\beta_{\text{j}} \ge$ 0 for every j, and $\sum\beta_{\text{j}} =$ 1. A unit sum can hide negative coefficients.

**Reference**

LO 89.e (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.3, “Style Analysis”): “Describe style analysis.” GARP Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.2, Style Analysis (constraints paragraph). Schweser: Module 89.3, Style Analysis, steps 1 and 3. Schweser: slopes “constrained to be nonnegative and to sum to 100%” so they are “effective” allocations. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 e, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error, drops a condition.** It checks only the sum constraint and ignores nonnegativity. A would be correct if all four coefficients were zero or positive.

b.reason: **Condition error.** It treats negative coefficients as short positions, but the fund (and Sharpe’s setting) bars short selling; that is the very reason for the nonnegativity constraint. B would be correct only for an unconstrained factor regression of a fund allowed to short, which is not Sharpe’s style analysis.

c.reason: A no-short fund cannot hold −12% in cash or value; the coefficients must be zero or positive and sum to 100%. Meeting the sum constraint alone is not enough.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It substitutes holdings-based weights for the regression’s implicit allocations. Style analysis infers effective allocations from returns; it does not require them to equal reported holdings. D would describe a holdings-based check, a different technique.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe style analysis.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 e Q5
questions.question: The CRO of a Canadian public sector pension plan is presenting the style analysis of an external CAD equity manager to the investment committee. The regression R-square is 99%. One committee member argues: “With an R-square of 99%, the manager’s stock picking clearly contributes nothing, so we should replace the mandate with a passive mix of the style indexes.” Which response by the CRO is most accurate?

options.text: The R-square measures only the share of return variability explained by style; the intercept, which measures the average return from security selection, can be positive even with an R-square of 100%, so it must be examined first.
The member is right, because with an R-square of 99% at most 1% of the manager’s average return can have come from security selection, which is too little to justify active fees.
The member is wrong, because the 1% of variability that style does not explain is itself the manager’s annual return from security selection, so the manager adds about 1% per year.
The member is wrong, because in Sharpe’s method the share of return variability attributable to style is measured by the sum of the coefficients, which is always 100%, not by the R-square.

questions.solution:
Canadian pension CRO: responding to the claim that R-square 99% means stock picking adds nothing.

**Concept and theory**

R-square and intercept answer different questions. R-square tells you how much of the variability of returns moves with the style indexes. The intercept tells you the average level of return earned on top of the style mix, which GARP calls the average return from security selection. A manager can track the style mix very closely month to month (R-square near 100%) while beating it by a steady margin every month (positive intercept). GARP warns that a high R-square “is commonly interpreted as evidence against the importance of security selection, but such a conclusion misses the important role of the intercept”; “the R-square of the regression can be 100%, and yet the intercept can be positive due to consistently superior stock selection”. Magellan is the example: R-square 97.5%, intercept 32 basis points per month.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee member infers “no stock-picking value” from R-square alone. The deciding fact is that value from selection shows up in the intercept, which has not been looked at. The CRO should examine the intercept (and its consistency) before recommending a passive replacement.

**Fragile fact.** High R-square does not mean zero selection value: R-square is about variability, the intercept is about average return.

**Reference**

LO 89.e (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.3, “Style Analysis”): “Describe style analysis.” GARP Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.2, Style Analysis (“This sort of result is commonly interpreted as evidence against the importance of security selection. . . ”). Schweser: Module 89.3, Style Analysis, steps 1 and 3. Conflict of emphasis: Schweser (LO 89.i key concept) says returns to timing and selection are “minimal at best”; GARP cautions that this reading ignores the intercept. GARP followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 e, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: A states both halves of GARP’s warning: R-square measures the share of variability due to style; the intercept measures average selection return and can be positive at an R-square of 100%.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: variability share read as return share.** The 1% is a share of variance, not a cap on average return. B would be right only if variance shares and return contributions were the same quantity, which they are not.

c.reason: **Wrong input twin.** It reads 1 $- \text{R}^{2} =$ 1% as an annual return. The average selection return is the intercept, a return figure; 1 $- \text{R}^{2}$ is a proportion of variability. C would be correct if the stem said the intercept was about 1% per year.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** The sum of the coefficients is fixed at 100% by construction; it is the R-square that measures the style share of variability. D would be correct if “sum of coefficients” were replaced by “R-square” and the conclusion reversed.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe style analysis.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 e Q6
questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Zurich private bank is reviewing a CHF-hedged fund marketed to clients as a “small-cap value” fund. She runs Sharpe’s style analysis on seven style portfolios and obtains the following output.

| Style portfolio | Coeff. (%) | Style portfolio | Coeff. (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| T-bill | 0 | High P/E (growth) | 16 |
| Small cap | 4 | Medium P/E | 0 |
| Medium cap | 22 | Low P/E (value) | 0 |
| Large cap | 58 | R-square | 95 |

Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: The fund is consistent with its small-cap value label, because an R-square of 95% shows that its returns are well explained by the style portfolios.
The fund’s effective style is mainly large cap with some medium cap and a growth tilt, which is inconsistent with its small-cap value label.
The fund’s style cannot be inferred, because Sharpe’s method requires a positive coefficient on every style portfolio included in the regression.
The fund’s label must be taken as its style, because style analysis estimates only the fund’s market beta and not its exposures to size or growth segments.

questions.solution:
Zurich PM: what the coefficients say about a fund labelled small-cap value.

**Concept and theory**

Because the coefficients are effective allocations to style portfolios, they reveal the manager’s investment style regardless of the label. Schweser’s step 3: the regression slopes are used to infer the investment style of the manager. GARP’s Magellan example shows the reading: of seven style portfolios only large cap (61), medium cap (35) and high P/E growth (5) had positive coefficients, so “the fund returns are well represented by three style portfolios”. Zero coefficients are normal: a fund need not load on every style. The R-square says how well the chosen mix describes the fund, not which mix it is.

**Applying it to this question**

Read the largest coefficients:

Size: $\beta_{\text{large}} =$ 58%, $\beta_{\text{medium}} =$ 22%, $\beta_{\text{small}} =$ 4%

Value or growth: $\beta_{\text{high P/E}} =$ 16%, $\beta_{\text{low P/E}} =$ 0%

Total: 0 + 4 + 22 + 58 + 16 + 0 + 0 = 100%, so the constraints hold. The effective style is mainly large cap, with medium cap and a growth tilt, and essentially no small-cap or value exposure. This is inconsistent with the “small-cap value” label (style drift or mislabelling).

**Fragile fact.** Read the style from the coefficients, not from the R-square; zero coefficients are permitted.

**Reference**

LO 89.e (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.3, “Style Analysis”): “Describe style analysis.” GARP Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.2, Style Analysis and Table 8.4 (Magellan). Schweser: Module 89.3, Style Analysis, steps 1 and 3. Schweser step 3 (style inferred from slopes, large-cap growth example). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 e, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error.** A high R-square says the fund is well explained by some style mix; it does not say the mix matches the label. A would be correct only if the large coefficients were on small cap and low P/E.

b.reason: B reads the style from the largest effective allocations, exactly as Schweser step 3 and GARP’s Magellan reading do.

c.reason: **Condition error.** No such requirement exists; zero coefficients are allowed and common (Magellan had positive coefficients on only three of seven). C would be correct only if zero coefficients were forbidden, which contradicts the nonnegativity (zero or positive) constraint.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It confuses style analysis with the single-index model. Style analysis is the multi-index generalization that measures exposures to several segments (size, growth or value). D describes the index model’s single beta.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe style analysis.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 e Q7
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a German insurer is evaluating an external EUR balanced fund. Sharpe’s style analysis over the previous five years gave the coefficients below, and she applies them to this year’s index returns. This year the fund returned 7.9%, and the broad euro area equity market index returned 8.0%. The regression R-square was 0.93.

| Style index | Coefficient (%) | Index return this year (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Cash | 0 | 3.0 |
| Euro government bonds | 20 | 2.0 |
| Euro large cap equity | 50 | 9.0 |
| Euro small cap equity | 30 | 4.0 |

What is the fund’s return this year relative to the passive portfolio that matches its style exposures?
questions.solution:
German insurer analyst: fund return relative to its passive style-matching portfolio.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s summary: “The coefficients on the style portfolios indicate a passive strategy that would match the risk exposures of the managed portfolio. These differences in returns between the managed portfolio and the matching portfolio measure performance relative to similar-style funds.” Figure 8.4 plots exactly this, the fund against the “tracking portfolio composed of the individual style portfolios”. The style benchmark return is the coefficient-weighted average of the style index returns:

$\text{r}_{\text{style}} = \sum_{\text{j}} \beta_{\text{j}} \text{r}_{\text{j}}$, Performance vs style $= \text{r}_{\text{P}} - \text{r}_{\text{style}}$,

where $\beta_{\text{j}}$ are the estimated style coefficients and $\text{r}_{\text{j}}$ the index returns for the period.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{r}_{\text{style}} =$ 0(3.0%) + 0.20(2.0%) + 0.50(9.0%) + 0.30(4.0%)

$\text{r}_{\text{style}} =$ 0 + 0.40% + 4.50% + 1.20% = 6.10%

$\text{r}_{\text{P}} - \text{r}_{\text{style}} =$ 7.90% − 6.10% = +1.80%

The fund beat the passive portfolio that matches its style exposures by 1.8 percentage points. The broad equity index (8.0%), the cash return (weight zero) and the R-square (0.93) are irrelevant inputs.

**Fragile fact.** The yardstick is the fund’s own style mix (coefficient-weighted), not the market index and not an equal-weighted mix.

**Reference**

LO 89.e (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.3, “Style Analysis”): “Describe style analysis.” GARP Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Summary point 4 (style analysis) and Section 8.2, Figure 8.4 (fund versus style benchmark). Schweser: Module 89.3, Style Analysis, steps 1 and 3. Schweser Module Quiz 89.3 Q1: style analysis measures performance relative to “a passive benchmark of the same style”. No conflict. The neutral-weight bogey and the split into allocation and selection effects belong to LO 89.i and are not used here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 e, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap, wrong benchmark.** 7.9% − 8.0% = −0.1% compares a balanced fund with a broad equity index that ignores its 20% bond exposure. Correct only if the stem asked for performance against the broad market index.

b.reason: **Intermediate result.** 6.1% is the style benchmark return itself, the intermediate step, not the difference. Correct only if the stem asked for the return of the passive style-matching portfolio.

c.reason: **Dropped term: the weights.** Equal-weighting the three non-zero indexes gives (2.0 + 9.0 + 4.0)/3 = 5.0% and 7.9% − 5.0% = 2.9%. Correct only if the style coefficients were one third each.

d.reason: +1.8% is the fund return minus the return of the coefficient-weighted passive style portfolio, the measure defined in GARP’s summary point 4.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe style analysis.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 e Q8
questions.question: The CCO of a Tokyo trust bank is reviewing two JPY funds sold by the bank. Sharpe’s style analysis gives an R-square of 99.5% for Fund P, an index-tracking fund, and 82% for Fund Q, an actively managed fund. Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: Fund Q’s lower R-square proves that its security selection added value, because the variability that style does not explain is the positive return earned from selection.
Fund P’s R-square near 100% proves that its intercept is zero, because a positive average return from selection would necessarily lower the R-square.
About 18% of Fund Q’s return variability is not explained by its style exposures and reflects selection within asset classes and timing, while Fund P’s variability is almost entirely due to style.
Fund P’s higher R-square shows that a larger share of its return variability comes from security selection within asset classes than is the case for Fund Q.

questions.solution:
Tokyo trust bank CCO: comparing style regression R-square of an index fund (99.5%) and an active fund (82%).

**Concept and theory**

The R-square measures the percentage of return variability attributable to style choice; 1 $- \text{R}^{2}$ is variability attributable to security selection within asset classes and to timing (periodic changes in allocation). A passively managed fund simply holds the style indexes, so almost all its variability is style and its R-square is close to 100%. An active fund departs from the indexes through selection and timing, so more of its variability is unexplained. Neither number, however, tells you whether the departures earned a positive return: that is the intercept’s job, and GARP stresses that R-square can be 100% with a positive intercept.

**Applying it to this question**

1 $- \text{R}^{2}_{\text{Q}} =$ 1 − 0.82 = 0.18 = 18%, 1 $- \text{R}^{2}_{\text{P}} =$ 1 − 0.995 = 0.005 = 0.5%.

Fund Q: 18% of variability from selection and timing, consistent with active management. Fund P: almost all variability is style, consistent with index tracking. No conclusion about value added is possible without the intercepts.

**Fragile fact.** Higher R-square means more style and less selection in the variability; it says nothing about the sign of selection return.

**Reference**

LO 89.e (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.3, “Style Analysis”): “Describe style analysis.” GARP Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.2, Style Analysis (R-square and intercept paragraphs); end-of-chapter Problem 19 asks the same passive versus active comparison. Schweser: Module 89.3, Style Analysis, steps 1 and 3. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 e, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: variability read as return.** Unexplained variability is not return; it can come from selection bets that lose money. The average selection return is the intercept. A would be right only if the stem gave Fund Q a positive intercept.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** GARP: “The R-square of the regression can be 100%, and yet the intercept can be positive.” A high R-square does not prove a zero intercept. B would be right only if the stem reported that the intercept was zero.

c.reason: C applies the R-square definition correctly to both funds and draws no conclusion beyond what R-square measures.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** A higher R-square means a smaller share of variability from selection. Reverse the comparison (Fund Q has the larger selection share) and D is correct.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe style analysis.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 e Q9
questions.question: A risk consultant at a US state pension fund is presenting a case study to trustees: the GARP reading’s style analysis of Fidelity’s Magellan Fund using monthly returns during Peter Lynch’s tenure, October 1986 to September 1991, with seven style portfolios (T-bill, small cap, medium cap, large cap, high P/E, medium P/E and low P/E). Which of the following statements about the results is most accurate?

options.text: All seven style portfolios had positive coefficients, so that Magellan’s returns could only be represented by a combination of every style portfolio.
The R-square of 97.5% showed that security selection was unimportant for Magellan, and its intercept was accordingly close to zero over the period.
Only three style portfolios had positive coefficients, namely small cap, medium cap and low P/E (value) stocks, and together they explained 97.5% of variance.
Only three style portfolios had positive coefficients and explained 97.5% of variance, yet the intercept of 32 basis points per month gave a cumulative abnormal return of about 19%.

questions.solution:
US pension consultant: what the GARP reading’s Magellan style analysis (October 1986 to September 1991) showed.

**Concept and theory**

GARP illustrates Sharpe’s approach with monthly returns on Fidelity’s Magellan Fund during Peter Lynch’s tenure, October 1986 to September 1991 (Table 8.4).

| Style portfolio | Coeff. (%) | Style portfolio | Coeff. (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| T-bill | 0 | High P/E (growth) | 5 |
| Small cap | 0 | Medium P/E | 0 |
| Medium cap | 35 | Low P/E (value) | 0 |
| Large cap | 61 | R-square | 97.5 |

Only three coefficients are positive (large cap, medium cap, high P/E growth), and these alone explain 97.5% of the variance of Magellan’s returns; residual variability is 100 − 97.5 = 2.5%. Yet the intercept was 32 basis points per month, giving a cumulative abnormal return over the five-year period of 19.19%. Figure 8.4 shows the cumulative residuals rising steadily against both the style benchmark and the SML benchmark.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are the count of positive coefficients (three), which three they are (large, medium, growth), the R-square (97.5%) and the sizeable positive intercept. As a check, 0.32% × 60 ≈ 19.2%, consistent with GARP’s 19.19%.

**Fragile fact.** Magellan in GARP: large 61, medium 35, growth 5; R-square 97.5%; intercept 32 bp per month; 19.19% cumulative.

**Reference**

LO 89.e (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.3, “Style Analysis”): “Describe style analysis.” GARP Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.2, Style Analysis, Table 8.4 and Figure 8.4. Schweser: Module 89.3, Style Analysis, steps 1 and 3. **Conflict:** Schweser reports Sharpe’s study of Magellan from January 1985 to December 1989 with 97.3% of returns explained by style and 2.7% by selection. GARP uses the authors’ own calculation for October 1986 to September 1991 with an R-square of 97.5% and residual 2.5%. This looks like a version difference (a different study in the newer edition of the source text); GARP followed, and the stem fixes the GARP period.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 e, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** Only three of seven coefficients were positive; four were zero. A would be correct if every style portfolio had received a positive weight.

b.reason: **Polarity flip of the interpretation.** This is the misreading GARP warns against: the high Rsquare was accompanied by a large positive intercept, evidence of consistently superior selection. B would be correct only for a fund with an intercept near zero.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It names the wrong style portfolios (small cap and low P/E value instead of large cap and high P/E growth). C would be correct for a small-cap value fund, not for Magellan.

d.reason: D combines all the correct facts: three positive coefficients, 97.5% of variance explained, and a 32 basis point monthly intercept producing about 19% cumulative abnormal return.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 e Q10
questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a UK university endowment is shown a chart for a GBP equity manager: the cumulative sum of the intercept plus monthly residuals from the manager’s Sharpe style regression over five years. The line rises steadily over the whole period, and the regression R-square is 97%. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: The manager consistently earned returns above its style tracking portfolio, which points to persistent success in security selection over the sample despite the very high R-square.
The line rises steadily because the style regression constrains the residuals to be zero or positive whenever the coefficients are constrained to sum to 100%.
The rising line shows that most of the manager’s return variability came from security selection rather than style, so the regression R-square cannot really be 97%.
The rising line is typical of mutual fund managers, because the average residual return relative to style benchmarks across funds is reliably and substantially positive.

questions.solution:
UK endowment committee member: interpreting a steadily rising cumulative intercept-plus-residual line with R-square 97%.

**Concept and theory**

Each month the fund return minus the style tracking portfolio equals the intercept plus that month’s residual, $\text{r}_{\text{P,t}} - \sum_{\text{j}} \beta_{\text{j}}\text{r}_{\text{j,t}} = \alpha+ \text{e}_{\text{t}}$. Cumulating this over time (GARP Figure 8.4) shows how the fund has done against its style benchmark. A line that rises steadily means the fund beat its style mix consistently, which is what a positive intercept (average return from security selection) produces. GARP’s point is that this can happen while the R-square is very high: Magellan had an R-square of 97.5% and a “consistently positive residual return (reflected in the steadily increasing plot of cumulative return difference)”. GARP also notes that this is “hardly common”.

**Applying it to this question**

Steady rise ⇒ persistently positive $\alpha+ \text{e}_{\text{t}} \Rightarrow$ consistent outperformance of the style tracking portfolio, pointing to selection success over the sample. The R-square of 97% only says the month-to-month variability is mostly style; it does not contradict a positive level of outperformance.

**Fragile fact.** Cumulative intercept plus residuals measures level of outperformance against the style mix; R-square measures co-movement. Both can be high together.

**Reference**

LO 89.e (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.3, “Style Analysis”): “Describe style analysis.” GARP Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.2, Style Analysis, Figure 8.4 (cumulative return difference, fund versus style benchmark and versus SML). Schweser: Module 89.3, Style Analysis, steps 1 and 3. No conflict; Schweser does not discuss the cumulative residual chart (GARP-only content).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 e, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: A gives GARP’s interpretation of Figure 8.4 and explicitly reconciles it with the high R-square.

b.reason: **Condition error.** The constraints (zero or positive, sum to 100%) apply to the coefficients, not to the residuals. B would make sense only if the constraint were placed on the residuals, which no version of the method does.

c.reason: **Sibling swap: return level read as variability share.** A rising cumulative line reflects the average level of excess return, not the share of variability; GARP states the R-square can be 100% with a positive intercept. C would be right only if the chart showed residual variance rather than cumulative residual return.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** Across 636 funds the average residual had a slightly negative mean (−0.074% per month), and Magellan’s steady rise is “hardly common”. D would be right only if the cross-fund mean were positive.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe style analysis.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 e Q11
questions.question: The treasurer of a Singapore family office is choosing between performance evaluation methods for an SGD equity manager. An adviser says the office should use Sharpe’s style analysis. Which of the following best describes the yardstick against which style analysis measures the manager’s performance?

options.text: The median return of a universe of actively managed peer funds with the same investment style, ranked by rate of return over the evaluation period.
The return required by the CAPM given the manager’s beta, as shown by the security market line, with performance measured as the vertical distance from it.
A passive portfolio of style indexes, weighted by the regression coefficients, that would match the risk exposures of the manager’s portfolio.
A passive portfolio of asset class indexes held at the neutral weights that the family office sets for the manager in consultation with its adviser.

questions.solution:
Singapore family office treasurer: the yardstick against which style analysis measures performance.

**Concept and theory**

Performance evaluation needs a benchmark. GARP describes several in Chapter 8, and they must not be confused:

| Method | Yardstick |
|---|---|
| Comparison universe | Rank of the fund’s return among peers of similar style (8.1) |
| Jensen’s alpha | CAPM required return on the SML given beta (8.1) |
| Style analysis | Passive mix of style indexes at the regression coefficients (8.2, summary 4) |
| Attribution (LO 89.i) | Neutral weights set with the client (bogey) (8.5) |

For style analysis, the coefficients “indicate a passive strategy that would match the risk exposures of the managed portfolio”, and the return differences between the managed portfolio and that matching portfolio measure performance. The weights are estimated from the fund’s own returns, not set by anyone.

**Applying it to this question**

The adviser recommends style analysis, so the yardstick is the coefficient-weighted passive style portfolio. The deciding fact is “passive” plus “weights from the regression”.

**Fragile fact.** Style benchmark weights are estimated (from returns), not chosen (by the client); and the benchmark is passive, not a peer average.

**Reference**

LO 89.e (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.3, “Style Analysis”): “Describe style analysis.” GARP Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Summary point 4 and Section 8.2, Style Analysis. Schweser: Module 89.3, Style Analysis, steps 1 and 3. GARP’s summary wording “performance relative to similar-style funds” refers to the matching passive portfolio, not to a peer average; Schweser’s quiz says so explicitly. Not a conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 e, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: comparison universe.** Ranking against actively managed peers is the comparison-universe method (and Morningstar-style peer groups), not style analysis. Correct if the adviser had recommended a universe comparison.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: Jensen’s alpha.** The SML distance is Jensen’s measure (LO 89.b). GARP’s Figure 8.4 shows the SML line only as a second, different benchmark. Correct if the stem asked about Jensen’s alpha.

c.reason: C restates GARP summary point 4 and Schweser’s Module Quiz 89.3 answer (“a passive benchmark of the same style”).

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** In style analysis the weights are estimated by the regression from the fund’s returns; neutral weights chosen by the client with the adviser define the attribution bogey of LO 89.i. Correct if the stem asked about the benchmark for performance attribution.
