questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 e Q12
questions.question: A regulator in Hong Kong is reviewing a fund’s marketing document, which states: “Like most mutual funds, our fund earns consistently positive residual returns relative to its style benchmark.” The regulator checks the claim against the evidence reported in the GARP reading on average residuals from style analysis across 636 mutual funds over 1985 to 1989. Which of the following assessments is most accurate?

options.text: The claim is supported: the distribution of average residuals across the funds had a positive mean, so consistently positive residual returns are common.
The claim is not supported: average residuals across the funds formed a bell-shaped distribution with a mean of about −0.074% per month, so consistently positive residual returns are hardly common.
The claim cannot be assessed: style analysis reports only the coefficients and the R-square, so it says nothing about a fund’s return relative to its style benchmark.
The claim is not supported: average residuals across the funds formed a bell-shaped distribution with a mean of about −0.074% per year, so consistently positive residual returns are hardly common.

questions.solution:
Hong Kong regulator: testing a marketing claim of “consistently positive residuals like most funds” against the 636-fund evidence.

**Concept and theory**

After the Magellan illustration GARP adds: “Of course, Magellan’s consistently positive residual return . . . is hardly common.” Figure 8.5 shows the frequency distribution of average residuals across 636 mutual funds (1985 to 1989, from Sharpe’s study, axis in % per month). “The distribution has the familiar bell shape, but with a slightly negative mean of −.074% per month.” So the typical fund did slightly worse than its style benchmark, and steady outperformance is the exception.

**Applying it to this question**

The claim has two parts: “most mutual funds” and “consistently positive”. The evidence: bell-shaped distribution, mean −0.074% per month (about −0.074 × 12 ≈ −0.9% per year in simple terms). Hence “most funds” do not earn positive residuals, and the claim is not supported.

**Fragile fact.** −0.074% per month, bell-shaped, slightly negative mean, 636 funds: consistent positive residuals are hardly common.

**Reference**

LO 89.e (Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.3, “Style Analysis”): “Describe style analysis.” GARP Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, Section 8.2, Style Analysis, Figure 8.5 (average residuals across 636 mutual funds, 1985 to 1989). Schweser: Module 89.3, Style Analysis, steps 1 and 3. Schweser does not report the 636-fund distribution (GARP-only content). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 e, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** The mean was slightly negative, not positive. A would be correct only if the cross-fund mean residual were positive.

b.reason: B states the shape, the sign, the size and the unit of the GARP evidence and draws GARP’s conclusion (“hardly common”).

c.reason: **Sibling swap / scope error.** Style analysis does report performance against the style benchmark: the intercept measures average selection return, and GARP’s Figures 8.4 and 8.5 are built on residuals. C would be correct only for a method that reported coefficients alone.

d.reason: **Time-unit slip.** GARP’s −0.074% is per month, not per year; the per-year figure would be roughly twelve times larger in magnitude. D would be correct only if the figure were stated per year.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 i Q1
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Frankfurt asset manager is presenting the firm’s performance attribution framework to newly hired analysts. She wants one slide that summarises how a standard attribution procedure is organised. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Attribution starts from the finest level, the choice of individual securities, and progressively aggregates upward until the broad asset market allocation is reached.

The difference between the managed portfolio and the bogey is expressed as the sum of the contributions of decisions taken at successive levels: asset market allocation, sector choice within each market, and security choice within each sector.
Attribution ranks each of the manager’s decisions by its contribution to the portfolio’s Sharpe ratio and Jensen’s alpha, so that every decision is judged on a risk-adjusted basis.
The difference explained by attribution is the gap between the managed portfolio and the median return of a comparison universe of funds following the same investment style.

questions.solution:
Induction slide: which statement best summarises how a standard performance attribution procedure is organised?

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens Section 8.5 by contrasting two questions. Risk-adjusted measures (Sharpe, Treynor, Jensen, information ratio, $\text{M}^{2}$) ask whether the manager’s return was adequate for the risk taken. Practitioners often want something different: they want to know which decisions produced superior or inferior performance. Portfolio managers make broad asset allocation decisions and then more detailed sector and security decisions within each asset class, so attribution decomposes overall performance into components that can each be identified with one level of the portfolio selection process.

The procedure has a direction and a structure. GARP: attribution “starts from the broadest asset allocation choices and progressively focuses on ever-finer details of portfolio choice.” The difference between the managed portfolio P and a benchmark portfolio B (the bogey) is expressed as the sum of the contributions of decisions at the various levels. One common system uses three components:

| Level | Decision | Measured against |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Broad asset market allocation (equity, fixed income, money market) | Neutral (benchmark) weights across markets |
| 2 | Industry (sector) choice within each market | Index sector weights within the market |
| 3 | Security choice within each sector | Sector returns of the index |

**Applying it to this question**

The slide must describe how the procedure is organised. The deciding facts are the direction (broad to fine), the object explained (managed portfolio minus bogey) and the three named levels. Only B carries all three without distortion.

**Fragile fact.** Direction is broad to fine (asset allocation first, securities last), and the residual explained is P minus the bogey, not minus a peer median or the risk-free rate.

**Reference**

LO 89.i: “Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.5 Performance Attribution Procedures, opening paragraphs. Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.3 (step 2 under “Style Analysis”) describes only the two-way split into asset allocation and selection; consistent with GARP, which is fuller.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 i, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the direction. GARP starts from the broadest asset allocation choice and moves to finer detail. A would be correct if the stem asked for the reverse of the standard procedure, or described a bottom-up aggregation report rather than attribution.

b.reason: GARP: “The difference between a managed portfolio’s performance and that of a benchmark portfolio then may be expressed as the sum of the contributions to performance of a series of decisions made at the various levels of the portfolio construction process,” with the three components (1) asset market allocation, (2) industry (sector) choice within each market and (3) security choice within each sector. B restates exactly this.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attaches the properties of the risk-adjusted measures (Section 8.1) to attribution. GARP introduces attribution precisely as the alternative: “Rather than focus on risk-adjusted returns, practitioners often want simply to ascertain which decisions resulted in superior or inferior performance.” C would be correct for a question about ranking managers with risk-adjusted measures.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** It replaces the bogey by a comparison universe. A comparison universe (median return of similar-style funds) is a separate, simpler performance yardstick in GARP’s chapter summary. The bogey is a passive portfolio built from neutral weights and index returns. D would be correct for a question on universe comparisons.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 i Q2
questions.question: A risk consultant engaged by a Singapore family office is designing the bogey against which an external balanced manager will be evaluated. The office’s investment committee has agreed neutral weights across equities, bonds and money market instruments with the consultant. Which of the following bogey designs is most consistent with the purpose of the bogey in performance attribution?

options.text: The manager’s actual asset class weights each month, applied to the return of the passive index for each asset class.
The agreed neutral weights, applied within each asset class to the median return of active funds investing in that class.
Weights that are reset each month to the manager’s tactical view of each market, applied to the return of the passive index for each class.
The agreed neutral weights, applied within each asset class to an indexed portfolio such as a broad market index for equities.

questions.solution:
Singapore family office: which bogey design fits the purpose of the bogey in attribution?

**Concept and theory**

The bogey is designed to measure the return the manager would earn by following a completely passive strategy. GARP says “passive” has two attributes here:

| Attribute | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 1. Across markets | Funds are allocated across broad asset classes at a usual or neutral allocation (passive asset market allocation). |
| 2. Within markets | Within each asset class the manager is assumed to hold an indexed portfolio, for example the S&P 500 for equities. |

Because the bogey rules out both asset allocation and security selection decisions, “any departure of the manager’s return from the passive benchmark must be due to either asset allocation bets (departures from the neutral allocation across markets) or security selection bets (departures from the passive index within asset classes).” Both attributes are needed for that clean split.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each design against the two attributes. Weights must be the agreed neutral weights (attribute

1) and the within-class return must be a passive index (attribute 2). Only D satisfies both.

**Fragile fact.** Two passive attributes: neutral weights across markets and an index within each market; drop either and one of the two decisions vanishes from the attribution.

**Reference**

LO 89.i: “Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.5 Performance Attribution Procedures, paragraph defining the bogey and the two attributes of “passive”. Schweser Reading 89 (step 2) uses benchmark weights and benchmark asset class returns implicitly; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 i, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error.** Actual weights at index returns is the hypothetical portfolio GARP uses inside the asset allocation step, not the bogey. Using it as the bogey makes the asset allocation contribution zero by construction, so allocation bets disappear from the attribution. A would be correct if the question asked which portfolio is compared with the bogey to isolate the allocation effect.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** The median active fund is a comparison-universe yardstick and is not passive; it fails attribute 2. Selection would then be measured against other managers’ active choices. B would be correct only if the stem were about a universe comparison.

c.reason: **Condition dropped.** Weights that follow the manager’s tactical views fail attribute 1: the bogey would absorb the very allocation bets the attribution is meant to measure. GARP requires neutral weights, and any deviation from them must be justified by a market view. C would be correct if the question asked what the managed portfolio’s weights reflect.

d.reason: D uses the agreed neutral weights and indexed portfolios within each class, which is GARP’s definition of the passive bogey. Departures then split exactly into allocation bets and selection bets.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 i Q3
questions.question: The chief investment officer of a Shanghai wealth management subsidiary is setting the neutral weights for two discretionary mandates. Client X, a young entrepreneur, is highly risk tolerant; Client Y, a retired couple, is risk averse. Both mandates will be evaluated with the same three-market attribution procedure. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The neutral weights should be determined in consultation with each client and will differ with risk tolerance, and any departure from them must be justified by a belief that a market will over- or underperform its usual risk-return profile.

The neutral weights should be chosen by the manager at the start of each period to maximise the mandate’s expected excess return, and the clients should then confirm that the chosen weights are acceptable.
The neutral weights should be identical for both clients and equal to the market-capitalisation weights of the three markets, since only a common bogey allows the two mandates to be compared.
The neutral weights may differ between the clients, but any departure from them during the period is credited to sector and security selection rather than to the asset allocation decision.

questions.solution:
Two clients with different risk tolerance: how should neutral weights be set and how are departures interpreted?

**Concept and theory**

The neutral weights are the first attribute of the bogey. GARP explains that weights designated as neutral “will depend on the risk tolerance of the investor and must be determined in consultation with the client.” Its illustration: risk-tolerant clients may direct neutral weights of 75% equity, 15% bonds and 10% cash equivalents; more risk-averse clients may set 45%/35%/20%, so their portfolios in normal circumstances carry less risk. “Any deviation from these weights must be justified by a belief that one or another market will either over- or underperform its usual risk-return profile.” Only intentional bets on market performance cause departures from the neutral profile, and those departures are what the asset allocation contribution measures.

**Applying it to this question**

Clients X and Y have very different risk tolerance, so their neutral weights should differ and be agreed with each client. During the period, departures are allocation bets that require a market view. A states both facts.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the client (in consultation) fixes the neutral weights; the manager’s departures from them are allocation bets.

**Reference**

LO 89.i: “Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.5 Performance Attribution Procedures, paragraph “It is worth briefly explaining the determination of the neutral allocation”. Schweser does not discuss neutral weights; GARP-only content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 i, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: A combines GARP’s two statements: neutral weights reflect the client’s risk tolerance and are set in consultation with the client, and any deviation must be justified by a belief about a market’s over- or underperformance.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** It gives the choice of neutral weights to the manager, period by period, to chase excess return. GARP assigns the decision to the client (in consultation), on the basis of risk tolerance; if the manager reset the neutral weights to his views, his allocation bets would be hidden inside the bogey. B would be correct if it described how the manager chooses the actual weights.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** It forces one set of weights on all clients. GARP’s own example gives different neutral weights to risk-tolerant and risk-averse clients. C would be correct only for two clients with identical risk tolerance and an agreed market-weight policy.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Departures from neutral weights are allocation bets, credited to the asset allocation decision; selection measures departures from the passive index within each class. D would be correct if it referred to departures from the index within a market.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-7 i Q4
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at an Australian superannuation fund is attributing one month of performance of an external balanced mandate (AUD 640 million). The bogey uses neutral weights and passive index returns; the mandate’s actual weights and its returns within each asset class are also shown.

| Market | Actual weight | Benchmark weight | Index return (%) | Portfolio return (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equity | 0.65 | 0.55 | 4.20 | 3.60 |
| Fixed income | 0.15 | 0.35 | 0.90 | 1.30 |
| Cash | 0.20 | 0.10 | 0.35 | 0.35 |

What is the contribution of the manager’s asset allocation decision to performance for the month?
questions.solution:
AUD balanced mandate: asset allocation contribution from actual and benchmark weights, with within-class portfolio returns as excess data.

**Concept and theory**

To isolate the asset allocation decision, GARP compares the performance of a hypothetical portfolio invested in the passive index for each market at the actual weights with one invested in each index at the benchmark weights. The difference measures the effect of shifting away from the benchmark weights “without allowing for any effects attributable to active management of the securities selected within each market.” Hence

Asset allocation contribution $= \sum_{\text{i}} (\text{w}_{\text{P,i}} - \text{w}_{\text{B,i}}) \text{r}_{\text{B,i}}$,

the excess (active) weight in each market times the index return of that market (GARP Table 8.7, Panel A: e.g. 0.10 × 5.81 − 0.23 × 1.45 + 0.13 × 0.48 = 0.3099%).

Active weights: equity 0.65 − 0.55 = +0.10; fixed income 0.15 − 0.35 = −0.20; cash 0.20 − 0.10 = +0.10.

Equity = +0.10 × 4.20 = +0.420%

Fixed income = −0.20 × 0.90 = −0.180%

Cash = +0.10 × 0.35 = +0.035%

Asset allocation = 0.420 − 0.180 + 0.035 = 0.275%

Meaning: the overweight in equity, the best-performing market, added 27.5 basis points. The AUD 640 million and the portfolio’s own returns are not used. (For the record: $\text{r}_{\text{P}} =$ 0.65(3.60) + 0.15(1.30) + 0.20(0.35) = 2.605%, $\text{r}_{\text{B}} =$ 0.55(4.20) + 0.35(0.90) + 0.10(0.35) = 2.660%, total excess −0.055%, so selection is −0.330%.)

**Fragile fact.** Allocation uses active weight times the index return; the portfolio’s own returns belong to selection.

**Reference**

LO 89.i: “Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.5 Performance Attribution Procedures, “Asset Allocation Decisions” and Table 8.7 Panel A. Schweser Reading 89 step 2 gives the same definition (formula image lost in extraction; the text “difference in returns attributable to active asset allocation decisions” and the zero-weight-difference remark pin it down). No conflict.

Valuing the weight shift at the manager’s own returns mixes selection into the allocation effect. A would be correct only if the manager had earned the index return in every market.

b.reason: **Intermediate or total result.** −0.055% is the aggregate contribution $\text{r}_{\text{P}} - \text{r}_{\text{B}}$, allocation plus selection (0.275 − 0.330). It would be correct if the question asked for total excess return over the bogey.

c.reason: C applies GARP’s rule: sum over all markets of the active weight times the index return of that market.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Japanese corporate pension fund is checking the attribution report for a balanced mandate of JPY 1.2 trillion. The mandate’s ex post tracking error over the past year was 2.1%. Data for the latest month are shown below.

| Market | Actual wt | Benchmark wt | Portfolio return (%) | Index return (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Domestic equity | 0.45 | 0.25 | 2.90 | 2.30 |
| Foreign equity | 0.30 | 0.25 | 1.10 | 1.60 |
| Bonds | 0.20 | 0.45 | 0.80 | 0.50 |
| Cash | 0.05 | 0.05 | 0.02 | 0.02 |

What is the contribution of selection within markets to the mandate’s performance relative to the bogey?
questions.solution:
JPY pension mandate: contribution of selection within markets, with AUM and tracking error as irrelevant inputs.

**Concept and theory**

Once asset allocation has been isolated, the rest of the excess return “must be attributable to sector selection and security selection within each market.” GARP measures it market by market as the managed portfolio’s excess performance within that market (portfolio return minus index return) weighted by the portfolio’s weight in that market (Table 8.7, Panel B: 1.47 × 0.70 + 0.44 × 0.07 = 1.06%):

Selection within markets $= \sum_{\text{i}} \text{w}_{\text{P,i}} (\text{r}_{\text{P,i}} - \text{r}_{\text{B,i}})$.

The actual weight is used because the selection skill was exercised on the money actually invested in each market.

**Applying it to this question**

Domestic equity = 0.45 × (2.90 − 2.30) = 0.45 × 0.60 = +0.270%

Foreign equity = 0.30 × (1.10 − 1.60) = 0.30 × (−0.50) = −0.150%

Bonds = 0.20 × (0.80 − 0.50) = 0.20 × 0.30 = +0.060%

Cash = 0.05 × 0 = 0

Selection = 0.270 − 0.150 + 0.060 = 0.180%

Check: allocation = 0.20(2.30) + 0.05(1.60) − 0.25(0.50) + 0 = 0.460 + 0.080 − 0.125 = 0.415%; $\text{r}_{\text{P}} =$ 1.796%, $\text{r}_{\text{B}} =$ 1.201%, total 0.595% = 0.415 + 0.180. The AUM and the 2.1% tracking error play no part.

**Fragile fact.** Selection is weighted by the actual portfolio weight, not by the benchmark weight (benchmark weights would give 0.25(0.60) + 0.25(−0.50) + 0.45(0.30) = 0.16%).

**Reference**

LO 89.i: “Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.5 Performance Attribution Procedures, “Sector and Security Selection Decisions” and Table 8.7 Panel B. Schweser step 2 “selection attribution” agrees (it includes sector allocation within asset classes in selection, as GARP’s 1.06% does). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 i, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: A weights each market’s excess over its index by the actual weight, as in GARP Table 8.7 Panel B.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: allocation for selection.** 0.415% is the asset allocation contribution. It would be correct if the question asked for the allocation decision.

c.reason: **Intermediate result: aggregate.** 0.595% is the total excess return over the bogey, allocation plus selection. Correct only if the question asked for the aggregate contribution.

d.reason: **Dropped term: weights omitted.** 0.60 − 0.50 + 0.30 + 0 = 0.40% adds the unweighted return differences. It would be correct only if every market carried a weight of 1, which is impossible in a portfolio whose weights sum to 1.

questions.question:
A member of the risk committee of a Canadian insurer is reviewing a validation memo on how the firm’s attribution system measures the asset allocation decision. The memo makes four statements.

I. The effect is isolated by comparing a hypothetical portfolio invested in the passive index for each market at the actual weights with one invested in each index at the benchmark weights.

II. The contribution equals the sum over all markets of the active (excess) weight in each market times the return of the index for that market.

III. A positive contribution arises from overweighting markets that turn out to perform well and underweighting markets that perform poorly.

IV. The contribution is calculated with the managed portfolio’s actual return in each market, so that it also captures the manager’s skill within each market.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
II and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Validation memo: which statements on how the asset allocation effect is measured are correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP describes the asset allocation step in three linked sentences: (1) to isolate the effect of the departure from neutral allocation, compare a hypothetical portfolio invested in a passive index for each market at the actual weights with one invested in each index at the benchmark weights; (2) this measures the shift away from benchmark weights “without allowing for any effects attributable to active management of the securities selected within each market”; (3) superior performance relative to the bogey comes from overweighting markets that turn out to perform well and underweighting poorly performing ones, and the contribution equals the sum over all markets of the excess (active) weight times the return of the index for that market.

**Applying it to this question**

I restates sentence (1): correct. II restates the formula: correct. III restates the source of a positive contribution: correct. IV says actual returns are used and that skill within markets is captured: this contradicts sentence (2). So I, II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Allocation is valued at index returns precisely to keep within-market skill out of it.

**Reference**

LO 89.i: “Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.5 Performance Attribution Procedures, “Asset Allocation Decisions”. Schweser step 2 adds that equal weights give zero allocation attribution; consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 i, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: **Incomplete set.** It omits III, which is a direct GARP statement. A would be correct if III had been corrupted (for example “overweighting markets that perform poorly”).

b.reason: B is the only option containing all three true statements and excluding IV.

c.reason: **Includes the false statement IV, omits I and III.** IV is a wrong input twin: it swaps the index return for the portfolio return, which would mix selection into allocation. C would be correct only if IV described the selection contribution and I were false.

d.reason: **Includes IV, omits II.** D would be correct only if the allocation effect were measured at actual returns, which GARP explicitly excludes.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Paris asset manager is attributing the equity component of a balanced fund for one month. The equity component returned 3.35% against 2.47% for its benchmark equity index. The equity component represents 60% of the total fund. Sector data are as follows.

| Sector | Portfolio weight (%) | Index weight (%) | Sector return (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Financials | 22 | 18 | 3.0 |
| Technology | 30 | 24 | 6.5 |
| Healthcare | 10 | 16 | 1.0 |
| Energy | 8 | 14 | −2.5 |
| Consumer | 30 | 28 | 2.0 |

What is the contribution of security selection within sectors to the performance of the equity component?
questions.solution:
Equity component of a EUR balanced fund: security selection within sectors after removing sector allocation.

**Concept and theory**

The selection contribution of a market can be partitioned further. GARP’s Table 8.8 analyses the equity component: for each sector, the contribution of sector allocation equals the active sector weight (portfolio weight minus index weight) times the sector’s return:

Sector allocation (within equity) $= \sum_{\text{s}} (\text{w}_{\text{P,s}} - \text{w}_{\text{I,s}}) \text{r}_{\text{s}}$.

The equity component’s total excess over its index is then split as

$\text{r}_{\text{P,eq}} - \text{r}_{\text{I,eq}} = \text{sector allocation} +$ security selection within sectors,

so security selection within sectors is the residual. In GARP, equity outperformed the S&P 500 by 1.47%, sector allocation gave 1.29%, and “the effect of security selection within sectors must have contributed an additional 1.47% − 1.29%, or .18%, to the performance of the equity component.”

**Applying it to this question**

Active sector weights (%): +4, +6, −6, −6, +2 (they sum to zero).

Sector allocation = 0.04(3.0) + 0.06(6.5) − 0.06(1.0) − 0.06(−2.5) + 0.02(2.0)

= 0.120 + 0.390 − 0.060 + 0.150 + 0.040 = 0.64%

Equity excess = 3.35 − 2.47 = 0.88%

Security selection within sectors = 0.88 − 0.64 = 0.24%

Check: the index return $\sum_{\text{s}} \text{w}_{\text{I,s}}\text{r}_{\text{s}} =$ 0.18(3.0) + 0.24(6.5) + 0.16(1.0) + 0.14(−2.5) + 0.28(2.0) = 2.47%, matching the stem. The underweight in energy (a falling sector) helps, as GARP’s “good performance derives from overweighting well performing sectors” implies.

**Fragile fact.** Within equity, security selection is the residual (excess minus sector allocation) and is stated per unit of the equity component until multiplied by the equity weight.

**Reference**

LO 89.i: “Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.5 Performance Attribution Procedures, “Sector and Security Selection Decisions”, Table 8.8. Schweser describes sector allocation as part of “selection” but gives no sector table; GARP used. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 i, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: **Intermediate result.** 0.64% is the sector allocation effect. It would be correct if the question asked for the sector allocation contribution.

b.reason: **Unit or scope slip.** 0.24 × 0.60 = 0.144% converts the effect into a contribution to the total fund. The question asks for the equity component. B would be correct if it asked for the contribution to total portfolio performance.

c.reason: **Intermediate result.** 0.88% is the equity component’s whole excess return, sector allocation plus security selection. Correct only if the question asked for the equity component’s excess over its index.

d.reason: D is the equity excess minus the sector allocation effect, the residual GARP attributes to security selection within sectors, expressed for the equity component as asked.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Toronto pension plan is preparing the attribution summary for the board. The fund’s benchmark weight in equity is 0.50 and its actual weight was 0.60. Within the equity component, sector allocation contributed 85 basis points and security selection within sectors contributed −20 basis points, so the equity component beat its index by 65 basis points. The fixed-income component, with an actual weight of 0.30, beat its index by 30 basis points.

How many basis points should the summary report as the equity component’s sector and security selection contribution to the total portfolio’s excess return?

options.text: 65.0 basis points
32.5 basis points
39.0 basis points
51.0 basis points

questions.solution:
CAD pension board summary: equity component’s sector and security selection contribution to total portfolio excess.

**Concept and theory**

Sector allocation and security selection within a market are measured per unit of that market’s component. To express them as a contribution to the total portfolio, GARP multiplies the component’s excess by the portfolio’s actual weight in that market. In Table 8.9: “The total equity excess performance of 147 basis points is multiplied by the 70% weight in equity to obtain contribution to portfolio performance,” giving 147 × 0.70 = 102.9 bp; fixed income adds 44 × 0.07 = 3.1 bp; with allocation of 31 bp, the total is 137 bp.

**Applying it to this question**

Equity component excess = 85 + (−20) = 65 bp

Contribution to total portfolio = 65 $\times\text{w}_{\text{P,eq}} =$ 65 × 0.60 = 39.0 bp

The fixed-income line is irrelevant to the equity contribution (it would add 30 × 0.30 = 9 bp of its own).

**Fragile fact.** Multiply by the actual market weight (0.60), and include both sector allocation and security selection.

**Reference**

LO 89.i: “Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.5 Performance Attribution Procedures, “Summing Up Component Contributions”, Table 8.9. Schweser has no equivalent table; GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 i, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: **Dropped scaling: unit slip.** 65 bp is the equity component’s excess over its index, not its contribution to the total portfolio. Correct if the question asked for the equity component’s own excess.

b.reason: **Wrong input twin: benchmark weight.** 65 × 0.50 = 32.5 bp uses the benchmark weight. Selection is weighted by the money actually invested, $\text{w}_{\text{P}}$. Correct only if the actual equity weight were 0.50.

c.reason: C scales the equity excess by the actual equity weight, exactly as in GARP Table 8.9.

d.reason: **Dropped term.** 85 × 0.60 = 51 bp scales only sector allocation and ignores the −20 bp security selection. Correct if the question asked for the sector allocation part alone.

questions.question:
A CRO at a US endowment is reviewing a global equity manager benchmarked to a world equity index. The manager may hold the four countries in any proportions. Results for the quarter are below.

| Country | Index wt | Manager wt | Manager return (%) | Country index return (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| UK | 0.15 | 0.25 | 9.0 | 6.0 |
| Japan | 0.20 | 0.10 | 4.0 | 5.0 |
| US | 0.55 | 0.50 | 7.0 | 8.0 |
| Germany | 0.10 | 0.15 | 3.0 | 1.0 |

Which of the following correctly states the contributions of the country allocation decision and of stock selection within countries?

options.text: Country allocation +0.30%; stock selection +0.45%
Country allocation −0.25%; stock selection −0.10%
Country allocation +0.25%; stock selection +0.45%
Country allocation −0.25%; stock selection +0.45%

questions.solution:
US endowment, global equity manager: country allocation and stock selection contributions.

**Concept and theory**

The same two-component attribution applies when the “markets” are countries: the bogey holds each country index at its index weight; country allocation is the active country weight times the country index return; stock selection is the manager’s weight in each country times her return in that country minus the country index return. Their sum is the aggregate contribution, the manager’s return minus the bogey (GARP Problem 12 sets up exactly this structure; the numbers here are original).

**Applying it to this question**

Country allocation = (0.25 − 0.15)6.0 + (0.10 − 0.20)5.0 + (0.50 − 0.55)8.0 + (0.15 − 0.10)1.0

= 0.60 − 0.50 − 0.40 + 0.05 = −0.25%

Stock selection = 0.25(3.0) + 0.10(−1.0) + 0.50(−1.0) + 0.15(2.0)

= 0.75 − 0.10 − 0.50 + 0.30 = +0.45%

$\text{r}_{\text{P}} =$ 0.25(9) + 0.10(4) + 0.50(7) + 0.15(3) = 6.60%

$\text{r}_{\text{B}} =$ 0.15(6) + 0.20(5) + 0.55(8) + 0.10(1) = 6.40%

Aggregate = 6.60 − 6.40 = 0.20% = −0.25 + 0.45 ✓

Meaning: underweighting the US, the best market, cost 25 bp; stock picking in the UK and Germany more than made up for it.

**Fragile fact.** Active weight is actual minus benchmark; allocation uses index returns, selection uses the manager’s weights. Check: the two must sum to $\text{r}_{\text{P}} - \text{r}_{\text{B}}$.

**Reference**

LO 89.i: “Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.5 Performance Attribution Procedures, Tables 8.6 and 8.7; end-of-chapter Problem 12 (structure only). Schweser: “the combination of the two attribution components (asset allocation plus selection) equals the aggregate contribution.” No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 i, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: **Wrong input twin in allocation.** Valuing active weights at the manager’s own returns: 0.10(9) − 0.10(4) − 0.05(7) + 0.05(3) = 0.90 − 0.40 − 0.35 + 0.15 = +0.30%. Correct only if the manager had earned the index return in every country.

b.reason: **Wrong input twin in selection: index weights.** 0.15(3) + 0.20(−1) + 0.55(−1) + 0.10(2) = 0.45 − 0.20 − 0.55 + 0.20 = −0.10%. Selection must use the manager’s weights. Correct only if her weights equalled the index weights.

c.reason: **Sign error in allocation.** Computing $(\text{w}_{\text{B}} - \text{w}_{\text{P}})\text{r}_{\text{B}}$ gives +0.25%. Correct only if the definition of active weight were reversed, which GARP does not do (active weight = actual minus benchmark).

d.reason: D gives both components correctly, and they sum to the aggregate contribution of +0.20%.

questions.question: A risk analyst at a London insurer is drafting a training note on the aggregate contribution in a two-component attribution (asset allocation and selection) of a multi-asset portfolio against its bogey. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.text: The selection contribution weights each market’s excess return over its index by the benchmark (neutral) weight of that market, so that it is independent of the manager’s allocation bets.
If the managed portfolio’s weights in every market equal the benchmark weights, the asset allocation contribution is zero.
If the manager earns exactly the index return within every market, the selection contribution is zero.
The asset allocation contribution plus the selection contribution equals the managed portfolio’s return minus the return of the bogey.

questions.solution:
Training note on aggregate contribution: which statement is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

Schweser’s step 2 states three properties of the two-component attribution, each consistent with GARP’s tables:

- If the managed portfolio’s estimated allocations equal the benchmark’s (passive asset allocation), the asset allocation attribution is zero, since every active weight is zero.
- If the manager has no superior selection ability, the returns earned within each asset class equal the benchmark asset class returns and the selection attribution is zero.
- Asset allocation plus selection equals the aggregate contribution, $\text{r}_{\text{P}} - \text{r}_{\text{B}}$.

The selection term is $\sum_{\text{i}} \text{w}_{\text{P,i}}(\text{r}_{\text{P,i}} - \text{r}_{\text{B,i}})$, with the portfolio’s actual weights (GARP Table 8.7 Panel B, column (4) “Portfolio Weight”).

**Applying it to this question**

B, C and D restate the three properties. A replaces the actual weights by the benchmark weights in the selection term. With benchmark weights the two components no longer sum to $\text{r}_{\text{P}} - \text{r}_{\text{B}}$ (a cross term would be left over), so A is the false statement.

**Fragile fact.** Qualifier is NOT: pick the false statement. The false one swaps actual weights for benchmark weights in the selection term.

**Reference**

LO 89.i: “Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.” Schweser Reading 89, Module 89.3, step 2 under “Style Analysis” (the zero conditions and the aggregate contribution); GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.5 Performance Attribution Procedures, Table 8.7 Panel B. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 i, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: GARP weights each market’s excess performance by the portfolio weight (0.70 for equity, 0.07 for fixed income, giving 1.06%). A misassigns the weight, so it is not correct.

b.reason: **True.** Zero active weights give a zero allocation term. It would become false under an absolute-claim corruption such as “the allocation contribution is zero whenever the total weight in risky assets is unchanged”.

c.reason: **True.** Zero within-market excess returns give a zero selection term. It would become false if it said selection is zero whenever the weights equal the benchmark weights (a sibling swap).

d.reason: **True.** The identity $\text{r}_{\text{P}} - \text{r}_{\text{B}} = \text{allocation} +$ selection holds exactly with actual-weight selection (see the notation section). It would be false if “bogey” were replaced by “risk-free rate”.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Brazilian pension fund finds that the bogey for a balanced mandate was built with neutral weights of 60% equity, 30% bonds and 10% cash, whereas the investment policy agreed with the trustees specifies 50% equity, 40% bonds and 10% cash. The mandate’s actual weights, its returns within each market and the index returns are unaffected. If the attribution for the month is rerun with the correct neutral weights, which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The contribution of selection within markets changes, because each market’s excess return over its index is now weighted by the corrected neutral weights.
The asset allocation contribution is unchanged, because the manager’s actual weights and the index returns used to value them are unaffected by the correction.
The bogey return and the asset allocation contribution change, the selection contribution is unchanged, and the change in total excess return equals the change in the asset allocation contribution.
Neither the asset allocation contribution nor the total excess return changes, because the aggregate contribution is fixed by the portfolio’s actual return.

questions.solution:
BRL pension: rerunning the attribution with corrected neutral weights, which effects change?

**Concept and theory**

The neutral weights enter the attribution in exactly two places: the bogey $\text{r}_{\text{B}} = \sum_{\text{i}} \text{w}_{\text{B,i}}\text{r}_{\text{B,i}}$ and the active weights in the asset allocation term $\sum_{\text{i}}(\text{w}_{\text{P,i}} - \text{w}_{\text{B,i}})\text{r}_{\text{B,i}}$. The selection term $\sum_{\text{i}} \text{w}_{\text{P,i}}(\text{r}_{\text{P,i}} - \text{r}_{\text{B,i}})$ contains no benchmark weight. GARP’s Concept Check 8.5(a) changes the benchmark weights to 70/25/5: the bogey rises to 4.45% and the asset allocation contribution becomes −0.17%, while the selection result is changed only in part (b), where the S&P 500 return itself changes.

**Applying it to this question**

Moving 10 points of neutral weight from equity to bonds changes $\text{r}_{\text{B}}$ by −0.10 $\text{r}_{\text{B,eq}} +$ 0.10 $\text{r}_{\text{B,bd}}$ and changes the allocation term by the same amount with the opposite sign. $\text{r}_{\text{P}}$ is unchanged, so the change in total excess $\text{r}_{\text{P}} - \text{r}_{\text{B}}$ equals the change in the asset allocation contribution; selection is untouched.

**Fragile fact.** Neutral weights live in the bogey and the allocation term only; selection uses actual weights.

**Reference**

LO 89.i: “Describe and apply performance attribution procedures, including the asset allocation decision, sector and security selection decision, and the aggregate contribution.” GARP Chapter 8, Section 8.5 Performance Attribution Procedures, Concept Check 8.5 and its solution. Schweser has no equivalent; GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-7 i, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Selection is weighted by the actual portfolio weights, not the neutral weights, so it does not change. A would be correct if the index return within a market were corrected (as in Concept Check 8.5(b)).

b.reason: **Scope error.** The allocation term depends on $\text{w}_{\text{P,i}} - \text{w}_{\text{B,i}}$, so correcting $\text{w}_{\text{B,i}}$ changes it even though $\text{w}_{\text{P,i}}$ is unchanged. B would be correct if only the managed portfolio’s actual returns were corrected.

c.reason: C states all three consequences: bogey and allocation change, selection does not, and the change in total excess equals the change in allocation. This follows from GARP’s definitions and is illustrated by Concept Check 8.5(a).

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** $\text{r}_{\text{P}}$ is fixed but $\text{r}_{\text{B}}$ is not, so the aggregate contribution $\text{r}_{\text{P}} - \text{r}_{\text{B}}$ changes. D would be correct only if the corrected weights happened to give the same bogey return (for example if equity and bonds had equal index returns).

| Equity: security selection within sectors (within equity component) | 90 |

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Singapore pension fund is preparing an onboarding slide for newly hired analysts that explains how the fund’s external equity long/short manager builds and manages its portfolio. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Because the long and short books are matched to hedge market risk, the manager’s factor exposures beyond beta are removed automatically, so factor models add little.
If two long positions offer the same expected revaluation, the one expected to converge to the manager’s forecast value sooner is the more valuable position.
Holding-period discipline matters most on the long side, since that is where adverse price moves trigger costly margin calls or a forced exit at a large loss.
The manager’s alpha comes mainly from forecasting the direction of the broad equity market, with individual positions chosen chiefly to express that view.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst’s onboarding slide on how an equity long/short manager builds and manages positions.

**Concept and theory**

An equity long/short strategy is built on fundamental company analysis that weighs the risks and opportunities coming from a firm’s industry, geography and the wider macroeconomic environment. The manager buys securities it judges underpriced and sells short related securities it judges overpriced. Two goals sit side by side: exploit mispricings (the alpha) and hedge overall market risk (the short book offsets much of the long book’s beta). When security selection is good, alpha is earned on both sides of the book.

Two further building blocks matter:

- **Investment horizon.** For every position the manager sets the period over which it expects the price to converge to its forecast value. A position that delivers its expected revaluation sooner is worth more, because the same gain is earned over less time and capital is freed for the next idea.
- **Residual factor exposures.** Hedging beta does not remove every common exposure. Managers use advanced factor models to mitigate the factor exposures that remain beyond beta. The GARP Fung and Hsieh chapter adds that long/short equity funds empirically keep some directional market exposure and a long small-cap, short large-cap tilt, which is exactly the kind of residual exposure a factor model is meant to manage.

| Feature | What the source says |
|---|---|
| Return engine | Security selection (alpha) on longs and shorts |
| Market risk | Reduced by the short book, not eliminated |
| Residual factors | Managed with advanced factor models |
| Horizon | Set per position; faster convergence is more valuable |
| Most horizon-sensitive side | Shorts (margin calls, short squeeze) |

**Applying it to this question**

The slide must describe how the manager builds and manages positions. Test each statement against the source: (A) claims residual factor exposures vanish automatically; (B) concerns the horizon and speed of convergence; (C) concerns which side of the book is most sensitive to the holding period; (D) concerns where alpha comes from. Only B matches the source without alteration.

**Fragile fact.** Horizon matters most for the short side; faster convergence makes a position more valuable; factor models handle exposures beyond beta.

**Reference**

LO 90.a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.1, “Equity Long/Short Strategy”. GARP text in the project has no matching section for this Stowell and Stowell reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. Supplementary GARP passage (Chapter 9 Hedge Funds, Fung and Hsieh, long/short equity discussion, garp\_rmim.txt lines 14648 to 14687): directional exposure and small-cap tilt; consistent with Schweser, no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 a, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** The source says the primary goal is to reduce market risk, and that managers also use advanced factor models to mitigate remaining factor exposures beyond beta. Matching books does not remove those exposures automatically. The statement would be correct only for a hypothetical book hedged on every factor, which is not what the strategy promises.

b.reason: Schweser states that managers set an investment horizon for each position, the period over which valuation is expected to converge to the forecast, and that “positions that realize their expected revaluation more quickly are considered more valuable.” With identical expected revaluation, the faster-converging long is therefore the more valuable position.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** The holding period is described as especially important for short positions, because rising prices can trigger costly margin calls or a short squeeze that forces closure at a large loss. Assigning that sensitivity to the long side moves the risk to the wrong actor. It would be correct if the stem asked about the short book.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Forecasting the direction of broad markets and expressing it in positions is the global macro engine. Long/short equity earns alpha from security selection while hedging market direction. The statement would fit a global macro manager.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Canadian life insurer is reviewing how the administrator of an equity long/short fund classified four items in the fund’s annual return attribution.

| Item | Description | Classified as |
|---|---|---|
| I | Interest earned on the cash proceeds of short sales, net of broker and securities-lender fees | Source of return |
| II | Dividends on the shares the fund has borrowed and sold short | Source of return |
| III | Interest earned on the liquidity buffer posted at the start of the strategy to cover daily mark-to-market adjustments | Cost |
| IV | Fees paid to borrow shares for the short positions | Cost |

Which of the items are classified correctly?

options.text: I, II and IV only
I, III and IV only
IV only
I and IV only

questions.solution:
Auditor checks how four items in a long/short fund’s return attribution were classified.

**Concept and theory**

A long/short fund’s economics are more than its stock-picking alpha, because the short book creates cash flows of its own. When the fund sells borrowed shares, it receives cash. That cash, held with the broker, earns interest, and the fund keeps that interest after the broker’s and securities lender’s fees: this is the **interest rebate**. At the start of the strategy the fund also posts a **liquidity** **buffer** to cover daily mark-to-market adjustments, and that buffer earns interest too.

Against these, the fund bears costs created by borrowing and by leverage: financing charges on margin loans, fees paid to borrow shares, any **dividends owed on borrowed shares** (the short seller must compensate the lender for dividends paid while the shares are on loan), and transaction costs.

| Sources of return | Costs |
|---|---|
| Alpha on long positions | Financing charges on margin loans |
| Alpha on short positions | Fees to borrow shares for shorts |
| Interest rebate (net of broker and lender fees) | Dividends owed on borrowed shares |
| Interest on the liquidity buffer | Transaction costs |

**Applying it to this question**

- I, interest on short proceeds net of fees, classified as a source: **correct** (interest rebate).
- II, dividends on borrowed shares, classified as a source: **incorrect**; the fund owes these to the lender, so they are a cost.
- III, interest on the liquidity buffer, classified as a cost: **incorrect**; it is a source of return.
- IV, fees to borrow shares, classified as a cost: **correct**.

Correctly classified: I and IV only.

**Fragile fact.** Dividends on borrowed shares flow out of the fund; liquidity-buffer interest flows in; the rebate is income after fees.

**Reference**

LO 90.a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.1, “Equity Long/Short Strategy” (sources of return and costs); Key Concepts LO 90.a. GARP text in the project has no matching section for this Stowell and Stowell reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 a, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Accepting II means treating dividends on the shorted shares as received. The short seller pays them to the lender, so the direction is reversed. Dividends would be a source only for shares the fund owns, for example in a long position.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Accepting III treats the liquidity buffer’s interest like its sibling, the financing charge on margin loans. The buffer is cash the fund posts and earns interest on; the margin loan is money the fund borrows and pays interest on. B would be right if item III described margin loan financing.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Rejecting I because the rebate is “net of fees” confuses the condition attached to the item with its sign. The netting reduces the rebate but it remains income. C would be right only if the fees exceeded the interest so the net figure were a charge.

d.reason: Schweser lists the interest rebate “net of broker and securities-lender fees” as a source of return and “fees paid to borrow shares for short positions” as a cost. Items I and IV match; II and III are reversed.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Japanese life insurer that is invested in an equity long/short fund is estimating the fund’s return for the year, before management and performance fees, as a percentage of beginning capital. The long and short books were beta-matched, and the alpha figures already exclude all market and factor contributions.

| Item | JPY million |
|---|---|
| Beginning capital | 10,000 |
| Alpha on long positions | 640 |
| Alpha on short positions | 330 |
| Interest on short-sale cash proceeds, before fees | 150 |
| Broker and securities-lender fees charged against that interest | 35 |
| Interest earned on the liquidity buffer | 55 |
| Financing charges on margin loans | 90 |
| Dividends on borrowed shares | 70 |
| Transaction costs | 45 |
| Broad equity index return for the year | 11.0% |

What is the fund’s return for the year before management and performance fees?
questions.solution:
Treasury analyst computes a JPY long/short fund’s pre-fee annual return from alpha, short-side income and costs.

**Concept and theory**

The return of an equity long/short fund (before management and performance fees) is the sum of its sources of return less its costs, divided by capital. With beta-matched books and alpha stated net of market and factor effects, the market return contributes nothing further.

R $= \frac{\alpha_{\text{L}} + \alpha_{\text{S}} + (\text{I}_{\text{short}} - \text{F}_{\text{lend}}) + \text{I}_{\text{buffer}} - \text{C}_{\text{margin}} - \text{D}_{\text{borrowed}} - \text{C}_{\text{trans}}}{\text{K}}$

where $\alpha_{\text{L}}$, $\alpha_{\text{S}}$ are alpha on long and short positions; $\text{I}_{\text{short}}$ is interest on short-sale proceeds before fees; $\text{F}_{\text{lend}}$ is broker and securities-lender fees (so $\text{I}_{\text{short}} - \text{F}_{\text{lend}}$ is the interest rebate); $\text{I}_{\text{buffer}}$ is interest on the liquidity buffer; $\text{C}_{\text{margin}}$ is margin financing; $\text{D}_{\text{borrowed}}$ is dividends owed on borrowed shares; $\text{C}_{\text{trans}}$ is transaction costs; K is beginning capital.

**Applying it to this question**

All figures in JPY million.

Total alpha = 640 + 330 = 970

Interest rebate = 150 − 35 = 115

Total sources = 970 + 115 + 55 = 1,140

Total costs = 90 + 70 + 45 = 205

Net result = 1,140 − 205 = 935

R = 935/10,000 = 9.35%

The broad index return of 11.0% is irrelevant: the books are beta-matched and alpha already excludes market and factor contributions. The fund earned 9.35% on capital, of which about 9.70 percentage points came from stock selection, with the short-side income and costs netting to a small drag.

**Fragile fact.** The rebate is income net of fees; dividends on borrowed shares are a cost; with beta-matched books the index return is a distractor.

**Reference**

LO 90.a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.1, “Equity Long/Short Strategy” (sources of return and costs). GARP text in the project has no matching section for this Stowell and Stowell reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 a, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: It applies exactly the Schweser classification: alpha on both books, the interest rebate net of broker and lender fees, and buffer interest as sources; margin financing, dividends owed on borrowed shares and transaction costs as costs.

b.reason: Treating dividends on borrowed shares as income instead of a cost: 935 + 2 × 70 = 1,075, giving 10.75%. It would be right only if the fund held those shares long rather than owing their dividends to the lender.

c.reason: Using the gross short-sale interest and dropping the broker and lender fees: 935 + 35 = 970, giving 9.70% (coincidentally equal to the alpha figure). It would be right if the stem gave the interest already net of fees.

d.reason: Stopping at total sources, 1,140, before deducting the 205 of costs. It would be right if the question asked for gross income before costs.

| Short 2 | 30 | 3.75 | 3 |
| Short 3 | 22 | 2.75 | 4 |
| Short 4 | 18 | 2.25 | 2 |

Which recommendation is most consistent with the management of short-position risk described for equity long/short strategies?

- Short 2: 30, 3.75%: above the band; cut.
- Short 3: 22, 2.75%: inside the band.
- Shorts 4 and 5: 2.25% and 1.75%: at or below the band.

The expected holding periods are context only; they do not change the size limit.

questions.solution:
Consultant’s presentation on a GBP allocation to a dedicated short fund; find the least accurate statement.

**Concept and theory**

A dedicated short (short-biased) strategy specialises in identifying overpriced securities and selling them short. Why does such a niche exist? Mutual funds are built to find positive-alpha stocks. They typically do not short; at most they underweight stocks with negative alpha. Overvalued securities therefore receive little attention, which leaves room for specialists who develop expertise in reading the signs of overvaluation: aggressive accounting, potential legal issues, and management attempts to obscure negative information. The GARP Fung and Hsieh chapter adds that detailed company research is the core alpha driver and that a focus on firms with weak cash flow generation is common; such funds take more short positions than long ones and so hold net short exposure.

The risk profile is harsh. Positions can be forced shut by margin calls, short squeezes and forced covering driven by risk-management constraints, regardless of whether the valuation thesis is still right. And there is a structural headwind: **market prices tend to rise over time**, so short positions carry a bias toward negative returns. Without specialised insight, a short seller is likely to lose money while taking significant risk. GARP’s regression of the dedicated short bias index on the S&P index gives a slope of −0.81, confirming strong negative correlation with equities.

The qualifier is least accurate, so three statements match the source and one corrupts it. A (mutual funds underweight rather than short), B (accounting, legal and disclosure red flags) and C (margin calls, squeezes, risk-limit covering) each restate the source. D states the direction of the long-run market drift backwards and draws the wrong conclusion from it.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Frankfurt hedge fund running a nonhedged equity strategy believes a mid-cap industrial stock trading at EUR 50.00 is modestly undervalued and will rise about 12% over six months. She implements a bull call spread using the EUR 50 and EUR 56 strike six-month calls. Each call pays max$(\text{S}_{\text{T}} -$ K, 0) at expiry; ignore financing costs and fees.

| Strike (EUR) | Call premium (EUR) |
|---|---|
| 50 | 3.20 |
| 56 | 0.90 |
| 60 | 0.40 |

If the stock ends at exactly EUR 56.00 at expiry, what is the return on the net premium paid for the spread?
questions.solution:
EUR nonhedged equity manager uses a 50/56 bull call spread; return on net premium if the stock ends at EUR 56.

**Concept and theory**

A nonhedged equity strategy is long only and based on fundamental analysis of individual firms or industries. Unlike a mutual fund, which may find a small expected gain not worth detailed analysis, a hedge fund can concentrate on one stock, assess its upside and downside, and use leverage to amplify even a small mispricing. One tool the source names is the **bull call spread**: buy a call with a lower strike and sell a call with a higher strike. The sold call cheapens the position by giving up gains above the higher strike, which costs little if the expected rise is modest (the source cites 10% to 15%). The payoff at expiry, for strikes $\text{K}_{1} < \text{K}_{2}$ with premiums $\text{c}_{1} \text{and c}_{2}$:

Short 56 call payoff $= - \text{max}($56 − 56, 0) = 0.00

Spread payoff = 6.00

Profit = 6.00 − 2.30 = 3.70

The nonhedged fund relies mainly on broad diversification to manage risk, whereas the mutual fund concentrates on a few high-conviction stocks.

| Emphasis | Expected returns | Upside and downside of each stock |
| Risk management | Portfolio diversification | Concentrated, researched positions |
| Small mispricings | May not justify detailed analysis | Worth pursuing, amplified with leverage |
| Tools | Long stock | Long stock, leverage, derivatives (e.g., bull call spread) |

A global macro fund makes large, leveraged bets on anticipated price movements across broad equity and fixed-income markets, interest rates, foreign exchange and commodities, often through options, swaps and futures on a wide range of underlying asset classes and indices. Its defining freedom is **broad discretion**: unlike mutual funds restricted to their mandated areas, global macro managers can allocate across sectors, regions and asset classes. The source adds that these funds tend to trade **more liquid** instruments, which suits large positions that must be resized as views change.

**Fragile fact.** Global macro trades more liquid instruments and has broad discretion; mutual funds are the ones bound by mandates.

The CRO of a US university endowment is comparing a global macro fund with an emerging markets fund before a USD 75 million allocation and has written four statements.

I. Both strategies may take positions in fixed-income instruments.

II. The global macro manager has broad discretion across regions and asset classes, whereas the emerging markets manager’s universe is the securities of developing countries.

III. The emerging markets manager needs deep insight into the specific markets it invests in, in addition to fundamental valuation skill.

IV. Global macro funds tend to trade less liquid instruments than emerging markets funds, so liquidity constraints are a smaller concern for emerging markets funds.

II and III only

| Dimension | Global macro | Emerging markets |
|---|---|---|
| Universe | Equity and fixed-income markets, rates, FX, commodities, globally | Corporate securities and sovereign debt of developing countries |

| Edge | Anticipating international macro trends | Fundamental valuation plus deep local insight |

- III: the source requires both fundamental valuation skill and deep insight into the specific markets. **Correct.**

An emerging markets strategy invests in the securities of developing countries, both corporate securities and sovereign debt. These economies are typically characterised by rapid growth and ongoing industrialisation, which is the source of the higher expected return. Success requires strong fundamental valuation skill and deep insight into the specific markets. |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| Q | Global macro | 400 | 1,300 | 700 | Futures, swaps and options on bond and equity indices, currencies and commodities | 2.0 |

Fund Q

| Strategy | Footprint |
|---|---|
| Equity long/short | Longs and shorts in related securities; market risk reduced, not zero; factor models for residual exposures |
| Nonhedged equity | Long only, may be leveraged and use derivatives; full market exposure |
| Global macro | Large, leveraged positions across equity, fixed income, rates, FX and commodities, often in derivatives |
| Emerging markets | Corporate securities and sovereign debt of developing countries |

- Q: gross notional 1,300 + 700 = 2,000 on capital of 400, i.e. 5×, in multi-asset derivatives: consistent with global macro.
- R: (290 − 280)/300 ≈ 3% net long, every long paired with a related short: a hedged book.
- S: long only in developing-country equities, corporate bonds and sovereign debt: consistent with emerging markets.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a US endowment is stress testing three equity-based hedge fund holdings against a sudden 15% rally in the broad equity market, with no change in the fundamentals of any position. Assume every position has a beta of about 1.

| Fund | Long (% of capital) | Short (% of capital) |
|---|---|---|
| Nonhedged equity | 130 | 0 |
| Equity long/short | 110 | 90 |
| Dedicated short | 0 | 100 |

Which of the following statements about the likely effect of the rally is most accurate?

options.text: The nonhedged fund would gain roughly 1.3 times the market move, while the long/short fund’s market-driven gain would be far smaller, since its short book offsets most of the move.
The long/short fund would be the most exposed of the three, because holding a short book leaves an equity long/short fund net short the market by design.
The dedicated short fund would be largely protected, because the interest rebate on its short-sale proceeds offsets the losses caused by rising prices.
The nonhedged fund would be largely unaffected, because its returns depend on fundamental analysis of individual firms rather than on the market.

questions.solution:
Stress test of three equity-based funds against a sudden 15% market rally.

**Concept and theory**

The three equity-based strategies sit at different points on the market-exposure spectrum, and that position drives their response to a broad market move.

- **Nonhedged equity**: long only, often leveraged; retains full market exposure, and leverage amplifies it.
- **Equity long/short**: shorts in related securities offset much of the long book’s market exposure; the aim is to reduce market risk, so the market-driven result is small relative to the move (GARP notes some directional exposure remains).
- **Dedicated short**: net short; rising prices cause losses and trigger margin calls, short squeezes and forced covering.

With all betas near 1, the first-order market effect is Net exposure × market move, where net exposure is long minus short as a fraction of capital.

**Applying it to this question**

First-order market effect $= \text{net exposure} \times$ 15%:

Nonhedged: (1.30 − 0) × 15% = +19.5%

Long/short: (1.10 − 0.90) × 15% = +3.0%

Dedicated short: (0 − 1.00) × 15% = −15.0%

The nonhedged fund gains about 1.3 times the market move; the long/short fund gains far less because its 90% short book offsets most of the 110% long book; the dedicated short fund loses and faces margin calls and squeeze risk.

**Fragile fact.** Ranking of market exposure: nonhedged (full, levered) > long/short (reduced) > dedicated short (negative).

**Reference**

LO 90.a: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles. Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.1, “Equity Long/Short Strategy”, “Dedicated Short (Short-Biased) Strategy”, “Nonhedged Equity Strategy”; Key Concepts LO 90.a. GARP text in the project has no matching section for this Stowell and Stowell reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The interest rebate is a modest income stream on short-sale proceeds; it cannot offset a 15% loss on a 100% short book, and rising prices are precisely what trigger the strategy’s margin calls and squeezes. C would need a tiny market move relative to the rebate.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a multi-strategy hedge fund in Singapore is preparing onboarding notes on which situations the fund’s arbitrage desks look for. She lists four situations recently observed on the trading floor.

I. Shares of one company, listed on two exchanges, trade at SGD 12.40 on one and at the equivalent of SGD 12.58 on the other, with negligible conversion and settlement costs.

II. Two bonds of the same issuer, whose remaining coupons and principal are virtually identical in amount and timing, trade 1.6 points apart.

III. A contract that will pay a known SGD 1,000,000 in one year trades today at SGD 951,000, while discounting that known amount at the one-year risk-free rate gives about SGD 968,500.

IV. An analyst’s discounted cash flow model values a stock 20% above its market price because she expects margins to expand faster than the consensus forecast.

Which of these situations fit the description of the opportunities that arbitrage strategies look for?

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Singapore analyst classifies four situations (dual listing, twin bonds, known future payoff, DCF view) against the arbitrage definition.

**Concept and theory**

An arbitrage strategy does not bet on where a price is going; it bets on a relationship between prices that should hold but temporarily does not. Schweser opens Module 90.2 by naming three situations that arbitrageurs look for:

| Situation | What should hold |
|---|---|
| Same asset, different prices in different markets | One price for one asset (law of one price) |
| Two assets with similar cash flows, priced differently | Equal cash flows deserve equal prices |
| Asset with a known future price whose current value does not equal its risk-free discounted price | Price today = known future value discounted at the risk-free rate |

In each case the arbitrageur can buy the cheap side, sell the rich side (or the replicating position), and earn a profit when the relationship is restored. The view needed is about convergence, not about the direction of the market or about a firm’s future fundamentals.

**Applying it to this question**

I: one company’s shares at SGD 12.40 and SGD 12.58 in two markets with negligible frictions is the first situation. II: two bonds of the same issuer with virtually identical cash flows priced 1.6 points apart is the second. III: a known SGD 1,000,000 in one year should be worth about SGD 968,500 today; it trades at SGD 951,000, so its price does not reflect the risk-free discounted value, which is the third. IV: the analyst’s DCF value is a forecast of fundamentals (margin expansion); there is no second price, twin asset or known future value to converge to, so it is a directional, fundamental view, not an arbitrage situation.

**Fragile fact.** “Mispriced relative to my forecast” is not arbitrage; arbitrage needs a pricing relationship (same asset, same cash flows, or a known future value) to converge to.

**Reference**

LO 90.b: “Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.” Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.2, opening paragraph of “Arbitrage Strategies”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 b, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: **Scope error, condition dropped.** It keeps the first two situations but drops the third, the known-future-price case. It would be right only if the definition were limited to the law of one price and twin cash flows.

b.reason: **Scope error, condition dropped.** It drops situation I, the same asset in two markets, which is the purest of the three. It would be right only if the stem said the two listings carried materially different rights or significant conversion costs.

c.reason: I, II and III map one to one onto the three situations Schweser lists (“the same asset trades at different prices in different markets, two assets with similar cash flows are priced differently, or an asset with a known future price trades today at a value that does not reflect its risk-free discounted price”). IV fits none of them.

d.reason: **Scope error, overextension.** It treats any perceived mispricing as an arbitrage. A fundamental valuation gap is the domain of long-only or long/short stock picking (LO 90.a), not arbitrage. D would be right only if IV described a second, near-identical instrument trading at a different price.
