| W | Buys S&P/TSX 60 index futures trading cheap to the index and shorts an algorithm-selected subset of the constituents | Relative value arbitrage |
| X | Buys a CAD convertible bond and shorts the issuer’s common shares in a delta-based quantity | Fixed-income arbitrage, since the long leg is a bond |
| Y | Shorts the newest benchmark government bond and buys a slightly older, cheaper issue of almost the same maturity | Relative value arbitrage, specifically pairs trading |
| Z | Buys one bank stock and shorts a competing bank stock after their historically correlated prices diverge with no news | Statistical arbitrage, since it relies on a factor model across many positions |

Which of the analyst’s labels is correct?

options.text: Trade W
Trade X
Trade Y
Trade Z

questions.solution:
Canadian pension CRO checks an analyst’s labels for four hedge fund trades (index futures vs constituents, convertible, on-the-run, bank pair).

**Concept and theory**

Schweser groups the arbitrage strategies of this LO into three families, distinguished by what is traded and what relationship is expected to restore itself.

| Family | What it trades | Examples in the reading |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed-income arbitrage | Long/short among fixed-income securities whose yields or prices have diverged | Hedged Italian bonds vs Treasuries; on-the-run vs off-the-run Treasuries |
| Convertible arbitrage | Long the convertible, short the issuer’s stock, delta hedged | Monetizing volatility, carry, cheap embedded options |
| Relative value arbitrage | Pricing inefficiencies across related assets | Pairs trading (two peers); statistical arbitrage (many positions, factor models, liquidity provision); index futures vs constituents |

Within relative value, pairs trading is two firms that are competitors or peers; statistical arbitrage “extends this idea across a large number of long and short positions, often using factor models”. GARP Chapter 9 describes fixed-income arbitrage in the same way, as exploiting price anomalies “between related fixed income securities” while hedging market and interest rate risk, and convertible arbitrage as buying convertibles and shorting the corresponding stock.

**Applying it to this question**

W: buying index futures and shorting an algorithm-selected subset of constituents is the reading’s own example of relative value arbitrage, so the label is right. X: the trade is the definition of convertible arbitrage; that one leg is a bond does not make it fixed-income arbitrage. Y: shorting the newest benchmark and buying a slightly older, cheaper issue is the on-the-run/off-the-run trade, listed under fixed-income arbitrage. Z: one bank against a competing bank after an unexplained divergence is pairs trading, not statistical arbitrage, which spans many positions.

**Fragile fact.** Classify by what is traded and what converges: two peers = pairs; many names with factor models = statistical arbitrage; bonds against bonds = fixed-income arbitrage; convertible against its own stock = convertible arbitrage.

**Reference**

LO 90.b: “Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.” Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.2, sections “Fixed-Income Arbitrage”, “Convertible Arbitrage” and “Relative Value Arbitrage”; Key Concepts LO 90.b. No GARP chapter matches this reading; GARP used for depth only: GARP Ch. 9 Hedge Funds, “Relative Value and Arbitrage-like Hedge Fund Styles” (fixed-income and convertible arbitrage index descriptions). No conflict with Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 b, where it is Q2 of 14.

a.reason: Schweser places “trading equity index futures and their underlying constituents when mispricing occurs” under Relative Value Arbitrage, including the use of algorithms to select “an optimal subset to trade”. Trade W is labeled exactly that.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attributes the fixed-income arbitrage label to convertible arbitrage because of the bond leg. The label would be right only if both legs were fixed-income securities, for example two bonds of different issuers whose hedged yields diverged.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It moves the on-the-run/off-the-run trade from fixed-income arbitrage into pairs trading. Pairs trading in the reading is about two peer firms’ shares. The label would be right if the trade were in two peer companies’ stocks.

d.reason: **Sibling swap within relative value.** It gives the two-stock trade the defining property of statistical arbitrage (a large number of positions selected with factor models). The label would be right if the desk ran hundreds of long and short positions chosen by a factor model.

questions.question:
A risk consultant at an Australian superannuation fund is validating an external manager’s fixed-income arbitrage book. Over the past five years the AUD-hedged yield on a foreign government bond (Bond P) has stayed within 10 bp of the yield on an Australian Commonwealth bond of similar maturity (Bond Q). It has recently moved to 41 bp above Q, with no change in either issuer’s fundamentals.

| Bond | Yield (%) | Coupon (%) | Modified duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| P (hedged into AUD) | 4.62 | 3.00 | 7.8 |
| Q (Commonwealth) | 4.21 | 4.50 | 7.9 |

Which of the following best describes the position consistent with fixed-income arbitrage and its source of profit?

options.text: Buy Bond Q and short Bond P; profit if the yield gap narrows back toward its historical range.
Buy Bonds P and Q with leverage; profit from P’s higher yield as the level of yields falls.
Buy Bond P and short Bond Q; the trade is riskless because the two yields must converge before maturity.
Buy Bond P and short Bond Q; profit if the yield gap narrows back toward its historical range.

questions.solution:
Australian consultant reviews a fixed-income arbitrage trade after a hedged foreign bond’s yield moves 41 bp above a Commonwealth bond.

**Concept and theory**

Fixed-income arbitrage is “a long/short approach that targets pricing inefficiencies among fixed-income securities”. Two securities that should trade at about the same yield (here, once currency risk is hedged) drift apart for reasons that are not fundamental. The arbitrageur buys the security that has become cheap (higher yield, lower price) and shorts the one that has become rich (lower yield, higher price), expecting the yields to converge. Because the legs offset, the position is largely insensitive to the overall level of rates; the profit comes from the gap closing. GARP Chapter 9 says the same: such funds exploit anomalies between related fixed-income securities and “often seek to limit volatility by hedging out exposure to the market and interest rate risk”. GARP also notes that these funds depend on leverage and are exposed to credit market conditions, so the trade carries risk.

**Applying it to this question**

Bond P yields 4.62% against 4.21% for Q, a 41 bp gap against a 10 bp historical range, with no change in fundamentals. Higher yield means lower price, so P is cheap and Q is rich. Convergence means P’s yield falls relative to Q’s, so P’s price rises relative to Q’s. The trade is long P, short Q. Coupons and durations are not needed to choose the trade: they are excess data.

**Fragile fact.** Higher yield $= \text{cheaper bond} =$ the long leg. Say it aloud: “buy the high-yield twin, short the low-yield twin”.

**Reference**

LO 90.b: “Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.” Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.2, “Fixed-Income Arbitrage”. No GARP chapter matches this reading; GARP used for depth only: GARP Ch. 9 Hedge Funds, “Relative Value and Arbitrage-like Hedge Fund Styles”, description of fixed-income arbitrage funds and their exposure to credit conditions. No conflict with Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 b, where it is Q3 of 14.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** The legs are reversed: buying the rich bond and shorting the cheap one loses if the gap narrows. A would be right if P’s hedged yield had fallen 41 bp below Q’s.

b.reason: **Scope error, long/short condition dropped.** Buying both bonds is a leveraged directional bet on the level of yields, not an arbitrage on their relationship. B would describe a macro or long-only duration trade, not fixed-income arbitrage.

c.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** The legs are right but the claim that convergence is certain is wrong: the reading speaks of an expectation of convergence, and GARP stresses leverage and exposure to credit conditions. C would be right only for a true riskless arbitrage, which this is not.

d.reason: D is the long/short convergence trade Schweser describes (positions “based on the expectation that these yields will eventually converge”), with the legs the right way round and the profit tied to the gap narrowing, not guaranteed.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a UK asset manager is reviewing a strategy memo from a fixed-income arbitrage fund. The fund holds a trade between the on-the-run 30-year US Treasury bond and the off-the-run 29½-year Treasury bond issued six months earlier. The memo contains the four statements below. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The fund buys the on-the-run bond and shorts the off-the-run bond, because the on-the-run issue is expected to keep its price premium as it ages.
The fund shorts the more expensive on-the-run bond and buys the cheaper off-the-run bond, and earns small, positive profits as the on-the-run premium fades over time.
The fund shorts the on-the-run bond and buys the off-the-run bond, and earns large profits because the on-the-run premium widens as the bond ages.
The fund shorts the on-the-run bond and buys the off-the-run bond, and the trade is free of risk because both bonds are issued by the same government.

questions.solution:
UK auditor checks four memo statements on an on-the-run 30-year vs off-the-run 29.5-year Treasury trade.

**Concept and theory**

The most recently issued (“on-the-run”) Treasury of a maturity is the most actively traded and so commands a price premium. A bond of almost the same maturity issued six months earlier (“off-the-run”) pays nearly the same cash flows but trades cheaper. As the on-the-run bond ages and a newer issue replaces it, its premium fades. Schweser’s example: short the more expensive on-the-run 30-year bond, buy the cheaper off-the-run 29½-year bond; as the premium fades, the trade “can produce small, positive arbitrage profits”. GARP Chapter 9 describes a related family of yield-curve trades that bet that bond prices deviate from the curve “only for short-run, tactical liquidity reasons, which dissipate over time”.

**Applying it to this question**

Three facts must all be right: (1) the legs (short on-the-run, long off-the-run); (2) the mechanism (the on-the-run premium fades); (3) the size and certainty of the profit (small and positive, not large and not risk free). Only one statement gets all three right.

**Fragile fact.** On-the-run $= \text{rich} =$ short leg; off-the-run $= \text{cheap} =$ long leg; profit is small and comes from the premium fading.

**Reference**

LO 90.b: “Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.” Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.2, “Fixed-Income Arbitrage”. No GARP chapter matches this reading; GARP used for depth only: GARP Ch. 9 Hedge Funds, “Relative Value and Arbitrage-like Hedge Fund Styles”, description of yield-curve spread trades. No conflict with Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 b, where it is Q4 of 14.

a.reason: **Polarity flip on the legs and the premium.** Being long the rich bond and short the cheap one pays only if the premium persists or widens, the opposite of the expected fade. A would be right only if the premium were expected to grow.

b.reason: B states the legs, the mechanism and the size as Schweser does: short the rich on-the-run bond, buy the cheap off-the-run bond, and earn small, positive profits as the premium fades.

c.reason: **Polarity flip on the premium, plus wrong magnitude.** The legs are right, but the premium fades rather than widens, and the reading calls the profits small. C would be right only if the on-the-run premium were expected to increase, in which case the stated legs would in fact lose.

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** Same issuer does not mean no risk: the trade relies on an expected convergence over time and is typically leveraged. D would be right only if the two bonds were perfectly identical and could be delivered against each other.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian insurer is presenting convertible bonds to newly hired analysts before they cover a BRL-denominated convertible issued by a domestic utility. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.text: Because the embedded option is a call on the utility’s shares, the convertible’s price is sensitive to the share price but not to the volatility of the share price.
The value of the convertible can be described as coming from three components: investment value, conversion value and option value.
Until the holder exercises the conversion option, the holder keeps receiving coupon payments just as a holder of a conventional bond would.
The convertible’s price responds both to a change in BRL interest rates and to a change in the utility’s credit risk.

questions.solution:
Brazilian insurer analyst: which statement about a BRL convertible’s sensitivities and value components is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

A convertible bond is a bond with an embedded call option on the issuer’s equity. The holder may convert into a fixed number of shares and will do so when the shares received are worth more than the cash redemption value; until then, the holder receives coupons like any bondholder. Because it is part bond and part equity option, its price is sensitive to:

| Driver | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Interest rates | The bond part is a stream of fixed coupons and principal |
| Issuer’s credit risk | The bond part can default |
| Share price | Drives the value of the shares received on conversion |
| Share price volatility | Drives the value of the embedded call option |

Schweser lists the three value components as investment value, conversion value and option value.

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is NOT correct, so three statements are true and one is false. B (three components), C (coupons until conversion) and D (rates and credit) repeat the source. A drops volatility from the list of drivers, although Schweser names “movements in the issuer’s common share price and price volatility”.

**Fragile fact.** Four price drivers: rates, credit, share price and share price volatility. Volatility is the one most often forgotten and the one convertible arbitrage earns from.

**Reference**

LO 90.b: “Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.” Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.2, “Convertible Arbitrage” (opening paragraphs). GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 b, where it is Q5 of 14.

a.reason: The convertible’s price is sensitive to the share price and its volatility, because the embedded call option is worth more when volatility is higher. Volatility is also what convertible arbitrage monetizes. A is therefore false, which makes it the answer.

b.reason: **True statement.** Investment value, conversion value and option value are exactly the three components Schweser lists. B would become false only if a component were swapped for one not in the list, for example “credit value”.

c.reason: **True statement.** Schweser: “Until the conversion option is exercised, the investor continues to receive coupon payments just like a traditional bondholder.” C would be false if it said coupons stop when the share price exceeds some level.

d.reason: **True statement.** Interest rates and the issuer’s credit risk are the first two sensitivities listed. D would be false if it denied either.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Singapore fund bought a convertible bond and holds it to maturity, when the holder must choose between the bond’s cash redemption value and conversion into shares.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Face value and cash redemption value at maturity | SGD 1,000 |
| Conversion ratio | 18.5 shares per bond |
| Purchase price | 101.5% of par |
| Annual coupon | 2.5% of face |
| Share price at issue | SGD 45.00 |
| Share price at maturity | SGD 56.20 |

Ignoring coupon income, what is the fund’s gain or loss per bond on its principal investment if it acts rationally at maturity?
questions.solution:
Singapore fund holds a convertible bought at 101.5% of par to maturity: convert or redeem, and the gain per bond.

**Concept and theory**

At maturity the holder of a convertible compares two values: the cash redemption value, and the value of the shares received on conversion. Schweser: the bondholder “will exercise this option when the value of the shares received exceeds the bond’s cash redemption value”. A rational holder therefore receives

Value at maturity $= \text{max}($Cash redemption value, CR $\times\text{S}_{\text{T}} )$,

where CR is the conversion ratio (shares per bond) and $\text{S}_{\text{T}}$ is the share price at maturity. The gain on the principal investment is that value minus the price paid.

**Applying it to this question**

Step by step:

Value of shares received $= \text{CR} \times\text{S}_{\text{T}} =$ 18.5 × 56.20 = SGD 1,039.70

Cash redemption value = SGD 1,000.00

Rational choice $= \text{max}($1,000.00, 1,039.70) = SGD 1,039.70 (convert)

Price paid = 1.015 × 1,000 = SGD 1,015.00

Gain on principal = 1,039.70 − 1,015.00 = SGD 24.70

The fund converts, because the shares are worth SGD 39.70 more than the cash, and its gain over what it paid is SGD 24.70. The coupon and the share price at issue are excess data.

**Fragile fact.** The comparison is shares value against the cash redemption value, not against the purchase price; the purchase price only enters when computing the gain.

**Reference**

LO 90.b: “Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.” Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.2, “Convertible Arbitrage” (conversion right). GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 b, where it is Q6 of 14.

a.reason: **Polarity flip on the decision.** SGD −15.00 = 1,000.00 − 1,015.00 is the result of taking cash redemption, the wrong choice when the shares are worth more. A would be right if the share price at maturity were below 1,000/18.5 = SGD 54.05.

b.reason: B applies the source’s conversion rule (convert when the shares are worth more than the cash redemption value) and then nets the purchase price.

c.reason: **Dropped term, wrong cost basis.** SGD 39.70 = 1,039.70 − 1,000.00 measures the gain against par, ignoring the 1.5-point premium paid. C would be right if the bond had been bought at par.

d.reason: **Intermediate result.** SGD 1,039.70 is the value received on conversion, not the gain. D would be right if the question asked what the fund receives per bond at maturity.

questions.question:
A junior analyst on the convertible arbitrage desk of a London hedge fund is setting up a new position. The fund buys convertible bonds of a UK retailer and hedges the equity exposure by shorting the retailer’s shares in the delta-neutral quantity.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Convertible bonds bought | 400 |
| Face value per bond | GBP 1,000 |
| Convertible price | 102.25% of par |
| Conversion ratio | 25.6 shares per bond |
| Convertible delta | 0.62 |
| Share price | GBP 38.40 |
| Annual coupon | 1.75% of face |

Approximately what are the short sale proceeds of the initial hedge?
questions.solution:
London desk buys 400 convertibles (CR 25.6, delta 0.62) and shorts the delta-neutral number of shares: short sale proceeds.

**Concept and theory**

Convertible arbitrage buys a convertible bond and simultaneously shorts the underlying stock so that the combined position is insensitive to small moves in the share price. Each bond converts into CR shares, and its delta ∆ measures how much of that equity exposure the bond carries at current prices. The delta-neutral short is therefore

Shares to short $= \text{N} \times\text{CR} \times\Delta$, Short sale proceeds = Shares to short × S,

where N is the number of bonds and S the share price. Schweser’s worked example uses this sizing (delta 53% and conversion ratio 21.2037, giving about 11.24 shares per bond, which reproduces its USD 1.37 hedged gain). GARP Chapter 9 says “the number of shares sold short usually reflects a delta neutral or market neutral ratio”.

**Applying it to this question**

Step by step:

Shares to short $= \text{N} \times\text{CR} \times\Delta=$ 400 × 25.6 × 0.62 = 6,348.8 shares

Short sale proceeds = 6,348.8 × 38.40 = GBP 243,793.92 ≈ GBP 243,794

These proceeds are what earns the interest rebate in the carry calculation. The convertible price and coupon are excess data.

**Fragile fact.** Hedge $= \text{N} \times\text{CR} \times\Delta$: both the conversion ratio and the delta multiply; dropping either is the classic slip.

**Reference**

LO 90.b: “Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.” Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.2, “Convertible Arbitrage” and its worked example (the example’s tables are not in the text file; the sizing is reconstructed from its stated inputs and its USD 1.37 result). No GARP chapter matches this reading; GARP used for depth only: GARP Ch. 9 Hedge Funds, “Relative Value and Arbitrage-like Hedge Fund Styles” (delta-neutral short). No conflict with Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 b, where it is Q7 of 14.

a.reason: **Dropped term: conversion ratio.** GBP 9,523 = 400 × 0.62 × 38.40 treats each bond as one share. A would be right only if each bond converted into a single share.

b.reason: **Sign or complement error on delta.** GBP 149,422 = 400 × 25.6 × (1 − 0.62) × 38.40 uses 1 − ∆ instead of ∆, a complement that has no role in hedge sizing. B would be right only if the delta were 0.38.

c.reason: C sizes the short at delta times the conversion ratio per bond, the delta-neutral quantity, and values it at the current share price.

d.reason: **Dropped term: delta.** GBP 393,216 = 400 × 25.6 × 38.40 shorts every share the bonds convert into, over-hedging. D would be right only if the convertible’s delta were 1.

questions.question: An internal model validator at a Canadian bank is reviewing the procedures of a hedge fund to which the bank provides prime brokerage. The fund’s convertible arbitrage manual states: “At inception we short the number of shares given by the convertible’s delta times the conversion ratio. Because the hedge is delta neutral at inception, we leave the short position unchanged until the bond is converted or redeemed.” Which recommendation should the validator make?

options.text: No change: a hedge that is delta neutral at inception stays neutral for as long as the conversion ratio is fixed.
Replace the short stock position with a short position in government bonds, since the convertible’s main sensitivity is to interest rates.
Rebalance only after large falls in the share price, since rises in the share price leave the convertible’s delta unchanged.
Rebalance the short stock position as the share price moves, since changes in the share price alter the convertible’s delta.

questions.solution:
Canadian bank validator reviews a fund manual that sets a delta-neutral short at inception and never rebalances.

**Concept and theory**

The short stock position in convertible arbitrage is sized from the convertible’s delta. Delta, however, is not fixed: Schweser states that the hedge “must be actively managed as changes in the stock price alter the delta of the convertible bond, requiring continuous rebalancing, a process known as delta hedging”. The reason is the nonlinear relationship between the share price and the convertible price: the convertible’s sensitivity to the share price changes as the share price changes, so a hedge that is neutral today will not be neutral after the share price has moved. GARP Chapter 9 adds that, under normal conditions, the delta-neutral position is expected to be insensitive to fluctuations in the share price, and that the strategy still lost over 12% a month in September and October 2008 when leveraged positions were forced to unwind.

**Applying it to this question**

The manual’s logic is “neutral at inception, so neutral forever”. That fails because the delta, and so the required short, changes whenever the share price changes. The validator should require rebalancing as the share price moves.

**Fragile fact.** Delta-neutral is a moment, not a state: any move in the share price changes the delta, so the short must be reset.

**Reference**

LO 90.b: “Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.” Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.2, “Convertible Arbitrage” (delta hedging). No GARP chapter matches this reading; GARP used for depth only: GARP Ch. 9 Hedge Funds, “Relative Value and Arbitrage-like Hedge Fund Styles” (delta-neutral ratio; insensitivity under normal conditions) and the 2008 passage on convertible arbitrage losses. No conflict with Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 b, where it is Q8 of 14.

a.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** A fixed conversion ratio fixes the number of shares per bond, not the delta. Neutrality at inception is not neutrality for life. A would be right only if the convertible behaved linearly in the share price.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It swaps the equity hedge for a rate hedge. Convertible arbitrage shorts the underlying stock to neutralize equity risk; rates are one sensitivity of the bond, but replacing the stock short leaves the equity exposure unhedged and turns the trade into something else. B would be right only if the aim were to hedge interest rate risk alone.

c.reason: **Scope error, condition narrowed.** The source says changes in the stock price alter the delta, in either direction; C limits this to large falls. C would be right only if the delta changed only when the share price fell.

d.reason: D restates the source: changes in the stock price alter the convertible’s delta, so the short must be rebalanced (delta hedging).

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of an Australian fund manager is reviewing draft marketing material for its convertible arbitrage fund, which buys AUD convertible bonds and shorts the issuers’ shares. Which statement in the draft is most accurate?

options.text: Dividends declared on the shares we have borrowed and sold short add to the fund’s income alongside the bond coupons.
Our only return sources are the bond coupons and interest on short sale proceeds; share price volatility is purely a risk for a hedged book.
Beyond the coupons and interest on short sale proceeds, we can earn from monetizing volatility and from buying convertibles whose embedded call is priced below fair value.
The stock borrowing fee on our short position is paid to the fund by the stock lender and adds to the interest earned on short sale proceeds.

questions.solution:
Australian CCO reviews four marketing statements on convertible arbitrage return sources and costs.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser lists what a convertible arbitrage position earns and what it pays.

| Sources of return | Costs |
|---|---|
| Coupon payments on the convertible | Borrowing fees paid to the stock lender |
| Interest earned on the short sale proceeds | Dividends paid to the lender on the borrowed shares |
| Monetizing volatility through delta hedging (nonlinear payoff) |  |
| The convertible itself being undervalued, for example an embedded call priced below fair value |  |

GARP Chapter 9 describes the same undervaluation source as buying convertibles and shorting the stock “when there is a pricing error made in the conversion factor of the security”, and reports research that interprets the strategy’s return as a liquidity premium paid by issuers to funds that hold and hedge convertible inventories.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement for who pays whom and for completeness. A turns a cost into income. B leaves out two sources. D reverses the direction of the borrowing fee. C lists all four sources correctly.

**Fragile fact.** On the short leg, money flows out twice (borrow fee and dividends to the lender) and in once (interest on the proceeds).

**Reference**

LO 90.b: “Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.” Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.2, “Convertible Arbitrage” (sources of return and costs). No GARP chapter matches this reading; GARP used for depth only: GARP Ch. 9 Hedge Funds, “Relative Value and Arbitrage-like Hedge Fund Styles” (pricing error in the conversion factor; liquidity premium interpretation). GARP’s “pricing error in the conversion factor” and Schweser’s “embedded call priced below fair value” describe the same idea of a cheap convertible; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 b, where it is Q9 of 14.

a.reason: **Polarity flip, cost into income.** The short seller must pay the lender the dividends on borrowed shares; they are a cost. A would be right for a fund that owned the shares, not one that had borrowed and sold them.

b.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** “Only” excludes monetizing volatility and undervaluation. For a delta-hedged convertible, volatility is a source of return, not just a risk. B would be right only for a position whose payoff were linear in the share price.

c.reason: C names the two income sources (coupons and short interest) and the two further sources Schweser lists: “monetizing volatility” and the convertible being undervalued “when the embedded call option is priced below its fair value”.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** The borrowing fee is paid by the fund to the stock lender, not the other way round. D would be right only from the stock lender’s point of view.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Frankfurt hedge fund is estimating the annual carry of a convertible arbitrage position, assuming the share price and the positions stay unchanged for one year.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Convertible bonds held | 1,000 bonds, face EUR 1,000 each |
| Annual coupon | 2.0% of face |
| Convertible price | 104% of par |
| Convertible delta | 0.55 |
| Shares sold short | 12,000 |
| Share price | EUR 42.00 |
| Interest earned on short sale proceeds | 3.0% per year |
| Stock borrow fee (on market value of borrowed shares) | 0.5% per year |
| Dividend per share | EUR 0.80 per year |

What is the expected annual net carry of the position?
questions.solution:
Frankfurt analyst computes one year of carry on a convertible arbitrage position (coupon, short interest, borrow fee, dividends).

**Concept and theory**

With the share price and positions unchanged, the convertible arbitrage position earns or pays only its carry. From Schweser’s lists of returns and costs:

$\text{Net carry} = \underbrace{\text{c} \times \text{F} \times \text{N}}_{\text{coupons}} + \underbrace{\text{r}_{\text{s}} \times \text{Q} \times \text{S}}_{\text{interest on short proceeds}} - \underbrace{\text{b} \times \text{Q} \times \text{S}}_{\text{borrow fee}} - \underbrace{\text{D} \times \text{Q}}_{\text{dividends paid}},$

where c is the coupon rate on face value F, N the number of bonds, Q the shares sold short, S the share price, $\text{r}_{\text{s}}$ the interest rate earned on short proceeds, b the borrow fee rate and D the dividend per share. Coupons are paid on face value, not on the market price.

**Applying it to this question**

Step by step:

Coupons = 0.020 × 1,000 × 1,000 = EUR 20,000

Short proceeds = 12,000 × 42.00 = EUR 504,000

Interest on short proceeds = 0.030 × 504,000 = EUR 15,120

Borrow fee = 0.005 × 504,000 = EUR 2,520

Dividends paid to lender = 12,000 × 0.80 = EUR 9,600

Net carry = 20,000 + 15,120 − 2,520 − 9,600 = EUR 23,000

The position carries EUR 23,000 a year before any gains from rebalancing. The convertible price and delta are excess data.

**Fragile fact.** Dividends on the shorted stock carry a minus sign for the arbitrageur; coupons are on face value.

**Reference**

LO 90.b: “Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.” Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.2, “Convertible Arbitrage” (coupon payments, interest on short sale proceeds, borrowing fees, dividends paid to the lender). GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 b, where it is Q10 of 14.

a.reason: A includes both income items Schweser lists (coupon and interest on short proceeds) and deducts both costs (borrow fee and dividends paid to the lender).

b.reason: **Wrong input twin: price for face.** EUR 23,800 computes the coupon on the market price: 0.02 × 1,040 × 1,000 = 20,800, then 20,800 + 15,120 − 2,520 − 9,600. B would be right if the coupon were paid on market value, which it is not.

c.reason: **Dropped term: dividends.** EUR 32,600 = 20,000 + 15,120 − 2,520 forgets the dividends owed to the stock lender. C would be right if the stock paid no dividend.

d.reason: **Sign error on dividends.** EUR 42,200 = 20,000 + 15,120 − 2,520 + 9,600 treats the dividends as income. D would be right only for a fund that owned the shares.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-8 b Q11
questions.question:
A risk consultant at a Tokyo hedge fund is explaining to the risk committee how the convertible arbitrage book behaves when the issuer’s share price moves. For one convertible bond, the fund’s pricing model gives the following.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Convertible price today | JPY 1,018,000 |
| Conversion ratio | 400 shares per bond |
| Share price today | JPY 2,500 |
| Convertible delta | 0.60 |
| Annual coupon | 1.0% of face |
| Model convertible price if the share price rises 6% | JPY 1,056,400 |
| Model convertible price if the share price falls 6% | JPY 984,100 |

The fund holds one convertible and is short the delta-neutral number of shares. Ignoring coupons, short sale interest, borrow fees and dividends, which pair gives the P&L (JPY) of the hedged position if the share price rises 6% and if it falls 6%?
questions.solution:
Tokyo consultant shows the P&L of a delta-hedged convertible for a 6% rise and a 6% fall in the share price.

**Concept and theory**

The convertible’s price is a nonlinear (convex) function of the share price, while the short stock leg is linear. Near today’s price, the delta-neutral short offsets the convertible’s first-order sensitivity. After a move in either direction, convexity makes the convertible do better than the linear hedge predicts: on a rise the convertible gains more than the short loses, and on a fall it loses less than the short gains. The hedged position therefore gains in both directions; this is “monetizing volatility”, which Schweser likens to the convexity of the bond price-yield relationship. Schweser’s example shows the effect: when the stock falls 5%, the hedged trade earns USD 1.37 while the unhedged long loses USD 19.47. GARP Chapter 3 (“Non-Linear Payoffs”) notes that convertible bond arbitrage has payoffs that resemble nonlinear option volatility strategies.

Hedged P&L $= \Delta\text{P}_{\text{CB}} - \text{h} \times\Delta$S, h $= \text{CR} \times\Delta$

**Applying it to this question**

Step by step:

h = 400 × 0.60 = 240 shares short

$\Delta\text{S} =$ 0.06 × 2,500 = JPY 150 per share

Short leg P&L = ∓ 240 × 150 = ∓ JPY 36,000 (loss on rise, gain on fall)

Rise: $\Delta\text{P}_{\text{CB}} =$ 1,056,400 − 1,018,000 = +38,400 ⇒ 38,400 − 36,000 = +JPY 2,400

Fall: $\Delta\text{P}_{\text{CB}} =$ 984,100 − 1,018,000 = −33,900 ⇒ −33,900 + 36,000 = +JPY 2,100

The hedged book gains in both scenarios: that is volatility being monetized. The coupon is excess data (and is excluded by the stem).

**Fragile fact.** Long convexity, short delta: the hedged convertible makes money on both up and down moves; the price of that is the carry costs and the need to rebalance.

**Reference**

LO 90.b: “Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.” Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.2, “Convertible Arbitrage” (monetizing volatility) and its worked example. No GARP chapter matches this reading; GARP used for depth only: GARP Ch. 3, “Non-Linear Payoffs”. Schweser wording flag: its sentence that “when the stock price falls or rises, the gain or loss on the short stock position tends to exceed the corresponding loss or gain on the convertible” holds for the fall but not for the rise; its own example (USD 1,038.07 model price, about USD 24.32 convertible gain against about USD 23.34 short loss) shows the convertible gain exceeding the short loss on the rise, which is what this solution uses. The example also appears to include the USD 2.50 coupon in the unhedged result (USD −19.47) but not in the hedged one (USD +1.37).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 b, where it is Q11 of 14.

a.reason: **Dropped term: the hedge leg.** +38,400 and −33,900 are the convertible’s own price changes, the unhedged position. A would be right for a long convertible with no short stock, Schweser’s “unhedged” scenario.

b.reason: **Sign error on the fall.** B treats the hedged P&L as moving with the stock, as if the residual were linear. On a fall the short gains 36,000 and the convertible loses only 33,900, so the result is +2,100, not −2,100. B would be right only if the convertible were concave in the share price.

c.reason: **Sign error on the rise.** On a rise the convertible gains 38,400 and the short loses 36,000, a net +2,400. C reverses that sign, as if the short loss exceeded the convertible gain. C would be right only if the convertible gained 33,600 on the rise.

d.reason: D gives a gain in both directions, the payoff profile Schweser’s example illustrates for a delta-hedged convertible.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Shanghai hedge fund is presenting four candidate trades in CNY-listed shares to newly hired analysts. Which trade is most consistent with pairs trading as a relative value arbitrage strategy?

options.text: Two dairy producers whose prices have historically moved closely together diverge by 9% after one announces a product recall; the fund shorts the recalling firm and buys its peer, expecting the gap to close.

Two cement producers whose prices have historically moved closely together diverge by 9% over two weeks with no company news; the fund shorts the outperformer and buys the laggard, expecting the gap to close.

A cement producer and a software developer whose prices have historically moved closely together diverge by 9% with no company news; the fund shorts the outperformer and buys the laggard, expecting the gap to close.

Two cement producers whose prices have historically moved closely together diverge by 9% with no company news; the fund buys the outperformer and shorts the laggard, expecting the gap to widen further.

questions.solution:
Shanghai PM shows four candidate CNY share trades; which is a pairs trade?

**Concept and theory**

Pairs trading is “a long-established relative value arbitrage strategy”. Schweser’s conditions are precise:

| Condition | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Two firms that are competitors or peers in the same industry | Common drivers justify a stable price relationship |
| Historically strong price correlation | Evidence that the relationship exists |
| Temporary divergence without fundamental news | The gap is noise, so it should close |
| Short one, buy the other; expect the spread to revert and converge | Profit from convergence, not direction |

The natural legs are short the stock that has run ahead (rich) and long the one that has lagged (cheap). GARP Chapter 3 (“Non-Linear Payoffs”) lists pairs trading among strategies whose payoffs resemble nonlinear option volatility strategies.

**Applying it to this question**

All four options show a 9% divergence. Check each condition: are they peers, is there no news, and is the trade a convergence bet? Only the two cement producers with no company news, short the outperformer and long the laggard, meet every condition.

**Fragile fact.** Pairs trading needs “no fundamental news”. A divergence explained by news is not a pairs signal.

**Reference**

LO 90.b: “Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.” Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.2, “Relative Value Arbitrage” (pairs trading). No GARP chapter matches this reading; GARP used for depth only: GARP Ch. 3, “Non-Linear Payoffs” (mentions pairs trading only in passing; no conflict).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 b, where it is Q12 of 14.

a.reason: **Scope error, “without fundamental news” dropped.** A product recall is fundamental news, so the gap may be a justified repricing rather than a temporary divergence. A would be right if the divergence had occurred with no company-specific news.

b.reason: B has peers in the same industry, a historically strong relationship, a temporary divergence with no fundamental news, and a convergence trade, matching every element of Schweser’s description.

c.reason: **Scope error, peer condition dropped.** A cement producer and a software developer are not competitors or peers in the same industry, so a past correlation gives no economic reason to expect convergence. C would be right if both firms were in the same industry.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** Buying the outperformer and shorting the laggard while expecting the gap to widen is a momentum bet, the opposite of the reversion pairs trading relies on. D would be right only for a trend-following strategy.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a London hedge fund is reviewing a trade booked by the statistical arbitrage desk. A large mutual fund sold a GBP 40 million block, several days’ normal volume, of a UK mid-cap engineering stock, and the stock fell 4% within the hour with no news about the company. The desk bought the stock and shorted a closely related engineering stock, planning to hold both until the first stock’s price normalizes. Which statement best describes the trade?

options.text: The desk earns a return for providing liquidity to a large institutional seller, using the related short to hedge market risk until the price normalizes.
The desk earns a return from a permanent revaluation of the engineering stock, so the long position should be held indefinitely.
The desk should instead short the stock being sold and buy the related stock, since a large block sale shows the stock is overvalued.
The desk faces no market or price risk on the trade, because a fund providing liquidity is always compensated by the seller.

questions.solution:
London stat arb desk buys a mid-cap stock hit by a mutual fund’s GBP 40 million block sale and shorts a related stock.

**Concept and theory**

Statistical arbitrage “extends” the pairs idea “across a large number of long and short positions, often using factor models to identify mispricings”. Schweser adds a specific source of return: providing liquidity to large mutual funds or other institutions. When a large block is sold, the price may fall temporarily because the seller needs liquidity, not because the stock’s value has changed. A hedge fund can buy the temporarily mispriced stock, short a related stock to hedge market risk, and hold until the price normalizes. The fund is paid for absorbing a block that others would not.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem has every element: a large institutional seller (a mutual fund), a block of several days’ volume, a 4% fall with no news, a long in the depressed stock, a short in a related stock, and a plan to hold until the price normalizes. The block size in GBP is context, not a calculation input.

**Fragile fact.** In liquidity provision the hedge fund buys what the large institution is selling, and the short in a related stock hedges market risk, not all risk.

**Reference**

LO 90.b: “Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.” Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.2, “Relative Value Arbitrage” (statistical arbitrage and liquidity provision). GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 b, where it is Q13 of 14.

a.reason: A describes the trade as Schweser does: return from providing liquidity, the related short hedging market risk, and a hold until the price normalizes.

b.reason: **Polarity flip, temporary into permanent.** The reading calls the mispricing temporary: the price “may temporarily decline” and is held “until the price normalizes”. B would be right only if the block sale revealed new information about the firm’s value.

c.reason: **Polarity flip on the legs.** C reverses the legs on the theory that the seller is informed. The reading’s trade buys the stock being sold and shorts the related stock. C would be right only if the seller were trading on fundamental information.

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** The related short hedges market risk but cannot remove all price risk; the price may not normalize as expected, and no one guarantees compensation. D would be right only for a riskless arbitrage.

questions.question: The CRO of a US bank, whose asset management and brokerage arms hold large long positions in US equities, is reviewing a proposal from the bank’s arbitrage desk. S&P 500 index futures trade below fair value relative to the constituent stocks by more than estimated trading costs, and the desk proposes to buy the futures and short the constituents. Which statement in the proposal is most accurate?

options.text: The desk must short all 500 constituents in exact index weights; shorting a subset means the position is no longer an arbitrage.
The desk’s algorithm should choose the constituents to short by index weight alone, without reference to transaction costs.
The desk can source shares to short from long positions held elsewhere in the bank at lower cost, a competitive advantage over standalone funds.
Standalone hedge funds with no existing equity holdings have the cost advantage in this trade, since they are not tied to internal positions.

questions.solution:
US bank CRO reviews an index futures vs constituents arbitrage proposal by a desk whose bank already holds long equity positions.

**Concept and theory**

When index futures trade away from the value of the constituent stocks, the arbitrageur buys the cheap side and shorts the rich side. Schweser’s example buys S&P 500 futures and shorts the constituents. Two practical points follow. First, shorting all 500 stocks is impractical, so “computer algorithms evaluate transaction and other costs relative to the mispricing and select an optimal subset to trade”. Second, firms that already hold long positions in the constituents elsewhere in the organization “can source the required shares internally at a lower cost, giving them a competitive advantage”.

**Applying it to this question**

The futures are cheap relative to the stocks by more than the costs, so the desk buys futures and shorts stocks. The bank’s asset management and brokerage arms hold large long US equity positions, which is exactly the internal sourcing advantage the reading describes. The task is to find the one statement that matches both practical points.

**Fragile fact.** The advantage sits with whoever already owns the constituents: they can source the shares to short internally.

**Reference**

LO 90.b: “Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies.” Schweser Reading 90, Module 90.2, “Relative Value Arbitrage” (index futures vs constituents). GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 b, where it is Q14 of 14.

a.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** Shorting all 500 names in exact weights is impractical; the reading has algorithms pick an optimal subset. A would be right only if a complete replication were required for the trade to count.

b.reason: **Scope error, condition dropped.** The algorithms weigh transaction and other costs against the mispricing; B removes that condition. B would be right only if trading were costless.

c.reason: C restates the source: existing long positions elsewhere in the firm allow cheaper internal sourcing of shares to short, which is a competitive advantage.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** It gives the cost advantage to the wrong party. The advantage belongs to firms with existing long positions, not to standalone funds without them. D would be right only if the standalone fund had cheaper internal access to shares.

questions.loText: Describe the mechanics and risks of event-driven strategies such as merger arbitrage.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-8 c Q1
questions.question:
A junior analyst at a pension consultancy is preparing a training note that sorts event-driven opportunities into the categories used in the reading (strategic, financial, operational, legal/regulatory and technical). She drafts the following list of events:

I. A credit re-rating of an issuer by a rating agency

II. A change in the firm’s accounting methods

III. Expected synergies from a merger

IV. A secondary offering of equity

Which of the events above would be correctly placed under financial opportunities?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Training note: which of four events belong in the “financial” category of event-driven opportunities.

**Concept and theory**

Event-driven strategies focus on specific corporate events that create pricing discrepancies and market inefficiencies. The manager is not betting on the market or on a macro view; the bet is that a particular event (a deal, a re-rating, a restructuring, a court ruling) will move the price of a security in a way the market has not fully priced. Schweser sorts the sources of these opportunities into five categories:

| Category | Examples listed in the reading |
|---|---|
| Strategic | Hard catalysts: risk arbitrage; evaluating a firm’s strategic alternatives; potential spin-offs; likely takeover targets; proxy contests and activist campaigns; stub trades |
| Financial | Credit re-ratings or liquidity events; changes in accounting methods; financial recapitalisations; primary offerings of debt or equity; bankruptcy reorganisations |
| Operational | Synergies from mergers; turnarounds and restructurings; senior management changes |
| Legal/regulatory | Litigation outcomes; regulatory changes; anticipated legislation |
| Technical | Broken risk arbitrage situations; secondary offerings of equity or equity-linked notes |

The logic of the grouping: financial events change the firm’s financing, credit standing or reported numbers; operational events change how the business is run; technical events create temporary supply and demand pressure on a security (a broken deal dumping target shares, or a secondary offering adding shares to the float) rather than changing the firm itself.

**Applying it to this question**

I. A credit re-rating is a financial opportunity. II. A change in accounting methods is a financial opportunity. III. Merger synergies are listed under operational opportunities. IV. A secondary offering of equity is listed under technical opportunities; only primary offerings of debt or equity are financial. So only I and II belong under financial.

**Fragile fact.** Primary offering = financial; secondary offering = technical. Synergies and management changes = operational, not strategic or financial.

**Reference**

LO 90.c: Describe the mechanics and risks of event-driven strategies such as merger arbitrage. Schweser, Reading 90, Module 90.3 “Event-Driven and Distressed Strategies”, opening list of opportunity categories. GARP text in the project has no matching section for Schweser Reading 90; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the assigned reading’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 c, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: Schweser’s “Financial opportunities” list contains credit re-ratings or liquidity events and changes in accounting methods, and contains neither merger synergies nor secondary offerings. I and II only.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Adds IV by taking the property of the neighbouring item “primary offerings of debt or equity” (financial) and attaching it to secondary offerings, which the reading places under technical opportunities. B would be correct if statement IV read “a primary offering of equity”.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Adds III, moving merger synergies from operational to financial. The word “merger” tempts you because mergers feel like a financing event, but synergies are about how the combined business runs. C would be correct if statement III read “a financial recapitalisation”.

d.reason: **Scope error.** Treats every listed event as financial, overextending the category to cover operational and technical events. D would be correct only if the question asked which events are event-driven opportunities of any category.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a multi-strategy hedge fund in Singapore is reviewing a position in Tembusu Holdings, a holding company whose only material asset is a 60% stake in the listed Merlion Logistics. The manager buys Tembusu shares and sells short Merlion shares in proportion to Tembusu’s look-through stake, so that the position isolates and profits from the gap shown below.

| Item | Value (SGD) |
|---|---|
| Tembusu share price | 2.10 |
| Look-through value of the Merlion stake per Tembusu share | 2.90 |
| Merlion share price | 4.35 |

Which of the following best describes this trade and its classification?

options.text: A pairs trade, classified as a relative value arbitrage strategy
A stub trade, classified as a technical event-driven opportunity
A stub trade, classified as a strategic (hard catalyst) event-driven opportunity
A risk arbitrage trade, classified as a strategic (hard catalyst) event-driven opportunity

questions.solution:
Long a holding company, short its listed subsidiary to isolate the holding-company discount: name and category.

**Concept and theory**

A holding company’s share price should, in a frictionless market, reflect the value of the assets it owns. In practice it often trades at a discount to that look-through value. A stub trade isolates and profits from the discount between a holding company’s share price and the value of its underlying assets. The manager is long the holding company and hedges the exposure to the underlying listed asset, so that what remains is a bet on the discount narrowing, typically because some corporate event (a restructuring, distribution of the stake, a takeover) forces the value to be recognised. Schweser lists stub trades under strategic (hard catalyst) opportunities, alongside risk arbitrage, spin-offs, likely takeover targets and proxy contests. Hard catalysts are events tied to the firm’s corporate strategy and ownership that can force a re-pricing.

Two siblings look similar. Pairs trading (LO 90.b, relative value arbitrage) trades two competitors with a strong historical price correlation that has diverged without news, expecting reversion. Risk arbitrage trades the spread in an announced acquisition. Neither is defined by a parent/subsidiary ownership link.

**Applying it to this question**

Tembusu’s only material asset is the Merlion stake, worth SGD 2.90 per Tembusu share, while Tembusu trades at SGD 2.10: a discount of SGD 0.80 (about 27.6% of look-through value). Buying Tembusu and shorting Merlion in proportion to the stake removes exposure to Merlion’s price and leaves the discount: that is the definition of a stub trade. The Merlion share price (SGD 4.35) is not needed to classify the trade. No acquisition has been announced, so this is not risk arbitrage, and the two securities are linked by ownership, not by being peers.

**Fragile fact.** Stub trades sit with the hard catalysts (strategic), not technical; broken risk arbitrage is the technical one.

**Reference**

LO 90.c: Describe the mechanics and risks of event-driven strategies such as merger arbitrage. Schweser, Reading 90, Module 90.3 “Event-Driven and Distressed Strategies”, “Strategic (hard catalysts) opportunities”. Pairs trading: Schweser LO 90.b, “Relative Value Arbitrage” (boundary item, used only as a distractor). GARP text in the project has no matching section for Schweser Reading 90; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the assigned reading’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 c, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Imports the label of a neighbouring LO 90.b strategy. A long/short pair is present, but pairs trading is defined by two peer firms whose historically correlated prices have diverged without fundamental news. A would be correct if the stem described two competing logistics firms whose price spread had widened without news.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Names the trade correctly but attaches it to the technical category, which in the reading holds broken risk arbitrage situations and secondary offerings. B would be correct if the trade were buying target shares dumped after a failed deal.

c.reason: Schweser: “Stub trades, which isolate and profit from the discount between a holding company’s share price and the value of its underlying assets” are listed under “Strategic (hard catalysts) opportunities”.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Keeps the right category but uses the wrong trade name: risk arbitrage needs an announced acquisition with an offer price. D would be correct if Merlion had announced a bid for Tembusu and the fund were capturing the offer spread.

questions.question: A member of a university endowment’s investment committee is reviewing a pitch from an activist hedge fund manager before approving an allocation. Which of the following statements about the activist strategy is most accurate?

options.text: The activist typically presses management to reduce leverage and cut dividends so that the firm can rebuild its balance sheet.
Once the board adopts the activist’s proposed initiatives, the strategy has succeeded, whatever the subsequent response of the share price.
The activist seeks to replace the board and take over day-to-day management, so that it runs the firm itself to implement its initiatives.
The activist may hold an equity or a derivative position and may solicit proxy votes, and the strategy fails when no meaningful changes are made.

questions.solution:
Endowment committee reviewing an activist manager: which statement about the activist strategy is most accurate.

**Concept and theory**

An activist strategy is an event-driven strategy in which the manager creates the event. The activist takes an equity or derivative position in a company and then seeks to influence management or the board to pursue initiatives the activist believes will raise the share price. The tools are pressure and persuasion: soliciting proxy votes to pressure the board, and advocating changes such as better corporate governance, spin-offs of business units, cost reductions, share repurchases, higher dividends or increased leverage. The common thread is shareholder value: return more cash to shareholders, use the balance sheet harder, shed businesses the market undervalues.

Success has two conditions in the Key Concepts: management must adopt the initiatives, and the share price must respond positively. The strategy fails when no meaningful changes are made. The activist does not itself run the company; management and the board implement.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against three facts: what position the activist holds (equity or derivative), who implements (management and the board, pressured by the activist), and what counts as success (adoption plus a positive price response). Only D states all of its facts consistently with the reading.

**Fragile fact.** Activists push for more leverage, higher dividends and buybacks; success needs adoption and a price response; position can be equity or derivative.

**Reference**

LO 90.c: Describe the mechanics and risks of event-driven strategies such as merger arbitrage. Schweser, Reading 90, Module 90.3 “Event-Driven and Distressed Strategies”, “Activist Strategy” and Key Concepts LO 90.c. GARP text in the project has no matching section for Schweser Reading 90; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the assigned reading’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 c, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** The reading lists higher dividends and increased leverage among the actions activists advocate; A reverses both directions. A would be correct only for a creditor-side investor seeking to protect bondholders, which is not the activist strategy described.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** Drops the second success condition. Adoption is necessary but not sufficient: success also requires the share price to respond positively. B would be correct if it read “once the board adopts the initiatives and the share price responds positively”.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** Right action (implementing value-enhancing initiatives), wrong actor. The activist seeks to influence management or the board; management implements. C would be correct for a private equity buyout, where the buyer takes control.

d.reason: Schweser: “taking an equity or derivative position in a company”, “Activist investors may solicit proxy votes to pressure the board”, and in Key Concepts “failure occurs when no meaningful changes are made”.

questions.question:
A risk consultant at a Canadian asset manager is validating a junior trader’s proposed merger arbitrage tickets for two deals announced this week.

| Deal | Offer terms | Target price (CAD) |
|---|---|---|
| X | CAD 40.00 cash per target share | 38.60 |
| Y | 1.5 acquirer shares per target share (acquirer at CAD 25.00) | 36.40 |

Which of the following set-ups is most appropriate for capturing the deal spread in each case?

options.text: X: buy the target and short the acquirer one for one; Y: buy the target and hold it unhedged until closing.
X: buy the target and tender it for cash at closing; Y: buy the target and short 1.5 acquirer shares per target share.
X: buy the target and tender it for cash at closing; Y: short the target and buy 1.5 acquirer shares per target share.
X: buy the target and tender it for cash at closing; Y: buy the target and short 0.67 acquirer shares per target share.

questions.solution:
Validating trade tickets for a cash deal (X) and a 1.5-for-1 share deal (Y).

**Concept and theory**

Merger (risk) arbitrage aims to profit from the spread between the acquirer’s offer and the target’s stock price after an acquisition is announced. The target trades below the offer because the market charges for the risk that the deal fails. How the arbitrageur captures the spread depends on what the acquirer pays:

| Deal type | Trade | What is isolated |
|---|---|---|
| Cash deal | Buy the target; tender it for the offer price at closing | Offer price minus purchase price |
| Fixed exchange ratio stock deal | Buy the target; short the acquirer according to the merger ratio | Ratio × acquirer price minus target price; market risk hedged |

In a stock deal the target is worth (exchange ratio) × (acquirer price) at closing. Buying one target share and shorting ratio acquirer shares locks in the spread: at closing the target converts into exactly the number of acquirer shares needed to cover the short, whatever the acquirer’s price has done.

**Applying it to this question**

Deal X pays cash, so there is no acquirer share to hedge against: buy at CAD 38.60 and tender at CAD 40.00, a spread of CAD 1.40. Deal Y pays 1.5 acquirer shares, so each target share becomes 1.5 acquirer shares at closing. Implied value 1.5 × 25.00 = 37.50; spread 37.50 − 36.40 = CAD 1.10. The hedge is long 1 target share, short 1.5 acquirer shares.

**Fragile fact.** Short ratio acquirer shares per target share (ratio = acquirer shares offered per target share); cash deals need no acquirer short.

**Reference**

GARP (2025 text in the project), Chapter 9 “Hedge Funds” (Fung and Hsieh), section “Event-Driven Hedge Fund Styles: Risk Arbitrage and Distressed”: an older reading, not a chapter for Schweser Reading 90, used only where it bears directly on merger arbitrage; no conflict with Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 c, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Swaps the mechanics of the two deal types: it hedges the cash deal with an acquirer short (unnecessary, and it adds exposure to the acquirer’s price) and leaves the stock deal unhedged (exposed to the acquirer’s price, so the spread is not isolated). A would be correct if X were the share deal and Y the cash deal.

b.reason: GARP Ch 9: in a cash deal the manager purchases the target and tenders it for the offer price; in a fixed exchange ratio stock merger, one goes long the target and short the acquirer according to the merger ratio to isolate the spread and hedge out market risk. Schweser: in a share-for-share merger the arbitrageur may short the acquirer while buying the target.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** Reverses both legs of Y. Short target, long acquirer profits if the spread widens (deal fails), which is a bet against completion, not the merger arbitrage trade. C would be correct if the question asked how to bet that deal Y will break.

d.reason: **Wrong input twin: inverted ratio.** Uses 1/1.5 = 0.67 instead of 1.5. At closing each target share delivers 1.5 acquirer shares, so a 0.67 short leaves 0.83 acquirer shares of unhedged long exposure per target share. D would be correct if the terms were 1 acquirer share for every 1.5 target shares.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Frankfurt hedge fund is estimating the payoff of a share-for-share merger arbitrage position. The acquirer has offered 0.8 of its own shares for each target share. Immediately after the announcement, the fund buys 10,000 target shares and sells short the matching number of acquirer shares implied by the exchange ratio, both at the post-announcement prices below.

| Item | Price (EUR) |
|---|---|
| Target, pre-announcement | 38.00 |
| Acquirer, pre-announcement | 63.00 |
| Target, post-announcement | 45.00 |
| Acquirer, post-announcement | 60.00 |
| Acquirer, on the closing date | 55.00 |

Neither firm pays dividends; ignore interest on short proceeds, borrowing fees and transaction costs. If the deal closes on the original terms, what is the fund’s profit on the position?
questions.solution:
EUR share-for-share deal, 0.8 ratio, 10,000 target shares: profit if the deal closes.

**Concept and theory**

In a share-for-share merger the target share converts into R acquirer shares at closing, where R is the exchange ratio. The arbitrageur buys N target shares at $\text{P}_{\text{T}}$ and shorts RN acquirer shares at $\text{P}_{\text{A}}$ at the same time. At closing the N target shares become RN acquirer shares, which are delivered to close the short. The profit is therefore fixed at entry:

Profit if the deal closes $= \text{N} (\text{R P}_{\text{A}} - \text{P}_{\text{T}} )$,

where $\text{P}_{\text{A}}$ is the acquirer’s short-sale price and $\text{P}_{\text{T}}$ the target’s purchase price, both post-announcement. This mirrors Schweser’s AWI and CI example (buy 100 CI at \$95, short 200 AWI at \$50, profit \$5 per CI share). Additional return can come from target dividends, interest on short proceeds (net of borrowing costs and dividends owed on the shorted acquirer stock) and a raised bid; the stem removes these.

**Applying it to this question**

Acquirer shares shorted = 0.8 × 10,000 = 8,000

Short-sale proceeds = 8,000 × 60.00 = EUR 480,000

Cost of target shares = 10,000 × 45.00 = EUR 450,000

Spread per target share = 0.8 × 60.00 − 45.00 = EUR 3.00

Profit = 480,000 − 450,000 = EUR 30,000

At closing, the 10,000 target shares become 8,000 acquirer shares, which exactly cover the short, so the acquirer’s closing price of EUR 55.00 never enters the profit. The pre-announcement prices (EUR 38 and EUR 63) are also irrelevant to the payoff on completion. Meaning: the fund locked in EUR 3 per target share on the day it put on the hedged trade.

**Fragile fact.** In a ratio-hedged stock deal the acquirer’s price at closing does not matter; the spread uses the post-announcement short-sale price times the ratio.

**Reference**

LO 90.c: Describe the mechanics and risks of event-driven strategies such as merger arbitrage. Schweser, Reading 90, Module 90.3 “Event-Driven and Distressed Strategies”, “Merger Arbitrage” and “EXAMPLE: Merger arbitrage” (AWI and CI). GARP text in the project has no matching section for Schweser Reading 90; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the assigned reading’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 c, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: **Wrong input twin.** Uses the acquirer’s closing-date price instead of its short-sale price: 10,000 × (0.8 × 55 − 45) = 10,000 × (−1) = −10,000. This treats the position as if the target were sold at the closing value of the acquirer shares without the short. A would be correct for an unhedged long target position valued at closing at an acquirer price of EUR 55.

b.reason: **Wrong input twin.** Uses the target’s pre-announcement price as the purchase price: 10,000 × (48 − 38) = 100,000. This counts the announcement jump, which the fund did not capture because it bought after the announcement. B would be correct if the fund had bought the target before the announcement at EUR 38.

c.reason: Schweser’s “Merger Arbitrage” section and worked example: buy the target, short the acquirer in the exchange ratio, unwind at the merger; the profit is the spread captured at entry.

d.reason: **Dropped term: exchange ratio.** Ignores the 0.8 ratio and treats one target share as one acquirer share: 10,000 × (60 − 45) = 150,000. D would be correct only if the terms were one acquirer share per target share (and the short were 10,000 shares).

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a fund of hedge funds is checking a manager’s return attribution for a share-for-share merger arbitrage position (long the target, short the acquirer) in a deal that has just closed. The attribution report lists the following items:

I. The spread between the target’s price at the announcement and the final bid price at closing

II. Dividends paid on the target shares held during the deal

III. Dividends paid on the acquirer shares that the fund sold short

IV. An increase in the bid after a competing bidder emerged

Which of the items should be reported as contributing positively to the arbitrageur’s return?

options.text: I, II and IV only
I, II, III and IV
I and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Auditing a return attribution for a closed share-for-share deal: which items add to return.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser lists what the arbitrageur may benefit from if the deal closes:

| Benefit if the deal closes | Comment |
|---|---|
| The arbitrage spread | Announcement price vs final bid at closing |
| Dividends received on the target’s stock | Received on the long leg |
| Interest on short-sale proceeds | Net of borrowing costs and any dividends owed on the shorted acquirer stock |
| Possibility of an increased bid | Especially when competing bidders emerge |

The asymmetry in dividends follows from the positions: a long holder receives dividends; a short seller must pay the lender any dividends on the borrowed shares. So acquirer dividends appear in the list only as a deduction from the interest benefit.

**Applying it to this question**

I (arbitrage spread): positive. II (dividends on the long target leg): positive. III (dividends on the short acquirer leg): owed to the stock lender, so they reduce return. IV (raised bid from a competing bidder): positive. Items I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Target dividends are received (long leg); acquirer dividends are owed (short leg) and are netted against short-proceeds interest.

**Reference**

LO 90.c: Describe the mechanics and risks of event-driven strategies such as merger arbitrage. Schweser, Reading 90, Module 90.3 “Event-Driven and Distressed Strategies”, “Merger Arbitrage”, list of benefits if the deal closes. GARP text in the project has no matching section for Schweser Reading 90; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the assigned reading’s framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-8 c, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: Schweser lists the arbitrage spread, dividends received on the target firm’s stock, and the possibility of an increased bid as benefits, and lists dividends owed on the shorted acquirer’s stock as a deduction from interest on short proceeds.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Includes III, reversing the direction of the acquirer dividend: dividends on borrowed shares are paid by the short seller, not received. B would be correct if the fund were long the acquirer, which it is not in this trade.

c.reason: **Scope error.** Drops II and so narrows the benefits to the spread and the higher bid, leaving out dividends received on the target. C would be correct if the target paid no dividends during the deal.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** Assigns the dividend benefit to the wrong leg: it credits the acquirer dividends (short leg) and drops the target dividends (long leg). D would be correct only if the positions were reversed (long acquirer, short target).
