questions.loText: Explain benefits and challenges of investing in private markets through an intermediated investment vehicle such as a private equity or private debt fund.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-11 f Q1
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Singapore family office is presenting to newly hired analysts. The office has no in-house deal team and has decided to gain private debt exposure through a pooled private debt fund rather than by lending directly to private companies. Which of the following statements about the expertise benefit of investing through the fund is most accurate?

options.text: The manager’s skills in sourcing and structuring deals mainly reduce the illiquidity risk the office would otherwise bear, because the manager can exit positions whenever the office needs cash.
The manager’s skills in sourcing, due diligence, structuring, monitoring and exiting eliminate operational risk for every investor that allocates through the fund, whatever its own capabilities.
The manager’s skills in sourcing, due diligence, structuring, monitoring and exiting can reduce operational risk, a reduction that matters most for investors that, like the office, lack such skills.
The manager’s skills are concentrated in sourcing and due diligence, so the office must still build its own team to monitor the loans and manage exits once the fund has invested.

questions.solution:
Singapore family office with no deal team uses a private debt fund: which statement on the expertise benefit is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Private markets are complex: there is no exchange that lists the opportunities, no standardized disclosure, and every deal must be found, examined, negotiated, watched and eventually sold or refinanced. An intermediated vehicle (a private equity or private debt fund) exists partly because most investors cannot do all of this well themselves. Schweser lists four benefits and seven challenges of intermediation:

| Benefits | Challenges |
|---|---|
| Expertise | High fees |
| Risk reduction | Principal-agent risk |
| Deal flow access | Lack of transparency |
| Cost and resource sharing | Blind pool risk Illiquidity risk Due diligence demands Potential conflicts of interest |

The expertise benefit has three parts. First, the scope: fund managers bring expertise in five activities across the whole life of an investment, namely sourcing, due diligence, structuring, monitoring and exiting. Second, the reason it matters: these capabilities are valuable given the complexity of private markets. Third, the risk it reduces and for whom: it can reduce operational risk for investors who lack specialized skills.

**Applying it to this question**

The office has no deal team, which is exactly the condition under which the source says expertise reduces operational risk. The deciding facts are (i) the full five-stage list of capabilities, (ii) the risk named is operational risk, not illiquidity risk, (iii) the verb is “can reduce”, not “eliminate”, and (iv) the benefit is tied to investors lacking specialized skills.

**Fragile fact.** Expertise reduces operational risk, it does so for investors lacking skills, and the verb is can reduce. The manager covers the full chain: sourcing, due diligence, structuring, monitoring, exiting.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 93.f: Explain benefits and challenges of investing in private markets through an intermediated investment vehicle such as a private equity or private debt fund.

**Schweser:** Reading 93, Private Markets Investing; Module 93.3, Private Market Co-Investing and Intermediated Vehicles; section “Intermediated Private Market Investment”, Benefits: “Expertise”. **GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this item.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 f, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** A attaches the expertise benefit to the wrong risk. Illiquidity is a listed challenge of intermediation: capital is committed for long periods with no redemption rights. A manager’s skill in exiting portfolio companies does not let the limited partner get its cash out on demand. A would only be correct if the stem asked about an open-ended, redeemable vehicle, which is not what the reading describes.

b.reason: **Absolute claim and scope error.** “Eliminate” overstates the hedged “can reduce”, and “every investor, whatever its own capabilities” drops the condition that the benefit applies to investors who lack specialized skills. B would be closer to correct if it said “can reduce operational risk for investors lacking such skills”.

c.reason: C reproduces all four elements: the five activities, the hedged verb “can reduce”, the correct risk (operational), and the condition (investors that lack such skills). This matches the Schweser text: fund managers bring expertise in sourcing, due diligence, structuring, monitoring and exiting, which can reduce operational risk for investors who lack specialized skills.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** D cuts the manager’s list down to sourcing and due diligence and assigns monitoring and exiting back to the investor. The source lists monitoring and exiting among the manager’s capabilities. D would describe a co-investor or direct investor, who must carry out these tasks with its own resources.

questions.question:
The CRO of a Canadian university endowment is reviewing a board memo that recommends committing CAD 150 million to a diversified private equity fund instead of making three direct buyouts of CAD 50 million each. The memo makes the following statements about the risk reduction benefit of the fund:

I. Pooling capital with other investors gives the endowment exposure to a wider range of deals, sectors and geographies than it could assemble on its own.

II. Professional management may lead to lower loss ratios, which further reduces risk.

III. Because the fund holds many deals across sectors and geographies, the endowment’s private equity exposure is no longer affected by economic downturns or interest rate changes.

IV. A further source of risk reduction is that limited partners can redeem their interests at NAV if the fund’s losses begin to mount.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
II and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
Canadian endowment memo on the risk reduction benefit of a diversified private equity fund: which of statements I to IV are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

The risk reduction benefit rests on two mechanisms. The first, which Schweser calls the key benefit of intermediation, is diversification: pooling capital from many investors gives each of them access to a wider range of deals, sectors and geographies than any one of them could assemble alone. A CAD 50 million direct buyout is one company; a share of a pooled fund is a slice of many. The second is professional management, which may lead to lower loss ratios, further reducing risk. Two limits matter. Diversification reduces deal-specific risk but does not remove exposure to the broad economy; elsewhere in the same reading (LO 93.d) Schweser stresses that private assets, despite low correlation with public indices, remain exposed to economic downturns, inflation and interest rate policy. And intermediation does not make the investment liquid: illiquidity, with no redemption rights, is one of the listed challenges.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against the two mechanisms and the two limits.

- I: pooling gives access to a wider range of deals, sectors and geographies. True (mechanism 1).
- II: professional management may lead to lower loss ratios. True (mechanism 2, with the hedge “may”).
- III: diversification removes exposure to downturns and interest rates. False (limit 1).
- IV: LPs can redeem at NAV. False (limit 2).

Only I and II survive.

**Fragile fact.** Risk reduction comes from diversification (deals, sectors, geographies) plus professional management that may lower loss ratios; it reduces deal-specific risk, not systematic risk, and it does not create liquidity.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 93.f: Explain benefits and challenges of investing in private markets through an intermediated investment vehicle such as a private equity or private debt fund.

**Schweser:** Reading 93, Private Markets Investing; Module 93.3, Private Market Co-Investing and Intermediated Vehicles; section “Intermediated Private Market Investment”, Benefits: “Risk reduction”; also Challenges: “Illiquidity risk”. The limit in statement III uses LO 93.d, “Major Risk Categories: Systematic risk” (same reading).

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this item.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 f, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: Statements I and II restate the two parts of the Schweser risk reduction paragraph: diversification through pooled capital across deals, sectors and geographies, and the possibility of lower loss ratios from professional management.

b.reason: **Absolute claim in statement III.** B accepts III, which turns “risk reduction” into immunity from systematic risk. Pooling diversifies away deal-specific risk only. B would be right only if III said that pooling reduces exposure to deal-specific risk.

c.reason: **Polarity flip in statement IV, and drops I.** IV reverses the illiquidity challenge: capital is committed for long periods with no redemption rights, and selling usually means a significant discount to NAV. C would be right only for a vehicle with redemption rights, which a private equity fund in the reading does not have; it also omits the true statement I.

d.reason: **Accepts III, drops II.** D includes the absolute claim in III and excludes the true statement II about lower loss ratios. It would be correct only if the reading had not listed professional management as a second source of risk reduction.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Japanese life insurer is preparing a report for the investment committee explaining why the insurer will access mid-market private debt through an established fund manager rather than originating loans itself. She must include one statement on the deal flow benefit. Which statement should she include?

options.text: Deal flow access matters less as private markets become more competitive, because competition makes attractive opportunities widely available to individual investors.
Deal flow access means the manager gives each limited partner the right to select which individual loans the fund will originate on its behalf.
Deal flow access means the manager spreads the costs of sourcing and analyzing loans across many investors, which lowers each investor’s fee burden.
Managers often have access to attractive opportunities that most individual investors cannot reach, a benefit that grows as private markets become more competitive and specialized.

questions.solution:
Japanese life insurer report on accessing mid-market private debt: which statement on the deal flow benefit should be included?

**Concept and theory**

In public markets every investor can buy the same listed bond. In private markets, opportunities are found through networks and relationships, and the best ones often never reach a wide audience. The deal flow access benefit says that managers often have access to attractive investment opportunities that are not available to most individual investors. Schweser adds a direction: this benefit becomes especially important as private markets grow more competitive and specialized. The logic is that, as more capital competes for deals and strategies become narrower, the advantage of an established manager’s network rises rather than falls. Deal flow access is distinct from the other three benefits: expertise is about skill in handling deals, risk reduction is about diversification and loss ratios, and cost sharing is about spreading the cost of sourcing and oversight.

**Applying it to this question**

The analyst must choose the statement that describes deal flow access and its direction correctly. The deciding facts are: the benefit is access to opportunities that most individual investors cannot reach, and its importance increases with competition and specialization.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: deal flow access becomes more important as private markets grow more competitive and specialized.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 93.f: Explain benefits and challenges of investing in private markets through an intermediated investment vehicle such as a private equity or private debt fund.

**Schweser:** Reading 93, Private Markets Investing; Module 93.3, Private Market Co-Investing and Intermediated Vehicles; section “Intermediated Private Market Investment”, Benefits: “Deal flow access”.

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this item.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 f, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** A reverses the direction: Schweser says the benefit becomes especially important as markets become more competitive. A would be right only if competition made deals easier for individuals to find, the opposite of the reading’s logic.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** B gives deal selection to the limited partner. In a fund, the manager decides how capital is deployed (see blind pool risk). Choosing individual deals is a feature of co-investing or direct investing, not of fund intermediation.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** C describes the cost and resource sharing benefit (spreading sourcing and analysis costs), not deal flow access. It also adds an unsupported claim that fees fall; the reading lists high fees as a challenge. C would describe cost and resource sharing if the fee claim were removed.

d.reason: D states both parts of the Schweser text: managers often have access to attractive opportunities not available to most individual investors, and this matters more as private markets become more competitive and specialized.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at an Australian superannuation fund is validating a recommendation to invest in private equity through a pooled fund rather than building a direct investment program. The recommendation cites the following annual cost estimates for a stand-alone direct program, together with a market statistic:

| Item | AUD million or % |
|---|---|
| Deal sourcing team (AUD million) | 4.2 |
| Transaction analysis and legal review (AUD million) | 2.8 |
| Ongoing portfolio oversight (AUD million) | 1.9 |
| Dividend yield on the fund’s listed equity portfolio (%) | 3.1 |

Which statement best describes the benefit of intermediation on which this part of the recommendation relies?

options.text: The pooled fund removes these costs from investors entirely, because the manager absorbs the sourcing, analysis and oversight costs without passing any of them on through fees.
Pooling assets lets the fund share the substantial sourcing, analysis and oversight costs with other investors, costs that might otherwise prevent it from investing directly.
Pooling assets means the manager’s analysis budget covers all review work, so the fund no longer needs to perform its own due diligence on the manager it selects.
Pooling assets lowers these costs mainly because the manager has access to attractive deals that are not available to most individual investors.

questions.solution:
Australian superannuation fund validating a pooled-fund recommendation with a table of direct-program costs: which benefit does it rely on?

**Concept and theory**

Running a private markets program is expensive in its own right: someone must find deals (sourcing), examine them (analysis, legal review) and watch them after purchase (ongoing oversight). For a single investor these fixed costs can be so large that they make direct participation uneconomic. The cost and resource sharing benefit says that pooling assets lets investors share the substantial costs associated with sourcing, analysis and ongoing oversight, costs that might otherwise prevent individual investors from participating directly in private markets. Note that sharing a cost is not the same as removing it: investors still pay for professional management through management fees and carried interest, which the reading lists as the “high fees” challenge.

**Applying it to this question**

The three cost lines in the table map one for one onto the three cost types named in the source: sourcing (AUD 4.2 million), analysis (AUD 2.8 million) and ongoing oversight (AUD 1.9 million). Their total of AUD 8.9 million a year is the burden the fund would carry alone. The dividend yield of 3.1% on listed equities is irrelevant to the question. No calculation is needed; the decision is which benefit the cost data support.

**Fragile fact.** Costs are shared, not removed; the three named cost types are sourcing, analysis and ongoing oversight.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 93.f: Explain benefits and challenges of investing in private markets through an intermediated investment vehicle such as a private equity or private debt fund.

**Schweser:** Reading 93, Private Markets Investing; Module 93.3, Private Market Co-Investing and Intermediated Vehicles; section “Intermediated Private Market Investment”, Benefits: “Cost and resource sharing”; Challenges: “High fees” and “Due diligence demands”.

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this item.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 f, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** A says the costs are removed entirely and never passed on. The reading says the costs are shared, and that investors typically pay both management fees and carried interest. A would only hold for a vehicle with no fees, which the reading does not describe.

b.reason: B names the mechanism (pooling), the cost types (sourcing, analysis, ongoing oversight) and the consequence (costs that might otherwise prevent direct participation), exactly as in the Schweser cost and resource sharing paragraph.

c.reason: **Scope error, contradicts a listed challenge.** C extends cost sharing to the investor’s own due diligence on the manager. Due diligence demands are a separate challenge: investors must still review fund strategies, manager track records, governance and operations. C would be right only if the reading had said intermediation removes the need for manager due diligence, which it does not.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** D explains cost savings through deal flow access. Deal flow access is a real benefit but concerns access to opportunities, not the sharing of sourcing, analysis and oversight costs. D would be right if the stem had cited exclusive deals rather than cost lines.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a German pension fund compares the gross returns earned on the portfolio companies of a EUR buyout fund with the net returns received by the fund’s limited partners and finds a persistent gap. A board member asks for the reason. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.text: Limited partners pay both management fees and carried interest, so the underlying investments must earn enough to clear a natural performance hurdle before investors earn an attractive net return.
Limited partners pay a management fee to the fund and a second layer of fees to the underlying funds it holds, a double fee layer present in any intermediated private equity fund.
The general partner pays carried interest to the limited partners out of its management fee, and this payment reduces the gross returns reported for the portfolio companies.
Carried interest is charged mainly when the fund underperforms, so it widens the gap in weak years while lowering the hurdle the manager must clear in strong years.

questions.solution:
German pension fund sees a persistent gap between gross portfolio-company returns and LP net returns in a EUR buyout fund: which explanation is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Professional management is not free. The high fees challenge says that accessing professional management teams is expensive, and that investors typically pay both management fees and carried interest. The two fees differ in nature. A management fee is paid regardless of results. Carried interest is a performance-based fee (Schweser LO 93.b describes carried interest as “performance-based fees”), paid to the general partner out of the gains. Together they create what Schweser calls a natural performance hurdle: the underlying investments must earn enough to cover both before the limited partners’ net return is attractive. In simple terms:

LP net return ≈ gross return on investments $- \text{management fees} -$ carried interest.

The direction of payment matters: fees flow from the limited partners (LPs) to the general partner (GP).

**Applying it to this question**

The stem describes a single buyout fund that owns portfolio companies directly; it is not a fund of funds. The gap between gross and net is the fee wedge. The deciding facts are: two fee types, paid by LPs to the GP, with carried interest tied to performance, creating a hurdle.

**Fragile fact.** Payer and payee: LPs pay the GP both a management fee and carried interest; carry is performance-based. The double fee layer is a fund-of-funds feature, not a single-fund feature.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 93.f: Explain benefits and challenges of investing in private markets through an intermediated investment vehicle such as a private equity or private debt fund.

**Schweser:** Reading 93, Private Markets Investing; Module 93.3, Private Market Co-Investing and Intermediated Vehicles; section “Intermediated Private Market Investment”, Challenges: “High fees”. Carried interest as a performance-based fee and the fund-of-funds extra fee layer: LO 93.b, “Private Market Investment Structures” (same reading).

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this item.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 f, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: A states that LPs pay both management fees and carried interest and that this creates a natural performance hurdle, which is the Schweser high fees challenge almost word for word.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** B describes the extra layer of management fees that belongs to a private fund of funds (LO 93.b). A direct buyout fund holds companies, not other funds, so there is no second fund layer. B would be correct only if the stem described a fund of funds.

c.reason: **Role misassignment.** C reverses who pays whom. Carried interest is paid by the LPs to the GP, not by the GP to the LPs. C would be correct only if the roles of payer and payee were swapped, which no structure in the reading does.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** D reverses the trigger for carried interest. As a performance-based fee, carry is earned on gains, so it bites in strong years and adds to, rather than lowers, the hurdle. D would be right only for a fee charged on losses, which the reading does not describe.

questions.question: A risk consultant advising a Brazilian family office with BRL 400 million of liquid assets is preparing a slide on the economics of investing in private markets through intermediated vehicles. Which of the following statements on the slide is NOT correct?

options.text: Pooling assets allows investors to share sourcing, analysis and ongoing oversight costs that might otherwise prevent them from participating directly in private markets.
Accessing a professional management team is expensive, and investors in such vehicles typically pay both management fees and carried interest.
Because pooling spreads costs across many investors, the fees of a private equity or private debt fund are too small to act as a meaningful hurdle to net performance.
The fees investors pay are the cost of accessing professional management teams, whose expertise and deal flow are themselves listed benefits of intermediation.

questions.solution:
Brazilian family office slide on the economics of intermediated private markets: which statement is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

Intermediation has an economic tension built into it. On one side, the cost and resource sharing benefit: pooling assets lets investors share the substantial costs of sourcing, analysis and ongoing oversight, costs that might otherwise prevent them from participating. On the other side, the high fees challenge: accessing professional management teams is expensive, investors typically pay both management fees and carried interest, and this creates a natural performance hurdle. Both are true at once. Sharing costs makes participation possible; it does not make the fee burden small. The fees are, in effect, what investors pay to obtain the expertise and deal flow that are listed benefits.

| Cost and resource sharing (benefit) | High fees (challenge) |
|---|---|
| Spreads sourcing, analysis, oversight costs | Management fees plus carried interest |
| Makes participation feasible | Creates a natural performance hurdle |

**Applying it to this question**

The question uses a NOT qualifier, so the answer is the single false statement. A restates cost sharing (true). B restates high fees (true). D links fees to access to professional management teams, whose expertise and deal flow are listed benefits (true). C claims that cost sharing makes fees too small to be a hurdle, which contradicts the high fees challenge.

**Fragile fact.** Cost sharing and high fees coexist: sharing makes participation possible, and fees still form a natural performance hurdle.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 93.f: Explain benefits and challenges of investing in private markets through an intermediated investment vehicle such as a private equity or private debt fund.

**Schweser:** Reading 93, Private Markets Investing; Module 93.3, Private Market Co-Investing and Intermediated Vehicles; section “Intermediated Private Market Investment”, Benefits: “Cost and resource sharing”, “Expertise”, “Deal flow access”; Challenges: “High fees”.

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this item.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 f, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: **True; restates cost and resource sharing.** This is the Schweser benefit almost verbatim. It would become false only if it claimed the costs were removed rather than shared.

b.reason: **True; restates high fees.** Accessing professional management teams is expensive, and investors typically pay both management fees and carried interest. It would become false if it named only one of the two fees as typical, or said carried interest is paid to LPs.

c.reason: Schweser states that investors typically pay both management fees and carried interest, which creates a natural performance hurdle. C uses the cost-sharing benefit to deny that hurdle, so it is the statement that is NOT correct.

d.reason:
**True; links the challenge to the benefits.** The high fees paragraph opens by saying that accessing professional management teams is expensive; the benefits paragraph lists the expertise and deal flow such teams provide. D would become false if it claimed the fees bought liquidity or transparency, both of which are listed as challenges.

The trap in C is a polarity flip on the fee hurdle, triggered by a sibling benefit (cost sharing) that sounds as if it should lower the fee burden.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee at a UK insurer reviews a case involving a GBP private debt fund in which the insurer is a limited partner. The general partner raised a successor fund early and shifted its senior staff to the new vehicle, which increased its own fee income, while the original fund’s portfolio received less attention and its loan workouts slowed. Which of the following best describes the challenge of intermediation illustrated by the case?

options.text: Principal-agent risk, in which the limited partners act as agents for the general partner, and the limited partners’ goals may not align with those of the manager they serve.

Principal-agent risk, in which the goals of the general partner may not align with those of the limited partners, creating governance and performance concerns, including potential abuse or misconduct.
Blind pool risk, in which the limited partners committed capital before knowing the assets, so the misalignment is simply a feature of the fund’s strategy guidelines.
Principal-agent risk, which arises only when the fund invests in both the equity and the debt of the same company and therefore faces competing incentives between the two claims.

questions.solution:
UK insurer, GBP private debt fund: GP raises a successor fund early and shifts staff, raising its fee income while the original fund’s workouts slow. Which challenge is illustrated?

**Concept and theory**

A principal-agent relationship exists when one party (the principal) delegates work to another (the agent) whose interests may differ. In a private fund, the limited partners provide the capital and delegate investment decisions to the general partner; the LPs are the principals and the GP is the agent. The principal-agent risk challenge, as Schweser states it, is that the goals of the general partner may not always align with those of the limited partners, and that this misalignment can create governance and performance concerns, including the potential for abuse or misconduct. It is a structural feature of delegation and does not depend on any particular asset mix. It is related to, but distinct from, the separate challenge of potential conflicts of interest, whose examples in the reading are a fund that holds both the equity and the debt of the same company, and the allocation of co-investment opportunities.

**Applying it to this question**

The GP’s action raised its own fee income while the existing LPs’ portfolio suffered (slower workouts). That is a divergence between the GP’s goals and the LPs’ goals, with a performance consequence. The fund did not invest in both the debt and equity of one company, and the issue is not about committing capital before knowing the assets. The deciding facts are the actor (GP’s goals) and the direction (GP’s goals diverge from those of LPs).

**Fragile fact.** Actor and direction: the GP’s goals may not align with the LPs’ goals; LPs are principals, the GP is the agent.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 93.f: Explain benefits and challenges of investing in private markets through an intermediated investment vehicle such as a private equity or private debt fund.

**Schweser:** Reading 93, Private Markets Investing; Module 93.3, Private Market Co-Investing and Intermediated Vehicles; section “Intermediated Private Market Investment”, Challenges: “Principal-agent risk” and “Potential conflicts of interest”.

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this item.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 f, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** A names the right challenge but swaps the roles: it makes the LPs the agents of the GP. In a fund, the GP acts for the LPs, who delegate control. A would be correct only in a structure where investors managed money on behalf of the manager, which does not exist in the reading.

b.reason: B states the Schweser definition with the correct actors and direction: GP goals may not align with LP goals, creating governance and performance concerns, including potential abuse or misconduct.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Blind pool risk concerns committing capital before knowing which assets will be acquired; it explains unwanted exposures, not a GP putting its own fee income ahead of the LPs. C would be correct if the stem had described acquisitions within the guidelines that the insurer would not have chosen.

d.reason: **Scope error.** D narrows principal-agent risk to the equity-and-debt case, which the reading gives as an example of the separate challenge of conflicts of interest. Principal-agent risk arises from delegation itself. D would describe conflicts of interest if “principal-agent risk” were replaced by that name and “only” were dropped.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Chinese sovereign wealth fund is drafting notes for a CNY 2 billion commitment program to private equity funds. The notes cover the lack-of-transparency challenge of intermediated investing. Which of the following notes is NOT correct?

options.text: Intermediation places layers between investors and the underlying assets, which limits the investors’ ability to monitor or influence the investments.
Limited disclosure and infrequent valuations by the manager are sources of the information asymmetry that investors in the funds face.
Proprietary management practices are a further source of information asymmetry, alongside the limited disclosure and infrequent valuations.
The timing of a fund’s cash flows is fixed in the fund documents at closing, so, unlike disclosure and valuation, it is not a source of uncertainty for investors.

questions.solution:
Chinese sovereign wealth fund notes on the lack-of-transparency challenge: which note is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

When an investor holds a company directly, it can look at the company itself. When it holds a share of a fund, the manager stands in between. The lack of transparency challenge says that intermediation introduces layers between investors and the underlying assets, limiting investors’ ability to monitor or influence investments. Schweser then names four sources of the resulting information asymmetry:

1. limited disclosure;
2. infrequent valuations;
3. proprietary management practices;
4. uncertainty regarding the timing of cash flows.

The fourth is easy to forget. The same reading (LO 93.c) notes that managers may delay capital calls by drawing on credit lines and that funds often do not call the full committed amount, so the investor cannot know in advance exactly when, or how much, cash will move.

**Applying it to this question**

With a NOT qualifier, look for the note that contradicts the list. A restates the layering point. B names sources 1 and 2. C names source 3. D denies source 4 by claiming the timing of cash flows is fixed at closing.

**Fragile fact.** Four sources of information asymmetry: limited disclosure, infrequent valuations, proprietary practices, and uncertain timing of cash flows.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 93.f: Explain benefits and challenges of investing in private markets through an intermediated investment vehicle such as a private equity or private debt fund.

**Schweser:** Reading 93, Private Markets Investing; Module 93.3, Private Market Co-Investing and Intermediated Vehicles; section “Intermediated Private Market Investment”, Challenges: “Lack of transparency”.

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this item.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 f, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: **True.** This is the opening sentence of the Schweser lack-of-transparency paragraph. It would become false if it said layers improve monitoring, for example by crediting the GP’s monitoring to the LP.

b.reason: **True.** Limited disclosure and infrequent valuations are the first two listed sources. It would become false if it said valuations were frequent or disclosure extensive.

c.reason:
**True.** Proprietary management practices are the third listed source. It would become false if it said the manager’s practices were shared in full with LPs.

The trap in D is a scope error: it drops one of the four stated sources and supports the omission with a plausible but unsupported claim about fund documents.

d.reason: Schweser lists uncertainty regarding the timing of cash flows as a source of information asymmetry. D asserts the opposite, so D is the note that is NOT correct.

questions.question: The CIO of a US charitable foundation committed USD 75 million to a newly raised private equity fund. Eighteen months later the fund has acquired two companies in a sector the foundation would not have chosen if it had invested directly, although both acquisitions fall within the strategy guidelines set out in the fund documents. Which statement best describes the challenge the foundation faces?

options.text: Blind pool risk: the foundation committed capital before knowing which assets would be acquired and, although guidelines were provided, the manager ultimately decides how the capital is deployed.
Blind pool risk: the foundation committed capital without receiving any strategy guidelines, so the manager was free to invest outside any stated mandate when it chose the sector.
Lack of transparency: the foundation held a veto over each acquisition but could not use it, because infrequent valuations prevented it from assessing the two target companies.
Principal-agent risk: the manager breached the fund’s stated strategy guidelines, so the sector exposure reflects misconduct by the manager rather than the structure of the fund.

questions.solution:
US foundation commits USD 75 million to a new private equity fund, which then buys companies in a sector the foundation would not have chosen but within the guidelines: which challenge?

**Concept and theory**

Many private equity and private debt funds are raised before they own anything. Investors sign a commitment and the manager then finds and buys the assets over the following years. Schweser calls this a blind pool: investors commit capital before knowing exactly which assets will be acquired. Two details define the risk precisely. First, investors are not blind to everything: strategy guidelines are provided. Second, within those guidelines the fund manager ultimately decides how capital is deployed, which may result in exposures an investor would not have chosen directly. The risk is therefore a structural consequence of delegating selection, not evidence of wrongdoing.

**Applying it to this question**

Three facts in the stem decide the answer: the commitment was made to a newly raised fund (assets unknown at commitment), the acquisitions fall within the stated strategy guidelines (guidelines were provided and respected), and the foundation would not have chosen the sector itself (an exposure the investor would not have chosen directly).

**Fragile fact.** Blind pool: guidelines are provided, but the manager decides deployment; the risk is unwanted exposure, not misconduct.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 93.f: Explain benefits and challenges of investing in private markets through an intermediated investment vehicle such as a private equity or private debt fund.

**Schweser:** Reading 93, Private Markets Investing; Module 93.3, Private Market Co-Investing and Intermediated Vehicles; section “Intermediated Private Market Investment”, Challenges: “Blind pool risk”. Advisory mandates with investor veto: LO 93.b, “Managed accounts” (same reading). **GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this item.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 f, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: A states each element of the Schweser blind pool paragraph: commitment before knowing the assets, guidelines provided, the manager ultimately deciding deployment.

b.reason: **Condition error.** B removes the stated condition that strategy guidelines are provided, and contradicts the stem, which says the deals fall within those guidelines. B would be correct only for a fund with no stated strategy at all.

c.reason: **Sibling swap with role error.** C relabels the problem as lack of transparency and gives the foundation a veto over each acquisition. A veto belongs to an advisory managed account (LO 93.b), not to an LP in a pooled fund, where the manager decides deployment. C would fit an advisory managed account whose investor lacked information to exercise its veto.

d.reason: **Sibling swap contradicting the facts.** D calls the outcome principal-agent misconduct based on a breach of the guidelines, but the stem says the acquisitions were within them. D would be correct only if the manager had invested outside the mandate for its own benefit.

questions.question:
The treasurer of a Singapore corporate pension plan needs cash and wants to exit the plan’s limited partner interest in a private debt fund well before the end of the fund’s term. She gathers the following data (SGD million):

| Item | SGD million |
|---|---|
| Reported NAV of the plan’s interest | 64.0 |
| Best bid received in the secondary market | 49.6 |
| Plan’s undrawn commitment to the fund | 16.0 |
| Distributions received over the past 12 months | 5.2 |

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The bid is at a 22.5% discount to NAV, but the plan can avoid this loss by exercising its right to redeem the interest from the fund at NAV instead of selling it.
The bid is at a 29.0% discount to NAV, which reflects the long commitment period, the absence of redemption rights and the limited secondary market of the fund.
The bid is at a 22.5% discount to NAV, which reflects the long commitment period, the absence of redemption rights and the limited secondary market of the fund.
The bid is at a 38.0% discount to NAV, which reflects the long commitment period, the absence of redemption rights and the limited secondary market of the fund.

questions.solution:
Singapore pension plan wants to exit an LP interest in a private debt fund early: NAV SGD 64.0 million, secondary bid SGD 49.6 million. Which statement is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

A limited partner in a private equity or private debt fund makes a long-term commitment. The illiquidity risk challenge, as Schweser states it, has three parts: capital is committed for long periods, there are no redemption rights, and secondary market options are limited. The consequence: if liquidity is needed, investors may have to accept significant discounts to NAV. The discount is measured against NAV, the reported value of the interest:

Discount to NAV $= \frac{\text{NAV} - \text{Price}}{\text{NAV}}$ ,

where NAV is the reported net asset value of the interest being sold and Price is the amount the buyer pays for it.

**Applying it to this question**

Only two inputs matter: the NAV of the interest and the bid. The undrawn commitment is capital not yet called, so it is not part of the interest’s NAV, and the 12-month distributions are past cash flows; both are irrelevant here.

Shortfall = 64.0 − 49.6 = SGD 14.4 million

Discount to NAV $= \frac{14.4}{64.0} =$ 0.225 = 22.5%

Meaning: to raise cash now, the plan gives up 22.5% of reported value. Because the fund offers no redemption and the secondary market is limited, this discount is the price of exiting early.

**Fragile fact.** The base is NAV, not the bid; there are no redemption rights, so an early exit means a secondary sale, often at a significant discount to NAV.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 93.f: Explain benefits and challenges of investing in private markets through an intermediated investment vehicle such as a private equity or private debt fund.

**Schweser:** Reading 93, Private Markets Investing; Module 93.3, Private Market Co-Investing and Intermediated Vehicles; section “Intermediated Private Market Investment”, Challenges: “Illiquidity risk”. Uncalled capital as distinct from deployed capital: LO 93.c, “Common Limitation of PE Performance Metrics” (same reading).

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this item.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 f, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip on redemption rights.** A computes the discount correctly but claims the plan can redeem at NAV. Schweser states there are no redemption rights. A would be correct only for an open-ended fund with redemption rights, which the reading does not describe.

b.reason: **Wrong base.** B divides the shortfall by the bid instead of NAV: 14.4/49.6 = 0.2903 = 29.0%. A discount to NAV must use NAV as the base. B would be correct if the question asked for the premium of NAV over the bid.

c.reason: C has the right number (22.5%) and the right explanation: long commitment, no redemption rights, limited secondary market, which together lead investors to accept significant discounts to NAV when they need liquidity.

d.reason: **Wrong input: irrelevant figure added to NAV.** D adds the undrawn commitment to NAV: (64.0 + 16.0 − 49.6)/(64.0 + 16.0) = 30.4/80.0 = 0.380 = 38.0%. The undrawn commitment is capital not yet called and is not part of the interest’s NAV. D would be correct only if the bid were for an interest whose value was SGD 80.0 million.

questions.question: At a meeting of a regional bank’s pension plan, a trustee argues that because the private debt fund manager the plan has shortlisted performs detailed due diligence on every loan, the plan can skip its own review before committing. The plan’s risk officer disagrees. Which of the following best states the risk officer’s position?

options.text: The manager’s due diligence expertise is itself a benefit of intermediation, so once a reputable manager is shortlisted, a separate review by the plan adds little.
The plan must perform its own due diligence on each borrower before the fund lends, because a blind pool fund needs limited partner approval for every loan.
The plan need only review the manager’s track record, because past returns already capture the quality of the fund’s strategy, governance and operational processes.
The plan must still review the fund’s strategy, the manager’s track record, the governance structure and the operational processes to reduce the risk of underperformance or misconduct.

questions.solution:
Bank pension plan trustee says the manager’s deal-level due diligence lets the plan skip its own review: what is the risk officer’s correct position?

**Concept and theory**

Intermediation moves deal-level work to the manager, but it creates a new task for the investor: choosing and checking the manager. The due diligence demands challenge says that investors must conduct thorough due diligence on four objects:

1. fund strategies;
2. manager track records;
3. governance structures;
4. operational processes;

and that the purpose is to reduce the risk of underperformance or misconduct. Two levels of due diligence must be kept apart. The manager’s expertise in due diligence on deals is a benefit; the investor’s due diligence on the fund and manager is a challenge that intermediation does not remove.

| Level | Who performs it | Where in the reading |
|---|---|---|
| Deals and portfolio companies | Fund manager | Benefit: expertise |
| Fund, manager, governance, operations | Investor (LP) | Challenge: due diligence demands |

**Applying it to this question**

The trustee conflates the two levels. The risk officer’s correct answer is that the plan still owes a full review of the fund on all four objects, for the stated purpose.

**Fragile fact.** Deal-level due diligence is the manager’s (a benefit); fund-level due diligence on strategy, track record, governance and operations is the investor’s (a challenge).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 93.f: Explain benefits and challenges of investing in private markets through an intermediated investment vehicle such as a private equity or private debt fund.

**Schweser:** Reading 93, Private Markets Investing; Module 93.3, Private Market Co-Investing and Intermediated Vehicles; section “Intermediated Private Market Investment”, Challenges: “Due diligence demands” and “Blind pool risk”; Benefits: “Expertise”.

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this item.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-11 f, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: benefit used to cancel a challenge.** A uses the expertise benefit (the manager’s deal-level due diligence) to dismiss the investor-level due diligence challenge. A would be correct only if the reading treated manager selection as risk-free, which it does not.

b.reason: **Role misassignment, contradicts blind pool.** B makes the LP perform due diligence on each borrower and claims LP approval is needed for each loan. In a blind pool the manager ultimately decides how capital is deployed. B would describe a co-investor or direct lender.

c.reason: **Scope error.** C narrows due diligence to the track record alone. Schweser names four objects; the track record is only one. C would be correct only if the stem asked for one element of the review rather than its full scope.

d.reason: D lists the four objects named by Schweser and the stated purpose, reducing the risk of underperformance or misconduct.

questions.question:
A risk consultant reviews three findings from the private markets funds held by a client. She must classify each finding under the challenge of intermediated investing whose description in the reading it matches.

1. Fund X holds both a senior loan to, and the majority of the equity of, the same portfolio company, which is now negotiating a restructuring of its debt.
2. Fund Y’s general partner offered co-investment rights in its most attractive deal of the year to two of its limited partners only, without a stated basis for the choice.
3. Fund Z valued two of its holdings only once in 18 months and declined to share its internal underwriting models with its limited partners.

Which classification is most accurate?

options.text: 1: principal-agent risk; 2: conflicts of interest; 3: lack of transparency
1: conflicts of interest; 2: conflicts of interest; 3: lack of transparency
1: conflicts of interest; 2: conflicts of interest; 3: blind pool risk
1: conflicts of interest; 2: deal flow access; 3: lack of transparency

questions.solution:
Consultant classifies three fund findings (debt and equity in one company; selective deal offer to two LPs; infrequent valuations and undisclosed models): which classification is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

The seven challenges of intermediation sound alike, so each is defined by its own trigger in the reading:

| Challenge | Trigger in the Schweser text |
|---|---|
| Principal-agent risk | GP goals may not align with LP goals (delegation) |
| Conflicts of interest | A fund investing in both equity and debt of the same company; allocation of co-investment opportunities |
| Lack of transparency | Layers; limited disclosure, infrequent valuations, proprietary practices, uncertain cash-flow timing |
| Blind pool risk | Commitment before assets are known; manager decides deployment |

Potential conflicts of interest is a named challenge of its own. Schweser gives two examples: a fund that invests in both the equity and the debt of the same company may face competing incentives between debtholders and equity holders, and conflicts can arise in the allocation of co-investment opportunities.

**Applying it to this question**

Finding 1 is the equity-and-debt example: in a restructuring, the senior lender and the equity holder want different outcomes, and the same fund holds both. Finding 2 is a selective allocation of co-investment rights among LPs, which is the co-investment allocation example. Finding 3 combines infrequent valuations and undisclosed proprietary models, two of the listed sources of information asymmetry under lack of transparency. Classified by the description each matches: conflicts of interest, conflicts of interest, lack of transparency.

**Fragile fact.** Both named examples of conflicts of interest: equity and debt of the same company, and allocation of co-investment opportunities. Principal-agent risk is the general GP versus LP misalignment.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 93.f: Explain benefits and challenges of investing in private markets through an intermediated investment vehicle such as a private equity or private debt fund.

**Schweser:** Reading 93, Private Markets Investing; Module 93.3, Private Market Co-Investing and Intermediated Vehicles; section “Intermediated Private Market Investment”, Challenges: “Potential conflicts of interest”, “Principal-agent risk”, “Lack of transparency”, “Blind pool risk”; Benefits: “Deal flow access”.

**GARP:** GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. No GARP versus Schweser conflict can therefore arise on this item.

a.reason: A files the equity-and-debt case under principal-agent risk. Principal-agent risk is about the GP’s goals versus the LPs’ goals in general; the reading places the equity-and-debt case explicitly under conflicts of interest. A would be correct if finding 1 described the GP putting its own fee income ahead of LPs.

b.reason: B matches each finding to the challenge whose description in the reading it reproduces: both examples given under potential conflicts of interest, and two of the sources listed under lack of transparency.

c.reason: C files infrequent valuations and undisclosed models under blind pool risk. Blind pool risk concerns committing before the assets are known; finding 3 concerns information about assets already held. C would be correct if finding 3 described LPs learning only after commitment which companies the fund would buy.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager.
questions.reading: IM-12: Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds
questions.topic: Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds
questions.source: High quality paper IM-12 c Q1
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Frankfurt bank’s EUR 2.4 billion hedge fund allocation programme is preparing a training slide for newly hired analysts. The slide sorts sample due diligence questions into the four themes used to evaluate a hedge fund manager: strategy, ownership, track record and investment management. Which of the following pairings of question and theme is most accurate?

options.text: “Are most of the staff who generated the past results still employed by the firm?”: strategy.
“Has the fund ever been soft or hard closed, or returned capital to investors?”: strategy.
“Do the traders, portfolio managers and research analysts hold equity in the firm?”: investment management.
“Did former employers find the manager to be a leader or a follower?”: track record.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst sorting sample due diligence questions into the four manager evaluation themes.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser organises manager evaluation into four themes. Strategy asks what the manager does and how: style, current themes, how the portfolio has evolved, turnover and liquidity, loss-limiting mechanisms, quantitative models, short sales, derivatives, trade execution, private investments, the trade-off between current returns and fund growth, and whether the fund has ever been closed or returned capital. Ownership asks whether the investment team (traders, portfolio managers, research analysts) hold equity in the firm. Track record asks whether past results are comparable, verified, long enough, achieved through stress, scaled to asset size and produced by a team still in place. Investment management covers manager interviews, reference checks and background checks. GARP’s section 10.6 uses the same structure under four headings: “What Is Your Strategy, and How Does It Work?”, “How Is Equity Ownership Allocated. . . ?”, “Is the Track Record Reliable?” and “Who Are the Principals, and Are They Trustworthy?”.

| Theme | Core question it answers |
|---|---|
| Strategy | What is the process and how does it work? |
| Ownership | Who owns the firm, and how does that shape talent and performance? |
| Track record | Are the past results reliable and repeatable? |
| Investment management | Are the principals who they say they are (interviews, references, background)? |

**Applying it to this question**

Classify each quoted question by the theme it serves. Team continuity is about whether the record is repeatable (track record). Closure or return of capital is GARP strategy question 15 and Schweser’s last strategy item. Equity held by traders and analysts is ownership. “Leader or follower” is what Schweser says to ask former employers in a reference check, which sits under investment management.

**Fragile fact.** Reference and background checks are investment management, not track record; team continuity is track record, not ownership.

**Reference**

LO 94.c (Schweser Reading 94, Module 94.1, “Manager Evaluation): “Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager. GARP Ch10, section 10.6 Investment Management, subsections “What Is Your Strategy, and How Does It Work?” (question 15), “Is the Track Record Reliable?” and “Who Are the Principals, and Are They Trustworthy?”. Schweser uses “investment management” for interviews, references and background checks, while GARP uses “Investment Management” as the name of the whole section 10.6; the four-theme labels are Schweser’s.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 c, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Whether the staff who generated past results are still employed is a track record question (GARP: “if the team that produced the historical track record is still in place today”). It would be correct if the theme were track record.

b.reason: GARP lists “Has the fund ever been soft or hard closed or returned capital to investors?” as question 15 of the strategy list, and Schweser’s strategy list ends with “Has the fund ever been closed or provided investors with a return of capital?”. The pairing is therefore correct.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Equity held by the investment team is the ownership theme itself. The pairing would be correct if the theme named were ownership.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** “Leader or follower” is a reference check question put to former employers, which belongs to investment management. It would be correct if the theme named were investment management. Track record does include “how it relates to the portfolio manager’s experience at previous firms”, which makes D tempting, but that concerns performance, not personal conduct.

questions.question:
The CIO of a Japanese corporate pension plan with JPY 310 billion in alternatives is drafting the strategy section of an interview guide for an equity long/short manager. A consultant proposes four entries:

I. Ask what triggers a reversal or an exit decision, and whether those triggers are hard coded into the risk management process or are just guidelines.

II. Ask whether stop losses are used at the position level, the portfolio level or both, and whether they are always executed or are subject to exceptions.

III. Ask whether short sales are used as hedges or as alpha generators, and screen out any manager who answers that they are used as both.

IV. Ask how proprietary models are developed and back-tested, but leave out how they are allocated capital or decommissioned, since those are business model questions.

Which of the entries are consistent with the strategy questions an investor can consider when evaluating the manager?

options.text: I only
I and III only
II and IV only
I and II only

questions.solution:
CIO drafting strategy interview entries on exit triggers, stop losses, short sales and models.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s strategy list is designed to make the manager explain how the portfolio is actually run, not just what the pitch book says. Several questions probe the mechanics of discipline. Question 5 asks about turnover, days to liquidate and “the triggers that result in a reversal and a sell or buy to cover or exit decision”, and whether the triggers are “hard coded into the risk management process or just guidelines”. Question 6 asks how stop losses are used: “at the position level, portfolio level, or both? Are they always executed or are there exceptions?”. Question 7 asks how quantitative the process is and how proprietary models are “developed, back-tested, and allocated capital, or decommissioned when failing to perform”. Question 8 asks whether short sales are used “as hedges, alpha generators, or both” and whether the firm has been hurt by a short squeeze, recall or buy-in. Schweser condenses these into questions on market signals for entering and exiting, mechanisms to limit losses, the use of quantitative models, and whether short sales are used to generate excess profits or to hedge.

**Applying it to this question**

Entry I reproduces the substance of GARP question 5. Entry II reproduces question 6. Entry III asks the right question but adds a screening rule: GARP lists “both” as one of the possible answers, not as a disqualification. Entry IV truncates question 7 by removing capital allocation and decommissioning, which GARP explicitly includes in the strategy question.

**Fragile fact.** Short sales: “hedges, alpha generators, or both”; models: developed, back-tested, allocated capital, or decommissioned. Both full lists sit in the strategy theme.

**Reference**

LO 94.c (Schweser Reading 94, Module 94.1, “Manager Evaluation): “Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager. GARP Ch10, section 10.6 Investment Management, “What Is Your Strategy, and How Does It Work?”, questions 5 to 8. Schweser’s version is condensed (“market signals”, “mechanisms in place to limit potential losses”, “excess profits or to hedge”); GARP’s wording is used here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 c, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error, too narrow.** “I only” omits II, which is an exact strategy question in GARP (stop losses at position or portfolio level, and exceptions). It would be correct if II had been corrupted, for example by saying stop losses need only be checked at the portfolio level.

b.reason: **Absolute claim in III.** III turns a question into an exclusion rule. GARP asks whether shorts are hedges, alpha generators “or both”; using both is a normal answer. III would be correct if it simply asked the question without the screening rule.

c.reason: **Scope error in IV.** IV drops part of a stated question and relabels it as a business model matter. GARP’s question 7 explicitly covers how models are allocated capital and decommissioned when failing to perform. IV would be correct if it kept those elements.

d.reason: Only I and II match the source questions without alteration of their scope. Hence “I and II only”.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Singapore insurer is reviewing a global macro fund in which the insurer already holds SGD 150 million. Her notes on the manager are summarised below.

| Item | Observation |
|---|---|
| Assets under management | SGD 0.9 billion three years ago; SGD 4.2 billion today |
| Investor relations headcount | Increased from 2 to 9 |
| Fund status | Has never been closed to new subscriptions |
| Management and incentive fees | 1.5% and 20%, unchanged since launch |

Her concern is that continued subscriptions may dilute the returns earned by existing investors such as the insurer. Which strategy question most directly addresses her concern?

options.text: How does the firm manage the conflict between generating returns for existing investors and growing assets under management, and is the strategy capacity constrained?
Has the fund’s track record been audited, and is it long enough for statistical evaluation and inference about the manager’s skill?
Does the firm manage the fund to specific gross and net exposure targets, and where does the fund stand today versus those targets and why?
Is equity ownership shared among the portfolio managers, traders and research analysts as part of the firm’s talent retention program?

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst worried that new subscriptions will dilute returns for existing investors in a fast-growing macro fund.

**Concept and theory**

A hedge fund manager earns management fees on assets and incentive fees on performance, so the firm can be return oriented, asset growth oriented or both. Growth in assets can conflict with existing investors’ interests if the strategy has limited capacity: more capital may have to be deployed in less attractive positions. GARP therefore includes in the strategy list: “Is the strategy capacity constrained?” (Q11), “Is the firm more return oriented, asset growth oriented, or both?” (Q13), “How does it manage the conflict between generating returns for existing investors versus growing the assets under management?” (Q14) and “Has the fund ever been soft or hard closed or returned capital to investors?” (Q15). Schweser condenses these as “What is the tradeoff between maximizing current returns versus long-term fund growth?” and the closure question.

**Applying it to this question**

The table shows rapid asset growth (SGD 0.9 billion to SGD 4.2 billion), a larger investor relations team and no closure ever. All point to asset gathering. The fee row is a deliberately irrelevant input: fees are unchanged and say nothing about dilution. The concern is dilution of existing investors’ returns, which is exactly GARP’s question 14, paired with capacity (question 11).

**Fragile fact.** Return orientation vs asset growth orientation, and capacity, are strategy questions; “whether returns were impacted by fund size” is the related track record question about the past.

**Reference**

LO 94.c (Schweser Reading 94, Module 94.1, “Manager Evaluation): “Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager. GARP Ch10, section 10.6 Investment Management, “What Is Your Strategy, and How Does It Work?”, questions 4, 11 and 13 to 15. Schweser omits the capacity question and states the conflict as a “tradeoff between maximizing current returns versus long-term fund growth”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 c, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: Option A states GARP questions 14 and 11, which directly address whether growth in assets under management is being pursued at the expense of returns for existing investors.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Audit and length of record are track record questions. They test whether past results are reliable, not whether future growth dilutes returns. B would be correct if her concern were whether the reported record could be trusted.

c.reason: **Scope error.** Gross and net exposure targets are a genuine strategy question (GARP question 4), but they address how the portfolio is positioned, not the growth versus return conflict. C would be correct if her concern were that the fund’s leverage or net market exposure had drifted.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Equity sharing as a talent retention tool is the ownership theme. It does not address dilution from asset growth. D would be correct if her concern were retention of key investment staff.

questions.question: A member of the investment committee of a Canadian university endowment (CAD 3.1 billion) is reviewing two hedge fund managers. Manager P grants equity in the management company to its portfolio managers, traders and research analysts; Manager Q keeps all equity with its founder. The committee member asks how the ownership theme should be applied. Which statement best describes the appropriate approach?

options.text: Manager Q should be screened out, because equity ownership by the investment team is a required condition for aligning the interests of the team with investors.
The ownership structure is an administrative detail with little bearing on the manager, so the committee should give it no weight in the evaluation.
Neither model is necessarily better; the committee should understand each firm’s ownership philosophy and how it affects performance, talent acquisition and retention.
Only the founder’s equity matters, because ownership held by traders and research analysts has no effect on how a firm attracts and retains its talent.

questions.solution:
Endowment committee member applying the ownership theme to one firm that shares equity and one that does not.

**Concept and theory**

Ownership is about who holds equity in the management company. GARP calls “the participation of the investment team in some form of ownership” “a critical area of differentiation among firms”. Some firms do not share equity with portfolio managers or traders; others use equity ownership “as a key feature of their professional talent retention program and to attract and groom new talent for future leadership positions”. GARP then states: “One model is not necessarily better than the other. Each has its pros and cons.” The investor’s task is “to understand the firm’s philosophy and how it impacts performance, talent acquisition, and retention.” Schweser presents the positive side: ownership interests “often help align the interests of the investment team and the investors” and help attract and retain quality staff, so investors should ask whether team members have ownership interests.

**Applying it to this question**

Manager P uses the shared equity model; Manager Q the founder-only model. Under GARP, neither is disqualifying; the committee should ask why each firm chose its model and how it affects performance and talent.

**Fragile fact.** GARP: “One model is not necessarily better than the other.” Team ownership is a question to understand, not a pass or fail test.

**Reference**

LO 94.c (Schweser Reading 94, Module 94.1, “Manager Evaluation): “Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager. GARP Ch10, section 10.6 Investment Management, “How Is Equity Ownership Allocated among the Portfolio Management, Trading, and Research Teams?”. Difference: Schweser frames ownership as beneficial (alignment, staff attraction and retention), whereas GARP is neutral between models; GARP is followed. This looks like condensation by Schweser rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 c, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** It converts Schweser’s “often help align” into a required condition. GARP explicitly says some firms do not share equity and that neither model is necessarily better. A would be correct only if the investor had a stated policy requiring team ownership, which GARP notes investors sometimes hold (“Investors often have a view one way or another”), but that is a preference, not the source’s rule.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP calls ownership “critical” and a key area of differentiation. B reverses that to “little bearing”. It would be correct if the statement said ownership has significant bearing.

c.reason: C restates GARP’s conclusion that one model is not necessarily better and that the investor should understand the philosophy and its impact on performance, talent acquisition and retention.

d.reason: **Scope error.** GARP’s heading names the portfolio management, trading and research teams, and the talent retention model works precisely through equity for those staff. Restricting the theme to the founder drops the condition the source states.

questions.question: An internal auditor at an Australian superannuation fund (AUD 48 billion) is validating the track record section of the fund’s manager evaluation checklist, which was built from the Greenwich Roundtable’s recommendations and related guidance on hedge fund due diligence. Which of the following checklist items is NOT consistent with the questions investors should ask about a manager’s track record?

options.text: Whether the track record is long enough to support statistical evaluation and inference.
Whether the fund’s returns were affected by the size of the fund over time.
How the track record relates to the portfolio manager’s experience at previous firms.
Whether the record excludes periods of market stress, so that unusual episodes do not distort it.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor validating track record checklist items.

**Concept and theory**

A track record is only useful if it is reliable and repeatable. GARP, citing the Greenwich Roundtable, says investors should inquire whether the track record “is comparable to similar strategies, has been audited, and is long enough for statistical evaluation and inference, whether returns were impacted by fund size, and if the team that produced the historical track record is still in place today.” It adds two more questions: “how it performed during periods of market stress and how it relates to the portfolio manager’s experience at previous firms, if applicable.” Schweser’s list matches: peer comparison, third-party audit or verification, sufficient history for trend and attribution analysis, performance in downturns, returns relative to the size of assets, and continuity of staff.

| Question | Risk it guards against |
|---|---|
| Comparable to similar strategies | Strategy beta mistaken for skill |
| Audited | Fabricated or mis-calculated returns |
| Long enough | Luck in a short sample |
| Impacted by fund size | Returns not scalable |
| Team still in place | Record not repeatable |
| Market stress | Hidden tail risk |
| Previous firms | Unverified claims of skill |

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and C each match a listed question. D asks whether stress periods are excluded; the source asks how the record performed during stress periods.

**Fragile fact.** Stress periods are included and examined, not filtered out: “how it performed during periods of market stress”.

**Reference**

LO 94.c (Schweser Reading 94, Module 94.1, “Manager Evaluation): “Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager. GARP Ch10, section 10.6 Investment Management, “Is the Track Record Reliable?”. Schweser phrases length as “sufficient performance history to perform trend and/or attribution analysis” and stress as “market downturns”; GARP’s “previous firms” question is GARP only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 c, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: **True statement.** “Long enough for statistical evaluation and inference” is on the Greenwich Roundtable list. It would be the answer if it said a record of any length suffices.

b.reason: **True statement.** “Whether returns were impacted by fund size” is listed (Schweser: returns relative to the size of investment assets). It would be the answer if it said size is irrelevant.

c.reason: **True statement.** The relation to the portfolio manager’s experience at previous firms is one of GARP’s additional questions. It would be the answer if it restricted the record to the current fund only.

d.reason: D reverses a listed item. Excluding stress periods removes the very evidence GARP wants examined, so D is not consistent with the guidance.
