questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a London life insurer is arranging an on-site visit to a hedge fund in which the insurer may invest GBP 200 million. The fund proposes a single meeting with its head of investor relations, who will walk through the marketing pitch book; it says the CIO and the traders are too busy to meet. Which response is most consistent with the guidance on evaluating a manager’s investment process?

options.text: Accept the meeting, because investor relations staff are best placed to give a consistent, approved message on the investment process.
Ask to meet in person the actual decision makers and risk takers and staff of mixed seniority, noting that poor access now signals poor access if things go wrong.
Replace the visit with written answers, because questions about the investment process are best answered in writing rather than in person.
Insist on meeting the founder alone, because the founder’s account is sufficient and meetings with other staff add little to the evaluation.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst offered only an investor relations pitch-book meeting.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s section on the investment process says the questions “should be done in person with as many people of mixed seniority as possible. The goal is to find out what is really going on at the fund and not just have a pitch book recitation by the investor relations staff.” It warns: “if you cannot get access to the actual decision makers when you are trying to invest, it is unlikely you will have access if something goes wrong!” Hearing it from the founder and lieutenants “is always best”, but getting “the same message from a diverse number of people” who perform tasks day to day “is also quite useful”. GARP closes the section: investors must deal “directly with the actual risk takers and decision makers and not just investor relations, salespeople, or junior staff”. Schweser lists manager interviews as part of investment management, asking about the strategy for generating excess returns and how the manager coped with tough markets.

**Applying it to this question**

The fund offers exactly what GARP warns against: a pitch book recitation by investor relations, with no access to the CIO or traders.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the actual decision makers and risk takers, plus mixed seniority; not investor relations, salespeople or junior staff alone.

**Reference**

LO 94.c (Schweser Reading 94, Module 94.1, “Manager Evaluation): “Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager. GARP Ch10, section 10.6 Investment Management (introductory paragraph and closing paragraph of “Who Are the Principals, and Are They Trustworthy?”). Schweser mentions manager interviews but not the mixed seniority point; GARP is the content source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 c, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: **Role misassignment.** It gives the investment process discussion to investor relations, the actor GARP says is not sufficient. A would be correct for a question about logistics or the fund’s marketing materials, not the investment process.

b.reason: B asks for in-person access to decision makers, risk takers and staff of mixed seniority, and draws GARP’s inference about access if things go wrong.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says investment process questions should be done in person. Written answers suit a questionnaire stage (a different LO), not the interview.

d.reason: **Scope error.** The founder’s account is “always best”, but GARP adds that the same message from diverse staff is “quite useful” to test consistency. Restricting to the founder drops that condition. D would be correct if it said the founder should be included.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Singapore fund of hedge funds (SGD 5.6 billion) is planning reference checks on two candidates. Fund X was launched 14 months ago by a former proprietary trader at two investment banks. Fund Y has been run by the same founders for 12 years. Which reference-check plan is most consistent with the guidance on evaluating the principals?

options.text: Apply an identical process to both, questioning Fund Y’s founders about employers from the distant past as closely as Fund X’s founder.
For Fund X, rely on the reference list supplied by the manager, since independently obtained references are needed only for established managers.
For Fund X, verify bank references, both listed and independently obtained; for Fund Y, focus on motivation, stress behaviour, communication and investor experience.
For Fund Y, focus on verifying prior employment at the founders’ former banks; for Fund X, focus on the experiences other investors have had over the life of the fund.

Fund of funds PM planning reference checks for a new manager and an established manager.

GARP: “Newer managers are a bit trickier than established ones. New managers need to have references from previous hedge funds or banks verified, both those that are on the manager’s reference list and those that the investor can obtain independently.” By contrast, “more established managers won’t need to be interrogated about previous firms or employers from the distant past as much as start-ups or firms lacking a reliable track record.” For established managers, focus “more on the manager’s motivation, behavior during crisis or stress periods, ability to communicate to investors, and experiences other investors have had, including both positive and negative over the life of the fund.”

| Manager | Reference focus |
|---|---|
| New | Verify prior employers (funds, banks); listed and independently obtained references |
| Established | Motivation; behaviour in stress; communication; other investors’ experiences |

**Applying it to this question**

Fund X is a start-up whose manager came from two banks: verify bank references, listed and independent. Fund Y has 12 years: focus on motivation, stress behaviour, communication and investor experience.

**Fragile fact.** New manager: verify past employers (listed and independent references). Established manager: motivation, stress behaviour, communication, investor experience.

**Reference**

LO 94.c (Schweser Reading 94, Module 94.1, “Manager Evaluation): “Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager. GARP Ch10, section 10.6 Investment Management, “Who Are the Principals, and Are They Trustworthy?”. The new vs established distinction is GARP only; Schweser lists reference sources (former employers, colleagues, clients, investors) without it.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 c, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error.** GARP explicitly differentiates; established managers need less interrogation about distant past employers. A would be correct if both managers were start-ups.

b.reason: **Role misassignment and condition error.** GARP requires new managers’ references to be verified both from the manager’s list and independently. B would be correct if it said “both on the list and independently obtained”.

c.reason: C applies each half of GARP’s distinction to the right manager.

d.reason: **Sibling swap of conditions.** D reverses the two focuses: prior employment verification belongs to the new manager, and other investors’ experiences over the life of the fund belong to the established manager (a 14-month fund has little life to report on). D would be correct with X and Y swapped.

questions.question: A risk consultant advising a Dutch pension fund (EUR 900 million hedge fund budget) is conducting reference checks on a portfolio manager who claims to have run the book at her previous fund. Four former colleagues confirm that she made the final trading decisions. Her former head of desk says she mainly implemented ideas generated by others. Which next step is most appropriate?

options.text: Vet the difference of opinion thoroughly and then discuss it directly with the manager, since there is often, but not always, a good explanation.
Set aside the former head of desk’s view, because the majority of references agree and that consistency removes the need for any follow-up.
Treat the difference as conclusive evidence of misrepresentation and reject the manager without discussing it with her.
Ask the fund’s investor relations team to nominate further references who can confirm the manager’s role at her previous fund.

questions.solution:
Consultant facing conflicting references on whether a manager was the decision maker.

**Concept and theory**

Verifying prior employment is “just the beginning”. GARP asks: “Did they do what they described? Were they the trigger puller or acting in a support role? Did they generate ideas or implement ideas? Did they operate individually or within a group?” The best way to find out is to ask former colleagues, partners, managers, clients or other independent parties, treating reference checks “as a 360-degree review of what a person has claimed”. “If enough people are saying the same thing about a person or a firm, then an investor can take some comfort. If significant differences of opinion. . . are uncovered, they should be thoroughly vetted and then discussed directly with the manager. Most often, there is a good explanation, but not always!” Schweser: ensure consistency, and if reviews are mixed, follow up for explanations and obtain clarification from the manager.

**Applying it to this question**

The manager claims to have been the trigger puller. Four colleagues agree; the former head of desk says she implemented others’ ideas. That is a significant difference of opinion on exactly GARP’s “generate or implement” question.

**Fragile fact.** Sequence: vet thoroughly, then discuss directly with the manager. Consistency gives “some comfort”, not proof.

**Reference**

LO 94.c (Schweser Reading 94, Module 94.1, “Manager Evaluation): “Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager. GARP Ch10, section 10.6 Investment Management, “Who Are the Principals, and Are They Trustworthy?”. Schweser’s equivalent: references from former employers (leader or follower, proactive or reactive, team player or individualist) and colleagues (“ensure consistency, but if there are mixed reviews, follow up”). Consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 c, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: A follows GARP’s prescribed sequence: vet thoroughly, then discuss directly with the manager, recognising that there is often, but not always, a good explanation.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** Agreement gives “some comfort”, not certainty, and a significant difference must still be vetted. B would be correct if all references had agreed.

c.reason: **Absolute claim, opposite direction.** GARP says most often there is a good explanation; the difference is a reason to investigate, not proof of misrepresentation. C would be correct only after vetting and discussion failed to resolve it.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** Asking the fund’s own investor relations team for more references defeats the independence of a 360-degree review; GARP says to discuss the difference directly with the manager after vetting it with independent parties.

questions.question:
The CRO of a US single-family office with USD 1.2 billion of assets is reviewing the background-check section of the office’s manager evaluation procedure. The procedure pairs each check with its purpose:

I. Personal credit reports and bankruptcy records: assess whether the manager has shown personal financial responsibility.

II. Public databases and the SEC website: look for past or current litigation, criminal accusations or civil disputes bearing on integrity.

III. Contacting auditors, administrators and prime brokers: verify what the manager represents in fund documents or verbally.

IV. Reviewing the manager’s Form ADV: confirm that the fund’s historical track record has been audited by a third party.

Which of the pairings are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
I, II and III only
III and IV only

questions.solution:
CRO reviewing pairings of background checks with their purposes.

**Concept and theory**

Background checks test whether the principals are trustworthy. Schweser lists: obtaining comprehensive background reports; reviewing the Form ADV filed with the SEC and state securities authorities, which contains general business information and details such as fees, services provided, conflicts of interest and background of key personnel; examining public databases and the SEC website for litigation or criminal behaviour (integrity); examining personal credit and bankruptcy reports (personal financial responsibility); inquiring with auditors and brokers to check the manager’s representations; and the extent of related party transactions. GARP says investors should “call former employers, track down credit reports, and contact auditors, administrators, and prime brokers to verify what a manager is representing in fund documents or through verbal communication”, search SEC websites and read the Form ADV in detail.

**Applying it to this question**

I, II and III each pair a source with the purpose the readings give it. IV assigns to Form ADV a purpose that belongs to the track record theme: third-party audit of performance.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a Brazilian pension fund (BRL 14 billion) receives a background search report on a credit hedge fund manager. The fund charges a 2% management fee and has delivered 11% a year in BRL since launch. The report finds that the fund executes most trades through a broker owned by the manager’s holding company and that its administrator is a subsidiary of the same group. Neither link appears in the materials the manager provided. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: This is related party activity that background searches should look for; affiliated brokers or administrators can lead to real problems, especially when not disclosed in advance.
Because the broker and the administrator are separate legal entities from the fund, no related party question arises for the evaluation of the manager.
Affiliated service providers become a concern only after the manager has been sued, so a clean litigation search resolves the issue.

A fund that uses affiliated brokers or administrators can lead to real problems, especially if the manager did not disclose it in advance.” Schweser’s background check list ends with: “What is the extent of the manager’s involvement in any related party transactions?” The concern is that affiliated providers are not independent of the manager, so execution, pricing and record keeping lose their independent check.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: affiliated brokers or administrators owned by the manager or principal; aggravating condition: not disclosed in advance.

**Reference**

LO 94.c (Schweser Reading 94, Module 94.1, “Manager Evaluation): “Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager. GARP Ch10, section 10.6 Investment Management, “Who Are the Principals, and Are They Trustworthy?”. Boundary: related party factors also appear in LO 94.f (fraud risk); here they are tested only as a background-check item, as both sources place them in manager evaluation.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 c, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: A states GARP’s point directly: this is related party activity that background searches should look for, and non-disclosure aggravates it.

b.reason: **Scope error.** GARP’s test is whether the manager or principal owns other businesses that deal with the fund. Separate legal form does not remove common ownership. B would be correct if the broker and administrator were unaffiliated.

c.reason: **Condition error.** Litigation searches test integrity; related party activity is a separate item to look for whether or not there has been litigation. C would be correct if the question asked what a clean litigation search shows.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a Chinese life insurer (CNY 60 billion of alternatives) is assessing the track record of an Asian equity long/short fund. Her data are below.

| Item | Finding |
|---|---|
| Length of record | 9 years of monthly returns |
| Verification | Returns audited annually by an independent auditor |
| Peer comparison | Top quartile against funds with a similar strategy |
| Stress periods | Drawdowns in 2020 and 2022 in line with peers |
| Assets under management | CNY 0.6 billion in 2017; CNY 9.5 billion today |
| Investment team | Lead PM and two of three analysts behind the 2016 to 2021 returns left in 2023 |
| Fees | 1.75% management fee and 20% incentive fee |

Which two track record questions do her findings most clearly flag for further work?

options.text: Whether the record has been audited, and whether it is long enough for statistical inference.
Whether the record is comparable to similar strategies, and how it performed under market stress.
Whether the fee terms are in line with peers, and whether returns were affected by fund size.
Whether returns were affected by fund size, and whether the team that produced the record is still in place.

questions.solution:
Risk analyst reading a track record data table with excess data.

**Concept and theory**

The track record questions (Solution 5) each guard against a specific failure: comparability (beta mistaken for skill), audit (fabricated returns), length (luck), fund size (scalability), team in place (repeatability), stress (tail risk), and previous firms (unverified skill). Applying them to data means checking which conditions the data show as satisfied and which show as at risk.

**Applying it to this question**

Row by row:

- 9 years of monthly data: long enough; no flag.
- Independent annual audit: satisfied; no flag.
- Top quartile vs similar strategies: comparable; no flag.
- Stress drawdowns in line with peers: no flag.
- Assets rose from CNY 0.6 billion to CNY 9.5 billion (about 16 times): flag “whether returns were impacted by fund size”.
- Lead PM and two of three analysts behind 2016 to 2021 returns have left: flag “if the team that produced the historical track record is still in place”.
- Fees: irrelevant input; fees are not a track record question.

**Fragile fact.** Asset growth is a track record flag because it asks whether past returns depended on a smaller fund; team departures mean the record may not be repeatable.

**Reference**

LO 94.c (Schweser Reading 94, Module 94.1, “Manager Evaluation): “Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager. GARP Ch10, section 10.6 Investment Management, “Is the Track Record Reliable?”. Schweser: “investment returns relative to the size of the investment assets” and “Are most or all of the staff on the investment team that generated those past results still employed by the firm?”. Consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 c, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **Condition error.** Audit and length are both satisfied in the table. A would be correct if the record were 18 months long and unaudited.

b.reason: **Condition error.** Peer comparison and stress performance are both satisfied. B would be correct if the fund lagged peers or had outsized drawdowns in 2020 and 2022.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Fund size is right, but fee terms belong to the assessment of fund terms in the risk management process (LO 94.d), not to the track record theme; the fee row is excess data. C would be correct if the question asked about fund terms and track record together.

d.reason: Only the fund size and team continuity questions are flagged by the data, and D names exactly those two.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a US public pension plan (USD 22 billion) is reviewing a staff memo on background checks of hedge fund managers. Which of the following statements in the memo is NOT correct?

options.text: A fairly comprehensive background report on a manager can be obtained for as little as USD 750, and greater depth costs more but may be worth it.
Background checks matter mainly for start-up managers; once a manager has a long, established record, litigation and SEC searches add little.
In many hedge fund frauds, simple searches of public databases would have revealed litigation, criminal accusations or civil disputes.
Investors should search websites maintained by the SEC and read the manager’s Form ADV in detail before deciding to invest.

questions.solution:
Risk committee member auditing a memo on background checks.

**Concept and theory**

GARP explains why background checks matter regardless of a manager’s standing: “The high-profile blowups of several hedge funds, including Bayou Management and Madoff, have raised important questions about what can be done to uncover fraud in advance.” “Background checks can certainly be obtained. Most investors can get a pretty comprehensive report on a manager for as little as \$750. More depth requires more money, but in some cases, it certainly may be worth it.” “In many hedge fund frauds, investors could simply have searched public databases and found litigation, criminal accusations, or civil disputes.” Investors should “include searches of websites maintained by the SEC and read the manager’s Form ADV in detail before deciding to invest.” The new vs established distinction in GARP applies to reference interrogation about distant past employers, not to background checks.

**Applying it to this question**

A, C and D restate GARP. B carries the new vs established distinction over to background checks and concludes that searches add little for established managers.

**Fragile fact.** The new vs established distinction applies to reference checks about distant past employers, not to background checks.

**Reference**

LO 94.c (Schweser Reading 94, Module 94.1, “Manager Evaluation): “Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager. GARP Ch10, section 10.6 Investment Management, “Who Are the Principals, and Are They Trustworthy?”. The USD 750 figure and the Bayou and Madoff examples are GARP only; Schweser lists comprehensive background reports, Form ADV, public databases, credit and bankruptcy reports, and auditors and brokers. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 c, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: **True.** GARP gives the USD 750 figure and says greater depth costs more but may be worth it. It would be the answer if it said a comprehensive report is not obtainable at low cost.

b.reason: B is not correct: GARP frames background checks (public databases, SEC, Form ADV) as something investors should always do before investing; its lighter touch for established managers concerns only questioning about distant past employers in reference checks.

c.reason: **True.** GARP says many frauds could have been flagged by simple public database searches. It would be the answer if it said such searches rarely reveal anything.

d.reason: **True.** GARP says to search SEC websites and read the Form ADV in detail before investing. It would be the answer if it said the Form ADV need only be read after investing.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a UK defined benefit pension scheme is presenting to newly hired analysts who will join the scheme’s hedge fund operational due diligence (ODD) team. One slide summarizes the primary purpose of ODD. Which of the following statements best describes that purpose?

options.text: To confirm that the manager’s investment process can generate returns, net of fees, that exceed those of a comparable strategy index over a full market cycle.
To confirm that management fee revenue covers the management company’s operating expenses, so that the firm can survive a period without performance fees.

To ensure that no significant additional risk of loss arises for investors from settlement, corporate actions, theft by employees or agents, or breakdowns in confirmation, valuation or reconciliation.
To ensure that every risk of loss from settlement, corporate actions, theft or reconciliation breakdowns is eliminated before capital is committed, leaving investors with market risk only.

questions.solution:
Q1: Presenting to new analysts, which statement best describes the primary purpose of operational due diligence?

**Concept and theory**

Mirabile splits hedge fund due diligence into four parts: investment process, risk management, operational environment, and business model. Each answers a different question. Investment due diligence asks whether the manager can make money; risk management review asks whether the risks taken are understood and controlled; business model review asks whether the management company can survive as a business. Operational due diligence (ODD) asks something narrower and more mechanical: even if the strategy works, can investors lose money through the plumbing of the fund?

GARP states the primary purpose of ODD as ensuring that no significant additional risk of loss is created for investors related to the settlement of securities, the process of corporate actions, misappropriation or theft by employees or agents, or any other breakdown in the manager’s confirmation, verification, valuation and reconciliation process. To do this the investor generally focuses on three things:

| GARP focus | Schweser heading |
|---|---|
| Adequacy of the manager’s internal controls | Internal control assessment |
| Consistency of fund documents and legal representations | Documents and disclosure |
| Risk of loss from counterparty or service provider failure | Service provider evaluation (counterparty risk sits under internal controls) |

Note the wording “significant additional”. ODD does not promise zero operational loss; it aims to keep operational risk from adding materially to the risk the investor chose to take.

**Applying it to this question**

The slide is about the primary purpose of ODD. Only one option describes the operational loss channels (settlement, corporate actions, theft, confirmation, valuation and reconciliation) with the correct “no significant additional risk” standard. The other options either describe other due diligence pillars or overstate the goal.

**Fragile fact.** The standard is “no significant additional risk of loss”, not “no risk of loss”; and the target is the fund’s processes (settlement, corporate actions, theft, reconciliation), not returns or business viability.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, opening paragraphs. Schweser R94, Module 94.2 introduction (three focus areas). The purpose statement is GARP-only; Schweser lists only the three focus areas. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q1 of 16.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Generating returns above a comparable index is the subject of investment process and manager evaluation (LO 94.b and 94.c), not ODD. It would be correct if the stem asked for the purpose of investment due diligence.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Whether management fees cover operating expenses is a business model risk test (LO 94.f, GARP 10.9). It would be correct if the slide covered business model risk.

c.reason: C restates GARP’s purpose statement: ensure that no significant additional risk of loss is created for investors through settlement, corporate actions, theft by employees or agents, or breakdowns in confirmation, verification, valuation and reconciliation.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** D lists the right loss channels but promises that every such risk is eliminated. GARP’s standard is no significant additional risk, and no review can remove all operational risk. It would be correct only if “eliminated” were replaced with “kept from adding significantly to the investor’s risk”.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Canadian fund of hedge funds is validating the ODD file on a target fund (NAV CAD 1.2 billion). The file contains the following notes:

- Background checks were completed on the portfolio manager and two research analysts.
- In the site meeting, the CEO described compliance as “a cost we keep to the legal minimum.”
- The COO and CFO joined three months ago from a global bank; no background checks were run on them.
- The fund has outperformed its peer group in each of the last five years.

Which recommendation by the auditor is most consistent with sound operational due diligence?

options.text: Extend background checks to the COO, CFO and other key back and middle office staff, and record the CEO’s attitude as a significant finding on the fund’s control culture.
Extend background checks to the COO and CFO, but treat the CEO’s attitude as acceptable, because responsibility for the control culture rests with the COO and CFO.
Keep background checks limited to the investment team as normal practice, and run checks on the COO and CFO only if the fund’s peer-relative performance deteriorates.
Treat the COO’s and CFO’s global bank experience as sufficient evidence that they are qualified, and focus any remaining checks on the investment and research team.

questions.solution:
Q2: Auditor validating an ODD file: checks on the investment team only, a CEO who dislikes compliance, new COO and CFO unchecked.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens the internal control assessment with people, because a good plan is useless if the people running it are not qualified or do not believe in it. “It is not enough to have a good plan. The people must be qualified, and the process must be followed every day.” Three ideas follow.

- Tone from the top. Does the CEO support a culture of control and compliance, or is he someone who does not like to follow the rules? The message from the top down should be one of safeguarding assets and treating investors with respect.
- Qualifications beyond the investment team. Operations, accounting, treasury, technology and compliance staff must be qualified for their positions and for the products the fund trades; managers in these areas must have experience managing.
- Background checks and training. It is not unusual for background checks to be done on the COO, CFO, accounting managers and other key back and middle office staff, in addition to the investment and research team. GARP also asks whether the firm hires experienced people and how it trains them and grows their skills outside the big-firm environment most of them came from.

**Applying it to this question**

Note 1 shows the checks stop at the investment team. Note 2 is a direct signal about the CEO’s attitude to compliance, which GARP treats as central. Note 3 shows that key back office leaders are new and unchecked. Note 4 (performance) is an irrelevant input: strong returns do not address operational risk. The recommendation must fix the coverage gap and flag the tone problem.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: tone from the top is the CEO’s. Scope: background checks extend to the COO, CFO, accounting managers and key back and middle office staff, not only to the investment team.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Internal Control Assessment. Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Internal Control Assessment (qualifications and attitudes of personnel). Consistent; GARP is more detailed on roles and training.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q2 of 16.

a.reason: A extends checks to the COO, CFO and other key back and middle office staff (GARP lists exactly these roles) and treats the CEO’s view of compliance as a significant control culture finding, matching GARP’s question whether the CEO supports a culture of control and compliance.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** B fixes the checks but moves responsibility for the control culture to the COO and CFO. GARP places the tone with the CEO, from the top down. B would be right only if the CEO’s attitude were not at issue and the question concerned operating staff alone.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** C limits checks to the investment team and attaches a performance trigger that GARP never mentions. Back and middle office checks are part of the normal assessment, not a contingency. It would be right only for a review restricted by mandate to investment staff.

d.reason: **Assumption error.** D treats previous employment at a global bank as proof of qualification. GARP asks whether staff are qualified for the positions they hold and the products traded, and how the firm trains them outside the big-firm environment. Experience elsewhere is an input, not a verification. It would be right only if checks had already confirmed their qualifications.

questions.question: A risk consultant advising an Australian superannuation fund is on a site visit to a credit hedge fund that seeks an AUD 150 million allocation. The fund hands over a 140-page manual of written procedures covering trading, derivatives, cash and securities processing, and position servicing. The consultant must advise the trustee on how much assurance this provides. Which advice is most accurate?

options.text: The manual’s length and its coverage of trading, derivatives and cash processing give strong assurance that controls are effective, so further control testing is not needed.
The manual is the best available evidence of control effectiveness, and an outside audit opinion adds little because outside auditors review only whether controls are designed well.
The manual matters mainly for measuring and monitoring market risk, so its review belongs to the fund’s risk committee rather than to the investor’s operational review.
The manual mainly shows whether management takes control seriously; better assurance comes from evidence the procedures are followed daily and an outside audit opinion on their operation.

questions.solution:
Q3: Consultant on a site visit is given a 140-page procedures manual; how much assurance does it provide?

**Concept and theory**

Written procedures describe what the fund intends to do. The risk ODD addresses is what the fund actually does each day. GARP notes that reviewing procedures for trading, derivatives, cash and securities processing and position servicing is now routine on site visits, and investors look for evidence of how the written policies are being followed. But such reviews “are not really comprehensive or efficient”; they only give a sense of whether management takes the control process seriously. Schweser says the same thing: the documents tend to be general and only demonstrate the intention of a strong control environment.

The stronger evidence is independent testing. Some managers have an outside audit firm evaluate their procedures and controls periodically and issue an opinion on whether the controls are well designed, have been tested and are operating effectively. Schweser calls it a good sign when a fund has proactively obtained such a report, and says the report should be reviewed.

| Evidence | What it tells the investor |
|---|---|
| Written procedures manual | Intention; a sense of how seriously control is taken |
| Evidence procedures are followed | Whether the plan is executed every day |
| Outside audit opinion on controls | Independent view on design, testing and operating effectiveness |

**Applying it to this question**

The fund offered a long manual. The question is how much assurance this alone provides. The deciding fact is that written documents show intention, not effectiveness; assurance must come from evidence of execution and from an independent controls opinion.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: written procedures show intention (weak evidence); an outside audit opinion on design and operating effectiveness is the stronger evidence.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Internal Control Assessment. Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Internal Control Assessment (policies and procedures). Consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q3 of 16.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** A turns length and coverage into “strong assurance” and drops testing. The source says reading documents gives little assurance that policies are followed or effective. It would be right only if the manual were backed by test evidence.

b.reason: **Scope error and polarity flip.** B ranks the manual above the outside opinion and says auditors only look at design. GARP’s outside opinion covers design, testing and operating effectiveness. It would be right only for a design-only review, which is not what GARP describes.

c.reason: **Sibling swap and role misassignment.** C moves the review to market risk measurement and to the fund’s risk committee. Written risk policies for measuring and monitoring risk belong to LO 94.d; operational procedures for trading, cash and securities processing belong to the investor’s ODD. It would be right if the document were a risk measurement policy and the question concerned LO 94.d.

d.reason: D matches GARP: the manual mainly gives a sense of whether management takes control seriously; better assurance comes from evidence the procedures are followed daily and from an outside audit firm’s opinion on whether controls are well designed, tested and operating effectively.

questions.question:
The chief compliance officer of a Singapore family office is reviewing an ODD memo on a SGD 90 million equity hedge fund that outsources its compliance function to a compliance service provider. The memo contains these statements:

I. The fact that compliance is outsourced is not by itself a deficiency; the investor should examine which compliance practices exist and whether they can be verified.

II. Compliance practices that the investor can verify include the existence of a code of ethics, the prohibition of related-party transactions, and restrictions on employee trading.

III. Because compliance is outsourced, responsibility for verifying the fund’s related-party restrictions passes from the investor to the compliance service provider.

IV. Only the largest hedge fund firms dedicate resources to compliance, so the absence of compliance resources at a fund of this size should not be a concern.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and III only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
Q4: CCO reviewing an ODD memo on a fund with outsourced compliance; which statements are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Compliance is a critical area of operational investigation. GARP notes that most firms today have either their own in-house compliance function or an outsourced relationship with a compliance service provider, and that all but the smallest firms have some resources dedicated to compliance. The location of the function is not the test; the test is whether specific compliance practices exist and can be verified. GARP lists the verifiable practices: the existence of a code of ethics, the prohibition of related-party transactions, and restrictions related to employee trading. Schweser frames it as examining the in-house or outsourced compliance system, including the code of ethics and restrictions on employee trading and related-party transactions.

The investor performs the due diligence. Outsourcing changes who runs compliance for the fund; it does not transfer the investor’s job of verifying it.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement: I (outsourcing not a deficiency) true. II (verifiable practices list) true. III shifts the investor’s verification duty to the provider: false. IV says only the largest firms dedicate resources: GARP says all but the smallest do, so false. Accurate: I and II.

**Fragile fact.** “All but the smallest” firms have compliance resources; in-house or outsourced is acceptable; the investor still verifies.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Internal Control Assessment (compliance). Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Internal Control Assessment (compliance system). Minor wording difference: GARP says “prohibition of related-party transactions”; Schweser says “restrictions on” them. Not decisive here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q4 of 16.

a.reason: **I only.** Omits II, which is GARP’s list of verifiable practices; the error is rejecting a true statement (treating “related-party” as belonging only to fraud risk). It would be right if II named items outside the source.

b.reason: Statements I and II restate GARP: firms have in-house or outsourced compliance, and code of ethics, related-party prohibition and employee trading restrictions are practices that can be verified.

c.reason: **I, II and III.** Accepts III, a role misassignment: the investor, not the compliance provider, performs due diligence. C would be right only if III said the provider operates the related-party restrictions while the investor verifies them.

d.reason: **II and IV.** Accepts IV, a polarity flip of “all but the smallest firms have some resources dedicated to compliance”, and rejects the true statement I. It would be right only if GARP said compliance resources were rare outside large firms.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Japanese life insurer is reviewing a global macro fund in which the insurer plans to invest JPY 8 billion. The fund holds all of its excess cash and all up-front margin on its OTC derivatives with a single dealer. The fund reviews that dealer’s credit rating once a month. Which recommendation is most consistent with operational due diligence guidance?

options.text: Spread the exposure across several dealers, move excess cash out of firms that may be at risk, and monitor counterparties daily, since past dealer failures left funds recovering only part of their cash.
Keep the single dealer, since cash held at a dealer is safe as a receivable on the fund’s balance sheet, provided the monthly rating reviews continue to show investment grade.
Spread the exposure across several dealers, after which monthly monitoring is sufficient, because diversification across dealers eliminates losses from a dealer default.
Leave the exposure to the market risk review rather than operational review, since counterparty exposure from OTC derivatives is a market risk issue and not an operational one.

questions.solution:
Q5: Macro fund holds all excess cash and OTC margin at one dealer, monitored monthly; what to recommend?

**Concept and theory**

Counterparty risk from OTC derivatives and other trade counterparties is now a routine part of ODD. A fund that posts up-front margin, or leaves cash with a dealer, holds an unsecured claim on that dealer. GARP’s lesson from the Lehman, MF Global and Refco failures: firms holding up-front margin failed and closed out fund positions without returning the margin. When a dealer goes bust the fund may never get the money back; at a minimum there may be a lengthy court battle, and recovery may only be 30 or 40 percent of an amount the fund thought was safe as cash or a dealer receivable.

GARP’s three responses:

1. Diversify the exposure among several firms.
2. Move excess cash out of firms that may be at risk.
3. Have a process to monitor the risks of these counterparties every day.

Schweser condenses this to: is the risk mitigated by dealing with more than one counterparty, and are counterparties monitored daily?

**Applying it to this question**

The fund breaks all three rules: single dealer, all excess cash at that dealer, and monthly (not daily) monitoring. The right recommendation fixes all three and is grounded in the lesson that dealer failures leave funds with only partial recovery.

**Fragile fact.** Frequency: counterparties are monitored every day, not monthly; recovery after a dealer failure may be only 30 to 40 percent.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Internal Control Assessment (counterparty risk). Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Internal Control Assessment. Consistent; the failure examples, recovery range and “move excess cash” step are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q5 of 16.

a.reason: A lists GARP’s three actions (diversify across several firms, move excess cash out of at-risk firms, monitor daily) and gives GARP’s reason: past dealer failures left funds recovering only part of their cash.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** B treats cash at a dealer as safe because it shows as a receivable. GARP makes the opposite point: cash the fund thought was safe as a dealer receivable may be lost or only partly recovered. B would be right only if the cash were held in segregated custody outside the dealer’s estate, which the stem does not say.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** C keeps diversification but claims it eliminates default losses, and so keeps monthly monitoring. Diversification reduces concentration; GARP still requires daily monitoring. It would be right only if “eliminates” became “reduces” and daily monitoring were kept.

d.reason: **Sibling swap and scope error.** D moves counterparty exposure out of ODD. GARP says counterparty risk from OTC derivatives and other trade counterparties is now routinely covered in the operational due diligence function. It would be right only for market risk sensitivities of the derivatives, not for the credit exposure to the dealer.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a Brazilian pension fund is reviewing an ODD report on a BRL 600 million hedge fund. The report notes that the fund’s board consists of the CEO (as chair), the CEO’s long-time business partner, and one independent director appointed last month. Board minutes show that service provider appointments have never been discussed. Two NAV calculation breaks in the past year were logged and closed without root-cause analysis or remediation. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: Governance is adequate because a board exists and includes an independent director, so the unremediated NAV breaks are a matter for the fund’s auditor alone.
Governance weakness matters only if the NAV breaks caused investor losses; since both breaks were closed, the investor does not need to take further action.
Governance appears to lack teeth: it does not extend meaningfully beyond the CEO, directors are not engaging with service provider decisions, and breaches are not remedied.
Governance weakness is a business model risk, so it should be assessed through the fund’s succession plan and key person insurance rather than in the operational review.

questions.solution:
Q6: Board of CEO, his business partner and a new independent director; no discussion of service providers; NAV breaks closed without remediation.

**Concept and theory**

Governance is the last line of the internal control assessment. GARP asks: is there a governance structure that extends beyond the CEO, and if so, does it have any teeth? Investors increasingly hold fund directors and advisors accountable for the decisions a fund manager makes on service providers, and for actions that lead to style drift or even fraud. A board that exists on paper but does not challenge the CEO offers no protection.

Schweser adds a test of effectiveness: is governance pervasive throughout the organization, and are internal control breaches followed up with actions to remedy them and prevent recurrence? GARP’s opening to the internal control review makes the same point about the team’s ability to execute procedures daily and clear any breaks or exceptions.

**Applying it to this question**

Three facts decide it. (1) Two of three directors are the CEO and his partner, and the independent director is one month old: the structure barely extends beyond the CEO. (2) The board has never discussed service provider appointments, exactly the decisions directors are increasingly held accountable for. (3) Breaks were closed without root cause or remediation: breaches are not followed up. The NAV size is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: investors increasingly hold fund directors and advisors accountable for service provider decisions and for style drift or fraud.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Internal Control Assessment (governance). Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Internal Control Assessment (corporate governance, breaches). The breach follow-up test is Schweser’s wording; GARP refers to clearing breaks and exceptions.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q6 of 16.

a.reason: **Scope error.** A treats the existence of a board with an independent director as sufficient and hands the breaches to the auditor. GARP asks whether governance has teeth, not whether it exists. A would be right if the board were independent in substance and breaches were remedied.

b.reason: **Condition error.** B makes governance relevant only once losses occur. Follow-up of breaches is meant to prevent recurrence, before losses. B would be right only if the question were about recognizing a realized loss.

c.reason: C applies GARP’s two questions (beyond the CEO? any teeth?) and the Schweser breach test to the facts.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Succession plans and key person insurance are business model risk items (LO 94.f). Governance beyond the CEO is an internal control item in ODD. D would be right if the finding were the absence of a successor to the CEO.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a German insurer is preparing the documents section of an ODD checklist for a EUR 75 million hedge fund allocation. The offering memorandum names a law firm on its cover and carries an as-of date of March 2025. Which set of procedures should the analyst include?

options.text: Accept the memorandum as current because it names a reputable law firm, and skip contacting the firm, since law firms do not disclose whether they represent a client fund.
Confirm with the listed law firm that it drafted the original content and all updates, check for changes made after the as-of date, and confirm the firm is still retained.
Confirm with the listed law firm that it drafted the original content, but skip later amendments, since the manager is entitled to update the fund documents on its own.
Ask the fund administrator to confirm that the listed law firm drafted the documents and is still retained, since the administrator keeps the fund’s legal records.

questions.solution:
Q7: Building the documents checklist; what to do with the law firm named on the offering memorandum.

**Concept and theory**

Investors generally rely on the quality of the law firm that created or amended the fund documents. That reliance is only valid if the law firm really did write what the investor is reading. GARP warns that managers have been known to change fund documents without the consent or even the knowledge of the drafting law firm. So the investor:

1. verifies with the listed law firm that it was responsible for the original content and for any updates;
2. checks the document for changes made after the as-of date on its face, and discusses any such changes immediately with the manager and the law firm;
3. verifies that the law firm is still under a retainer agreement with the manager or fund. Most law firms will at least indicate whether they currently represent the fund.

**Applying it to this question**

The memorandum names a law firm and has a March 2025 as-of date. Neither fact proves anything by itself. The checklist needs all three procedures, carried out directly with the law firm.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the law firm confirms; scope: original content and updates; check for changes after the as-of date.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Documents and Disclosures. Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Documents and Disclosure. Consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q7 of 16.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** A says law firms will not disclose representation. GARP says most will at least indicate whether they currently represent the fund. A would be right only if the firm refused to confirm, which would itself be a finding.

b.reason: B lists GARP’s three steps: confirm original content and updates with the law firm, check for post-as-of-date changes, confirm the firm is still retained.

c.reason: **Scope error.** C confirms the original but drops updates. GARP’s warning is precisely about later changes made without the law firm’s knowledge. C would be right only for a document never amended since launch.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** The confirmation is obtained from the listed law firm itself, not from the administrator. D would be right only if the question asked who keeps copies of fund records.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a US university endowment is comparing the terms of a long/short credit fund across its documents before a USD 40 million subscription:

| Document | Lock-up | Redemption notice | Management fee |
|---|---|---|---|
| Offering memorandum (2024) | 1 year, soft | 90 days | 1.5% |
| Subscription agreement (2024) | 1 year, soft | 90 days | 1.5% |
| Investment management agreement | 1 year, soft | 90 days | 1.5% |
| Fund website (2026) | None | 30 days | 1.5% |

On a call, the manager says the website shows the “current” terms. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: The website is the most recent document, so its terms govern, and the endowment can rely on a 30-day notice period and no lock-up once it has subscribed.
The mismatch is immaterial to document review, because lock-up and notice terms belong to the risk management review of whether terms fit the strategy.
The manager’s verbal confirmation settles the matter, because verbal confirmation is the final step of document review and supersedes the written fund documents.
The mismatch is a red flag: the documents should say the same thing at the same time, and since the offering memorandum governs, the verbal terms must be reconciled to it.

questions.solution:
Q8: Lock-up and notice terms differ between the offering memorandum and the website; manager says the website is current.

**Concept and theory**

Fund terms appear in several documents: the offering memorandum (OM), subscription agreement, limited partnership agreement, investment management agreement, Form ADV and website. GARP says it is very important to ensure that they are all saying the same thing at the same point in time. Documents often change after launch, and some may no longer match the OM, which ultimately governs an investor’s rights and obligations. Particular attention goes to fees, liquidity, side pockets, gates, suspension rights, creation of subfunds or SPVs, and changes in offshore investment managers.

GARP also requires a complete read of all fund documents to ensure the terms reflect the investor’s discussions with the manager. Redemption rights, notice periods, lock-ups, early redemption fees, gates and payout timing (there may be a 5 to 10 percent holdback pending the annual audit) should be confirmed verbally with the manager and reconciled to the fund documents. Schweser: corroborate the OM against the Form ADV, subscription agreement and investment management agreement; examine fee, redemption, liquidity and lock-up terms closely and clarify them with the manager.

**Applying it to this question**

Three legal documents agree (1-year soft lock-up, 90 days notice); the website disagrees. The management fee column is the same in every document and is an irrelevant input. The manager’s verbal claim does not resolve anything: verbal terms must be reconciled to the documents, and the OM governs.

**Fragile fact.** Direction of reconciliation: verbal terms are reconciled to the documents, and the OM governs.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Documents and Disclosures. Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Documents and Disclosure. Consistent; GARP’s document list is longer (adds LPA and website).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q8 of 16.

a.reason: **Sibling swap of documents.** A treats the most recent document as governing. The OM governs investor rights; a website is marketing. A would be right only if the OM had been formally amended to match the website.

b.reason: **Sibling swap of LO.** Whether terms make sense for the strategy is LO 94.d; whether documents agree with each other is LO 94.e, and GARP names liquidity and redemption terms as items to watch. B would be right if the question were whether a 1-year lock-up fits a liquid credit strategy.

c.reason: **Polarity flip of the reconciliation step.** GARP says verbal confirmations are reconciled to the documents, not that they supersede them. C would be right only if the written documents were amended to reflect the verbal terms.

d.reason: D identifies the inconsistency as a red flag, states that documents should say the same thing at the same time, names the OM as governing, and requires reconciliation of the verbal terms to it.

questions.question: A risk analyst at the wealth management arm of a Chinese bank is reviewing the conflicts of interest section of an offering memorandum for a CNY 300 million allocation. The section reads, in full: “Affiliates of the Investment Manager may from time to time have commercial dealings with service providers to the Fund; all such dealings are conducted on normal commercial terms.” Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Accept the clause, since the assurance that all dealings are on normal commercial terms means that any conflict arising from these relationships has been neutralized.
Disregard the clause as boilerplate drafted to protect the law firm, since the fund’s real conflicts are normally set out in the risk factors section of the memorandum.
Query the clause with the manager, since vague wording can cover anything from benign shared services to a personal rebate paid to the manager by a service provider.
Reject the fund, since any affiliate dealing with a fund service provider is a disqualifying conflict, whatever explanation of the arrangement the manager provides.

questions.solution:
Q9: Vague conflicts of interest clause on affiliates’ dealings with fund service providers.

**Concept and theory**

The conflicts of interest section of the OM is where the drafting law firm most clearly states any concern about nonstandard arrangements with managers, co-investors and others. GARP tells investors to query these representations, especially when they are vaguely worded. GARP’s example is a clause saying certain principals or affiliates may have relationships with fund counterparties but will always deal at arm’s length. Such wording can mean anything from something harmless (the administrator also does accounting for the bank holding the fund’s operating accounts) to something serious (the manager takes a personal rebate from the prime broker). Schweser: lack of clarity in the disclosure may be a red flag that warrants further discussion with the manager and possibly independent information.

**Applying it to this question**

The clause is vague in two ways: it does not say which affiliates, which providers or what dealings, and it relies on an unverifiable assurance (“normal commercial terms”). The appropriate response is neither acceptance nor automatic rejection, but a query, with independent information if needed.

**Fragile fact.** Vague conflicts wording is a reason to query, not to accept or reject outright.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Documents and Disclosures (conflicts of interest). Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Documents and Disclosure. Consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q9 of 16.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** A takes the clause’s own assurance as proof the conflict is neutralized. A self-declared assurance is exactly what must be queried. A would be right only after the arrangements were disclosed specifically and verified.

b.reason: **Sibling swap of sections.** GARP says the conflicts section is where the law firm most clearly flags nonstandard arrangements; the “protect itself” concern belongs to overly broad risk factors. B would be right if it described a long list of irrelevant risk factors.

c.reason: C applies GARP’s instruction to query vague conflicts wording and gives GARP’s reason: the same words can cover harmless shared services or a personal rebate to the manager.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** Not every affiliate relationship is disqualifying; some are benign. GARP asks for clarification, not automatic rejection. D would be right only if the query revealed, for example, a personal rebate to the manager.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a UK insurer is comparing the risk factor sections of three offering memoranda:

- Fund X (leveraged emerging market credit, uses OTC derivatives): four short, generic risk factors on “market conditions” and “general economic risk”; nothing on leverage, derivatives or emerging markets.
- Fund Y (US large-cap long/short equity): 70 pages of risk factors, including risks of real estate development and agricultural commodities.
- Fund Z (merger arbitrage): 18 risk factors, each specific to the strategy.

Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: X and Y both raise red flags, X’s more so; Y’s broad and irrelevant factors suggest the law firm drafted mainly to protect itself rather than the investor.
X and Y both raise red flags, Y’s more so; too many risk factors are more of a red flag than too few, as they bury the material risks of the strategy.
Only Y raises a red flag; X’s short list is acceptable, because brief risk disclosure normally indicates a simple strategy with few material risks.
Only X raises a red flag; Y’s long list protects the investor, because the more risks the memorandum discloses, the better informed the investor is.

questions.solution:
Q10: Comparing a very short generic risk section, a very long irrelevant one, and a specific one.

**Concept and theory**

Risk factor disclosure tells the investor how well the drafting law firm understood the manager’s program. GARP: caution is advised when there are either insufficient or extremely broad risk disclosures. Insufficient risk factors are more of a red flag than too many. Overly broad and irrelevant risk factors are also a red flag: the law firm may not have looked properly at the manager’s program, or may be drafting the OM so broadly that it is mainly protecting itself, not the investor. Schweser: lack of clarity or sufficiency in risk disclosure may warrant investigation, and very general or irrelevant risk factors may be cause for concern. GARP adds that registration and compliance language should be checked with independent counsel.

| Pattern | Red flag? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Too few, generic | Yes (greater) | Material strategy risks not disclosed |
| Too many, irrelevant | Yes | Law firm may be protecting itself; program not studied |
| Specific to strategy | No | Shows the program was understood |

**Applying it to this question**

Fund X uses leverage, OTC derivatives and emerging markets but discloses none of these: insufficient. Fund Y’s equity strategy lists real estate development and agricultural risks: overly broad and irrelevant. Fund Z is specific. Both X and Y are flags, X more serious.

**Fragile fact.** Ranking: too few is worse than too many, but both are red flags.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Documents and Disclosures (risk disclosures). Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Documents and Disclosure. Difference: Schweser flags both patterns but does not rank them; the ranking is GARP’s and decides this question.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q10 of 16.

a.reason: A ranks the two flags as GARP does (insufficient worse than too many) and gives GARP’s reason for Y’s problem (law firm protecting itself).

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** B reverses the ranking. GARP says insufficient risk factors are more of a red flag than too many. B would be right if the source said the reverse.

c.reason: **Scope error.** C dismisses X on the theory that short disclosure implies a simple strategy, but X is leveraged and uses derivatives. C would be right only for a genuinely simple strategy whose few risks were all disclosed.

d.reason: **Polarity flip on breadth.** D treats more disclosure as always better. GARP says overly broad and irrelevant factors are also a red flag. D would be right only if Y’s factors were long but all relevant.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at an Australian insurer is reviewing the limited partnership agreement of a GBP 500 million multi-strategy fund. It contains these clauses:

- Clause 1: The fund indemnifies the manager and directors for all losses from their acts or omissions, other than losses from fraud.
- Clause 2: The manager may invest in any instrument, in any market, with no limit on leverage or concentration.
- Clause 3: The manager may amend this agreement on 10 business days’ notice to investors.
- Clause 4: The manager will deliver audited annual financial statements and report the tax implications of the fund’s investments to investors.

Which of the following assessments is most accurate?

options.text: Clause 1 is consistent with typical practice, because fraud is the carve-out that indemnification provisions are normally expected to contain.
Clause 2 carries less risk than narrow provisions, because broad powers allow the manager to respond freely as market conditions change.
Clause 3 is acceptable, because a manager’s right to amend fund documents is a concern only when investors receive no notice of changes.
Clause 4 is what the investor should expect, because the documents should state the manager’s duties to report audited statements and tax effects.

questions.solution:
Q11: Four limited partnership agreement clauses on indemnification, powers, amendment and reporting.

**Concept and theory**

Beyond terms, the documents define what the manager may do and what it owes investors. GARP’s checklist on the powers of the manager:

- Are the powers very broad or relatively narrow? (Schweser: very broad provisions are potentially more risky.)
- Are there restrictions on leverage or concentration?
- Can the manager amend fund documents, such as the limited partnership agreement?
- What are the key man event rights or notice to investors?
- Does the fund have indemnification provisions, and to what extent does the fund indemnify the manager and directors? Typical indemnifications should not extend to the gross negligence, bad faith, fraud or willful misconduct of the manager.

The documents should also clearly state the manager’s obligations for reporting to investors, including audited financial statements and any tax implications of the fund’s investments that can affect investors.

**Applying it to this question**

Clause 1 excludes only fraud, so it covers gross negligence, bad faith and willful misconduct: too wide. Clause 2 gives the broadest possible powers with no leverage or concentration limits: higher risk. Clause 3 lets the manager amend the agreement, which GARP says to question, and notice alone does not cure it. Clause 4 is the reporting obligation GARP says documents should state. The GBP fund size is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Four carve-outs from indemnification: gross negligence, bad faith, fraud, willful misconduct (Schweser: fraud, gross negligence, malicious intent).

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Documents and Disclosures (powers of the manager, indemnification, reporting). Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Documents and Disclosure. Wording differs (Schweser: “fraud, gross negligence, or malicious intent”); GARP’s fuller list used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q11 of 16.

a.reason: **Scope error.** A drops three of the four exclusions. Indemnification should not extend to gross negligence, bad faith, fraud or willful misconduct. A would be right if Clause 1 excluded all four.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** B calls broad powers lower risk. Schweser says very broad provisions are potentially more risky, and GARP asks whether leverage and concentration are restricted. B would be right only if “less” were “more”.

c.reason: **Condition error.** C adds a condition (no notice) that the source does not state. GARP asks whether the manager can amend the fund documents at all; notice does not remove the concern. C would be right if the amendment required investor consent.

d.reason: Clause 4 is what investors should expect: the documents should state the manager’s duty to report audited financial statements and tax implications.

questions.question:
A credit risk officer at a Canadian bank is training analysts on how to review a hedge fund’s audited financial statements during ODD. Her draft notes contain these statements:

I. The review should start by reading the auditor’s opinion and confirming that it is unqualified, meaning the statements were issued without material caveats or concerns.

II. The footnotes are not audited, so they deserve less weight than the balance sheet and income statement when assessing the fund.

III. The footnotes are often where the really important items are clarified, such as the use of derivatives or litigation, so they should be read with care.

IV. An unqualified opinion confirms that no fraud has occurred at the fund, so further analysis of the statements by the investor is unnecessary.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I only
I and III only
I, II and III only
III and IV only

questions.solution:
Q12: Training notes on audit opinion and footnotes; which statements are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

The fund’s latest financial statements give the investor information about both manager and fund. GARP’s order of work:

1. Read the opinion and confirm it is unqualified: the independent auditor reviewed the records and issued the statements without material caveats or concerns. (Schweser: the auditor believes they contain no material misstatements.)
2. Examine the balance sheet and income statement for consistency with the strategy (see Q13).
3. Discuss unusual line items with the manager or even the auditor; unique or different material items are usually explained in the footnotes.
4. Read the footnotes. GARP calls this critical, as it is often where the really important items get clarified, such as use of derivatives or litigation. Schweser adds that footnotes are also audited and give more detail than the statements on items such as contingent liabilities and related-party transactions.

An unqualified opinion is the starting point, not the conclusion: the source asks for further analysis after it.

**Applying it to this question**

I matches step 1. II is false twice: footnotes are audited (Schweser) and are critical (GARP). III matches GARP. IV treats the opinion as a fraud guarantee and ends the review, but the source continues the analysis after the opinion. Accurate: I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Footnotes are audited and are where the really important items get clarified; an unqualified opinion starts the review, it does not end it.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Documents and Disclosures (financial statements). Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Documents and Disclosure. “Footnotes are also audited” is stated by Schweser only; GARP does not contradict it. Footnote examples differ (GARP: derivatives, litigation; Schweser: contingent liabilities, related-party transactions).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q12 of 16.

a.reason: **I only.** Rejects III, a true statement nearly verbatim from GARP. A would be right if III claimed footnotes replace the statements.

b.reason: I and III restate the source: start with an unqualified opinion; read the footnotes because they clarify the really important items such as derivatives and litigation.

c.reason: **I, II and III.** Accepts II, a polarity flip: footnotes are audited and are where key items are clarified, so they deserve more attention, not less. C would be right only if II said footnotes give more detail than the statements.

d.reason: **III and IV.** Accepts IV, an absolute claim (an unqualified opinion means no material caveats, not proof of no fraud, and analysis continues), and rejects the true statement I. D would be right only if IV said the opinion is the starting point.
