| Strategy | Equity long/short | Global macro | Buy-and-hold |
| Manager’s stated leverage | 1.3x, declining | 2.0x, stable | None |
| Total assets (this year / last year) | 840 / 600 | 500 / 480 | 410 / 405 |
| Net assets (this year / last year) | 280 / 300 | 250 / 240 | 400 / 390 |
| Interest expense (this year / last year) | 2.9 / 1.1 | 0.3 / 0.3 | 0.0 / 0.0 |
| Interest income (this year) | 0.4 | 4.2 | 0.2 |
| Realized / unrealized gains (this year) | 9.0 / 6.0 | 14.0 / 3.0 | 38.0 / 2.0 |
| Management fee rate | 1.5% | 2.0% | 1.0% |

Which funds’ statements are inconsistent with their strategy or the manager’s representations and call for immediate questions?

options.text: Fund P only
Funds P, Q and R
Fund R only
Funds P and R only

questions.solution:
Q13: Three funds’ statements: recalculate leverage and check interest and realized gain patterns against each strategy.

**Concept and theory**

Investors can examine the balance sheet and income statement to see whether they make sense for the fund’s strategy, because different strategies leave different footprints. GARP’s examples:

- An equity fund claiming low and declining leverage should not report a high and rising interest expense.
- A global macro fund most likely shows interest income.
- A long-term buy-and-hold fund should not generate large realized gains or losses each year; it should have sizable unrealized gains or losses instead.
- Leverage on the balance sheet can be recalculated and compared with the leverage expected for the strategy or represented by the manager.

If a fund does not make sense, questions must be asked immediately. Schweser’s version: a high leverage fund should show high interest expense and high liabilities. Leverage as defined in the stem:

L $= \frac{\text{Total assets}}{\text{Net assets}}$

**Applying it to this question**

Fund P:

$\text{L}_{\text{last}} =$ 600/300 = 2.0x

$\text{L}_{\text{this}} =$ 840/280 = 3.0x

Interest expense : 1.1 → 2.9 (rising)

The manager says 1.3x and declining; the statements show 2.0x rising to 3.0x with interest expense up. Inconsistent.

Fund Q: L = 500/250 = 2.0x this year and 480/240 = 2.0x last year, matching “2.0x, stable”. Interest income of 4.2 is what GARP expects for global macro. Consistent.

Fund R: L = 410/400 ≈ 1.03x, consistent with no leverage. But realized gains are 38.0 against unrealized gains of 2.0, which is the opposite of what a buy-and-hold fund should show. Inconsistent.

Management fee rates are an irrelevant input. Funds needing immediate questions: P and R.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: buy-and-hold means mainly unrealized gains; macro means interest income; stated low leverage must match low interest expense.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Documents and Disclosures (financial statements). Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Documents and Disclosure. Consistent; macro and buy-and-hold examples are GARP-only. The leverage ratio definition is given in the stem because the source does not specify one.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q13 of 16.

a.reason: **P only; dropped check.** Misses R’s realized versus unrealized pattern by checking only leverage and interest. A would be right if R’s gains were mainly unrealized.

b.reason: **P, Q and R; polarity flip on Q.** Treats Q’s interest income as an anomaly. GARP says a macro fund most likely earns interest income, and Q’s leverage matches the representation. B would be right only if Q were an unlevered equity fund.

c.reason: **R only; assumption error.** Accepts the manager’s stated 1.3x for P instead of recalculating it from the balance sheet (3.0x). C would be right if P’s statements showed leverage near 1.3x and flat interest expense.

d.reason: P’s recalculated leverage and interest expense contradict the manager’s representation; R’s realized gains contradict a buy-and-hold strategy. Q fits GARP’s expected macro pattern.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a French fund of funds is recalculating the fees charged by an underlying fund for the year. The offering memorandum and pitch book both state: management fee of 1.5% per year on opening NAV; incentive fee of 20% of annual net profit above the high-water mark, calculated and paid once a year. Data (EUR millions):

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Opening NAV (equal to the high-water mark) | 400.0 |
| Trading result before fees, first half | 15.0 |
| Trading result before fees, second half | −21.0 |
| Fund operating expenses | 1.1 |
| Management fee reported | 6.0 |
| Incentive fee reported | 3.0 |

Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: Recalculated fees total EUR 9.0 million, matching the statements, because the incentive fee equals 20% of the first-half gain.
Recalculated fees total EUR 0.6 million: the management fee is overcharged by EUR 5.4 million and no incentive fee is due.
Recalculated fees total EUR 6.0 million: the EUR 3.0 million incentive fee should not arise in a loss year and must be raised.
Recalculated fees total EUR 7.2 million: the incentive fee is EUR 1.2 million, so it is overcharged by EUR 1.8 million.

questions.solution:
Q14: Recalculate management and incentive fees for a year with a first-half gain and a full-year loss.

**Concept and theory**

GARP: investors can and should recalculate the fees the fund pays the manager and make sure they make sense. Fees should be compared with the pitch book and other fund documents such as the OM. “There should never be incentive fees earned in years when the fund lost money.” Schweser: fees should be scrutinized, recalculated and corroborated with the OM, with a specific check for incentive fees paid in loss years. Document review also confirms management and incentive fees subject to a high-water mark (HWM) or hurdle rate.

Fee formulas as stated in this fund’s OM:

MF $= \text{m} \times\text{NAV}_{0}$, IF $= \text{k} \times\text{max}($0, annual net profit above HWM)

where m = 1.5%, k = 20%, $\text{NAV}_{0}$ = opening NAV, and the incentive fee is calculated once a year.

**Applying it to this question**

MF = 0.015 × 400.0 = 6.0

Annual trading result = 15.0 + (−21.0) = −6.0

Annual net profit above HWM $= \text{max}($0, −6.0 − 6.0) = 0

IF = 0.20 × 0 = 0

Correct total fees = 6.0 + 0 = 6.0

Overcharge = (6.0 + 3.0) − 6.0 = 3.0

Operating expenses of 1.1 are an irrelevant input. The reported EUR 3.0 million incentive fee equals 0.20 × 15.0, the first-half gain: the fund charged an incentive fee in a year it lost money, against an OM that calculates the fee annually. This must be raised with the manager.

**Fragile fact.** Incentive fees in a loss year are a red flag, whatever happened in a sub-period, when the OM calculates them annually.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Documents and Disclosures (fee recalculation). Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Documents and Disclosure. Consistent. The fee formulas are the OM terms given in the stem, not a source formula.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q14 of 16.

a.reason: **Intermediate result.** 0.20 × 15.0 = 3.0 uses the first-half gain, an intermediate figure, instead of the annual result. A would be right only if the OM crystallized the fee semi-annually.

b.reason: **Unit slip.** Reads 1.5% as 15 bps: 0.0015 × 400 = 0.6, so “overcharged” by 6.0 − 0.6 = 5.4. B would be right only if the fee were 0.15%.

c.reason: C gives the correct recalculated total (6.0) and applies GARP’s rule that incentive fees should never be earned in a loss year.

d.reason: **Sign error.** Applies the incentive rate to the size of the loss: 0.20 × \|−6.0\| = 1.2, total 6.0 + 1.2 = 7.2, overcharge 3.0 − 1.2 = 1.8. A loss produces no incentive fee. D would be right only if the year had a 6.0 gain above the HWM before the management fee and the fee were charged on gross profit.

questions.question:
The CRO of a Singapore insurer is reviewing the equity section of a hedge fund’s audited statements. The general partner’s (GP’s) capital account is shown below (SGD millions).

|  | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| GP opening capital | 20.0 | 27.0 | 22.0 |
| GP contributions | 5.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 |
| GP withdrawals | 0.0 | 6.0 | 9.0 |
| Profit allocated to GP | 2.0 | 1.0 | 2.5 |
| GP closing capital | 27.0 | 22.0 | 15.5 |
| Total fund NAV, year end | 400 | 460 | 520 |

Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: The GP made net withdrawals of SGD 10.0 million over the three years, a big red flag to be discussed thoroughly with the manager.
The GP’s capital fell by only SGD 4.5 million, under 1% of year 3 NAV, so the change in the GP’s equity is not a concern.
The GP made net contributions of SGD 10.0 million over the three years, which shows continued commitment by the manager.
The GP’s withdrawals are not relevant to the review, provided the auditor has issued an unqualified opinion on the statements.

questions.solution:
Q15: GP capital account over three years shows contributions, withdrawals and profit allocations.

**Concept and theory**

The general partner (GP) investing its own money in the fund is a sign of alignment. GARP: check the equity section to see whether the GP is continuing to invest in the fund. Withdrawals or reductions in equity are a big red flag. Investors should thoroughly discuss and understand changes in the capital accounts of the GP and any significant key people who run the fund. Schweser: check the level of net contributions by the GP; any withdrawals should be questioned.

The capital account roll-forward:

Closing $= \text{Opening} + \text{Contributions} - \text{Withdrawals} +$ Profit allocated

Net contributions isolate the GP’s own decisions from investment results:

$$\text{Net contributions} = \sum \text{Contributions} - \sum \text{Withdrawals}$$

**Applying it to this question**

Year 1: 20.0 + 5.0 − 0.0 + 2.0 = 27.0

Year 2: 27.0 + 0.0 − 6.0 + 1.0 = 22.0

Year 3: 22.0 + 0.0 − 9.0 + 2.5 = 15.5

Net contributions = 5.0 − (6.0 + 9.0) = −10.0

Change in GP capital = 15.5 − 20.0 = −4.5

The GP withdrew SGD 10.0 million net, which profits of 5.5 partly hid. Fund NAV growth is an irrelevant input. This is a big red flag.

**Fragile fact.** Judge the GP by contributions minus withdrawals, not by the closing balance, which profits can prop up.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Documents and Disclosures (equity section). Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Documents and Disclosure. Consistent; GARP is stronger (“big red flag”; key people’s accounts too).

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q15 of 16.

a.reason: A gives the correct net contribution figure (net withdrawals of 10.0) and GARP’s conclusion that GP withdrawals are a big red flag to discuss thoroughly.

b.reason: **Intermediate result plus scale error.** 15.5 − 20.0 = −4.5 nets profit allocations against withdrawals, and 4.5/520 ≈ 0.87% adds an invented materiality test. GARP looks at withdrawals, not net change relative to NAV. B would be right only if the GP had made no withdrawals.

c.reason: **Sign error.** Reverses the sign of −10.0. C would be right only if contributions and withdrawals were swapped.

d.reason: **Scope error.** An unqualified opinion confirms the statements are fairly presented; it says nothing about whether the GP is exiting. GARP tells investors to check the equity section separately. D would be right for a question about whether the figures are reliable.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Canadian public pension plan is planning the service provider review for a CAD 250 million hedge fund that uses an external administrator for valuation, a prime broker for custody and execution, and an outside technology vendor. Which plan is most consistent with operational due diligence guidance?

options.text: Rely on the fund’s own description of each provider’s role, since investors contacting a fund’s service providers directly would breach the fund’s confidentiality terms.
Get the key provider contacts from the fund, verify the scope of services, obtain each provider’s control letters and audited statements, and interview them on their roles.
Obtain the fund’s own audited statements, which give an independent check on its providers, so that a separate review of each provider’s control letters is unnecessary.
Confirm that each provider is affiliated with the manager, since affiliated providers give the manager closer control over trade execution, valuation and custody.

questions.solution:
Q16: Planning the review of a fund’s administrator, prime broker and technology vendor.

**Concept and theory**

Funds hire third parties for trade execution, technology, valuation, verification and safeguarding assets. A failure at any of them can cause loss, so ODD checks the providers themselves. GARP:

- Investors should expect the fund to make all key contacts at its service providers available so they can verify the scope of services.
- Investors can obtain internal control letters and audited financial statements from the providers, so that there is an independent check on the service providers themselves.
- It is common for investors to interview providers and discuss their role in executing trades, providing technology, performing valuations or verification, and safeguarding assets.

Schweser: start with the internal control letters issued by the providers’ auditors and their audited financial statements; then hold in-person discussions on the provider’s role.

**Applying it to this question**

The fund uses three providers covering valuation, custody and execution, and technology, exactly GARP’s list of roles. The plan must reach each provider directly, verify scope, obtain each provider’s own control letters and audited statements, and interview them.

**Fragile fact.** The independent check on a service provider uses the provider’s own internal control letters and audited statements, not the fund’s.

**Reference**

LO 94.e: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment. GARP Part II RMIM, Chapter 10 (Performing Due Diligence on Specific Managers and Funds), Section 10.8 Fund Operating Environment, Documentation, Financials, and Service Providers, subsection Service Provider Evaluation. Schweser R94, Module 94.2, Service Provider Evaluation. Consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-12 e, where it is Q16 of 16.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** GARP says investors should expect the fund to make provider contacts available. Relying on the fund’s own description defeats the purpose of an independent check. A would be right only if the fund refused access, which would itself be a red flag.

b.reason: B follows GARP’s steps in order: key contacts, scope, providers’ control letters and audited statements, interviews on roles.

c.reason: **Sibling swap of documents.** C uses the fund’s audited statements in place of the providers’ own control letters and audited statements. The independent check on a provider comes from that provider’s documents. C would be right if it named the providers’ statements.

d.reason: Related-party providers are a fraud risk factor (LO 94.f), and independence from the manager is what the investor wants. D would be right only if “affiliated” were replaced by “independent”.

questions.question: A senior credit analyst at a US asset manager is presenting to newly hired analysts on the early detection of financial distress in corporate borrowers. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Early detection matters less than post-default analysis, because by the time the key accounting questions can be answered, the borrower has usually already defaulted.
It can be difficult to distinguish symptoms of distress from the underlying problems, and to judge whether observed changes are temporary, seasonal fluctuations or more permanent, cyclical issues.
The primary distinction in identifying symptoms of credit deterioration is between temporary and permanent changes, with the split into financial and nonfinancial indicators a secondary refinement.
Once a change has been confirmed in the audited financial statements, it can always be treated as the underlying problem rather than a symptom, so that distinction no longer needs to be judged.

questions.solution:
Briefing for new analysts on early detection of financial distress: which statement is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Financial distress rarely arrives without warning. The reading opens with the claim that early detection of financial distress is critical: the earlier a lender or investor sees credit deterioration, the more remedies remain available and the more value can be protected. Early detection is hard for two reasons, both named in the source:

- **Symptoms vs underlying problems.** What the analyst observes (a covenant breach, a late filing, falling margins) is often a symptom. The cause (a weak business model, excessive leverage, a fraud) sits underneath, and the two are easy to confuse.
- **Temporary vs permanent.** A change may be a temporary, seasonal fluctuation (which reverses) or a more permanent, cyclical issue (which persists). The same reported number can mean either.

To structure the search, the reading gives a set of key accounting questions (core earnings, accounting policies, reserves, restructuring adjustments, creditor behaviour, bad debts, the tax charge) and then states that the primary distinction in identifying symptoms of credit deterioration is between **financial** and **nonfinancial** indicators.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks which framing statement is accurate. Each option is a true source statement with one corruption, except one, which restates the two detection difficulties exactly.

**Fragile fact.** Primary distinction = financial vs nonfinancial indicators; temporary/seasonal vs permanent/cyclical is a difficulty, not the primary distinction.

**Reference**

LO 95.a (verbatim): “Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 95, Module 95.1, section “Early Warning Signals and Indicators of Financial Distress”. Schweser Key Concepts LO 95.a. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 a, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** The source calls early detection critical; A reverses its importance and invents a rationale. It would be correct only in a stem about analysis performed after a default, which is not what the reading describes.

b.reason: B restates the source: it “can be difficult to distinguish between symptoms of distress and underlying problems, and it can also be challenging to determine whether observed changes reflect temporary, seasonal fluctuations or more permanent, cyclical issues.”

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** The temporary vs permanent issue is one of the detection difficulties; the primary distinction for identifying symptoms is financial vs nonfinancial indicators. C swaps the two. It would be correct if the stem asked for one of the difficulties of early detection, not the primary distinction.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** Confirmation in audited statements does not convert a symptom into a cause; the reading stresses that the distinction is difficult and must be judged. “Always” and “no longer needs to be judged” promise a certainty the source denies. It would be correct only if the source said the distinction becomes clear once data are audited, which it does not.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Japanese bank is reviewing a JPY 40 billion loan to a manufacturer and lists four observations from its latest annual report and from discussions with its suppliers.

I. Operating profit was flat, but net income rose 30% because of a one-time gain on the sale of an equity stake.

II. The tax charge is in line with, and slightly above, what the statutory rate applied to reported pre-tax earnings would imply.

III. The firm changed the method it uses to set its warranty reserves, which reduced the reserve charge for the year.

IV. Several trade suppliers have shortened payment terms and now require cash on delivery.

Which of the observations should the auditor flag in response to the key accounting questions used for early detection of financial distress?

options.text: III and IV only
I, II, III and IV
I and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Auditor reviewing a JPY loan to a manufacturer: which four observations answer the key accounting questions?

**Concept and theory**

The reading lists seven key accounting questions for early detection of distress. Each asks whether reported numbers overstate the firm’s health or whether outsiders are already reacting:

| Key question | What it is looking for |
|---|---|
| Are earnings generated from core operations? | Profit propped up by one-off or noncore items |
| Do accounting policies artificially increase profitability? | Aggressive policies inflating reported profit |
| Any changes in reserve accounting policies? | Reserve changes that release or reduce charges |
| Any restructuring or reorganisation adjustments? | Adjustments that obscure the underlying trend |
| Are creditors showing signs of concern? | Suppliers or lenders tightening terms |
| Are bad debts being written off? | Deteriorating receivables quality |
| Does the tax charge appear low relative to reported earnings? | Reported earnings that tax authorities do not see |

The logic of the last question: if reported earnings are high but the tax charge is low, the reported earnings may not reflect real taxable profit.

**Applying it to this question**

- I: net income rises only because of a one-time gain while operating profit is flat. Earnings are not coming from core operations. **Flag.**
- II: the tax charge is in line with, or above, the statutory charge on reported earnings. The question flags a low tax charge; this one is not low. **Do not flag.**
- III: a change in the warranty reserve method that lowers the charge is a change in reserve accounting policy. **Flag.**
- IV: suppliers shortening terms and demanding cash on delivery are creditors showing concern. **Flag.**

Flagged set: I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: the warning is a tax charge that is low relative to reported earnings, not high.

**Reference**

LO 95.a (verbatim): “Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 95, Module 95.1, section “Early Warning Signals and Indicators of Financial Distress”. Focus: list of key accounting questions. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 a, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: **Scope error, dropped condition.** Omitting I treats a one-time gain as legitimate earnings, ignoring the first key question (are earnings generated from core operations?). A would be correct if the gain had come from the firm’s normal operating activity.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** Including II flags a tax charge that is high relative to reported earnings, whereas the key question flags a tax charge that is low relative to reported earnings. B would be correct if observation II described a tax charge well below what reported earnings would imply.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Omitting IV treats supplier behaviour as a commercial matter outside the accounting review. The source lists “Are creditors showing signs of concern?” among the key accounting questions. C would be correct if suppliers had kept their terms unchanged.

d.reason: D matches the three observations that answer the source’s questions on core earnings, reserve policy changes and creditor concern, and excludes the tax observation, which does not meet the “tax charge appears low” condition.

questions.question: A credit analyst at a Brazilian bank is screening a BRL-denominated borrower for earnings enhancements, one group of financial indicators of credit deterioration. Which of the following practices is least likely to be one of the earnings enhancements that signal credit deterioration?

options.text: Accelerating the recognition of operating costs into the current period.
Writing an asset down and later selling it and recording a gain on the sale.
Recognising revenue earlier than the delivery of the related goods would justify.
Selling a warehouse to an investor and immediately leasing it back.

questions.solution:
Screening a BRL borrower for earnings enhancements: which practice is least likely to be one?

**Concept and theory**

Financial indicators of credit deterioration are signals that show up in the financial reporting itself. Schweser lists four groups: covenant breaches; late submission of financial statements; creative accounting (for example off-balance-sheet financing or contingent liabilities); and **earnings** **enhancements**. An earnings enhancement is a practice that makes current reported profit look better than the underlying business justifies. The source gives four examples:

- sale-leaseback arrangements;
- asset write-downs followed by gains on sale (write the asset down, sell it later at above the reduced book value, and book a gain);
- accelerated revenue recognition (bring revenue forward into the current period);
- deferral of costs (push costs out of the current period).

The common direction is that each moves profit into the current period.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each practice against the direction of the effect on current profit. B, C and D raise current reported profit and appear in the source list. A moves costs into the current period, which lowers current profit; that is the opposite of the source’s “deferral of costs”.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: deferral of costs and acceleration of revenue are the enhancements; accelerating costs or deferring revenue is the opposite.

**Reference**

LO 95.a (verbatim): “Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 95, Module 95.1, section “Early Warning Signals and Indicators of Financial Distress”. Focus: financial indicators. Schweser Module Quiz 95.1 Q1 also treats a sale-leaseback as a financial indicator. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 a, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: Accelerating cost recognition is the reverse of the listed enhancement “deferral of costs”, so it is the practice least likely to be an earnings enhancement.

b.reason: **True source item.** “Asset write-downs followed by gains on sale” is listed verbatim as an earnings enhancement. B would be the answer only if the stem asked which practice the source does not list, and it does list it.

c.reason: **True source item.** Recognising revenue early is “accelerated revenue recognition”, a listed earnings enhancement. C would be the answer only if the revenue were deferred rather than accelerated.

d.reason: **True source item, sibling trap.** A sale-leaseback is a listed earnings enhancement. Candidates often reject it because the reading also discusses sale-leasebacks as a way to raise cash (LO 95.b). Here the stem is about indicators, so it belongs in the list. D would be the answer only if the stem asked for a remedy rather than an indicator.

questions.question:
A risk consultant at a German bank is classifying three items found in a EUR-reporting borrower’s accounts. Within the financial indicators of credit deterioration, she separates creative accounting from earnings enhancements.

(i) A guarantee of an affiliate’s EUR 300 million borrowing, not recognised on the balance sheet.

(ii) Deferring the recognition of EUR 45 million of operating costs to later periods.

(iii) Recognising the full revenue on multi-year service contracts at signing.

| Option | Item (i) | Item (ii) | Item (iii) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Creative accounting | Creative accounting | Earnings enhancement |
| B | Earnings enhancement | Earnings enhancement | Earnings enhancement |
| C | Creative accounting | Earnings enhancement | Earnings enhancement |
| D | Creative accounting | Earnings enhancement | Creative accounting |

Which row classifies the three items correctly?

options.text: Row A
Row B
Row C
Row D

questions.solution:
Classifying three EUR items as creative accounting or earnings enhancement.

**Concept and theory**

Within the financial indicators, Schweser separates two groups that are easy to confuse:

| Group | What it does | Source examples |
|---|---|---|
| Creative accounting | Keeps obligations or risks out of view | Off-balance-sheet financing; contingent liabilities |
| Earnings enhancements | Inflates current reported profit | Sale-leasebacks; write-downs then gains on sale; accelerated revenue recognition; deferral of costs |

A useful test: creative accounting hides what the firm owes or might owe; an earnings enhancement changes when profit is reported.

**Applying it to this question**

- (i) An unrecognised guarantee of an affiliate’s borrowing is a contingent liability kept off the balance sheet: **creative accounting**.
- (ii) Deferring EUR 45 million of operating costs is the listed “deferral of costs”: **earnings** **enhancement**.
- (iii) Booking all multi-year revenue at signing is “accelerated revenue recognition”: **earnings** **enhancement**.

questions.question:
A member of the risk committee at a US insurer asks which of the following developments at a USD bond issuer are nonfinancial indicators of credit deterioration.

I. The issuer moved its fiscal year-end from December to March.

II. The issuer submitted its annual financial statements late.

III. The issuer replaced its auditors.

IV. The issuer made a material change to its risk tolerance.

options.text: I and III only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Risk committee question: which of four developments are nonfinancial indicators?

**Concept and theory**

Nonfinancial indicators are signals about the firm’s governance, organisation and behaviour rather than its reported numbers. Schweser lists six: an unnecessarily complex corporate structure; resignations of board members or senior management; a change in the firm’s fiscal year-end date; a change in auditors; failure to meet commitments in a timely manner; and material changes in risk tolerance. Several of these sound accounting-related (auditors, fiscal year-end), which is where the classification traps sit. Conversely, late submission of financial statements sounds like a behavioural lapse but is listed as a financial indicator.

**Applying it to this question**

I (fiscal year-end change): nonfinancial. II (late financial statements): financial. III (auditor change): nonfinancial. IV (material change in risk tolerance): nonfinancial. Nonfinancial set: I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Late submission of financial statements is financial; change in auditors and change in fiscal year-end are nonfinancial.

**Reference**

LO 95.a (verbatim): “Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 95, Module 95.1, section “Early Warning Signals and Indicators of Financial Distress”. Focus: nonfinancial indicators. Schweser Key Concepts LO 95.a. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 a, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: **Sibling swap on IV.** Omitting IV treats a change in risk tolerance as a financial indicator, perhaps because risk tolerance sounds quantitative. The source lists it as nonfinancial. A would be correct if IV described a covenant breach instead.

b.reason: **Sibling swap on I and II.** It treats the fiscal year-end change as financial and late submission as nonfinancial, reversing the source on both. B would be correct only if the source’s two lists were exchanged for those items.

c.reason: **Sibling swap on II.** It includes late submission of financial statements, which the source lists as a financial indicator. C would be correct if II described, for example, failure to meet commitments in a timely manner.

d.reason: D contains exactly the three developments the source lists as nonfinancial indicators and excludes late submission, which the source lists under financial indicators.

A treasury analyst at a Singapore bank is reviewing a logistics borrower with annual revenue of SGD 1.2 billion and an average debt maturity of 4.5 years. She records seven observations.

| No. | Observation |
|---|---|
| 1 | Requested a waiver after breaching its leverage covenant |
| 2 | Filed its annual financial statements six weeks after the deadline |
| 3 | The CFO and two independent directors resigned within one quarter |
| 4 | Replaced its auditors |
| 5 | Recorded a gain on selling a depot that it had written down two years earlier |
| 6 | Guaranteed a joint venture’s debt and kept the guarantee off the balance sheet |
| 7 | Moved its fiscal year-end from December to June |

How many of the seven observations are financial indicators of credit deterioration?
questions.solution:
SGD logistics borrower: how many of seven observations are financial indicators?

**Concept and theory**

The primary distinction in identifying symptoms of credit deterioration is financial vs nonfinancial:

| Financial indicators | Nonfinancial indicators |
|---|---|
| Covenant breaches | Unnecessarily complex corporate structure |
| Late submission of financial statements | Resignations of board members or senior management |
| Creative accounting (off-balance-sheet financing, contingent liabilities) | Change in fiscal year-end date; change in auditors |
| Earnings enhancements (sale-leasebacks, writedowns then gains on sale, accelerated revenue, deferred costs) | Failure to meet commitments in a timely manner; material changes in risk tolerance |

**Applying it to this question**

- 1 Covenant breach and waiver: financial (count 1).
- 2 Late annual financial statements: financial (count 2).
- 3 CFO and directors resign: nonfinancial.
- 4 Auditor change: nonfinancial.
- 5 Gain on a previously written-down depot: earnings enhancement, financial (count 3).
- 6 Off-balance-sheet guarantee: creative accounting (contingent liability), financial (count 4).
- 7 Fiscal year-end change: nonfinancial.

Financial indicators = 4; nonfinancial = 3. Revenue (SGD 1.2 billion) and average maturity (4.5 years) are irrelevant inputs.

**Fragile fact.** “Accounting-sounding” is not the test: auditor and fiscal year-end changes are nonfinancial, late filing is financial.

**Reference**

LO 95.a (verbatim): “Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 95, Module 95.1, section “Early Warning Signals and Indicators of Financial Distress”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 a, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: Counting late filing as nonfinancial (a governance lapse) gives 4 − 1 = 3. A would be correct if observation 2 were replaced by a nonfinancial item such as failure to meet commitments on time.

b.reason: Four observations (1, 2, 5, 6) fall in the source’s financial list; the other three fall in the nonfinancial list.

c.reason: Counting the auditor change as financial because it concerns the accounts gives 4 + 1 = 5. C would be correct if observation 4 were a covenant breach.

d.reason: Treating every accounting-sounding change (auditors and fiscal year-end) as financial gives 4 + 2 = 6, leaving only the resignations as nonfinancial. D would be correct only if the source classified both changes as financial, which it does not.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a UK credit fund is assessing a GBP bond issuer that has just defaulted. The issuer has a market-leading product line and margins that were stable before the default, but its debt facilities were fully drawn and the default followed a cyclical downturn. Which combination of outcomes is most consistent with this profile?

| Option | Cash flow relative to the point of default | Revenue recovery |
|---|---|---|
| A | More than 50% below | 5 to 10 years |
| B | About 10% below | 5 to 10 years |
| C | About 10% below | Within 3 years |
| D | 70% or more below | An extended period |

options.text: Row A
Row B
Row C
Row D

questions.solution:
GBP issuer with a strong product line, fully drawn facilities and a downturn-triggered default: expected cash flow and recovery.

**Concept and theory**

The first group of causes is the interaction of **leverage and business performance**. There is always a trade-off between debt levels and operating performance, and the reading describes three broad outcomes:

| Profile | Facilities and operations | Trigger | Cash flow vs point of default | Revenue recovery |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Excessive leverage, solid model | Fully drawn | Typically a cyclical downturn | Stabilises about 10% below | Within 3 years |
| 2 Average leverage, weak operations | Revenues and margins fall significantly | In a downturn or independently of one | May fall more than 50% below | 5 to 10 years |
| 3 Excessive leverage, weak operations | Often fully drawn; revenues and margins drop substantially | Likely a cyclical event | May fall 70% or more below | An extended period |

Intuition: in profile 1 the business is sound and only the capital structure is wrong, so once the cycle turns the cash flow recovers quickly. When operations are weak, the decline is deep and slow to reverse, and high leverage makes it worse.

**Applying it to this question**

Market-leading products and stable margins indicate a solid business model; fully drawn facilities indicate excessive leverage; the trigger is a cyclical downturn. That is profile 1: cash flow stabilising about 10% below the point of default and revenue recovering within 3 years.

**Fragile fact.** Profile 1 numbers: about 10% below default, recovery within 3 years. Do not attach 5 to 10 years to it.

**Reference**

LO 95.a (verbatim): “Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 95, Module 95.1, section “Causes of Financial Distress: Leverage and business performance”. Note: Schweser’s Module Quiz 95.1 Q2 answer says profile 3 recovery is “often beyond 10 years”, while the main text says only “an extended period”; this paper uses the main text. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 a, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: More than 50% and 5 to 10 years belong to average leverage with weak operations. A would be correct if the stem described average leverage and significantly falling revenues and margins.

b.reason: **Sibling swap on one column.** It pairs the right cash flow decline with profile 2’s recovery period. No single profile combines about 10% with 5 to 10 years, so B mixes two profiles. B would be correct only if the stem asked separately for profile 1’s cash flow outcome and profile 2’s recovery period.

c.reason: Row C reproduces the source’s profile 1 outcomes: “Cash flows usually stabilize at about 10% below the point of default, and revenues tend to recover within 3 years.”

d.reason: 70% or more and an extended recovery belong to excessive leverage with weak operations. D would be correct if margins and revenues had dropped substantially.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at an Australian superannuation fund is classifying three defaulted issuers by the interaction of leverage and business performance. Cash flows are in AUD million.

| Issuer | Leverage and facilities | Operations and trigger | CF at default | Trough CF | Coupon (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P | High, fully drawn | Revenue and margins fell sharply; default in a cyclical downturn | 400 | 100 | 7.5 |
| Q | In line with sector average | Revenue and margins fell significantly; no downturn at default | 250 | 110 | 6.0 |
| R | High, fully drawn | Margins stable; default in a cyclical downturn | 180 | 162 | 8.0 |

Profiles: (1) excessive leverage with a solid business model; (2) average leverage with weak business operations; (3) excessive leverage with weak business operations. Which assignment is most consistent with the data?

options.text: P: profile 3; Q: profile 2; R: profile 1
P: profile 2; Q: profile 3; R: profile 1
P: profile 1; Q: profile 2; R: profile 3
P: profile 3; Q: profile 1; R: profile 2

questions.solution:
Mapping three AUD issuers P, Q and R to the three leverage and performance profiles.

**Concept and theory**

The three profiles (see the table in Solution 7) differ on four features: leverage and facility use, what happened to revenues and margins, the trigger, and the depth of the cash flow decline below the point of default. The decline is measured relative to cash flow at the point of default:

Decline below default $= \frac{\text{CF}_{\text{default}} - \text{CF}_{\text{trough}}}{\text{CF}_{\text{default}}}$

where $\text{CF}_{\text{default}}$ is cash flow at the point of default and $\text{CF}_{\text{trough}}$ is the lowest cash flow afterwards. Benchmarks: about 10% (profile 1), more than 50% (profile 2), 70% or more (profile 3).

**Applying it to this question**

P: $\frac{400 - 100}{400} = \frac{300}{400} =$ 75%

Q: $\frac{250 - 110}{250} = \frac{140}{250} =$ 56%

R: $\frac{180 - 162}{180} = \frac{18}{180} =$ 10%

- P: high leverage, fully drawn, sharp fall in revenue and margins, cyclical trigger, 75% decline: **profile 3**.
- Q: sector-average leverage, significant fall in revenue and margins, default without a downturn (only profile 2 allows default independently of a downturn), 56% decline (above 50%, below 70%): **profile 2**.
- R: high leverage, fully drawn, stable margins, cyclical trigger, 10% decline: **profile 1**.

The coupon column is an irrelevant input. Meaning: the qualitative features and the size of the decline point the same way for each issuer.

**Fragile fact.** Measure the decline from the point-of-default cash flow, and remember only profile 2 allows default independently of a downturn.

**Reference**

LO 95.a (verbatim): “Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 95, Module 95.1, section “Causes of Financial Distress: Leverage and business performance”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 a, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: P matches profile 3, Q profile 2 and R profile 1 on every feature in the source.

b.reason: It treats Q’s default without a downturn as the worst case and P as average leverage. P’s leverage is high and its decline (75%) reaches the 70% marker; Q’s leverage is average. B would be correct if P had sector-average leverage and Q had fully drawn facilities with a 70%+ decline.

c.reason: P and R share high leverage and a cyclical trigger, so keying only on those features confuses them. The deciding facts are margins (sharp fall vs stable) and the decline (75% vs 10%). C would be correct if P’s margins were stable and R’s had collapsed.

d.reason: It assigns Q to the solid-model profile and R to weak operations, although Q’s revenues and margins fell significantly with a 56% decline and R’s margins were stable with a 10% decline. D would be correct if the operating data of Q and R were exchanged.

questions.question: A risk consultant advising a Chinese bank is preparing a report on a CNY bond issuer that faces product liability claims from consumers. Which of the following statements on tort liabilities should she include as most accurate?

options.text: Financial markets typically wait for a final court award before discounting the issuer’s securities, because the probability of a large loss is low.
Insurance coverage removes the cash flow risk of tort claims, so they matter for credit analysis only when the issuer is uninsured.
Tort exposures are mainly inherited through acquisitions, and are hard to guard against because the problematic contract terms are unknown in advance.
Management often underestimates tort exposures because they are low-probability events, and awards, sometimes bundled through class actions, frequently exceed expectations.

questions.solution:
Report on a CNY issuer facing product liability claims: most accurate statement on tort liabilities.

**Concept and theory**

**Unexpected liabilities** are a separate cause of distress: obligations usually not directly related to debt that can still hit cash flows hard. The two examples are tort and contract liabilities.

**Tort liabilities** arise from legal claims involving harm to individuals or property. Key points in the source:

- They may take the form of class action lawsuits, which bundle many individual claims into a potentially large settlement.
- Management often underestimates them, because they are low-probability events and awards frequently exceed expectations.
- Insurance may or may not cover the losses.
- Financial markets typically assume the worst and discount security prices accordingly.

**Contract liabilities**, by contrast, arise when contractual arrangements become unfavourable as circumstances change; they may be inherited in an acquisition and are hard to protect against because the problematic terms are often unknown in advance.

**Applying it to this question**

Product liability claims from consumers are claims of harm to individuals: a tort exposure. The accurate statement must reflect underestimation by management, awards above expectations, possible class actions, uncertain insurance and a market that assumes the worst.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: management underestimates tort exposures; markets assume the worst.

**Reference**

LO 95.a (verbatim): “Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 95, Module 95.1, section “Causes of Financial Distress: Unexpected liabilities”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 a, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** The source says markets typically assume the worst and discount prices accordingly, not that they wait for a final award. A would be correct only if the stem described a market that ignores the claims until they are settled.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** The source says insurance may or may not cover the losses; B promises full protection. B would be correct if the stem stated that the issuer’s policy fully covered all awards.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Inheritance through acquisitions and unknown problematic terms are properties of contract liabilities. C would be correct if the stem asked about contract liabilities.

d.reason: D combines three source facts: underestimation by management, the reason (low probability), and awards frequently exceeding expectations, with class actions as the bundling mechanism.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Canadian bank is reviewing a CAD borrower that acquired a competitor two years ago. The acquired company had signed a long-term fixed-price supply agreement, and after input costs rose sharply the agreement now produces large cash outflows. Which statement best describes this source of distress?

options.text: It is a tort liability, because the obligation arises from a legal claim that the agreement harms the counterparty’s property.

It is a contract liability: an arrangement that became unfavourable as circumstances changed, here inherited through an acquisition, and hard to protect against fully because such terms are often unknown in advance.
It should be analysed as part of the borrower’s leverage, because unexpected liabilities of this kind are usually directly related to the borrower’s debt.
It could have been fully protected against through acquisition due diligence, so its emergence shows that it is not an unexpected liability at all.

questions.solution:
CAD borrower with an inherited, loss-making fixed-price supply agreement: which statement describes this source of distress?

**Concept and theory**

Contract liabilities are the second type of unexpected liability. They occur when contractual arrangements become unfavourable due to changes in circumstances. Sometimes the risk is inherited when acquiring another firm, and because the problematic terms are often unknown in advance, it is difficult to protect fully against this exposure. Like tort liabilities, they are usually not directly related to debt, yet they can severely reduce cash flow.

|  | Tort liability | Contract liability |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | Legal claim of harm to people or property | Agreement turned unfavourable by changed circumstances |
| Typical route | Class actions bundling claims | Inherited through an acquisition |
| Why hard to manage | Underestimated; awards exceed expectations; insurance uncertain | Terms often unknown in advance |

**Applying it to this question**

The obligation is a fixed-price supply agreement (a contract), it turned costly because input costs rose (changed circumstances), and it came with the acquired company (inherited). No harm to people or property is claimed, and the obligation is not debt.

**Fragile fact.** Inherited via acquisition and unknown terms belong to contract liabilities, not tort liabilities.

**Reference**

LO 95.a (verbatim): “Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 95, Module 95.1, section “Causes of Financial Distress: Unexpected liabilities”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 a, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It labels a contractual loss as a tort, which requires a legal claim of harm to individuals or property. A would be correct if the counterparty had sued for physical damage caused by the borrower’s products.

b.reason: B restates all three source features of contract liabilities and applies them to the facts.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** The source says unexpected liabilities are usually not directly related to debt. C would be correct only if the obligation were a borrowing.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** The source says it is difficult to protect fully because the problematic terms are often unknown in advance; D promises that due diligence would have removed the exposure. D would be correct only if the terms had been known and fully disclosed before the acquisition, which the source says is often not the case.

questions.question: The CRO of a US pension fund is reviewing a USD bond holding in a national retailer whose sales and margins have fallen during a recession. The investment team says the problem is “performance well below expectations”. Which statement about this cause of distress is most accurate?

options.text: It is the most common cause of financial distress, and in a downturn the key challenge is to determine whether the downturn itself or management’s decisions and strategies are driving the deterioration.
It is the least common cause of financial distress, because recessions occur only rarely, so the analyst should look first for fraud or unexpected liabilities.
Because the business cycle can be avoided by prudent management, any deterioration during a recession should be attributed to management’s decisions and strategies.
Products and services become uncompetitive mainly when high margins attract too many new entrants, so the retailer’s problem is the oversupply that follows.

questions.solution:
USD retailer with falling sales and margins in a recession: most accurate statement about performing well below expectations.

**Concept and theory**

**Performing well below expectations** is, per the source, the most common cause of financial distress. Two trigger events are given:

- **Economic downturns.** The business cycle is unavoidable and recessions occur periodically. The key challenge is to determine whether the downturn itself is driving the deterioration, or whether management decisions and strategies are the underlying cause. This links back to the early-detection difficulty of separating symptoms from underlying problems.
- **Uncompetitive products or services.** Demand evolves over time, and shifts in customer preferences can render existing products or services obsolete.

This differs from the “too many new entrants” story, which the source places under unrealistic business plans: high margins attract entrants, entry exceeds demand, and oversupply hurts all competitors.

**Applying it to this question**

The retailer’s sales and margins have fallen in a recession. The analyst must judge whether the recession explains the decline or whether management’s choices are the real cause.

**Fragile fact.** Most common cause = performing well below expectations; obsolescence is driven by shifting demand, not by new entrants.

**Reference**

LO 95.a (verbatim): “Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 95, Module 95.1, section “Causes of Financial Distress: Performing well below expectations”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 a, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: A states both source facts: most common cause, and the downturn-vs-management judgement as the key challenge.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** The source calls it the most common cause and says recessions occur periodically. B would be correct only if the source ranked it the least common, which it does not.

c.reason: **Absolute claim, polarity on the cycle.** The source says the business cycle is unavoidable; C says it can be avoided and attributes every deterioration to management, removing the judgement the source requires. C would be correct only if the stem had established that peers were unaffected and management’s strategy was the sole cause.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** Oversupply from too many entrants belongs to unrealistic business plans. Under this cause, products become uncompetitive because demand and customer preferences shift. D would be correct if the stem asked about the “too many new entrants” plan.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a French credit fund holds EUR bonds of an industrial group that has just disclosed fraudulent revenue recognition at one subsidiary over the past two years. Which approach best reflects how a crisis of confidence of this kind should be analysed?

options.text: Limit the review to the two restated years, because figures for earlier years were audited and therefore remain reliable.
Concentrate on restating earnings, because accounting fraud changes reported profits but leaves the likelihood of bankruptcy unchanged.

Treat all previously reported information as suspect, assess informational contagion and whether a practical cutoff point for reliable data exists, and evaluate cash balances, credit lines and the risk of loan acceleration.
Treat the fall in the bond price as the full measure of the damage, because markets typically assume the worst, and so skip the review of historical data.

questions.solution:
EUR bonds of an industrial group that disclosed revenue fraud at a subsidiary: how to analyse a crisis of confidence.

**Concept and theory**

A **crisis of confidence** is a cause of distress often associated with fraud (the source cites Enron). The reading names two areas of focus:

1. **Reliability of historical information.** Once financial fraud is uncovered, all previously reported financial information becomes suspect. The analyst must assess the potential for informational contagion (doubts spreading from the restated items to everything else) and determine whether there is a practical cutoff point for data reliability.
2. **Liquidity and likelihood of bankruptcy.** The analyst must evaluate whether the fraud could trigger liquidity problems or raise the risk of bankruptcy. Key considerations are cash balances, the availability of credit lines and the risk of loan acceleration.

Why liquidity matters: a loss of confidence can cause lenders to withdraw lines or accelerate loans, so a reporting problem can quickly become a cash problem.

**Applying it to this question**

The fraud is confirmed for two years at one subsidiary. The source does not let the analyst assume earlier years are clean: every earlier figure is suspect until a reliable cutoff is established. In parallel, the analyst must check cash, credit lines and acceleration risk.

**Fragile fact.** Scope: after fraud, all prior information is suspect, not only the restated period; then look for a cutoff point.

**Reference**

LO 95.a (verbatim): “Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 95, Module 95.1, section “Causes of Financial Distress: Crisis of confidence”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 a, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: **Scope error.** It limits suspicion to the restated period, while the source says all previously reported information becomes suspect. A would be correct only after the analyst had established that a practical cutoff point exists at the start of the fraud period.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** The source requires assessing whether the fraud could trigger liquidity problems or increase bankruptcy risk; B says that risk is unchanged. B would be correct only if the stem stated that credit lines and loan terms are unaffected by the disclosure, which the source does not assume.

c.reason: C contains both focus areas in the source’s own terms: all prior information suspect, contagion, cutoff point, and cash balances, credit lines and loan acceleration.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** “Markets typically assume the worst” is the source’s statement about tort liabilities, and in any case the crisis of confidence requires a review of historical data. D would be correct if the stem asked how markets typically price tort exposures.

X: A sponsor bought a firm with heavy debt, planning to repay it from the sale of two divisions; buyers did not pay the expected prices.

Z: High margins in battery recycling attracted many firms; capacity soon exceeded demand.

Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Case X is best classified as a roll-up, because the plan depended on combining the acquired firm’s divisions to achieve economies of scale.
In Case Z, the oversupply is a problem mainly for late entrants, while the early, high-margin firms are protected from it by their head start.
Case Y is best classified as a leveraged buyout, because the consolidator planned to repay acquisition debt from asset sales.
In Case X, distress arose because the financing structure assumed that cash from asset sales would reduce leverage, and that cash was not generated as expected.

questions.solution:
Three GBP borrowers that failed on unrealistic business plans: most accurate statement.

**Concept and theory**

Setting realistic expectations is essential. Schweser names three types of business plan that often prove unrealistic:

| Plan |  | What it assumes | How distress arises |
|---|---|---|---|
| Leveraged buyout |  | Enough cash, from asset sales or ongoing operations, to reduce leverage | The expected cash is not generated |
| Roll-up |  | Combining several smaller firms creates economies of scale | The expected cost savings fail to materialise |
| Too many new trants | en- | High margins justify entry | Entry exceeds demand; oversupply creates problems for all competitors |

**Applying it to this question**

Case X is debt-financed, with deleveraging planned from division sales that fell short: an LBO. Case Y combined many smaller clinics expecting savings, and was equity-funded: a roll-up. Case Z had high margins that attracted entry beyond demand: too many new entrants.

**Fragile fact.** LBO = deleveraging cash not generated; roll-up = scale savings not realised; new entrants = oversupply hurting all competitors.

**Reference**

LO 95.a (verbatim): “Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 95, Module 95.1, section “Causes of Financial Distress: Unrealistic business plans”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 a, where it is Q13 of 13.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Economies of scale from combining firms is the roll-up mechanism. Case X combined nothing; it relied on selling divisions to repay debt. A would be correct if X had bought several smaller firms to cut costs.

b.reason: **Scope error.** The source says oversupply creates problems for all competitors; B narrows the damage to late entrants. B would be correct only if the source limited the effect to some competitors.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Repaying acquisition debt from asset sales is the LBO mechanism, and the stem says Y was funded by a share issue and failed because savings never appeared. C would be correct if Y had been debt-funded with planned disposals.

d.reason: D restates the source’s LBO mechanism exactly: the financing structure assumed cash from asset sales would reduce leverage, and the cash was not generated.

questions.question: A junior analyst at a Singapore-based distressed debt fund is preparing onboarding notes for new analysts on how remedies for financial distress are organized. A senior colleague asks her to keep only the statement that matches the fund’s reference text. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Solutions to distress fall into three categories, and the right restructuring approach depends mainly on the firm’s legal jurisdiction, whether it files in or out of court, and the size of its creditor committee.
Solutions to distress fall into two categories, restructuring and reducing leverage, with raising additional capital treated as one form of reducing leverage through equity.

Solutions to distress fall into three categories, and the right restructuring approach depends on whether the deterioration is temporary, whether the distress is a first episode, or whether a prior turnaround has failed.

Solutions to distress fall into three categories, and the right restructuring approach is the same whatever the cause of distress, because every restructuring pathway ends in a reduction of the firm’s debt.

questions.solution:
Onboarding notes at a Singapore distressed debt fund: how remedies for distress are organized.

**Concept and theory**

When a firm is in financial distress, the reading groups the possible cures into three families: restructuring, raising additional capital, and reducing leverage. They answer different questions. Restructuring changes how the business or its obligations are organized. Raising capital brings in cash (asset sales, secured financing, sale-leasebacks, equity sponsors), mainly to buy time. Reducing leverage changes the balance between debt and equity, either by adding equity or by cutting debt (open market repurchases, direct purchases, cash tender offers, exchange offers).

Within restructuring, the right approach depends on where the firm is in its distress history. Schweser names three pathways:

| Pathway | What it tells the analyst |
|---|---|
| Temporary deterioration | The fall in performance is expected to reverse |
| First episode of distress | No turnaround has yet been attempted |
| Failed prior turnaround | An earlier rescue has already been tried and has not worked |

This is the sense in which the LO speaks of remedies “at different stages of distress”: a fix that suits a temporary dip differs from one that suits a firm whose previous turnaround failed. (The detailed mapping is in Schweser’s Figure 95.1, adapted from Whitman and Diz, which is not legible in the project text and is not tested.)

**Applying it to this question**

All four options open with a claim about the number of categories and then say what drives the choice of restructuring approach. Two checks decide the answer: is the count three (restructuring, raising capital, reducing leverage), and is the driver the three-pathway history of the distress? Only C passes both checks.

**Fragile fact.** Three categories (restructure, raise capital, reduce leverage) and three pathways (temporary, first-time, failed turnaround); do not merge raising capital into reducing leverage.

**Reference**

LO 95.b: “Describe methods firms can use to remedy a financial distress situation at different stages of distress and explain the potential implications and challenges to using each method.” Schweser Reading 95, Module 95.2, “Remedies for Financial Distress” and “Restructuring”; Key Concepts LO 95.b. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 b, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** The count is right, but the drivers named (jurisdiction, in-court vs out-of-court filing, creditor committee size) are the material of LO 95.c on legal challenges, not the cause-based pathways of LO 95.b. A would be right if the stem asked which considerations shape the choice between an out-of-court and an in-court restructuring.

b.reason: **Scope error.** It drops a whole category by folding raising capital into reducing leverage. The trap is that “increasing equity” does appear under reducing leverage; but raising additional capital (asset sales, secured financing, sale-leasebacks, sponsors) is a separate category whose main role is to buy time. B would be right only for a text that recognized two categories.

c.reason: Schweser: “Solutions to financial distress can include restructuring, raising additional capital, and reducing leverage” and “The appropriate restructuring approach depends on whether the performance deterioration is temporary, whether the firm is experiencing distress for the first time, or whether a previous turnaround effort has already failed.” C restates both.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** It says one approach fits every cause. The source says the approach depends on the pathway. D would be right only if the source had said restructuring choice is independent of the cause of distress.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Japanese trust bank is screening three distressed issuers for its JPY credit opportunities fund. She has the data below and must choose one statement for her screening memo on how the debt data can be used.

| Issuer | Debt instrument | Price per 100 of face | Coupon (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | Listed senior bonds, actively traded | 91 | 2.40 |
| Y | Listed senior bonds, actively traded | 38 | 3.10 |
| Z | Bilateral bank loan, not traded | n/a | 2.75 |

Which of the following statements is most appropriate for the memo?

options.text: For X and Y, the trading level compares the debt’s current market price with its full repayment value and signals the market’s expectations about the severity of distress and the potential restructuring options.

For X and Y, the trading level compares the debt’s current market price with its full repayment value and signals each management team’s own expectations about the severity of distress and its preferred options.
For X, Y and Z alike, the trading level compares the debt’s current market price with its full repayment value, so it gives the same insight into distress severity for each of the three issuers.
For X and Y, the trading level compares the debt’s current market price with its full repayment value and determines, by itself, the single restructuring solution that each issuer must adopt.

questions.solution:
Japanese trust bank screening three distressed issuers’ debt prices.

**Concept and theory**

When a distressed firm’s debt is actively traded, its price is a live, collective forecast. Schweser defines the debt trading level as the current market price of the firm’s debt relative to its full repayment value (par). It “serves as an indicator of the market’s expectations about distress severity and potential restructuring options”. Intuitively (an illustration, not a statement in the source), a bond quoted near par says the market expects to be repaid nearly in full, so mild remedies may suffice; a bond quoted far below par says the market expects a deep loss, which points toward heavier remedies. Three features matter: (1) it is a market signal, not a management view; (2) it requires a traded instrument; (3) it offers insight into problems and a range of solutions, not a single prescription. (Schweser’s Figure 95.2, adapted from Moyer, pairs price bands with problems and solutions; it is not legible in the project text and is not tested.)

**Applying it to this question**

X (91) and Y (38) are actively traded, so their prices can be read as trading levels: the market sees Y’s distress as far more severe than X’s. Z’s loan has no market price, so the tool does not apply. The coupons are a deliberately irrelevant input: the trading level is a price relative to full repayment value, not a yield or coupon measure. The deciding facts are: market’s (not management’s) expectations, actively traded debt only, and insight into a range of options (not a single answer).

**Fragile fact.** Actor: the market. Condition: actively traded debt. Output: insight into severity and a range of options, never one answer.

**Reference**

LO 95.b (verbatim as in Q1). Schweser Reading 95, Module 95.2, “Restructuring” (text around Figure 95.2); Key Concepts LO 95.b (“Debt trading levels can also provide insight into the likely causes of distress and the feasible set of solutions”). GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 b, where it is Q2 of 14.

a.reason: A limits the reading to the traded issuers and repeats the source: price relative to full repayment value, indicating “the market’s expectations about distress severity and potential restructuring options”.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** Right measure, wrong actor: the trading level reflects the market’s expectations, not management’s. B would be right if the stem described management guidance on expected recoveries.

c.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the condition “If a firm’s debt is actively traded”. Z’s bilateral loan has no price, so no trading level exists. C would be right only if Z’s loan were also actively traded.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** The source says the trading level offers “insight into the underlying issues and the range of potential solutions”. Saying it determines, by itself, a single required solution overstates it. D would be right only for a rule that mapped each price to one mandatory remedy.

questions.question: An independent board member of a Brazilian apparel retailer in financial distress is reviewing management’s proposal to raise BRL 450 million of additional capital. The board has not yet agreed on what is causing the decline in margins. Which of the following statements best describes the potential implications of raising additional capital?

options.text: Raising capital resolves the underlying problem, because the new cash removes the cause of the distress and so ends the need for any further restructuring of the business.
Raising capital buys the firm time, and that extra time always works in the creditors’ favor, because difficult periods end and business conditions eventually improve.
Raising capital reduces leverage directly, so it is one of the debt reduction methods, alongside open market repurchases, cash tender offers and exchange offers.
Raising capital may not fix the underlying problem but can buy time to work through a difficult period, although it may also give ineffective management more time to erode value.

questions.solution:
Brazilian retailer’s board weighing a BRL 450 million capital raise without agreement on the cause of distress.

**Concept and theory**

Raising additional capital is the second family of remedies, and the reading is candid about what it does and does not do. New cash does not by itself fix whatever caused the distress (a weak business model, poor management, a cyclical slump). What it buys is time. Time has two faces:

| Good use of time | Bad use of time |
|---|---|
| The firm works through a difficult period, or conditions improve | Ineffective management gets longer to keep eroding value |

This is the core “implication” the LO asks you to explain. The four ways of raising cash (asset sales, secured financing, sale-leasebacks, equity sponsors) each carry their own challenges, tested in Q4 to Q7.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem flags that the board does not know the cause of the decline. That is exactly the situation in which the two faces of time matter: if the cause is cyclical, time helps; if it is management, time may hurt. The answer must therefore say that capital may not fix the problem, buys time, and can cut both ways.

**Fragile fact.** Raising capital buys time; it does not fix causes, and the time can help recovery or let poor management destroy more value.

**Reference**

LO 95.b (verbatim as in Q1). Schweser Reading 95, Module 95.2, “Raising Additional Capital” (opening paragraph). GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-13 b, where it is Q3 of 14.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses “may not resolve the underlying problem” into “resolves the underlying problem”. A would be right only if the source said fresh cash cures the cause of distress.

b.reason: **Absolute claim.** It keeps the time-buying idea but promises time “always” helps creditors, deleting the warning that ineffective management can use the time to erode value. B would be right only if management were known to be effective and recovery certain.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It moves raising capital into the reducing-leverage family and lists it among the debt reduction methods. Open market repurchases, direct purchases, cash tender offers and exchange offers are debt reduction methods; raising capital is a separate category. C would be right if the stem described increasing equity as part of a leverage reduction plan, which is a different method.

d.reason: Schweser: raising capital “may not resolve the underlying problem, it can buy the firm more time. Ideally, that time allows the business to work through a difficult period, or for conditions to improve. However, it may also give ineffective management more time to further erode value.” D states all three parts.
