questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a UK building society reconstructs what a single reported split-strike conversion cycle would have produced in a falling market. The basket tracks the S&P 100 exactly, the option notional equals the basket value, and dividends, interest and transaction costs are ignored. All figures are in USD.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Equity basket value at inception | USD 300 million |
| S&P 100 level at inception | 600 |
| Strike of calls written | 612 |
| Premium per call (index points) | 2.40 |
| Strike of puts bought | 576 |
| Premium per put (index points) | 1.80 |
| S&P 100 level at expiry | 552 |
| Days to expiry at inception | 24 |

What is the profit or loss on the combined position over the cycle?

options.text: A loss of USD 12.0 million
A loss of USD 23.7 million
A profit of USD 6.3 million
A loss of USD 11.7 million

questions.solution:
Building society analyst computes the USD profit or loss of one collar cycle when the index falls through the put strike.

**Concept and theory**

The profit or loss of the collared basket at expiry is the sum of three legs plus the net premium. With N index units of exposure (N $= \text{V}_{0}$/S$_{0}$ when the option notional equals the basket value $\text{V}_{0}$):

P&L $= \text{N}[(\text{S}_{\text{T}} - \text{S}_{0}) - \text{max}(\text{S}_{\text{T}} - \text{K}_{\text{c}}$, 0$) + \text{max}(\text{K}_{\text{p}} - \text{S}_{\text{T}}$, 0$) + (\text{c} - \text{p})]$

where $\text{S}_{\text{T}}$ is the index at expiry, $\text{K}_{\text{c}} \text{and K}_{\text{p}}$ the call and put strikes, c the call premium received and p the put premium paid. Below $\text{K}_{\text{p}}$, the stock loss beyond the put strike is offset one for one by the put, so the loss is locked at $(\text{K}_{\text{p}} - \text{S}_{0})$ plus net premium (Schweser: the long put “establishes a floor”).

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1, index units:

N = 300,000,000/600 = 500,000

Step 2, equity leg:

(552 − 600) × 500,000 = −USD 24.0 million

Step 3, long put (in the money, $\text{K}_{\text{p}} =$ 576 > 552):

(576 − 552) × 500,000 = +USD 12.0 million

Step 4, short call $\text{(K}_{\text{c}} =$ 612 > 552, expires worthless): 0. Step 5, net premium:

(2.40 − 1.80) × 500,000 = +USD 0.3 million

Step 6, total:

−24.0 + 12.0 + 0 + 0.3 = −USD 11.7 million (= −3.9% of USD 300 million)

Meaning: an 8% fall in the index costs the collared basket only 3.9%, which is the floor (−4.0%) improved by the 0.1% net credit. The 24 days to expiry is an irrelevant input; the call strike matters only to confirm the call expires worthless.

**Fragile fact.** Below the put strike the loss is fixed at $(\text{K}_{\text{p}} - \text{S}_{0})$ plus net premium; check which strike is the put’s before computing.

**Reference**

GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. The payoff arithmetic applies the long put and short call described there; no figures come from the source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-14 a, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: −24.0 + 12.0 = −12.0: the net premium of +0.3 million is omitted. It is also the floor loss (576 − 600) × 500,000 on its own. A would be correct for a zero-cost collar.

b.reason: −24.0 + 0.3 = −23.7: the put is treated as expiring worthless, as if the analyst forgot it is in the money at 552. B would be correct only for a basket that had written the calls but bought no puts.

An examiner at a securities regulator is writing a case study on how BMIS collapsed in December 2008. She lists the following events.

I. Madoff tries to raise additional capital but cannot do so quickly enough.

II. Madoff’s sons report him to US authorities.

III. Amid market turmoil, redemption requests arrive faster than BMIS can meet them.

IV. Madoff tells his sons, wife and brother that the advisory business is “a giant Ponzi scheme.”

V. Madoff is arrested and charged with securities fraud; his family’s assets are frozen and a receiver is appointed for BMIS.

Which sequence correctly orders these events from first to last?

options.text: III, IV, I, II, V
III, I, IV, II, V
I, III, IV, II, V
III, I, II, IV, V

questions.solution:
Regulator’s case study orders five events in the December 2008 collapse.

**Concept and theory**

A Ponzi scheme pays withdrawals with other investors’ money rather than with investment returns, so it survives only while inflows cover outflows. Schweser’s account of the end is a causal chain, not just a list of dates:

1. By late 2008 markets were in turmoil and redemption requests flooded in faster than BMIS could meet them.
2. Madoff tried to raise additional capital but could not do so quickly enough.
3. “At that point,” on December 10, 2008, he admitted to his sons, wife and brother that it was “all a big lie,” a “giant Ponzi scheme.”
4. That evening his sons reported him to US authorities.
5. He was arrested the following day, charged with securities fraud; his family’s assets were frozen and a receiver was appointed to oversee BMIS.

Schweser stresses that Madoff “was not discovered through an investigation”; the trigger was his own confession under liquidity pressure.

**Applying it to this question**

Map the statements: III (redemptions) → I (failed capital raise) → IV (confession) → II (sons report) → V (arrest, charges, freeze, receiver). The sequence is III, I, IV, II, V.

GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing. GARP cross-check: “Predicting Fraud,” Section 11.1 Introduction (“On December 11, 2008, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) charged Bernard Madoff with securities fraud”); consistent with Schweser.

a.reason: Schweser places the failed attempt first and the confession “at that point.” A would be correct only if Madoff had confessed and then sought money to repay investors.

b.reason: B is the only option that keeps cause before response (redemptions before the capital raise), response before confession (“At that point, he admitted”), and confession before the sons’ report.

c.reason: The capital raise was a response to redemptions he could not meet. C would be correct only if the scheme had sought new money before the redemption wave, which is not how the source tells it.

d.reason: **confession).** Placing II before IV means the sons reported him before he confessed, i.e., that they uncovered the fraud themselves. They reported him the evening of his confession to them. D would be correct only if the family had found the fraud independently.

**Concept and theory**

In a normally structured fund, the functions that create and record value are split among separate entities: the investment manager decides what to buy, an executing broker carries out the trades, a custodian holds the assets, and a fund administrator values the portfolio and calculates NAV. The point of the split is not efficiency; it is verification. Each independent party produces records that the others cannot alter: the custodian can confirm that the securities exist, the broker that the trades happened, the administrator that the NAV reflects real prices. Schweser lists “lack of independent service providers” as the first operational red flag: BMIS performed all of these roles in-house, which “made it far easier to manipulate performance results and potentially misappropriate assets.”

| Function | Typical fund | BMIS |
|---|---|---|
| Investment management | Manager | BMIS |
| Trade execution | Independent broker | BMIS |
| Custody | Independent custodian | BMIS |
| Administration and NAV | Independent administrator | BMIS |

The table shows that every function that could verify the manager’s claims is performed by the manager or an entity it owns. The question asks how this indicates fraud risk, so the answer must name the mechanism (no independent verification, therefore easier manipulation and misappropriation) without overclaiming. The year of first launch is irrelevant data.

**Fragile fact.** The red flag is the absence of independent verification across execution, custody, administration and management, and it signals fraud risk, not proof.

Two operational red flags concern governance. First, the conflict of interest: BMIS acted as both broker-dealer and market maker for some of its own strategies. Which of the following best explains how this fee structure can indicate potential fraud risk?

$\text{F}_{\text{total}} = \text{m} \times\text{A}_{0} + \text{p} \times(\text{R}_{\text{g}} \times\text{A}_{0})$,

Gross reported gain = 0.10 × 200 = BRL 20.0 million

Performance fee = 0.20 × 20.0 = BRL 4.0 million

She explains that, before 2008, investors offered several explanations for the manager’s near-perfect record: superior stock selection, use of market-making profits to smooth results, leverage, and front running. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: A genuine split-strike strategy would inevitably produce some negative months; none of the explanations was legitimate, and Markopolos argued the returns were impossible without front running or a Ponzi structure.
The long put in a split-strike strategy eliminates all losing months, so the absence of negative months was consistent with the strategy, and the red flag lay only in the level of returns.

**Concept and theory**

A split-strike conversion holds a stock portfolio, sells out-of-the-money calls and buys out-of-the-money puts. Because the puts are out of the money, the portfolio can still lose value between the current price and the put strike, and the calls cap the upside. Such a strategy “can be profitable over time but will inevitably produce some negative months”. Madoff’s reported record had essentially none, which is why Schweser calls it a black box strategy red flag. Investors rationalised the record in four ways: superior stock selection, using market-making profits to smooth results, leverage, and front running (an illegal practice in the United States). The source’s conclusion is that “no legitimate explanation could account for his results”. Harry Markopolos, a former portfolio manager, repeatedly warned the SEC, including in his 2005 report The World’s Largest Hedge Fund Is a Fraud, arguing that the returns were impossible without either front running or a Ponzi structure; regulators dismissed his warnings.

| Rationalisation | Why it fails as a legitimate explanation |
|---|---|
| Stock selection, leverage | Cannot remove the losing months a collar produces |
| Smoothing with market-making profits | Misstates the strategy’s real results |
| Front running | Illegal in the United States |

**Applying it to this question**

Deciding facts: a genuine split-strike strategy must produce some negative months, none of the four explanations was legitimate, and Markopolos warned while the SEC dismissed.

questions.question: A risk consultant at a Toronto quantitative advisory firm runs a returns-based style analysis on a CAD feeder fund whose manager claims to hold a stock portfolio highly correlated with the S&P 100, written out-of-the-money index calls and bought out-of-the-money index puts. The pattern shows that the manager was front running client orders, which explains both the high returns and the unusual exposures.
Because reported returns were similar to the S&P 100, style analysis carries little information here, and the exposure mismatch can be set aside.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Hong Kong insurer is checking a manager’s quarter-end Form 13F filings against its stated strategy. The data are summarised below.

| Item | Observation |
|---|---|
| Stated strategy | Split-strike conversion on S&P 100 stocks |
| Assets under management | About USD 17 billion |
| Holdings shown on Form 13F | Small positions in minor, non-S&P 100 companies |
| Manager’s explanation | Portfolio converted to cash at each quarter end |
| Insurer’s proposed allocation | HKD 400 million |

Which of the following assessments is most accurate?

options.text: The explanation is plausible, because the strategy was mostly held in cash anyway; the red flag lies only in the identity of the non-S&P 100 names.
The non-S&P 100 holdings contradict the stated focus, and converting such enormous sums to cash every quarter would have been impractical and implausible at this scale.
The filings are a red flag because they show large S&P 100 holdings at quarter end, which contradicts the manager’s claim to be in cash.
The filings are an operational red flag because they are mailed on paper, which lets the manager fabricate the holdings shown after the fact.

questions.solution:
Hong Kong treasury analyst: Form 13F filings showing small non-S&P 100 holdings and a quarter-end cash explanation.

**Concept and theory**

Form 13F is a required quarterly filing of equity holdings. It gives an outside view of what a manager actually held at quarter end. BMIS’s filings showed small holdings in minor, non-S&P 100 companies, inconsistent with a strategy built on S&P 100 stocks. Madoff’s explanation was that he converted the portfolio to cash at the end of each quarter to avoid public scrutiny of his positions. Schweser rejects this: moving such enormous sums each quarter “would have been impractical and implausible, given the scale of AUM.” The red flag thus has two layers: the holdings contradict the strategy, and the excuse for the contradiction is itself implausible at the manager’s size.

**Applying it to this question**

The table gives both layers: non-S&P 100 holdings and a quarter-end cash explanation for a manager with about USD 17 billion. The HKD allocation is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** 13F showed small, non-S&P 100 holdings; the quarter-end cash excuse fails on scale.

**Reference**

LO 96.b: Identify characteristics of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund that can serve as warning signs or potential “red flags” and explain how they can indicate potential fraud risk. Schweser Reading 96, Module 96.2, Investment Red Flags, “Illogical Form 13F filings”. GARP: no matching section in the project’s GARP text; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-14 b, where it is Q12 of 14.

a.reason: **Scope error.** A accepts the explanation because the strategy was “mostly held in cash”. Madoff did claim to hold cash most of the time, but the source’s point is that converting such enormous sums at every quarter end was implausible given the AUM. A would be right only for a small manager whose quarter-end liquidation is feasible.

b.reason: B states both sourced points: the holdings contradict the stated focus, and converting such sums to cash every quarter was impractical and implausible at that scale.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C says the filings showed large S&P 100 holdings. They showed small holdings in minor, non-S&P 100 companies. C would be right if the filings had contradicted the cash claim by showing the stated holdings.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** D borrows the paper-confirmation mechanism, an operational red flag, and attaches it to the 13F filings, which are an investment red flag about inconsistency with the strategy. D would be right for a stem about mailed trade tickets.

questions.question: The CRO of a Japanese bank is asked whether the bank could have been an OTC counterparty to a manager claiming to trade S&P 100 index options against about USD 17 billion of equity. The proposed notional with the bank would have been JPY 150 billion. Which of the following is the least accurate reason why the claimed option trading was implausible?

options.text: S&P 100 options are more liquid and more widely traded than S&P 500 options, so trades of this size would have been absorbed without any visible effect on prices.
Trades sized for about USD 17 billion of equity would have moved the option market significantly, yet no such movements were observed.
OTC counterparties would have lost money year after year, faced enormous credit exposures and needed to hedge, yet there was no evidence of any of this.
No counterparties to the claimed trades were ever confirmed, which suggested that the trades had never actually been executed.

questions.solution:
Japanese bank CRO: which reason for the implausibility of Madoff’s claimed S&P 100 option trading is least accurate.

**Concept and theory**

A strategy can be ruled out by checking whether the market could have carried it. Madoff claimed to use S&P 100 options rather than S&P 500 options. S&P 100 options are less liquid and less widely traded, so the strategy would have been prohibitively expensive and virtually impossible at his size. With about \$17 billion under management, his trades would have moved the market significantly, yet no such movements were observed. To explain the lack of visibility, Madoff claimed to trade OTC. That explanation fails too: the counterparties would have suffered losses year after year, faced enormous credit exposures and needed to hedge their positions, and there is no evidence that any of this occurred. No counterparties were confirmed, suggesting the trades were never executed.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the least accurate reason. Three options restate sourced reasons; one reverses the liquidity comparison. The JPY notional is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** S&P 100 options are less liquid than S&P 500 options; the OTC excuse fails on counterparty losses, credit exposure and hedging.

**Reference**

LO 96.b: Identify characteristics of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund that can serve as warning signs or potential “red flags” and explain how they can indicate potential fraud risk. Schweser Reading 96, Module 96.2, Investment Red Flags, “Impossible use of S&P 100 options”. GARP: no matching section in the project’s GARP text; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-14 b, where it is Q13 of 14.

a.reason: A reverses the direction of the liquidity comparison. The source says S&P 100 options are less liquid and less widely traded than S&P 500 options; that is precisely why trading them at Madoff’s size was implausible.

b.reason: **Accurate.** Matches the source: trades of that size would have moved the market, and no movements were observed. B would be the answer if it claimed large trades would have no effect.

c.reason: **Accurate.** Matches the source’s three-part rebuttal of the OTC claim: recurring counterparty losses, enormous credit exposures and the need to hedge, with no evidence of any of it. C would be the answer if it said counterparties profited.

d.reason: **Accurate.** Matches the source: the absence of confirmed counterparties suggested the trades were never executed. D would be the answer if it claimed counterparties had been identified.

questions.question:
A board risk committee member at a UK insurer is preparing a GBP briefing note on lessons from Madoff. A consultant has proposed four statements.

I. Illogical Form 13F filings are classified as an investment red flag, because they reveal an inconsistency with the stated strategy.

II. The use of paper trade confirmations is classified as an investment red flag, because it reveals an inconsistency with the stated strategy.

III. Even using only the publicly available information in BMIS’s Form ADV, a methodology developed by Brown, Goetzmann, Liang and Schwarz (2008) would have identified BMIS as a problematic fund.

IV. Harry Markopolos’s 2005 report led the SEC to open the investigation that exposed the fraud in December 2008.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I only
I, II and III only
I and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
UK insurer board member: classifying red flags and judging whether they were detectable from public information.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser groups the red flags in two families. Operational red flags concern how the firm was run and verified: lack of independent service providers, conflict of interest, questionable auditing firm, family members in key roles, unusual fee structure, lack of transparency, late SEC registration and paper trade confirmations. Investment red flags are those that “pointed to inconsistencies in Madoff’s strategy and performance”: black box strategy, questionable style exposure, illogical Form 13F filings and impossible use of S&P 100 options.

| Operational (how the firm was run) | Investment (strategy and performance) |
|---|---|
| Independent service providers; conflict of interest; auditor; family roles; fees; transparency; late registration; paper confirmations | Black box strategy; style exposure; Form 13F filings; S&P 100 options |

The closing paragraph adds that the flags were detectable: Markopolos warned the SEC repeatedly (regulators dismissed the warnings), a few banks declined to do business with BMIS, and even using only public Form ADV information, a methodology developed by Brown, Goetzmann, Liang and Schwarz (2008) would have identified the firm as problematic. The fraud did not come to light through these warnings; Madoff confessed to family members in December 2008 when he could not meet redemptions (LO 96.a content, used here only to judge statement IV).

Context only (neighbouring GARP chapter, not the assigned reading): GARP’s “Predicting Fraud by Investment Managers” reports that the predicted fraud risk of BMIS from Form ADV data is above the 95th percentile (GARP text line 17273, footnote 2), which supports the same point using a different study.

**Applying it to this question**

I: 13F filings are an investment red flag (true). II: paper confirmations are an operational red flag (false). III: the Form ADV statement restates the source (true). IV: Markopolos’s warnings were dismissed and did not expose the fraud (false). Accurate: I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Paper confirmations are operational; Form 13F is investment; Markopolos’s warnings were dismissed.

**Reference**

LO 96.b: Identify characteristics of Bernie Madoff’s hedge fund that can serve as warning signs or potential “red flags” and explain how they can indicate potential fraud risk. Schweser Reading 96, Module 96.2, “Operational Red Flags” and “Investment Red Flags” headings; closing paragraph (Markopolos, banks, Form ADV methodology). Statement IV also draws on Module 96.1, “Fund Collapse and Confession” (LO 96.a), for the fact that disproves it. GARP: no matching section in the project’s GARP text; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-14 b, where it is Q14 of 14.

a.reason: **Rejects III, a polarity flip on detectability.** A treats the Form ADV statement as false, implying the fraud could not be detected from public data. The source says the opposite. A would be right if the source had said public filings gave no useful signal.

b.reason: **Accepts II, sibling swap.** B moves paper trade confirmations into the investment family. They are listed under operational red flags. B would be right if the classification were by what the flag reveals about returns rather than how the firm operated, which is not the source’s grouping.

c.reason: Only I and III match the source’s classification and its statement on Form ADV.

d.reason: **Accepts IV, role and causation error.** D credits Markopolos’s report with triggering the investigation that exposed the fraud. Regulators dismissed his warnings; the fraud surfaced through Madoff’s own confession. D would be right if the SEC had acted on the 2005 report.

questions.question: The head of risk at a Canadian public pension plan is presenting to newly hired analysts on why the plan replaced the stress testing framework it used before the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) of 2007 to 2009. Which of the following statements best describes the pre-GFC practice and the reason it proved unreliable?

options.text: Stress testing was the primary risk tool and value at risk (VaR) was an add-on to it; the framework failed because the expert views that drove the stress tests proved too subjective during the crisis.

Stress testing was an add-on to VaR or ex ante tracking error used to estimate the P&L impact of tail risks; the framework failed because its forward-looking scenarios did not materialise during the crisis.

Stress testing was an add-on to VaR or ex ante tracking error, with model-consistent stress tests that depended heavily on historical data; the framework failed because historical relationships between key market variables broke down entirely.

Stress testing was an add-on to VaR or ex ante tracking error and depended heavily on historical data; the framework failed because the historical samples were too short to estimate VaR at high confidence levels, although historical relationships between market variables held.

questions.solution:
Pension plan head of risk explaining pre-GFC stress testing and why it failed; which statement is best.

**Concept and theory**

Before the GFC, stress testing was not a stand-alone discipline. It sat on top of statistical risk models, typically value at risk (VaR) or ex ante tracking error, and its job was to estimate the P&L impact of tail risks. The stress tests were model-consistent: they used the same machinery and the same inputs as the statistical models, which meant that everything, the models and the stress tests alike, depended heavily on historical data. That design has a hidden assumption: the relationships between market variables observed in the past will hold in the stress. During the GFC that assumption failed. Schweser states that historical relationships between key market variables broke down entirely, which made these models unreliable. This failure is the motivation for the rest of the reading: a framework is needed that can describe forward-looking events that history does not contain.

| Feature | Pre-GFC practice (Schweser) |
|---|---|
| Role of stress testing | Add-on to VaR or ex ante tracking error |
| Purpose | Estimate the P&L impact of tail risks |
| Construction | Model-consistent stress tests |
| Data dependence | Heavy reliance on historical data |
| Failure in the GFC | Historical relationships between key market variables broke down entirely |

**Applying it to this question**

Each option has two halves: what the practice was, and why it failed. The first half must place stress testing as the add-on (not the primary tool) and tie it to historical data. The second half must name the breakdown of historical relationships. Only C gets both halves right.

**Fragile fact.** Direction of the add-on: stress testing was bolted on to VaR or tracking error, not the other way round; the failure was a breakdown of historical relationships, not too little data.

**Reference**

LO 97.a (verbatim): “Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 97, Module 97.1, section “Market-Driven Scenario Approach”, first paragraph; Key Concepts LO 97.a; Module Quiz 97.1 Q1. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing (Schweser cross-references Golub, Chapter 5). No GARP versus Schweser conflict can arise for this LO.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-15 a, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Role misassignment, plus sibling swap of the failure cause.** A reverses which tool was the add-on: VaR was the base model and stress testing the add-on. It also blames subjective expert views, which is a criticism that applies to the MDS approach that came after the crisis, not to the historical, model-driven framework that failed in it. A would describe a post-GFC scenario framework criticised for subjectivity, not the pre-GFC regime.

b.reason: **Sibling swap: forward-looking for historical.** The first half is right, but the failure is attributed to forward-looking scenarios. Pre-GFC stress tests were model-consistent and historical; the forward-looking property belongs to scenario analysis, the replacement. B would fit a question about a scenario framework whose forward-looking scenarios did not occur.

c.reason: Schweser: stress testing “was typically used as an add-on to statistical models such as value at risk (VaR) or ex ante tracking error”; pre-GFC risk management “relied on VaR and tracking-error models with model-consistent stress tests, all of which depended heavily on historical data”; in the GFC “historical relationships between key market variables broke down entirely, rendering these models unreliable.” C restates all three points.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error: wrong failure mechanism, and denies the stated breakdown.** D correctly describes the practice but substitutes a sample-length problem and explicitly says that historical relationships held. The source says the opposite: the relationships broke down entirely. D would be correct only in a stem about estimation error in a stable regime, which is not the GFC story.

questions.question:
A risk consultant engaged by a UK insurer is drafting a briefing note on the case for scenario analysis and the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach. She considers the following statements.

I. Scenario analysis emerged as an alternative to purely historical models because it allows the estimation of forward-looking events.

II. A challenge for scenario analysis is the lack of an established framework for constructing scenarios.

III. The MDS approach removes subjectivity from scenario analysis by replacing expert judgement with statistical aggregation.

IV. The MDS approach provides a structured framework designed to reduce subjectivity in scenario analysis.

Which of the statements should she include as accurate?

options.text: I, II and IV only
I and II only
II and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Consultant’s briefing note on scenario analysis and the MDS approach; which Roman-numeral statements are accurate.

**Concept and theory**

Once historical models proved unreliable, scenario analysis emerged as the alternative, because it allows the estimation of forward-looking events: a scenario can describe something that has never happened. Its weakness is structural, not statistical. Schweser notes there is no established framework for constructing scenarios, so scenarios tend to be ad hoc and dependent on whoever writes them. The MDS approach is offered as the answer: a structured framework designed to reduce subjectivity in scenario analysis. The precise word is “reduce”. The Key Concepts say subjectivity is unavoidable; MDS makes it quantified and transparent rather than making it disappear.

|  | Plain scenario analysis | MDS approach |
|---|---|---|
| Looks forward? | Yes | Yes |
| Established framework? | No | Structured framework |
| Subjectivity | Unstructured | Reduced, quantified, transparent (not removed) |

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement. I is the stated reason scenario analysis emerged: true. II is the stated challenge: true. III says MDS removes subjectivity: false, an absolute claim. IV says MDS is designed to reduce subjectivity: true. The accurate set is I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Verb discipline: MDS reduces subjectivity; it never removes it.

**Reference**

LO 97.a (verbatim): “Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 97, Module 97.1, section “Market-Driven Scenario Approach”, second and third paragraphs; Key Concepts LO 97.a. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing (Schweser cross-references Golub, Chapter 5). No GARP versus Schweser conflict can arise for this LO.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-15 a, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: Schweser: “Scenario analysis has emerged as an alternative approach because it allows for the estimation of forward-looking events. One challenge, however, is the lack of an established framework for constructing scenarios.” The MDS approach “provides a structured framework designed to reduce subjectivity in scenario analysis.” Statements I, II and IV are these sentences; option A selects exactly them.

b.reason: **Scope error: rejects a true statement by over-reading it.** B drops IV, as if “designed to reduce subjectivity” were the same overclaim as III. “Reduce” is the source’s word and is correct. B would be right only if IV said “eliminate”.

c.reason: **Polarity flip on statement I.** C rejects I, which amounts to treating scenario analysis as backward-looking. Forward-looking estimation is the very reason it emerged. C would be right only if I described scenario analysis as dependent on historical relationships.

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** D accepts III. Schweser says subjectivity remains (“Although this scenario approach contains an element of subjectivity”) and the Key Concepts say it is unavoidable. Note also that III and IV cannot both be true, so D also drops IV. D would be right only in a world where statistical aggregation removed judgement entirely.

questions.question: A board member of a Brazilian asset manager asks the CRO which conditions, according to James Surowiecki’s The Wisdom of Crowds, must hold for aggregating information from many individuals to improve decision-making. Which list is accurate?

options.text: Each individual has specialised knowledge not available to others; individuals discuss their opinions as a group until they reach consensus; there is an objective mechanism for aggregating private views into a collective assessment.

Each individual has specialised knowledge that is shared with all other participants; individual opinions are independent and not influenced by groupthink; there is an objective mechanism for aggregating private views into a collective assessment.

Each individual has specialised knowledge not available to others; individual opinions are independent and not influenced by groupthink; private views are aggregated by the judgement of the most senior expert in the group.

Each individual has specialised knowledge not available to others; individual opinions are independent and not influenced by groupthink; there is an objective mechanism for aggregating private views into a collective assessment.

questions.solution:
Board member asks the CRO for Surowiecki’s three wisdom-of-crowds conditions; which list is accurate.

**Concept and theory**

The MDS approach borrows its logic from James Surowiecki’s The Wisdom of Crowds, which argues that decision-making improves when information is aggregated from many individuals, but only under three conditions. Think of each condition as guarding against one way a crowd can fail.

| # | Criterion (Schweser) | Failure it guards against |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Each individual has specialised knowledge not available to others | A crowd that knows the same things adds no information |
| 2 | Opinions are independent, not influenced by groupthink | Correlated opinions repeat one view many times |
| 3 | An objective mechanism aggregates private views into a collective assessment | Aggregation by authority or politics overrides the crowd |

The MDS approach is said to meet all three: it gathers input from a diverse group of professionals and has the risk management department aggregate it through a centralised process.

**Applying it to this question**

All four options share the three-slot structure, and each wrong option corrupts exactly one slot. Check each slot: knowledge must be not available to others; opinions must be independent; aggregation must be by an objective mechanism. Only D has all three.

**Fragile fact.** Three words carry the list: not available to others, independent, objective. Each distractor flips exactly one.

**Reference**

LO 97.a (verbatim): “Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 97, Module 97.1, section “Market-Driven Scenario Approach”, second paragraph (Surowiecki’s three criteria). GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing (Schweser cross-references Golub, Chapter 5). No GARP versus Schweser conflict can arise for this LO.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-15 a, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: Group discussion until consensus is the mechanism that produces groupthink, the opposite of independence. A would describe a committee process, not a wisdom-of-crowds aggregation.

b.reason: Knowledge “shared with all other participants” reverses “not available to others”. If everyone knows the same thing, aggregation adds nothing. B would be correct only if the criterion were common knowledge, which it is not.

c.reason: Aggregation by the most senior expert’s judgement is subjective and lets one person override the crowd. The source requires an objective mechanism. C would describe a hierarchical decision process, not the third criterion.

d.reason: Schweser’s list: “Each individual should possess specialized knowledge that is not available to others. Individual opinions must be independent and not influenced by groupthink. There must be an objective mechanism for aggregating private views into a collective assessment.” D matches all three.

An internal auditor at a Singapore asset manager (assets under management SGD 84 billion) is reviewing the firm’s new market-driven scenario process. The scenario panel is summarised below.

The objective aggregation criterion is at risk, because the risk management department, rather than the CIO, aggregates the views.

Independence is about how views are formed: are they formed before anyone is exposed to a dominant opinion? a.reason: **Polarity flip on the role of diversity.** Diversity across asset classes and regions is what supports criterion 1; the aim is knowledge not available to others, not a common view. A would be right only if the panel were drawn from a single desk.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Japanese life insurer is presenting to newly hired staff on how a market-driven scenario is first framed, using JPY interest rate policy as the issue. Which statement best describes the opening stage of the process?

options.text: The issue is identified once, when the framework is first set up, and is then used for all later stress tests; the outcomes are translated into instantaneous shocks on policy variables such as equity, bond and commodity indices.

Risk managers, investors and economists periodically identify the issue, and then define the single most likely outcome, which is translated into instantaneous shocks on policy variables such as equity, bond and commodity indices.

Risk managers, investors and economists periodically identify the issue, define a set of idealised outcomes covering a broad spectrum of plausible possibilities, and translate these outcomes into instantaneous shocks on policy variables such as equity, bond and commodity indices.

Risk managers, investors and economists periodically identify the issue, define a set of idealised outcomes covering a broad spectrum of plausible possibilities, and translate them into gradual multi-year paths for macroeconomic series such as GDP growth and unemployment.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst explains how an MDS scenario on JPY rate policy is first framed; which opening-stage description is best.

**Concept and theory**

The MDS process opens in three moves. First, risk managers, investors and economists periodically identify current issues that could affect financial markets, for example inflation, trade policy or monetary policy. Periodic identification keeps the scenario set current. Second, once an issue is chosen, they define a set of idealised outcomes covering a broad spectrum of plausible possibilities: not one forecast, but the range of ways the issue could play out. Third, the outcomes are translated into instantaneous shocks on policy variables, such as equity, bond or commodity indices. Instantaneous shocks to traded market variables are what a valuation engine can apply to a portfolio later.

| Move | What the source says | Common corruption |
|---|---|---|
| Identify issue | Periodically, by risk managers, investors, economists | Once, at set-up |
| Outcomes | A set covering a broad spectrum | A single most likely outcome |
| Translation | Instantaneous shocks on policy variables (equity, bond, commodity indices) | Gradual paths for macro series |

**Applying it to this question**

Check the three moves in each option. A fails on frequency, B on the number of outcomes, D on the form of the shocks. C passes all three. The JPY rate policy framing is context only: monetary policy is one of the issues Schweser lists.

**Fragile fact.** Three qualifiers: periodically, a set of outcomes across a broad spectrum, instantaneous shocks on policy variables.

No GARP versus Schweser conflict can arise for this LO.

These outcomes are then translated into instantaneous shocks on policy variables, such as equity, bond, and/or commodity indices.” C restates each move.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a EUR multi-asset fund is reviewing the fund’s market-driven scenario documentation and recommending improvements. One section describes how judgement and statistics interact. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Statistical tools generate the candidate scenarios first, and creativity is applied afterwards to interpret the resulting P&L for the investment committee.

The process requires creativity in envisioning potential scenarios, followed by statistical tools that constrain and refine those ideas, with the Mahalanobis distance used to assess the plausibility and magnitude of each shock.
The process requires creativity in envisioning potential scenarios, and the Mahalanobis distance is then used to translate each idealised outcome into instantaneous shocks on the policy variables.
The process requires creativity in envisioning potential scenarios; the covariance matrix then produces the portfolio P&L, and the valuation engine is used to check the plausibility of the shocks.

questions.solution:
EUR fund PM reviews how creativity and statistical tools interact in the MDS process; which statement is most accurate.

**Concept and theory**

The MDS process combines two different kinds of work in a fixed order. Creativity comes first: people envision potential scenarios and the outcomes they imply. Statistics comes second: tools constrain and refine those ideas so that they stay plausible. Schweser names the tools and gives each a role. The Mahalanobis distance, a multivariate measure, assesses the plausibility and magnitude of each shock. The shocks to policy variables are passed through a covariance matrix, which is reviewed for plausibility. After several iterations a collective version is agreed, and only then do the shocks go into a valuation engine, which produces the P&L.

| Element | Role (Schweser, LO 97.a level) |
|---|---|
| Creativity | Envision potential scenarios (first) |
| Statistical tools | Constrain and refine the ideas (second) |
| Mahalanobis distance | Assess plausibility and magnitude of each shock |
| Covariance matrix | Shocks to policy variables passed through it; reviewed for plausibility |
| Valuation engine | Applies finalised shocks to the portfolio, producing the P&L |

The formula for the Mahalanobis distance and the z-scores built from it belong to LO 97.b and are not needed here.

The deciding facts are the order (creativity, then statistics) and the role of each tool. A reverses the order; C gives the Mahalanobis distance a translation role it does not have; D swaps the roles of the covariance matrix and the valuation engine. B has the right order and the right role.

**Fragile fact.** Order and job: humans propose, the Mahalanobis distance judges plausibility and magnitude, the valuation engine prices.

**Reference**

b.reason: Schweser: “The process requires creativity in envisioning potential scenarios, followed by the use of statistical tools to constrain and refine those ideas. A multivariate measure called the Mahalanobis distance is used to assess the plausibility and magnitude of each shock.” B is a direct restatement.

Swiss private bank committee member asks what the MDS process finally delivers; which answer is most accurate.

**Concept and theory**

The MDS process ends in a portfolio P&L, not in a probability or a VaR figure. Schweser’s sequence: the shocks are refined through several iterations until a collective version is agreed; the finalised shocks are then entered into a valuation engine and applied to the portfolio under analysis, “producing a P&L that helps identify the key underlying risk drivers.” The P&L is therefore a diagnostic: it shows which exposures drive the loss or gain under a plausible, collectively agreed scenario. Iteration is not optional; it is how the collective version is reached and how views get challenged and refined.

**Applying it to this question**

Two facts decide: the output is a P&L from the valuation engine, and it comes after iteration to a collective version. A and B name the wrong output; C drops the iteration. The currencies in the stem are context only.

**Fragile fact.** Output equals P&L that reveals risk drivers, produced only after the collective version is agreed through iteration.

**Reference**

LO 97.a (verbatim): “Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 97, Module 97.1, section “Market-Driven Scenario Approach”, fifth paragraph. The covariance matrix in MDS is used to review shocks for plausibility, not to produce a VaR. A would be right in a stem about a parametric VaR model.

**Concept and theory**

The “evaluate” half of the LO turns on one balanced judgement. Weakness: the approach contains an element of subjectivity, and the Key Concepts say subjectivity is unavoidable. Strength: it is still highly valuable, because it forces risk takers through a structured process that quantifies their subjective views. Quantified views are transparent; transparent views can be challenged and refined; and that iterative feedback is described as an essential component of effective portfolio risk management. |---|---|

| Mechanism | Views become transparent, so they can be challenged and refined |
| Status of the feedback loop | Essential component of effective portfolio risk management |

**Concept and theory**

The wisdom-of-crowds argument needs all three criteria at once, and the MDS approach meets them through its design: a diverse group of investment professionals across asset classes, regions and areas of expertise provides the input, and the risk management department’s centralised process aggregates it. Diversity is what makes knowledge “not available to others”: people from different desks, regions and specialisms know different things. A process can be perfectly independent and perfectly objective and still add little, if every contributor has the same knowledge.

| Four analysts, one background, one office, risk department only | 1: specialised knowledge | Falls short of MDS diversity |
| Each writes separately, no discussion | 2: independence | Met |
| Fixed, documented statistical procedure | 3: objective aggregation | Met |

The only gap against the MDS design is the narrow input group: no portfolio managers, traders or economists, no spread across asset classes, regions or expertise.

An internal auditor at a US endowment is validating the order of the stages in the endowment’s market-driven scenario procedure manual. The manual lists the following stages, not in order.

I. Translate the outcomes into instantaneous shocks on policy variables.

II. Periodically identify a current issue that could affect financial markets.

III. Enter the finalised shocks into a valuation engine and apply them to the portfolio to produce a P&L.

IV. Define a set of idealised outcomes covering a broad spectrum of plausible possibilities.

V. Assess the shocks with the Mahalanobis distance, pass them through a covariance matrix reviewed for plausibility, and iterate until a collective version is agreed.

Which sequence is correct?

options.text: II, I, IV, V, III
II, IV, I, III, V
II, IV, I, V, III
IV, II, I, V, III

questions.solution:
Auditor validates the order of five stages in an endowment’s MDS manual; which sequence is correct.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser describes the MDS process as one chain, each stage needing the output of the one before.

| Order | Stage | Why it comes here |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Periodically identify a current issue (II) | Nothing can be framed without an issue |
| 2 | Define a set of idealised outcomes across a broad spectrum (IV) | Outcomes are outcomes of the issue |
| 3 | Translate outcomes into instantaneous shocks on policy variables (I) | Shocks are the quantified form of outcomes |
| 4 | Mahalanobis distance, covariance matrix review, iterate to a collective version (V) | Statistics constrains and refines the proposed shocks |
| 5 | Valuation engine applies finalised shocks to the portfolio, producing the P&L (III) | Only finalised shocks are priced |

**Applying it to this question**

Map the stages: II first, then IV, then I, then V, then III. This is option C. Each wrong option swaps one adjacent pair.

**Fragile fact.** Issue, outcomes, shocks, statistical refinement and iteration, then valuation. Pricing waits for the finalised collective version.

GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress GARP’s framing (Schweser cross-references Golub, Chapter 5). No GARP versus Schweser conflict can arise for this LO.

The source says the shocks entered into the valuation engine are the finalised ones, after a collective version is agreed. B would describe pricing a first draft.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Dutch pension fund is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on the statistic the fund uses to check whether a vector of expert-proposed policy variable shocks in a market-driven scenario (MDS) is plausible. Which of the following statements best describes the Mahalanobis distance (MD) as used in the MDS approach?

options.text: It measures how many standard deviations the shock vector lies from the center of the distribution after setting all correlations between the shocks to zero, so it isolates the pure magnitude of the shocks.

It measures how many standard deviations the shock vector lies from the mean vector, using the inverse covariance matrix of the policy variables so that correlations shape the distance, and it is used to flag multivariate outliers.

It measures how far the shock vector lies from the mean vector, using the inverse covariance matrix of the policy variables, and converts that distance directly into an absolute probability of occurrence without further assumptions.

It measures how many standard deviations the shock vector lies from the mean vector, using the inverse covariance matrix of all M risk factors, including the implied nonpolicy factors, and it is used to flag multivariate outliers.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst at a Dutch pension fund describing the Mahalanobis distance for new hires.

**Concept and theory**

In the MDS approach, experts propose a vector of shocks r to a small set of policy variables. The first question is whether that vector is plausible. Schweser defines an implausible shock as one that is highly inconsistent with historical data, that is, an outlier. A single variable is easy to judge: a z-score $(\text{r} - \mu)$/$\sigma$ counts how many standard deviations the shock is from its mean. With several variables, judging each one alone is not enough, because the variables are correlated: an equity fall of 3 standard deviations together with a fall in bond yields may be quite ordinary if the two usually move together, while the same equity fall with a sharp rise in yields may be extraordinary.

The Mahalanobis distance is the multivariate generalization of the z-score that handles this. It is a distance metric that accounts for the correlations among data points and the shape of the distribution:

MD $= \sqrt{(\text{r} - \mu)^{'} \Sigma^{-1} (\text{r} - \mu)}$

where r is the shock vector, $\mu$ is the mean vector and $\Sigma^{-1}$ is the inverse covariance matrix of the policy variables. With one variable it collapses to \|r $- \mu|$/$\sigma$, the ordinary z-score.

| Element | Role in the MD |
|---|---|
| r $\mu$ $\Sigma^{-}$1 | expert-proposed policy variable shocks center (mean) of the historical distribution inverse covariance matrix of the policy variables; it rescales by volatil- |
| Output Use | ities and builds in correlations number of standard deviations from the center, given the shape of the data identify multivariate outliers, that is, implausible shock vectors |

**Applying it to this question**

The analyst wants the statistic that checks plausibility of the whole shock vector. Three features must all be present in the right option: (1) distance in standard deviations from the mean vector, (2) computed with the inverse covariance matrix of the policy variables, so correlations matter, and (3) used to flag outliers. Only B has all three without an added false claim.

**Fragile fact.** MD uses the inverse covariance matrix of the policy variables and keeps correlations; the zero-correlation version is the volatility z-score.

**Reference**

LO 97.b (verbatim): “Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 97, Module 97.1 (Statistical Tools for MDSs), section “Mahalanobis Distance”; Module Quiz 97.1, Q2 answer explanation. Formula reconstructed as stated in the source note. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-15 b, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Setting all correlations to zero is the defining feature of the volatility z-score, which isolates the magnitude of the shocks. The MD keeps the correlations; that is its purpose. A would be correct if the stem asked for the volatility z-score.

b.reason: B restates Schweser: the MD “identifies how many standard deviations a point is from the center of a distribution, considering the shape of the data,” uses $\Sigma^{-1}$ of the policy variables, and is the most common statistical method for identifying multivariate outliers. Schweser’s Module Quiz 97.1 answer confirms MD is the primary outlier tool.

c.reason: **Absolute claim / scope error.** The first half is right, but no z-type measure converts directly into an absolute probability. Schweser says scenario z-scores measure relative probability under an elliptical distribution, and additional assumptions (parametric or nonparametric) are needed for an absolute probability. C would be correct only if it said “can be converted into a probability after assuming a distribution for the scores.”

d.reason: **Scope error.** The matrix in the MD is the covariance matrix of the policy variables, the small set of K shocked variables. The nonpolicy factors are implied afterwards; they are not inputs to the plausibility check on the proposed policy shocks. D would be correct if the MD were defined over the full perturbation vector, which Schweser does not do.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee at an Australian superannuation fund sends the chief risk officer four questions about a proposed market-driven scenario. The CRO replies to each with the statistic she intends to use. Which of the following pairings of question and statistic is most appropriate?

options.text: “Is this shock vector a multivariate outlier relative to history, once correlations among the policy variables are taken into account?” Answer: the volatility z-score.
“How large are these shocks if we ignore how they co-move with one another?” Answer: the correlation z-score.
“Do these shocks move together in the way our chosen covariance matrix expects them to?” Answer: the Mahalanobis distance.
“How severe is this scenario in standard deviations, on a basis that does not rise simply because more policy variables are shocked?” Answer: the scenario z-score.

questions.solution:
CRO of an Australian superannuation fund matching four committee questions to statistics.

**Concept and theory**

Reading 97 gives four related statistics. Each answers a different question, and the exam habitually swaps them.

| Statistic | What it measures | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| Mahalanobis distance | SDs from the center using $\Sigma^{-1}$ (correlations included) | Is the shock vector a multivariate outlier? |
| Scenario z-score | Severity in SDs, rescaled so it does not grow with $\sqrt{\text{n}}$ | How severe or plausible is the scenario? Lower is more plausible. |
| Volatility z-score | Scenario z-score with all correlations set to zero | How big are the shocks, ignoring co-movement? |
| Correlation z-score | Scenario z-score normalized for magnitude | Are the shocks consistent with the covariance structure? |

The scenario z-score exists because the MD increases at a rate proportional to the square root of the number of policy variables n. Kinlaw and Turkington (2014) then split the scenario z-score into a magnitude component (volatility z-score) and a consistency component (correlation z-score).

**Applying it to this question**

Read each committee question for its key phrase: “outlier, correlations taken into account” points to MD; “ignore how they co-move” points to the volatility z-score; “move together as the covariance matrix expects” points to the correlation z-score; “severity in SDs, not rising with the number of variables” points to the scenario z-score. Only D pairs its question correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Volatility z-score = magnitude (zero correlations); correlation z-score = consistency (magnitude removed). Swapping these two is the commonest trap.

**Reference**

LO 97.b (verbatim): “Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 97, Module 97.1 (Statistical Tools for MDSs), section “Mahalanobis Distance; Scenario Z-Score; Volatility Z-Score; Correlation Z-Score”; Module Quiz 97.1, Q2 answer explanation. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-15 b, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** The multivariate outlier test with correlations is the MD. The volatility z-score deliberately sets correlations to zero, so it cannot account for them. A would be correct with the answer “Mahalanobis distance.”

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Magnitude ignoring co-movement is the volatility z-score. The correlation z-score is the opposite: it removes magnitude and keeps the co-movement information. B would be correct with the answer “volatility z-score.”

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Consistency with the covariance structure is read from the correlation z-score (and its contrast with the volatility z-score). The MD mixes magnitude and correlation into one distance and cannot by itself tell you whether a large value comes from large shocks or from inconsistent co-movement. C would be correct with the answer “correlation z-score.”

d.reason: Schweser: the scenario z-score is applied to prevent the MD from increasing at a rate proportional to $\sqrt{\text{n}}$, and it “represents the severity of a given scenario (in standard deviations).”

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at an Australian bank reviews two hypothetical scenarios evaluated with the same covariance matrix. The bank’s trading book is worth AUD 6.2 billion.

| Scenario | Number of policy variables | Mahalanobis distance |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario 1 | 3 | 3.2 |
| Scenario 2 | 12 | 3.6 |

A colleague concludes that Scenario 1 is clearly the more plausible of the two because its Mahalanobis distance is lower. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: The comparison is not like-for-like, because the Mahalanobis distance tends to rise in proportion to the square root of the number of policy variables; the scenarios should be compared on their scenario z-scores, where the lower value is the more plausible.
The comparison is valid as it stands, because the Mahalanobis distance already uses the inverse covariance matrix and therefore needs no further adjustment before two scenarios are compared.

The comparison is not like-for-like, because the Mahalanobis distance tends to rise in proportion to the number of policy variables; dividing each distance by its number of policy variables makes the scenarios comparable.

The comparison is not like-for-like; the scenarios should be compared on their volatility z-scores, because the volatility z-score is the measure built to remove the effect of the number of policy variables.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst at an Australian bank comparing MDs of a 3-variable and a 12-variable scenario.

**Concept and theory**

The MD adds up squared standardized deviations (adjusted for correlations) across all policy variables. Every extra variable contributes another nonnegative term, so a scenario that shocks more variables tends to have a larger distance even if no single shock is unusual. Schweser states the MD increases at a rate proportional to the square root of the number of policy variables n.

A simple illustration with uncorrelated variables, each shocked by exactly one standard deviation:

MD $= \sqrt{\sum^{\text{n}}_{\text{i}=1} 1^{2}} = \sqrt{\text{n}}$ : n = 4 ⇒ 2, n = 9 ⇒ 3, n = 16 ⇒ 4.

The scenarios are equally “ordinary” per variable, yet the distance grows with $\sqrt{\text{n}}$. To remove this dimension effect, the MDS approach applies the scenario z-score, which represents scenario severity in standard deviations on a basis that does not drift upward with n. Between two scenarios, the one with the lower scenario z-score is more plausible.

**Applying it to this question**

Scenario 1 shocks 3 variables and has MD 3.2; Scenario 2 shocks 12 variables and has MD 3.6. The raw distances are not comparable because Scenario 2’s distance is inflated by its larger n. Indeed, with four times as many variables, a “baseline” MD would be about $\sqrt{4} =$ 2 times larger, so an MD only slightly above Scenario 1’s could well correspond to the less severe scenario. The correct step is to compare scenario z-scores. The AUD 6.2 billion book value is irrelevant: plausibility does not depend on position size.

**Fragile fact.** MD grows with $\sqrt{\text{n}}$ (not n); the scenario z-score is the fix; lower scenario z-score = more plausible.

**Reference**

LO 97.b (verbatim): “Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 97, Module 97.1 (Statistical Tools for MDSs), section “Scenario Z-Score”. The $\sqrt{\text{n}}$ illustration is derived from the reconstructed MD formula. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-15 b, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: A combines both source facts: the MD rises in proportion to $\sqrt{\text{n}}$, and the scenario z-score is the measure used to compare scenarios, lower meaning more plausible.

b.reason: **Scope error.** Using $\Sigma^{-1}$ adjusts for volatilities and correlations, not for the number of dimensions. B drops the condition that the scenarios have the same number of policy variables. It would be correct if both scenarios shocked the same number of variables.

c.reason: **Unit or convention slip.** The growth rate is $\sqrt{\text{n}}$, not n, and the source remedy is the scenario z-score, not an ad hoc division. Dividing by n would give 3.2/3 = 1.07 and 3.6/12 = 0.30, over-penalizing the smaller scenario. C would be closer to correct only if MD grew linearly with n.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** The volatility z-score is the scenario z-score with correlations set to zero; it isolates magnitude, not dimension. The measure built to stop growth with $\sqrt{\text{n}}$ is the scenario z-score itself. D would be correct with “scenario z-scores” in place of “volatility z-scores.”

I. The scenario z-score expresses the severity of a scenario in standard deviations.

II. When two scenarios are compared, the one with the higher scenario z-score is the more plausible.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor at a Swiss private bank checking four statements about the scenario z-score.

**Concept and theory**

The scenario z-score is the MDS approach’s headline severity measure. Its properties, as given by Schweser:

- It represents the severity of a scenario in standard deviations.
- It is built so that it does not rise merely with the square root of the number of policy variables, as the MD does.
- Lower is more plausible: when two scenarios are compared, the one with the lower scenario z-score is more plausible; higher values indicate more severe or less plausible stresses.
- It depends on the covariance matrix: the same event gets different z-scores under slow, fast or recent data, so each choice produces a different risk ruler.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian asset manager must assign a severity to a hypothetical scenario proposed by the firm’s economists: a sudden loss of central bank independence. No comparable event exists in the firm’s history. The analyst has a risk ruler listing past market events with their scenario z-scores. The fund’s assets are BRL 14 billion. Which of the following approaches is most consistent with how a risk ruler is used?

options.text: Estimate the loss the hypothetical scenario would cause on the current portfolio, find the historical event on the ruler with the closest portfolio loss, and assign that event’s scenario z-score.
Treat events higher up the ruler, with larger scenario z-scores, as the more plausible ones, and place the hypothetical scenario above every historical event the economists consider less likely.
Read the scenario z-score straight off the ruler as a fixed value, since each historical event’s z-score on the ruler is the same whichever covariance matrix was used to build it.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at a Brazilian asset manager sizing a no-precedent scenario with a risk ruler.

**Concept and theory**

Hypothetical future events have no data of their own, so analysts often scale them subjectively by comparison with past outliers that seemed implausible beforehand but still occurred. A risk ruler is a spectrum of historical events arranged from most plausible to least plausible, each tagged with its scenario z-score computed under a chosen covariance matrix (historical or more recent data). Lower z-scores are the more plausible events.

How it is used: the analyst decides how likely the hypothetical event feels, finds the historical event of similar perceived likelihood on the ruler, and assigns that event’s scenario z-score as the target severity for the hypothetical scenario. Shocks are then sized to hit that target. Because z-scores depend on the covariance matrix, slow, fast and recent data each produce a different ruler for the same events.

**Applying it to this question**

There is no comparable historical event, which is exactly when the ruler helps: the analyst benchmarks on likelihood, not on similarity of content. The deciding facts are (1) matching is on perceived likelihood, (2) the matched event’s z-score becomes the target, and (3) the ruler is covariance-matrix-specific. The BRL 14 billion asset figure is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** The ruler is ordered most plausible (low z) to least plausible (high z) and is specific to the covariance matrix used.

**Reference**

LO 97.b (verbatim): “Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 97, Module 97.1 (Statistical Tools for MDSs), section “Scenario Z-Score” (Figure 97.1, Risk Ruler of Scenario Z-Scores); also “Covariance Matrix Selection”. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-15 b, where it is Q5 of 12.

Portfolio P&L is the output of the stress test after the shocks are set; using it to size the shocks reverses the process. A would be correct if the ruler were a P&L ranking, which it is not.

C would be correct only if a single covariance matrix were fixed by policy, and even then the values would be specific to that matrix.

She asks the chief risk officer: “Does that mean this scenario has roughly the probability of a three-standard-deviation move under a normal distribution?” Which of the following responses by the CRO is most accurate?

options.text: Yes. Because scenario z-scores are measured in standard deviations, a standard normal table converts them directly into absolute probabilities without any further assumption.

Not without more assumptions. Scenario z-scores measure relative probability assuming elliptically distributed returns; an absolute probability needs either an assumed distribution for the z-scores or an empirical distribution of z-scores over a historical horizon.

Not without more assumptions. The parametric approach estimates an empirical distribution of z-scores over a historical horizon, while the nonparametric approach assumes a probability distribution for the z-scores.

Board member of a Japanese life insurer asking whether a scenario z-score of 3.0 gives a normal-table probability.

**Concept and theory**

A scenario z-score is a severity in standard deviations, so it is tempting to look it up in a normal table. Schweser warns against this. Scenario z-scores are designed to measure the relative probability of events under the assumption that asset returns follow an elliptical distribution (a broad family that includes, but is not limited to, the normal). Relative probability means they rank scenarios: a z of 2 is more plausible than a z of 4. Converting a z-score into an absolute probability requires additional assumptions. Two approaches:

| Approach | What it does |
|---|---|
| Parametric | assumes a probability distribution for the z-scores |
| Nonparametric | estimates an empirical distribution of z-scores over a historical time horizon |

**Applying it to this question**

The board member is asking for an absolute probability. questions.question:
A model validator at a Canadian pension plan compares two scenarios built on the same three policy variables and evaluated with the same covariance matrix. The individual factor z-scores (each shock divided by its own volatility) are shown below. The plan’s assets are CAD 48 billion.

| Scenario | Equity index | 10-year yield | CAD/USD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scenario 1 | −2.0 | −1.5 | 1.0 |
| Scenario 2 | −2.0 | 1.5 | 1.0 |

The two scenarios have materially different scenario z-scores. Which of the following statements about their volatility z-scores is most accurate?

options.text: They differ, because the volatility z-score measures how consistent each set of shocks is with the chosen covariance structure, and reversing the yield shock changes that consistency.
They differ, because the volatility z-score is the Mahalanobis distance before adjusting for the number of policy variables, and that distance uses the full covariance matrix.
They are equal, because the volatility z-score is the scenario z-score computed with all correlations set to zero, so it reflects only the shock magnitudes, which are the same here.
They are equal, because the volatility z-score depends only on the signs and relative magnitudes of the factor z-scores, and not on their absolute size.

questions.solution:
Model validator at a Canadian pension plan comparing volatility z-scores of two sign-pattern scenarios.

**Concept and theory**

Kinlaw and Turkington (2014) propose decomposing the scenario z-score into two components:

- **Magnitude**: how large the shocks are. Isolated by computing the scenario z-score under the assumption that all correlations between shocks are zero. This is the volatility z-score.
- **Consistency**: how well the shocks fit the chosen covariance structure. Captured by the correlation z-score, which normalizes the scenario z-score for the magnitude of the shocks.

With all correlations set to zero, the distance underlying the score is built only from the squares of each factor z-score, $\text{z}_{\text{i}} = (\text{r}_{\text{i}} - \mu_{\text{i}})$/$\sigma_{\text{i}}$:

$\text{MD}_{\rho}=_{0} = \sqrt{\sum_{\text{i}} \text{z}^{2}_{\text{i}}}$,

so squaring removes signs, and the volatility z-score depends only on the sizes of the individual standardized shocks. The sign pattern (whether shocks move with or against the usual correlations) enters only through the correlation terms, that is, through the consistency component.

**Applying it to this question**

The two scenarios share the absolute factor z-scores (2.0, 1.5, 1.0); only the sign of the yield shock differs. Zero-correlation distance for both:

$\sqrt{2.0^{2} + 1.5^{2} + 1.0^{2}} = \sqrt{4 + 2.25 + 1} = \sqrt{7.25} =$ 2.69.

Identical inputs to the magnitude component give identical volatility z-scores. The material difference in scenario z-scores therefore comes from the consistency component: reversing the yield shock changes how the scenario sits against the covariance matrix. The CAD 48 billion is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Volatility z-score: sign-blind, size-sensitive. Correlation z-score: sign-sensitive, size-blind (to uniform scaling).

**Reference**

The zero-correlation distance in

(a) and (b) is derived from the reconstructed MD formula with a diagonal covariance matrix; it illustrates the magnitude component and is not the volatility z-score formula itself, which is not recoverable from the text. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-15 b, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** Consistency with the covariance structure is the job of the correlation z-score. The volatility z-score ignores correlations, so a sign reversal cannot change it. A would be correct if it referred to the correlation z-score.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** Describes the MD (full covariance matrix, before the $\sqrt{\text{n}}$ adjustment), not the volatility z-score. The MD of the two scenarios would indeed differ. B would be correct as a statement about Mahalanobis distances.

c.reason: C uses the source definition (scenario z-score with all correlations zero, isolating magnitude) and draws the right conclusion that equal magnitudes give equal volatility z-scores.

| Scenario | Policy variables | Volatility z-score | Correlation z-score |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alpha | 3 | 3.8 | 0.1 |
| Beta | 3 | 1.9 | 1.6 |

Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: Beta’s shocks co-move in a way that the chosen covariance matrix may not adequately capture, whereas Alpha’s shocks are broadly consistent with it, even though Alpha’s shocks are larger.
Alpha’s shocks are the ones that are inconsistent with the chosen covariance matrix, because Alpha has the higher volatility z-score of the two scenarios.
Alpha’s correlation z-score close to zero shows that its policy variables are uncorrelated with one another, so the covariance matrix adds no information for Alpha.

**Concept and theory**

Having both the scenario z-score and the volatility z-score lets the risk manager normalize the scenario z-score for the magnitude of the shocks; the result is the correlation z-score. It answers: given the sizes of the shocks, do their joint directions fit the covariance matrix? Schweser’s interpretation rule:

| Correlation z-score | Reading |
|---|---|
| Close to zero | shocks are consistent with the covariance structure |
| High positive (e.g., above 1.0) | covariance matrix may not adequately capture the true co-movement of the policy shocks |

Because it is normalized for magnitude, it does not change if all shocks are scaled up or down together.

**Applying it to this question**

Alpha: volatility z-score 3.8 (large shocks), correlation z-score 0.1 (near zero, consistent). Beta: volatility z-score 1.9 (smaller shocks), correlation z-score 1.6 (above 1.0, co-movement not well captured). Size and consistency are separate dimensions, so the bigger scenario is not the inconsistent one. The SGD 2.4 billion AUM and the equal number of policy variables do not affect the reading.

**Fragile fact.** Above about 1.0 = covariance matrix may not capture the co-movement; near 0 = consistent. Uniform rescaling never changes it.
