questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Canadian corporate bond fund is estimating how long it would take to unwind one holding under the fund’s liquidity policy, which uses the days-to-liquidate approach with a 60-day average daily volume (ADV) and a 15% market participation rate. All volumes are in face value.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Position held (face value) | CAD 45 million |
| Clean price (per 100 face) | 97.50 |
| Modified duration | 6.2 |
| 20-day ADV (face value) | CAD 18 million |
| 60-day ADV (face value) | CAD 12 million |

Under the policy, the estimated number of days to liquidate the full position is closest to:

options.text: 3.8 days
25.0 days
16.7 days
250.0 days

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst, Canadian bond fund: CAD 45m face, 15% participation, 60-day ADV CAD 12m.

**Concept and theory**

The days-to-liquidate approach turns a liquidity question into a time: the trading days needed to unwind a position without moving the market. Schweser builds it from three inputs: (1) the size of the intended trade, (2) an assumed market participation rate, and (3) the asset’s average daily volume (ADV). The participation rate is the percentage of ADV that can be sold each day without causing significant market impact, so the fund’s daily selling capacity is the participation rate times ADV. Dividing the trade size by that capacity gives the days:

Days to liquidate $= \frac{\text{Size of intended trade}}{\text{Participation rate} \times\text{ADV}}$

Formula rebuilt from Schweser’s text (the printed formula is an image): the text names exactly these three inputs and defines the participation rate as a share of ADV, which fixes the form. ADV is measured over a specified window (e.g., 20-day or 60-day), which must match the policy; size and ADV must share units.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula as in (a), one step per line:

Daily capacity = 0.15 × CAD 12 million = CAD 1.8 million face per day

Days to liquidate $= \frac{45}{1.8} =$ 25.0 days

Price and duration are irrelevant (all figures are in face value; duration measures rate risk, not tradability), as is the 20-day ADV. Interpretation: selling at no more than 15% of a typical day’s volume, the fund needs about five trading weeks to exit.

**Fragile fact.** Participation rate and ADV sit together in the denominator: a lower participation rate or a lower ADV means more days, and the ADV window must be the one the policy specifies.

**Reference**

LO 98.c: Describe and apply different approaches to model asset liquidity, including an approach to modeling infrequently traded bonds and the t-cost model to calculate transaction costs for corporate bonds. Schweser Reading 98, Module 98.2, “Days-to-Liquidate Approach”; Key Concepts LO 98.c. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-16 c, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: **Dropped term.** 45/12 = 3.75, about 3.8 days: the participation rate is ignored, as if the fund could absorb a whole day’s volume. It would be correct only with a 100% participation rate.

b.reason: B applies trade size over participation rate times ADV with the ADV window the policy names, exactly as Schweser’s three-input description requires.

c.reason: **Wrong input twin.** 45/(0.15 × 18) = 16.7 days uses the 20-day ADV. It would be correct if the policy specified a 20-day window.

d.reason: **Unit slip.** 45/(0.015 × 12) = 250 days enters 15% as 0.015. It would be correct only for a 1.5% participation rate.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at the investment arm of a Japanese insurer is presenting to newly hired analysts on why days-to-liquidate estimates for corporate bonds must be interpreted with care. Which of the following statements about latent liquidity is most accurate?

options.text: It is the gap between the volume the market could theoretically support and the volume actually traded, so estimates based on observed ADV tend to overstate the days needed to liquidate.
It is the gap by which the volume actually traded exceeds the volume the market could theoretically support, so estimates based on observed ADV tend to understate the days needed.
It is the gap between the executed price of a trade and its pre-trade benchmark price, so it measures the market impact cost incurred when a bond position is liquidated.

**Concept and theory**

The participation rate and ADV are estimated from what actually traded. Schweser stresses that actual trading volume is usually lower than the volume the market could theoretically support. The difference between observable liquidity and this potential capacity is called latent liquidity:

Latent liquidity = Potential (supportable) volume − Observed traded volume (≥ 0)

Because the observed volume is the smaller of the two, an estimate built on observed ADV gives a smaller daily capacity than the market could really absorb, so it gives more days than are truly needed. That is why Schweser calls ADV a conservative measure. The latent part cannot be observed directly; it must be inferred, for example from dealer inventory or a tail measure such as the 90th percentile of the ADV distribution.

**Applying it to this question**

Two facts decide the answer: the direction of the gap (potential exceeds observed) and its consequence for days (observed ADV overstates the days). Only A has both right.

**Fragile fact.** Observed volume is below potential volume, so observed ADV makes days-to-liquidate longer (conservative), not shorter.

**Reference**

LO 98.c: Describe and apply different approaches to model asset liquidity, including an approach to modeling infrequently traded bonds and the t-cost model to calculate transaction costs for corporate bonds. b.reason: **Polarity flip.** B reverses the direction: Schweser says actual volume is lower than theoretical volume. With the direction reversed, the conclusion about days also flips. B would describe a market where reported prints were inflated beyond what could really trade, which is not the source’s case.

| Item | Bond X | Bond Y |
|---|---|---|
| Benchmark bid | 61.20 | 101.10 |
| Benchmark ask | 62.00 | 102.30 |
| Last traded price (9 days ago for X) | 60.10 | 101.80 |

Bond X, about 130 bp
Bond Y, about 120 bp
Bond X, about 65 bp

**Concept and theory**

Schweser splits t-costs into fixed costs (commissions and bid-ask spreads) and realized market impact costs (how position size affects execution costs). A raw spread in price points is not comparable across bonds trading at different price levels, so the spread “can be normalized by the midprice of benchmark quotes”:

Normalized spread $= \frac{\text{Ask} - \text{Bid}}{\text{Mid}}$ , Mid $= \frac{\text{Bid} + \text{Ask}}{2}$

(Rebuilt from Schweser’s wording.) Schweser adds that comparability across bonds becomes less reliable when the securities trade infrequently.

Formula as in (a), one step per line:

Bond X: Mid = (61.20 + 62.00)/2 = 61.60; spread = 0.80; 0.80/61.60 = 1.299% ≈ 130 bp

Bond Y: Mid = (101.10 + 102.30)/2 = 101.70; spread = 1.20; 1.20/101.70 = 1.180% ≈ 118 bp

Y has the larger raw spread (1.20 vs 0.80) but X has the larger normalized spread because it trades at a much lower price. Last traded prices are irrelevant: the denominator is the midprice of benchmark quotes, and X’s last trade is nine days stale.

**Fragile fact.** Divide by the midprice of benchmark quotes, not par and not the last trade; the bond with the bigger raw spread need not have the bigger normalized spread.

A quantitative analyst at a US corporate bond fund is estimating the average market impact cost for one bond by regressing observed impact on a constant only. Following good practice for t-cost regressions, she weights each observation by the dollar amount traded. Prices are per 100 face.

| Trade | Face traded (USD million) | Price | Market impact (bp) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.05 | 104 | 45 |
| 2 | 0.08 | 103 | 38 |
| 3 | 6.00 | 70 | 12 |
| 4 | 2.00 | 110 | 24 |

**Concept and theory**

Bond trade data contain many small odd-lot trades which, if every trade counts equally, dominate the estimate. Schweser therefore recommends weighting regression observations by the dollar amount traded. In a weighted least squares regression on a constant only, the fitted intercept equals the weighted mean of the dependent variable:

$\hat{\alpha}$ $= \frac{\sum_{\text{i}} \text{w}_{\text{i}} \text{MI}_{\text{i}}}{\sum_{\text{i}} \text{w}_{\text{i}}}$ , $\text{w}_{\text{i}} = \text{Face}_{\text{i}} \times\frac{\text{Price}_{\text{i}}}{100}$

$\sum\text{w} =$ 6.5344

$\sum\text{w MI} =$ 0.0520(45) + 0.0824(38) + 4.20(12) + 2.20(24)

= 2.340 + 3.131 + 50.400 + 52.800 = 108.671

$\hat{\alpha}$ = 108.671/6.5344 = 16.6 bp

Meaning: dollar-representative impact is about 17 bp; the odd lots carry almost no weight.

**Fragile fact.** Weight by dollar amount traded (face times price), not by face and not equally.

Transaction costs are a critical part of liquidity risk assessment and a key component of best-execution verification. The model has two components:

| Component | Content |
|---|---|
| Fixed costs | Commissions and bid-ask spreads (spread normalized by benchmark midprice). |
| Market impact costs | How position size affects execution cost; measured by implementation shortfall against a pre-trade benchmark. |

Inputs are intraday benchmark prices, empirical transaction data and bond-specific attributes, with regression for some components; the first component of the standard form is fixed costs, the second market impact. The primary purpose is to estimate market impact. Schweser also notes the trade-off: liquidating quickly on a pro rata basis may cause undesirable price effects, while holding higher ongoing liquidity can constrain return objectives. (The exact functional form is an image in the source and is not reconstructed here.)

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-16 d Q1
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Canadian asset manager is presenting to newly hired analysts on how the firm should prepare for unanticipated redemption requests across its funds. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Extraordinary measures, rather than advance planning, are the most effective way for a fund to manage unexpected redemption requests.
Extraordinary measures are permitted in every jurisdiction whenever a fund’s redemption requests exceed its average daily outflows.
Although extraordinary measures are rarely invoked, they may be needed on short notice, so legal, operations, risk management and trading should run break-glass tests.
Because extraordinary measures are rarely invoked, break-glass testing can be left to the risk management function alone, without legal or operations.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst at a Canadian asset manager briefs new analysts on preparing for unanticipated redemptions; which statement is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

A fund that offers investors the right to redeem promises liquidity on demand, yet it holds assets that may take days or weeks to sell without moving prices. When redemptions arrive unexpectedly and in size, the fund faces a choice between selling assets fast (and at a discount, harming those who stay) and failing to pay those who leave. Schweser frames the response in two tiers:

- **Advance planning** is the most effective way to manage unexpected redemption requests. The fund’s ordinary liquidity tools do the everyday work.
- **Extraordinary measures** are a second tier that some jurisdictions permit when ordinary liquidity tools prove insufficient. The five named measures are temporary borrowing, in-kind redemptions, gates, price mechanisms (swing pricing and PRVs) and suspension.

Because these measures are rarely invoked, the people who must activate them may never have done so. Yet they may be needed on short notice. Schweser therefore says that legal, operations, risk management and trading teams should conduct “break glass” testing so that each measure can be activated quickly. The analogy is a fire alarm behind glass: rarely pulled, but everyone must know where it is and what happens when it is pulled.

| Feature | Schweser statement |
|---|---|
| Best defence | Advance planning |
| When extraordinary measures apply | Some jurisdictions permit them when ordinary liquidity tools prove insufficient |
| Frequency and urgency | Rarely invoked, but may be needed on short notice |
| Preparation | Break-glass testing by legal, operations, risk management and trading |

**Applying it to this question**

The analyst is teaching the framing, not a single tool. The deciding facts are three: the ranking (planning first, measures second), the condition (some jurisdictions, when ordinary tools are insufficient) and the actors in break-glass testing (four teams). Only one option keeps all three intact.

**Fragile fact.** Advance planning ranks first; break-glass testing is a four-team exercise (legal, operations, risk management, trading), not a risk-only task.

**Reference**

LO 98.d (verbatim): “Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 98, Module 98.3, section “Meeting Unanticipated Redemption Requests”, opening paragraph. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-16 d, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the ranking. Schweser says the most effective way to manage unexpected redemptions is advance planning; extraordinary measures are the fallback. A would be right only if the stem asked what a fund turns to after its ordinary plan has failed.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It overextends two conditions. The measures are permitted in some jurisdictions (each measure has its own regime), and only when ordinary liquidity tools prove insufficient, not whenever requests exceed an average. B would be right only if every measure were available in all jurisdictions and keyed to a flow average; the nearest true statement is that swing pricing, where permitted, is triggered when net flows exceed a threshold.

c.reason: C restates the source almost exactly: the measures are rarely invoked, may be needed on short notice, and legal, operations, risk management and trading teams should run break-glass tests so that each measure can be activated quickly.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** Right action, wrong actor. Break-glass testing involves legal, operations, risk management and trading together; it is not a risk-only exercise. Note also the inverted logic: rarity is the reason testing matters, not a reason to narrow it. D would be right only if the source assigned break-glass testing to the risk function alone, which it does not.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-16 d Q2
questions.question: A treasury analyst at a U.S.-based retail bond fund is preparing a contingency memo. The fund holds a sizable sleeve of less liquid corporate bonds and has just received redemption requests that its ordinary liquidity tools cannot fully meet. The CRO asks the analyst to describe temporary borrowing as an extraordinary measure. Which statement should the analyst include?

options.text: It gives the fund a short-term liquidity buffer and more time to sell the less liquid bonds in an orderly manner, and it can be arranged through overdrafts, repos, bank credit facilities or interfund lending.

It removes the need to sell the less liquid bonds by transferring specific holdings directly to the redeeming investors, and it relies on specialized electronic transfer systems to move those securities.

It permanently replaces asset sales as the fund’s source of redemption cash, and it can be arranged through overdrafts, repos, bank credit facilities or interfund lending, so the bonds never need to be sold.
It gives the fund a short-term liquidity buffer and more time to sell the less liquid bonds in an orderly manner, and it is equally available to a European UCITS bond fund facing the same outflows.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst at a U.S.-based retail bond fund describes temporary borrowing for the CRO; which statement belongs in the memo?

**Concept and theory**

Temporary borrowing is the bridge among the extraordinary measures. When redemptions arrive faster than the fund can sell its less liquid assets without price damage, the fund borrows cash for a short period, pays the redeeming investors, and then sells the less liquid assets in an orderly way over the time it has bought. The borrowing does not replace the sale; it spreads it out.

| Element | Schweser content |
|---|---|
| Purpose | Short-term liquidity buffer; additional time to sell less liquid assets in an orderly manner |
| Common tools | Overdrafts, repurchase agreements (repos), bank credit facilities, interfund lending arrangements |
| U.S.-based retail funds | Permitted |
| European UCITS funds | Not allowed |

Why it matters for fairness: a fire sale to meet redemptions transfers costs to the investors who stay. Borrowing for a short window lets the fund avoid that fire sale.

**Applying it to this question**

The fund is U.S.-based and retail, so temporary borrowing is permitted. The stem stresses less liquid corporate bonds, which points to the purpose: buy time for orderly sales. The question is which description is complete and correct on purpose, tools and jurisdiction.

**Fragile fact.** Borrowing: U.S. retail yes, UCITS no (the mirror image of gates). Interfund lending counts as temporary borrowing.

**Reference**

LO 98.d (verbatim): “Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 98, Module 98.3, section “Meeting Unanticipated Redemption Requests”, paragraph “Temporary borrowing”; Key Concepts LO 98.d. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-16 d, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: A matches the source on all three: a short-term buffer, time to sell less liquid assets in an orderly manner, and the four named tools (overdrafts, repos, bank credit facilities, interfund lending).

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attributes the in-kind redemption mechanism (transferring specific assets directly to the redeeming investor, relying on specialized electronic transfer systems) to temporary borrowing. B would be right if the stem asked the analyst to describe in-kind redemptions.

c.reason: **Scope error, absolute claim.** It turns a short-term buffer into a permanent replacement for sales. Schweser’s purpose is to give the fund additional time to sell; the less liquid assets are still sold, only more slowly. C would be right only if the stem described a permanent leverage facility, which is not an extraordinary redemption measure at all.

d.reason: **Sibling swap of jurisdiction.** The first half is correct, but temporary borrowing is not allowed for European UCITS funds. D applies the U.S. retail regime to UCITS. D would be right if the comparison fund were another U.S.-based retail fund.

questions.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-16 d Q3
questions.question: An internal auditor at a fund group that manages both an Irish UCITS equity fund and a U.S.-based mutual fund is reviewing the redemption policies of the two funds. The draft audit report contains four statements about redemption gates. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: A gate halts all redemptions from the fund until the board judges that market conditions have normalized, and it is available to the UCITS fund.
A gate allows partial redemptions up to a predetermined threshold of fund assets, and it is available to the U.S.-based fund but not to the UCITS fund.
A gate allows partial redemptions up to a predetermined threshold of fund assets, and it guarantees that the UCITS fund can never experience a run.
A gate allows partial redemptions up to a predetermined threshold of fund assets, and it is available to the UCITS fund but not to the U.S.-based fund.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor reviews gate statements for an Irish UCITS fund and a U.S.-based mutual fund; which statement is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

A gate is a cap on how much can leave in a given period. Instead of paying every redemption request at once, the fund pays redemptions up to a predetermined threshold, such as 10% of fund assets, and the rest waits. The motivation is the run dynamic: if investors fear that early leavers will get a better deal than late leavers, everyone rushes for the exit. Limiting the pace of outflows can temporarily slow or prevent such a run.

| Element | Schweser content |
|---|---|
| Mechanism | Partial redemptions up to a predetermined threshold (e.g. 10% of fund assets) |
| Effect | Temporarily slows or prevents a run by limiting the pace of outflows |
| UCITS funds (Europe) | Permitted |
| U.S.-based funds | Not allowed (Key Concepts: not for U.S. mutual funds) |

Contrast with suspension: a gate still pays partial redemptions; a suspension halts all of them.

**Applying it to this question**

The auditor sees one UCITS fund and one U.S.-based mutual fund. The deciding facts are the mechanism (partial, up to a threshold), the strength of the claim (slows or prevents, temporarily) and the jurisdiction (UCITS yes, U.S. no).

**Fragile fact.** Gates: UCITS yes, U.S. no; partial redemptions, not a full halt.

**Reference**

LO 98.d (verbatim): “Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 98, Module 98.3, section “Meeting Unanticipated Redemption Requests”, paragraph “Gates”; Key Concepts LO 98.d. Schweser’s body says “U.S.-based funds” while Key Concepts says “U.S. mutual funds”; the stem uses a U.S.-based mutual fund, which satisfies both. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-16 d, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** “Halts all redemptions” is the definition of suspension, the most extreme measure. A gate allows partial redemptions. A would describe suspension if the word “gate” were replaced.

b.reason: **Polarity flip of jurisdiction.** It reverses the regimes: gates are permitted for UCITS and not for U.S.-based funds. B would be right only if the two fund labels were swapped.

c.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** Schweser says a gate can temporarily slow or prevent a run by limiting the pace of outflows; it does not guarantee that a run can never occur. C would be right if “guarantees . . . never” were replaced with “can temporarily slow or prevent”.

d.reason: D gives the correct mechanism and the correct jurisdiction: gates are permitted for UCITS funds in Europe but are not allowed for U.S.-based funds.

questions.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-16 d Q4
questions.question:
A risk consultant is advising a group whose Luxembourg UCITS fund and U.S.-based mutual fund each received unanticipated redemption requests on the same dealing day. Both funds’ offering documents contain a clause for a gate set at 10% of fund assets, and neither fund’s ordinary liquidity tools can meet the requests in full.

| Item | UCITS fund (EUR m) | U.S. fund (USD m) |
|---|---|---|
| Total fund assets | 1600 | 900 |
| Redemption requests received | 260 | 140 |
| Cash and highly liquid assets | 70 | 45 |
| Five-day average redemptions | 18 | 9 |

If each fund applies a gate only where a gate is permitted for that fund, how much of each fund’s requests can be deferred under a gate today?

options.text: UCITS fund EUR 100 million; U.S. fund USD 50 million.
UCITS fund EUR 100 million; U.S. fund USD 0.
UCITS fund EUR 0; U.S. fund USD 50 million.
UCITS fund EUR 234 million; U.S. fund USD 0.

questions.solution:
Consultant to a group with a Luxembourg UCITS fund and a U.S.-based mutual fund, both with 10% gate clauses; how much of each fund’s requests can be deferred today?

**Concept and theory**

A gate permits partial redemptions up to a predetermined threshold expressed as a share of fund assets. The mechanics are:

Gate threshold $= \text{g} \times$ A,

Paid today $= \text{min}($R, g $\times\text{A})$,

Deferred $= \text{R} -$ Paid today,

where g is the gate percentage, A is total fund assets and R is redemption requests received. Two conditions sit in front of the arithmetic. First, the gate must be a measure the fund’s regime permits: gates are permitted for UCITS funds but are not allowed for U.S.-based funds, whatever a document clause says. Second, the base of the threshold is fund assets, not the requests.

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1, permission. UCITS fund: gate permitted. U.S.-based mutual fund: gate not allowed, so nothing can be deferred under a gate.

Step 2, UCITS threshold:

g $\times\text{A} =$ 0.10 × EUR 1,600m = EUR 160m.

Step 3, UCITS payout and deferral:

Paid today $= \text{min}($260, 160) = EUR 160m,

Deferred = 260 − 160 = EUR 100m.

Step 4, U.S. fund: no gate, so deferred under a gate = USD 0. (It must meet the USD 140m through measures it is permitted to use, such as temporary borrowing.)

The cash rows (EUR 70m, USD 45m) and the five-day average redemptions are irrelevant to the gate arithmetic: the threshold depends only on fund assets.

Meaning: the UCITS fund pays EUR 160m today and the remaining EUR 100m waits; the U.S. fund cannot gate at all.

**Fragile fact.** The gate threshold is a percentage of fund assets, and a gate clause is irrelevant for a U.S.-based fund because gates are not allowed there.

**Reference**

LO 98.d (verbatim): “Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 98, Module 98.3, section “Meeting Unanticipated Redemption Requests”, paragraph “Gates”. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-16 d, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error: ignores the jurisdiction condition.** It applies the document clause to the U.S. fund: 0.10 × 900 = 90, deferred 140 − 90 = USD 50m. A would be right if both funds were UCITS funds.

b.reason: B applies the 10% threshold to the UCITS fund’s assets and recognizes that gates are not allowed for U.S.-based funds, so the U.S. deferral is zero.

c.reason: **Polarity flip of jurisdiction.** It gates the U.S. fund (USD 50m, as in A) and treats the UCITS fund as unable to gate. C would be right only if the regimes were reversed.

d.reason: **Wrong input twin: base of the threshold.** It applies 10% to the requests instead of fund assets: paid = 0.10 × 260 = 26, deferred = 260 − 26 = EUR 234m. D would be right only if the gate were defined as 10% of each day’s requests.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a U.S.-based asset manager is reviewing two unanticipated redemption requests from the same fund. The first comes from a large Australian sovereign pension plan that holds 8% of the fund and already receives securities directly through specialized electronic transfer systems. The second is a wave of small requests from thousands of retail investors. Which statement best describes the use of in-kind redemptions here?

options.text: In-kind redemption is permitted, but it is practical mainly for the pension plan and for appropriate asset types, and it spares the fund from selling the holdings that are transferred.
In-kind redemption is permitted, but it is practical mainly for the retail investors, because many small transfers of specific assets are easier to settle than one large transfer.
In-kind redemption is not permitted for this U.S.-based fund, because regulators allow it only for European UCITS funds that redeem large institutional investors.
In-kind redemption is permitted for any asset type and any investor, so the fund can meet both requests this way and will not need any other extraordinary measure.

questions.solution:
Risk analyst at a U.S.-based manager weighs in-kind redemption for a large Australian pension plan versus many retail investors; which statement is best?

**Concept and theory**

An in-kind redemption pays the leaving investor with securities instead of cash. Specific assets are transferred directly to the redeeming investor, so the fund does not have to sell those holdings and does not incur the price impact of selling them. The limits are practical, not legal:

| Element | Schweser content |
|---|---|
| Mechanism | Specific assets transferred directly to the redeeming investor; no need to sell them |
| Asset types | Generally used only for certain asset types |
| Investors | Most common with large institutional investors |
| Why | Relies on specialized electronic transfer systems |
| Regulation | Permitted by regulation (Key Concepts: allowed in both the United States and Europe) |

The investor must be able to receive and hold the securities. A large institution with the right infrastructure can; a retail investor typically cannot.

**Applying it to this question**

The pension plan is large, institutional and already connected to specialized electronic transfer systems: the textbook case. The retail requests are many and small: the case where in-kind is impractical. The fund is U.S.-based, and in-kind redemption is permitted there.

**Fragile fact.** In-kind: legally permitted on both sides of the Atlantic, but practically limited to certain assets and large institutional investors with specialized transfer systems.

**Reference**

LO 98.d (verbatim): “Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 98, Module 98.3, section “Meeting Unanticipated Redemption Requests”, paragraph “In-kind redemptions”; Key Concepts LO 98.d. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-16 d, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: A states that the measure is permitted, that it is practical mainly for the large institutional investor and appropriate assets, and that it spares the fund from selling the transferred holdings, exactly as Schweser describes.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** Right measure, wrong investor. In-kind redemption is most common with large institutional investors because it relies on specialized electronic transfer systems; many small retail transfers are the hard case. B would be right only if the stem said the retail investors, not the pension plan, had the transfer infrastructure.

c.reason: **Scope or jurisdiction error.** In-kind redemption is permitted by regulation and, per Key Concepts, allowed in both the United States and Europe. C wrongly confines it to UCITS funds. C would be right for a measure such as gates, which UCITS funds may use and U.S.-based funds may not.

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** In-kind redemption is generally used only for certain asset types and investors capable of receiving securities directly; it is not universal and does not make other measures unnecessary. D would be right only if every holding were transferable and every investor could receive securities.

questions.question: A member of the board of a Luxembourg UCITS equity fund asks the fund’s CRO how swing pricing protects investors who stay in the fund when large redemptions arrive. Which explanation by the CRO is most accurate?

options.text: The fund adjusts its NAV on every dealing day regardless of the size of net flows, so that transacting investors bear trading costs and the incentive to run on the fund is reduced.
The fund adjusts its NAV when net flows exceed a threshold, so that the remaining shareholders bear trading costs and the incentive to run on the fund is reduced.
The fund adjusts its NAV when net flows exceed a threshold, so that transacting investors bear trading costs and the incentive to run on the fund is reduced.
The fund adjusts its NAV when net flows exceed a threshold, so that no investor bears trading costs and the possibility of a run on the fund is removed.

questions.solution:
Board member of a Luxembourg UCITS equity fund asks how swing pricing protects remaining investors; which CRO explanation is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

When large flows hit a fund, the fund must trade, and trading costs money (spreads, market impact). Without any adjustment, the fund’s NAV absorbs those costs, so the investors who stay pay for the trading caused by those who leave or arrive. That is unfair, and it creates a first-mover advantage: leaving early, before costs pile up, is cheaper than leaving late. That incentive is what fuels a run.

Price mechanisms fix the allocation. Swing pricing adjusts the fund’s NAV when net flows exceed a threshold, so that the costs of trading are absorbed by transacting investors (subscribing or redeeming) rather than by remaining shareholders. By raising the cost of rapid exits, the mechanism reduces the incentive for a run.

| Element | Schweser content |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Net flows exceed a threshold |
| Action | NAV adjusted |
| Who bears trading costs | Transacting (subscribing or redeeming) investors, not remaining shareholders |
| Effect on runs | Raises the cost of rapid exits, reducing the incentive for a run |
| UCITS | Permitted and widely used |

**Applying it to this question**

The fund is UCITS, so swing pricing is available. The board member asks how it protects stayers. Three details decide: the trigger (a threshold on net flows), the cost bearer (transacting investors) and the strength of the effect (reduces the incentive, does not eliminate the possibility).

**Fragile fact.** Costs move to transacting investors and away from remaining shareholders; the trigger is net flows above a threshold.

**Reference**

LO 98.d (verbatim): “Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests, and explain when each measure may be allowed.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 98, Module 98.3, section “Meeting Unanticipated Redemption Requests”, paragraph “Price mechanisms”; Key Concepts LO 98.d. GARP: the GARP text in the project has no matching section for this reading; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-16 d, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** It drops the condition: Schweser says the NAV is adjusted when net flows exceed a threshold, not on every dealing day regardless of flow size. A would be right only for a regime that swings on every flow, which the source does not describe.

b.reason: **Polarity flip, role misassignment.** It assigns the costs to the remaining shareholders, the group the mechanism exists to protect. That is the no-swing outcome. B would describe the situation without swing pricing.

c.reason: C has the threshold trigger, places trading costs on transacting investors, and describes the run effect as a reduced incentive, matching the source.

d.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** Swing pricing reallocates trading costs; it does not make them disappear, and it reduces the incentive to run rather than removing the possibility of a run. D would be right only if “no investor bears” read “transacting investors bear” and “removed” read “reduced”.

questions.question:
A chief compliance officer at a U.S. asset manager oversees three vehicles: a mutual fund regulated by the SEC, a collective trust fund (CTF) under OCC oversight, and a European UCITS fund. She is preparing a summary of price-based mechanisms and considers the following statements:

I. Swing pricing is permitted for, and widely used by, the UCITS fund.

II. Purchase redemption values (PRVs) are allowed for the collective trust fund.

III. The SEC currently allows the mutual fund to apply swing pricing.

IV. PRVs shift transaction costs from transacting investors to remaining shareholders.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
I and II only
II and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
CCO with an SEC mutual fund, an OCC collective trust fund and a UCITS fund audits four statements on price mechanisms; which are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Schweser names two price mechanisms, swing pricing and purchase redemption values (PRVs). Both shift transaction costs to subscribing or redeeming investors, which reduces first-mover incentives. Each is tied to a specific vehicle and regulator:

| Vehicle | Swing pricing | PRV |
|---|---|---|
| European UCITS fund | Permitted and widely used | Not stated in source |
| U.S. collective trust fund (OCC oversight) | Not stated in source | Allowed |
| U.S. mutual fund (SEC) | Not currently allowed by the SEC (under consideration in a rulemaking planned for 2025) | Not stated in source |

**Applying it to this question**

|---|---|

questions.solution:
Portfolio manager at a UCITS fund wants to activate a 10% gate with requests of GBP 132m on assets of GBP 2,400m; which evaluation is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Two layers of “when” govern any extraordinary measure. The general condition: some jurisdictions permit extraordinary measures when ordinary liquidity tools prove insufficient; advance planning and ordinary tools come first. The measure-specific condition for a gate: it allows partial redemptions up to a predetermined threshold of fund assets, so it only restricts payments when requests exceed that threshold.

Gate threshold $= \text{g} \times$ A,

Gate binds if R $> \text{g} \times$ A.

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1, permission: the fund is UCITS, so a gate is permitted.

Step 2, threshold:

g $\times\text{A} =$ 0.10 × GBP 2,400m = GBP 240m.

Step 3, does it bind:

R = GBP 132m \< GBP 240m.

All requests fall within the threshold, so nothing would be deferred.

Step 4, general condition: cash and highly liquid assets of GBP 300m exceed the GBP 132m of requests, so ordinary liquidity tools are sufficient. The less liquid bond holding (GBP 610m) is irrelevant, because no sale of those bonds is required.

Meaning: the gate is permitted but would not bind, and the trigger for extraordinary measures (ordinary tools proving insufficient) is not met.

**Fragile fact.** A gate threshold is a share of fund assets and binds only when requests exceed it; extraordinary measures come in only when ordinary tools prove insufficient.

Which of the following statements should the analyst include in the briefing as most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Redemption risk is the risk that investors ask for their money back in amounts, or at speeds, that the fund cannot meet without harming the investors who stay. Schweser frames the starting point as preparation: a fund must be ready to meet redemption requests under all market conditions. That requires knowing what drives unusually large outflows. The reading lists five drivers:

| Driver | What it means |
|---|---|
| Macroeconomic developments | Economy-wide shocks that lead many investors to withdraw at once |
| Poor fund performance | Investors leave a fund that is underperforming |
| Manager reputation | Deterioration in a manager’s reputation triggers withdrawals |
| Peer fund underperformance | Severe underperformance by peer funds can create contagion risk |
| Fund-specific characteristics | Investor profiles and concentration levels (a few large holders can redeem in size) |

The reading also contrasts regimes. Under normal conditions, redemption demand is typically low before a strategy reaches maturity; stressed markets can produce large and highly correlated redemption requests (many investors leave together, so the requests do not offset each other). Finally, the ultimate objective of redemption management is fairness across three investor categories: those redeeming, those subscribing and those remaining in the fund, all treated fairly and equitably. The intuition, which the wider reading supports, is that more than one group can be disadvantaged: remaining investors if liquidity is created for departing investors in a way that leaves them with an illiquid portfolio (LO 98.a), and transacting investors versus stayers when the costs of trading are not allocated to those who cause them (the price mechanisms of LO 98.d).

| Item | Description |
|---|---|
| I | Absorbing routine or unplanned redemption “noise” while minimizing transaction costs |
| II | Drawing on reverse repos, overdraft facilities or lines of credit |
| III | Selling less liquid holdings so that the remaining portfolio keeps approximately the same risk profile |
| IV | Supporting an investment strategy that uses a derivatives overlay for return enhancement |

Which of the following assignments is correct?

Assigning four liquidity uses and sources to the layers of a ’40 Act fund’s redemption waterfall.

**Concept and theory**

A redemption waterfall, typically used by U.S.-based ’40 Act funds, is a sequence of liquidity layers accessed in order to meet redemption requests. When one layer does not hold enough assets to satisfy demand, the fund moves to the next layer. The order runs from cash, through asset sales, to borrowing as the final option:

| Layer | Content | Purpose or condition |
|---|---|---|
| Layer 1 | Cash and highly liquid assets | Three uses: (i) meeting routine or unplanned redemption “noise” while minimizing transaction costs; (ii) supporting an investment strategy that uses a derivatives overlay for return enhancement; (iii) responding strategically to market conditions |
| Layer 2 | Pro rata or risk-constant asset sales | Used when requests exceed Layer 1; sells less liquid holdings so the remaining portfolio keeps approximately the same risk profile as before |
| Layer 3 | Short-term borrowings | Final option: backup sources such as reverse repos, overdraft facilities or lines of credit; ’40 Act funds may borrow no more than 33.3% of total fund assets |

The point to remember is that Layer 1 is not idle cash: besides absorbing noise it can support a derivatives overlay strategy or a strategic response to market conditions.

**Applying it to this question**

Item I (redemption noise at minimal transaction cost) is the first listed Layer 1 use. Item II (reverse repos, overdrafts, credit lines) is the list of Layer 3 backup sources. Item III (sales that keep the risk profile constant) is the definition of Layer 2. Item IV (derivatives overlay for return enhancement) is the second listed Layer 1 use. The correct mapping is therefore I: 1, II: 3, III: 2, IV: 1.

**Fragile fact.** Layer 1 has three uses, and the derivatives overlay is one of them; borrowing is Layer 3, the last resort, not Layer 2.

**Reference**

To raise the balance quickly, he proposes selling only the fund’s most liquid Treasury and agency holdings, leaving its high-yield and structured holdings untouched. The fund’s risk manager objects to the proposal. Which of the following best explains the risk manager’s objection?

options.text: Sales in the second layer should be pro rata or risk-constant so that the remaining portfolio keeps approximately the same risk profile; selling only the most liquid holdings leaves remaining investors with a less liquid, riskier portfolio.
The fund should draw on short-term borrowing before selling any less liquid holdings, because borrowing is the second layer of the waterfall and asset sales are the final option.
The second layer exists to absorb routine redemption noise at minimal transaction cost, so the most liquid holdings must be held back for that purpose rather than sold to meet large requests.
Pro rata sales are required by the ’40 Act limit of 33.3% of total fund assets, which caps the proportion of any single holding that a fund may sell to meet redemption requests.

**Concept and theory**

Once redemptions exceed the cash and highly liquid assets of Layer 1, a waterfall fund must sell less liquid holdings in Layer 2. Schweser calls this layer “pro rata or risk-constant asset sales” and adds the key condition: care must be taken so that the remaining portfolio maintains approximately the same risk profile as it had before the redemptions.

Why this matters: if a fund meets redemptions by selling only its most liquid assets, departing investors receive cash cheaply and quickly, but the investors who stay are left holding a portfolio that is more concentrated in illiquid and riskier positions. This is exactly the outcome the fairness objective (treat redeeming, subscribing and remaining investors fairly) is designed to prevent. A pro rata sale sells the same fraction of each holding, so portfolio weights, and hence the risk profile, are unchanged; the reading groups pro rata and risk-constant sales together under the single aim of keeping the remaining portfolio’s risk profile approximately the same.

|  | Sell most liquid first | Pro rata or risk-constant |
|---|---|---|
| Cost to redeemers | Low | Higher (less liquid assets sold too) |
| Remaining portfolio | Less liquid, riskier, distorted | Approximately the same risk profile |
| Fairness to stayers | Poor | Preserved |

The proposal sells only Treasuries and agencies, so the remaining portfolio is tilted toward high yield and structured products. The deciding fact is the Layer 2 condition that the remaining portfolio keep approximately the same risk profile.

**Fragile fact.** Layer 2’s condition is about the remaining portfolio: approximately the same risk profile as before the redemptions. The 33.3% figure belongs to Layer 3 borrowing.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a U.S. ’40 Act fund is preparing a report on how the fund’s redemption waterfall would handle an unplanned redemption request of USD 290 million received today. The fund’s data are:

| Item | USD million |
|---|---|
| Total fund assets (before the redemption) | 1,200 |
| Cash and highly liquid assets | 60 |
| Pro rata or risk-constant sale proceeds available in the settlement window | 150 |
| Notional of the fund’s derivatives overlay | 400 |
| Historical redemption-at-risk (99th percentile, five-day) | 240 |

The ’40 Act limit restricts borrowing to no more than 33.3% of total fund assets, measured before the redemption, and the fund has no existing borrowings. Which of the following best describes how the waterfall meets the request?

options.text: Layer 1 USD 60 million, Layer 2 nil, Layer 3 USD 230 million; remaining borrowing headroom about USD 170 million.
Layer 1 nil, Layer 2 USD 150 million, Layer 3 USD 140 million; remaining borrowing headroom about USD 260 million.
Layer 1 USD 60 million, Layer 2 USD 150 million, Layer 3 USD 80 million; remaining borrowing headroom about USD 320 million.
Layer 1 USD 60 million, Layer 2 USD 150 million, Layer 3 USD 80 million; remaining borrowing headroom about USD 17 million.

questions.solution:
Running a USD 290 million redemption through a ’40 Act fund’s waterfall and checking the 33.3% borrowing limit.

**Concept and theory**

The waterfall is sequential: the fund uses Layer 1 (cash and highly liquid assets) first; if that is insufficient it moves to Layer 2 (pro rata or risk-constant sales); only then does it access Layer 3 (short-term borrowing), the final option. For U.S. ’40 Act funds, borrowing is limited to no more than 33.3% of total fund assets. With R the redemption request, $\text{L}_{1}$ the Layer 1 assets, $\text{L}_{2}$ the proceeds available from Layer 2 sales and A total fund assets:

Layer 3 draw $= \text{max}($0, R $- \text{L}_{1} - \text{L}_{2})$

Borrowing limit = 0.333 × A

Remaining headroom = 0.333 $\times\text{A} -$ Layer 3 draw (with no existing borrowings)

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then one step per line (USD million):

Layer 1 used $= \text{min}($290, 60) = 60

Still required after Layer 1 = 290 − 60 = 230

Layer 2 used $= \text{min}($230, 150) = 150

Layer 3 draw = 230 − 150 = 80

Borrowing limit = 0.333 × 1,200 = 399.6

Remaining headroom = 399.6 − 80 = 319.6 ≈ 320

The derivatives overlay notional (USD 400 million) and the HRaR estimate (USD 240 million) are irrelevant to this calculation: the overlay is a use of Layer 1 cash, not an additional source, and HRaR is a stress signal, not a liquidity layer. Meaning: the fund meets the full request, borrowing USD 80 million, and still has about USD 320 million of ’40 Act borrowing capacity.

**Fragile fact.** Order: cash, then pro rata sales, then borrowing. The 33.3% limit is on total fund assets, not on the redemption request.

**Reference**

LO 98.e (Schweser Reading 98, Module 98.3): “Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund, including the redemption waterfall, approaches to model a fund’s level of redemption-at-risk, and approaches to optimize liquidity to meet redemption requests.”

Schweser section: Module 98.3, “Understanding and Managing Redemption Risk”, Layers 1 to 3 and the ’40 Act borrowing limit.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a London-based asset manager is reviewing the redemption stress-testing program of the firm’s EUR-denominated bond fund, which the risk team describes as a natural extension of its redemption modeling. The program documentation contains the following statements:

|  | Statement |
|---|---|
| I | Stress scenarios are applied both to the fund’s assets and to redemption volumes. |
| II | Stress scenarios are applied to the ADV assumptions and to transaction costs. |
| III | The program considers investor concentration, relevant historical redemption events and the potential effects of any gates in place. |
| IV | Stress scenarios can be omitted for share classes whose redemption history shows no meaningful outflows, because their history already demonstrates low redemption risk. |

Which of the statements are consistent with sound redemption stress testing?

options.text: I and II only.
I, II, III and IV.
II and III only.
I, II and III only.

questions.solution:
Auditing four statements in a EUR bond fund’s redemption stress-testing program.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser describes stress testing as a natural extension of redemption modeling. The waterfall and the redemption estimates tell the fund what happens under expected conditions; stress testing asks whether the layers still work when inputs move against the fund at the same time. The reading names what to stress and what else to consider:

| Stress scenarios applied to | Also important to consider |
|---|---|
| Fund assets | Investor concentration |
| Redemption volumes | Relevant historical redemption events |
| ADV assumptions Transaction costs | Potential effects of any gates in place |

Why stress the liquidity inputs as well as the redemption volumes: the reading notes that stressed markets can produce large and highly correlated redemption requests, so the waterfall must be checked in scenarios where the selling side (ADV and transaction costs) is also adverse, not only on normal-market inputs.

**Applying it to this question**

Statements I, II and III restate the reading’s list. Statement IV proposes dropping stress tests where history shows no meaningful outflows. The reading treats the absence of meaningful outflows (new or rapidly growing funds) as a challenge for history-based redemption modeling, which is a reason for stress testing rather than an exemption from it.

**Fragile fact.** Four stressed inputs: assets, redemption volumes, ADV, transaction costs; three further considerations: concentration, historical events, gates. A benign flow history is a weakness to stress, not a reason to skip stress tests.

**Reference**

LO 98.e (Schweser Reading 98, Module 98.3): “Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund, including the redemption waterfall, approaches to model a fund’s level of redemption-at-risk, and approaches to optimize liquidity to meet redemption requests.”

Schweser section: Module 98.3, “Understanding and Managing Redemption Risk”, final paragraph on stress testing; “Modeling Redemption-at-Risk”, first challenge.

A risk analyst at an Australian fund manager is applying the historical redemption-at-risk (HRaR) approach to an AUD 2,400 million fixed-income fund. From the fund’s daily flow history over its 12-year life, the analyst has computed percentiles of rolling net redemptions, expressed as a percentage of net asset value:

| Horizon | 95th percentile (%) | 99th percentile (%) |
|---|---|---|
| One day | 1.1 | 2.0 |
| Five days | 3.5 | 6.0 |
| Twenty days | 8.0 | 12.5 |

The largest single investor holds 9% of the fund’s net asset value. Which of the following best describes the HRaR estimate the analyst should report and how it is used?

options.text: AUD 84 million, used to generate a potential stress signal for the fund’s managers.
AUD 144 million, used to generate a potential stress signal for the fund’s managers.
AUD 144 million, an upper limit that five-day outflows cannot exceed, so further stress testing is unnecessary.
AUD 48 million, used to generate a potential stress signal for the fund’s managers.

questions.solution:
Reading the HRaR estimate for an AUD 2,400 million fund from a table of historical redemption percentiles.

**Concept and theory**

Modeling redemption demand is complex. In an ideal setting analysts would estimate worst-case outflows from historical fund flows. The example Schweser gives is the 99th-percentile, five-day redemption scenario over the life of the fund. This is the basis of the historical redemption-at-risk (HRaR) model, which “generates potential stress signals for fund managers”. In symbols, with $\text{Q}_{0.99}$ the 99th percentile of the distribution of rolling five-day net redemptions (as a fraction of NAV) over the fund’s history:

HRaR $= \text{Q}_{0.99}($five-day net redemptions$) \times$ NAV

Two features matter. First, the percentile and horizon are specific: 99th, five days. Second, the output is a stress signal, not a guaranteed ceiling: the reading immediately lists challenges (short or benign histories, idiosyncratic behavior, poor visibility of end investors) that mean actual outflows can exceed history.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then steps:

HRaR $= \text{Q}_{0.99}(\text{five-day}) \times$ NAV

$\text{Q}_{0.99}(\text{five-day}) =$ 6.0%

HRaR = 0.060 × 2,400 = AUD 144 million

The largest-investor holding (9%) is irrelevant to the HRaR number; concentration matters for stress testing but does not enter the historical percentile. Meaning: on the fund’s own history, a five-day outflow of AUD 144 million is the 1-in-100 case, and the managers should treat it as a signal against which to check Layer 1 cash and Layer 2 capacity.

**Fragile fact.** HRaR example: 99th percentile, five-day, over the life of the fund; it produces a stress signal, not a ceiling.

**Reference**

LO 98.e (Schweser Reading 98, Module 98.3): “Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund, including the redemption waterfall, approaches to model a fund’s level of redemption-at-risk, and approaches to optimize liquidity to meet redemption requests.”

| 5 | A large pension investor’s discretionary need for cash |
| 6 | Regulatory sanctions imposed on the asset manager |

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a Canadian asset manager runs the liquidity optimizer for a CAD multi-asset fund that must raise CAD 200 million from asset sales over the next two trading days (day 1 and day 2). Prices are at par, so notional equals market value. The risk constraint is not binding.

| Security | Sector | Holding (CAD m) | ADV (CAD m) | Bid-ask (bp) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bond K | Investment grade | 300 | 100 | 12 |
| Bond L | Investment grade | 250 | 150 | 9 |
| Bond M | High yield | 120 | 50 | 45 |
| Stock N (IPO stake) | Equity | 90 | 150 | 6 |

| Sector | Participation rate (%) | Sector capacity per day (CAD m) |
|---|---|---|
| Investment grade | 40 | 80 |
| High yield | 20 | 25 |
| Equity | 10 | 60 |

The IPO lockup on Stock N expires at the end of day 3. Applying the ADV, sector capacity and time-lag constraints, which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: At most CAD 220 million can be raised over the two days, so the requirement can be met with CAD 20 million to spare.
At most CAD 210 million can be raised over the two days, so the requirement can be met with CAD 10 million to spare.
At most CAD 90 million can be raised over the two days, so the requirement is missed by CAD 110 million.
At most CAD 180 million can be raised over the two days, so the requirement is missed by CAD 20 million.

questions.solution:
Maximum two-day sale proceeds for a CAD fund under ADV, sector capacity and time-lag constraints.

**Concept and theory**

The optimization approach adds market-based constraints to the daily sale fractions $\text{p}_{\text{i,t}}$. The formulas in Schweser are images that did not survive the text extraction, so the relations below are reconstructed from the reading’s verbal description, which pins down the direction of each constraint:

- **ADV constraint.** Security i has ADV $\text{v}_{\text{i}}$ and belongs to sector j, which has participation rate $\text{r}_{\text{j}}$. The amount of i sold on any day cannot exceed the participation rate times ADV: $\text{p}_{\text{i,t}} \text{n}_{\text{i}} \le\text{r}_{\text{j}} \text{v}_{\text{i}}$.
- **Sector capacity constraint.** Sector $\text{S}_{\text{j}}$ has capacity $\text{c}_{\text{j,t}}$ on day t, because large simultaneous sales of similar fixed-income securities can quickly exhaust the market’s ability to absorb supply: $\sum_{\text{i}\in\text{S}_{\text{j}}} \text{p}_{\text{i,t}} \text{n}_{\text{i}} \le\text{c}_{\text{j,t}}$.
- **Time-lag constraint.** Strategies with fixed time constraints, such as IPO lockups, carry a lag $\text{d}_{\text{i}}$ in days; no sale of i is possible until the lag has elapsed.
- **Liquidation requirement.** Proceeds over the period must reach the required amount v (here CAD 200 million over two days).

The binding constraint for each sector is the tighter of the sum of security-level ADV limits and the sector capacity.

**Applying it to this question**

Daily limits first (CAD million; notional equals market value because prices are at par):

Bond K: $\text{r}_{\text{IG}} \text{v}_{\text{K}} =$ 0.40 × 100 = 40

Bond L: $\text{r}_{\text{IG}} \text{v}_{\text{L}} =$ 0.40 × 150 = 60

Investment grade: min(40 + 60, $\text{c}_{\text{IG}}) = \text{min}($100, 80) = 80

Bond M: min$(\text{r}_{\text{HY}} \text{v}_{\text{M}}$, $\text{c}_{\text{HY}} ) = \text{min}($0.20 × 50, 25$) = \text{min}($10, 25) = 10

Stock N: lockup to end of day 3 ⇒ 0 on days 1 and 2

Maximum per day = 80 + 10 + 0 = 90

Maximum over two days = 2 × 90 = 180

Shortfall = 200 − 180 = 20

Holdings (300, 250, 120) are never binding, and the bid-ask spreads are irrelevant to feasibility (they would matter for the cost objective, not for the constraints). Meaning: the constraints make the CAD 200 million two-day requirement infeasible from asset sales alone; the fund must extend the period, relax a constraint or turn to another waterfall layer.

**Fragile fact.** Participation rate $\text{r}_{\text{j}}$ is set at sector level but multiplies each security’s own ADV $\text{v}_{\text{i}}$; sector capacity $\text{c}_{\text{j,t}}$ then caps the sector’s total; a lockup removes the security until the lag $\text{d}_{\text{i}}$ has passed.

questions.loText: Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-17 c Q1
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Singapore family office is reviewing a commercial database of private equity and hedge fund returns before using it to set return assumptions. She notes four features of the data:

I. Funds are not required to report to the database, and several funds stopped submitting returns after a run of poor performance.

II. Some funds with weak early track records never began reporting to the database.

III. The provider’s long-horizon study includes only funds that operated over the entire 15-year sample, omitting funds that failed.

IV. Funds tend to record the value of portfolio companies mainly when those companies are sold or listed at high valuations.

Which of the features above contribute to survivorship bias in the database’s reported returns?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV
II and III only

questions.solution:
Family office analyst: which of four database features contribute to survivorship bias.

**Concept and theory**

Reported returns in illiquid asset markets are generally overstated, so Schweser tells investors to be skeptical of them. Three main biases do the damage: survivorship bias, sample selection bias and infrequent trading. Each bias works through a different channel, and keeping the channels apart is the key to this LO:

| Bias | What goes wrong in the data | Main effect |
|---|---|---|
| Survivorship | Which funds are in the sample: poor funds drop out or never enter | Reported returns too high |
| Sample selection | When values are recorded: mainly when they are high | Alpha too high; beta and variance too low |
| Infrequent trading | How often prices are observed: rarely | Betas, volatilities and correlations too low |

Survivorship bias exists because certain types of funds (private equity, hedge funds, buyout funds) have no requirement to report returns to database providers. Four routes feed it: (1) poorly performing funds tend to stop reporting; (2) some funds never begin reporting because their returns are not high enough to appeal to investors; (3) many poorly performing funds ultimately fail; and (4) performance studies generally include only funds that survived the whole period of analysis, leaving out funds that no longer exist. Non-surviving funds have below-average returns and surviving funds above-average returns, yet only survivor returns are reported, so reported returns are too high.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each feature against the question “does it change which funds appear in the data?” Feature I (no reporting requirement, funds stop reporting after poor results) is route (1): survivorship. Feature II (weak funds never began reporting) is route (2), which Schweser explicitly files under survivorship bias. Feature III (the study keeps only funds that lasted the full 15 years) is routes (3) and (4): survivorship. Feature IV concerns when values are recorded (at sale or listing, at high valuations): that is sample selection bias, not survivorship.

**Fragile fact.** “Never began reporting” is survivorship bias in Schweser, not selection bias; selection bias is about when prices are recorded (when high), survivorship about which funds stay in the sample.

**Reference**

LO 99.c (verbatim): “Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, section “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Survivorship Bias”; Key Concepts LO 99.c point 1; Module Quiz 99.1 Q3. GARP text in the project has no matching section (no Illiquid Assets chapter); content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 c, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error.** It drops feature II. Funds that never begin reporting because returns are weak are, in Schweser’s words, part of the reporting problem that “is called survivorship bias”. A would be correct only if feature II described something else, for example funds that never reported because they were closed to new investors regardless of performance.

b.reason: Features I, II and III are the three survivorship routes Schweser lists (stop reporting, never begin reporting, failure with survivor-only studies). Feature IV is Schweser’s description of sample selection bias (“asset values and returns tend to be reported when they are high”). So the answer is I, II and III only.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It adds feature IV, attributing sample selection bias to survivorship. C would be correct if the question asked which features contribute to overstated reported returns in general, because selection bias also overstates returns.

d.reason: **Scope error.** It leaves out feature I, the textbook survivorship case: funds without a reporting requirement that stop reporting after poor performance (Schweser’s own module quiz uses a fund that quits reporting after poor returns as its survivorship example). D would be correct only if feature I described funds that stopped reporting for reasons unrelated to performance.

questions.question:
An investment analyst at an Australian superannuation fund is checking a vendor’s performance figure for the 2016 vintage of private equity funds. The vendor’s figure is the equally weighted average return of the funds that reported through the end of the period. Because the superannuation fund is a limited partner in all six funds of the vintage, the analyst has the returns of every fund from its own records:

| Fund | Commitment (AUD m) | Annualized return (%) | Status in vendor database |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 | 120 | 14.0 | Reporting |
| F2 | 85 | 11.0 | Reporting |
| F3 | 200 | 9.0 | Reporting |
| F4 | 60 | 2.0 | Stopped reporting in 2021 |
| F5 | 45 | −6.0 | Liquidated in 2022 |
| F6 | 150 | −3.0 | Never submitted returns |

Using equal weights, by how much does the vendor’s figure overstate the average return of the full 2016 vintage?

options.text: 4.50 percentage points
5.33 percentage points
6.83 percentage points
13.67 percentage points

questions.solution:
Superannuation analyst: overstatement of a vintage average by a vendor figure that keeps only reporting funds.

**Concept and theory**

Survivorship bias is a missing-data problem. If the funds that drop out (stop reporting, fail) or never enter (never begin reporting) have below-average returns, an average computed only over the funds still reporting is too high. The size of the bias is the gap between the survivor average and the full-universe average. With S the set of surviving (reporting) funds, U the full universe of funds in the vintage, $\text{n}_{\text{S}} \text{and n}_{\text{U}}$ their counts and $\text{r}_{\text{i}}$ the return of fund i:

$\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{S}} = \frac{1}{\text{n}_{\text{S}}} \sum_{\text{i}\in\text{S}} \text{r}_{\text{i}}$, $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{U}} = \frac{1}{\text{n}_{\text{U}}} \sum_{\text{i}\in\text{U}} \text{r}_{\text{i}}$,

Survivorship bias = $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{S}} -$ $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{U}}$ .

Schweser stresses that the obvious cure, observing the entire universe of funds, is impossible in illiquid asset markets. This question is the rare case where an investor can do it, because a limited partner in every fund knows every fund’s return.

**Applying it to this question**

Survivors (still reporting): F1, F2, F3. Non-survivors: F4 (stopped reporting), F5 (liquidated) and F6 (never submitted). All six belong to the 2016 vintage. Equal weights are specified, so the commitment column is irrelevant.

$\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{S}} = \frac{14.0 + 11.0 + 9.0}{3} = \frac{34.0}{3} =$ 11.33%

$\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{U}} = \frac{14.0 + 11.0 + 9.0 + 2.0 - 6.0 - 3.0}{6} = \frac{27.0}{6} =$ 4.50%

Bias = 11.33% − 4.50% = 6.83 percentage points

Meaning: the vendor’s figure overstates the vintage’s true average return by about 6.8 percentage points, because the three funds missing from the database averaged −2.33%.

**Fragile fact.** The benchmark is the whole universe (survivors plus all non-survivors, including funds that never reported), and the bias is positive: the reported figure is too high.

**Reference**

LO 99.c (verbatim): “Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, section “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Survivorship Bias”. GARP text in the project has no matching section (no Illiquid Assets chapter); content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 c, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: This is $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{U}}$, the full-vintage average itself, not the overstatement. A would be correct if the question asked for the true average return of the vintage.

b.reason: This drops F6 from the universe on the reasoning that a fund that never submitted returns was never “in” the database: $\bar{\text{r}}^{'}_{\text{U}} = ($14 + 11 + 9 + 2 − 6)/5 = 30/5 = 6.00% and 11.33 − 6.00 = 5.33. Schweser counts funds that never begin reporting as part of survivorship bias, so they belong in the benchmark. B would be correct if the question asked for the bias relative to funds that ever appeared in the database.

c.reason: C is the survivor average minus the full-universe average, with the full universe including funds that stopped reporting, failed and never began reporting, exactly the three routes Schweser lists for survivorship bias.

d.reason: This is the survivor average minus the non-survivor average: $\bar{\text{r}}_{\text{NS}} = ($2 − 6 − 3)/3 = −2.33%, and 11.33 − (−2.33) = 13.67. It measures the gap between the two groups, not the bias in the reported average. D would be correct if the question asked how much better the surviving funds did than the missing ones.

questions.question: The chief risk officer of a Canadian university endowment is drafting a note for the investment committee on how survivorship bias affects the reported returns it uses for alternative investments. Which of the following statements is most accurate for inclusion in the note?

options.text: Studies show that mutual fund returns are about 1% to 2% lower than reported, and that the shortfall may be as much as 4% in illiquid asset markets.
Studies show that mutual fund returns are about 4% lower than reported, and that the shortfall is only 1% to 2% in illiquid asset markets because those funds report less often.
Studies show that true returns in illiquid asset markets exceed reported returns by as much as 4%, because the funds that stop reporting are mostly the strongest performers.
Survivorship bias in illiquid asset markets is readily eliminated in practice by observing the entire universe of funds, including those that failed or never reported.

questions.solution:
Endowment CRO: most accurate statement on the size of survivorship bias and whether it can be removed.

**Concept and theory**

Survivorship bias arises because funds without a reporting requirement drop out of databases when performance is poor, never begin reporting when returns are weak, or fail; studies of the survivors then overstate returns. Schweser gives two quantitative markers: studies show mutual fund returns are 1% to 2% lower than reported, and returns may be as much as 4% lower for illiquid asset markets.

Schweser also addresses the remedy. The solution “seems obvious” (observe the entire universe of funds), but it is impossible to do in illiquid asset markets, because the funds that never report or that disappear cannot be observed. So the bias can be removed in principle, not in practice.

| Market | True return below reported return by |
|---|---|
| Mutual funds | about 1% to 2% |
| Illiquid asset markets | as much as 4% (and the full universe cannot be observed) |

**Applying it to this question**

The CRO needs a statement that has the right direction (reported returns too high), the right magnitudes attached to the right markets, and a realistic view of the remedy. Only A has all three.

**Fragile fact.** 4% belongs to illiquid asset markets, 1% to 2% to mutual funds, and both are amounts by which true returns fall below reported returns.

**Reference**

LO 99.c (verbatim): “Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, section “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Survivorship Bias”. GARP text in the project has no matching section (no Illiquid Assets chapter); content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 c, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: It reproduces Schweser’s evidence: mutual fund returns 1% to 2% lower than reported, and as much as 4% lower in illiquid asset markets.

b.reason: **Sibling swap of magnitudes.** It swaps the two figures, giving 4% to mutual funds and 1% to 2% to illiquid markets, and invents a reason. B would be correct only if the markets were labeled the other way round.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the direction of the mechanism. The funds that stop reporting are poor performers, so true returns are below reported returns, not above. C would be correct only if strong performers, rather than poor ones, were the funds leaving the sample, which is the reverse of the Schweser mechanism.

questions.question:
A credit risk analyst at a Canadian bank uses a regional house-price return index, built only from completed sales, to track the value of residential mortgage collateral. For the most recent downturn year she gathers the following:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Reported index return (%) | −1.5 |
| Change in number of completed sales versus prior year (%) | −55.0 |
| Average five-year mortgage rate (%) | 6.2 |

Local agents report that most owners kept their homes off the market until prices recovered. Which assessment of the reported −1.5% return is most accurate?

options.text: It is likely to overstate the true return because of survivorship bias, as the properties of owners who default are dropped from the index.
It is likely to understate the true return because of sample selection bias, as the few sales in a downturn are mostly distressed sales at low prices.
It is likely to be an unbiased estimate of the true return, because infrequent trading distorts only the volatility and correlations of the index.
It is likely to overstate the true return because of sample selection bias, as sales, and so recorded prices, are concentrated among properties whose values are high.

questions.solution:
Bank credit analyst: whether a sales-based house-price index overstates or understates the downturn-year return.

**Concept and theory**

Sample selection bias arises because asset values and returns tend to be reported when they are high. For illiquid real assets, a price is only observed when a sale happens, and the decision to sell is not random: houses and office buildings are typically sold when values are high, and a seller will often wait until property values recover before selling. Those higher selling prices are then used to calculate returns. The observed sample is therefore tilted toward high-value outcomes, so reported returns overstate true returns and, as Schweser adds, reported risk (beta and variance) is understated.

The mechanism differs from survivorship bias (which funds remain in a database) and from infrequent trading (how often prices are observed, which mutes measured risk). Here the issue is which prices get recorded.

**Applying it to this question**

The index uses only completed sales. In the downturn year, sales fell 55%, and agents report owners held homes off the market until prices recovered. So the properties that did sell are disproportionately ones whose values held up, and the falls on the unsold properties are never recorded. The reported −1.5% is therefore likely to be higher than the true change in collateral values: the true decline is probably deeper. The mortgage rate of 6.2% is irrelevant to the direction of the bias.

**Fragile fact.** Selection bias pushes reported returns up: sellers wait for recovery, so the prices that get recorded are the high ones.

**Reference**

LO 99.c (verbatim): “Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, section “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Sample Selection Bias”; Key Concepts LO 99.c point 2. GARP text in the project has no matching section (no Illiquid Assets chapter); content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 c, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attributes the problem to survivorship bias. Survivorship bias concerns funds that stop reporting, never report or fail, so that only survivors enter performance studies. A would be correct if the index were an average of fund returns from which failed funds had been removed.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** It assumes the downturn sales are distressed sales at low prices, so the index understates returns. Schweser’s mechanism is the opposite: owners wait for values to recover before selling, so recorded prices are high. B would be correct only if owners were forced to sell at depressed prices, which the stem rules out.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** It treats infrequent trading as the only issue and concludes the return is unbiased. Infrequent trading does mute measured risk, but the stem describes a selection mechanism that biases the recorded prices themselves. C would be correct only if sales were a random draw of properties rather than chosen by owners waiting for recovery.

d.reason: D names the right bias (sample selection), the right direction (reported return overstates the true return) and Schweser’s mechanism (sellers wait for recovery, so recorded prices are high).
