questions.question: A risk consultant advising a Chinese insurer on a CNY 2 billion venture capital allocation receives a vendor’s capital asset pricing model estimates for the venture capital asset class. The vendor computed log returns only at exit events (initial public offerings and trade sales), which occur mainly when valuations are high, and reports an annual alpha of 28% and a beta of 0.6. Which of the following best describes the likely bias in these estimates relative to the true values?

options.text: Alpha and beta are both overstated, because high recorded prices raise both the measured excess return and the measured co-movement with the market.
Alpha is overstated, while beta and return variance are understated; the bias flattens the security market line relative to the true one.
Alpha is unbiased because it is measured relative to the market, while beta and return variance are understated, flattening the security market line.
Alpha is overstated, while beta and return variance are understated; the bias steepens the security market line relative to the true one.

When returns are only observed at exits that occur mainly when valuations are high, the sample omits the low-value outcomes. Schweser lists three impacts of this sample selection bias:

| Estimate | Reported versus true | Schweser’s reason |
|---|---|---|
| Alpha | Higher | Only high prices are recorded |
| Beta | Lower | Fewer (only high) prices recorded; flattens the SML |
| Variance of returns | Lower | Only high returns are counted (risk underestimated) |

In sum, sample selection bias overestimates expected returns and underestimates risk, whether risk is measured by beta or by standard deviation. Schweser’s evidence: one study finds a venture capital alpha of more than 90% on log returns, falling to −7% after correction.

The security market line (SML) plots expected return against beta. Intuition (an explanatory gloss): if the data assign high returns to assets whose betas look low, the risk-return relationship estimated from those data is flatter than the true one; Schweser states that the lower reported betas flatten the SML.

**Applying it to this question**

The vendor computed returns only at IPOs and trade sales, which occur mainly at high valuations: a textbook sample selection setting (Schweser notes that buyout funds take companies public when prices are high and venture capitalists sell companies when values are high). So the 28% alpha is likely too high, the 0.6 beta is likely too low, and the variance is likely too low. The allocation size (CNY 2 billion) does not affect the direction of the bias.

**Fragile fact.** Selection bias: alpha up, beta down, variance down, SML flatter.

**Reference**

GARP text in the project has no matching section (no Illiquid Assets chapter); content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 c, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip on beta.** It says beta is overstated. Schweser says reported betas are lower than true betas because only high prices are recorded. A would be correct for alpha alone.

b.reason: B states all three Schweser impacts (alpha up, beta and variance down) and the SML consequence (flattened).

c.reason: **Scope error.** It claims alpha is unbiased. Schweser’s first impact is “higher reported alphas relative to true alphas”; measuring alpha relative to the market does not protect it, because the missing low-value observations are exactly what pushes alpha up. C would be correct if the question asked only about beta and variance.

questions.question:
A member of the risk committee of a Dutch pension fund is reviewing a consultant’s memo on sample selection bias in private equity returns. The memo contains the following statements:

I. One study estimates a venture capital alpha of more than 90% using log returns, which falls to about −7% after correcting for sample selection bias.

II. Another study estimates that correcting for sample selection bias decreases returns by 2% to 5% per month.

III. Because only high returns are counted, sample selection bias raises the reported variance of returns relative to the true variance.

IV. Sample selection bias is especially prevalent in private equity because buyout funds tend to take companies public when stock prices are low.

Which of the statements in the memo are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
I only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Pension risk committee: which statements on sample selection bias in a consultant’s memo are correct.

**Concept and theory**

Sample selection bias is especially prevalent in private equity. Exits are chosen by the general partner: buyout funds take companies public when stock prices are high, and venture capitalists sell companies when values are high. Distressed companies are often not liquidated and are left as shell (“zombie”) companies, whose status is hard to judge from old data. Because returns are recorded mainly at high values, the bias raises reported alpha and lowers reported beta and variance.

Schweser’s quantitative evidence:

| Study | Before correction | After correction |
|---|---|---|
| Venture capital, log returns | Alpha above 90% | Alpha about −7% |
| Second study | Reported returns | Returns decreased by 2% to 5% per month |

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I matches the first study (alpha above 90% falls to −7%): correct. Statement II matches the second (correction decreases returns by 2% to 5% per month): correct. Statement III says variance is raised: Schweser says “lower reported variance of returns than the true variance” because only high returns are counted, so III is wrong. Statement IV says buyout funds list companies when prices are low: Schweser says they do so when prices are high, so IV is wrong.

**Fragile fact.** Correcting for selection bias decreases returns (2% to 5% per month), and the bias lowers reported variance; exits happen when prices are high.

**Reference**

LO 99.c (verbatim): “Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, section “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Sample Selection Bias”. GARP text in the project has no matching section (no Illiquid Assets chapter); content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 c, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: Only I and II reproduce Schweser’s statements with the correct direction and numbers.

b.reason: **Includes III, polarity flip.** III reverses the variance effect. Counting only high returns removes the low tail of the distribution, so reported variance is lower than true variance (risk is underestimated). B would be correct if III said “lowers”.

c.reason: **Rejects II, polarity flip.** It treats statement II as false, which happens if the reader expects the correction to raise returns. Correcting for selection bias allows for the low-value outcomes that the recorded data omit, so the corrected returns are lower; Schweser says they decrease by 2% to 5% per month. C would be correct if II said that the correction increases returns.

d.reason: **Includes IV, polarity flip.** I and II are right, but IV is wrong for the reason above. Note that IV’s conclusion (selection bias is especially prevalent in private equity) is true; it is the reason that is flipped. D would be correct if IV said “when stock prices are high”.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a Singapore insurer receives the following ten-year statistics for an SGD core real estate fund, computed from its quarterly appraisal-based returns:

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean annual return (%) | 7.80 |
| Annualized volatility (%) | 4.10 |
| Beta to the listed equity index | 0.18 |
| Correlation with the listed equity index | 0.12 |
| Average portfolio occupancy (%) | 94.00 |

Which assessment of these statistics is most accurate?

options.text: The true volatility is likely above 4.10%, but the beta and correlation are reliable, because infrequent trading distorts dispersion and not co-movement.
The true volatility, beta and correlation are all likely above the reported values, because infrequent trading makes risk measures from reported returns too low.
The reported risk measures are reliable, because quarterly appraisals are frequent enough; the infrequent trading bias arises only with less than annual valuation.
The true volatility is likely below 4.10%, because quarterly appraisal revisions add noise that daily transaction prices of the same assets would average away.

questions.solution:
Singapore insurer analyst: assessing volatility, beta and correlation computed from quarterly appraisal returns.

**Concept and theory**

Illiquid assets, by definition, trade infrequently, and infrequent trading results in underestimated risk. Reported returns of infrequently traded assets are smoothed: values move only when an appraisal or transaction updates them. Schweser’s comparison: quarterly returns of an asset appear (and are) less volatile than its daily returns, so the computed standard deviation is often lower; prices will often have been higher or lower within the horizon than the quarterly figures show. Because measured volatility is muted, betas and correlations with other asset classes (for example, large-cap stocks) are also artificially low.

| Risk measure from reported returns | Bias | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Volatility (standard deviation) | Too low | Total risk understated |
| Beta | Too low | Systematic risk understated |
| Correlation with liquid assets | Too low | Diversification looks better than it is |

(How to undo this, unsmoothing, belongs to LO 99.d and is not tested here.)

**Applying it to this question**

The statistics come from quarterly appraisal-based returns, the setting of Schweser’s quarterly versus daily comparison. The reported volatility (4.10%), beta (0.18) and correlation (0.12) are therefore all likely to be below their true values. Occupancy (94%) is irrelevant, and the mean return is not what the options assess.

**Fragile fact.** Infrequent trading biases all three risk measures downward: volatility, beta and correlation.

**Reference**

LO 99.c (verbatim): “Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, section “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Infrequent Trading”; Key Concepts LO 99.c point 3. GARP text in the project has no matching section (no Illiquid Assets chapter); content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 c, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error.** It confines the bias to dispersion. Schweser lists betas and correlations as well as volatility, and says correlations with liquid assets are artificially low precisely because volatility is muted. A would be correct only for the volatility half of the statement.

b.reason: It states Schweser’s result in full: “betas, return volatilities, and correlations are too low when they are computed using the reported returns of infrequently traded assets.”

c.reason: **Condition error.** It invents a frequency threshold. Schweser’s own illustration shows that quarterly returns are already less volatile than daily returns, so quarterly appraisal does not remove the bias. C would be correct only if the assets were valued from daily market prices.

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** It reverses the direction: smoothed, infrequent valuations reduce measured volatility; daily prices would reveal more variation, not less. D would be correct if the reported series were noisier than the true one.

questions.question:
The chief investment officer of a Brazilian pension fund reviews three data issues raised by internal audit in the BRL-denominated alternatives program:

I. A hedge fund database’s ten-year average return is computed only from funds that were still operating and reporting at the end of the decade.

II. A venture capital index records a return for a portfolio company only when it is listed or sold, and such exits cluster in years of high valuations.

III. A timberland index, valued by annual appraisal, shows a correlation of only 0.05 with listed equities.

Which of the following correctly matches each issue with the bias it creates and its main effect?

options.text: I: survivorship, returns overstated; II: sample selection, alpha overstated and beta understated; III: infrequent trading, correlation understated.
I: sample selection, returns overstated; II: survivorship, alpha overstated and beta understated; III: infrequent trading, correlation understated.
I: survivorship, returns overstated; II: infrequent trading, alpha overstated and beta understated; III: sample selection, correlation understated.

**Concept and theory**

Diagnosing a data issue means asking what has gone wrong with the sample:

| Signal in the data | Bias | Schweser’s stated effect |
|---|---|---|
| Funds missing because they stopped reporting, never reported or failed | Survivorship | Reported returns too high |
| Prices recorded mainly when values are high (sales, exits) | Sample selection | Alpha too high; beta and variance too low |
| Values updated rarely (appraisals) | Infrequent trading | Betas, volatilities, correlations too low |

**Applying it to this question**

Issue I: only funds still operating and reporting at the end of the decade are averaged, which is survivorship bias, so returns are overstated. Issue II: returns are recorded only at listing or sale, and exits cluster at high valuations, which is sample selection bias, so alpha is overstated and beta understated. Issue III: annual appraisals produce smoothed values, which is infrequent trading, so the 0.05 correlation with equities is artificially low.

**Fragile fact.** Survivorship acts on which funds, selection on which prices, infrequent trading on how often; the last two both push measured risk down.

LO 99.c (verbatim): “Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, section “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsections “Survivorship Bias”, “Sample Selection Bias” and “Infrequent Trading”. GARP text in the project has no matching section (no Illiquid Assets chapter); content from Schweser, a condensed source.

Infrequent trading is about how often values are observed, selection bias about which (high) values are recorded. C would be correct if issue II described stale appraisals and issue III described exits at high prices.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a UK insurer is reviewing a manager’s pitch for a private real estate fund. The pitch reports the figures below, computed from the fund universe’s reported returns:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Reported mean annual return (%) | 11.0 |
| Reported annualized volatility (%) | 7.0 |
| Risk-free rate (%) | 2.0 |
| Fund assets under management (GBP m) | 850.0 |

The insurer’s risk team estimates that survivorship bias overstates the reported mean return by 3.0 percentage points, and that the true annualized volatility, once the effect of stale appraisals is removed, is 14.0%. What is the fund’s Sharpe ratio after both corrections?
questions.solution:
UK insurer analyst: Sharpe ratio of a private real estate fund after correcting reported return and volatility.

**Concept and theory**

The biases in this LO hit a risk-adjusted measure from both sides. Survivorship (and selection) bias inflates the reported mean return; infrequent trading deflates the reported volatility. The Sharpe ratio divides excess return by volatility:

SR $= \frac{\bar{R}_{\text{P}} - \text{R}_{\text{F}}}{\sigma_{\text{P}}}$ ,

where $\bar{\text{R}}_{\text{P}}$ is the mean portfolio return, $\text{R}_{\text{F}}$ the risk-free rate and $\sigma_{\text{P}}$ the standard deviation of returns. An overstated numerator and an understated denominator both push the reported Sharpe ratio up, so reported risk-adjusted performance of illiquid assets is overstated twice over.

**Applying it to this question**

Reported Sharpe ratio (for comparison):

$\text{SR}_{\text{rep}} = \frac{11.0 - 2.0}{7.0} = \frac{9.0}{7.0} =$ 1.29

Correct the return for survivorship bias:

$\bar{\text{R}}^{\text{adj}}_{\text{P}} =$ 11.0% − 3.0% = 8.0%

Corrected excess return:

$\bar{\text{R}}^{\text{adj}}_{\text{P}} - \text{R}_{\text{F}} =$ 8.0% − 2.0% = 6.0%

Divide by the corrected volatility:

$\text{SR}_{\text{adj}} = \frac{6.0}{14.0} =$ 0.43

Meaning: the fund’s risk-adjusted performance is about one third of what the pitch implies (0.43/1.29 ≈ 0.33). The AUM figure (GBP 850 million) is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Both biases push the reported Sharpe ratio up: returns too high in the numerator, volatility too low in the denominator.

**Reference**

LO 99.c (verbatim): “Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, section “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, introduction and subsections “Survivorship Bias” and “Infrequent Trading”. GARP text in the project has no matching section (no Illiquid Assets chapter); content from Schweser, a condensed source. The Sharpe ratio definition is from GARP RMIM Chapter 8, Portfolio Performance Evaluation, section “Risk-Adjusted Performance Measures” (garp\_rmim.txt lines 10300 to 10352), used only for the formula.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 c, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: (11.0 − 3.0 − 2.0)/7.0 = 6.0/7.0 = 0.86. It fixes the return but keeps the smoothed 7.0% volatility. A would be correct if volatility had been measured from frequently traded prices.

b.reason: (11.0 − 2.0)/14.0 = 9.0/14.0 = 0.64. It fixes volatility but keeps the survivorship-inflated mean. B would be correct if the return data covered the full fund universe.

c.reason: (11.0 − 3.0)/14.0 = 8.0/14.0 = 0.57. It divides the total return, not the excess return, by volatility. C would be correct if the risk-free rate were zero.

d.reason: D applies both corrections: the return correction for survivorship bias (reported returns too high) and the risk correction for infrequent trading (reported volatility too low).

questions.question: A due diligence analyst at a US university endowment is reviewing the reported net asset value of a USD venture capital fund. Of the fund’s 22 portfolio companies, 9 have had no financing round, sale or other transaction for more than five years and are still carried at their last-round valuations. Several of these 9 are known to be distressed but have not been liquidated. Which assessment of the fund’s reported returns is most accurate?

options.text: They are likely understated, because last-round valuations lag current values, which venture funds realize only when they sell at high prices.
They are likely overstated because of survivorship bias, since distressed companies that are liquidated are dropped from the fund’s records.
They are likely overstated because of sample selection bias, since distressed companies left as shells cannot be told apart from live ones using old data.
They are likely unbiased, because infrequent trading affects only risk estimates and the fund’s net asset value includes all 22 companies.

questions.solution:
Endowment due diligence: venture fund with many companies carried at stale last-round values, some distressed but not liquidated.

**Concept and theory**

Within sample selection bias, Schweser highlights a private equity feature: distressed companies are often not liquidated but left as shell companies, sometimes called zombie companies. Because nothing trades, it is difficult to tell, from old data without any recent transactions, whether a company is alive or a zombie. Combined with the tendency of venture capitalists to sell companies when values are high and of buyout funds to list companies when prices are high, the recorded values skew high and the low outcomes stay unrecorded. The net effect, as for all sample selection bias, is overestimated returns and underestimated risk.

Distinguish this from survivorship bias: survivorship bias drops funds (or, in studies, non-surviving entities) from the data. Zombies are not dropped; they stay in the portfolio at values that no recent transaction has tested.

**Applying it to this question**

Nine of 22 companies have had no transaction for five years and sit at last-round valuations; several are distressed but not liquidated. That is the zombie problem: the old marks cannot reveal which of the nine are alive. The fund’s reported returns are therefore likely overstated through sample selection bias.

**Fragile fact.** Zombie companies sit under sample selection bias, not survivorship: they are not liquidated, and they stay in the data at untested values.

**Reference**

LO 99.c (verbatim): “Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, section “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Sample Selection Bias” (zombie companies). GARP text in the project has no matching section (no Illiquid Assets chapter); content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 c, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** It says the stale marks understate returns. Schweser’s mechanism points the other way: distressed companies carried at old values, and exits taken only when values are high, push reported values up. A would be correct only if the stale companies were known to be thriving and marked conservatively.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It attributes the problem to survivorship bias through liquidated companies that are dropped, yet the stem says the distressed companies have not been liquidated. B would be correct if the fund had written off and removed failed companies from its reported track record.

c.reason: C names sample selection bias, the right direction (overstated) and Schweser’s zombie mechanism (shell companies cannot be told apart from live ones using old data without recent transactions).

d.reason: **Scope error.** It reasons only from infrequent trading (which Schweser links to understated risk) and ignores the selection mechanism that biases the values themselves. questions.loText: Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-17 c Q12
questions.question:
A model validation analyst at a Swiss private bank is reviewing a model that estimates the CHF beta of the bank’s illiquid holdings by regressing their reported returns on a listed equity index. She considers three biases in the reported returns:

I. Survivorship bias

II. Sample selection bias

III. Infrequent trading

Which of these biases, acting alone, would cause the beta estimated from reported returns to be lower than the true beta?

options.text: III only
I and III only
I, II and III
II and III only

questions.solution:
Swiss bank model validator: which biases, acting alone, lower the beta estimated from reported returns.

**Concept and theory**

The three biases do not all act on the same statistic. Schweser’s stated effects:

| Bias | Effect on returns | Effect on beta |
|---|---|---|
| Survivorship | Reported returns too high | None stated |
| Sample selection | Alpha (expected return) too high | Reported beta lower than true beta |
| Infrequent trading | Not its stated channel | Betas too low (with volatility and correlation) |

Selection bias lowers beta because only high prices are recorded (fewer observations, flattening the SML). Infrequent trading lowers beta because smoothed returns mute measured co-movement with liquid markets. Survivorship bias, in Schweser, is a return-level problem: missing poor funds make reported returns too high.

**Applying it to this question**

The validator regresses reported returns on a listed index. Bias II records mainly high prices and lowers the estimated beta. Bias III smooths reported returns and lowers the estimated beta. Bias I removes poor performers and raises the average return, but Schweser attaches no beta effect to it.

**Fragile fact.** Two of the three biases lower beta: selection and infrequent trading; survivorship’s stated effect is on returns.

**Reference**

LO 99.c (verbatim): “Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, section “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsections “Sample Selection Bias” and “Infrequent Trading”. GARP text in the project has no matching section (no Illiquid Assets chapter); content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 c, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: **Scope error.** III only leaves out selection bias, whose second listed impact is a lower reported beta. A would be correct if the question asked only about biases that arise from stale or smoothed prices.

b.reason: **Sibling swap.** It substitutes survivorship bias for selection bias. B would be correct if survivorship bias, rather than selection bias, were the bias that records only high prices.

c.reason: **Absolute claim.** It assumes every bias lowers beta. Survivorship bias acts on the level of reported returns. C would be correct if the question asked which biases make reported illiquid asset performance look better than it is.

d.reason: Schweser lists “lower reported betas than true betas” under sample selection bias and “betas . . . are too low” under infrequent trading. Those are II and III.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-17 d Q1
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Canadian public pension plan is presenting to newly hired analysts on how the plan prepares the appraisal-based quarterly returns of its CAD 14 billion private real estate portfolio before they enter the plan’s risk models. One step in the process is labelled “unsmoothing”. Which of the following statements best describes that step?

options.text: It applies a filtering algorithm that strips noise out of the reported returns, so the cleaned series is smoother and its estimated volatility is lower than that of the reported series.
It runs a filtering algorithm in the opposite direction to its usual purpose, adding noise back to the reported returns to uncover the true, noisier returns, which raises the risk estimates.
It adds back the returns of funds and properties that dropped out of the reporting database, so the series covers the full universe and its average reported return falls.
It adds noise back to the reported returns, but the adjustment is confined to the volatility estimate, so the returns reported for individual quarters are left unchanged.

questions.solution:
Pension plan analyst presenting to new hires: what the “unsmoothing” step does to appraisal-based quarterly real estate returns.

**Concept and theory**

Illiquid assets, by definition, trade infrequently. When an asset is not traded, its reported value is an appraisal or a stale price, and the return computed from those values moves less than the underlying value really does. Schweser’s illustration: if you compare quarterly returns with the daily returns of the same asset, the quarterly returns appear (and are) less volatile, and the price within the horizon will often have been higher or lower than the quarterly figures suggest. The reported series is therefore smoothed: it understates volatility, beta and correlation with other asset classes.

Unsmoothing (also called de-smoothing) is the correction. Schweser describes it through the language of filtering:

|  | What it does to a series |
|---|---|
| Ordinary filtering | Removes noise from a signal, leaving a cleaner, smoother series. |
| Unsmoothing | Uses filtering algorithms the other way: adds noise back to the reported returns to uncover the true, noisier returns. |

The point of the reversal is that the smooth look of the reported data is itself the distortion. The true returns are noisier, so recovering them must increase measured dispersion. Schweser adds that unsmoothing affects both risk and return estimates and can have a dramatic effect on returns.

**Applying it to this question**

The plan’s input is appraisal-based quarterly returns: exactly the infrequently traded, smoothed data the procedure is built for. The question asks what the step does. Two facts decide it: the direction (noise is added back, not removed) and the breadth (both risk and return estimates change). Only one option has both right.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: unsmoothing adds noise back (ordinary filtering removes it), so volatility, beta and correlation go up, and individual period returns can change sharply.

**Reference**

LO 99.d (verbatim): “Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Infrequent Trading”. Schweser Key Concepts LO 99.d. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 d, where it is Q1 of 10.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** A describes ordinary filtering, which removes noise. Reversing “adds” to “strips out” flips every consequence: a smoother series and lower volatility. A would be correct if the stem asked what a standard noise filter does to a signal, not what unsmoothing does to smoothed returns.

b.reason: B states the source process exactly: filtering algorithms, used in reverse of their usual noise-removing purpose, add noise back to the reported returns to uncover the true, noisier returns, so risk estimates rise. This matches Schweser: “unsmoothing adds noise back to reported returns to uncover the true, noisier returns.”

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Adding back funds that left the database is the remedy one would want for survivorship bias, a different bias in the same Schweser section (and one Schweser says cannot in practice be fixed in illiquid markets, because the entire universe cannot be observed). C would describe a survivorship correction if the stem asked how to deal with funds that stopped reporting.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D gets the direction right but narrows the effect to volatility only. Schweser says unsmoothing affects risk and return estimates and can have a dramatic effect on returns (for example, a reported −8.3% quarter became −36.3%). D would be correct only if the question were restricted to the effect on the volatility estimate.

questions.loText: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-17 d Q2
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Singapore life insurer is reviewing a memo from the private markets team on the return data used for the insurer’s SGD 6.2 billion of illiquid holdings. The team lists three problems and proposes to apply an unsmoothing procedure to all reported returns:

I. The quarterly returns of the core real estate fund rest on infrequent appraisals, so they look much steadier than the property values would if the properties were priced daily.

II. Several buyout funds in the peer database stopped reporting after weak years, and some of them later failed.

III. Venture investments enter the database mainly at exits, which tend to occur when valuations are high.

Which of the problems can the unsmoothing procedure address?

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III
I only

questions.solution:
Singapore insurer auditor: of three data problems (appraisal smoothing, funds that stopped reporting, exit-driven sampling), which can unsmoothing address?

**Concept and theory**

Schweser lists three main biases in the reported returns of illiquid assets. They differ in what goes wrong, and therefore in what could correct them:

| Bias | What goes wrong | Effect on reported numbers |
|---|---|---|
| Survivorship | Poor performers stop reporting, never start, or fail and drop out | Average returns too high |
| Sample selection | Values are recorded mainly when they are high (sales, IPOs, exits) | Returns and alphas too high; beta and variance too low |
| Infrequent trading | Values that exist are updated rarely, so returns are smoothed | Volatility, beta and correlations too low |

Unsmoothing is presented by Schweser inside the infrequent-trading discussion as the way to undo smoothing: it works on an existing return series and adds back the variation that infrequent valuation hid. It cannot create observations that were never reported. The survivorship problem needs the returns of funds that left (Schweser: observing the entire universe is impossible in illiquid markets), and the selection problem needs the low values that were never recorded.

**Applying it to this question**

Problem I: infrequent appraisals make returns look steadier than daily pricing would. That is infrequent trading: unsmoothing applies. Problem II: buyout funds stopped reporting and some failed. That is survivorship bias: the missing funds are absent from the data, and no transformation of the surviving series brings them back. Problem III: venture investments recorded mainly at high-valuation exits. That is sample selection bias: the low-value states were never observed, so unsmoothing the recorded values does not supply them.

**Fragile fact.** Unsmoothing fixes the measurement of an existing series (smoothing from infrequent trading); it does nothing for missing observations (survivorship, sample selection).

**Reference**

LO 99.d (verbatim): “Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Infrequent Trading”; context from “Survivorship Bias” and “Sample Selection Bias” (LO 99.c, used only to mark the boundary). GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 d, where it is Q2 of 10.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** A treats survivorship bias as if it were a smoothing problem. Survivorship is about which funds are in the database, not how their returns are measured. A would be correct if problem II instead described funds whose returns were reported only from quarterly appraisals.

b.reason: **Sibling swap, applied to both other biases.** B picks exactly the two problems unsmoothing cannot touch and drops the one it was designed for. It would be correct only if the question asked which problems require better data coverage rather than unsmoothing.

c.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** C assumes one statistical fix cleans every bias. Schweser presents three distinct biases with distinct causes; unsmoothing addresses one. C would be correct only if all three problems were forms of infrequent valuation.

d.reason: Only problem I is a smoothing problem, and smoothing from infrequent trading is what unsmoothing corrects (“It is possible to unsmooth or de-smooth returns using filtering algorithms”, in the Infrequent Trading subsection).

questions.question: A risk consultant engaged by a UK university endowment is reviewing its GBP 900 million allocation to private real estate. A member of the investment committee notes that the allocation’s reported quarterly return volatility is 2.4%, against 7.6% for the endowment’s listed equities, and concludes that real estate is a low-risk holding. The consultant plans to unsmooth the reported returns before giving a view. Which of the following statements most accurately describes what the consultant should expect?

options.text: The unsmoothed volatility will be well above 2.4% and may move much closer to the equity level, because the reported series mutes price swings that occur between infrequent valuations.
The unsmoothed volatility will be below 2.4%, because unsmoothing removes appraisal noise from the reported series, which supports the committee member’s conclusion.
The unsmoothed volatility will be well above 2.4% and will exceed 7.6%, because unsmoothed real estate returns are always more volatile than listed equity returns.
The unsmoothed volatility will stay close to 2.4%, because unsmoothing changes the allocation’s correlation with listed equities but leaves its own volatility unchanged.

questions.solution:
UK endowment: reported real estate volatility 2.4% vs 7.6% for equities; what should the consultant expect after unsmoothing?

**Concept and theory**

Reported returns of infrequently traded assets are smoothed, so their computed standard deviation is too low: prices within the period were often higher or lower than the reported figures show. Unsmoothing adds that hidden variation back, so the estimated volatility rises. Schweser’s documented magnitudes (quarterly figures for a US property index):

| Series | Quarterly volatility (%) |
|---|---|
| Raw (reported) property returns | 2.25 |
| Unsmoothed property returns | 6.26 |
| Stock returns, for comparison | about 7.5 |

So the unsmoothed volatility was nearly three times the raw figure (6.26/2.25 ≈ 2.78) and moved from about 30% of equity volatility (2.25/7.5) to about 83% (6.26/7.5), yet it stayed below the equity level.

**Applying it to this question**

The endowment’s reported 2.4% versus 7.6% for equities resembles Schweser’s raw 2.25% versus 7.5%. The committee member reads the low reported figure as low true risk. The consultant should expect the unsmoothed volatility to be substantially higher than 2.4%, and possibly much closer to the equity figure. Nothing in the source says it must exceed equity volatility; in the documented case it did not.

**Fragile fact.** Unsmoothed property volatility rose sharply (2.25% to 6.26% per quarter) but remained below stock volatility (about 7.5%): “closer to equities”, not “above equities”.

**Reference**

LO 99.d (verbatim): “Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Infrequent Trading” (unsmoothing paragraph and its volatility figures). GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 d, where it is Q3 of 10.

a.reason: A gets the direction (well above 2.4%), the hedged magnitude (“may move much closer to the equity level”) and the reason (the reported series mutes swings between valuations), all of which follow Schweser’s Infrequent Trading subsection and its 2.25% vs 6.26% vs about 7.5% comparison.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** B reverses the direction of the process: unsmoothing adds noise back rather than removing it, so volatility rises, not falls. B would describe an ordinary noise filter, and would only be right if the stem’s series were noisier than the truth.

c.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** C promises that unsmoothed real estate volatility will exceed equity volatility, “always”. The source evidence shows unsmoothed property volatility of 6.26% against about 7.5% for stocks: higher than reported, still below equities. C would be correct only for a stem that supplied an unsmoothed figure above the equity level.

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** D attributes to unsmoothing a property of a neighbouring effect: it moves correlation but supposedly leaves volatility alone. In fact volatility is the most directly affected estimate; correlation rises as well. D would be correct only if the question asked about an input that unsmoothing leaves unchanged, such as the volatility of the liquid equity index.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Brazilian bank’s asset management arm attends a board meeting on its BRL 3.1 billion private property fund. In the worst quarter of a recent crisis, the fund’s appraisal-based reported return was −7.9%, while the local equity index fell 24%. A board member concludes that property protected the portfolio in the crisis, because its loss in that quarter was under 8%. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: The conclusion is sound, because appraisal-based returns already reflect all price information, and unsmoothing would change only the volatility estimate, not the return reported for that quarter.
The conclusion is sound, because unsmoothing strips appraisal noise out of reported returns, so the unsmoothed loss for that quarter would probably be smaller than the reported 7.9%.
The conclusion is unreliable, because smoothed returns can badly understate losses in a downturn; in one documented case a property index’s reported −8.3% quarter was −36.3% once unsmoothed.
The conclusion is unreliable, but only modestly so, because studies show that correcting reported returns for such biases typically lowers them by about 1 to 2 percentage points.

questions.solution:
Brazilian bank board: a property fund reported −7.9% in a crisis quarter while equities fell 24%; did property really protect the portfolio?

**Concept and theory**

Smoothed, appraisal-based returns dampen the true changes in value. The distortion is not confined to the volatility estimate: in a downturn the reported return itself is muted, so the reported loss in the worst quarter can be far smaller than the true loss. Schweser stresses that unsmoothing affects risk and return estimates and “could have a dramatic effect on returns”, with two documented cases:

| Episode | Reported (%) | Unsmoothed (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Real estate, 1990s downturn | −5.3 | −22.6 |
| NCREIF, quarter to December 2008 | −8.3 | −36.3 |

In the 2008 case the unsmoothed loss was about 4.4 times the reported loss (36.3/8.3 ≈ 4.37); in the 1990s case about 4.3 times (22.6/5.3 ≈ 4.26).

**Applying it to this question**

The board member compares a smoothed −7.9% with a market-priced −24% and concludes that property was a shelter. The comparison mixes a smoothed series with an unsmoothed one. Given the source cases, the true crisis-quarter loss on the property fund could be several times the reported figure. The conclusion is therefore unreliable, and the reason is the smoothing of reported returns.

**Fragile fact.** In the source cases the unsmoothed downturn loss was roughly four times the reported loss (−8.3% to −36.3%; −5.3% to −22.6%); do not confuse these with the 1% to 2% (up to 4%) survivorship figures.

**Reference**

LO 99.d (verbatim): “Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Infrequent Trading” (unsmoothing paragraph, 1990s and December 2008 figures); survivorship figure from “Survivorship Bias” (LO 99.c). GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 d, where it is Q4 of 10.

a.reason: **Scope or condition error.** A confines unsmoothing to the volatility estimate and treats the reported return for the quarter as final. Schweser says it affects risk and return estimates, and the documented cases show large changes in single-quarter returns. A would be correct only if the question asked about the effect on a volatility figure alone.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** B reverses the process: unsmoothing adds noise back, so the true loss is larger, not smaller. B would be correct only if the reported series exaggerated swings, which is the opposite of smoothing.

c.reason: C identifies the right mechanism (smoothed returns understate losses in a downturn) and cites the source evidence correctly (NCREIF, reported −8.3%, unsmoothed −36.3%), consistent with Schweser’s statement that unsmoothing can have a dramatic effect on returns.

d.reason: **Sibling swap of a number.** The “1 to 2 percentage points” figure is Schweser’s estimate of how much survivorship bias inflates mutual fund returns (LO 99.c), not the effect of unsmoothing. The documented unsmoothing effects in crisis quarters are 17 to 28 percentage points (22.6 − 5.3 = 17.3; 36.3 − 8.3 = 28.0). D would be correct if the stem asked about survivorship bias in mutual fund return studies.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at an Australian superannuation fund is assessing an AUD 2 billion unlisted infrastructure holding that is revalued only quarterly. Using the reported returns, the holding’s correlation with the domestic equity index is 0.08. Before commissioning an unsmoothing exercise, the manager drafts four conclusions. Which of the following conclusions is least likely to be correct?

options.text: The raw correlation of 0.08 is likely to be artificially low, because the holding’s return volatility is muted by its infrequent valuations.
The unsmoothed correlation is likely to be lower than 0.08, because the noise that unsmoothing adds back is unrelated to equity market movements.
The unsmoothed correlation is likely to be higher than 0.08, in line with evidence that unsmoothing raised a property index’s correlation with the S&P 500.
The raw volatility of the holding is likely to be understated as well, because the infrequent valuation that depresses the correlation also mutes measured volatility.

Australian superannuation fund: unlisted infrastructure with a raw equity correlation of 0.08; which conclusion about unsmoothing is least likely to be correct?

Infrequent trading lowers three risk estimates together: volatility, beta and correlations with other asset classes. Schweser explains the correlation effect directly: “correlations with other asset classes (e.g., liquid assets such as large-cap stocks) will be artificially low because return volatility is muted by infrequent trades.” Unsmoothing recovers the true, noisier returns, and the evidence goes the same way: the correlation between the S&P 500 and NCREIF returns rose from 9.2% to 15.8% when returns were unsmoothed. The “noise” that unsmoothing adds back is not random static unrelated to markets: it is the true variation in value that the reported series concealed, and in the documented case that variation co-moved more with equities than the smoothed series did.

**Applying it to this question**

This is a “least likely” question: three conclusions are consistent with the source and one is not. Check each against the source: raw correlation artificially low (true), unsmoothed correlation lower than raw (contradicts the 9.2% to 15.8% evidence), unsmoothed correlation higher than raw (true), raw volatility understated too (true).

**Fragile fact.** Unsmoothing raises correlation with liquid assets (9.2% to 15.8% for NCREIF vs the S&P 500); “adding noise” here means restoring true variation, not adding unrelated static.

**Reference**

LO 99.d (verbatim): “Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Infrequent Trading” (correlation sentence and unsmoothing paragraph). Schweser Key Concepts LO 99.c item 3. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 d, where it is Q5 of 10.

Schweser’s evidence shows the opposite direction (9.2% to 15.8%), and its explanation ties the artificially low raw correlation to muted volatility, which unsmoothing reverses. B therefore fails.

c.reason: **True statement.** Direction and evidence both match the source (NCREIF correlation with the S&P 500 up from 9.2% to 15.8%). It would be false if it said “lower than 0.08”.

**True statement.** Schweser lists betas, return volatilities and correlations together as too low when computed from reported returns of infrequently traded assets. It would be false if it claimed volatility was overstated.

B itself is a **polarity flip** supported by a plausible-sounding but unsourced statistical rationale: the trap is that adding independent noise to a series does dilute correlation in general, but unsmoothing is not adding independent noise.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a Japanese life insurer is re-estimating the equity market beta of a JPY 85 billion private real estate fund. The analyst uses $\beta= \rho\sigma_{\text{f}}$ /$\sigma_{\text{m}}$, where $\rho$ is the fund’s correlation with the equity index, $\sigma_{\text{f}}$ the fund’s quarterly return volatility and $\sigma_{\text{m}}$ the index’s quarterly return volatility. The fund’s loan-to-value ratio is 35%. Statistics from the two return series:

| Statistic | Reported series | Unsmoothed series |
|---|---|---|
| Fund quarterly volatility, $\sigma_{\text{f}}$ (%) | 2.00 | 5.60 |
| Correlation with equity index, $\rho$ | 0.10 | 0.18 |
| Equity index quarterly volatility, $\sigma_{\text{m}}$ (%) | 8.00 | 8.00 |

Which beta should the analyst report for the fund on the unsmoothed basis?
questions.solution:
Japanese life insurer: re-estimating a private real estate fund’s equity beta with $\beta= \rho\sigma_{\text{f}}$ /$\sigma_{\text{m}}$ on unsmoothed inputs.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser states that betas, return volatilities and correlations are too low when computed from the reported returns of infrequently traded assets, and that unsmoothing uncovers the true returns, so all three estimates rise. Beta combines two of these. With $\beta= \text{cov}(\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ , $\text{r}_{\text{m}})$/$\sigma^{2}_{\text{m}}$ and cov$(\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ , $\text{r}_{\text{m}}) = \rho\sigma_{\text{f}} \sigma_{\text{m}}$:

$\beta= \frac{\rho\sigma_{\text{f}} \sigma_{\text{m}}}{\sigma^{2}_{\text{m}}} = \rho\frac{\sigma_{\text{f}}}{\sigma_{\text{m}}}$ ,

where $\rho$ is the fund’s correlation with the index, $\sigma_{\text{f}}$ the fund’s volatility and $\sigma_{\text{m}}$ the index volatility. Because unsmoothing raises both $\rho$ and $\sigma_{\text{f}}$ , while $\sigma_{\text{m}}$ (a liquid, market-priced index) is unaffected, the beta rises multiplicatively. (The beta formula is supplied in the stem; Reading 99 gives no formula. The covariance definition of beta is in GARP Chapter 1, “Factor Theory”.)

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: $\beta= \rho\sigma_{\text{f}}$ /$\sigma_{\text{m}}$, using the unsmoothed column for $\rho$ and $\sigma_{\text{f}}$ , and the index volatility for $\sigma_{\text{m}}$.

Volatility ratio: $\sigma_{\text{f}}$ /$\sigma_{\text{m}} =$ 5.60/8.00 = 0.70

Unsmoothed beta: $\beta_{\text{u}} =$ 0.18 × 0.70 = 0.126

Raw beta, for comparison: $\beta_{\text{r}} =$ 0.10 × 2.00/8.00 = 0.10 × 0.25 = 0.025

Ratio: $\beta_{\text{u}}$/$\beta_{\text{r}} =$ 0.126/0.025 = 5.04

The 35% loan-to-value ratio is irrelevant: the volatilities are of the fund’s reported and unsmoothed returns, and no leverage adjustment is asked for. Meaning: on unsmoothed data the fund’s equity beta is about five times the reported estimate, because unsmoothing lifts the volatility ratio by 2.8 times and the correlation by 1.8 times.

**Fragile fact.** Unsmoothing raises beta through two channels at once, $\rho$ and $\sigma_{\text{f}}$ ; the market volatility $\sigma_{\text{m}}$ does not change.

**Reference**

LO 99.d (verbatim): “Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Infrequent Trading”; Schweser Key Concepts LO 99.c item 3 (betas, volatilities and correlations too low). Beta formula supplied in the stem (covariance definition in GARP Chapter 1, “Factor Theory”). GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 d, where it is Q6 of 10.

a.reason: 0.10 × 2.00/8.00 = 0.025 is the raw, reported beta: a step of the comparison, computed entirely from the smoothed column. It would be correct if the stem asked for the beta on the reported basis.

b.reason: 0.10 × 5.60/8.00 = 0.070 unsmooths the volatility but keeps the raw correlation, as if unsmoothing left correlation unchanged. It would be correct if the unsmoothed correlation were still 0.10.

c.reason: 0.18 × 2.00/8.00 = 0.045 takes the unsmoothed correlation but the reported volatility. It would be correct if unsmoothing had raised only the correlation and left the fund’s volatility at 2.00%.

d.reason: 0.126 uses the unsmoothed values of both inputs that infrequent trading biases downward, consistent with Schweser’s statement that beta, volatility and correlation are all understated on reported data and that unsmoothing recovers the true returns.

questions.question:
A member of the risk committee of a Swiss charitable foundation (CHF 1.4 billion) reads an analyst memo on the foundation’s private equity and real estate holdings. The memo makes four statements about the effects of unsmoothing the holdings’ reported returns:

I. Unsmoothing raises the estimated return volatility of the holdings.

II. Unsmoothing leaves the estimated correlation with listed equities unchanged, because it alters only the variance of the illiquid series itself.

III. Unsmoothing can change the returns shown for individual quarters dramatically, especially in downturns.

IV. Unsmoothing removes the upward bias in average reported returns that arises because poorly performing funds stop reporting.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I, II and III
I and III only
I, III and IV

questions.solution:
Swiss foundation risk committee: which of four memo statements on the effects of unsmoothing are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Summary of what Schweser says unsmoothing does, and does not do:

| Estimate | Effect of unsmoothing (source) |
|---|---|
| Volatility | Rises (2.25% to 6.26% per quarter in the property example) |
| Correlation with liquid assets | Rises (9.2% to 15.8%, NCREIF vs S&P 500) |
| Beta | Rises (beta is too low on reported data) |
| Returns in individual periods | Can change dramatically (1990s: −5.3% to −22.6%; Dec 2008: −8.3% to −36.3%) |
| Survivorship or selection bias | Not addressed: these concern which data are reported |

Key Concepts LO 99.d: unsmoothing “affects risk and return estimates and could have a dramatic effect on returns.”

**Applying it to this question**

I: volatility rises, correct. II: correlation unchanged, incorrect; Schweser shows correlation rising, because the raw correlation is low precisely due to muted volatility. III: dramatic changes in single-quarter returns, especially in downturns, correct. IV: unsmoothing does not fix survivorship bias (funds that stop reporting are missing data), incorrect. Correct set: I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Unsmoothing moves volatility, beta, correlation and period returns; it does not touch survivorship or sample selection bias.

**Reference**

LO 99.d (verbatim): “Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Infrequent Trading”; Schweser Key Concepts LO 99.d; “Survivorship Bias” (LO 99.c) for the boundary. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 d, where it is Q7 of 10.

a.reason: A rejects III, treating unsmoothing as a pure risk adjustment. The source says it affects risk and return estimates and can have a dramatic effect on returns. A would be correct only if the memo restricted itself to volatility.

b.reason: Accepting II assigns to correlation an “unaffected” status that belongs to none of the risk estimates; correlation is one of the three estimates that smoothing depresses. B would be correct only if unsmoothing left co-movement with equities unchanged.

c.reason: Statements I and III restate Schweser’s unsmoothing paragraph (higher standard deviation; dramatic effect on returns in the 1990s and 2008 downturns). II and IV each fail on a source fact.

d.reason: Accepting IV attributes a survivorship remedy to unsmoothing. Survivorship bias arises from funds that stop reporting or fail; unsmoothing works on the series that exists. D would be correct only if IV described smoothing from infrequent valuation.

questions.source: High quality paper IM-17 d Q8
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a US state pension fund receives two quarterly return series for the same USD 1.8 billion private real estate fund, labelled X and Y. One is the fund’s appraisal-based reported series and the other is its unsmoothed version. The fund charges a 1.1% annual management fee. Summary statistics over the same 72 quarters:

| Statistic | Series X | Series Y |
|---|---|---|
| Quarterly return volatility (%) | 5.8 | 2.1 |
| Worst quarterly return (%) | −29.4 | −6.9 |
| Correlation with the S&P 500 | 0.21 | 0.11 |

Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: X is the unsmoothed series and every gap in the table is consistent with unsmoothing; series Y understates both the fund’s total risk and its co-movement with equities.
X is the unsmoothed series, but the gap in correlations is inconsistent with unsmoothing, which should leave the correlation with equities unchanged, so the data need checking.
Y is the unsmoothed series, because unsmoothing filters appraisal noise out of returns; series X is the reported series and overstates the fund’s total risk.
X is the unsmoothed series, but the gap in worst-quarter returns is inconsistent with unsmoothing, which should change only risk estimates, so the data need checking.

questions.solution:
US pension fund analyst: two series X and Y for the same property fund; which is unsmoothed and what does the table imply?

**Concept and theory**

Because unsmoothing adds back the variation that infrequent valuation hid, an unsmoothed series has a recognisable signature relative to the reported series it came from:

| Statistic | Unsmoothed relative to reported |
|---|---|
| Volatility | Higher (property example: 6.26% vs 2.25%) |
| Worst-period return | More negative (Dec 2008: −36.3% vs −8.3%) |
| Correlation with equities | Higher (15.8% vs 9.2%) |

**Applying it to this question**

Series X has higher volatility (5.8% vs 2.1%), a deeper worst quarter (−29.4% vs −6.9%) and a higher correlation with the S&P 500 (0.21 vs 0.11). Every one of these gaps points the same way, the way unsmoothing moves each statistic. So X is the unsmoothed series and Y is the reported one. The reported series therefore understates total risk (volatility) and co-movement with equities (correlation), and also understates the loss in the worst quarter. The 1.1% management fee and the 72-quarter length are irrelevant: both series cover the same fund and period.

**Fragile fact.** All three statistics move the same way on unsmoothing: volatility up, worst-period return down (more negative), correlation up.

**Reference**

LO 99.d (verbatim): “Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Infrequent Trading” (unsmoothing paragraph); Schweser Key Concepts LO 99.d. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 d, where it is Q8 of 10.

a.reason: A identifies X correctly and reads all three gaps as consistent with unsmoothing, which matches the source: higher standard deviation, larger downturn losses and higher correlation after unsmoothing.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** B accepts that X is unsmoothed but treats the correlation gap as an anomaly, assuming unsmoothing leaves correlation unchanged. Schweser documents the correlation rising (9.2% to 15.8%). B would be right only if the source showed correlation as invariant to unsmoothing.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** C runs the process backwards: unsmoothing “filters noise out”, so the calmer series must be unsmoothed. Unsmoothing adds noise back. C would be correct only if unsmoothing were an ordinary noise filter.

d.reason: **Scope or condition error.** D accepts X as unsmoothed but treats the gap in worst-quarter returns as an anomaly, assuming unsmoothing changes only risk estimates. Schweser says it affects risk and return estimates and can have a dramatic effect on returns. D would be right only if the question confined unsmoothing to second moments.

questions.question: The CRO of a German bank’s asset management subsidiary is reviewing a model validation report on a EUR 650 million fund of private real estate holdings. The properties are revalued only once a quarter, and the risk model uses the resulting quarterly returns. Which of the following statements in the validation report is most accurate?

options.text: Quarterly revaluation adds appraisal noise to the reported returns; unsmoothing removes that noise, so the unsmoothed volatility will be lower than the reported volatility.
Quarterly revaluation affects only when gains and losses are reported, not how dispersed they are, so unsmoothing is needed only to correct the average return of the fund.
Quarterly revaluation understates volatility, and unsmoothing removes the bias exactly, so the unsmoothed series equals the returns the fund would show if priced daily.
Quarterly revaluation misses price swings that occur within each quarter, so reported volatility is too low; unsmoothing adds that variation back, so the unsmoothed volatility is higher.

questions.solution:
German bank CRO: properties revalued only quarterly; which validation statement about smoothing and unsmoothing is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

The need for unsmoothing starts with how infrequent trading distorts measurement. Schweser’s example: compare quarterly returns of an asset with its daily returns. The quarterly returns appear (and actually are) less volatile; the price within the horizon will often have been higher or lower than the quarterly figures show; and the standard deviation computed from quarterly returns is often lower than from daily returns. The reported series is smoothed, so measured risk is too low. Unsmoothing (via filtering algorithms) adds that variation back to uncover the true, noisier returns. It is an estimation procedure: it moves the estimates towards the truth and can change them dramatically, but the source makes no claim that it reproduces the true series exactly.

**Applying it to this question**

The fund’s properties are revalued once a quarter, so the risk model sees only quarter-end values. Price swings inside each quarter never appear, and measured volatility is too low. The accurate statement must say: reported volatility is understated because within-quarter variation is missed, and unsmoothing adds variation back, raising volatility. It must not claim that unsmoothing removes noise, that only the mean is affected, or that the correction is exact.

**Fragile fact.** Infrequent valuation removes variation (so reported risk is too low); unsmoothing adds it back, as an estimate, not an exact reconstruction.

**Reference**

LO 99.d (verbatim): “Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Infrequent Trading” (quarterly vs daily example and unsmoothing paragraph). Schweser Key Concepts LO 99.c item 3 and LO 99.d. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 d, where it is Q9 of 10.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** A says quarterly revaluation adds noise and unsmoothing removes it, lowering volatility. Both directions are reversed: infrequent valuation removes variation, and unsmoothing adds it back. A would describe an ordinary filter applied to a genuinely noisy series.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** B claims infrequent revaluation affects only timing, not dispersion, and that unsmoothing corrects only the mean. Schweser states that the standard deviation computed from quarterly returns is often lower than from daily returns, and that betas, volatilities and correlations are too low. B would be correct only if dispersion were unaffected by sampling frequency.

c.reason: **Absolute-claim trap.** C promises an exact correction, so that the unsmoothed series equals the daily-priced returns. The source says unsmoothing uncovers the “true, noisier returns” and affects risk and return estimates; it gives no guarantee of exactness, and filtering is an estimate. C would be correct only if stated as “closer to” rather than “equals”.

d.reason: D follows the source chain step by step: infrequent valuation misses swings within the period (“prices will often be higher or lower in a given investment horizon than it appears”), so reported volatility is too low, and unsmoothing adds that variation back, so unsmoothed volatility is higher.

questions.loText: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-17 d Q10
questions.question:
A treasurer at a Chinese insurer’s investment subsidiary is estimating the quarterly return volatility of a CNY 40 billion portfolio holding 70% listed equities and 30% private real estate. The treasurer uses

$\sigma_{\text{p}} = \sqrt{\text{w}^{2}_{\text{E}}\sigma^{2}_{\text{E}} + \text{w}^{2}_{\text{R}}\sigma^{2}_{\text{R}} + \text{2w}_{\text{E}}\text{w}_{\text{R}} \rho\sigma_{\text{E}}\sigma_{\text{R}}}$.

| Input | Reported basis | Unsmoothed basis |
|---|---|---|
| Equity quarterly volatility, $\sigma_{\text{E}}$ (%) | 7.00 | 7.00 |
| Real estate quarterly volatility, $\sigma_{\text{R}}$ (%) | 2.00 | 5.50 |
| Correlation, $\rho$ | 0.10 | 0.20 |
| Real estate annual income yield (%) | 4.20 | 4.20 |

Which estimate of the portfolio’s quarterly volatility should the treasurer report on the unsmoothed basis?
questions.solution:
Chinese insurer treasurer: portfolio volatility of 70% equities and 30% private real estate, recomputed with unsmoothed real estate inputs.

**Concept and theory**

Unsmoothing raises two of the inputs that feed a portfolio risk estimate: the illiquid asset’s own volatility and its correlation with liquid assets (Schweser: 2.25% to 6.26% quarterly volatility; 9.2% to 15.8% correlation with the S&P 500). The equity volatility, measured on a liquid, market-priced index, does not change. For a two-asset portfolio,

$\sigma_{\text{p}} = \sqrt{\text{w}^{2}_{\text{E}}\sigma^{2}_{\text{E}} + \text{w}^{2}_{\text{R}}\sigma^{2}_{\text{R}} + \text{2w}_{\text{E}}\text{w}_{\text{R}} \rho\sigma_{\text{E}}\sigma_{\text{R}}}$,

where $\text{w}_{\text{E}}$, $\text{w}_{\text{R}}$ are the equity and real estate weights, $\sigma_{\text{E}}$, $\sigma_{\text{R}}$ their quarterly volatilities and $\rho$ their correlation. Unsmoothing raises the second term (through $\sigma_{\text{R}}$) and the cross term (through both $\rho$ and $\sigma_{\text{R}}$). (Formula supplied in the stem; Reading 99 gives no formula. The two-asset portfolio risk formula appears, in VaR form, in GARP Chapter 5, “Portfolio Risk: Analytical Methods”, Eq. 5.12.)

**Applying it to this question**

Unsmoothed inputs: $\text{w}_{\text{E}} =$ 0.70, $\text{w}_{\text{R}} =$ 0.30, $\sigma_{\text{E}} =$ 7.00, $\sigma_{\text{R}} =$ 5.50, $\rho=$ 0.20 (volatilities in %).

Equity term: $\text{w}^{2}_{\text{E}}\sigma^{2}_{\text{E}} =$ 0.49 × 49.00 = 24.0100

Real estate term: $\text{w}^{2}_{\text{R}}\sigma^{2}_{\text{R}} =$ 0.09 × 30.25 = 2.7225

Cross term: $\text{2w}_{\text{E}}\text{w}_{\text{R}}\rho\sigma_{\text{E}}\sigma_{\text{R}} =$ 2 × 0.70 × 0.30 × 0.20 × 7.00 × 5.50 = 0.084 × 38.50 = 3.2340

Variance: $\sigma^{2}_{\text{p}} =$ 24.0100 + 2.7225 + 3.2340 = 29.9665

Volatility: $\sigma_{\text{p}} = \sqrt{29.9665} =$ 5.474 ≈ 5.47%

The 4.20% income yield is irrelevant to a volatility estimate. Meaning: on the reported inputs the portfolio volatility is 5.00%; unsmoothing lifts it to 5.47% per quarter, about 9.6% higher, even though real estate is only 30% of the portfolio, because both the real estate volatility and its correlation with equities were understated.

**Fragile fact.** On unsmoothing, change $\sigma_{\text{R}}$ and $\rho$ together; $\sigma_{\text{E}}$ (liquid equities) stays the same.

**Reference**

LO 99.d (verbatim): “Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.1, “Illiquid Asset Return Biases”, subsection “Infrequent Trading” (unsmoothed volatility and correlation figures). Portfolio formula supplied in the stem (GARP Chapter 5, “Portfolio Risk: Analytical Methods”, Eq. 5.12). GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 d, where it is Q10 of 10.

a.reason: 5.47% uses the unsmoothed values of both inputs that unsmoothing moves ($\sigma_{\text{R}}$ and $\rho$), which is what Schweser’s evidence requires (volatility and correlation both rise on unsmoothing).

b.reason: Keeping $\rho=$ 0.10 gives a cross term of 0.042 × 38.50 = 1.6170, variance 24.0100 + 2.7225 + 1.6170 = 28.3495, $\sigma_{\text{p}} =$ 5.32%. This treats unsmoothing as if it left correlation unchanged. Correct only if the unsmoothed correlation were still 0.10.

c.reason: Ignoring the covariance term gives 24.0100 + 2.7225 = 26.7325, $\sigma_{\text{p}} =$ 5.17%, which is the answer for zero correlation. Correct only if $\rho$ were 0.

d.reason: With the reported inputs $\sigma_{\text{R}} =$ 2.00 and $\rho=$ 0.10, the real estate term is 0.09 × 4.00 = 0.3600 and the cross term is 2 × 0.70 × 0.30 × 0.10 × 7.00 × 2.00 = 0.5880, so the variance is 24.0100 + 0.3600 + 0.5880 = 24.9580 and $\sigma_{\text{p}} =$ 4.996 ≈ 5.00%. This is the reported-basis comparison figure, not the unsmoothed answer. Correct only if the stem asked for the reported basis.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-17 e Q1
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Canadian public pension plan is presenting to newly hired analysts on Antti Ilmanen’s figure relating the liquidity of asset classes to their average returns over 1990 to 2009, as discussed in the reading. Which of the following statements about the figure is most accurate?

options.text: Because each asset class sits at one point on the illiquidity scale, an investor can assume that any private equity fund is less liquid than any hedge fund or infrastructure investment.
The figure implies a positive relationship between illiquidity and expected return, although real estate, roughly as liquid as hedge funds, earned a markedly lower return than hedge funds.
Timber was the least liquid asset class in the figure and earned the highest average return, ahead of venture capital and buyout funds.
Hedge funds, although more liquid than buyout funds, earned a higher average return than buyout funds over the period covered by the figure.

questions.solution:
Presentation to new analysts on Ilmanen’s liquidity versus expected return figure: which statement is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

An illiquidity risk premium is the extra expected return an investor demands for holding an asset that cannot be sold quickly, cheaply and in size. The simplest way to look for it is to line asset classes up from most liquid to least liquid and see whether returns rise along the line. The reading does this with a figure from Antti Ilmanen’s 2011 book Expected Returns: each asset class is plotted with an illiquidity estimate on one axis and its average return over 1990 to 2009 on the other.

| Asset class | Liquidity, per the reading | Approximate return, 1990 to 2009 |
|---|---|---|
| Venture capital | Least liquid | 16% to 17% (highest) |
| Buyout funds | Illiquid | about 13% |
| Timber | Illiquid | close to 12% |
| Hedge funds | More liquid than the above | a little more than 12% |
| Real estate | On par with hedge funds | nearly 8% |
| Equities | Much more liquid | a bit more than 4% |
| Cash | Most liquid | a little over 4% |

The reading’s conclusion from the figure is that Ilmanen’s work “does imply a positive relationship” between illiquidity and expected return. The relationship is not one for one, though: real estate is about as liquid as hedge funds but earned roughly 4 percentage points less. The reading also attaches caveats (tested in Q2) and, more importantly, four reasons why this cross-class picture may overstate the premium (tested in Q3 and Q4).

**Applying it to this question**

The analyst is describing what the figure shows. Each option makes a claim about the ordering of liquidity or return. The deciding facts are: venture capital (not timber) is the least liquid and highest return class; buyouts (about 13%) earned more than hedge funds (a little more than 12%); real estate, on par with hedge funds in liquidity, earned nearly 8%; and the reading warns that classes cannot be pigeonholed.

**Fragile fact.** Venture capital is the least liquid and highest return class (16% to 17%); real estate is the outlier: as liquid as hedge funds but nearly 8% versus a little over 12%.

**Reference**

LO 99.e (verbatim): “Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.2, section “Illiquidity Risk Premiums Across Asset Classes”. Figure 99.1 (Liquidity vs. Expected Returns). GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 e, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** The reading explicitly says “we cannot completely pigeonhole asset classes based on illiquidity (e.g., some private equity funds are more liquid than some hedge funds or infrastructure investments).” A turns a class-level average into a guarantee about every fund. It would be correct only if the stem asked about the typical position of the asset classes in the figure, with no claim about every fund.

b.reason: B states the source’s two facts together: the figure implies a positive relationship between illiquidity and expected return, and “real estate is on par with hedge funds in terms of liquidity but commands a lower return of nearly 8%” versus a little more than 12% for hedge funds.

c.reason: **Sibling swap.** Timber’s property is swapped with venture capital’s. Venture capital is the least liquid class with the highest return (16% to 17%); timber is illiquid but earned close to 12%, below buyouts. C would be correct if “timber” were replaced by “venture capital” (and “venture capital” in the comparison by “timber”).

d.reason: **Polarity flip.** The return order is reversed. Buyout funds earned about 13%, hedge funds a little more than 12%, so the less liquid class (buyouts) earned more, in line with the positive relationship. D would be correct if it said hedge funds earned slightly less than buyout funds.
