questions.loText: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-17 e Q2
questions.question:
A member of the risk committee at a UK university endowment is reviewing a slide that reproduces Ilmanen’s liquidity versus expected return figure in support of a GBP 400 million increase in the allocation to private markets. The slide carries four footnotes.

I. The average returns shown are computed over the period 1990 to 2009.

II. The illiquidity estimates on the horizontal axis represent Ilmanen’s opinions rather than measured values.

III. Asset classes cannot be completely pigeonholed by illiquidity: some private equity funds are more liquid than some hedge funds or infrastructure investments.

IV. Because the returns are averaged over two decades, the positive slope in the figure is free of the reporting biases that affect illiquid asset returns.

Which of the footnotes are consistent with the reading?

options.text: I and II only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Risk committee member checking four footnotes on a slide reproducing Ilmanen’s figure: which are consistent with the reading?

**Concept and theory**

A chart is only as good as its inputs. The reading presents Ilmanen’s figure (Q1) but immediately qualifies it in three ways before discussing whether a premium really exists across asset classes:

- **Sample period.** Returns are computed over 1990 to 2009, a specific 20-year window.
- **Nature of the horizontal axis.** The illiquidity estimates “are just estimates (i.e., they represent Ilmanen’s opinions)”. There is no single measured number for the liquidity of an asset class.
- **No pigeonholing.** Liquidity varies within classes: some private equity funds are more liquid than some hedge funds or infrastructure investments.

Separately, the reading’s first reason for doubting a cross-class premium is that the returns themselves are biased: “reported returns of illiquid assets are too high (i.e., overstated if using raw, unsmoothed data) and risk and correlation estimates are too low.” These reporting biases (survivorship, sample selection, infrequent trading, analysed in LO 99.c) do not disappear when returns are averaged over a long period; averaging a biased series gives a biased average.

**Applying it to this question**

Footnotes I, II and III restate the three qualifications. Footnote IV claims the long averaging window cleans the figure of reporting biases. The reading says the opposite: the raw returns of illiquid assets are overstated, which is why the positive slope may overstate the premium.

**Fragile fact.** The bias direction for illiquid assets: reported returns too HIGH, risk and correlations too LOW. A long sample does not remove this.

**Reference**

LO 99.e (verbatim): “Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.2, section “Illiquidity Risk Premiums Across Asset Classes”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 e, where it is Q2 of 14.

a.reason: **Scope error: drops a true footnote.** I and II are true, but A leaves out III, the pigeonholing caveat that the reading states in the same paragraph. A would be correct only if footnote III had been corrupted, for example to say that every private equity fund is less liquid than every hedge fund.

b.reason: **Absolute claim accepted, true footnote dropped.** B includes IV, which promises that the figure is “free of” reporting biases, a certainty the reading denies, and drops the true footnote I. B would be correct only if footnote I misstated the period and footnote IV said the figure is affected by the biases.

c.reason: **Absolute claim accepted.** C accepts all four, so it accepts IV. It would be correct if IV read: “The reported returns of the illiquid classes are likely overstated, so the slope may overstate the premium.”

d.reason: I (1990 to 2009), II (Ilmanen’s opinions) and III (cannot completely pigeonhole; some private equity funds more liquid than some hedge funds or infrastructure) are each stated in the source. IV is false, so “I, II and III only” is the only correct combination.

questions.loText: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.
questions.source: High quality paper IM-17 e Q3
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Singapore sovereign fund is reviewing a consultant’s memo that lists reasons why the conventional view of an illiquidity premium ACROSS asset classes may not hold. Which of the following reasons in the memo is least accurate?

options.text: Reported returns of illiquid asset classes tend to be understated, and their risk and correlation estimates overstated, so raw data hide part of the true premium.
Illiquid asset classes such as private equity, buyout funds and timber carry significant risks beyond liquidity risk, and after adjusting for them they look much less attractive.
Private equity, hedge fund and real estate indices are not investable, so no investor is actually earning the index return of these asset classes.
Investors must rely on manager skill, because without cheap tradeable index funds they cannot separate factor risk from the talents of fund managers.

questions.solution:
Auditor reviewing a memo listing reasons the cross-class illiquidity premium may not hold: which reason is least accurate?

**Concept and theory**

The conventional view is that illiquid asset classes pay a premium over liquid ones. The reading says “this may not be true” and gives four reasons:

1. **Illiquidity biases.** Reported returns of illiquid assets are too high and risk and correlation estimates are too low. The raw premium is therefore inflated.
2. **Other risks.** Private equity, buyout funds and physical assets such as timber contain significant risks beyond liquidity risk. After adjusting for them, illiquid classes are much less attractive; one study finds most investors would be better off in the S&P 500 than in a private equity portfolio.
3. **No market index.** Private equity, hedge fund and real estate indices are not investable, so no investor earns the index return. NCREIF contains thousands of properties; an individual owner of a few properties bears idiosyncratic risk.
4. **Reliance on manager skill.** With no cheap tradeable index fund, factor (systematic) risk cannot be separated from manager talent, so passive returns cannot be separated from alpha.

Together these “imply that it may not be possible to generate substantial illiquidity risk premiums across illiquid asset classes.”

**Applying it to this question**

The question is “least accurate”. Three options restate reasons 2, 3 and 4. One option states reason 1 with the direction of both biases reversed. Reversing the bias direction also reverses the conclusion: if returns were understated, the true premium would be larger than it looks, which would support the conventional view rather than undermine it.

**Fragile fact.** Polarity: illiquid asset returns are reported too high; risk and correlations too low. The bias makes the cross-class premium look BIGGER than it is.

**Reference**

LO 99.e (verbatim): “Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.2, section “Illiquidity Risk Premiums Across Asset Classes”. Key Concepts LO 99.e. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 e, where it is Q3 of 14.

a.reason: A is the inaccurate reason. The source says reported returns of illiquid assets “are too high” and risk and correlation estimates “are too low”. A says returns are understated and risk overstated, the exact opposite.

b.reason: This is the source’s second reason almost word for word (private equity, buyout funds, timber; risks beyond liquidity risk; much less attractive after adjustment). It would be the answer only if it claimed these classes carry only liquidity risk.

c.reason: The source: “Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate indices are not investable, so no investor is actually earning the index return.” It would be the answer only if it claimed the indices were investable.

d.reason: The source: there is no way, as with tradeable, cheap bond and equity index funds, to separate factor risk from the talents of fund managers. It would be the answer only if it said manager skill can be isolated by benchmarking.

questions.loText: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.

questions.question: The CRO of an Australian superannuation fund is reviewing a proposal to invest AUD 600 million in a directly held portfolio of 12 office and logistics properties. The proposal sets the expected return of the portfolio equal to the long-run average return of a national property index that contains thousands of properties, similar to the NCREIF index. Which critique of the proposal is most accurate?

options.text: The index return understates what the portfolio can expect, because appraisal-based index returns are smoothed and smoothing biases reported returns downward.
The concern about index returns applies to individual investors; a fund of this size can buy the index directly and will therefore earn the index return.
The index is not investable, and with only 12 properties the portfolio is far more exposed to idiosyncratic risk and less diversified within the asset class than the index.
Benchmarking the property manager against the index will cleanly separate the manager’s alpha from real estate factor risk, as it would for an equity index fund.

questions.solution:
CRO reviewing a proposal that assumes a 12-property portfolio will earn a broad property index’s average return: which critique is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

In liquid markets an investor can buy the market: a cheap index fund delivers the index return, and any extra return from an active manager can be measured against it. Illiquid asset classes have no such “market index”. The reading’s third and fourth reasons against a large cross-class premium are built on this:

- **Not investable.** Private equity, hedge fund and real estate indices cannot be bought, so “no investor is actually earning the index return.” NCREIF includes thousands of properties; because individual investors do not own thousands of properties, “they are much more subject to idiosyncratic risks and are less diversified within the asset class.”
- **Manager skill is unavoidable.** Without an investable index, factor (systematic) risk cannot be separated from manager talent; an investor “has no way of separating passive returns from alpha”.

So the published index return of an illiquid class is not a return an actual investor can lock in, and a small portfolio within the class carries a risk profile that differs sharply from the index.

**Applying it to this question**

The proposal treats the broad index average as the expected return of a portfolio of only 12 properties. The deciding facts are that the index is not investable and that holding a few properties instead of thousands exposes the fund to idiosyncratic, property-specific risk. Fund size (AUD 600 million) does not create an investable index.

**Fragile fact.** No investable index means BOTH problems at once: idiosyncratic risk for the actual holder, and no way to split factor return from alpha.

**Reference**

LO 99.e (verbatim): “Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.2, section “Illiquidity Risk Premiums Across Asset Classes”. Third and fourth reasons. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 e, where it is Q4 of 14.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** Smoothing and the other reporting biases make reported returns of illiquid assets too high, not too low. The index average therefore, if anything, overstates what the portfolio can expect. A would be correct if it said the index return may overstate the expected return.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** The reading gives the individual investor as an example, but the underlying condition is that the index is not investable for anyone: “no investor is actually earning the index return.” Size does not make an index of thousands of appraised properties buyable. B would be correct only for a liquid asset class with a tradeable index fund.

c.reason: C restates the reading’s NCREIF argument: the index is not investable and a small number of properties makes the holder “much more subject to idiosyncratic risks and . . . less diversified within the asset class.”

d.reason: **Sibling swap.** D gives the real estate index a property of liquid equity index funds. The reading says that, unlike with tradeable, cheap bond and equity index funds, there is no way in illiquid classes to separate factor risk from manager talent. D would be correct for a listed equity manager benchmarked against an investable index.

questions.question: A senior risk consultant at a Japanese life insurer is preparing a report for the investment committee comparing illiquidity premiums within and across asset classes. Which of the following statements is most appropriate to include in the report?

options.text: A formal equilibrium theory explains why the premium appears within asset classes but not across them: multi-asset investors arbitrage away any cross-class premium.
The cross-class premium is absent because capital moves quickly between asset classes and institutions manage their portfolios as one cohesive whole.
Within-class premiums are confined to illiquid asset classes such as private equity; in liquid classes such as Treasuries and listed equities there is no within-class premium.
No formal theory explains the gap; investors may overpay for illiquid asset classes, while siloed management, slow-moving capital and limits to arbitrage may sustain it.

questions.solution:
Consultant’s report comparing illiquidity premiums within and across asset classes: which statement is most appropriate?

**Concept and theory**

The reading reaches two contrasting conclusions:

|  | Across asset classes | Within asset classes |
|---|---|---|
| Evidence | Little evidence of a large premium once biases, other risks, non-investable indices and manager skill are considered | Large premiums: less liquid assets generally earn more than more liquid assets of the same class |
| Examples | Ilmanen figure (raw, biased) | Off-the-run vs on-the-run Treasuries; wide-spread corporate bonds; illiquid stocks; OTC vs listed stocks |

Why would a premium exist within classes but not between them? The reading is explicit that “there is no formal theory”. It offers possible explanations:

- investors may simply overpay for illiquid asset classes, chasing the illusion of higher returns;
- firms may not manage portfolios as a cohesive whole but put asset classes in separate silos;
- the cross-class mispricing may persist because of slow-moving capital across classes, limits to arbitrage and institutional constraints (for example, the fixed-income desk does not talk to the equity traders).

**Applying it to this question**

The report must state the comparison and its explanation correctly. The deciding facts are: there is no formal theory; overpaying (not underpaying) for illiquid classes; silos and slow-moving capital (not integrated management and fast capital); and within-class premiums are found in liquid markets too (Treasuries, equities).

**Fragile fact.** Investors OVERPAY for illiquid asset classes (killing the cross-class premium); within-class premiums show up even in the most liquid markets.

**Reference**

LO 99.e (verbatim): “Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.2, section “Illiquidity Risk Premiums Within Asset Classes”. Key Concepts LO 99.e. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 e, where it is Q5 of 14.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** The source says “currently, there is no formal theory” about why premiums exist within but not across asset classes. A asserts a formal equilibrium theory and a complete arbitrage mechanism. Ironically, the reading cites limits to arbitrage as a reason the gap persists. A would be correct only if the stem asked for a hypothesis to be tested, framed as a possibility.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** The source’s explanations are the reverse: slow-moving capital across classes and firms that do not manage portfolios as a cohesive whole. B would be correct if it said capital moves slowly and asset classes are managed in silos.

c.reason: **Scope error.** The reading’s within-class evidence comes largely from liquid markets: U.S. Treasuries (“one of the largest and most liquid in the world”) and listed equities (less liquid stocks earn more, with a premium of about 1% even for listed equities). C confines the within-class premium to illiquid classes. It would be correct only if the stem were restricted to private markets.

d.reason: D combines the source’s “no formal theory” with its candidate explanations: overpaying for illiquid asset classes, managing asset classes in silos, and slow-moving capital and limits to arbitrage sustaining the cross-class mispricing.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Swiss private bank is asked to find one piece of evidence that illustrates the illiquidity premium WITHIN an asset class, as opposed to evidence about the premium ACROSS asset classes. She shortlists four findings discussed in the reading. Which finding best meets the brief?

options.text: Venture capital earned an average return of about 16% to 17% over 1990 to 2009, compared with a little over 4% for cash.
Among listed stocks, those that are less liquid, for example with low turnover and wide bid-ask spreads, earn higher returns than more liquid stocks.
After adjusting for risk, most investors would have been better off investing in the S&P 500 than in a portfolio of private equity.
Real estate, about as liquid as hedge funds, earned nearly 8% over 1990 to 2009, compared with a little more than 12% for hedge funds.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst choosing one finding that illustrates a WITHIN-class illiquidity premium: which finding fits?

**Concept and theory**

A cross-class comparison sets one asset class against another (venture capital against cash, real estate against hedge funds). Such comparisons mix illiquidity with everything else that differs between the classes: risks beyond liquidity risk, reporting biases, the absence of investable indices and manager skill. That is why the reading doubts the cross-class premium.

A within-class comparison sets more liquid and less liquid assets of the same class against each other: on-the-run against off-the-run Treasuries, liquid against illiquid corporate bonds, liquid against illiquid stocks. The reading concludes that “less liquid assets generally have higher returns than more liquid assets, within asset classes”, and in equities that “less liquid stocks earn higher returns than more liquid stocks”, measured by characteristics such as bid-ask spreads, volume and turnover.

**Applying it to this question**

Classify each finding by what it compares. A and D compare two different asset classes. C compares private equity with the S&P 500 (two classes) and is evidence against a cross-class premium. Only B compares more and less liquid securities inside one class (listed stocks).

**Fragile fact.** “Within” means same asset class, different liquidity (stocks vs stocks, bonds vs bonds, Treasuries vs Treasuries); anything comparing two asset classes is cross-class evidence.

**Reference**

LO 99.e (verbatim): “Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.2, section “Illiquidity Risk Premiums Within Asset Classes”. Also section “Illiquidity Effects in Equity Markets”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 e, where it is Q6 of 14.

a.reason: **Sibling swap: across presented as within.** Venture capital versus cash is the extreme ends of Ilmanen’s cross-class figure, and those raw returns are subject to reporting biases. A would meet the brief if it had been asked for evidence used in the cross-class discussion.

b.reason: B is the within-class equity finding: less liquid stocks earn higher returns than more liquid stocks, using illiquidity characteristics the reading lists (turnover, bid-ask spreads).

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** This is the reading’s risk-adjustment finding: after adjusting for risk, most investors are better off in the S&P 500 than in private equity. It is cross-class and points against a premium. It would fit a brief asking for evidence that the cross-class premium may not exist.

d.reason: **Scope error.** Real estate versus hedge funds again compares two classes, and it actually shows that equal liquidity does not imply equal return. It would fit a brief asking for a limitation of Ilmanen’s cross-class figure.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Singapore bank that holds USD government securities is preparing a note on illiquidity effects in the U.S. Treasury market. Which of the following statements is most appropriate for the note?

options.text: On-the-run (newly issued) T-bills are less liquid than seasoned off-the-run T-bills and therefore trade at higher yields.
During the 2007 to 2009 financial crisis, T-note prices were more than 5% lower than the prices of T-bonds of the same maturity.
On-the-run T-bills are more liquid and have lower yields than off-the-run T-bills, and in the 2007 to 2009 crisis T-bond prices were more than 5% below same-maturity T-note prices.
Because the Treasury market is among the largest and most liquid in the world, illiquidity effects in it are negligible, even in a crisis.

questions.solution:
Treasury analyst’s note on illiquidity effects in the U.S. Treasury market: which statement is most appropriate?

**Concept and theory**

The U.S. Treasury market is a clean laboratory for illiquidity because credit risk is held constant: every security has the same issuer. Any price difference between two Treasuries with the same cash flow timing is therefore mostly a liquidity effect. The reading gives two examples:

- **On-the-run vs off-the-run.** Newly issued (on-the-run) T-bills are more liquid and have lower yields than seasoned (off-the-run) T-bills. The difference is the on-the-run/off-the-run spread. Investors pay up (accept a lower yield) for the more liquid bill; the less liquid bill must offer more.
- **T-bonds vs T-notes in 2007 to 2009.** Same-maturity T-bonds and T-notes traded at different yields; although prices should have been the same, T-bond prices were more than 5% lower than T-note prices.

The reading calls it surprising to see large illiquidity effects in one of the largest and most liquid markets in the world, which is the point: within-class premiums exist even there.

**Applying it to this question**

Check the direction (which bill yields more), the actor (which instrument was cheaper in the crisis) and the size of the effect (not negligible). Only one option gets all three right.

**Fragile fact.** On-the-run = more liquid = LOWER yield. In the crisis, T-BONDS were the cheap ones (more than 5% below T-notes).

**Reference**

LO 99.e (verbatim): “Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.2, section “Illiquidity Effects in U.S. Treasury Markets”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 e, where it is Q7 of 14.

a.reason: **Polarity flip.** The liquidity and yield ranking are reversed. On-the-run bills are the more liquid ones and have the lower yields. A would be correct if “on-the-run” and “off-the-run” were swapped.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** The effect is right (a price gap of more than 5% between same-maturity instruments) but it is attributed to the wrong instrument: it was T-bond prices that were lower than T-note prices. B would be correct with “T-bond” and “T-note” exchanged.

c.reason: C states both source facts with the correct directions: on-the-run T-bills are more liquid with lower yields, and in the crisis T-bond prices were more than 5% lower than same-maturity T-note prices.

d.reason: **Absolute claim.** The reading’s point is the opposite: even in this very large, liquid market, illiquidity effects were large during 2007 to 2009, and the on-the-run/off-the-run spread exists in normal times. D would be correct only if the reading had found no on-the-run/off-the-run spread and no crisis price gaps.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a German insurer holds the following EUR corporate bond and observes a widening of its quoted bid-ask spread.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Credit rating | A (investment grade) |
| Coupon | 4.25% |
| Remaining maturity | 7 years |
| Issue size | EUR 500 million |
| Bid-ask spread, last month | 40 bp |
| Bid-ask spread, this month | 55 bp |

Based on the evidence in the reading, which pair best describes (1) the change in the bond’s yield spread associated with this widening and (2) the share of the variation in yields that illiquidity explains for bonds of this credit quality?

options.text: (1) An increase of more than 30 bp; (2) about 7%
(1) An increase of about 15 bp; (2) about 7%
(1) An increase of more than 30 bp; (2) about 22%
(1) An increase of more than 110 bp; (2) about 7%

questions.solution:
Insurer’s A-rated EUR bond: bid-ask spread widens from 40 bp to 55 bp; yield-spread effect and share of yield variation explained by illiquidity?

**Concept and theory**

In corporate bond markets the reading reports that “larger bid-ask spreads and infrequent trading led to higher yields”. Investors who may need to sell into a wide bid-ask spread demand compensation up front in the form of a higher yield. Three quantitative findings are given:

| Finding | Value in the reading |
|---|---|
| Share of variation in investment grade yields explained by illiquidity | 7% |
| Share of variation in junk (high-yield) bond yields explained by illiquidity | 22% |
| Yield spread response to a 1 bp increase in the bid-ask spread | more than 2 bp |

The sensitivity rule is a statement about changes: $\Delta(\text{yield spread}) >$ 2 $\times\Delta(\text{bid-ask spread})$. Illiquidity matters more for junk bonds than for investment grade bonds.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first: $\Delta(\text{yield spread}) >$ 2 $\times\Delta(\text{bid-ask spread})$.

$\Delta(\text{bid-ask spread}) =$ 55 − 40 = 15 bp

2 $\times\Delta(\text{bid-ask spread}) =$ 2 × 15 = 30 bp

$\Delta(\text{yield spread}) >$ 30 bp

Second part: the bond is rated A, investment grade, so illiquidity explains about 7% of the variation in yields for bonds of this quality. The coupon (4.25%), maturity (7 years) and issue size (EUR 500 million) are irrelevant inputs. Meaning: a 15 bp deterioration in trading cost is associated with a yield spread move of more than twice that size, even though illiquidity explains only a small part of the overall variation in investment grade yields.

**Fragile fact.** Change in yield spread is MORE THAN TWICE the change in bid-ask spread; illiquidity explains 7% (investment grade) vs 22% (junk) of yield variation.

**Reference**

LO 99.e (verbatim): “Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.2, section “Illiquidity Effects in Corporate Bond Markets”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 e, where it is Q8 of 14.

a.reason: A pairs the correct sensitivity (more than 2 × 15 = 30 bp) with the investment grade figure (7%), both stated in the source.

b.reason: **Dropped term: the multiplier.** Treating the response as one for one gives 1 × 15 = 15 bp. The source says the yield spread rises by “more than double the amount”. B would be correct if the relationship were one basis point of yield spread per basis point of bid-ask spread.

c.reason: **Wrong input twin: junk for investment grade.** The sensitivity is right, but 22% is the share for junk bonds. C would be correct if the bond were rated below investment grade (for example BB).

d.reason: **Wrong input: level instead of change.** Applying the multiplier to the new spread level gives 2 × 55 = 110 bp. The rule links changes, not levels. D would be correct only if the bid-ask spread had widened from zero to 55 bp.

questions.question:
A quantitative analyst at a Korean asset manager is building a stock-level illiquidity screen for KRW equities. She writes four descriptions of candidate illiquidity variables.

I. The Amihud measure is the ratio of a stock’s dollar trading volume to its absolute return.

II. A large number of zero returns indicates illiquidity, because returns in liquid markets are usually not zero.

III. Return autocorrelations are used as a measure of stale prices.

IV. Quote size and quote depth are illiquidity characteristics of an individual stock.

Which of the descriptions are consistent with the reading?

options.text: I, II, III and IV
II and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Analyst building a stock-level illiquidity screen checks four variable descriptions: which are consistent with the reading?

**Concept and theory**

Liquidity in equities has many dimensions (cost, speed, size, price impact, information), so no single variable captures it. The reading lists the illiquidity variables shown to affect equity returns:

| Variable | What it captures |
|---|---|
| Bid-ask spreads | Direct cost of a round trip |
| Volume; turnover | How much trades |
| Signed volume (buyer vs seller initiated) | Order-flow direction |
| Amihud measure | Ratio of absolute returns to dollar volume: price move per unit traded |
| Price impact of large trades | Cost of trading in size |
| Informed trading measures | Adverse selection |
| Quote size; quote depth | Size available at the quotes |
| Frequency of trades | How often it trades |
| Number of zero returns | No trade or no price change (liquid stocks rarely show zero returns) |
| Return autocorrelations | Stale prices |

All of these are characteristics unique to each stock. The Amihud measure in formula form is

Amihud $= \frac{|\text{r}|}{\text{dollar volume}}$ ,

where \|r\| is the absolute return. A higher value means a given dollar volume moves the price more, so a higher Amihud value means a less liquid stock.

**Applying it to this question**

I inverts the Amihud ratio: dollar volume over absolute return would be a liquidity measure (more volume per unit of price move), the reciprocal of the reading’s definition. II, III and IV match the list: number of zero returns (with the reason given in the source), return autocorrelations as a measure of stale prices, and quote size and depth.

**Fragile fact.** Amihud = absolute return DIVIDED BY dollar volume (higher = less liquid). The relevant count is of ZERO returns.

**Reference**

LO 99.e (verbatim): “Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.2, section “Illiquidity Effects in Equity Markets”. Module Quiz 99.2 Q1 answer. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 e, where it is Q9 of 14.

a.reason: **Polarity flip accepted.** A accepts I, which flips the numerator and denominator of the Amihud measure. A would be correct if I read “ratio of absolute returns to dollar volume”.

b.reason: **Scope error: drops a true item.** B omits III, but return autocorrelations are explicitly listed “(which are a measure of stale prices)”. B would be correct only if III had said autocorrelations measure, for example, informed trading.

c.reason: Only II, III and IV are consistent with the source list; I misdefines the Amihud measure, which the reading defines as the “ratio of absolute returns to dollar volume”.

d.reason: **Polarity flip accepted, true item dropped.** D accepts the inverted Amihud definition and drops the true statement III. D would be correct only if I were correctly defined and III were false.

questions.question: A risk analyst at a Brazilian pension fund is summarising the research on illiquidity premiums in equity markets for a BRL equity mandate review. Which of the following statements best describes that research?

options.text: Illiquidity risk betas are characteristics unique to each stock, such as its bid-ask spread, turnover and frequency of trades.
Studies find an illiquidity risk premium of about 20% for listed equities, compared with about 1% for OTC stocks.
Estimated illiquidity risk premiums in equities range from 1% to 8% and have risen over time as markets became more liquid.
Illiquidity risk betas are covariances of stock returns with illiquidity factors, and estimated premiums range from 1% to 8% depending on the measure used.

questions.solution:
Pension fund analyst summarising equity illiquidity premium research: which statement best describes it?

**Concept and theory**

The reading distinguishes two ways illiquidity enters equity returns:

| Concept | Definition in the reading |
|---|---|
| Illiquidity characteristics | Stock-specific measures such as bid-ask spreads, volume, turnover, the Amihud measure, quote depth, frequency of trades: “characteristics of illiquidity that are unique to each stock” |
| Illiquidity risk betas | “Covariances of stock returns with illiquidity factors”: co-movement of the stock’s return with an illiquidity factor |

A characteristic describes how illiquid the stock itself is; a beta describes how the stock’s return co-moves with an illiquidity factor. On magnitudes, researchers estimate illiquidity risk premiums at **1% to 8%**, depending on the illiquidity measure used; research also indicates that premiums have **declined**, although studies still find about **1%** for listed equities versus about **20%** for OTC stocks.

**Applying it to this question**

Four claims to check: the definition of illiquidity risk betas, the listed versus OTC figures, the direction of change over time, and the 1% to 8% range with its dependence on the measure.

**Fragile fact.** Betas are COVARIANCES with illiquidity factors; characteristics are stock-specific levels. Premium 1% to 8%, declining; 1% listed vs 20% OTC.

**Reference**

LO 99.e (verbatim): “Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.2, section “Illiquidity Effects in Equity Markets”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 e, where it is Q10 of 14.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** A attaches the definition of stock-level characteristics (bid-ask spread, turnover, trade frequency) to illiquidity risk betas. A would be correct if it began “Illiquidity characteristics are . . . ”.

b.reason: **Role misassignment.** The figures are right but attached to the wrong markets: about 1% is for listed equities and about 20% for OTC stocks. B would be correct with “listed” and “OTC” exchanged.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** The range is right, but the reading says premiums have declined, not risen. C would be correct if “risen” were replaced by “declined”.

d.reason: D gives the source definition of illiquidity risk betas (covariances of stock returns with illiquidity factors) and the source range (1% to 8% depending on the illiquidity measure used).

questions.question: A risk consultant advising a US foundation on its private equity program is explaining how liquidity can be obtained in private equity. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Secondary buyouts let funds exit specific deals and may give limited partners cash and a better view of portfolio company values, but limited partners leaving the fund itself must use a small, immature and opaque secondary market.
Secondary buyouts, which represented about 15% of all private equity buyout deals in 2005, allow limited partners to exit the private equity fund itself without selling their fund interests.
The secondary market in which limited partners sell their fund interests is large, mature and transparent compared with the market for secondary buyouts of portfolio companies.
In the 1990s, sellers of limited partnership interests were called vultures, because they exploited buyers by forcing them to accept discounts of 30% to 50%.

questions.solution:
Consultant explaining how a foundation can obtain liquidity in private equity: which statement is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Private equity is illiquid at two levels, and the reading treats the secondary market at each level separately:

|  | Secondary buyouts (deal level) | LP secondary market (fund level) |
|---|---|---|
| What trades | Portfolio companies, sold by one PE fund to another | Limited partners’ interests in a PE fund |
| Size | About 15% of all PE buyout deals in 2005 | Immature, small and more opaque |
| What it does | Lets funds exit specific deals; may give LPs some cash; may help LPs understand portfolio company values | Lets LPs exit the fund itself |
| Limitation | Does not let LPs get out of the fund | Discounts: 30% to 50% in the 1990s; below 20% in the early 2000s; up again in 2007 to 2009 |

In the 1990s the buyers in the LP secondary market were called “vultures”: they took advantage of distressed sellers, buying at discounts of 30% to 50%. The buyer earns the discount: this is supplying liquidity and harvesting the illiquidity premium.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are: what secondary buyouts can and cannot do for LPs, the character of the LP exit market (small, immature, opaque), and which side of the trade was called vultures.

**Fragile fact.** Secondary buyouts = deal-level exit for the FUND, not a fund exit for the LP. Vultures were BUYERS.

**Reference**

LO 99.e (verbatim): “Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.2, section “Secondary Markets for Private Equity and Hedge Funds”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 e, where it is Q11 of 14.

a.reason: A restates the source: secondary buyouts “allow funds to get out of specific deals, may give limited partners (LPs) some cash . . . and may allow LPs to better understand the values of portfolio companies”, but “do not allow limited partners to get out of the private equity fund itself”; LPs exit in secondary markets that “are immature, small, and more opaque”.

b.reason: **Scope error.** The 15% figure for 2005 is correct, but B extends what secondary buyouts do to the fund level. The source says they do not let LPs out of the fund. B would be correct if it said secondary buyouts let funds exit specific deals.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** The LP secondary market is described as immature, small and more opaque; C reverses all three. It would be correct if it read “small, immature and opaque”.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** The label and the discount range are right, but the actor is wrong: vultures were the buy-side firms that took advantage of distressed sellers. D would be correct if it said buyers were called vultures because they bought from distressed sellers at discounts of 30% to 50%.

questions.question:
The treasurer of a Canadian university endowment must raise cash for operations during a financial crisis and is comparing secondary-market sales of fund interests. Discounts are to net asset value (NAV).

|---|---|
| Endowment value at start of fiscal year | CAD 12.0 billion |

| Cash required for operations | CAD 300 million |
| Discount on private equity LP interests, early 2000s | 18% |

Using current-crisis discounts, by approximately how much does the NAV that must be sold to raise the cash entirely from private equity interests exceed the NAV that must be sold to raise it entirely from hedge fund interests?

options.text: CAD 129.0 million
CAD 277.4 million
CAD 600.0 million

**Concept and theory**

Secondary-market discounts measure the price of immediacy, and they differ sharply between private equity and hedge funds:

- **Private equity LP interests.** Discounts of 30% to 50% in the 1990s, below 20% in the early 2000s, then up again in 2007 to 2009. Harvard’s endowment fell by more than \$8 billion, or 22%, between 1 July and 31 October 2008; when its managers tried to sell private equity stakes to raise operating cash they faced discounts of 50%.
- **Hedge fund interests.** Because hedge fund investors can typically redeem at predetermined dates, secondary discounts are much smaller: 6% to 8% on average in the crisis, and some funds closed to new investors even traded at a premium.

To raise cash C by selling an interest at discount d to NAV, the seller receives (1 $- \text{d})$ per unit of NAV, so

NAV sold $= \frac{\text{C}}{1 - \text{d}}$ .

**Applying it to this question**

Use the current-crisis discounts (50% and 7%). The endowment value (CAD 12.0 billion), its 22% decline and the early-2000s discount (18%) are not needed.

NAV sold, hedge funds $= \frac{300}{1 - 0.07} = \frac{300}{0.93} =$ 322.58 CAD million

Excess NAV sold = 600.00 − 322.58 = 277.42 ≈ 277.4 CAD million

A board member of a multi-employer pension plan asks the CIO to classify four mandates by the way each harvests illiquidity premiums.

(i) Buys small-cap shares at a discount from investors who want to sell quickly and sells them at a premium to investors demanding shares.

(ii) Within the corporate bond sleeve, tilts toward issues with wide bid-ask spreads that trade infrequently.

(iii) Sets a fixed strategic weight of 15% to real estate and timber.

(iv) Holds long positions in illiquid assets and short positions in liquid assets at the aggregate portfolio level, rebalancing countercyclically.

| Row | (i) | (ii) | (iii) | (iv) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | Liquidity security selection | Market making | Passive allocation | Dynamic factor strategy |
| B | Market making | Passive allocation | Liquidity security selection | Dynamic factor strategy |
| C | Dynamic factor strategy | Liquidity security selection | Passive allocation | Market making |
| D | Market making | Liquidity security selection | Passive allocation | Dynamic factor strategy |

Which row classifies the four mandates correctly?

options.text: Row A
Row B
Row C
Row D

questions.solution:
Board member asks the CIO to classify four mandates by illiquidity-harvesting method: which row is correct?

**Concept and theory**

The reading lists four ways investors can harvest illiquidity premiums. They differ by level (asset class, security, trade, whole portfolio) and by whether they exploit the across-class or the within-class premium:

| Method | What it means in the reading |
|---|---|
| 1. Passive allocation | Allocate a portion of the portfolio to illiquid asset classes such as real estate |
| 2. Liquidity security selection | Choose more illiquid assets within an asset class |
| 3. Market making | Act as a market maker for individual securities: buy at a discount from those wanting to sell quickly, sell at a premium to those demanding shares (e.g., DFA in small caps; also sovereign wealth funds and large pension funds) |
| 4. Dynamic factor strategies | At the aggregate portfolio level, long illiquid assets and short liquid assets, rebalancing to exploit liquidity differences; rebalancing is countercyclical |

Given the earlier comparison, method 1 relies on the cross-class premium, which the reading doubts, while method 2 targets the within-class premium, for which there is strong evidence.

**Applying it to this question**

(i) Buying at a discount from quick sellers and selling at a premium to buyers is the DFA description: market making. (ii) Tilting toward less liquid bonds inside the bond sleeve: liquidity security selection. (iii) A fixed strategic weight to illiquid asset classes: passive allocation. (iv) Long illiquid and short liquid at the aggregate level with countercyclical rebalancing: dynamic factor strategy. That is Row D.

**Fragile fact.** Passive allocation = TO illiquid classes (relies on the doubtful cross-class premium); liquidity security selection = WITHIN a class.

**Reference**

LO 99.e (verbatim): “Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.2, section “Secondary Markets for Private Equity and Hedge Funds”. Four ways to harvest illiquidity premiums; Key Concepts LO 99.e. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 e, where it is Q13 of 14.

b.reason: **Row B (sibling swap of (ii) and (iii)).** Passive allocation and liquidity security selection are exchanged: tilting within a sleeve is selection within a class, while a strategic weight to real estate and timber is allocation to illiquid classes. Row B would be correct if the two mandates’ descriptions were exchanged.

c.reason: **Row C (sibling swap of (i) and (iv)).** Market making and dynamic factor strategy are exchanged. Market making is trade by trade in individual securities; the dynamic factor strategy works at the aggregate portfolio level. Row C would be correct if (i) described aggregate long-short rebalancing and (iv) described buying from quick sellers.

d.reason: Row D maps each mandate to the method the reading describes for it: market making, liquidity security selection, passive allocation, dynamic factor strategy.

options.text: Passive allocation to illiquid asset classes is the easiest method to implement and can have the greatest effect on portfolio returns, since it needs no trading after the initial purchase.
A liquidity provider such as Dimensional Fund Advisors avoids adverse selection by trading mainly with anonymous counterparties, so that its information cannot be exploited.
Dynamic factor strategies at the aggregate portfolio level are the easiest to implement and can have the greatest effect, because rebalancing is countercyclical when buying as others sell.
Acting as a market maker is reserved for specialist firms; sovereign wealth funds and large pension funds cannot provide liquidity by buying at discounts and selling at premiums.

questions.solution:
CIO choosing among methods of harvesting illiquidity premiums: which statement is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Of the four methods (Q13), the reading ranks one above the others: “Of the four ways investors can harvest the illiquidity premium, this \[dynamic factor strategies at the aggregate portfolio level\] is the easiest to implement and can have the greatest effect on portfolio returns.” The mechanism is rebalancing. “Rebalancing the portfolio is the simplest way to provide liquidity. As long as buyers buy when others want to sell and sell when others want to buy, rebalancing is countercyclical.” A rebalancer automatically supplies liquidity when it is scarce and is paid for doing so.

Market making in individual securities is the third method. The reading’s example is Dimensional Fund Advisors (DFA), which buys stock at a discount from those wanting to sell quickly and sells small caps at a premium. DFA avoids adverse selection “by choosing counterparties who fully disclose information about stocks”, is trustworthy, and does not manipulate prices or front run. The reading adds that sovereign wealth funds, large pension funds and other large asset owners can also act as market makers.

**Applying it to this question**

Check which method is ranked easiest with the greatest effect (dynamic factor strategies, not passive allocation), how DFA handles adverse selection (full-disclosure counterparties, not anonymity) and who can make markets (large asset owners as well as specialists).

**Fragile fact.** Easiest AND greatest effect = dynamic factor strategies (countercyclical rebalancing), not passive allocation; DFA picks FULL-DISCLOSURE counterparties.

**Reference**

LO 99.e (verbatim): “Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.2, section “Secondary Markets for Private Equity and Hedge Funds”. Four ways to harvest illiquidity premiums; Key Concepts LO 99.e; Module Quiz 99.2 Q2 answer. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 e, where it is Q14 of 14.

a.reason: **Sibling swap.** A attaches the “easiest, greatest effect” ranking to passive allocation (method 1). Passive allocation is also exposed to the cross-class premium that the reading doubts. A would be correct if it named dynamic factor strategies.

b.reason: **Polarity flip.** DFA avoids adverse selection by choosing counterparties who fully disclose information, the opposite of anonymous counterparties. Anonymity would increase the risk of trading against better-informed sellers. B would be correct if it said DFA trades with counterparties who fully disclose information about the stocks.

c.reason: C states the source ranking and its reason: dynamic factor strategies at the aggregate portfolio level are the easiest to implement and can have the greatest effect, and rebalancing is countercyclical as long as the investor buys when others want to sell.

d.reason: **Role misassignment.** The action is right (buy at discounts, sell at premiums) but the actors are wrongly excluded: the reading says sovereign wealth funds, large pension funds and other large asset owners can also act as market makers. D would be correct only if the reading restricted market making to specialist firms, which it does not.

The source lists four things that shape the illiquid allocation in particular: (1) the investor’s investment horizon, (2) the lack of tradeable indices (you cannot buy “the private equity market” the way you buy an equity index fund), (3) the need to hire talented active managers, because without an index the only way in is through a manager, and (4) the need to monitor those managers.

| Aspect the model must capture | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Long time horizons between trades (infrequent trading) | The investor cannot rebalance, hedge or consume the asset until a liquidity event arrives. |
| Large transaction costs | Entry and exit are expensive; models built on this alone wrongly assume the asset always trades if the cost is paid. |

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Canadian public pension plan is validating the plan’s strategic asset allocation model. The model treats every asset class as saleable on any date at a fixed proportional cost, shown below, and its documentation states: “In a forced-sale scenario, any position can be converted to cash within one week by paying the stated cost.”

| Asset class | Exit cost (% of value) | Weight (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Listed equities | 0.1 | 45.0 |
| Real estate | 2.0 | 15.0 |
| Timber | 3.0 | 5.0 |
| Infrastructure | 4.0 | 10.0 |

Which of the following recommendations should the auditor make?

options.text: Retain the assumption but raise the exit costs for real estate, timber and infrastructure to stressed levels, since any asset can be sold within the week if the seller pays a high enough cost.

Replace the one-week assumption for the illiquid classes with a fixed due diligence delay, after which each sale is assumed to complete at the stated cost, because a counterparty that completes due diligence is committed to buy.
Revise the assumption because it overstates the time needed to exit real estate, timber and infrastructure, which a seller willing to pay the stated cost can normally complete within a few days.

Replace the assumption: for the illiquid classes a buyer may not be found quickly or at all, and a counterparty must complete due diligence and may then decline; in stress, even listed markets can freeze.

questions.solution:
Auditor validating an allocation model that assumes every asset class can be sold within one week at a fixed proportional cost.

**Concept and theory**

Many asset allocation models acknowledge that markets are imperfect by adding a transaction cost: to sell, you pay a percentage, and then the trade happens. The source’s criticism is that this hides a strong assumption, namely that an asset will always trade if the cost is paid. In private equity, infrastructure, real estate and timber, that is false for three reasons:

- a buyer may not be found quickly, or may not be available at all;
- a counterparty that is found must perform due diligence, which takes time;
- after due diligence the counterparty may choose not to buy.

In addition, in periods of stress even liquid asset classes can face liquidity freezes in which it becomes impossible to find buyers at any price. So illiquidity is a question of whether and when a trade can occur, not only of how much it costs.

**Applying it to this question**

The model documentation states the flawed assumption almost word for word: “any position can be converted to cash within one week by paying the stated cost.” The cost levels and portfolio weights in the table are irrelevant to the audit finding; changing them does not fix the assumption. The right recommendation must attack the assumption itself, for the illiquid classes (no buyer, due diligence, walk-away) and for listed equities in stress (freezes).

**Fragile fact.** Direction: transaction-cost models are too optimistic about exit. Paying more does not guarantee a trade; the buyer can be absent or can walk away after due diligence.

**Reference**

LO 99.f (verbatim): “Evaluate the impact of allocating illiquid assets to a portfolio, including the impact on rebalancing and trading and on optimizing the proportion of illiquid assets.” Schweser Book 5, Reading 99, Module 99.2, section “Portfolio Allocation to Illiquid Assets”, subsection “Asset Allocation to Illiquid Asset Classes With Transaction Costs”. GARP text in the project has no matching section; content from Schweser, a condensed source whose wording may compress the original framing.

**Source:** High quality question set, Risk Management and Investment Management: the paper for IM-17 f, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: **Absolute claim.** A keeps the very assumption the source rejects, that any asset can be sold if a high enough cost is paid. Raising the cost does not create a buyer. A would be correct only in a world where every market always clears at some price, which the source explicitly denies for illiquid markets and for liquid markets in stress.

b.reason: **Scope or condition error.** B recognizes due diligence but drops the condition that the counterparty “upon completion of due diligence, chooses not to buy” in some cases, and it ignores that a buyer may never be found. B would be correct if completion of due diligence created a binding obligation to purchase.

c.reason: **Polarity flip.** The source’s problem is that the model understates how long exit can take (weeks, months, or never), not that it overstates it. C reverses the direction. It would be correct only if exit in these markets were faster than one week, which contradicts the source.

**Concept and theory**

The source puts it bluntly: one cannot “eat” illiquid assets. Spending, whether a university’s operating budget or an individual’s living costs, is paid in cash, and only liquid assets can be turned into cash on demand. Illiquid assets are consumed only after a liquidity event arrives.

A second consequence follows. A liquid investor whose assets are falling in value can sell or hedge. An illiquid investor cannot, because the asset cannot be traded. To offset that unhedgeable risk, the source states that illiquid asset investors must consume less than liquid asset investors. The Harvard example in the reading shows the practical side: when cash was needed during the crisis, the only way to raise it from illiquid holdings was to sell at huge discounts.

Portfolio I moves 40% of assets into private equity and directly held real estate. The BRL 120 million payout is a fixed cash need that must come from liquid assets. Because 40% of Portfolio I cannot be traded to hedge declines, the foundation bears a risk it cannot offset, so the source’s rule applies: plan lower consumption with Portfolio I. The payout amount itself is context; the deciding fact is the direction (illiquid investor consumes less).

- Allocation: W highest, Z lowest (allocation falls as the wait lengthens).

$\text{w}_{\text{ill}} = \frac{\text{V}_{\text{ill}}}{\text{V}_{\text{liq}} + \text{V}_{\text{ill}}}$ ,

Because an illiquid position cannot be traded when its value falls, its holder cannot hedge the decline and must consume less than an otherwise similar investor in liquid assets.
The illiquidity risk premium an investor should demand on an asset falls as the frequency with which that asset can be traded rises.
An investor can lock in the illiquidity premium as an arbitrage by buying an illiquid asset and shorting a similar liquid asset, because the position does not require continuous trading.

**Concept and theory**

The source lists the effects of illiquidity (infrequent trading) on portfolio choice:

- It reduces optimal holdings: the rarer the liquidity event, the lower the allocation.
- It makes allocations vary significantly between liquidity events (too high or too low vs optimal).
- Holders cannot hedge declining values, so they must consume less than liquid investors.
- There are no illiquidity “arbitrages”: to construct an arbitrage, an asset must be continuously traded, and illiquid assets are not.
- Investors must demand an illiquidity premium; the more frequently the asset trades, the lower the premium.

An arbitrage locks in a riskless profit by trading offsetting positions and adjusting them as prices move. If one leg cannot be traded, the position cannot be adjusted or closed when needed, so the profit is not locked in.

This is a four-statement audit with a NOT qualifier. D claims an arbitrage that “does not require continuous trading”, which contradicts the no-arbitrage bullet.

b.reason: Correct statement, from the bullet that investors cannot hedge declining values and so must consume less. It would be the answer if it assigned the lower consumption to the liquid investor (a role misassignment).
